# <term>PRIVILEGE</term>. <note>Original: "Octroy." In the 17th century, authors or publishers had to apply to the government for a "privilege," an early form of copyright that gave them the exclusive right to print and sell a specific book for a set number of years.</note>

THE <term>States General</term> <note>The "Staten Generael" was the high governing body of the Dutch Republic, representing the various provinces.</note> of the United Netherlands, to all those who shall see these presents or hear them read, Greetings: LET IT BE KNOWN, that we have consented, agreed, and granted a privilege; as we do consent, agree, and grant by these presents to the surviving sons and common heirs of the late Master **WILLEM TEELLINCK**, in his life Minister at Middelburg in Zeeland, that for the term of fifteen consecutive and following years, to the exclusion of all others within these United Provinces, associated territories, cities, and members thereof, they may have printed, vended, and sold all the works of the aforementioned Master **WILLEM TEELLINCK**: Prohibiting any and all residents of the aforementioned United Netherlands, associated territories, cities, and members thereof, within the aforementioned term of fifteen following years, from reprinting, causing to be reprinted, or selling the aforementioned works in whole or in part, or bringing into the aforementioned lands such works reprinted elsewhere, upon the forfeiture of all pirated copies, and in addition a sum of three hundred <term>Carolus Guilders</term> <note>A gold or silver coin named after Emperor Charles V; 300 guilders was a substantial fine in 1651, intended to deter book piracy.</note>, etc. Done at the assembly of the high-mentioned States General. At The Hague, October 22, 1651.

J. Schuylenborgh,

->Beneath was written,<-
->By Order of the same,<-

N. RUYSCH.

# Preface to the Reader.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'B' containing a landscape scene with figures and foliage.</image-desc>

**B**eloved Reader, since many of the writings of this author still remain among us which have never before seen the light of day <note>A common idiom for being published.</note>; of which you have a remarkable treatise here present; and as we would not gladly see the labor of that over-diligent man remain in part hidden under a bushel <note>original: "onder een koren-mate." A biblical reference to Matthew 5:15; the editors are saying Teellinck's wisdom shouldn't be hidden away.</note>; so we gladly take the effort upon ourselves to place his light, which God had given him and which shines in his godly and learned treatises, upon the candlestick; so that it might shine for all who are in the house of God. 

We shall then, by God’s grace—if God spares us in life and we remain sitting in rest and peace for so long—subsequently give all his works to the light in various volumes. Those which have been published before, we shall oversee, correcting printing errors, and setting the passages of Holy Scripture according to the *New Translation* <note>The "New Translation" refers to the *Statenvertaling* (States Translation) of the Bible, first published in 1637, which became the standard Dutch Bible.</note>; making the others fit for printing and so bringing them to light. 

And we shall also add to each volume two indices <note>original: "Regiſters."</note>: one of the matters contained in this specific treatise; and another alphabetically of all the matters contained in the entire volume, as you see the beginning of it here. For we give you here the first part of his treatises on particular texts of Holy Scripture, which contains *Adam right-formed, misshapen, re-formed*—a glorious treatise making man known to himself, as it discovers how glorious man was before the fall in the first Adam; how entirely miserable he is now in himself through the fall of that, his first forefather; and how he shall be placed in a much more blessed state through the *second Adam*, Christ <note>A theological concept from 1 Corinthians 15, contrasting the fall of Adam with the redemption of Jesus.</note>, than he had in the first Adam. 

With this treatise we have joined those treatises which deal with the entirely mournful and troubled state in which both the Land and the Church were in the time of this author, and now are much more so:

<summary>In this preface, the editors explain their mission to publish Willem Teellinck's remaining manuscripts to benefit the "House of God." They describe their editorial process, including updating biblical citations to the 1637 States Translation and providing indices for the reader's convenience.</summary>
<keywords>Preface, Willem Teellinck, publishing history, States Translation, Adam, Fall of Man, Second Adam, Dutch Republic, Church history</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Preface to the Reader," completing the editors' explanation for publishing these works and introducing a secondary preface by the famous theologian Gilbertus Voetius. ### Preface to the Reader.

...where you shall find revealed not only the hardships that weigh upon us; but also the sins that are the causes of them; and the remedies and means which must be used by everyone so that the Land and the Church might be delivered from these oppressive hardships. The troubling condition of the Country and the Church in our days has moved us to place these **Treatises** <term>Tractaten: formal written works dealing with specific religious subjects</term> in the first section; in the hope that the good **God** might yet grant that, by reading these once again, our careless age might finally wake up, and that by following the counsel which this **Author** prescribes from the word of **God**, **God's** wrath might still be turned away from our Land and Church.

We consider it unnecessary to say much in recommendation of the writings of this **Author**; for they recommend themselves sufficiently, provided they are read with a spiritual heart. And since the praise that children give to their parents' work is usually held in suspicion by many, we have preferred to include here—after prior communication with Master **Professor Gilbertus Voetius** <note>Gilbertus Voetius (1589–1676) was one of the most influential Dutch Reformed theologians of the 17th century and a leading figure in the "Nadere Reformatie" or Dutch Further Reformation.</note>—a certain preface which that world-renowned and highly learned man wrote in the year 1631 for a certain **Treatise** written by this **Author** concerning the seventh chapter of the **Romans**, from which you will be able to see that man’s judgment concerning the works of this **Author**. Read and use, then, for the benefit of your own and other people's souls, the labor of this **Author**, and then we shall not regret our own labor either.

This <insert>10th</insert>/20th of February, 1659.

->Your Honors' humble servants in the Lord,<-
->**THEODORUS TEELLINCK.**<-
->**JOHANNES TEELLINCK.**<-

# PREFACE BY GISBERTUS VOETIUS, Written in the year 1631, placed before the Treatise of Mr. Willem Teellinck, regarding the 7th Chapter of Romans.

### *Foreword to the Pious Reader.*

<image-desc>Decorative drop cap 'G' featuring a seated figure, possibly a scholar or saint, inside the letter amidst elaborate foliage and scrollwork.</image-desc>

Pious Reader, among all writers who concern themselves with the treatment of Religion, those have always been held as the most pleasant and profitable—in the judgment of the right-minded—who treat the *practice* <note>original: "practijcke"</note> of Religion; that is, the particular application to the cases of conscience and of human life. It has been seen how even amidst the darkness of the Papacy <note>A common 17th-century Protestant term for the Roman Catholic Church.</note> such Practical-writers (although deficient in our judgment) were held in high esteem, such as *Bernard, Bonaventure, William of Paris, Harphius, Ruysbroeck, Schoonhovia, Carthusianus, Tauler, Thomas à Kempis, etc.* And after the rise of the Reformation (when the world was filled with polemical writings) there nevertheless appeared and were eagerly received by many various practical writings of the *contemplative* <note>original: "complative," likely a printer's error for "contemplative"</note> people (as they are called there), especially from the Carmelite, Carthusian, and Augustinian Orders, which are unnecessary to recount all here. The single little book by *Thomas à Kempis*, on the *Imitation of Christ*, has for some time now been published anew in print almost every year, now by these, then by others of the Papacy, and highly recommended to everyone. Just as also for a long time the Reformed in the Dutch, French, English, and other languages, with prefaces, notes, and all necessary adornments, have made the three books of the aforementioned *Imitation* very common among their own people. The aforementioned Reformed also formerly received with great desire and zeal the excellent Treatises of *William Perkins*. Just as our fellow Netherlanders also used to read with wonder and attention that excellent book by *Jean Taffin, on Repentance*, when it first came out, because it—above many other writers of our Church—very earnestly and particularly presses for the *reformation of life*. But just as no good things remain in a steady good state due to the cunning of Satan and our human sluggishness: so it has also gone with the kindled zeal [inspired] by these and similar Practical-writers, while the desire for the practice—

<summary>Gisbertus Voetius introduces Willem Teellinck's work by emphasizing the historical importance of "practical" divinity—the application of faith to daily life—citing both medieval mystics and early Reformed authors.</summary>
<keywords>Gisbertus Voetius, Willem Teellinck, Practical Divinity, Cases of Conscience, Thomas à Kempis, William Perkins, Jean Taffin, Reformation of Life, Dutch Further Reformation</keywords>

# TO THE READER.

of godliness, and consequently the inclination toward publishing and reading **Practical writings** gradually began to vanish, especially due to the turmoil caused by the *Remonstrants* <note>The Remonstrants were a Dutch theological group whose disputes with orthodox Calvinists led to the Synod of Dort (1618-1619).</note>, who would have almost reduced the entire practice of Theology to mere hair-splitting, legal proceedings, and pleadings. Yet the Lord God, both during and after these distractions among the Reformed, has nevertheless raised up various learned and godly men, specifically in England and the Netherlands, who have labored to renew and support the fallen *Practice* <note>term: "Practice" (Practijcke) refers to "Practical Divinity," the application of theology to daily Christian living and the conscience.</note> through their sermons and writings. Those in England who have done this learnedly, thoroughly, powerfully, and clearly are many, among whom in my judgment these stand out far above others, and can be most profitably read by candidates, ministers, and other scholars: *Perkins* <note>William Perkins (1558–1602)</note> mentioned before, *P. Baines*, *Daniel Dyke*, *Preston*, *R. Bolton*—whose deep practice alongside his powerful and affectionate style one can never sufficiently admire—*John Downame*, who with unspeakable diligence has treated all parts of *Practice* at great length, and *William Ames* who briefly and in a scholarly manner presented the chief points of *practice* and cases of conscience in his *Treatise on Conscience and its Cases* <note>original: "Tractaet de Conscientiâ ejusque casibus"</note>, recently published. Among our fellow Netherlanders, *practice* has been especially awakened and advanced through the sermons and writings of *Wilhelmus Teellinck*; (*G. Udemans* and other writers who are still living I shall now pass over for certain reasons) to whom was joined his brother *Mr. Eeuwout Teellinck*, in his lifetime Receiver General of Zeeland, under the name of *Iraeneus Philalethius* <note>A Greek pseudonym meaning "Peaceful Lover of Truth."</note>, in his *Philemetor* <note>Greek: "Mother-lover."</note>, *Laments of the Church*, and the following small treatises, especially in his book named *Cloud and Pillar of Fire*. How scriptural, thorough, powerful, sensitive, and moving the sermons of *Wilhelmus Teellinck* were can best be testified by all godly souls who heard him, and to whom he was so often, and still is, a sweet savor of Christ. I shall not say much of that, as I have heard but two or three of his sermons to my recollection; nevertheless, I received such an impression and feeling from his manner of preaching that since that time it has been my heart's entire wish that I and all teachers in this Land might follow such a fashion and power of preaching. Of his writings I can speak more closely, as I have read them. In these he has abundantly shown how his senses were exercised in the Holy Scriptures, his heart accustomed to a deep feeling of Divine things, and his spirit lifted up from the vain turmoil of the world to Heavenly contemplations; in short, what a brave and experienced practi-

<summary>The author discusses the revival of "Practical Divinity" following theological disputes, praising influential English and Dutch authors like William Perkins and Wilhelmus Teellinck for their focus on the heart and conscience.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the preface, likely written by a contemporary or successor, praising the life and literary contributions of the Dutch divine Willem Teellinck.</meta>

-># TO THE READER.<-

how excellent he was in his profession: so that he might rightly be regarded as a second **Thomas à Kempis** <note>original: "Thomas à Kempis"; a 15th-century mystic known for 'The Imitation of Christ'</note> (though of the Reformed faith) of our age. It is true that he was by no means deficient in **textual, dogmatic, or catechetical Theology, likewise Polemics**, and therein could have gone quite far alongside the "heroes of David" <note>A biblical reference to King David's elite warriors, implying Teellinck could have been a top-tier academic debater</note> had he wished to write more on those subjects—as is sufficiently shown by his explanations of various Scripture texts, his work on the Small Catechism, his *Eubulus*, his work on *Perseverance* against the Remonstrants <note>The Remonstrants were a theological group whose views were condemned at the Synod of Dort (1618-1619)</note>, and the treatises on the *Gaping at Idols* against Popery. But that in which he truly and singularly excelled above many others was **Practical Theology**, whether he wished to present it distinctly in its form and method, or through **preachable concepts** <note>original: "conceptus predicabiles"</note> to instill it and make it savory even to the simplest members of the Congregation. Among his first published practical writings was the little book named **Christian Exercises**,

<margin>*</margin>

with the preface, through which he began to raise such a banner that many Teachers and members of Christ in this land have since that time held this Man of God in great esteem, and have not neglected to earnestly and more closely observe many things which they had previously hardly thought of, and which they would have sought in vain in various **commonplaces** <note>original: "locis communibus"; standard theological textbooks</note>, commentaries, or collections of sermons. So that, following upon his other writings—such as *Eubulus, Fasting-Prayer-Day, Rest-Time, Wedding Garment*, etc.—one saw many public, solitary, and private exercises once again placed in **fresh observance** <note>original: "viridi observantia"</note>, and a new zeal for them kindled here and there. Also, many abuses and defects that still clung to the Reformed people from the "old leaven" <note>A biblical metaphor for lingering corrupt influences or old habits</note>, or had grown anew and were hardly judged as evil anymore, were disgraced afresh and poured out from the dregs upon which they lay. After he had applied great labor toward these and similar observations and improvements among God's people, and had published many treatises to that end, he equipped in his final years, as a crowning addition, his **Necessary Exposition**, being like a morning-alarm to those who watch over souls. Oh, if only it were read with as simple an eye by all Preachers, Candidates, Elders, and other loving Christians, as it is despised—unread and even unseen—by some who do not know what precious and necessary considerations are contained therein! At the end of his life, now hastening toward the set goal, he took his final leave by publishing his sweet soliloquies and "time-gainings," and his explanation of the 7th Chapter of Romans, and thus left his Congregation and all of us with a good taste of his inner devotion,

<summary>This preface praises Willem Teellinck as a "Reformed Thomas à Kempis," highlighting his shift from academic polemics to practical theology and his influence on Dutch spiritual life. It lists several of his key works and laments that some of his important later writings are overlooked by contemporary clergy.</summary>

--- Page 14 ---
<meta>The catchword "Syne" (His) from the previous page suggests the author was discussing the legacy or character of the deceased writer. This page continues the preface, specifically praising a new commentary on Romans 7.</meta>

->TO THE READER.<-

accompanied by a mournful longing, left behind. Of the *soliloquies* <note>original: *soliloquien*; private spiritual meditations</note> and *time-redeemings* <note>original: *tijt-winningen*; likely referring to works on the productive use of time for God</note>, which have now been in everyone's hands for a long time, I do not need to say much. Yet I cannot refrain from speaking a word in praise of the explanation of the 7th Chapter to the Romans, or a portion thereof, which is now brought to light from the Author's notes by the Heirs. I have found it in every way most excellent. The *Analysis* <note>original: *Analysis*; the systematic breakdown</note> or dissection of the Text is concise and well-aimed. The pressing and close explanation of the words used by the Holy Spirit is thorough, and yet suited to the understanding of the listeners. The Teachings and points of Religion are very aptly drawn from it, with necessary explanation and proof. The errors of the Socinians, Coornhertists, and Remonstrants <note>These were various theological groups—rationalists, followers of Dirck Coornhert, and Arminians—whom the Dutch Reformed orthodoxy considered heretical</note>, with their false glosses <note>interpretive comments</note>, are learnedly refuted. The applications to the practice of comfort on the one hand and improvement on the other, are very deep, elegant, moving, and suited to the circumstances of our people. The pronunciation and style of the words is generally also proper, clear, and consistent with the matters being handled. To sift every little word here and there, and to weigh them against my own or anyone else's Rhetoric (as they see fit), is not my habit; nor do I believe that such should happen in human writings by orthodox Authors—let alone that one should extract this or that absurdity against their meaning, or mock their supposed lack of learning, and thus with a mere pretense dismiss all the good reflections and observations. This treasure is shared with you through Printing, *Pious Reader*, especially those of you who labor in the Word, or prepare yourselves for it. If you seek and love from the heart the power of godliness, circumspection, and spiritual conduct in internal matters—at least if you are not too wise in your own eyes—you will without doubt be able to gain no small profit from this and the other Treatises of this venerable man. If time and your learning do not permit or require you to read all his Writings, at least make yourself familiar with those that orderly present the general concepts regarding the Practice and exercises of Godliness. Likewise, the Spiritual Policy, and *the conduct over and in God's Congregation*, such as:

### TO THE READER.

His other writings are mostly concerning some particular texts and points of Religion, which then can be very usefully employed by the Candidates <note>original: "Proponenten" — students who have passed their exams and are eligible to be called as ministers</note> and Preachers <note>original: "Predicanten"</note>, who have need of some assistance in the forming of their sermons upon such texts and points. Every person can use their own judgment, and act according to their circumstances, leaving another also to his freedom. Were it that we all had equally exercised senses in the Holy Scripture, and an equally great feeling and experience of its practice, then we could well do without such writings, and help ourselves with the Bible alone. But now that it is found to be quite otherwise, it is good that everyone, according to his situation, tests all things, and holds fast to that which is good. It is true, that just as all writers—even the best—experience various judgments, often also unjust ones, this author of ours has likewise had to endure the same. People have—I know not what—mumbled here and there in the dark behind his back, in order to make his labor and singular gifts unstable: *That he had wondrous new and strange things in his head.*

I. What he had in his head or in his heart I do not know, but one thing I know well: that with his writings, alongside countless others, he has opened my eyes and touched the heart through God's Grace, to understand many things more closely and to take them into consideration, of which previously nothing at all, or certainly very little, was thought. If you ask me what kind of things these were, I point you to his *Eubulus*, *Spiritual Exercises*, *Fast-day*, *Necessary Discourse*, and therein the Register on the 10 Commandments. For this, one always has the good God to thank, who had given his servant such gifts and such a mind. For the rest, I leave the investigation of his strange, wise concepts (if one wishes to call them that) to stay within his *Necessary Discourse*, approved by the Honorable Theological faculties at Leiden and Franeker, unless someone beyond that could give us any closer explanation. That which he urges there and shakes clearly enough from his bosom is nothing new or singular, but is the *Old-new* <note>A reference to the "Old Truth" of the Reformation being presented anew</note>, which we must all uphold, if there is but a drop of true Christianity in us. Let us, for the time being, read that book often, and learn from it what that man of God wants, what his aim, what his driving force, what his holy agitation has been, what he has practiced for so long, and with what he has occupied his pious soul. There you have, in my opinion, the sum and as it were the *quintessence* <note>original: "quinta essentia" — the purest or most essential part of something</note> of Teellinck's own temperament (if one wishes to call it that) and of his concepts. If there is anything else or anything special besides that, I know nothing of it, nor can or will I answer for the same. And in any case, if such were so (as I trust it is not), it would not

# TO THE READER.

therefore one should not fail to hold all his excellent concepts and writings in high esteem and to use them for good: just as one still knows how to make use of the writings of Jesuits and other corrupt heretics for certain purposes. To conclude, I pray all godly and conscientious readers in this matter to consider the golden proverb of Tertullian: <note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was an early Christian author from Carthage.</note> *It is more just to judge hidden things by those that are manifest, than to condemn manifest things because of what is hidden. Apology, Chapter 3.* <note>original Latin: "Iustius est occulta de manifestis prejudicare, quam manifesta de occultis prædamnare"</note>

II. Men have also sought to strip the pious man of his luster with unsavory chatter, claiming that he little regarded or urged the points of truth and faith, especially those in dispute between us and the Remonstrants. <note>The Remonstrants were followers of Jacobus Arminius who disagreed with certain Calvinist doctrines on predestination.</note> These are picked-up and clumsily fabricated trifles, hardly worthy of an answer. I believe that in his writings he has acquitted himself so well in the explanation and defense of the truth against the Remonstrants, that he may well pass muster alongside many others, not only in Zeeland (where by God's grace the conflict never existed) but even here in Holland. Just read his *Eubulus*, concerning perseverance, according to the demonstration, and this explanation of the 7th Chapter to the Romans, and you shall find what I say to be true. All faithful teachers have done their best in this struggle, according to their circumstances and gifts, although they have not all done an equal amount. For the rest, he has so laid the foundation of Jesus Christ in all his writings, and urged Him as being the first and last motive for godliness—to embrace Him with true faith, to taste His love, and to cling to Him again with unfeigned love—that I do not know what one could rightly accuse in practical writings of that sort: unless one would also wish to call into question the method of Taffijn’s *Repentance* <note>Jean Taffin (1529–1602), a prominent Walloon minister known for his works on practical piety.</note> and all similar writings, indeed even the letters of James, Peter, John, and Jude. But even if it were as they say, all the good pieces concerning practice should not therefore be rejected.

III. Above all, they have sought to obscure the light of the practice kindled by this Reverend Man, by alleging his new opinion concerning the Sabbath or Christian Day of Rest. What he felt regarding this I cannot know, except from his writings and some verbal reports he gave me in response to my propositions and questions on the matter. Concerning the Day of Rest, one can dispute either the practice and sanctification, or the day itself and its origin. Regarding the practice, you have an opening in his book named *Rest-Time*, which was approved by the Reverend faculties at Leiden, and the Deputies of the Classis <note>A "Classis" is a regional governing body in the Reformed Church.</note> of Walcheren, as also by the highly learned Franciscus Gomarus, <note>Gomarus (1563–1641) was a strict Calvinist theologian and opponent of Arminius.</note> with—

If anyone desires good information on this, let them not rely on rumors and chatter, but read for themselves the *Post-acts of the National Synod of Dordrecht* 1619 <note>original: "Post-acta Synodi Nationalis Dordracenae"; the official records of the famous Reformed synod</note>, the presentations and disputations of the Honorable Professors at Leiden, namely *Dr. Tysius* and *Dr. Rivet* on the *Sabbath* <note>original: "de Sabatho"</note>, and the treatises of *Dr. Gomarus* and *Dr. Walaeus* on the *Sabbath*. And even if it were true that—driven by the extreme and exorbitant profanities on the other side—he had spoken a word too strongly (as commonly happens in such cases) and thus pulled the string a bit too tight, or brought forward some considerations that do not hold or apply perfectly to every *case* <note>original: "casus"</note> (according to everyone's judgment), one should not therefore condemn or despise all the labor of this pious man in presenting and promoting the practice of Godliness. Just as the writings of *Piscator* and other excellent teachers among the High Germans and Scots do not cease to be used and esteemed everywhere by our people, although they promote a particular view regarding the *active righteousness of Christ* <note>original: "Iustitiâ activâ Christi"; the theological doctrine that Christ's legal obedience to the law is imputed to believers</note>. I now pass over many other similar matters, where the truth of Religion and a good conscience would suffer much more impact (even in the judgment of the complainers) than from this alleged opinion of *Teellinck*, which he holds in common with *Beza*, *Junius*, *Piscator*, *Diodati*, *Perkins*, *etc.* and more other excellent theologians, or from his particular decision and understanding regarding any specific *case*.

->TO THE READER.<-

understands, I do not wish to excuse it in him, nor in anyone in the world, just as I have roundly declared my feelings regarding such wisdom and precision <note>original: "precijsheyt" - here meaning a rigid, overly scrupulous adherence to rules or "Puritanical" strictness</note> in a certain meditation on James 2, verse 12. When our Author had read this with relish, as he declared, he completely approved of it in all parts in a letter sent to me at that time. But I cannot find that such precision dwelt in that Man of God, much less ruled him. I have seen and spoken to him little, yet I hear everything to the contrary from those who dealt with him most and knew him best. This must be enough for us: that his writings do not taste of such evil precision, but rather continually instill the opposite. But if someone were to understand a "precision" (Ephesians 5, verse 15) of keeping a close watch on all of God's commandments, without releasing himself or others from any of them (Matthew 5:19); likewise in the promotion and understanding of good order and discipline in God's congregation, without flattering anyone’s flesh or looking to anyone’s eyes, or to this or that worldly consideration: such precision and strictness is entirely laudable, and he must be quite loose and unbound who would declare himself an enemy of the same. In a word, such a "Precisian" <note>A term often used for the early Puritans or those favoring strict Reformed discipline</note> and of such a humor was *John Calvin*, and his fellow laborers in the Church at Geneva, who for that reason had to endure no small amount of outcry and adversity above many other reformed Teachers and Churches.

Besides these and similar unfriendly censures, there are also some complaints from some who otherwise do not think poorly of this honorable Man and his writings, to whom we shall also say a word.

<margin>❦</margin>The first complaint is, *that he wrote too much, and continually brought forth something new.* I do not wish to praise the writing of many books in general (especially those that provide little edification). But this cannot and should not make anyone turn against all the writings of our Author. For everyone can use their judgment here, and read those that suit them best. I assure you that none of them shall be read without learning some particular reflection therefrom. *Augustine*, *Jerome*, *Luther*, *Calvin*, *Beza*, *Martyr*, *Zanchius*, *Perkins*, *etc.* <note>A list of major Church Fathers and Protestant Reformers: Peter Martyr Vermigli, Jerome Zanchi, and William Perkins</note> also wrote much, and did not cease publishing Treatises until the end of their lives, notwithstanding that so much had been written before them; their footsteps are still followed by those who now daily make themselves known through learned writings. However, the Reader can see this complaint answered by the Author in his Preface to the *Necessary Demonstration* <note>original: "Nootwendich vertooch"</note>.

## TO THE READER.

The second complaint is, *that he is so lengthy in some Treatises*. I freely admit that those broad deductions, which were mostly delivered without the formal structure of Sermons, are not as necessary for learned and experienced Ministers, and therefore reading them may sometimes weary them; just as they are otherwise pleasant when impressed by the living voice and action. This is common to almost all published Sermons: they seem too short to those who hear them with relish, and yet too long to read for those who could sufficiently help themselves with the marrow and the *archetypes* <note>original: "archetypis" - the original patterns or primary drafts</note> or *outlines* <note>original: "dispositien" - the structural arrangement of a speech or sermon</note> of the same. So it goes with the published sermons of many other excellent Ministers, who otherwise in their lives were never heard with annoyance by pious and intelligent listeners. But for that reason, learned and practiced minds must not make such useful Treatises distasteful to others, who are not wearied by such long deductions and instillations—indeed, who without them would receive little instruction from the work. One sometimes sees those long and loose *preachable concepts* <note>original: "conceptus predicabiles" - ready-made sermon outlines or themes</note> of *Besseus* <note>Pierre de Besse (1567–1639), a French Catholic preacher known for his prolific and sometimes repetitive sermon collections</note>, and other Roman writers in the hands of our candidates for the ministry, and those do not seem too long, so it appears. But how much more usefully would they search our Author, in whose single quire <note>a small gathering of leaves in a manuscript or book</note>, or smallest Preface, more marrow of the Holy Scripture, more power of consolation and godliness is to be found, than in the entire Warehouses of such messy and lukewarm Theologians. If the polemical writings against the Papacy by the Lord of *Plessis* <note>Philippe de Mornay, Lord of Plessis-Marly (1549–1623), a prominent Huguenot leader</note>, of *Whitaker* <note>William Whitaker (1548–1595), an influential English Protestant theologian</note>, of *Chamier* <note>Daniel Chamier (1565–1621), a French Reformed theologian</note> etc. do not seem too long to us (as indeed they must not), why should practical writings be rejected for their length, where besides the motives, proofs, and means, all kinds of exceptions, distinctions, and excuses of Satan, the World, and the flesh must be dealt with.

The third complaint is, *that he does not provide much comfort, but always seems to urge the reformation of life*. It may be that our times and our congregations require it so. Otherwise, one could diminish *Taffin’s Repentance* <note>Jean Taffin (1529–1602), author of "The Marks of the Children of God" and works on repentance</note> and similar writings with the same pretext. When one deals with texts and subjects that properly belong to repentance and the explanation of the Ten Commandments, one cannot delve as deeply into the other part of practice, namely *consolations*. Now it is evident that our Author’s published Treatises are mostly of the first kind. He has, however, never been lacking when the texts and subjects gave opportunity for consolations, as his *Comfort for the Sick* <note>original: "Siecken-troost"</note>, and the little book of comfort by *Perkins* <note>William Perkins (1558–1602), a foundational English Puritan theologian whose works were widely translated into Dutch</note> translated by him, and besides his other writings, this explanation of the 7th Chapter to the Romans can testify. And even if our Author were not as bold in that part of practice

The fourth complaint is, *that his style and manner of speaking is often not as elegant, dignified, and pleasing as some might wish.* But one must know that everyone has their own style, according to their temperament, training, and subject matter. Our Author's style is indeed simple, sometimes a bit low, not too high-flown or sublime, yet nonetheless clear, powerful, and moving; when his voice and gestures were added to it, he was entirely tempered according to the manner, his temperament, and the circumstances of the common people, and accordingly pleasing enough. One can easily fulfill what is lacking here by reading the Treatises of *Irenæus Philalethy* <note>A pseudonym likely referring to a contemporary "peace-loving" theological writer</note>, which in my judgment have very gracefully expressed many points of practice and some particular *Political-Theological* <note>original: "Politico-Theologisch"</note> concepts with a dignified, moving, and almost prophetic style. Nor is anyone forbidden from further perfecting the reflections and style of these two Heroes, and to fulfill everything that, in anyone's judgment, is lacking. They have gone before and paved the way; it is all the easier to follow and to build something good upon their work. If only we brought a similar zeal and diligence with upright hearts to this task, and while they have been called home by the Lord, placed ourselves in their stead, we would be able to strengthen many hands through God's blessing and awaken many sleepy souls; we would see our Churches stand out like *Smyrna* and *Philadelphia* <note>References to two of the seven churches in the Book of Revelation, known for their faithfulness</note> in faith and works to the pleasure of God and all the pious. Now may our God and Father look down upon His Vineyard from Heaven and keep it in cultivation, sending many such Laborers; may He give us all an upright heart to gladly praise and follow that which is good. Amen, Amen. This 18th of October, 1631.

->Your Honor's willing servant in the Lord,<-

# ADAM
## Upright, Deformed, Reformed,

->That is:<-

### A naked discovery of the condition of Man, in his threefold state; namely, of innocence, of corruption, and of restoration, presented through the words of Moses.

->Genesis 2:7<-

>And the Lord God had formed Man from the dust of the earth, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; thus Man became a living soul.

## CHAPTER I.

->Introduction to the following treatise.<-

<margin>After God had created the entire visible world, he finally made man.</margin>
<note>The author follows the traditional "Hexameron" structure, explaining the six days of creation.</note>
Moses, having very modestly recounted the Creation of the entire visible world, with all that is therein—excepting man—begins first in Genesis 1:26, and again here in our text, the explanation of the creation of man himself. In this, he follows the order that God the Lord followed in the Creation itself; which He so arranged that He created man last of all, just when the entire world stood there

<column-break/>

perfect in all its parts; and was now abundantly provided and furnished with all such things as were useful, not only for necessary maintenance, but for the abundant delight of man.

<margin>In which he has shown his great kindness.</margin>
In this, the Lord God reveals his kindness toward man: namely, that he did not bring man into the world before the same was well-provided and furnished with everything, in order to properly accommodate this excellent inhabitant.

<margin>And manifold wisdom in creating man.</margin>
It also befitted the manifold wisdom of God <note>original: "menigerley wijstheit" - a reference to the 'multiform' or 'variegated' wisdom of God mentioned in Ephesians 3:10</note> that—having now created the Heaven and the Earth, which displayed the excellent

--- Page 26 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the original state of humanity, specifically focusing on the purpose of creation and the inherent abilities granted to Adam before the Fall.</meta>

# Adam, Upright
-><note>original: "Rechtſchapen" - meaning created in a state of moral perfection and integrity</note><-

<margin>
In order to recognize and to praise the skill of his Creator.
</margin>

...the craftsmanship of their Creator (but could not themselves take any knowledge of it), He would also make some excellent creatures who might behold, know, and recognize the skill of their Creator, revealed in the created things. To that end, the Lord created the Angels and humans, and endowed them with a very lofty understanding and an unrestricted will, so that they might be able to know and recognize not only the excellence of the created things, but also of their Creator Himself from other things and from themselves, and to love, cling to, and serve Him as is fitting. These He has appointed as inhabitants and as it were the Stewards <note>original: "Casteleynen" - keepers of a castle or estate</note> of these two glorious Palaces, Heaven and Earth; giving the Angels Heaven (Matthew 18:10) and the earth to the children of men for their dwelling (Psalm 115:16; Acts 17:26), so that they should be servants, witnesses, and proclaimers of the glory of God here on earth, just as the Angels are the same in Heaven.

<margin>
Therefore humans must also proclaim it: for they were created for that purpose.
</margin>

From this design of the Lord, man may indeed be fully convinced that it truly behooves him to make the proclamation of the honor of God his Creator his principal, indeed his only work in all that he does and can do (1 Corinthians 10:31). Since he alone, of all the creatures of this lower world, was specifically created by God for that purpose; so that also his principal, indeed his only work (in which the holiness of man consists) is that all the members and all the powers of man should agree with the will of God, and be entirely ready,

<column-break/>

alert, and capable of fulfilling the required duties with ease and joy. This should be well remembered here at the beginning, for it will be of great utility in the following discourse.

<margin>
And received sufficient capability for this from God in the first creation.
</margin>

Accordingly, the Lord God has also given to man all such gifts and powers as were necessary to be able to well and easily fulfill and carry out this glorious and excellent service of God, for which God the Lord created and made him. ### CHAPTER II.

#### Regarding the Creation of the Body in General.

By the Body we must understand that part of man which can be perceived with the outward senses, and in which man is in some way similar to the animals of the field.
   Regarding this, Moses testifies to us that God the Lord made man (that is, in this place, the body) out of a lump of the earth. Concerning this, we must now note three things: First, of what sort; secondly, out of what; thirdly, how the Lord made the Body of man.

#### Of what sort the Body of man was created.

<margin>The body of man was created by God very beautiful and capable, which is evident from the beauty it still possesses even after the Fall.</margin>
The Body of man was created by God in the beginning entirely beautiful, and entirely capable for all kinds of works for which God the Lord had created it; just as we can still somewhat deduce now, from the fact that our body—even such as it is now, so broken and marred by sin—still presents itself as beautiful. If the very most beautiful [today] were compared to what man's body was when it was freshly made by the hand of the Lord, it is merely like a withered flower that once stood and bloomed so beautiful and youthful. Nevertheless, man's body, as it still is now, presents itself so beautifully that there is truly no beauty—

### Of the Wonder and Convenience of the Members.

<margin>Indeed, all its members are very convenient.</margin>
And how convenient and useful the parts and members of the body are made and arranged, in order to properly carry out all kinds of physical work, is also beyond words; it would be infinite to explain and lay open all the particular circumstances of the parts of this little visible world <note>The "microcosm" or "klepnẽ ſichtbaren werelts," a common Renaissance idea that the human body mirrors the universe.</note>. We shall only briefly examine some of the most prominent parts and members thereof, which most often catch the human eye, from which one will then be able to judge the rest sufficiently.

The most evident members of the body are these: the eyes, the ears, the nose, the mouth, the hands, and the feet; all of them very wonderful, all of them very convenient instruments for the benefit of man and the service of the Creator.

<margin>The eyes are very miraculous instruments of the body.</margin>

How easily, how quickly can one open them and shut them again? What things can one also see through the eyes as soon as one opens them, provided it is clear day? The Regents of the Land, the Merchants, the Craftsmen, the Farmer, the City-folk, all House-holding people find that they have no more faithful servants than their own hands, which gladly, willingly, readily, and all their life long—without house-hire, only for their food—serve them, and sleep and labor for them. Man’s hand, in outward works, is all in all; it is a Soldier, a Carpenter, a Tailor, a Surgeon, a Cook, a Notary, and whatever one wishes; it knows all trades; it can do all things, if only it be practiced therein. And, that which is most wonderful of all, and has not yet been said: these hands of men, which are as soft and tender as silk or velvet can be, and yet are so entirely busy, and so continually practiced and used, they nevertheless do not wear out. They remain, when a man is healthy, in one condition, equally nimble, equally alert. There is no iron, no steel, which if it were used as continually as our hands, would not, within a year or two, be made completely blunt and useless; as those perceive who work with iron or steel tools. Consider then what wonderful, what excellent, what convenient tools Man’s Hands are.

But, to properly realize what convenience, what service, that man has from his hands, one only needs to see the condition of those who have no hands,

<column-break/>

**Column 2**

or useless hands through the "starving" <note>likely referring to atrophy or paralysis</note> or otherwise: what a discomfort, what an inconvenience that person has therefrom, everyone knows; and what a deformity the lack of them also brings to the body, each one can see with the eye: by which one may also, in some measure, realize the grace and beauty of the hands.

->Of the Feet.<-

<margin>The feet</margin>
Lastly, if we also wish to properly behold our feet—even the very lowest and, as it appears, the most base members of our body, with which we tread through thick and thin, as the saying goes—we shall indeed also have to confess that the same are very wonderful, useful creatures of God. For besides that they are in their making every bit as wonderful as man’s hands, they also have singular uses, and are like faithful and firm Pillars of the body, upon which it so certainly supports and rests itself, that people have been found who, setting themselves firmly on their feet, could be moved from their place by no other human strength alone. And also, what alert runners, what ready messengers are our feet? How willingly, how speedily do they carry us hither and thither, wherever we wish to be? How nimble are they also to ward off, and to "push with the foot," as we say, that which rises up against our bodies to damage them? And what a grace and beauty they also bring to man’s body can best be seen in those who are deprived of their feet, or are maimed. And—

# Adam, Righteous

Look there; from these few parts of the body—those which are most visible to the eye and present themselves so conveniently and beautifully—we can fully conclude that indeed the Lord, the almighty God, has made man's body entirely beautiful and entirely fit for all kinds of uses for which it was created. For He has also provided the entire body, as it stands there in all its members, with such keen sensation that nothing in the world may touch or come against it, however softly or gently, but that it immediately perceives and feels it. It knows how to distinguish very modestly <note>The author uses "bescheydentlijck" to mean with discernment or precision.</note> between an unpleasant scraping and a friendly caress; from which it subsequently receives great pleasure, or smarting and pain. Indeed, it is so delicate and so tender in feeling, that even the thin air against the body is very precisely felt, from which it then receives cold or heat, according to how the air is tempered. And

<margin>The entire body is also very artistically made.</margin>
to that end, the body is overlaid with a most artistic network, made of veins, nerves, and muscles; in such a manner that the sensation of man's body is situated just like the sensation of a spider, which, sitting in her spiderweb that she has spun out, immediately perceives if one touches even the slightest thread of her work. Which sensation the Lord God also implanted in man, so that he would be provided in every way with an unspeakable quickness to immediately perceive what is good or harmful to the body; and

<column-break/>

consequently would avoid the one and pursue the other, for the well-being of the body and all its members. And all these parts were in the beginning so well joined and fitted together by God, through the aforementioned veins, nerves, and muscles, that man possessed a very great power and strength in his arms, hands, and other limbs; just as the Lord has allowed us to see a glimpse and trace of this even after the Fall in the strong Samson. So too were all the limbs and all the parts of man's body so well tempered in their humors <term>humeuren: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) believed in early medicine to determine health and temperament</term> that he possessed a perfect and entirely vigorous health. Of this, the long lives of the first Patriarchs of the ancient world were still a small remnant; being closest to that first preceding vigor and health in which man was first created, they were also the healthiest and longest-lived of all men, Genesis 5.

<margin>So that every person can also be distinguished from the other.</margin>
And what is indeed still quite wonderful regarding the condition of the body: it is so arranged that while there are so many thousands, and thousands, and ten thousands of different people in the world, each having their own particular body, yet not one person is so like another (although they all have the same fashion, limbs, and color) that they cannot be easily distinguished from one another. This was also necessary in the highest degree to prevent a great confusion among the children of men, which would otherwise necessarily arise if one could not [tell] one person from the other.

# Deformed, Reformed.

When a great work is made, there falls a certain amount of scrap <note>original: "grups" - refers to the dross or waste material from a manufacturing process</note> that one sweeps up and throws away; this was gathered below into a lump, which we call the earth. From this, the body of man was made. And what is also worthy of note: man's body was not even made from any of the noblest of earthly things, such as from precious stones or pearls, or from silver or gold, which were abundant in the rivers of Paradise. Instead, it was made from the very dust of the earth, which the wind scatters and the worms churn up. For so says our text: *and God made man from the dust of the earth*. The word signifies a kind of red, dry, dusty earth. So it is that man's body was created and made from the scrap of the earth itself, and consequently from the very least of all God's creatures. Because of this, our body is also called in the Scripture an *earthly house* (2 Cor. 5:1), and we are said to *dwell in houses of clay, whose foundation is in the dust* (Job 4:19). And in this respect, the whole man is called earthly or dusty <note>original: "χοϊκὸς" (choikos) - a Greek term used by St. Paul meaning "made of dust" or "terrestrial"</note> (1 Cor. 15:47). Indeed, he is called dust itself (Gen. 3:19). Looking upon this, the godly have made many such confessions, as Abraham does in Genesis 18:27: *Behold now, I have taken upon me to speak unto the Lord, which am but dust and ashes.* See here, then, from what lowly material the glorious body of man was created, and learn from this to acknowledge that the humbler the material, the more excellent the Master-worker is.

<margin>Without it however having died</margin>
### Question.
Was man's body then not nonetheless mortal, being made only from the dust

<column-break/>

of the earth?

<margin>died</margin>
### Answer.
If one understands "mortal" as that which *could* die, we say yes; for the outcome teaches this inarguably. But if one understands "mortal" as that which *necessarily* had to die, and could not be kept in life for more than a few hundred years, then we say no to that. For the body of man, once having been made alive, could have lived always, and would have lived eternally, had sin not come upon it; for through sin, death first entered into the world (Rom. 5:12).

### Regarding the manner in which man's body was created.

<margin>Indeed, God fashioned it like a Potter.</margin>
Now follows thirdly, that we also examine how the Lord Almighty God made the body of man from a lump of earth so gloriously as we have now heard. Regarding this, the text explains to us that the Lord God did not create man's body simply by speaking the word—that it should come forth from the dust of the earth as He had created the beasts of the field—but He Himself fashioned and made man's body from the dust of the earth, as if with hands, into a fit vessel and dwelling for the excellent and noble soul which He wished to breathe into it. Just as a Potter <term>Potbacker: a traditional term for a potter, emphasizing the molding of clay</term> makes his vessels from clay, in which one might keep precious things; and Moses gives us this to understand when he says that the Lord God *formed* man from the dust of the earth (Gen. 2:7). And more expressively regarding the creation of the Woman: that the Lord God *built* or *constructed* the Woman (like one who [builds] a mag-

# Deformed, Reformed, 19

Is the situation not entirely different now? Are not those noble, those excellent members of man now—through the Fall—so miserably misshapen that they have become mere weapons of unrighteousness and servants of sin? Decency teaches this all too clearly: that indeed the members of the unregenerate <note>original: "onherbozen" — those not yet "born again" or spiritually renewed</note> and misshapen man have now become worthy instruments of all kinds of evil and sin. Their eyes are full of adultery **2 Pet. 2:14.** Indeed, their hands are full of blood. **Isaiah 1:15.** Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they practice deceit; the venom of asps is under their lips; their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness; their feet are swift to shed blood. **Rom. 3:13, 14, 15, 16.** Their entire bodies are vessels of impurity, of shameful passions **Rom. 1; 1 Thess. 4:5**, of gluttony, of drunkenness, and of intemperance; and all the members thereof have become entirely wicked, unfit for any good work. **Titus 1:16.** If the service of God is to be done—if one is to sing praises to God with a loud throat, or offer up prayers with heart and mouth—man's members are entirely unwilling for it; they are by nature so rude <note>original: "onbeschoft" — meaning unrefined, crude, or socially/spiritually clumsy</note> that they do nothing but mar and ruin the work at hand.

Thus it stands indeed with poor man now, since he has fallen away from his God. Sin does not quite take away the members of his body entirely, nor the use of them; the eye still sees; the ear still hears; but it misuses these same members for an entirely different purpose than that for which they were created. Sin has brought such confusion into that excellent clockwork <note>original: "Uer-werck" — a metaphor comparing the body's internal systems to the precision of a mechanical clock</note> or

<column-break/>

glorious organ of the body, that all the wheels or pipes thereof are disordered; they all take a wrong course. The lovely harmony of this musical instrument is broken; there is nothing but discord and confusion. This is truly altogether lamentable: that this so artistic, so beautiful, so glorious a masterpiece is so shamefully deranged, ill-treated, and misused for all kinds of foulness; that now the devil and sin reign in this glorious body, so that all the members have become mere weapons of unrighteousness. If we only see someone strike and break into pieces a beautiful, artistic painting made by human hands, it displeases us. When we read in Moses **Exod. 1:13, 14** that the tyrannical Pharaoh drove the children of Israel to such foul work as brick-making, it pains us. When we read in the prophet Jeremiah **Lam. 4:2** that the precious children of Zion, once valued against fine gold, were regarded as earthen pitchers, it affects us deeply. How much more, then, should it affect us that our noble and so very excellent members of the body (which, as we heard above, were all created alike to do the glorious and excellent work of the Most High God for eternal salvation) are so miserably misshapen by the Fall, that they plunge into all kinds of foul work of sin, to serve the devil unto damnation? Is this not altogether lamentable? Is that not also a great unfaithfulness regarding the most worthy talents of God, which He has entrusted to man? Shall this not also create a heavy accountability on that great Day of Judgment, when man

Well, all of this applies to every one of us, whichever mother's child we may be: we, we, every single one of us who have received a living body from God, stand guilty of this treachery. We have so miserably disordered our body that now the members of our body are merely damaged tools, from which no good work can be made; for through the misuse of them, we have disordered, damaged, and corrupted the same. This ought rightly to humble us to dust and ashes, and to awaken us to look out from our eyes and diligently inquire how we must be restored to our first uprightness; and having learned that, then also to practice it with all diligence before and above all other work.

### Of the restoration of the corrupted body through Christ.

<margin>How the corrupted body must now be restored again.</margin>
The human body (which formerly was created as a glorious vessel, and yet now, through the fall of Adam, is as if broken into pieces, and so crushed in regard to the Divine work) is such that it is true of it, in regard to the spiritual, what the Prophet says in an-

<column-break/>

other context: that from its shattering not a shard is found to take fire from the hearth, or to scoop water from any ditch (Isaiah 30:14). <note>original: "Esa. 30.14."</note> It cannot be raised up again into a vessel of honor, into a Temple of the Holy Spirit, into an instrument of righteousness and holiness, except by the same hand by which it was first made. If the human body were to be placed in good standing again, it must be re-created, which is solely the work of the Almighty God. So also the Son of God—who is God praised into eternity, and through whom all things were first created—came in the flesh to set upright again everything that is to be set upright. He Himself took on a human body, like unto our body of humiliation, in order to make our corrupted, damaged bodies conformable to His glorious body (Philippians 3:21). <note>original: "Phil. 3.21."</note> This He also begins to do for His own, even here in this life: for where their eyes, since the fall, saw nothing but vanity; and their ears stood open only to folly and sin; and their tongue spoke nothing but vanity or evil; there the Lord Jesus Christ pierces the ears of His own, so that they begin to hear His word; He opens their eyes, so that they begin to look toward the righteous who are in the land, and toward the work of the Lord; He unbinds their tongue, so that they begin again to speak of the great deeds of God, and to proclaim the virtues of Him who has called them out of darkness into His marvelous light. Yea, He makes their whole body serviceable and submissive unto good; in such a manner that, although there may still be some stiffness, even rebelliousness...

### CHAPTER IV.
### Of the Creation of the Soul.

<margin>Although the body of man is very glorious.</margin>
Up until now we have spoken of the wonderful condition, beauty, and fitness of Man’s Body: for even though it is now most miserably marred by the Fall, it is nevertheless still—even as it is now—the most wonderful, artistic, beautiful, and fit piece of work that can be seen with eyes.

<margin>Yet the soul of man is far more excellent than the body.</margin>
But man’s Body, as wonderful, as artistic, and as beautiful as it may be, compared with the soul of man, is as nothing at all; it differs as much as the Earth from the Heaven, or as the Beasts of the field from the Angels of God.

Truly, the body of man is but like an earthly Palace, very costly and gloriously made, 2 Cor. 5:1, but the soul is the Heavenly Inhabitant of this beautiful Palace: the body is merely like a most artistic cabinet of a Jeweler, but the worthy Jewel that is laid therein is the soul: indeed, the body is merely like the mask with which that most wonderful and beautiful face, the soul, is covered: the Body is merely like the Lantern, but the soul is that light—yes, the bright light—which shines through it: the body, as

<column-break/>

fit as it is for all kinds of works, is like the tool, but the soul itself is the Master-craftsman.

<margin>For the soul performs all the excellent and glorious actions that are wrought through the body.</margin>
So also truly belongs to the soul the praise and prize for all the excellent, glorious, wonderful, and artistic actions which we have explained above as being wrought through the body; for certainly the soul is like the eye of the eye. It is not so much our eye, which we see standing in the head, that sees; the eye is but like the window, but the soul that is within sees through the eye: the soul is the hand of the hand, and works therewith as with a tool all that is artistic, and so with the rest. For the eye does not see, the ear does not hear, the hand does not work, when the soul is no longer in the man, when the soul has departed from it. Consider then, what a glorious, what an excellent creature the soul must be, which is the inhabitant, the Lord and Master of that beautiful, of that most excellent Palace of the Body; yes, such a wonderful inhabitant of the Body, that by its indwelling it moves the Body itself, sets it going, and directs and governs all its powers and all its members: so that the soul is truly like a King in the Body; yes, the soul as it is in man is truly like an incarnate <term>bevleeschten</term> <note>Literally "enfleshed" or "made into flesh."</note> Angel of God, like an Angel of Heaven revealed in the flesh: the Body is like a Temple, like a house of devotion for the service of God; the soul is like the Priest, like the worshiper who rightly promotes and ordains all things.

# Deformed, Reformed

<margin>
And works very diligently within the Body.

If we could but once see with the eyes of the Body how the soul sets itself to work within the Body; indeed, if we could see it naked and bare before our eyes, the soul working diligently and busily within our Body, it would arouse such wonder and amazement in us that we would have to confess never in all the days of our lives to have seen anything more marvelous. In this way, the soul also makes the human being (whom we consider to be the most wonderful creature that can be imagined). Therefore, some are accustomed to say *non est homo quod videtur* <note>Latin: "Man is not what he appears to be."</note>; the body with which we are clothed is not the human being; it is merely the human being's dwelling. The human being himself, they said, dwells within that which we see. Nevertheless, we know that, strictly speaking, a human being is neither soul nor body, but consists of both.

</margin>

# Adam, Upright

->**The investigation of the same is quite difficult.**<- Just as it usually happens with all things of value, so too is this subject <note>the soul</note> a matter of difficult inquiry. For certainly our soul, through which we know all things, is not easily known by ourselves; just as we perceive that the eye of our body, with which we see all things, cannot see itself. There are primarily three causes that make it so that some things which are around us cannot be well known by us: the corruption of our own understanding, the hidden nature of the things themselves, and that they sometimes lie somewhat too close to us.

<margin>1. Because our understanding is so corrupt. 2. The soul is so hidden. 3. And the same lies so close to us.</margin> All of this meets here together, especially regarding these spiritual beings, their properties, and operations. The soul is an entirely heavenly, hidden thing, a spiritual and almost incomprehensible being; yet it lies so close to us that this also creates—I know not what—difficulty, so that we can know it the less; just as when something is placed so close to our eye that it touches it, we can then see and know that thing the least.

<margin>Yet we must not neglect the same while there is still a means to come to the knowledge of it.</margin> Nevertheless, we must not neglect to apply our diligence to this. For even though we cannot fully fathom the essence of our soul, there are nonetheless some means of knowledge at hand, through which we can learn to know and perceive the condition of our soul to some extent for our edification.

Now we come to the knowledge of things through two means: first through sensation, that is, through the help of the external senses, and thus we

<column-break/>

come to learn to know all those things that can fall under the external senses, which are all physical things. Secondly, through reflection upon those things which are not physical but spiritual, and therefore cannot be perceived with the external senses; if we wish to know their condition in any way, we must, through reflection and imagination, represent them to ourselves as being thus and so, and so carve and create in our mind a certain form and image of them, comparing the same with something that we have well perceived with our external senses, and which seems to come closest to that spiritual thing that we would gladly know and understand.

<margin>Namely, that we see them as in an image and as in a mirror.</margin> Therefore, if we would in some measure perceive and understand the condition of our worthy soul, we must endeavor to see it as in an image, as in a mirror, since we cannot see or perceive it in its own essence; just as we cannot see the eyes of our own body, with which we see all things, in their own essence, but only as they are represented to us in a mirror. What image of the soul shall we then make for ourselves? What mirror shall we set before us, in which we might in some way see and perceive the nature, the form, the essence, and the condition of the soul? For this, we must take something that is best known to us, and in which we might nonetheless see the likeness and the condition of the soul expressed. Now, that is the living human being.

<margin>Which mirror is the living human being in his operations.</margin> Yes, the living human being is the only true, right, and faithful mirror, in which, looking, we might in some measure...

# Adam, Righteous,

By this you shall, to some extent, perceive what the condition of the soul is. For everything that a living person can do more than a dead body of a person—from which the soul has departed—that, and all of that, comes from the soul. For that, and for all of that, the soul has certain working powers and <term>faculties</term> <note>The author uses "faculteyten" to refer to the inherent abilities of the soul, such as reason or will</note>, from which one can then to some degree deduce the essence and the condition of the soul.

Look then, this is how it stands: a dead body neither eats nor drinks; it can neither stir nor defend itself, nor move; it neither walks nor stands; it neither sees nor hears; it neither smells nor tastes; it does not feel; it does not desire; it has no reflection; it has no memory; it is neither joyful nor sad; it does not fear, it does not hope; it does not boast; it does not speak; it does not understand, nor does it notice or perceive. In short (to say it all in one word) it is just like one of the idols of the <term>Heathens</term> <note>Non-Christians</note> and the <term>Papists</term> <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics, common in 17th-century Dutch Protestant writing</note>; it has eyes but it does not see, it has ears but it does not hear; it is as unfeeling as a wooden block. In contrast, a living person, who has the soul within them, does all this: they walk, they stand, they see, they hear, they are now joyful, now sad; they speak; they edify or corrupt their neighbor; they praise or blaspheme their God. Indeed, the living person has something within them by which they soar far above and beyond the body, and elevate themselves above all that is called "world," and search and rummage through all the little shops and every corner of the entire world, and move in an instant—just as they wish and please—many thousands of miles away; being now in France, now in India; now beholding the beau-

<column-break/>

tiful Heaven, now looking into Hell; yes, even penetrating to God the Lord Himself, the almighty Creator of all, who indeed dwells in a Light that no one can approach. See, all this goes on in the living person; all this the living person does, and can do, which a dead Body, from which the soul has departed, neither does nor can do. Behold then, in this mirror of the living person, the condition of the soul, and understand that that, and all of that, which the living person can do more than a dead Body, are workings of the soul and are all brought about through certain internal powers and faculties of the soul. From this one can somewhat deduce what the condition of our soul may be: namely, that it is a spiritual, active, and busy essence, a creature and creation of God, created for that purpose and breathed into man, so that man through it should live, work, feel, and understand.

# CHAPTER V.

#### That the soul makes the body alive, and makes man into a living soul through her indwelling.

<margin>The first operation of the soul in man is that she makes the body alive.</margin>
The first operation of the soul in man is that she makes the body of man—and consequently the man himself—alive; our text testifies to this explicitly, saying: *and he had breathed into his nostrils the breath of life, thus man became a living soul.* Genesis 2:7. <note>The author cites the Dutch Statenvertaling phrasing of the creation of Adam.</note>

Now, what life is, each person experiences better within themselves than can be expressed through any description; there plays within a living human I know not what youthfulness, alertness, pleasantness, and grace, which one sees clearly with the eyes, and yet cannot well express what it is, wherein the life of man shows itself, and through which one (especially when alert) can immediately distinguish it from a dead body. And that comes from the soul: for also (to say a word on this) life is nothing other than a certain operation and youth of the soul and her instrument, the body, wrought through the operation of the soul and the body together in the creature. Indeed, the soul, through her indwelling and presence in the body, does not only set the body in motion, and does not only move and stir

<column-break/>

the body this way and that to all kinds of operations, just as a pilot steers and sets in motion a ship in which he is, to wherever he wishes; but the soul makes the body itself alive, youthful, and active; for so our text also says, that the Lord God having breathed the living breath into the nostrils of the earthly Adam, the man became a living soul—that is, his body itself became like a living soul or body; for the word "soul" is sometimes taken simply for the body, Acts 2:27, 31. <note>original: "Actor. 2. 27. 31." The author refers to the Greek/Biblical usage of 'psyche' (soul) to denote the whole person or physical being.</note> Thus the body without the soul is cold, stiff, and immovable of itself; but through the indwelling of the soul, the body itself becomes warm, nimble, alert, and active; one sees a dead body is entirely cold, all the limbs are stiff, even rigid and immovable: lay upon a dead body as many clothes as you wish, you shall not warm it; rub it with oil, you shall not be able to make the limbs nimble and alert; all of that must come from the soul.

<margin>Indeed, she makes all the instruments and powers thereof alive and youthful through her indwelling, provided only that the instruments are well-disposed.</margin>
So there is also not one limb, not one instrument, nor one power of the body, but that the soul through her indwelling makes it—and all of it—each according to its nature, alive and youthful, so that as long as the soul is in the body (and provided only that the instruments of the body are well-disposed) all the limbs, instruments, and powers of the body show themselves alive, and each is capable and well-ordered for the operations for which they were created by God; the eye to see, the ear to hear, the nose to smell, the mouth to speak, the hand to grasp, the foot to walk. **Question.** Since the soul works so excellently in the body, and makes it so lively and active in all ways; how does it happen then that the soul does not also make the body spiritual and intelligent?

<margin>As also, why the body is not made spiritual and intelligent.</margin>
**Answer.** Because the body by its own kind and nature is not disposed <note>original: "gheſchicht" - meaning suited or fashioned</note> to be able to be made spiritual and intelligent; otherwise the soul, through its indwelling, would make the body just as readily spiritual and intelligent as it makes the same living and feeling, if it were as capable of spirituality and understanding as it is of life and feeling.

Just as it is no fault in the master <note>referring to a schoolmaster</note> that he does not teach the chairs and benches to recognize letters and learn to read as well as the children, because the chairs and benches are not capable of any learning or instruction: so it is also no fault in the soul that it does not make the body spiritual and intelligent; because the body is not capable of it. Meanwhile, the soul, being in the body, nevertheless exercises understanding and reason; and further works out through the body—as we shall presently hear—very diverse operations, whenever the condition of the body and its instruments <term>instruments: the physical organs and senses</term> have suitable fitness for the same; and through its indwelling, it always makes the body capable, ready, and alert for all such operations for which it can be suitably used.

<margin>For the soul is like a spark—</margin>
And all this comes from the fact that our soul is truly like a

<column-break/>

<margin>—of the Divine nature</margin>
spark of the Divine nature itself, and thus also has some resemblance to the infinite condition of the Divine nature; it runs, it spreads itself, it sparkles through all the body, so that just as it is said of the course of the sun, that nothing remains hidden from its heat (Psalm 19:7), so it also goes with our noble soul; it spreads itself flying, swarming, sparkling (that I may speak so for the understanding of the simple) throughout the entire body, and makes living, alert, youthful, and active all the limbs, all the instruments, and all the powers thereof.

So that the soul in the body of man is like a candle in a lantern, which makes the whole lantern luminous, and shoots its light on all sides, to all parts of the lantern, provided it is transparent and capable of receiving the light; it is like the wind in the organ, which creeps through all the pipes, and all the nooks and corners thereof, and makes the same capable of giving all kinds of sound, each according to its kind.

<margin>And is in the body in a very noble way.</margin>
Yet the soul is in the body in a much nobler way than a candle is in a lantern, or the wind in the organ; for the soul is an ever-burning light, which never goes out, and never consumes itself as the candle does; it is also an ever-quickening wind (so to speak), a wind that always blows, and also does not vanish nor cease, even when it is already departed from the body. Yes, that which is most wonderful of all: the soul of man is such a light in the body of man, that it not only gives light through the body, like the candle through a lantern, but it makes the whole body itself...

-># Deformed, Reformed<-

The soul possesses the human being in this small world <note>The "small world" or microcosm refers to the human being as a reflection of the universe (macrocosm).</note>: all the duties and the activities that the human can do and carry out, not only do not happen well or properly, but cannot be done at all by the human without the soul—without the sovereign power of the soul joining in. Whatever actions or activities they might be, great or small, simple or of importance; without the power of the soul, the human can neither exercise judgment well, nor give good counsel, nor wage war well, nor practice medicine well, nor conduct trade well, nor practice any art well, nor keep any shop well, or do a craft well, even down to the smallest things. Without the power and the guidance of the soul, not a single garment, not a single shoe can be well made; so that truly the soul is the "all" in this small world. She is the only and best Judge, Councilor, Theologian, Jurist, Physician, Captain, Merchant, Artist, Shopkeeper, and Craftsman that emerges therefrom: all that is done through her is done; and without her, nothing is done of all that is done. The soul must let her breath pass over it; she must be with it, near it, over it, or what is done there will be of no value. Indeed, nothing, nothing in the world could be done; everything would stand completely still. Humans, even the most excellent of the Land, would be merely like wooden stakes if the soul were not beneath them and with them.
