describe the condition of the soul, have declared that the same is an *entelecheia* <note>original: "ἐντελέχεια"</note>, that is, a "possessor of perfection" <note>original: "perfectihabea"</note>. This was not to play games or to cover their ignorance of the soul's condition, as some take it; for they were truly too proud to allow themselves to appear ignorant in anything. Rather, it was to truly express in one word as much of the soul's condition as poor humans, who are greatly darkened by the Fall <note>Referring to the biblical Fall of Man, which was believed to have clouded human intellect.</note>, could say about it. It being a Greek word, composed of several words together, signifying as much as such a being which has within itself the perfection or completeness of the human. And it is borrowed, so it appears, from the usage and manner of speaking that was in the land of Greece, which consisted mostly of Republics. There they called *entelecheia* <note>original: "ἐντελέχεια"</note> that sovereign power which was among the people, by whose authority and vigor all things of the Republic gain their strength and power, and are kept in good order and fashion. By observing this sovereign power in the Republic, one is very aptly led to a closer understanding of the condition of the soul in this small world, the human being.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the human soul's superiority over other creatures, specifically focusing on how even physical actions are elevated by human reason and spirituality.</meta>

# Adam, Righteous

<columns>

Furthermore, even those activities which are otherwise purely physical—such as hungering, thirsting, seeing, and hearing—are transformed. While other creatures, who can also hunger, thirst, see, and hear, simply do so without further reflection, attending only to what the physical matter requires and indicates; the human being, by contrast, is accustomed to being drawn up from these outward things to very beautiful, heavenly, and spiritual matters. 

For example, while tasting the pleasantness of food at his own table, he is thereby reminded of how joyful and delightful it shall be to eat hereafter at God’s table with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Luke 14:15). Likewise, beholding the beautiful heavens, the stars, the sun, and the moon, etc., he is drawn up to consider what a wonderfully glorious Being the Lord our God must be, who knew how to bring forth and create such magnificent creatures with a single word (Psalm 8:2; Psalm 111:2, 3). 

Truly, even in those activities which seem purely physical, and which man has in common with the trees of the earth <note>The author likely refers to biological growth or "vegetative" functions shared with plants.</note> or the beasts of the field, there is found as great a difference between how they occur in man and how they occur in other creatures as there is between the sight that a Master of the House has of his very artistic and costly paintings, and the sight that a dog has of them. Both see the paintings, but the dog runs past them (as we say) with blind eyes; he sees neither art nor value in them.

<column-break/>

On the contrary, the Master of the House notices the art and ingenuity of them in every respect. Here that old saying particularly applies: *When two do the same work, it is nonetheless not the same work.* <note>original: "als twee het eygen werck doen / soo en is het doch eygen werck niet." A variation of the Latin proverb "Si duo faciunt idem, non est idem."</note>

And just as we know that whenever a mighty Prince or King is pleased to perform some common task—for example (as happens in some places), to wash the feet of some of his lowly subjects—one truly considers that work much more wonderful, glorious, and excellent than if it were performed by a common servant. 

Even so it stands with the common activities of man which he shares with other creatures; because of the great excellence and glory of his noble soul, they are much more glorious and excellent when they are done by man than when they are done by the trees of the earth, the beasts of the field, or the birds of the heaven.

This serves to be well-noted here at the beginning, where we commence speaking of the **activity of the soul**, and should always be kept in mind hereafter. For it will certainly bring great light and great utility to the handling of the matter; while we, attending to this, shall have occasion (as is fitting) to point out each time what further spiritual practice and discernment man ought reasonably to have over all these more lowly and common activities. Man, I say, who—through such a completely spiritual and noble soul—performs and works out even these lowest and slightest activities.

</columns>

<summary>This page argues that human physical sensations (like hunger or sight) are superior to those of animals because they serve as catalysts for spiritual reflection and worship. The author uses the analogy of a King washing feet to show how the dignity of the actor elevates even the most mundane task.</summary>

->Concerning the first sort of life, and its operations, which lead man, through the soul, in conformity with the trees and plants of the earth, yet in a nobler manner.<-

<margin>The plants of the earth also have a life whose operations are: 1. To draw nourishment to themselves.</margin>
The trees and plants of the earth are found in fact—and also testified in Scripture—to have a certain life: for we read in the Scripture of dead trees **Jude 1:12**, <note>original: "Jud. Ep. 12"</note> and so we also tend to say in our common speech of a tree that perishes, that it dies. Now the operations of life which the trees and plants of the earth possess are threefold: First, they draw nourishment to themselves, as is evident by the fact that one must have very good knowledge of the earth—reasonably rich, and yet not too rich, each according to its nature—lest the trees and plants of the earth perish: either through lack of nourishment, like wheat sown in sand; or through too great an abundance of nourishment, as when wheat is sown in much too rich a soil, so that it grows too luxuriantly, collapses, and turns to dung.

<margin>2. To grow and increase.</margin>
2. Secondly, they grow, wax, and increase in height and breadth: just as we see that a tree a year old, being well planted, is much sturdier than a little sprout which first comes out of the earth.

<margin>3. To bring forth fruit and seed.</margin>
3. Thirdly, they bring forth fruit and seed themselves, so that they procreate and perpetuate; as the Scripture also testifies to us, **Gen. 1:12.** Now all these three kinds of operations we also find in man; they draw nourishment to

<column-break/>

themselves; they grow up to their manly height or stature; they procreate and beget children who are like them. All these powers and operations are in man through the indwelling of the soul. We shall look into the nature of these, one after the other, somewhat more closely.

### Chapter IX.

->Concerning the power and operation of drawing nourishment to oneself, to which also, according to man's present condition, clothing belongs.<-

<margin>Man also has the power to draw nourishment to himself.</margin>
That man has this power appears abundantly from his daily eating and drinking. Now the power of eating and drinking was created in man by God; for it was so with man, even in the first creation itself, and still is, that the natural heat of life which is in him feeds and maintains itself upon the natural moisture which the Lord also first created in man; just as we see that a burning wick feeds itself with the oil that is in the lamp; which burning wick, if it is to be maintained forever, must have new oil constantly put into the lamp, in proportion to the amount of oil consumed and swallowed up by the burning wick: so it is likewise necessary, for the maintenance of man's life, that the natural moisture—which is constantly drawn upon, and in every way consumed and swallowed up by the natural heat within man—be renewed each time, and receive new succor from without, just as one puts oil in a lamp.

<margin>Which is necessary to him for the maintenance of his life.</margin>

Furthermore, the Lord our God has also arranged this power so very wisely within man, that He has provided for the possibility that man might at some time—the soul being taken up by other more glorious Spiritual and Heavenly preoccupations—forget or neglect the consumption of his necessary nourishment for the maintenance of his life. This was done so that through such neglect, the burning wick <note>original: "brandende wiecke"; a metaphor for the vital flame or metabolic heat of the body</note> which is within man, and which never neglects to draw its fuel to itself, would not be left without sustenance and thus go out, whereby the soul would then be separated from the body. To provide for this, the Lord God placed within man the power to hunger and to thirst. The condition of this is such that when the burning wick currently within man has consumed much of that moisture upon which it lives, the small veins (which are spread like a network throughout the entire man) immediately become aware of it. For they are then sucked upon too strongly by the other needy members of the Body, and this begins to pain and torment him; whereupon they then rouse themselves and begin more diligently to suck at the stomach to obtain some help from it. This in turn pains and torments the stomach, and as it has nothing else to which it can turn, it begins—being aided by the imagination <note>original: "phantaſije"; here meaning the mental faculty of forming images or desires</note>—to crave and long for nourishment, for food and drink, which might be brought to it from without. This is so that, being provided with it, the stomach might have something to pass on to the sucking small veins, which might then carry it over to all the

<column-break/>

members of the Body for its maintenance. And this desire and this longing for food and drink we call hunger and thirst, which are given by God to the children of men so that they might be warned and exhorted by them when the Body has need of nourishment, in order to provide the same. The Lord our wise God has further arranged it so that man, being thus hungry and thirsty, partakes of and receives the same nourishment with a singular delight, pleasantness, and taste. This is so that he—being on the one hand pressed by the painfulness of hunger and thirst, and on the other hand enticed by the delight and tastiness he finds in eating and drinking when he is truly hungry and thirsty—should by no means fail to consume his proper nourishment for the maintenance of his life.

And it was necessary that the Lord should so arrange it with man, seeing as the situation with man in this regard is quite different than with the trees and plants of the earth. Because of this, it can happen that the noble soul of man, being taken up with other more glorious and excellent contemplations, might come to neglect the consumption of necessary food. ### Of the corruption of the power to draw nourishment to oneself, and to clothe oneself through and in the Fall.

<margin>Man now carries himself against the laws of God.</margin>

As for his nourishment, or his power to take nourishment to himself, man most hideously abused the same in the beginning by eating of the forbidden fruit; so also since that time, because this power of man was employed against the command of **God**, and because he as it were withdrew the same from **God** and made it rebel against **God**, this same power has leaped as if beyond all bounds and beyond the management of man himself; and it is indeed now so unbound that man himself has great trouble and difficulty with it before he can restrain it in any measure: for it now often rebels as much through **God's** righteous permission and judgment against the will of man, as it was once used against the will of **God**.

We ought to accustom ourselves to remember the Lord our God in our food and drink, from whose hand we receive that eating and drinking, and to represent to ourselves that these are all His gifts, by which we are so kindly refreshed; that also the power to be able to eat and drink is granted to us by God Himself; that it is He also who gives us health and preserves our sense of taste, so that we may eat of all that is set before us, and that we find some sweetness therein; and that we, through the contemplation of all this, strive and endeavor, on the occasion of our food and drink, also to taste for ourselves how gracious the Lord is, thus applying ourselves to enjoy our nourishment in a more noble manner than the plants of the earth or the beasts of the field do.

If we then moreover think on those things: that if the Lord had wished to deal with us according to justice, He might indeed rightfully have ordained (since Adam set about eating of the forbidden fruit) that we should never again find any good taste in any food or drink; but if we then, notwithstanding all this kindness of the Lord, should nevertheless be gluttonous

### Chapter XI.

->Of the power to grow in size and in strength.<-

<margin>In man there is also the power to grow.</margin>
THAT this power exists in man is witnessed by the Scriptures, Genesis 1, Luke 1, and daily experience teaches irreducibly that the small and weak infants, being first born, grow up to manly and womanly strength. All those who now rule the world—cities, lands, churches, families—were previously small, powerless, helpless infants, and played there in the cradle; played there in the jumping-chairs <note>original: "hupfen" - likely referring to a baby walker or bouncer</note> and in the streets; just as we now see happening with young children; but in the progress of time, and through the power of growth, they have become what we now see them to be.

<margin>Just as in everything that has received life;</margin>
So we see then, that it is thus in nature, that every thing that has received life has also received a certain secret power to enlarge itself, to strengthen itself, and to grow and wax great until it has come to that perfection of size, thickness, length, and strength which was appointed to it by the Creator; just as is evident in the plants and trees of the earth.

Now this power was created into living creatures by God, for it pleased the manifold wisdom of the Creator to arrange the matter in nature so that each should bring forth its own kind,

<column-break/>

Genesis 1. However, so that there should always be found a great distinction between the production of the Creator and the procreation of the creatures; it is also so situated that, whereas the Lord our God the Creator created all things in their full size, strength, and as it were perfection according to their kind, the creatures bring forth their own kind, yet not in the first instance as large and perfect as they themselves are. For a tree does not in the first instance bring forth another tree; nor a man a man as strong <note>original: "vroom" - in 17th-century Dutch this often meant 'strong' or 'capable' rather than just 'pious'</note> and as large as he himself is: but they bring forth only the seed, in which then (a wonderful arrangement of our God) lies wound up, as it were, the entire condition of that creature which brings forth such seed: which seed, being well nurtured, receives such fashion as the living creature is from which that seed came, and grows on and on, until it actually becomes as large as that from which it came: and consequently is now also capable of procreating again itself; just as daily experience irreducibly teaches.

<margin>So that he might thereby come to the perfection of a full-grown man</margin>
So then this power of growth is given to man, so that the humans who are procreated should, through this growing power, come to the perfection of a full-grown man, and it happens thus: namely, that the nourishment which the human receives—more than he simply needs for present maintenance (therefore one also sees that growing youth requires more abundant nourishment than the adult)—is turned by the nourishing power into

# Adam, Righteous

The power of growing growth: man's body, being in this state, is like a small sponge which, though initially compressed and very tiny, can gradually be released to become larger and wider. If it could then also draw in some nourishment to fill that expansion, it would truly become firmer and larger; just as happens in the trees and plants of the earth, and in the body of man, until it has reached the perfection of a full-grown human.

<margin>So that it stops thereafter, although man does not lose the power itself.</margin>

When man has reached this stage, the power to grow and increase further ceases; however, man does not lose it, as is evident from this: if it should happen that a grown man receives some great wound in his body, so that a large portion of his flesh must be cut out, there immediately appears in him this concentrated power of growth. In place of the flesh he has lost, other and new flesh grows again, and the wound is filled. It is also to be thought that this power of growing and increasing exerts itself in man by ensuring that the human body—otherwise so soft and tender—is nevertheless not worn away. For do we not see that all other things wear out through use? Is it not wonderful that our hands, which are as soft as silk or velvet and are daily at the forefront and constantly used, nevertheless do not wear out, but always remain in the same condition? Truly, there is no iron or steel which, if it were as constantly employed,

<column-break/>

exerted, practiced, and used as our hands are, would not be made entirely blunt and useless at the end of a year or two, as goldsmiths and others realize; yet our hands endure. Many people pay very little attention to this; yet it is a wonderful work of our great God, and is brought about, as is to be thought, through the power of growing and increasing in man. And thus far, Adam and Eve also had this power of growth and increase in themselves, although they were created in their full adult size.

<margin>This power now has its place only in the body, not in the soul, which from the first birth is perfect in all its powers.</margin>

Now, all that we have said concerning the growing increase of man must be understood solely and only of man's body. For as far as the soul is concerned, it is in the first instance complete and perfect in all its parts and powers, even in the smallest and most tender child that is born. This immediately begins to show itself: even young children, regarding those things they are beginning to perceive, have certain reflections and from them make as firm a conclusion as the wisest men living know how to make from what they further perceive. For example: a child who has progressed far enough to know that fire burns, hurts, and scorches, immediately draws from that as firm a conclusion as any human can: that it will not willingly throw itself into the fire, but flee from it. ## CHAPTER XII.
### Concerning the nature of the power to grow in size and in strength, before, during, and after the Fall.

### The glory of this power before the Fall.

<margin>Through this power, man before the Fall would have reached a suitable size and strength of body; he would also have increased in knowledge as far as was useful to him.</margin>
Now, regarding this power to grow and increase, it was so ordained in the first creation that, as far as physical growth is concerned, it would have proceeded in all suitability; as must necessarily follow from the right and temperate use of nourishment, of which we have spoken previously. And as for the increase of the soul in knowledge, man would also have acquired that as far as it would have been useful and profitable to him; of which the Tree of Knowledge of Good and Evil was a certain and true pledge to him, Genesis 2, if he had properly abstained from it. So also Adam, before his fall, by occasion of the growth he could see in things, began to consider how much he, being the most noble, ought to increase in the things that had not yet been revealed to him.

### The corruption of the power of growth under the Fall.

<margin>But now, through sin, the power of growth is greatly weakened in respect to the body.</margin>
However, since Adam set himself to eat of the forbidden fruit, it has become quite piteous for man in this regard. The growth and increase of the body, although the same was not entirely taken away thereby (for God desires to have adults here on earth who carry out His counsel, Isaiah 7:3, Acts 13:2), it is nevertheless greatly

### Of the restoration of the power of growth through Christ.

<margin>To be restored in this, we must become partakers of the Lord Christ.</margin>
Should we then also be placed in a better condition in this regard, we must strive and endeavor in every way to become partakers of the second Adam, the Lord Jesus Christ, who has been given to us out of the great grace of God, so that we, having become one plant with him (Romans 6:5), might grow and increase to a perfect man in Christ (Ephesians 4:13). For truly, in the second Adam there is sap and nourishment enough to make all of us, who are grafted and joined into him, take a continual shoot and grow up in all that is good, according to soul and according to body (Romans 8:10-11).

The means now, which we must use so that we might enjoy this good from Christ, are these: 1. Regarding the body, that we be sober and temperate, as was explained above; and that shall make us grow up fittingly—if we still have stature to grow—to our full maturity, and in any case, it shall fittingly strengthen our body and preserve it against decay as much as shall be useful and soul-saving for us in our present situation; for just as immoderation weakens, as we heard above, so temperance restores (see Ecclesiastes 10:16-17). 2. Regarding the soul, that we continually awaken the powers of the same and the gifts that are in us, and employ <note>original: "imploreren" - here used in the sense of putting to use or calling upon</note> them for the contemplation and working out of necessary and useful matters, especially those which are Heavenly and concern our salvation.

## CHAPTER XIII.

### Concerning the power of procreation.

That this power has been given to man is testified by the Scripture, Genesis 1:28 <note>original: "Gen. 1. 28." — "Be fruitful and multiply."</note>, and experience teaches it; for we find nowhere now any men in the world—those who govern the Republic, the Church, or the Households—who were not all brought forth out of their mother's body as small, powerless, helpless children, having been begotten by their fathers; this is incontrovertible: everyone knows this.

And just as it now presents itself, the Lord our wise God also willed to use this way of procreation, through which men come into the world one after another; in order that in the progress of time there might always remain among men an irrefutable proof of the creation of the first humans. This was so that man, by observing the circumstances of his own coming into the world, might be led to a certain conviction regarding the creation of the first humans, and subsequently to the certain knowledge of God his Creator himself. For when man begins to observe this with understanding, with attention, and with discernment—that indeed truly no capable men are found or can be found anywhere, in any regions or coasts of the world, who were not previously small, young, underage, helpless, and distraught little children; who also would not have been procreated by other humans, having had both Father and Mother; in such a manner

<column-break/>

that since no small young children or rising youth are now found in the world who have not come forth from adults, he must necessarily go one step further if he is to be satisfied. For, as we now find the state of affairs with men—namely, that on the one hand there are no young children who are not procreated by adults, and on the other hand, there are no adults now who were not first young children—so human ingenuity (if it goes no further) can in no way comprehend how man could first have come into the world; indeed, how any humans at all could have come to be in the world. For since there are no adults who were not first young children, and no young children who were not brought forth by adults; it is in no way imaginable how either the adults or the young children could have first come into the world. For if one posits on the one hand that the adults existed before the young children, that cannot be, if one merely regards the common course of nature <note>original: "natuure"</note>, considering that no adults are found who were not first young children: if one posits on the other hand that the young children were first, that also cannot be, for no young children are found who are not procreated and brought forth. # Misshapen, Reshaped.

For we perceive with our eyes not only light, but also darkness; we become aware through our ears not only of sound, but also of silence; we discern through our taste and smell not only the things that one tastes and smells, but also that which one does not taste and does not smell. With our feeling <note>touch</note>, we feel not only whether a thing is hard or soft, but also whether it is not hard, or not soft, not hot, or not cold.

### The manner in which the external senses work.

<margin>2. Concerning the manner of the operation of the external senses, as far as is known: 1. That one and the same sense cannot perceive the object presented to another sense.</margin>
As to what the manner of the operation of the senses may be, many things are taken into consideration therein. We shall briefly touch upon the most necessary points for our purpose.

1. Whether one and the same sense would be able to perceive also the object presented to another sense; for example, whether the sight would also be able to perceive sounds?

Answer: No, not at all, just as experience teaches us; and the Apostle, <margin>1 Corinthians 12:17</margin> points out to us how God the Lord has arranged this in wisdom, in order to bind the members and instruments <note>organs</note> to one another in mutual love, as each has need of the other.

Now, it does not conflict with this that we sometimes know how to deduce through the eye whether a thing we see is hard or soft, hot or cold—which is the subject matter of feeling <note>touch</note>. For that knowledge does not come from the eye, but from the experience which the human being has previously had through feeling of a thing that presents itself in such and such a way—such as that iron is hot, or that ice is cold. Thus, this distinction does not come from the eye, but from the

<column-break/>

common sense <note>term: "common sense" (Latin: *sensus communis*); in historical psychology, this was the internal faculty that unified the data from the five individual senses</note>, being aided by the experience of feeling.

2. Whether the power of perceiving is in the external instrument <note>the physical organ</note>, such as in the eye or in the ear, or whether it is somewhere else.

<margin>2. That perceiving requires two things: 1. The receiving of that which is to be perceived, and that is the work of the external instrument.</margin>
Answer: Two things are necessary for perceiving: namely, first, that one receives the form <note>the sensory image or appearance</note> of that which should be perceived; secondly, that one pays attention to it and distinguishes it. As far as the first is concerned, it is the proper work of the external instrument—namely, to receive the form of that which one should perceive; as for the eye, to receive the color, the size, width, length, figures, and shape of the things presented to us. Therefore, when the instrument is damaged, the human being can in no way receive the form through that damaged instrument, such as through a ruined eye. This is evident when a person has one ruined eye and one good one; if he then closes the good one, he sees nothing at all. From this it further appears that this power to receive the form is located in the instrument. And it remains to be seen whether this does not extend so far that a well-constituted eye, even if the person is dead, can still receive the form like a mirror; although there is no one inside to rightly judge or speak of it.

<margin>2. The noticing and judging thereof, and that is the work of the common sense.</margin>
As far as the second point is concerned—the noticing and the judging of the same forms which one receives through the external senses—the instruments of the external senses do not do that, but that comes from the common sense, of which we shall speak hereafter; just as experience undeniably teaches, for it often happens to us,

# Adam, Righteous,

that we have there a sharp, alert, and open eye, with a living soul to accompany it, and also many things whose forms are cast before the eyes, and yet the human being does not see those things; namely, because the power of attention and observation does not apply itself to them.

<margin>So that in all actual perception there is not only a passion <note>original: "lijde" - here meaning a passive state of being acted upon</note> but also an action.</margin>
From which distinction we may also understand that truly perceiving a thing is not merely to suffer something <note>to be passive</note>, but to act. For when something is actually perceived by a human, the external instrument (it is true) suffers and is moved by the form of the things that occur before it; but the human being himself acts. For unless the soul and the common sense <note>term: "ghemeynen sin" - the internal faculty that unifies the data from the five external senses</note> act therein, unless they please to pay attention and observe it, then nothing is seen or heard by the human, etc.

So that in perceiving, the human being partly suffers something, namely, in the external instruments; and partly he acts himself, namely through his internal senses and through his soul. And from this it comes (which should be well noted) that although the human does not perceive the things that are cast before the external instruments of the senses unless the soul attends to them; nevertheless, the external instruments are often so powerfully moved by the things cast before them, that the soul must attend to them whether it wants to or not; as when a completely bright light suddenly shines around a person, or a terrifying voice strikes the ear, or a deadly wound is given to the body, then the soul must attend to it, whether it wants to or not; and that happens because the first principle

<column-break/>

and the first origin of perception comes from the suffering of the instruments, which are affected by the subject matters that come before them.

From this it also follows that the external senses affect the human much more powerfully than the fantasy <note>term: "phantasie" - the faculty of imagination or mental representation</note>; for they have massive and very substantial subjects, which sometimes violently affect their instruments, so that the human, whether he wants to or not, must attend to them; just as he also receives from them either great pleasure or great pain, which are the distinct consequences of the senses. And therefore it is also recounted as something special and wonderful when it happens to someone that they have a bowel movement just by seeing the purgative or the clyster <note>term: "klistierije" - an enema</note>, even if they do not take it; because the bowel movement must be awakened through feeling, although it can also happen through the Imagination.

<margin>All things cast before the senses give off certain forms and are not substances in that regard.</margin>

Just as the same is found in the voice, which spreads itself into a thousand ears, which then cannot happen without the multiplication of forms. Now, that such forms come off from all perceptible things is most clearly evident in visible things; for we see that a body, being placed before the Sun, casts a shadow; being placed before a mirror, or against the water, it gives a form of itself in the mirror and in that water: and furthermore, there remains in our hearts a form of that which we have seen, even when it has already vanished in its physical essence.

So also these forms (which must certainly be noted, in order to preserve their proper context) are merely like shadows, which take up no space, have no substance, and can depart by the thousands from those things without the things themselves being in the least altered or impaired thereby: just as one sees that the very same body, being placed against many mirrors, gives off various forms, or against many candles, gives off various shadows without any destruction or impairment of itself.

So that it proceeds here in much the same way as with the seal, which presses itself in form upon the wax, and that a thousand times over, without being in any way changed or

<column-break/>

impaired thereby; unless it be so far as one sees that time wears all things away; and that one might think that this happens through this giving off of forms, which in the course of time makes some slight wear; yet that is so little that it is not felt, nor can it reasonably be taken into account.

<margin>
4. That the report of the senses is firm when all things necessary for it are well-ordered.
</margin>

### 4. Whether the report of the Senses is firm and certain?

**Answer.** Yes, when all things necessary for it are well-ordered. 1. The perceptible thing must have a proper distance; because it is not so with the sun, the sun seems to us ten thousand times smaller than it is. 2. The instrument <note>The organ of sense, such as the eye.</note> must be rightly positioned. 3. The medium <note>The "between-thing" or environment through which one perceives.</note> must also be right. For if you look through a green glass, everything is green. 4. That the common sense <note>The internal faculty that processes sensory data.</note> pays attention to it.

Furthermore, we must know that there are three touchstones of truth: 1. Right sense, 2. Right reason, 3. Holy Scripture: these must each be applied according to their nature; right sense regarding perceptible things, as also regarding the perceptible elements of the Lord's Supper <note>original: "Avondtmaels"</note>. 2. The rational regarding the rational; such as that the Sun, being so far away, still appears so large, so that in itself it must be a thousand times larger than it appears to be. 3. Holy Scripture, regarding spiritual things.

Now, as concerns the closer nature of these outward senses, their wonderfulness, and their usefulness—from which it also appears what great and glorious gifts and favors of God they are, and consequently, how much we ought to watch over them, for we shall have to give a great account for them—of these we have spoken when we explained

And see, this is the condition of man's outward senses; which are also given to man by God for very excellent ends. So also man receives much good through the proper application of them, and conversely, much harm through the great abuse thereof.

Now the Lord God Almighty has given the outward senses to man, not only so that he should enjoy the physical comfort therefrom, of which we have spoken before; but especially so that he, through the help of his outward senses, should take closer knowledge of the Lord his God, and His things, and consequently be moved thereby as is fitting.

<column-break/>

To this end we must remember what we said above: that man comes to the knowledge of things through these two means; namely, through outward perception and inward reflection. Both must be applied wisely to learn to know the Lord our God and His things: for we are indeed bound to serve the Lord our God and to cling to Him with all our strength, Matthew 22:38. And that the outward senses are given to us for that purpose appears most singularly and clearly from the senses of seeing and hearing. For as far as sight is concerned, the Apostle <note>Paul</note> sets before us the entire created visible world, and desires that we should learn to know therefrom the eternal power and Godhead of the Creator, Romans 1:20. Hear also how the Prophet Isaiah reproaches man for this: "Lift up your eyes on high, and see who has created these things," Isaiah 40:26. And as far as hearing is concerned, for that purpose the Lord God has given His audible Word to man, so that all who had ears to hear should hear, and thereby perceive the sense and meaning of their God; just as we make our inner thoughts known to one another through speech and hearing. Yea, even smell (Song of Solomon 1:3), taste (Psalm 34:9), and feeling <note>touch</note> (Acts 17:27) are all awakened to take knowledge of the Lord our God: therefore the Apostle testifies that we ought to have well-exercised senses to rightly grasp and discern the things of God, Hebrews 5:12, 13, 14.

See there then, these are the noble outward senses which God the Lord has given to man, and that for such an excellent end as we have now...

### Concerning the righteousness of the external
### senses before the fall.

<margin>
These external senses were, in the first creation, very capable and ready instruments of the soul.

**W**ith regard to the first point, it stands firm and certain that the senses of man in the first creation were very well ordered, and in every way were capable and worthy instruments of the soul; on the one hand to work out all kinds of convenience for man, and on the other hand, also by the help of these, to penetrate more and more into the knowledge of God and His Divine things. If David, by observing created things, could perceive to some extent the wondrous nature of his God in Psalm 8, how much more was Adam able to do that? Who can doubt that Adam, seeing with a completely understanding eye the beautiful design <note>original: "ontwerp"</note> of created things, saw through them more and more the immeasurable wisdom, power, and goodness of his God? Hearing also the Divine discourses, how abundantly was he thereby advanced in the knowledge of the will of God; and so forth.

Thereby the noble soul itself, while it now dwells in the body, finds itself in many ways disturbed, confused, and misled: just as it often happens with mighty Princes and Kings, who, though they may be very wise and understanding, nevertheless (because they cannot be present everywhere themselves, but must see through other people's eyes and hear through their ears) are often deceived by their officers, who do not behave faithfully in the work for which they are employed.

And that which truly inconveniences the soul greatly, yes, confuses it in every way, is that all these sub-officers, all these senses of the flesh, have conspired as if in a plot <note>original: "Complot"</note> to simultaneously bring nothing but perverse and false impressions from all sides and directions to the internal senses; whereby man comes to wander most lamentably away from his God, and to break out into all kinds of wicked whims and practices.

How can man receive a heavier plague upon the ear in this life than that the **Noble ear**, which was given to him to receive the **Heavenly doctrine** for his eternal salvation, is now turned into a seducing ear, through which he receives the hellish impulses of wandering spirits to his eternal ruin? For behold, it stands thus: just as God the Lord out of great grace on the one hand, for the good of man, has so ordained it that man, giving diligent heed to edifying discourses <term>propoosten: topics of conversation or formal discourses</term>—which are the word of the Lord—thereby becomes more and more a partaker of God's good Spirit, which (I know not by what secret and Divine guidance) flows into our hearts at the same time as the good and wholesome words we hear; so on the other hand, when man sets himself to open his ear to foul speech—which is the word of the devil—so also the evil spirit of the devil shoots into man's heart at the same time as those foul words; he provides

->CHAPTER XVIII.<-

->Of the use of the Inner Senses, which man possesses through the indwelling of the soul;<-

<margin>If the external senses are to do their work well, the internal senses must help them.</margin>
Of the internal senses <term>internal senses: the cognitive faculties of the mind, as opposed to the physical organs</term> of men, and also of the animals of the outer image, simple and plain folk take no notice; yet it is certain and sure that without the help of the internal senses, man would perceive no discernment of things through the external senses. Daily experience teaches that whenever the internal senses of man do not come to the aid of the external ones, the latter in no way perform their work well. How often does it happen that a man passes by with his eyes that which is before him—even things of great importance to him—and does not notice it, but is like one who is seeing yet blind? How often is something spoken in his presence, while he stands by with open ears, and it is of great importance that he should know it, yet he does not notice it? All of this happens to man because, in these cases, the internal senses do not come to the aid of the external; therefore we are accustomed to say on such occasions: "Where are your senses?"

### Chapter XIX.

### Of the Common Sense.

<margin>
The common sense is that internal power of man through which he perceives and distinguishes the things that have occurred before the external senses.
</margin>

The common sense is that internal power of man with which man grasps, perceives, and distinguishes within himself the form and circumstances of the things that have occurred before the external senses.

So that the object presented to this common sense is every kind of form of all things that are perceived through the external senses; and therefore this inner sense is called the common sense; because it alone is <term>Capable</term> <note>original: "Capabel," meaning fit or suited</note> and prepared to receive within itself the form of all those things that are perceived by the external senses; not just one kind of perceptible matter, such as for example the colors with which the eyes occupy themselves, or the various voices and sounds with which the ear busies itself and not the eye (for just as the eye sees no voice, so the ear hears no colors); but this common sense alone perceives within itself all kinds of perceptible things; it re-

<column-break/>

ceives indeed the forms and images <note>original: "verbeeldinghen," often used in this period to mean mental representations or "species"</note> of all kinds of things that can be observed with any of the external senses.

Thus this common sense receives the image of all the various colors that the eye offers; of all the various voices that are carried to it through the ear; of all the various smells that the nose [perceives]; tastes that the tongue [perceives]; and feelings of hot or cold, wet or dry, hard or soft, smooth or rough, pleasant or unpleasant, painful or delightful, which the "upper-net" or the epidermis of man perceives. So that this common sense is like the <term>Center</term> <note>original: "Centrum," the middle point</note> or midpoint in which all the actions, forms, and images of all five external senses concur and meet together.

<margin>
Whereupon they then make the forms known more distinctly. Note this well.
</margin>

For it notices what is served to it by the external senses and makes a distinction between them; such as what is black, what is white; what sounds well or poorly; what smells good or stinks; what tastes good or bad; what hurts or what delights;

<margin>
For the external senses only receive the images of things without going further, like a mirror.

<meta>This page continues the philosophical discussion on the nature of human perception, specifically comparing the physical senses to a mirror and distinguishing them from the internal "common sense" or intellect.</meta>

# Deformities, Reformations,

in this part positioned simply like a **Mirror**; which only receives the forms and images that are presented to it, without making any distinction whatsoever, or noticing what is white or what is black, which is a beautiful and which is an ugly face; the mirror does not perceive or distinguish that; it only receives the form, and when it has done that, it has fulfilled its work.

It is exactly the same with the **outer senses**; the eye receives the colors presented to it; the ear, the voices; the nose, the smells; the tongue, the tastes, etc. But these outer instruments and senses make no distinction between these things—for example, whether they are pleasant or unpleasant; that comes from the **common sense** <note>original: "alghemeyne sin"; a philosophical term referring to the faculty that unifies and interprets data from the five physical senses</note>: and consequently, the human being is well or poorly disposed toward those things which the outer senses serve up. Indeed, these outer senses do not even know or perceive themselves that they receive those things into them; the eye does not know that it sees; the ear does not know that it hears; no more than a mirror knows that it receives forms or images; which, because it might seem strange to the simple-minded, even unbelievable, they shall be able to notice through experience from the following reflections.

<margin>
From the fact that a person sometimes receives many images in their outer senses.
</margin>
First and foremost, because it indeed often happens that a person has many things in their eye—various forms and images—which they notice no more than if they were not there; as for example: when a person runs diligently somewhere from one street to another to look for someone, many things encounter them, many things

<column-break/>

run into their eye, just as all kinds of things presented to a mirror are imaged therein; nevertheless, the person does not see the things, even though they have them in the eye just as well as the mirror they might carry on their chest; and all that because this **inner sense** <note>the mind or consciousness</note> being now occupied—not to watch this or that, or to see this doorstep or that cart—but solely to find the man whom the person seeks, it does not notice those things; thus those things are also not seen nor heard, properly speaking, although they have been in the person's eye or ear, each according to its situation. This is found to be indisputably so by experience; and that the simple-minded should think that in this case the eye truly does not receive that form into itself, that is an error <note>original: "abuys"</note>; for a person's eye is like a mirror; and just as it is impossible that if any things were presented to a mirror, the mirror would not receive the image of those things; so it is also impossible that an open eye would not receive into itself the form of those things that run into the eye, even though it takes no more knowledge of them than a mirror does, whenever the common sense does not attend to it.

<margin>
2. From the fact that mad and drunken people, who nevertheless have capable instruments of the outer senses, [judge] quite differently.
</margin>
2. Secondly, it also appears from this, because one daily finds that mad and drunken people—who otherwise have their outer instruments just as ready and sharp as if they were sober of mind—often judge many things served through the senses entirely differently than they are accustomed to do when they are sober. # Adam, Righteous

<margin>
Others judge things served to them by the senses only when they are sober and in their right mind.
</margin>

...others <note>The text continues from a previous page discussing mental impairment</note> do not recognize their own partners and spouses from other people; even though it is found that their sight is as good and as sharp as it has ever been in their lives. That mad people do not distinguish their best friends from their enemies; that Lot did not distinguish his daughters from his wife <note>A reference to the biblical story in Genesis 19:30-38</note>; this does not happen because their eye is damaged or because their sight is not good; but it happens because their brains are disturbed, which is the seat of this **common sense** <term>common sense: (Latin: sensus communis) a philosophical concept of a faculty that binds together the data from the five individual senses</term>; and consequently it happens because those who have this common sense within them as a damaged instrument do not rightly distinguish between otherwise known friends and enemies. By this it further appears that it is actually not the eye that notices that it sees, nor the ear that it hears, but it is the **common sense** that does and perceives all this.

<margin>
3. From the fact that people, when they sleep or lie in a faint, receive all images without discernment.
</margin>

3. Thirdly, this is also further proven by the fact that truly, when a person is dead, or sleeps, or lies in a faint, he nevertheless has all those instruments, and the eye like a mirror can still receive that image, and the ear the sound; but all without any discernment. This can be most clearly inferred from the wounds and stabs that are sometimes given to dead bodies; when this happens, the instrument of feeling is entirely present, it also actually receives those stabs and wounds; but it does not feel them, it does not suffer pain from them; because the **common sense** (being a power of the soul, although worked out through an internal physical instrument, just as animals have as well) is not there. And this one sees daily in sleep; the

<column-break/>

person, when he sleeps soundly, has the senses of hearing, feeling, etc., and yet he not only does not see—because his eyes are closed and sleep works particularly upon the eyes—but he also does not hear, he also does not smell, even though his ears and nostrils stand open; he does not taste, even if one puts something in his mouth; he also does not feel, even if one touches him; he does not notice these things until he begins to wake up. And all this happens to the person not because his soul sleeps (for that never sleeps, as we shall hear hereafter), but because his **common sense** sleeps; that is, it is actually stifled by the moist vapors that rise from the stomach into the brain, and is as if in a daze or sleep; just as when a person falls into a faint, and then the external senses do not perform their works.

<margin>
4. Also from the fact that people carry such diverse judgments over those things served to them by the external senses.
</margin>

4. Fourthly and lastly; this truth is also recognized here, as one daily perceives that people are so diverse in judgment regarding the things served to them through the external senses; one considers beautiful that which another does not consider so beautiful; one takes more pleasure in this music, and another in another; one has more taste for this food, another for another; and so forth. This diversity does not come from the external senses, for they receive the images just the same and do not contribute to the choice; but it comes from this **common sense**, according to which the person judges thus or so, depending on how his heart or brain is disposed; which we ourselves confirm when we (being asked why we want this thus or so, differently than others) answer that it is just our **sense** <note>original: "sin" - here meaning inclination or personal opinion</note>.

# Deformations, Reformations.

Now, against all this, it does not conflict that one finds in practice that whenever the external senses are damaged or wrongly positioned, the person then also judges wrongly regarding the things presented to him through those external senses. For even though it is true that it is not the eye that perceives what it sees, nor the ear what it hears, but rather that the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "ghemeyne sin"; the internal faculty that unifies the data from the five physical senses</note> does all this: it is nevertheless also true that this common sense does not judge, nor can it judge otherwise (for to subject the false presentation of the senses to scrutiny is the work of the <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "verstants"; the higher intellectual faculty</note>) than according to how the things are presented to it by the external senses. Just as we, when we look into a mirror, come to see nothing else in it but that form and image which the mirror has received, and the same just as it appears in color, shape, and size as it shows itself in the mirror; whether it be right and well, or whether it be poor or distorted: where it is nonetheless certain and sure that it is not the mirror that perceives what form it has received into itself, but the person who looks into the mirror.

See, it is exactly the same with this common sense. It uses all the five external senses as a mirror (so to speak) into which it comes to look; and it also cannot see anything else therein but those forms and images which the external senses—being well or poorly disposed—have received; and so it must take them up, and consequently it is moved, well or poorly: if then the eye, being damaged, views a thing wrongly, this common sense cannot better it, but must necessarily judge it just as the eye presents it to it. So

<column-break/>

likewise with the taste: if it is damaged, the sweet tastes bitter to him; the common sense can feel nothing else from it than what the taste presents. For it, as has now been said, uses these external senses as a mirror; and so it is still always the one that judges the forms and images, and not the external senses themselves.

Therefore it is also certain and sure that everything we have spoken of above regarding the operation of our external senses—which present false or correct reports to the soul—the senses do not do this immediately through themselves, but through the intervention of this common sense. Therefore also everything we have indicated above that we must observe in order to guide the external senses well, actually applies to the internal senses through which it must happen: but we have nonetheless seen fit to point it out through the occasion of the external senses, because the simple-minded can grasp it better that way, and because it also actually affects the external senses, whatever power it may be that guides them.

Thus, having now understood the nature of this common sense in general, we must yet briefly go and learn the wonder of it.

<margin>
The wonder of the common sense appears:
1. From that which receives all kinds of forms and images perceived through the five senses.
</margin>

### The wonder of the common sense.

**The** wonder of this common sense is truly great, whether we consider what it receives, or how.

As for the first: this general sense receives all kinds of forms and images of all kinds of things, which are perceived and presented through any of the five senses, or through them all together. So

# Adam, Upright

So that this common sense alone receives within itself all the forms of things with which all the five senses occupy themselves, and is consequently as if it were everything: eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and feeling. For it is quick and alert to receive all that: which is truly a most wonderful thing, that the Lord our wise God has placed such an excellent mirror within man, whereby he can perceive and notice so many things, which rightly ought to stir him to wonder at the great wisdom, power, and goodness of his Creator.

If we also, secondly, wish to look into the manner of how that happens, we shall also find something wonderful therein; that just as the aforementioned forms and images of size, of numbers, of colors, of tastes are made within us, through which we are then moved in this way or that; that we be-

## The utility of the common sense.

<margin>The utility of the common sense is seen by the deformity of the same.</margin>
The utility and the convenience / that man derives from this common sense / can be perceived and recognized nowhere better / than in those who are deformed <note>meaning impaired or disordered</note> in this common sense / as may be seen in drunken / and in mad people: how many things do they miss / or pass by / which they ought to heed in the highest degree? how erroneously do they also judge many other things / which they seem to want to notice? and what a confusion does that bring upon them? so that they would truly ruin / and destroy themselves to the very ground / if there were no other people / who, having their senses better intact / watched over and guided them more effectively.

<margin>It is the utility that makes the external senses perform their service and work.</margin>
The utility of this common sense also reveals itself in this / that through its help the external senses / which we have heard / are such highly excellent gifts of God / are turned to our benefit and service; in such a manner / that this common sense / is / like the chief officials of Solomon / who were set over his laborers / who worked on the Temple / and who saw to it / that each might do his things well: so likewise this common sense / sees to it / that the external senses might do their work well; although the same / just like Solomon's officials / cannot give to the senses themselves

<column-break/>

Now it is indeed a great convenience for man / that he has such a power within himself / wherewith he can sharpen his senses / and make each according to its capacity employ itself well / and apply itself to the works / to which they are called and appointed. Thus this common sense is to man / in regard to the external senses / what alertness is to man / in regard to all the active / and busy powers of his life; for just as those all rest / keep themselves still / and do nothing at all while sleeping (excepting the power of exercise / and some outward movement of the veins / nerves / and other internal parts / which man does not feel in that way / and in which the vigor of his life does not so manifest itself.) # Adam, Righteous
Do you not often say yourself, when you are sometimes sitting and chatting: "I am listening quite keenly" or "I looked as sharply as I could"? Thus you truly find that, even though you pass by many things unnoticed, nevertheless when you intend to pay attention to all the signs hanging out in this or that street, you are able to do so. And so it is with the other senses; since man has this power within himself, he shall have to give an account of it; he must then also consider to what end he has especially received this power from his God.

### The end for which God gave man the common sense.

<margin>For to that end God gave man the common sense,</margin>
Now the Lord God Almighty has given to man this common sense <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was historically understood as the internal faculty that binds together the data from the five external senses.</note>, and this power of attention and discernment of the things that occur to the external senses, so that man, being helped by this common sense, might alertly observe and properly heed everything that the external senses perceive. This is useful for learning to understand and retain more and more the wisdom, power, and goodness of our God, as well as our bounden duty toward God, toward ourselves, and toward our neighbor.

<margin>So that through the same he might perceive the opportunity of God and His will by an attentive noting of those things which the external senses receive.</margin>
For see, it stands thus: the external senses receive into themselves the forms and images of many remarkable and precious things, wherein the wisdom, the power, the goodness, the justice, the mercy, and the will of God reveal themselves most heartily. Yet men would pass all these by with blind eyes (as we are accustomed to say) if they did not, being helped by the common sense, attentively

<column-break/>

note them. Thus the Lord has placed this power of attention and discernment in man so that he might well heed and sharply notice that which is presented to him through the external senses, wherein he might more and more perceive the occasion and the will of his God. As for example: so that he might now and then fix his eyes to attentively notice the entire circuit of the Heavens, wherein the Lord our hidden God reveals Himself so notably (Psalm 8:4, Psalm 19:2, 3, 4, 5, etc.). Likewise, so that seeing how it goes with this one and that one, the godless and the godly, in this world—wherein God's mercy, justice, and unfathomable providence are discerned. But especially, if he can read, so that he might frequently read through God's Word with a keen eye and with attention, wherein he finds all the mysteries of God—His being, His works, and His will—abundantly revealed to us. So that he might attentively listen with his ears to what he hears told and recounted regarding the great deeds of God, and especially to go and listen to the preaching of God's Word and to all holy and edifying discourse, wherein the nature of our God, His being, His works, and His will are revealed to us quite faithfully and more powerfully than through any other sense. So that he might also sharpen his entire perception when he has something to smell, to taste, or to feel, in order to attentively note the particular quality thereof, so as to learn to notice from that also God's wonderful dealings, which [gave] such virtue and power of pleasant scent or...

### The righteousness of the common sense before the Fall.

<margin>This common sense was in the first creation a faithful Official over the outer senses, properly noting the things that were presented to him through the outer senses, in order to honor and know his God through the creatures.</margin>
As regards the first point, it is not to be doubted, seeing that Adam was created righteous in all his powers, so also was this <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "gemeyne sin"; the faculty that integrates data from the five physical senses</note> present in Adam in the first creation as a completely faithful and alert Official over the outer senses, which very diligently and discreetly gave heed to all their doings; and also with all attention noted, by the help of the outer senses, the situation of the things that were presented to humans thereby; so that the human beyond all doubt (if it could have remained so with him, and the Fall had not come over it, which has confused everything) through the quick alertness and observation of this common sense, would have increased from day to day more and more in the knowledge of many beautiful and glorious things of God, revealed in the creatures of the world, in <term>perceptible things</term> <note>original: "besinnelijcke dingen"; things that can be perceived by the senses</note>: for, although it is not to be doubted that Adam had from the first a great knowledge of natural things, as appears from the fact that he knew how to name all the animals, each according to its nature; yet one must also hold that there were still many things in the perceptible creatures which Adam, through the observation of the same, would have perceived more and more to his great delight, and to the greater wonder at the condition of his Creator.

<column-break/>

### The corruption of the common sense through and under the Fall.

<margin>But after the Fall the same is quite miserably damaged; so that the same now with most attention notes vanities and evil whims; and easily without observation lets pass those things which are most serviceable to the human.</margin>
But, however it stood with Adam in regard to this common sense and power of attention, so we poor, miserable children of Adam become aware on every side that the same power in us is now very weakened, indeed corrupted and damaged; that it is indeed so pitifully situated that we only have an alert attention and ready quickness for vanity and sinful whims, which only lead us to the loathsome Satan; and on the contrary have no kind of quickness or alertness in the observation of Holy things, that is, of the perceptible created things or histories, as they come from God and lead us to God.

Experience teaches this irreputably: if stage-players and jugglers come anywhere to a place; if there is any vanity or lightheartedness to be seen; if there are any <term>farces</term> <note>original: "boetserien"</note>, antics, or fabricated fables and trifles, or even worse things to be heard; there one sees wicked people very attentively present, there they know how to pay quick heed, there they swiftly perceive all that goes on, there they know how to listen diligently to all that is said: if, on the contrary, the Men of God come—the lovely feet of those who proclaim peace to us—if they administer the Lord’s Supper, if they proclaim the word of the Lord, our great God and Savior, on which all salvation, happiness, and welfare depends; there the people let their ears hang, there they can get neither heart nor mind to pay attention and give heed with quickness: there their senses are scattered by many wandering thoughts, there their senses often wander

# Delusions, Dominions.

Often [people are] far from the matters upon which they ought to attend with all seriousness; so that man may often perceive that their money <note>The author likely refers to the "price" of their attention or their worldly investments.</note> is that which the Lord reproaches the Israelites for: that they approached him with the mouth and with the ear, and yet their heart was far from him (Isaiah 29:13), so that their mind was not set upon him. For one, while he hears God’s word, has his mind in his warehouse; another in his account books; another on his field; another on his foul gain. Thus, that curse is also found in this part to have struck a multitude of people when they are in the house of the Lord: namely, that they have eyes and see not; they have ears and hear not (Isaiah 6:9). And this stupidity in Divine things has so strongly taken hold of man, that even when the men of God, in their addresses and exhortations, earnestly rouse the people to attention in order to call their obstructed <note>original: "verstropte," meaning choked or blocked</note> and straying senses back home again and again—crying out to them with a loud throat as the Lord Christ once did, saying: *He who has ears to hear, let him hear* (Luke 8:18); and saying with Isaiah to the people: *Give ear, and hear my voice; hearken, and hear my speech* (Isaiah 28:23); and with Peter: *Let this be known to you, and let my words enter into your ears* (Acts 2:14)—yet all this helps but little. For although, through such earnest rousing to attention, man lends his senses a bit better for a moment to observe that which is spoken, his senses immediately wander away again from the things of God toward vanity. So it is that the worldly and wicked man, who is so awake, and who with such untiring effort and attention

follows his own affairs—each according to where his heart leads him, for a long time and with much [effort]—cannot be attentive for a single hour to the things of his God, nor incline his ears to listen properly thereto.

### CHAPTER XXI.

### Of the Phantasy or the Power of Imagination.

Hitherto we have spoken of the <term>common sense</term> <note>original: "gemeynen sin"; the faculty that integrates data from all five physical senses</note>, whose work it is to receive into itself, to perceive, and to distinguish the things whose images are presented to man through the outward senses. But since this common sense (as has appeared from the preceding discourse) only receives the images of things that are present to the outward senses—such as the colors that the eye sees, the taste that the tongue tastes, etc.—and since it was nevertheless necessary, for the convenience of man, that he might have a perception not only of things present to his outward senses, but also of things which he formerly had present before his senses; in order that, through the perception thereof, when necessary, he might be able to make reflections therefrom, and consequently form conclusions, be moved in his <term>affections</term> <note>emotions or internal dispositions</note>, and bring forth actions toward his God, of gratitude or humiliation according to the nature of the matter; therefore the Lord God has implanted two other internal senses in man, namely the <term>phantasy</term> <note>imagination</note> and the <term>memory</term>, through which man knows how to represent to himself the things which he formerly had in his outward senses, but which are now not at hand; and that not only

<column-break/>

immediately after one has seen or heard them, etc. (which happens through the imagination), but even long, yes, many years thereafter, until the end of our lives, yes, always and eternally (which happens through the memory). We shall speak of both in the following discourse; and first of the phantasy.

<margin>What the phantasy is.</margin>
The phantasy is an internal sense and power of man, through which man can vividly bring before himself those things which he has perceived through his outward senses, perceiving and distinguishing them; and moreover, he is powerful enough, from those things which he formerly had before his outward senses, to form, to create, and to bring before himself such things as never were, shall be, nor can be according to the common course of nature, or experience and law.

<margin>The phantasy has two workings distinct from the common sense.
1. That it holds fast and presents to itself things that are now gone from the outward senses.</margin>
So that the phantasy has a twofold working, distinct from the common sense. First, that it holds fast those things which are now out of the sight or out of the other outward senses, and will not let them go, but causes them to remain there constantly, and represents them and brings them forward. As for example: I have seen a man there; he passes me by and goes into another street; as long as I see him, my eye, with the help of the common sense, has a perception of that man; but when he is now out of sight and has turned into another street, I would lose all perception of that man, were it not for the phantasy and the power of imagination; which not only receives the image when the thing is before the eyes, but also knows how to represent it firmly when the thing itself is out of sight: so likewise of mu-

The wonder of this power reveals itself also in its lack of temperance, and when it is disturbed, as one sees in many melancholic persons <note>referring to the "four humors" theory where an excess of black bile caused depression or delusions</note>, who tend to be very fantastical, each according to where the humor leads him; some being in such anxieties as if they were already cast into the abyss of hell; and others being as rejoiced as if they were raised into heaven, all this yet only through mere fantasy. Thus there have been found those who, through their fantasy, have imagined that every ship that came into the harbor was theirs, and rejoiced no less over it than the owner himself: others have imagined that they were made entirely of glass.

<column-break/>

In short, it would be endless to reckon up all the wonderful things which this fantasy has sometimes produced.

Whereby, just as its irregularity is known, so also is its wonder; and one can also conclude from this that since this power brings forth such wonderful, great, and terrible things when it is disturbed, that certainly the same power, when well-ordered, must also be very wonderful. There are trivial things, like a straw, a stubble, or the like, which, whether they are ordered or disturbed, cannot bring forth much wonder. It must then be something wonderful in itself, which knows how to bring forth such wonderful things even when it is disturbed.

<margin>Likewise also from dreams.</margin>
Now the wonder of this fantasy appears further in dreams. For when man's outward senses are all as if bound up by sleep, the fantasy nonetheless cannot rest, which often still plays very wonderfully and brings forth strange and very rare forms; therefore we are accustomed to say, when a matter appears very wonderful and strange to us: "it seemed to me to be a dream; it is merely a fantasy." Indeed, this power is also in some respect like unto God; it knows how to make all things present, even the past and the future. # Adam, Righteous,

### The convenience of the power of the imagination.

<margin>The convenience of the imagination; what [it is]</margin>
The convenience of this power is very great; for by the help of the imagination, our affections are stirred, and we are also helped to invent things, and to perform all our outward works well.

<margin>1. Through it we take to heart matters of weight that are not before our outward senses.</margin>
1. See, by the help of the imagination we are accustomed to still take to heart and to contemplate those things which are of weighty and necessary concern, which we otherwise would in no way take to heart since they are not always before our outward senses. For it goes with us as our proverb says: "out of sight, out of heart" <note>The Dutch "uyt der oogen uyt der herten" is equivalent to the English "out of sight, out of mind."</note>; for the imagination (as we have heard more) holds fast the image of things which are now gone, and are no longer before the outward senses; and so subsequently our heart is still moved thereby, and we are stirred; which (if we did not have this power of imagination) would not be stirred over anything that is not before our eyes; for then it would also immediately be out of our mind and out of our thoughts, which is now

<column-break/>

fulfilled through the imagination.

Thus we find that Nehemiah, hearing only how piteously it stood with the remnant in the Land of Judah, took that very much to heart and was moved thereby; representing vividly to himself through the power of imagination the piteous state of God's people there. Nehemiah 1 and 2.

Thus a youth, who has seen there the pleasantness of his beloved and has been moved thereby to seek her good, still keeps that pleasantness in his thoughts even when she is away, and subsequently contemplates her affairs and her welfare beyond measure.

<margin>2. Through it we also invent all beautiful arts.</margin>
2. Secondly, through the help of the imagination, all the beautiful arts and works that we see men produce are invented and wrought; and in this regard the imagination is very useful, yes, entirely necessary to man's life and sustenance.

For man, holding fast the images of things through the imagination, is helped thereby to do all fine things, and even to invent new ones. It is through the imagination that the little birds know how to make their little nests, and the beasts <note>original: "bossen," likely referring to forest creatures</note> to choose out their hollows; through it also it is that men know how to be helped to make the houses in which they dwell; and all craftsmen <term>ambachts-luyden: skilled manual laborers or artisans</term> do their trade-work by the help of the imagination. Thus a shoemaker makes his shoes, though he has no shoes before his eyes; for he has the fashion <note>the shape or design</note> in his imagination: so a tailor, a skillful Painter, a Goldsmith [do] all that handsome and wonderful work, which we have explained above,
