# Deformations and Reformations

Everything that humans have made or created, they do so through the aid of the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasie"</note>. It is by the help of the imagination that the pen of a swift writer so readily and so surely expresses the **image** <note>original: "verbeeldinghe"</note> of the letters upon the paper; for a human would not be capable of doing this if he had not first expressed the same in his brain through the help of the imagination, although it is impossible for us to explain how such a thing might occur.

Through this, new arts are also invented; namely, when a human—by representing all kinds of images which he knows how to skillfully create within himself through the imagination—casts things into all forms: the colors white, black, red, mixed thus and so; the sizes, breadths, lengths, and depths extended this way and that; and in strokes, the smell and the taste, struck together in various ways. From this, he then presents to himself such a rarity of new works and things. See, through this, the invented arts are perfected, or yet new ones are invented for the convenience of the children of men.

And, because we have heard that the imagination knows how to imagine not only massive and physical things, but also those which concern the understanding; it can imagine new forms of **Republics** <note>original: "Republijcken," referring to organized states or commonwealths</note>, new governments of lands, cities, and households. Thus, the human is also helped and moved by the imagination to strive for and seek to introduce this or that form which he has envisioned for himself. We shall say no more here; for the judging of which would be best, and the inventing of good

<column-break/>

forms of **Government**, properly belongs to the understanding.

<margin>3. Through this we are helped to walk prudently in many things and to prevent much misfortune.</margin>

3. Through the help of the imagination, the human is helped to walk prudently in many things and to prevent much misfortune; namely, when he knows how to vividly represent to himself that this or that business, such joy or sorrow, such pleasure or pain, is accustomed to bring about certain results. Having a vivid image of this within himself, he is subsequently moved and set in motion to see to it that he might obtain the pleasurable and avoid the painful.

<margin>The usefulness of the imagination is clearly perceived when one observes those who have a corrupted imagination.</margin>

But the great usefulness of this inward sense, the imagination, is perceived even more closely when one observes how it stands with those who are **vitiated** <note>original: "ghevitiëert," meaning impaired or corrupted</note> and corrupted in their imagination. How dull, how stubborn, how uncivil, how unfit are such people found to be for all kinds of dealings in human life? What wrong turns and reaches do they bring forth? How droll, how unseemly is their conduct? How difficult it is to somehow settle them and make them ready for any good exercises or manners? What a fuss, what trouble one has in a household, in a family, where such a person is!

Namely, when this powerful force of the soul is unbound, broken loose, and set out of order; what is there to be done with such a person? And when it goes to extremes, are such people not much worse to govern than the wild beasts of the field themselves? This is seen in **maniacs** <note>original: "dollupsen," referring to those suffering from acute madness or frenzy</note>. For indeed, most of the confusion that mad people cause arises from the fact that their imagination is wounded.

# Adam, Upright

That their common sense is disturbed, or that their memory is gone, might simply make them weak and simple, and in their speech like the innocent or like children; but that the imagination <note>original: "phantasie"; in this context, it refers to the mental faculty of forming images, not mere whimsy</note> is disturbed—from that comes what we call madness <note>original: "dollicheyt"</note>, all those wicked, evil blows, because of which people must be tied down, locked up, and kept in the dark: and then we say that their little senses are wandering, though they have all five of their outward senses perfectly well, but the imagination in them is singularly disturbed.

Thus we may now to some extent perceive the wonder and usefulness of this power of imagination; so also can everyone quickly become aware, if they only wish, that they have also received in their head from God the power of imagination, which is such a wonderful and useful power: for take note, can you not, when you wish, still hold fast and reflect upon the image of such a person who has passed you by: of such or such things that you have seen, heard, smelled, tasted, or felt there? Do you not have the power, when you wish, through the help of the imagination, to make appear before you to some extent the joy of Heaven, the pain of Hell, of which you have often heard spoken or preached? Can you not, when you wish, go and represent to yourself all such things as please you; beasts with seven heads, horses with wings, chests full of money, such or such costly clothes, precious stones, even if they are not at hand, even if you have never seen such things? Do you not nonetheless know, one better than the other, how to bring forth this or that convenience through the joining and fitting together of things, which did not exist before? Experience teaches this irreducibly.

<column-break/>

->The end for which God gave man<-
->the power of imagination.<-

So then every human has also received these noble gifts from God; it now remains to be seen to what end he has received this noble gift so singularly from God; beyond what we have indicated above regarding the usefulness of this power—which is also a general and natural end for which God the Lord gave the children of men this power, yes, even to the beasts of the field—so there is a singular and spiritual end for which this power was created in us by God, namely, so that we should be led thereby, according to the nature of this power, to the knowledge, the love, and the fear of God.

<margin>
This imagination is given to men so that he might be more led thereby to the knowledge, love, fear, and service of God.
</margin>

For let us note this here, which must be remembered everywhere, both what has been said before and what shall yet be said hereafter concerning the powers that God the Lord has given to men: all those powers that God the Lord has given to man are primarily given to him so that he, through the wonder and usefulness thereof, should be more and more led to the knowledge, the love, the fear, and the service of God the Creator, who created the power within him.

And consequently, our powers are only in their right form and in good condition when they lead us to that end, and are directed by us toward it, namely to the knowledge, love, fear, and service of God, who gave them to us: when they lead us there, and we apply them to that, then all is well.

So then also this power of imagination was given to us by the Lord for this purpose—

# Misshapen, Reshaped.

once had its seat in the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasie"; in the 17th century, this referred to the mental faculty that forms images and thoughts</note> of man; there it was well received; there it was nurtured; there it was dressed up; there it began to take its shape; there it received an eye; the imagination had to set it forward, so that it might have a form.
  The imagination of man is like a **watermill**, which not only can grind continuously, but also always grinds; and whatever is thrown into it, it grinds into dust; it makes it ready to produce some works from it. Indeed, the Lord disposes the affairs of the children of men such that none go free; or rather, just as they have all misused the noble power of their thoughts, so they all have—at one time or another, indeed some every day, though one more than another—things coming into their mind and thoughts that they would rather see otherwise, which beset and plague them, and by which their imagination is restless and tormented. And all this happens to the corrupt children of men in this way—although they think little of it—because they themselves have so often and frequently so miserably misused that noble power of their imagination for sin and vanity. What is then more righteous with God than that He should visit such people again in that same power? And since the Lord God does not get His will from man regarding the use of that noble power, is it not very just that men, in turn, should also not have their will over it?

So also these are but the beginnings of sorrow and the precursors of greater plagues; for this is certain and sure: if man does not bethink himself better in time, eternal heartache and eternal grief shall come upon him, which shall properly entangle his imagination and inflict all horrible pains and sorrows.

### CHAPTER XXIII.

->Of the Memory.<-

Until now we have heard how it stands with the imagination <note>original: "phantasie"</note>, through which we hold fast or bring before us things that are no longer present before the external senses. Now it follows that we speak of the memory; which is a very worthy servant to the imagination, serving the imagination as a tablet-book <note>A "tafel boecsken" refers to a small notebook or wax tablet used for quick jottings.</note>, in which are already firmly marked all those things which have been perceived by the external senses, or have been further formed by the imagination itself; and in which yet further things can be marked, as many things as man might perceive with his external senses, or form through his imagination itself, or even comprehend with his noble understanding; for the memory is serviceable to all of these.

<margin>What the memory is.</margin> So that the memory is an internal sense, which receives into itself the representation <note>original: "verbeeldinghe"</note> of all those things that we perceive with our external senses—seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, feeling—and further those things we have brought to mind or otherwise formed and created through our imagination, or that we have in any way comprehended and noted through our understanding; to hold all that fast, and at any time when there is occasion to take knowledge of it, to raise it up and bring it forth, is the work of the memory.

<column-break/>

->The Objects of the Memory.<-

<margin>The objects presented to the memory.</margin> Thus the objects presented to the memory consist of these three things:

1. In all that which one has perceived and grasped with the external senses, by help of the common sense <note>The "common sense" (sensus communis) was historically believed to be the faculty that unified the data from the five individual senses.</note>, such as what has been preached or spoken, etc.

2. In all that which the imagination has further formed and made itself out of particular things; as for example, Painters and Poets lie on their beds in the dark and think up strange, unheard-of, foreign things; well, their memory works upon those, holds them fast, and has them ready to bring forth when the Painter has risen and—after other things he has done—is now ready to go and draw them with his brush, or the Poet to express them with his pen.

3. In all that which the understanding of man comprehends or grasps, such as the things of the Kingdom of God, the government of the world, such and such excellent counsels, decisions, advices, etc.

->The Manner of the Memory's Operation.<-

<margin>The manner in which the memory holds things fast.</margin> Now the manner in which the memory comes to hold all these things fast, and to have them ready for when one might have need of them, is this:

The things that we grasp with our external senses—seeing, hearing, etc.—give off from themselves (as explained above regarding the nature of the senses in general) a representation of themselves, which representation makes an impression in the organ <note>original: "wercktuygh," literally "work-tool" or instrument</note> of the memory, so that a counter-impression and a footprint remains (like a seal that is pressed upon wax), and that stands there firmly ready, to raise it—

<meta>catchword: raise it—</meta>

How this further occurs, and is hindered, cannot be well grasped nor expressed; but that such a thing happens cannot be denied. For it would otherwise not be possible that one should remember anything, if those things which one has understood through the sense of the imagination <note>original: "phantaſie"; in 17th-century psychology, this refers to the faculty that forms mental images</note> or the intellect did not leave something behind in the soul, and in that vessel which we call the memory, which is ready to show itself again even if the matter which we had grasped with our senses is gone and no longer in existence. Like the words in the sermon which we hear delivered: they are finished, they are gone. The wedding which we saw held, or the feast, that is over, it is no more; nevertheless, an impression of it is left behind in our soul, through which we can represent the same to ourselves. So that the memory is to man like a prison <note>used here in the sense of a secure storehouse or chamber</note> in which the soul firmly lays up all such things as it will hereafter wish to have come before it, to examine, and thus to leave or keep as evil or good; and to reject or to use. The memory is indeed like the Office of the Lords States <note>original: "Cantoōr der Heeren Staten"; a reference to the administrative offices of the Dutch government, implying a highly organized archive</note> where notes are kept of all the business that occurs there in that little world, the human being; where the senses have been set, one may go to look up and read, and there bind it all up faithfully again, if only the memory faithfully does its own work.

By this we can now partly perceive the wondrousness and also the convenience of the memory. But we shall nevertheless reveal both of these somewhat more closely.

<column-break/>

<margin>The wondrousness of the memory. From its vastness.</margin>
THE wondrousness of the memory is singularly situated, and reveals itself in two things.

First, in the vastness, great comprehension, and exceeding roominess of this vessel of the memory; namely, that it is powerful enough to receive and lodge so many, yes, so many thousands and thousands of various kinds of things within itself, giving each its spacious place, to bring them forth at any time.

The receiving into the memory and lodging there means that we remember everything that we have seen and deemed worthy of remembering, such as so many cities, lands, houses, people, spectacles, and wonderful works; or have heard, such as so many instructions, admonitions, lovely or harsh speeches; and also what we have smelled, tasted, felt, even what we have devised through our imagination or understood with our intellect—that, and all of that, is lodged and laid up in the memory.

Consider then for once what a wondrously large, spacious vessel the memory must be, in which all those things lie lodged and laid up: whole cities, landscapes, mountains, valleys, rivers, seas, waters, ships; Paris, London (if you have been there), Amsterdam, Antwerp, all the streets, the houses, the fashions, the shapes thereof; and all that you have further seen, and all that you have heard, smelled, tasted, felt, suspected, and understood; that, and all of that, lies there all orderly, each in its place, gathered together in that vessel of the memory. -># Adam, Righteous<-

...miraculous vessel, in which everything rests as one. <margin>From the firm holding of all those things which she receives.</margin>
Indeed, truly, what a miraculous mirror this is: which can not only receive within itself all the aforementioned images, but knows how to hold them fast; so that they remain there, and do not depart, but are always there ready at hand to show themselves; even when the things themselves are gone, the **memory** still has her image fresh and new.

The common **mirrors** which we use are wonderful things, were it not that we were so accustomed to them and had them so commonly here; we would come to marvel at them in the highest degree if we were to see them for the first time; just as it is found that those peoples who do not yet have the instruments of mirrors were astonished by them in the highest degree, and were very much taken with them when they were first brought to them.

But what are our common mirrors compared to this mirror of the memory? Which not only receives all kinds of images while the things are before her, as our mirrors do; but (which should be well noted) holds the images fast, as if they were beautifully painted to the life upon a **panel** <note>original: "tafelreel," referring to a painting on a wooden board</note>; even when the things are now gone, are not present, yes, sometimes are no longer in existence, yet the memory still holds

<column-break/>

her images within herself, which is truly miraculous. If someone could make themselves a mirror which would hold fast all the images of the things that were placed before it, what admiration would that arouse? But such a thing is not possible to be made by the hand of man. Thus, this mirror of the memory is such an artistic masterpiece that it necessarily draws us up (if we pay proper attention to it) to the knowledge and acknowledgment of the Most High and only wise God.

<margin>From the order that is within the memory.</margin>
But that which further and more closely discovers the miraculous nature of this artistic Mirror (which truly could be made by none but the all-wise hand of the great God) is the good **order** which is kept by the memory in the lodging and storing of all these things. One might reasonably think, hearing of so very many diverse, changeable, and all sorts of things—of every kind and nature, all sorts of colors, sounds, smells, tastes, feelings, and yet a thousandfold imaginary things of the fantasy, and all kinds of things of weight, arts, sciences, lessons, instructions, customs—that all these being stored in one vessel, would lie there very confusedly through one another; but it is not so. They all lie there in that great vessel of the memory without confusion, without entanglement, each in its place, each in its order, each ready and prepared at hand to be brought forth without mixing with the others. And thus we may well speak of distinct places, of little drawers; for experience teaches that a Shopkeeper, if he does not have his particular places for each thing, everything lies there all tangled, and there is no managing it; more time is lost in searching than in any other work one has to do. Think, if in an Apothecary's shop all his things, his herbs, were not each in their particular place, but were all thrown together, would he not have a great deal of trouble before he could pick out what each customer needed? ## CHAPTER XXIV.

### Concerning the condition of memory, before, in, and after the fall.

NOW it follows that we go to look into how the same was created by God the Lord; how it has been situated since the fall; and how we might get it improved?

### Concerning the righteousness of memory before the fall.

<margin>The condition of memory in the first creation.</margin>
As regards the first, the memory of man was certainly created very good and holy in the first creation; even so that man, through the help of his memory, was able to hold fast all memorable things, and keep them well, in order to be promoted more and more in the knowledge, love, fear, and service of God through the remembering of the same, just as we see that the whole man was created righteous, Ecclesiastes 7:29. So that we must hold it to be so, that man's memory in the beginning would have given him all kinds of help toward the promotion of the fear and the love of God in man.

### Concerning the corruption of memory through and under the fall.

<margin>The condition of memory after the fall.</margin>
But alas, it does not stand thus now with the memory of poor fallen man; since man cast out of his esteem the commandment of his God and went and forgot the faithful counsel, and all the good that the Lord had done for him, so is his memory also quite miserably violated. This glorious, excellent, miraculous, and distinguished vessel has been greatly broken and damaged by the fall; manifold confusions and injustices have come over it, in such a way that not only is the power of memory greatly weakened, and this worthy vessel as if split and torn, so that

This shall cause us to easily forget the evil and well remember the good. We see that children do not remember many things, because they do not take many things to heart. Old people also forget many things, the reason for which, among others, is also this: that their heart is no longer so set upon them. For otherwise we see that old folk—however poorly it may stand with their memory—always know well enough how to remember where they have buried their treasure, upon which their heart is set; that they shall never forget.

This is also seen very clearly in Divine things. There is a simple person who is far surpassed in the power of memory by those of quick and clever intellects, who nevertheless carries away more from a Sermon <note>original: "Predicatie"</note> and knows how to recount more than those who are worldly-wise. And this is because these godly ones take the matters of God to heart; they esteem God's word greatly; they hold it for the nourishment of their souls, and so they preserve it with the utmost diligence. But the others do not take it to heart. If something is said to us there that we do not take to heart, we have hardly gone a street's length before it goes out of our mind, and it never occurs to us again in all our days. But on the contrary, let something be said to us in which our heart is invested—such as that our ship has been lost, or our beloved has died—that stays with us; we cannot forget it. And the reason for this is that, as we have heard, we remember things

<column-break/>

in this manner: that the images of things make deep impressions in our souls, and so leave the footprints and forms of them within us, even when the things are gone; and so we still hold them fast as if seeing or hearing them. When we then take a matter to heart, the things make a deep impression in our soul and remain lying there firmly; but if we do not take them to heart, they make only a superficial impression and soon vanish.

And this is the reason that we remember wicked and idle things much better; because we are much more moved by them—they tickle our heart more and consequently make deep impressions. Therefore, regarding what we say or the excuses we make about the defect of our memory in remembering spiritual things: the fault lies largely in the fact that we do not take them to heart. Therefore the Apostle, admonishing the Hebrews that they should strengthen themselves to hold fast what they had learned, and that they should not let it slip away <note>A reference to Hebrews 2:1, often translated as "let them slip" or "drift away."</note>, also testifies to them that the neglect of Divine things shall be heavily punished. By this he gives us sufficiently to understand that neglect is the entire cause of forgetfulness (Hebrews 2:1-2).

## CHAPTER XXV.
### On the power of desiring and of shunning.

UNTIL now we have spoken at length both of the outward and the inward senses; now it follows that we speak of the power of desiring and shunning, which is set in motion by the operation of the aforementioned senses.
For whatever man finds pleasant, sweet, and lovely through his senses, for that he conceives a lust and desire; whatever he finds unpleasant, that he rejects, and conceives a loathing against it. As for example, toward that which tastes well, smells well, strokes sweetly, or presents and offers itself inwardly through the imagination <term>phantasie: the faculty of forming mental images</term> as charming and attractive, for that man conceives a desire; whatever on the contrary tastes ill, smells ill, scrapes harshly, or presents itself inwardly through the imagination as foul, ugly, and deformed,

<column-break/>

for that he conceives an aversion.
<margin>
What the power of desiring and shunning is.
</margin>
Now the power of desiring and shunning is that power of the soul through which man is set in motion to move himself, to incline, and to reach out toward that which the previously discussed senses of man judge to be good and profitable for man; and on the contrary to turn away and avert himself from that which the same judge to be evil and shameful.

### On the objects of the power of desiring and shunning.

<margin>
What the objects of those powers are.
</margin>
SO then this power has for its object everything that falls under the senses of man, outward and inward; all things whatever man sees, hears, smells, tastes, feels, or knows how to think upon—concerning that, and all that, this power busies itself, to desire it or to reject it, according as it presents itself as good or evil.
And it matters not here whether the thing that presents itself is truly good or truly evil, or whether it is so only in appearance and in the opinion of man. For opinion and truth, appearance and being, count for the same here with this power; man desires as earnestly that which he firmly holds for good, even if it be evil, as that which is in fact good. Thus Eve desired the fruit of the forbidden Tree as much as if it had been in fact good for her to eat, because she held it to be so; whereas nevertheless the same was in truth very evil for her to eat of.
And from this it now comes that although everything that falls under the senses of man is the presented object of these powers of desiring and shunning; yet nevertheless every man is not accustomed to desire or shun the same things; for to...

Since in this life things do not always go—as we hope—according to truth (which is always simple and consistent), but also according to opinion and appearance; so it happens here that every human being, according to their disposition, opinion, and imagination, desires one thing and shuns another. In such a way that what tastes good to one, may not to another; what one flees from, another seeks; or indeed, what one greatly desires, another desires but little. Yes, the very same person, according as they perceive, retain, and observe things differently at different times, sometimes desires that which they previously rejected, and shuns that which they previously desired. As is evident in the case of Amnon in 2 Samuel 13:15 <note>Amnon’s intense "love" for Tamar instantly turned to intense hatred after he forced her.</note>. So we used to desire and follow different things when we became youths than we desired and followed when we were merely children; to this end serves what the Apostle says: *When I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child; but when I became a man, I put away childish things,* 1 Corinthians 13:11.

So then, these powers have this in common: that through them all people desire what seems good to them, and conversely reject what does not seem good to them; yet each according to their own opinion and imagination. One takes more pleasure in this, another in that. One is led by the throat <note>i.e., by gluttony or appetite</note> and sets everything upon feasting and carousing; another by the ear, and loves to be near music and talk; others by the eye, seeking beautiful paintings and flowers; others by smell; others by touch. Eagles seek the dead body <note>A reference to Matthew 24:28, "Wherever the carcass is, there the eagles will be gathered."</note>, but many other birds have a loathing for it; it does not agree with their character and nature to desire it or to eat of it. So likewise the born-again desire and seek the Lord Christ the Crucified; but the unregenerate, who are of a different character and nature, have an aversion to Him and seek something else.

### Concerning the usefulness of the power of desiring and shunning.

<margin>The power of desiring and shunning is also useful to man.</margin>Now it follows that we should also speak somewhat of the **usefulness** <note>original: "gerieffelĳckheydt"; refers to the practical benefit or convenience of these faculties</note> of these powers; the same is also very great. For through these powers it is that man is set in motion to chase after and obtain that which is good and useful for the well-being of man; and on the contrary, to shun and avoid that which is evil and harmful to man.

For, just as we have now heard that man perceives through the senses what is good and profitable for him, so through this power he desires it, and whatever is against him, he rejects. From this it follows that these powers, being so diligently served by all the other powers as

<column-break/>

we have now explained; man subsequently pursues with all his powers that which might do him good, and flees that which might harm him; which everyone can sufficiently observe to be in the highest degree not only useful, but necessary for his maintenance. We see this in little children themselves, who are stirred up by the desire for milk to cry for it, and so they get the full breast; through the aversion to pain they are also stirred up, when they are pricked by some pin or otherwise, to fret and cry over it, and are thus helped against it.

Were it not for the strength of this desire and aversion, man would be almost as immovable as a block of wood; whatever he saw or heard, if he did not desire or reject it, he would let it all go **at sixes and sevens** <note>original: "voor ses en seven"; an idiom meaning to let things fall into disorder or neglect</note> (as they say) and it would be all the same to him whether he were alive or dead; whether he were empty or full; wounded or whole. Whereas now, on the contrary, man is set in motion by desire and aversion to avoid that which is harmful to him and to chase after that which is beneficial to him.

And even though it is true that, as man is currently situated, man often very earnestly desires many things that are very harmful to him; and on the contrary avoids and flees some things that would be wonderfully good for him: that is an **abuse** of these powers; they do not cease to be useful in themselves when they are rightly used and directed.

# Adam, Upright

->**The powers of man stand ready**<-

What has caused you people to come to Church so early in this cold frost and wintry day, while others have remained lying in their warm beds, other than the desire that you have for God, His house, and Word, and for the assembly of the believers? That is what "made your legs," as the saying goes. <note>The author uses a Dutch idiom implying that desire provides the physical energy for action.</note>

The desire itself, which lay there quietly, is first—as we have now explained—awakened and set in motion by that which the outward and inward senses present to the person, and either praise or condemn. But once it has been stirred and awakened, this desire is like a master commander over all the types and powers of the soul; she causes them to arise and show themselves. She is like a field general; she puts them in battle array, she makes them march and depart toward that which she is set upon. And she herself, who was first awakened by the senses, being now set in motion, puts the senses themselves to work like pressed soldiers <note>term: "pressed soldiers" refers to conscripts or those forced into military service</note>; so that now the eye must look sharply, the ear must listen quickly to obtain that which the desire is set upon. And what is more, she awakens yet other powers of the soul and takes those also into her service, such as all those affects, passions, and inclinations of man, which—though they truly exist in this "little world" <note>term: "little world" (microcosm), a common Renaissance and Early Modern concept of the human being as a miniature version of the universe</note> of man—nevertheless keep themselves quiet and do not go to war, except when they are pressed and called up to it by this desire.

Whoever considers all this properly and with understanding, who does not then immediately see that truly this

<column-break/>

desire is a wonderful power within man. We hear of some Princes who have that power and authority over their subjects, that they may press them and make them march to war with them; we consider it a very great authority, as indeed it is. But the matter stands thus: those Princes and Kings who have such power and authority can indeed force their subjects to march with them, but they cannot make them *willing* to do so; they also cannot change their hearts so that what they must do, they might also do gladly. And it would be of even greater advantage to them if they also had that power.

Now, this power of desire has both; she has the power to press and to make all the powers of this "little world" march with her as a single man, and she can also immediately make them entirely willing and inclined. All those powers that she presses and forces to march with her, she also makes willing; they all march gladly. It would grieve them if they had to sit still. If there is any power which, through illness or accident, cannot properly bend itself to the execution of that to which the desire calls it, that power clings to it; it even torments itself because it cannot put itself to work along with the rest.

And even if the expedition to which the desire presses the powers of man—both of the soul and of the body—is very difficult in itself, nevertheless all the powers set themselves willingly to work: if they must break their sleep, and rise early for it...

### Concerning the usefulness of the power of desiring and shunning.

<margin>

Whereas now, on the contrary, man is set in motion by desire and aversion to avoid that which is harmful to him and to chase after that which is advantageous to him.

And even though it is true that, as man is currently situated, he often very earnestly desires many things that are very harmful to him; and on the other hand avoids and flees some things that would be wonderfully good for him: that is a **misuse** of these powers. They do not, because of that, cease to be useful in themselves, when they are rightly used and guided.

# Adam in Righteousness

Indeed, in all cases, when man recognizes a matter as good and worthy of pursuit, desire is again very useful to him in this instance, so that through it he knows how to awaken and set in motion all his powers.

And behold, this is the occasion, the character, and nature, the wonder and the usefulness of desire. We have all received these powers; we daily perceive all that we desire and loathe: thus we have received these noble gifts from God; this wonderful and useful power is also given to us; so we shall also have to give an account of this <term>Talent</term> <note>A reference to the Biblical Parable of the Talents, implying that natural faculties are gifts to be invested for God's glory.</note>. Let us now properly inquire to what end this power was given to us by God our Creator.

### The end for which God gave man the powers of desiring and shunning.

<margin>
This power of desire is given to man to desire all those things that lead him to God; and to shun those things that lead him away from God.
</margin>

The end for which this power of desiring and shunning was given to man is so that man, through this power, might relish, long for, and desire all those things, gifts, and means which might help him further and further toward the knowledge, love, fear, and service of his God and Creator; and would, on the other hand, recoil from and loathe all such things, parties, and ways as might lead him away from God; and that in such a manner and measure, that what leads him most to God, he would desire most; and what leads most away from God, he would most resist and loathe. See 1 Corinthians 12:31 and 14:1.

Yes, even more: so that man would do all this with delight and pleasure, with all dignity and alertness. For this we know, and experience teaches us, that that which

<column-break/>

the desire is set upon, one follows with pleasure and delight; just as Jacob served Laban for seven years for Rachel with pleasure, because his desire was set upon her. Genesis 29:20. See Psalm 119:40, 47, 48. So that man, with an untiring delight, might always cling to and serve the Lord his God. 1 Corinthians 7:35. To this end also was this power placed in man; just as God the Lord, on the grounds that He has given this gift to man, requires of him that he should serve Him with joy and delight of heart. Deuteronomy 28:47, 48.

From all of which it then also appears that desire, just as it is a power of the soul, is not evil, but very good; therefore the godly often boast that they have desired this or that; it is indeed often taken in the Scriptures for "evil lust," but that is because it is not directed toward that for which it was placed in man.

# Deformities, Reformed.

The [faculties of desire] were well-guided by the information of the senses and the higher powers, and were also obedient to them; so that these powers were very faithful and entirely diligent servants to man, ready and watchful for all that was truly good, and turned away from that which was truly evil; also maintaining proper proportion and measure in all things. # Adam, Upright

We have previously heard that there is such great power in man that it holds all human faculties under its will and command; yet since the Fall, it has become the most reckless and unrestrained force in man that can be imagined. It is like the blind Samson <note>A reference to the biblical judge Samson, who was physically powerful but spiritually and mentally blinded, eventually destroying himself and his enemies.</note>, full of strength, but also full of recklessness.

And although this power is somewhat more restrained in some, and breaks out more hatefully in others—depending on the particular temperament of the body, the education of one's life, the circumstances of affairs, or the guidance of the Spirit—it is nevertheless in all natural men without measure and without rule. One is led by the lust of the eyes and has set his heart on a lump of gold, or is infatuated with a beautiful face, or something else. Another is led by the lust of the flesh and is always out for a life of luxury, carnal pleasures, and all kinds of worldly delights and enjoyments. There are also those who are entirely taken up with the pride of life, with high contemplations, studies, and speculations; these are driven by the desire for high status and offices, for honor and reputation. All of this is so far beyond all proper measure and rule that they become mere slaves to their own desire, and are thereby led into all kinds of foul and contemptible work.

1. Either on evil things.

1. **Disorderly**: Truly, we maintain no right proportion between the various things we desire; between Heaven and Earth; Christ and the world; God and ourselves. The earthly, worldly, and physical things we desire earnestly with a burning passion; whereas the Heavenly, Christian, and Divine things we desire only faintly and weakly. What proportion is here? Indeed, our desires for Heavenly goods are never in any way proportioned to the weightiness of those very things; yet we are quite capable of desiring something earnestly. Thus, the very earnestness of desire that we apply to earthly things shall shame us in the judgment; for we desire most what should be desired least. We contemplate earthly and carnal things above the Heavenly, and seek the earth while pushing Christ to one side. This is a great disorder in desire, even if there were no excess in the desiring of earthly things, and even if we could do so "like a Philosopher" <note>original: "op sijn Philosoophs"; referring to the Stoic or academic ideal of rational moderation.</note> with reasonable temperance. Isaiah 55:2-3.

To this also belong false desires: namely, that we desire many things that we do not need, and which can do us no good. Indeed, we desire things that are very harmful to us, which might utterly destroy us.

# Deformed, Reformed.

It is truly a matter of great lamentation that this noble power—which is of such vast scope and potential, and was given to man by God for his greatest benefit—is now being employed so entirely for the worst ends.

God the Lord had given man, as we have now heard, this power of desire <note>original: "begeeren"</note> so that he might use it to desire above all the things of God, the welfare of God’s people, and all spiritual gifts; so that this great vessel of desire might be like a holy womb and matrix to receive the good seed of the Good Spirit, and subsequently to bring forth all kinds of good fruit with great delight and joy. Man, on the contrary, has misused and diverted it, using it to desire evil, base, idle, sinful, and abominable things which were forbidden and denied to him by God. And so this noble gift is turned into a foul vessel of Satan, into which he shoots his evil seed, and through which he brings forth many horrors and monsters. Shall this not bring a very heavy reckoning against us poor humans on the great Day of Judgment, since we are entirely faithless servants in this matter? If we had merely laid this precious talent away in a handkerchief <note>A reference to the Parable of the Talents in Luke 19:20</note>, our guilt would already be great; we would indeed be worthy to be bound hand and foot and cast into the outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth. But now we have made it even worse; we have not only uselessly laid this precious talent aside, but we have shamefully misused it against the Lord our God and Creator Himself. How great must our guilt now be? How shall

<column-break/>

we ever be able to answer for this in eternity, if we do not amend it in time?

### Of the reformation of the power of desiring and eschewing through Christ.

<margin>Therefore we must all strive to have the power of our desire improved.</margin>

Therefore, all the preceding discourse must especially serve to awaken us and set us in motion, so that we may strive and endeavor with all our might and to our utmost ability to bring this power of desire into a better state. Much depends on this for us; our very life hangs upon it. It withers our natural strengths if it is not moderated, and it takes away the spiritual life almost entirely. We are certainly ruined and corrupted to the core forever and eternally if we do not get our desire amended. But on the other hand, if we can get this power of desire improved and fixed upon its rightful objects, we shall thereby have won over almost all our powers and all our members; God will help us, and we shall be well. We shall then also be delivered from all that vexatious trouble which our untempered desires so miserably provoke. Conversely, being rightly ordered in our desires, we shall also obtain them, which will then be to us as a tree of life (Proverbs 13:12 and 19). For man has no greater delight than when his desire is fulfilled; and therefore the unregenerate man, who is led by unruly desire, is very miserable. Nay, what is more, we shall perform the work of God with delight if we can once get our desire fixed upon it: for what we do with a lust and desire, we do with pleasure; then also shall this power of

### CHAPTER XXVII.
->Concerning the Affections.<-

Irrational animals have nothing with which they can restrain or redirect their desires; however, for this purpose, humans have their **affections** <note>original: "affecten"; refers to the emotions or passions of the soul</note>; and when these are but weak, they are usually little able to restrain their desires, except by the will alone. Therefore, it is a useful thing for the restraint of evil desires to have strong affections toward the good: for the affections are like winds, which either make the ship go forward well, or hold it back, or turn it about; and they are given to us so that we should set them upon divine things. Thus, no contemplations can be regarded as established virtues <note>original: "doughtden"</note> in us, unless—proceeding from the knowledge of our understanding and the resolution of our will—they take a place in the affections of our hearts. So it is with man, who consists of soul and body, that even if he understood something thoroughly and distinctly, and earnestly desired it, he would nevertheless stand there firm and still, like a tree in its roots, if there were no other power in man through which the desire might work outward and make the man move externally.

Thus the Lord God has given man two active powers for this purpose, and that is—to speak thus—the **affections** and the **locomotive** <note>original: "locomotive"; the faculty of physical movement or self-motion</note> power, by which man is stirred, moved, and set going. The Affections move the inner man, or the heart, which being moved sets the locomotive power going, and through that power moves the outer man, and so everything is set in motion; and so things are sought out and

<column-break/>

brought to actual practice: and through these powers man—who otherwise until now is only inwardly active or busy in speculations <note>original: "speculatien"; theoretical or mental contemplation</note>—becomes also outwardly active.

<margin>What the affections are.</margin>
We shall now first speak of the first, that is, of the affections; which word we take here very broadly, and understand by it that power of the heart through which the heart can change itself, now this way, now that, according as the matter that comes before the heart requires; or through which the heart can receive within itself the representation <note>original: "verbeeldinghe"</note> of the things that come before the man, with such an impression that it does not only receive the bare representation, as the other powers (of which we have spoken until now) do; but receives moreover such a particular operation and working through the representation, that the heart itself works in feeling just as the thing—whose representation comes before the heart—is in deed and in truth, or at least appears to be such in deed and in truth. For in this matter of the affections, since the sorrowful fall of man which has confused everything, appearance and reality are of the same weight and operation.

In such a manner, the heart is bound by this power of the affections to be a true **Chameleon**, receiving all such colors, forms, and—what is more—even feelings, as the things that come before the heart have in truth or appearance within them; as for example, if something comes before a man that has within it the matter and material of joy, and it strikes the man, then the heart receives not only a bare and unfeeling speculation, a representation of joy; but it receives in deed, and in truth, and in

<margin>The nature and power of the affects.</margin>
From this it now appears that the nature of this power of the affects <note>term: "Affects" (Dutch: *affecten*) refers to what we would today call emotions, passions, or psychological impulses.</note> is to make such a sensible impression upon the heart of man—through those things which man has now perceived through his outward and inward senses—as the things possess in truth, or at least in appearance. If it is a joyful matter which man has perceived through his senses, it is the nature and work of this power of the Affects to make such a sensible, active impression of joy in the heart that the heart itself becomes joyful. If it is a terrifying matter in truth or in appearance, it is its nature to make such a sensible, active impression of terror in the heart that the heart itself is indeed and in truth terrified and made to tremble; and thus the heart is, as we say, like a Chameleon <note>The author uses the chameleon as a metaphor for the heart's ability to change its "color" or state based on its surroundings or perceptions.</note>.

To now better understand the nature and character of this power, we shall observe these four things regarding it: 1. The object presented. 2. The manner in which it occupies itself therewith. 3. The wonderousness. 4. The convenience of this power.

So it is that the affections and passions (of which so much is spoken in the Holy Scripture, and which we perceive in ourselves in all places and almost every moment, that they) mingle and involve themselves with all our conduct. In effect, they are nothing other than so many changes of our own heart, according to the circumstances of the things that come before a person. And it is a very wonderful thing that it is so with the heart, that it can receive such changes so speedily and also so sensibly; for see, it happens thus: a man goes on his way undisturbed and unmoved; there he meets a thoroughly beautiful, modest maiden, whom he begins to esteem highly; there-

<column-break/>

While he is in this meditation, this maiden falls and wounds herself severely; hereupon there arises in him great compassion for her misfortune. She, on the other hand, bears this very patiently and conducts herself very Christianly in this her mishap. When he notices this, being aware that he is not accustomed to behave so well or so Christianly in such or other misfortunes, there arises from this in him a holy emulation <note>original: "emulatie"; a righteous desire to imitate or match another's virtue</note> and a desire to follow her virtue.

And see, thus quickly and alertly is the human heart stirred and moved, and it receives all kinds of sensible impressions and receives, like a Chameleon, all those changes according to the circumstances of the things that come before it.

# Deformed, Reformed,

### On the wondrous nature of the passions.

<margin>
The wondrous nature and the power of the passions is evident from how the passions involve themselves with all things that are presented to us.
</margin>
THE wondrous nature of this power can be partly understood from what has already been said. We shall reveal it a bit further with a few words; and it is known from two observations.

First, from the fact that the heart can somehow, and knows how to, adapt itself to all things that happen to a person; yes, with everything that is in Heaven, on Earth, in the Sea, in all depths, and in Hell itself, and all that goes on there. See, our <term>passions</term><note>original: "affecten"; in the 17th century, this referred to strong emotions or "affections" that move the soul.</note> are like so many living, sensitive animals and creatures that lie there quietly, but listen very closely to everything that goes on around them, each of them being very ready to spring up and rouse themselves as soon as something occurs that resembles them, concerns them, or seems to come under their command or district. Is it not wondrous that the heart of man (which is laid so secretly in the bosom of man, and surrounded with so many covers, and as if coated with so many crusts, so that one would think that surely the heart of man could know or perceive nothing of anything) nevertheless busies itself so actively with everything, so that such a <term>busybody</term><note>original: "moeyal"; a person who meddles in everything.</note> as the heart is found to be through the working of the passions, is to be found nowhere else in the world? There is nothing in the world that concerns man, or the heart of man draws it in; it knows how to involve itself therein; yes, moreover, it also tends to involve itself and concern itself with things that truly do not concern the man in whom it resides; and not only with those things that are massive and weighty, but also with the occurrences and the circumstances of things.

<column-break/>

This is all wondrous and strange.
<margin>
2. From the wondrous nature of the manner of operation: namely, that man's heart is so powerfully moved only by the imagination of a thing.
</margin>
Secondly, from the manner in which this happens. That is also wondrous, and not easy to comprehend: namely, that the heart of man is so sensitively and violently moved to agitation only by the <term>imagination</term><note>original: "verbeeldinge"; here meaning the mental image or internal representation of a thing, rather than "fantasy."</note> of a thing, even when the thing itself does not yet reach the heart; and nevertheless the heart is moved and stirred not only in appearance, but in deed and in truth by the mere imagination of things, just as if one were fondling it in the loveliest way, or wounding and hurting it in the most cruel manner. As for example: the married woman sits there in great joy and luxury; she eats, drinks, and is of good cheer; but a harsh messenger comes upon her and brings her news that her ship with all the goods, and also her dear and worthy husband, has been lost and perished; this pierces her heart no less than if it were wounded with the point of a sword, and yet nothing comes to her but the imagination of the sorrowful things that are announced to her; she still sits in her luxury, among her friends, and no one does her harm, no one touches her; see here an example of this, <margin>Daniel 5:1-7; Acts 2:37.</margin> On the other side, the beauty of his bride does not reach the heart of the Bridegroom physically, yet his heart is thereby delighted, stroked, more kindly than anything that can be done to him externally. <margin>Song of Solomon 4:9.</margin>

That pleasure or torment comes to man from those things that touch his senses physically; as from the fact that he actually enjoys his dear bride, or that his body is pierced through with knives, or that he tastes what is flavorful to everyone, or what is very bitter and unpleasant...

# Adam, Upright,

It cannot seem so strange to a person; but that a person also receives such great pleasure or torment in his heart—indeed, much greater than through other external things—through the mere imagination of things, even though the things themselves do not reach his heart, that is truly, when one begins to notice it, entirely wonderful.

And even more especially, when one observes this alongside it: that not only does the pleasure and torment arising from this often far, far exceed all the pleasure and torment received through external touches; but moreover, that one receives just as true, certain, and sure pleasure or torment from the mere appearance of things that have no truth in them, provided we only hold them to be true. For instance, when it is falsely reported to us that our friends are there near the harbor, ready to land, healthy and well, it fills our heart with delight when we believe it, even though it often happens that they have all perished together on a sandbank; and so, on the contrary, if it is told to us, and so testified, that the ship with all our friends has perished, if we hold it to be true, it fills our heart with sadness and pain, even if the matter is not so, and our friends have arrived healthy and well in the harbor.

->Of the Usefulness of the Affections.<-

<margin>The usefulness of the power of the affections.</margin>
The usefulness of this power is also very great, and shows itself principally in these cases.

First and foremost, it serves to set a person in motion toward all kinds of contemplations, useful for obtaining that which might benefit the nature of man, and for avoiding that which might harm it. For desire sets a person in motion through the affections.

<margin>1. It appears from this, that they set a person in motion and dispose them to be able to do good works.</margin>
1. When this power is rightly ordered, it is very convenient, useful, and necessary for a person. For through it, as we have now heard, the heart rouses itself toward those things which are good for the nature of man; and conversely [away from the bad]: from which it is now very easy to perceive that it must bring a person great ease when it is rightly disposed. For just think, if a person always loved what he ought to love, hated what he ought to hate; if he feared from afar that which is fearful, in order to ward it off in time; hoped for that which is desirable, in order to pursue it; would not a person be set in motion in all ways by such a disposition of the heart, to seek most that which is most useful to him, and would that not also bring very great convenience and ease to the person?

Now, we have understood the objects of the affections presented to us to be of two kinds: 1. certain massive <note>substantial or physical</note> things that present themselves as very pleasant or unpleasant. 2. those things which we have to shun or to follow; namely the duties which

Now this power is the power of the affections, which, as we have heard, makes such impressions upon the heart as the nature of things brings with it; through which the heart is subsequently stirred and moved to such contemplations as those things require, each according to its nature. From this also comes the actual practice of godliness and that active life in all virtues, to which God the Lord continually exhorts us in His word, and for which we are created and reshaped <note>original: "herschapen"; refers to the spiritual rebirth or reformation of the soul</note>. So that the knowledge and discernment which we perceive through the imagination of things—which come before us through our outer and inner senses—would only serve us toward a heavier judgment if they did not make proper impressions upon our heart, to subsequently set all other powers in motion to carry out those things according to the truth of the matter and the will of our God. He requires of us that through this power of the affections, we love our wife and children, and most of all our God; that we hate all ungodliness and fear to anger God.

# Adam, Righteous

If we are then properly moved toward every object according to its nature and the truth of the matter, then all good works and all virtues arise from that; namely, when we love what we ought to love; and that first and most, which we also ought to love first and most, then we perform a good work. And if we persevere in doing so, there arises from it a virtue of love; and so it is with other things as well. Thus, it was merely madness for some to have urged that all <term>affections<note>The "affections" (Dutch: *affecten*) refer to the emotions, passions, or inclinations of the soul, which the author argues are necessary for true virtue.</note></term> must be rooted out.

And it is well worth noting here that truly nothing we do, or with which we concern ourselves, can be regarded as virtues if they are not accompanied by this power of the affections. This is what God the Lord gives us to understand when He teaches us that everything we do, if it is to please Him, must be done with the heart, to which this power properly belongs. "Whatever you do, do it from the heart," He says in Colossians 3:23. And He complains that some approach Him with their mouths, but that their heart was far from Him (Matthew 15:8), testifying that He had a loathing for such conduct (Isaiah 29:13-14). And this is also easy to perceive.

For that which we do is not good and virtuous in us simply because it is so in the truth of the matter and in its kind, nor because we judge it to be so in our brains, nor because we perform and fulfill it outwardly; but there is, beyond that, a requirement that we approve and hold it as good with our heart and affections (Romans 7:16). Our affection and heart must be set upon it, and set upon it rightly, or else the work

<column-break/>

that we do is not a good work for us, nor is it a virtue in us. For example: Simon the Sorcerer <note>original: "Simon de Tovenaer"; referring to Simon Magus from Acts 8.</note> makes a confession of the Christian faith; that work is good, and he may even judge it so in his understanding; but his heart is not in it—it is set upon his greed. Or if his heart is in it, it is not in it as it should be; it is in it from an evil principle, toward an evil end. Thus, it is not a good work for him, nor is it a virtue in him, and the reason for this is readily available.

For those who merely perform good and virtuous works outwardly, and do not do them from the heart—that is, with an affection and heart for the virtuousness of the work itself—but have another aim in mind, they have something other than that virtuous work upon which their heart is set. Such people will be very ready (if an evil, wicked work presents itself outwardly clothed with the same respect and regard that the virtuous work had, for which they did it) to go and do that evil work. For example, if some evil work presents itself which, according to the corruption of the times, would bring such a person honor and reputation, profit and advantage among men, then he will be ready to do it; for his heart is not actually set on the work he does, but on the "clothing" <note>The external rewards or social status attached to the action.</note> of the work; according to what those rewards are, so the person sets himself to work.

Therefore, if any work we do is to be judged as good and virtuous in us, our heart must be set upon the goodness and the virtue of that work itself; in such a way that even if it were stripped and bared of all other advantages, we would nonetheless take it to heart and practice it for the sake of the goodness and virtuousness which...

<margin>power of the affections to do good works and practice virtues: and to that end the affections must be set upon their right objects.</margin>
Now, to rightly apply these affections toward good works and virtues, two things are required.

First, that they be set upon their right objects.

Secondly, in a right measure and order.

As for the first: God has given us the power of the affections so that we should set our affections upon their right objects, and that each should occupy itself as if with its own work: love with that which is truly lovely; fear with that which is truly fearful; joy with that which is truly joyful; and so forth. Thus, this power of the affections is given by God to man to take on and clothe himself with such an imagination and form of things as the things themselves have in truth and in fact; to take up a lovely imagination from lovely things, to take up a fearful imagination from fearful things, and consequently to make such an impression and movement in the heart as the things themselves that come before man bring with them in truth and in fact: and thus move the heart to love, to fear, according to whether the things themselves are either lovely or fearful.

So also the power to hate is given to us to set it most of all upon that which God hates most: sin, the devil, the kingdom of Satan; and to be most sorrowful over it when sin is greatly committed.

This measure must be kept if the end is to be reached for which God gave us the affections: for if we should love our wife or children (for which God gave us love, to love them), whom we also may and must love, so much that we would love them more than God; then that love becomes sinful, although it does not fail in the object, because it nevertheless fails in the measure.

->Adam, Righteous<-

in two ways: either through persuasion or through compulsion.

Through persuasion: when man, informed by the higher powers he possesses—that is, his reason and understanding—and vividly perceiving that his affections <note>The term "affections" (affecten) refers to what we might call emotions, passions, or internal drives.</note> wish to take a wrong path, turns them back and makes them enter another way. Thus was the wrath of David—which would have made him rush into stray paths—guided through persuasion toward greater moderation. 1 Sam. 25:32, 33, 34.

<margin>Or through compulsion.</margin>
Through compulsion: when man cannot indeed prevent the internal movement of his affections, which he sees and senses are being led astray, but nevertheless restrains himself so that he does not run where his affections push him—such as his foolish love, to go visit his beloved; or his anger, to strike such a person. For thus far can the will rule over the affections: that, even if it cannot change the affections, it can nonetheless restrain the man so that he does not run off to follow his evil affections into wickedness.

It now follows that we should examine more closely and specifically what the condition of these affections was before the Fall, during the Fall, and how they might be set right again.

### Concerning the righteousness of the affections before the Fall.

The power of the affections before the Fall, as it was created by God the Lord, was so established that they were in every way entirely ready to take on

<column-break/>

such movements as the nature of the objects presented to man truly and actually required; and that also in such measure and order as they required, as was explained above. Thus, man was then so constituted that his heart immediately took on and clothed itself, through the power of the affections, with such a garment as the object in deed and truth demanded. In this regard, they were true Chameleons <note>The author uses "Chameleons" as a metaphor for the soul's ability to perfectly adapt its emotional state to match the spiritual reality before it.</note>, being most moved by God and the things that most concerned God; and so forth. Thus, all the affections of man then allowed themselves to be very readily guided by reason and by the will of God, in such a way that they all always harmonized perfectly with the nature of the objects that came before them. If an occasion for joy arose, the man rejoiced; for an occasion of great joy, greatly; and for an occasion of small joy, less so. We must necessarily posit this, since the Lord testifies to us that man was created upright (Ecclesiastes 7:29). And we also know that God the Lord made everything well; since this power was implanted in man by God, it was also perfect in its nature and fully answered the end for which it was made; for that is entirely fitting to the wisdom and goodness of the Creator.

# Misshapen, Reshaped

We have heard that from the **affections** <note>original: "affecten"; refers to the passions or emotions of the soul</note> flows either pleasure or torment; so it was with man, that from those very affections—which otherwise seem capable of bringing nothing but torment to people, such as the affections of fear and sadness—pleasure has come forth to man. Just as we explained above, that even out of sadness, indeed in the midst of sadness, man can take pleasure. Which is very worthy of note here in this place, and this comes from that excellent nobility of man's understanding, will, and conscience, through which these higher powers have very high authority over all the lower ones.

<margin>Question whether man was virtuous in his first creation?</margin>
Here now this question is moved: whether man in his first creation was also virtuous—that is, whether he truly had the habit of all virtues within himself, or whether he merely had very well-disposed and tempered powers to immediately learn and acquire all virtues.

<margin>Answer: Yes.</margin>
As far as this is concerned, we gladly maintain that man in the first creation had not only well-tempered powers, but also formal virtues; and that God the Lord also created man perfect in that respect, yet in such a way that the virtues could be further strengthened through exercise, and could fall away through evil oversight. For man was indeed created virtuous, yet changeable.

### Of the corruption of the affections through, and in the fall.

<margin>After the fall the affections are unregulated.</margin>
It was indeed thus excellently situated with the powers of the affections in the first creation; but

<column-break/>

now it does not stand so: for since man has set about to depart from his God, and so to let go of the fear of God—which is the most powerful bridle to well-restrain our affections, *Nehemiah 5:15*—so our affections, like so many galloping horses or wild animals, have broken loose, having cast off their bridle, so that they now in many things follow neither rule, nor measure, nor order; following all appearance instead of the truth, being all together misled by a corrupt **fantasy** <note>original: "phantaſie"; in this context, the faculty of imagination or sensory perception unguided by reason</note>, which, like a mad coachman, drives these galloping horses further and further.

So that now man often seems to vanish entirely and perish in smoke, in fumes, in turbulence, and passion; so that in all ways he seems to be more like the wild raging animals than the rational creatures.

For since Adam desired to be so much his own being that he did not want to be his God's, so he also rightfully lost the proper command of his own powers; these also escaped him, and like a raging madness broke away from his command; so that now the affections, which ought to be guided by the understanding and rationality, are often driven more by fantasy and lust; from which then great disorder and misery arise on all sides.

### Of the restoration of our affections through *Christ*.

Therefore, it also applies to every one of us, that one must not let the turbulent affections have their will, but must oneself rule over them; and there is also a means to achieve this; for although it is true that we are all alike entangled in Adam's fall, and that we are all alike so damaged by it that all our affections are turned into turbulent affections, there is nevertheless help against the same in the second Adam <note>A theological reference to Jesus Christ, who restores what was lost by Adam.</note>: for indeed all those who are born-again through the Lord Jesus Christ and made into new creatures, also receive a new power from the Lord, through which they are also to some extent capable of conquering their turbulent affections and guiding them better: For indeed the power and working of rebirth shows itself especially in this, that it turns all the powers of man away from sinful and perverse conduct, into which they were plunged by Adam's fall; and appropriates, exercises, and puts the same to work toward a godly conduct, and toward all that is good.

<margin>We must strive for our affections through Christ.</margin>

therefore we must still use some means to better help our turbulent passions.

<margin>Good instruction.</margin>

means to properly restrain our turbulent passions: for that purpose, there is nothing in the world more powerful, when it is well-impressed upon the heart—no better bit nor bridle—than the **fear of God**. The lack of the fear of the Lord causes many people to break out so recklessly into great, turbulent passions, and to proceed so boldly in following their evil passions; on the contrary, the fear of God causes a person to restrain themselves. Nehemiah testifies to this: that where the previous Governors followed their passions and had done great injustice to the people, he did not do so because of the fear of his God. <note>Nehemiah 5:15</note>. Here the proverb applies: *one learns by doing.*

Just as we see that a craftsman, who first begins to learn his craft or art, deals with it very awkwardly at first, and his hands and fingers are stiff and unformed for it, in such a way that in the beginning of his tasks he works very slowly; but the more he does it, the more he begins to do it with more pleasure, and also more nimbly and better, until at last he knows how to do it very well; and even with ease and pleasure, the work shoots very smoothly from his hand. So it is also with the management of the affections and with the practice of <term>godliness</term> <note>Original: "Godsalicheydt," referring to a life lived in accordance with God's will.</note>; at first it is difficult for us, and it does not go well from our hand, and many mistakes still slip in; but in the progress of time we become better practiced in it, and gradually gain more skill in doing well with ease and pleasure, and may therefore say with truth that for those who are truly born again, to live godlily and to tame one's passions is but a habit.

# From Creation to Recreation, 175

Therefore, we shall further hear most excellently how we may accustom ourselves to known and beloved virtue, and what we ought to do toward that end; for which purpose we must avoid certain things and practice others.

->The things we must avoid are these:<-

<margin>Making an idol of ourselves.</margin>
**F**IRST, that we do not make an idol of ourselves; that is, that we do not take matters in such a way that we wish to serve ourselves in everything, and merely measure all things according to our own convenience—what might be harmful or profitable to us. We shall never be able to properly accustom ourselves to virtue in the taming of our <term>affections</term> <note>The author uses "affections" to mean emotional impulses or passions that sway the will.</note> if we do not, above all, deny ourselves and our lusts and desires; if we are not minded to frequently break ourselves in the following of our own desires, whenever we perceive through sanctified reason that godliness requires something else. Therefore, we must accustom ourselves to frequently breaking off our lusts against our own liking and will; then breaking our fleshly joy through the fear of men, for the sake of the fear of God. And to this end, it is very profitable that we frequently look upon the Cross of Christ and consider how the Lord Christ denied himself in all his inclinations.

But he who pays no heed to their stings and gives no ear to their whinings finds himself best off and breaks the habit before long.

For here applies what Solomon says: *He who rules over his spirit is better than he who takes a city.* Proverbs 16:32.

And, thus acquitting ourselves in the good management of our affections, this blessing shall certainly come forth from it: that we shall have our affections very ready at hand for service, in such a way that when any occasions shall befall us to be moved in this or that way, we shall then also have ready affections to meet those occasions.

### CHAPTER XXIX.
### Of the Locomotive or movement of place.

<margin>What the Locomotive is.</margin>
Until now we have heard how man is moved through the senses to desire, and through desire to the affections; which power of the affections is nothing other than a particular internal power, through which the heart of man is thus stirred and moved. Now it follows that we also speak of that particular power of motion and stirring, which is also certainly internal and comes from the soul, but shows itself externally, through which the whole man and his external limbs are stirred and made to go from one place to another.

<margin>What its object of action is.</margin>
1. The object <note>original: "voor-gheworpen sake," literally the thing thrown before the faculty.</note> about which this power works is either the whole external man, or certain parts and limbs thereof.

The whole external man is moved by this power in many ways; backwards, forwards, sideways, upwards, downwards; just as it may seem

<column-break/>

good to the man.

The particular parts and limbs of man are moved by this power in many ways; every particular limb that has its joint <term>juncture: a joint or articulation point in the body</term> can be conveniently moved by this power for the service of man; but the principal parts and limbs of man, about which this power occupies itself, are these: the hands with their fingers, the feet, the tongue, and lips, jaws, eyes, eyelids, and nostrils: from which then also various very excellent operations of man arise, if only the aforementioned limbs are rightly applied.

<margin>What its manner of movement is.</margin>
2. The manner according to which this stirring and movement happens is this: no external stirring and movement occurs over the man except that which is commanded by a higher hand; when the higher powers of man—his understanding and will—find it good to make some movement concerning that which they have perceived with the senses and taken to heart with the desires and affections, then the living spirits <note>The "vital spirits" were thought in 17th-century physiology to be a subtle fluid or gas that carried signals from the brain to the muscles.</note> that are in man are awakened like a flickering wind; these strike the nerves; the nerves, being made to go, move the muscles, which have a power to contract or to extend themselves upon those joints of the parts of the human body that are movable, which we call limbs; and from that arises the external stirring and movement; namely, when the same is supported by something firm and immovable upon which the stirring and movement might happen; as in the movement of the whole man, the firm earth to walk upon; for man cannot walk on the water, nor in the air; although the fish that have fins swim through the water, and the birds fly in the air, and men swim through the water, but

### Concerning the Wonderfulness of the Power of Movement.

The wonderfulness of this power shows itself, both in regard to the manifold movements that are wrought thereby, as well as the manner in which it happens and proceeds.

<margin>and in regard to the movement.</margin>
As for the first, that man can stir and move himself in all sorts of ways—forwards, backwards, sideways, upwards, downwards, in a circle; and then even while sitting still can move many particular members so nimbly—that is very wonderful; although we are accustomed to seeing it; for truly, were we not accustomed to seeing it, it would seem to us the most wonderful thing in the world.

If man had been created with his feet rooted in the earth (just as we see the trees standing there, and as we can imagine such a thing of man), then all people would look on with great strangeness and have deemed it very wonderful if any man there had been able to

<column-break/>
