So too, if a dead man, who still has all his members and instruments <note>meaning the organs or mechanical parts of the body</note>, and is still young and strong of limb, stood up from the grave and began to walk through the streets of the city, what talk would there be of that? Everyone would marvel at it. But that we ourselves, being in life, do this daily—walking from one place to another, moving our hands hither and thither, and our whole body and all the members thereof as we wish—that we pass by with blind eyes, and are not even drawn to wonder at that wonderfully skillful Master, the Lord our God. Who, through the blowing in as if of a little wind, or something similar that we ourselves cannot understand what it might be in our being, has known how to make man—who was previously unfeeling—so walking and active. This we pass by, I say, with blind eyes, while nevertheless thousands upon thousands (mark well what I say) are not able to devise or give any distinct reason why they, who live and still have their soul (which they so often entirely forget) within them, can walk better than a wooden-made idol <note>original: "Afgodt"</note> or a dead man, who yet seems to have the outward instruments of the spirit and of movement.

### 2. Regarding the manner in which the movement occurs.
As for the second point, namely the manner—how this motion and movement is brought about in man—that is also very wonderful to observe. For just think: that the soul, which is so subtle and fine, so pure, thin, and spiritual, that one cannot in any way see it depart from the body, nor perceive that it takes up any place within the body, nevertheless possesses such massive, sensible, pressing power and movement—is that not very wonderful? Where does that power lie in man? Where does it hide while he possesses it? Where does it gather when man lies there like a block <note>i.e., motionless like a piece of wood</note>? This is wonderful.

Notice now what I say: all the strength, all the violence, all the power and might, all the force which the bravest and strongest heroes exert with the body, that and all of that comes from this secret, invisible power of the <term>Locomotive</term> <note>The faculty of self-motion or locomotion</note>. # V. Of Being Created and Recreated

The Lord lets us perceive things in this way so that we might be drawn up toward a contemplation: that we must not think of the Lord our God—who alone creates and performs such great things—in a gross or physical manner. It is not as if no one could perform such things regarding bodies unless they themselves were also physical. Rather, we should consider that the more pure, clean, fine, clear, thin, and spiritual a thing is, the more powerful its effects can be in its own strength. However, even if the Lord allows us to understand it this way, the matter is nonetheless wonderful; it remains a marvelous thing that the spiritual souls of men can exert such great force <term>force: power or physical energy</term> upon the body and cause so many various stirs and movements, and do so with such speed.

For notice this further: in order for even the hand of a person to be moved, all of this must take place: some of the outward senses must have perceived the object toward which the movement should occur; the imagination must grasp it and stir the desires and affections, and also awaken the understanding; these must petition the will to move the outward man. When the will has consented to this, the living spirits <note>The "animal spirits" believed in early modern medicine to be the fluid medium between soul and body</note> must be fanned into flame; they must then immediately fly through various arteries, nerves, and muscles, and stir them all and set them in motion—some extending, some contracting—and see, all of this is done in the blink of an eye. It can hardly be thought of before it is done. Thus, we have a demonstration in this "little world" <note>The "microcosm," a common Renaissance idea that the human body mirrors the universe</note> of the swift movement of the sun, moon, stars, and the heavenly orders which run rapidly along. Because some could not believe this speed, they have begun to argue that the globe of the Earth turns and the Sun stands still. <note>A reference to the Copernican theory, which was still a subject of intense debate at this time.</note>

<column-break/>

But to better observe this convenience, we must first consider the matter in general, and thereafter somewhat more closely in particular.

### Concerning the end for which this power is given to us.

From what has now been explained, we can perceive how excellent and convenient a power this power of outward motion is; thus, all of us who have received a living soul and body from our God have also received this power of motion. And although one may be stronger or more nimble in moving than another, this talent is nevertheless given to us all alike, and we shall also have to give an account of it; we shall certainly have to give an account of how we have walked, stood, worked, and remained still. For through these powers, all our outward works are wrought, which are also subject to this accounting (2 Corinthians 5:10). Let us, therefore, now examine to what end this power is specifically given to us, so that we might discern our duty from it and subsequently prepare our account before God appropriately.

<margin>
The end for which this power is given is to fulfill the commandments of God concerning outward works.
</margin>
The end for which this power of motion is given to us is namely so that we should, through this power, immediately put into practice and carry out all the commandments of God that require outward works from us; on the other hand, we must avoid, shun, and abstain from everything that God forbids regarding the outward man.

# Adam, Upright,

Behold, there are very many beautiful and glorious commandments of God, by which many outward works—which must be performed through the movement of our body and its members—are commanded of us. To this end, we have received this power of motion: to fulfill those commandments which were first written in the heart of Adam, and since then have been perfectly and clearly renewed and applied to various occasions in the Bible which we Christians possess.

<margin>James 1:27; Matt. 28:19; Jonah 1; Eph. 4:28; Rom. 15:9; Isa. 40:26; Heb. 10:25; Ps. 47:2; Joel 2:16, 17;</margin>
Such commandments are these: that we should visit widows and orphans in their distress (James 1:27). Thus the Apostles are sent to go throughout the whole world (Matt. 28:19); Jonah to journey to Nineveh (Jonah 1). Thus we are commanded to work with our hands (Eph. 4:28); to laud and praise the Lord our God with our tongue and mouth (Rom. 15:9); to open our eyes to see God’s wondrous works (Isa. 40:26). Our ears, to hear His word, for which purpose we must visit the assembly of believers (Heb. 10:25); to laugh and shout for joy over the welfare of God’s people (Ps. 47:2), and to weep and cry over their misfortune (Joel 2:16, 17); to greet one another with a <gloss>~</gloss>Holy kiss <note>The tilde in the gloss likely indicates a common liturgical or scriptural shorthand for "Holy".</note>, and whatever many more such commandments there are, which cannot be carried out except through the power of outward motion. To this also belongs that our fists should seize weapons, and our hands stretch out to bravely fight the battles of God <margin>Josh. 1:14, 16.</margin> and to fight a good fight for God’s people when necessity demands.

<margin>Prov. 5:8; Rev. 18:4.</margin>
On the other hand, we are commanded that we should turn our foot away from the house of the harlot (Prov. 5:8) and go out of Babylon (Rev. 18:4). We should not wickedly strike with the fist,

<column-break/>

<margin>Isa. 58:4; Eph. 4:29.</margin>
nor stick out the tongue, nor point with the finger (Isa. 58:4). We should speak no godless talk (Eph. 4:29), nor open our eyes or ears to vanity, nor mock, nor laugh at the upright, and whatever more such prohibitions there are.

So then, we have received this power of motion so that through it we might put into practice the aforementioned commandments and their like, each according to its occasion. From this it follows that it is our bounden duty that we should, with all diligence and industriousness, with all alertness and courage, embolden ourselves to promptly execute and put into work all these commandments and whatever more there are, each in its own time. To that end, we must exercise our members and make them ready, so that they might be willing servants of righteousness and fit <term>instruments</term> <note>original: "wercktuygen" - tools or organs of the body used for a specific purpose</note> to fulfill and do also the outward works of God (which He also justly requires of us, for He created both the outward and the inward man), according to the sound of the Lord’s commandments: that we should honor Him not only according to the spirit, but also according to the body <margin>1 Cor. 6:20.</margin> This then happens when we also, through the power of outward motion, practice with our bodies and the members thereof that which He commands us, and avoid and shun that which He forbids us.

## Concerning the integrity of local motion <note>original: "plaetſbeweginge"; the physical ability to move from place to place</note> before the fall.

<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:29.</margin>
With the same force, it stood quite well before the fall, just as with all the others; it was holy and blessed.

<margin>Holy.</margin>
1. The holiness of this power consisted in this (if one may speak thus regarding this power): that the entire body of man, with all its members, were not only entirely willing but also very capable instruments to perform and carry out those preceding outward good works which God the Lord had commanded; and to avoid and shun the evil. The hands and their actions were not limp, nor the knees sluggish, to practice the good and avoid the evil: there was then nothing lame in man's body that would have been inclined to limping (Hebrews 12:12-13). But the entire body of man, and all its members, were all equally quite ready instruments for good; such as is even now required (Romans 6:13, Romans 12:1).

And it is to be considered here (since it is certain that all actual movement originates from the readiness of the spirits <note>original: "geesten"; referring to the "animal spirits" thought in early modern medicine to flow through the nerves to cause motion</note> through the nerves like a wakeful, flying wind, and thus creating movement) whether the Apostle did not have his eye on this in 1 Thessalonians 5:23, when he speaks of the perfection of the spirit; and prays that these spirits might become as if perfected, so that they would be ready for nothing other than the good.

<margin>Blessed.</margin>
2. Blessed; the blessedness of this power consisted in these things:

<column-break/>

1. That it was very strong: it is not absurd to hold that Adam, before his fall, was as strong as Samson; for the soul has sufficient power, provided it finds a capable body.

2. That it was not misused for such foul, stinking, sinful, and destructive work as it is now frequently misused; which is merely a great dishonoring of the noble members (1 Thessalonians 4:5-6, Romans 3:14-15).

3. That it could do and carry out its affairs with great delight and pleasure, without weariness or torment: for that tormenting weariness has entered since the fall (Genesis 3:17), "in the sweat of your face," etc.

## Concerning the corruption of outward movement through and in the fall.

<margin>After the fall, this power is.</margin>
Now after the fall, it stands quite miserably with this power: since Adam and Eve stretched out their unhappy hand to the forbidden fruit, through the power of movement, to pluck and eat the same, a terrible disturbance and confusion has come over this same power; the devil has, as it were, inserted himself therein, and now stirs the same quite distressingly: for he rides, so to speak, on the wings of our *Spiritus* <note>Latin: "spirits" or "breaths"; the physiological vapors mentioned previously</note> and creates a terrible movement toward evil. Thus, this power of movement is found to be entirely unholy and entirely disastrous.

<margin>Entirely unholy.</margin>
1. Entirely unholy, according to the condition of the unholiness of the body: for the entire body of man is now a quite ready instrument of the devil for evil, and all its members are wakeful servants of unrighteousness: on the contrary, they are quite stiff, sluggish, and lame toward the good.

<column-break/>

with us leprous men / that although the power of healing is not in that which we can do / but solely in God's power and grace / yet we must nevertheless do what we can do / and if we will not do even that / then we shall not be helped for all eternity.

Therefore, seeing that the locomotive power must serve us in our actions / it behooves us / that we employ it as much as we can and may toward our improvement / and that shall be able to serve us / not to convert us immediately / but at least to acquit ourselves outwardly in that which we must do / like Naaman's washing.

So then the means here is / that we always outwardly, as well as we can / do those outward works / which are charged to us in the word of the Lord / and which the Lord requires as Naaman's washing / that they should be done / for our cleansing; although these have no power of cleansing in themselves / but that such comes from God.

<margin>
So we must, through this power, do much outwardly as we are able regarding that knowledge which God commands us in His word.
</margin>

# CHAPTER XXXI.
-> Concerning sleep and waking. <-

THUS have we now extensively discussed all the gifts and all the powers of man (through which he can bring forth wonderful effects in every way) which he has in common with the irrational animals of the field; although he possesses and uses the same in a much nobler manner.

There is yet one matter remaining pertaining to this (which arises from the aforementioned actions, all of which man performs while waking, due to the particular temperament and condition of the human body, whose instruments are applied and used in all the aforementioned things), namely **sleep**; concerning which the situation is as follows.

<margin>
What sleep is.
</margin>
Sleep is a binding-up of the outward senses and actions of man, or a suspension of man’s industrious activity, for the rest, refreshment, and renewal of the nerves, limbs, and the powers of man, which become weary through the constant contemplations of the waking man: for in sleep all the outward senses are laid down to rest; they all cease from their work; the eye from seeing, the ear from hearing, and so man rests (who is not of an infinite strength like the Creator, <note>Isaiah 40:28: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the Lord, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?"</note> Isaiah 40:28) from all his outward business.

This power, or rather this weakness, the first Adam also had, Genesis 2:21. <note>Refers to the "deep sleep" God caused to fall upon Adam.</note> So we also read of the second Adam <note>A common theological term for Jesus Christ.</note> that he slept, Matthew 8:24. We shall briefly examine the whole condition thereof somewhat more closely;

<column-break/>

and in particular these things: 1. The subject matter. 2. The manner. 3. The wonder. 4. And the convenience.

<margin>
The subject matter of sleep.
</margin>
1. The subject matter of sleep, upon which it works, are especially all the outward senses, which it causes to rest, and by occasion of that, all the outward limbs of man, through which they are essentially refreshed; only excepted the power of <term>Respiration</term> <note>Breathing</note> and that inward intermediate flow of the spirits for <term>digestion</term>; and so, these are not extinguished.

I say especially the outward senses; for the inward ones, such as the <term>phantasy</term> <note>The imagination or the faculty of forming mental images.</note>, often do not let themselves be laid down by sleep, but keep themselves somewhat awake and remain at play, and often arouse in man and show him very wonderful and strange, or even terrifying images in his sleep, which we call **dreams**, which commonly and generally are nothing but sudden phantasy, in which there is neither truth, nor understanding, nor reason; although the Lord our wise God and Creator also knows how to present great things to man in sleep through the phantasy, which are very wonderful, true, and firm, as he has many times done for his Prophets and dearest children.

<margin>
The manner of how sleep affects the senses.
</margin>
2. The manner of how sleep affects these senses happens thus: there are certain vapors sent up to the brain from the food that man consumes in the stomach, which are then condensed by the coldness of the brain, and thus the brain and the <term>common sense</term> <note>The "sensus communis," a theoretical faculty that unified the inputs of the five outward senses.</note> make the man drowsy and encumbered, and cause him to lie down for a time insensible, seeing that the common sense being encumbered, none of the outward senses can take knowledge of

<margin>The wondrous nature of sleep.</margin>
1. That it makes a person lie there for such a long time as if dead and makes all people equal: the King and the beggar; the miserable and the blessed; we are then, all that time, as if we did not live; and so sleep is a Brother of death.

2. Isaiah 29:7-8. It is a wondrous thing, this playing of the fantasy.

<margin>The benefit of sleep.</margin>
4. The benefit of this power is recognized by this: that through sleep all the bodily powers of man, which often decline through constant reflection and movement, are restored, refreshed, and recovered again through the calming of sleep; so that a person, after a good sleep, rises up very fresh and brisk, ready and alert for his work, as if all his instruments <note>referring to the organs or faculties of the body</note> were newly ground and sharpened.

->Of the end for which sleep is given to us by God.<-

The power of sleeping is given to the children of men so that, using it moderately, they might be refreshed thereby in all their powers, so that being better awake again, they might be able to do the work of the Lord their God; so that in all the preceding discourse it is explained where the works of wakefulness are indicated; therefore we shall not speak of that here.

So it is then our bounden duty that we use this sleep no further than as it is necessary and serviceable to our awakening in the work of the Lord: as is also said of food in Ecclesiastes 10:17.

<margin>The power of sleeping and waking was before the Fall.</margin>
These powers, like all others, were Righteous before the Fall, Ecclesiastes 7:29. <note>original: "Regtschapen"</note>

<margin>1. Holy.</margin>
1. Holy; man of his own accord, without effort, kept the right measure in sleep; and was also not made vain in dreaming.

<margin>2. Blessed.</margin>
2. Blessed. Precisely in that he had such good measure, and always attained the end for which sleep was given to him by God; which is the blessedness of all powers; which should be well noted throughout all the preceding discourse.

<margin>But is now after the Fall.</margin>
This power, like all others, is miserably damaged in the Fall.

<margin>1. Unholy; for it is immoderate; as some sleep too much.</margin>

# CHAPTER XXXIV.
## Concerning the Understanding of Man.

<margin>What the understanding is</margin>
THE understanding of man is a particularly excellent power of the soul, through which man takes knowledge of all those things that can be understood and perceived, recognizes them, distinguishes them, and judges them.

We say that it is a power of the soul through which man takes knowledge of all things that can be known; from this it appears that this noble power far surpasses all the other powers of knowledge of which we have spoken until now. For those only take knowledge of those things that can be perceived with the senses—that is, only of sensible things—which also fall under the knowledge of the beasts of the field, although man knows them more discretely. And whatever we have said further in the treatment of the aforementioned powers, which reaches higher than the sensible, we have done in consideration of the fact that man, who exercises the aforementioned powers, is a rational creature who possesses understanding. So all the excellence and preeminence which has appeared therein, above the beasts of the field, has proceeded from this power of man of which we now speak: that is, the understanding.

<margin>Which extends further than the aforementioned powers.</margin>
So it stands with the understanding thus: that it extends itself much further in the perceiving of things than all the other aforementioned powers.

<column-break/>

See, both the external and internal senses of man perceive only the upper side, the appearance, the shell, the exterior of those things that come before man; but the understanding penetrates and presses through to the substance, to the essence of the things themselves; it searches through the matter to the root, to the very kernel. It sees far beyond all those things that merely offer themselves to the external or internal senses; it draws conclusions, it makes deductions; it knows how to perceive what would follow and arise from those things joined together, and consequently what has been done or left undone before, and so forth.

And just as the external senses serve the imagination <note>original: "phantasie"; in 17th-century psychology, this refers to the faculty that forms mental images</note>, so the imagination serves the understanding, in such a way that just as we notice where the external and common sense stops, the imagination still goes forward and knows how to join things together—yet only as they are all externally sensible. So likewise, where the imagination stops—which can only occupy itself with things as they are external and sensible—there the understanding takes up the matter and goes further to investigate the essence of things, the causes, the effects, the consequences, and what more is to be done or left undone, which the beasts of the field do not do; but this is the work of the intelligent spirits, of the Angels, and of the rational soul.

Therefore it is necessary that we investigate all this somewhat more closely and thoroughly, and to that end we shall reveal these things: First, the nature and condition of the understanding in general; Second, the

# Deformed, Reformed.

## On the nature of the understanding.

As concerns the particular nature, condition, and quality of the understanding <note>Dutch: *verstant*; refers to the cognitive faculty of the intellect or reason</note>, in order to perceive it properly, we shall treat four things regarding it. 1. What the object is toward which the understanding occupies itself. 2. What the manner is in which it occupies itself therewith. 3. What the wondrousness of this power is. 4. What the usefulness of this power is.

### 1. On the object of the understanding.

<margin>The object of the understanding is everything that has being or can be known.</margin>
The object of the understanding is entirely extensive; even everything that has being or can be known—not only <margin>1 Kings 4:33</margin> from the high, great Cedar trees to the Hyssop that grows in the wall; from the great beasts to the worms that creep upon the earth; but from the great God and all His revealed things, to the smallest speck of dust of the earth that is blown away by the wind: all things which have being and can be understood belong to the knowledge of the understanding; general and particular things; things that are, or that can exist according to the grasp of man's understanding; past, present, future; necessary and accidental; good, evil; excellent, common; material, spiritual; all histories and events, workings, processes, arts, inventions, faculties <note>term: *faculteyten*; here meaning inherent powers or branches of knowledge</note>, circumstances of things;

<column-break/>

their manner of existence or operation; words, works, thoughts, conjectures, intentions, counsels, decrees; all kinds of things and all kinds of matters that can merely be known and recognized; with these the human understanding busies itself. The things of God, the depths of Satan, the condition of God's Kingdom, of the kingdom of darkness, of Heaven, of Hell, of the Earth, of the Sea, of all that can be grasped or known.

See this—all this, and whatever more of the like can be imagined—is the object of the understanding, which is like the eye of the rational soul; for just as the eye of the body, when well-disposed, can see all kinds of visible things (though not all at once, yet many at once), so it is also with the understanding; all that can be known belongs to the understanding.

Thus, the understanding is like an entirely great Court, Palace, or place of remembrance, where knowledge is taken of all things, of all events; where the same are examined, investigated, and each matter dealt with according to its merits, whether they enter through the hearing, the sight, the feeling, the smell, the taste, or the creation of the imagination <note>Dutch: *phantasie*; the faculty of forming mental images</note>; also all that the memory has retained, or that man has further perceived through his rational soul, all that belongs to this spiritual Court of the understanding, where all matters are investigated; where attention is paid not only to the shell, to the outward appearance—by which one could easily be deceived—but to the essence, the substance, the true truth of the things themselves: therefore, just as in wise courts many

A man who is intelligent observes outward sensible things in a different and more excellent way than the beasts of the field or simple and foolish men are accustomed to do: indeed, the understanding often corrects and improves the judgment of both the outward and inward senses. ->Adam, Upright<-

if one holds a stick in the water that is stirred and rippled, the stick shall appear to be crooked; and all the senses of man cannot perceive it otherwise so long as that stick is in the water, and a simple and foolish man shall also think it so. But he who is understanding shall know, and nevertheless hold for certain, that the water cannot make the stick crooked, just as it immediately appears as soon as one pulls it out. Likewise, if one distorts their eyes, they think all things are double; the senses can go no further here, and an animal would stand amazed by it, but an understanding person knows that it is not so.

And this happens thus because, as we said, the understanding does not only notice the upper side, or the shell, but penetrates to the essence and the kernel of the matter itself.

Indeed, thus we may now see to some extent which things the understanding concerns itself with. Now it follows that we examine the manner in which it keeps itself busy with these.

### The operations which the understanding exercises concerning the matters presented to it.

<margin>
1. The understanding makes distinction.

As for the first, the understanding makes a distinction between matter and matter, which distinction is twofold.

1. Between truth and falsehood, good and evil.

This serves to be properly noted; for truly much lies within it: the work then that the understanding has to do, concerning all the aforementioned things with which it is accustomed to occupy itself, is twofold: First, it must distinguish truth from falsehood, appearance from being <note>original: "schijn van sijn"</note>: Secondly, it must distinguish between two truths, two goodnesses, as to what serves to be presently taken in hand and practiced; for we can leave a thousand things at once, but only do and carry out one thing before the other: we shall say something of both, for this must be well known if one would live in any way decently.

# Misshapen, Reshaped.

->Concerning the distinction between two true and good things, and which of the two should presently be undertaken and practiced.<-

<margin>Concerning the distinction between two true and good things.</margin>
BEHOLD, it is so with man that he can only undertake and carry out one thing at a time; because of this, it happens in all human affairs that this consideration arises: which of those things—which one otherwise judges to be good, whether Spiritual, Civil, or Natural—should we now rather undertake and practice, since we cannot do all things at once? For example, man has many things to do: he must feed and maintain his own body; he must do his daily work to earn a living; he must take care of his household <note>original: "Weesen," referring to his being or estate</note> and those entrusted to his care; he must also observe the stately service of his God and care for his soul in a special way. Yet he can only do one thing at a time; here, then, deliberation arises as to which of these he shall take in hand. We know all things have their time; and—

<column-break/>

the fitness <note>original: "ghevallicheyt"</note> of a good thing is that it happens in its proper time, which is like golden apples in silver bowls <note>A reference to Proverbs 25:11</note>. Regarding this, the children of Issachar had a singular gift (1 Chronicles 12:32). Indeed, so much depends on this that some things, which would otherwise be good and well-done, are entirely evil and sinful if they are done outside the proper time—such as going to plow on the Lord's Day.

Then considerations arise not only regarding the time, but also in view of other circumstances that befall certain matters with which they are clothed; from this, much reflection arises as to what is profitable <term>expedient; original: "oorboor"</term> to be done or left undone.

<margin>Thereby the intellect judges what is profitably done or left undone.</margin>
The work of the intellect is then to judge here what were best done; and when the matter stands in great doubt, to keep the man in suspense <note>to hold judgment in abeyance</note>, the process of which shall also be explained in the manner of the intellect's operation.

Now, to be able to distinguish thoroughly and rightly between two things that occur to be done—what must not be done and what indeed must be done—therein great ingenuity is shown. It is, as it were, the most excellent operation of the intellect: namely, that in comparison of all things, one knows how to decide what is best done. This is especially true when many things present themselves, each offering and serving itself to be done first, and all alike desiring equally that they might have the upper hand, each clothing itself in the most beautiful manner to entice the man; indeed, many here particularly avail themselves of appearance instead of essence. Now, to give a right account <note>to make a correct decision</note> in this case is truly a very noble and useful work of the intellect, as we shall hear more broadly hereafter (Philippians 1:21 <note>The author likely intended Philippians 1:10, which discusses discerning what is best</note>).

# On the invention of new things.

<margin>2. The invention of new things.</margin>
Just as we have heard above, that the imagination <note>original: "phantasie"</note> knows how to join things to things, and plays with them in such a way that it is like a little Creator fashioning many things, which is very, very useful; just as the birds of the field know how to make nests, so man knows how to invent many convenient arts and practices for the benefit of mankind. Likewise, the understanding <note>original: "verstant"</note>—which goes even higher than the imagination—has a special work regarding those things that surpass even human imagination and are only properly perceived through the human understanding. These include the things of the Kingdom of God, and also the arts of governing cities and lands; regarding these, it knows how to find many good conclusions through comparison and the fitting together of things with things, which are found to be entirely useful and convenient for man; for man becomes very experienced and wise through that exercise. Thus, many excellent things have been invented in the governance of the civil state <note>original: "politie"</note>. However, man's understanding has no "play" in spiritual things to invent something different, but only that which God has revealed in His word; which then happens when we combine spiritual things with spiritual things (1 Corinthians 2:13). Through this, we are further led to find such practices and exercises as lie stored up in God's word for the good of God's people and their salvation. And to find this is truly no less than to find something in the civil state that is not written down; for just as he who finds that out merely discovers the truth of the matter which

<column-break/>

was hidden there in the course of nature in general, and now brings it back into practice; so he who finds out spiritual practice also finds the truth of the matter which was hidden in the Scripture, and applies it to spiritual practice.

# On being well-advised.

<margin>3. Advising the human being.</margin>
Since the situation with men is such that they are not all equally clever, it is also the work of the understanding—concerning the aforementioned things that one has properly grasped—to give instruction to others who are not very quick of comprehension. This would also have taken place among Adam's children, even if everything had remained in its original [unfallen] state, for they would not have been born as understanding as their parents. The children of Issachar had a great gift for this (1 Chronicles 12:32).
And to this belongs all learning and the instruction that is given from one person to another; and consequently the entire Ministry of Preaching <note>original: "Predickampt"</note> with all that pertains to it, besides all other ways of teaching and all kinds of sciences practiced among men.
And this is especially practiced upon our own selves; therefore we must always well advise and guide our understanding (to which special attention should be paid), seeking always to move and win it over to accept the good and reject the evil.

to learn, and to allow oneself to be well-advised by others, and also by ourselves, in regard to our **will**.

<margin>The manner in which the understanding works.</margin>
One must pay singular attention to the manner of the **operation** <note>original: "werckinghe"</note> of the understanding; for much is contained herein: and regarding this, two things must be examined: first, in general, how a person comes to understand and possess something; secondly, in particular, how he goes to work regarding the specific operations we just spoke of.

<margin>1. In general, the understanding grasps things by creating images of them, and through those, penetrates into their nature.</margin>
As for the first: the human understanding comes to perceive and understand things by receiving within itself the form and **images** <note>original: "verbeeldingen"</note> of things; and by occasion of these, it penetrates—according to its excellence and nobility—deeply and far into the nature of the matters themselves; observing those forms and images with a sharper and more ingenious eye than the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasie"</note> can do. For just as we know that human eyes, aided by human imagination, observe a precious painting hanging in the house quite differently than the eye of a dog running past the house, who otherwise beholds it with as clear an eye as the human; for the human notices the art therein, which the eye of an unreasoning animal does not and cannot do: so likewise the human imagination, aided by the human understanding (to put it thus), observes things even more deeply than the bare imagination is naturally capable of doing, and penetrates even to the essence and the core of the things themselves.

<margin>The power of reasoning.</margin>
As for the power of reasoning <term>reasoning: translated from "reden-kavelinghe," an older Dutch term for logic or discursive reasoning</term>; it is a certain power of the human understanding (or if one prefers, of the human soul) through which a person knows how to compare and arrange many different well-known things together in such a way that they advance themselves in the knowledge of that which was previously doubtful or unknown; and consequently knows how to distinguish truth from falsehood, appearance from reality, and good from evil. In this same way, the human also exercises those other operations, namely that they make a distinction between two good things to determine what is best to be done. For example: a consideration arises whether a person (being at a feast where there are also many pious Christians who they know are usually greatly grieved when a health-toast <note>original: "santeen instelt." A "Sante" or "Gezondheid" was a formal toast, often associated with worldly excess or vanity which bothered the more ascetic or "pious" Reformers.</note> is proposed) should also propose one, or not. Here the understanding person knows how to find the best course again, thus: God has testified that I must not grieve my brother for the sake of food <note>A reference to Romans 14</note>, for a matter that I can easily omit without causing offense. Such is the drinking of health-toasts at its very best; since I know then that pious Christians will be grieved by it, I must omit it.

And see, thus the human distinguishes various things, namely through the power of reasoning, from which it further appears that the same needs to be supported by certain other powers which are useful for that purpose; and these are especially—above the good and thorough knowledge of those first principles and of God’s testimonies in His word—the following:

Good things, without goodness; (for the fact that a person knows many good things does not fill his intellect with goodness, unless something else is added beyond simple understanding, as is evident in the Devil, who knows very many good things); sad things, without sadness: as is evident in a thousand cases, where a person knows very joyful or sad things with his intellect, yet he is neither sad nor joyful about them; or even quite the opposite: because he does not take them to heart, or has another perspective therein, being sad over the joyful things of his enemies, etc.
Now this is truly a most wonderful thing, that the intellect thus knows how to strip away all the outward trappings of things and make them entirely spiritual, just as the intellect itself is, and then to lodge them within itself; just as we see that fire changes all things into fire upon which it can have its full effect; but the intellect works more powerfully, and strips all things of their [material] essence, and transforms them into its own essence, and makes them spiritual.

<margin>4. The intellect stores things in the memory without confusion.</margin>
4. But that which is even most wonderful of all is this: namely, that the intellect is able to fix all those things—which it has once perceived and understood—through the intellectual memory in such a way that these same things do not confuse one another (as we heard above), nor push one another out of their place; but each arranges and fits itself there so well that there is always still room for even more. So that the intellect is not only like a mirror, which receives the image of the things placed before it and, as soon as they are taken away, the mirror also lets the image go; but it is like a painting <note>original: "tafereel"; specifically a panel painting or tableau</note>, which does not merely receive the image of this or that for a time, but forever, as long as the painting upon which this or that is depicted lasts. In such a manner, all things which the intellect has once grasped are, by the help of memory, always and eternally written there before the eyes of man. Now this is very wonderful: for how room can be found within the small human being to receive all of that, as if in a painting, can neither be explained nor imagined. Just as if a mirror held fast forever every image it received but once, and could receive as many as one wished to show it, and displayed and presented them all as clearly as if there were but one—that would indeed be entirely wonderful. It is also not possi-

<column-break/>

-ble with a natural mirror. Thus, the intellect is truly in this respect a miraculous reflection of the infinity of God, and leads us as if by the hand to His simple and incomprehensible being.

Now from this it also follows that where the eye and the other senses can no longer see except when the visible object is before the eye, the intellect can nevertheless understand and comprehend things even when they are no longer at hand, but are gone and passed away. For the intellect, having once received the image, does not let it go again as the senses do; but it holds it fast, and they all stand within it as if depicted in a painting. And what is more, even when a person is out of sight—yes, even if he is dead and gone from the world—man's intellect still knows how to display that person and represent him to itself. So that it makes all things—past and future, of which it has merely taken knowledge—present, and represents them vividly to itself; therein also showing, in some measure, the image of its Creator.

originally from the gift of understanding; through this, we are rational creatures, and more than the birds of the heavens <note>Reference to Job 35:11: "Who teaches us more than the beasts of the earth, and makes us wiser than the birds of the heaven?"</note>. If we have work to do, more than the animals of the field, that—and all of that—we must carry out through our understanding.

With our understanding, we perceive and comprehend the things of God, and of His Heavenly Kingdom, upon which our eternal welfare depends; with our understanding, we perceive the distinction between good and evil, and know the fundamental rules of government and conduct, in which our temporal welfare is situated, insofar as we are human beings; with our understanding, we also correct and improve many false impressions of the senses, through which we might otherwise be led astray, as sometimes happens to the animals of the field through lack of understanding. For the understanding serves us to frequently check the false impressions of the senses, which otherwise judge external things very erroneously; as when looking through a green glass, when that which is truly white appears green to the eye, the understanding lets us know that such a thing is not green but truly white; so also the understanding teaches us, when sailing in a ship, that it is not the land but the ship that moves away; hearing a voice which, through an echo, seems to come from behind, that it comes from the front; that sugar, which seems bitter to the sick, is sweet: and whatever other such mistakes of the senses there are, which the understanding corrects.

of the year turn out poorly; and those who do not apply their understanding thus, how confused, how distorted do their affairs eventually turn out? How do they fall into arrears? and likewise in all other dealings and things.

<margin>And man would walk in darkness.</margin>
Yes, without the right use of the understanding, man truly walks in darkness, both in spiritual and temporal matters, to his temporal and eternal ruin. He who has no understanding of things does not know where he is going; he must necessarily go astray and be ruined to the core. What ruins a merchant other than that he mistakes himself, takes the wrong turns, and enters into reckless paths, striving against the mysteries <term>mysteries: the specialized professional secrets or "tricks of the trade"</term> of proper commerce?

Indeed, when man is deceived in his understanding, he runs headlong to his own destruction; he works most industriously toward his own harm; he is very busy doing himself injury, and is much occupied with this or that scheme which will ruin him fundamentally. Thus we know that blind people in Religion persecute God’s own dearest children unto death, and boast of the fact that they would give their last penny to buy a faggot <note>A bundle of sticks used for burning heretics at the stake</note> so that they might be burned. ### Concerning the corruption of the understanding, through and under the fall.

SEE, thus gloriously did it stand in the beginning with man’s understanding; such a clear, beautiful light was kindled in man by God, so that he might walk by it and do all his things well.

<margin>
This is how man's understanding is now also corrupted through the fall.
</margin>
But oh, alas and alack! It does not stand thus now with man’s understanding; this beautiful, clear light has been extinguished through the Devil’s cunning and man’s poor oversight. He now sits in deep darkness and in the shadow of death; indeed, he is now called "darkness" in the Scripture, in the abstract <note>original: "in abstracto" - meaning he is not just dark, but darkness itself</note> Ephesians 5:8 and Matthew 6:23: *If then the light that is in you is darkness, how great shall that darkness itself be.*

But the holiness of the knowledge is gone; in such a way that even if they—like the Devil—still seem to know much, they nevertheless *know nothing as one ought to know.* 1 Corinthians 8:2. of God, of the Christian faith (just as the heathens themselves perceived entire truths of God), of the future life and Judgment; they nevertheless have no light to learn spiritual things as they ought—namely, so that the same might rightly serve them for the awakening of the true fear and love of God, and holy trust in him.

For this spiritual knowledge, the natural man now has no light within him: he has no principles <note>original: "principia" - fundamental starting points or foundations of thought</note> or beginnings in him through which he might grasp that knowledge; these are all corrupted and violated by the fall. In that regard, he sits not only in darkness, but he is blind—indeed, he is darkness itself—so that even if one brings the light before him, he nevertheless sees nothing. Therefore the Scripture says that *the natural man cannot understand the things that are of the Spirit of God, because they are spiritually discerned.* 1 Corinthians 2:14. For he has no such spiritual principles to be able to discern them.

So also the natural man is compared in the Scripture to a mule or a horse. Psalm 32:9. Show a mule or a horse the most beautiful painting; they will certainly see it, but they will not penetrate to the art that is within it; they will be able to take no knowledge of that. And even if you wished to discourse much with a mule or horse about the beauty of the work, they would hear the sound of your voice, but they would understand nothing of what you said. # Adam, Righteous,

The natural man—by his very nature—is blinded in his understanding. <note>See Ephesians 4:18 and 5:8.</note>

For consider how it is with a person who is born blind; he may well hear discussions about the light of the Sun, the glory of colors, and the beauty of flowers. By hearing this, he can perceive that there is something to it—that indeed the Sun must be a beautiful creature of God—and he can even begin to discuss these things with others based on what he has heard. But meanwhile, he cannot truly penetrate to a real knowledge of the light and the beauty of the sun. Even if he were eager to see the Sun out of curiosity, he still cannot truly love the Sun until he has actually seen it. Behold, such is also the knowledge of spiritual things that natural men can attain; it does not have such an effect within them toward the pursuit of salvation and the love of God as it ought to have.

# Adam, Righteous,

how can one escape? Thus, man becomes more and more indebted to hell through his corrupted understanding <note>original: "verdorven verstant"</note>, while he everywhere creates wondrous and great confusion in the world, and a very poor accounting for himself on the final day.

And this happens to him justly from the Lord, because he wished to know more than God; so that he now does not know as much as he must know; and because he did not wish to apply his understanding toward salvation, it shall serve him toward damnation.

->Of the restoration of the understanding through Christ.<-

**S**ince things stand so miserably with our understanding, we must indeed rightfully all be moved to strive for the improvement of our intellect.

For although we are so corrupted in understanding that we cannot, by nature, know spiritual things in a spiritual manner; nevertheless, like the blind, we come to perceive that there is something to the things of the Kingdom of God, and that they are well worth the effort of striving after.

<margin>So we must then sigh to God to have our understanding improved.</margin>
Let us then begin to look to the Lord; and just as we—like the sailors of Tarshish <note>A reference to Jonah 1:5, where the sailors cried out to their gods during the storm</note> and the ravens in the forest—learn to cry out to God when some physical hardship presses upon us, or when we lack something we desire; so, noticing like the blind that we lack this, let us also sigh to God over it, that He might be pleased to help us in this.

And this much we must confess, that even the natural man can do; for otherwise, we would

<column-break/>

have to judge all those who sometimes sigh to God for the Kingdom of God as being born again, which is a manifest untruth.

Now the Lord our gracious God has, for this purpose, caused the Sun of Righteousness, the Lord Jesus Christ, to rise upon the children of men in the world, to guide their feet into the way of peace, **Luke 1:78.** This light enlightens every man coming into the world, **John 1:9.** But we have loved the darkness more than the light; yet those who allow themselves to be advised by Him become wise toward God and unto salvation, **2 Timothy 3:15.** They know thereafter how to apply all things to join themselves more and more to God and to step toward Heaven.

We see the worldly-wise have a wonderful ingenuity and cleverness to turn all things that befall them to their own advantage and profit. The born-again <note>term: "weder gheborene" - those who have undergone a spiritual rebirth or conversion</note> receive that same cleverness in spiritual things, so that whatever befalls them—be it prosperity, be it adversity, be it whatever it may be—they weigh it all for their own spiritual advantage and profit.

Truly, we sometimes stand amazed and wondering to notice another's lowly and humble person, how they know—being taught by God—to turn all things to their edification and comfort, to the awakening of the fear and love of God, and trust in Him.

In order that we also may be enlightened in our understanding through the Lord Jesus Christ, and made capable in every way to grasp holy things in a holy manner; so must we follow the counsel of the Lord Christ, and shun many things that corrupt our understanding, and practice those things that improve it.

### Certain things that we must shun, in order to get our understanding rightly disposed in spiritual matters.

<margin>And to that end we must guard ourselves against false mirrors, which are:</margin>
THAT WHICH we must avoid / in order to get our understanding rightly disposed / may be considered in two ways.

In general; we must see to it / that we take no false touchstones of truth / no false mirrors / which show matters differently / than they are in truth; we are directed by James to the right mirror / the Law of truth / which judges without respect of persons. James 1:25. These false mirrors or touchstones now are:

<margin>1. The corrupted light of nature</margin>
1. The bare light of nature / which we nevertheless know / is miserably corrupted / and therefore by no means sufficient / to rightly distinguish good and evil: yet many here on earth go to work according to it; what seems good to them according to their natural understanding and light / that they call good; what is evil or indifferent / that they also judge as such / without more; these make their natural light their bible / whereas nevertheless their understanding errs in many things / since it is enmity against God. <note>The author refers to the Calvinist doctrine of Total Depravity, where human reason is seen as fundamentally flawed due to the Fall.</note>

<margin>2. The course of the world.</margin>
2. The course of the world: many think it must be right / what all the world does; and forget / that the world is set in wickedness 1 John 5:19. and that we may not be conformed to the world Rom. 12:2. so that we ought to hold it suspect for that very reason / because all the world does and practices it; for the good and the truth are not so common.

<margin>3. The decrees of the Roman Church,</margin>
3. The decrees of the Roman Church; many rely on these / and—

<column-break/>

—solely through their own noise <note>original: "beruyst," likely meaning the clamor or influence of tradition</note> and understanding / having no ground from God / nor His word / so they wish to hold for certain / first that there is a Church in the world / which cannot err; secondly that the Roman Church is that Church: both of which are false grounds; these must also be rejected.

<margin>4. The bare letter of the H. Scripture</margin>
4. The bare letter of scripture / which sometimes seems to be contradictory; there people then read / what best suits their fantasy; not once taking the trouble to properly compare scripture with scripture. 1 Cor. 2:13. By this the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wederdoopers"</note> / Libertines / and fanatics <note>term: "geestdrijvers" (spirit-drivers) - a derogatory term for radical reformers who claimed direct inspiration from the Holy Spirit over the written Word</note> are misled.

In particular there are principally five things to be shunned / above the general dullness of the understanding.

<margin>In particular the person must also guard themselves. 1. From blatant wickedness.</margin>
1. Hardened wickedness / and an evil conscience; namely when a person does not concern themselves with what might stand in the scripture / let stand there what will / he is minded to do what pleases him / and so he dares to give himself over to some things / which he knows are evil / for which he has received enough reason and understanding from God; such as in lying / deceiving / drunken drinking / whoring / usury / skipping out on debts <note>original: "upthuppen"</note> / false yardsticks / wares / or measures: and see / people know this / that it is evil / their understanding has light enough for that: So when a person still gives himself over to it / then he holds down the truth of God / which God had revealed to him; he extinguishes / in those cases / the light of nature / that God had still left remaining in him / Rom. 1:18. this displeases the Lord our God in the highest degree / therefore the Lord God also will not reveal other more precious truths to such a one / nor will He pour them in / nor trust them to him.

# Adam, Upright #

See, when man suppresses and holds down those worthy principles of truth—which he still possesses in a defiled state—then the Lord our God rightly thinks: "Should I go and trust these people further? Should I reveal to them the noble mysteries of my Kingdom? They would horribly defile and violate them; if they are so unfaithful in those small things, how should I dare to trust them with great ones?" Matthew 25:29. <note>The author references the Parable of the Talents to explain why divine insight is withheld from the ungodly.</note>

Indeed, the Lord God is the one who quite rightly punishes this unfaithfulness—through which one suppresses His truth by unrighteousness—by handing them over to strong delusion, so that they give belief to lies, just as the Apostle teaches in 2 Thessalonians 2:11, and by allowing false prophets and teachings to arise among such people.

<margin>2. Strong, perverse affections.</margin>
2. Strong, perverse affections; namely, when our heart is strongly fixed upon some matter which we would gladly do as if it were good, or promote as if it were truth; being preoccupied with a great inclination toward the matter before we have examined the matter itself for what it truly is.

Such affections, ignited by the lusts of the flesh or the curiosity of the intellect, greatly blind the understanding and estrange our intellect from the truth; they secretly and powerfully pull it to judge that as good and true upon which our heart is set.

See, we are very ready and prepared to hold as truth, and to believe, that which we would gladly have be true; and conversely: we have seen it in the recent sad tidings, which we were very reluctant to believe because we did not wish it to be so. Thus one finds by experience that

<column-break/>

stubborn <note>original: "stordighe," likely meaning headstrong or obstinate</note> people, because they would gladly be in Heaven, very readily believe—on small grounds and with little discernment—that they shall surely be saved. So we also find those who learn something with affection and desire, even if they are by no means the quickest of mind, nevertheless make good progress, better than those who have no desire for it, even if they have a bolder intellect.

See, our affections being now set in the innermost part of our heart, and lying so close to us—much more than our pillow, or our own spouse who lies in our bosom (who, as we are accustomed to say and also find, has much power to displace our judgment)—these advise us secretly with great effect, that we should not make acquaintance with those things for which they have no desire; on the contrary, that we should embrace and judge as good, faithful friends those things to which they are greatly inclined. And thus the truth is often shown the door, while lies and falsehood are pulled in and brought into the house. Do we not also find that hate, anger, hope, fear, and similar affections often make us judge matters suddenly and very perversely?

The Scripture testifies this to us: we read in 2 Timothy 3:7 that those who are driven by manifold lusts are always learning, and yet never come to the knowledge of the truth, being blinded by their affections and lusts. Speak against the pride in clothing to a woman or girl whose heart is set on finery <note>original: "mopicheyt," referring to vanity or excessive fashion</note>; her affection for dandyism <note>original: "toperije," referring to showy or foolish behavior</note>, her inclination, her attraction, her great sighing which she has for it, so blinds her understanding that she does not grasp the discernment of the reasons brought against it; she cannot perceive

See, the great God who made you has also made a book, and has written and revealed therein all the mysteries of His Kingdom for those who diligently investigate it; and yet man cannot take the trouble to search that book day and night, that he even dares to think that it is with God's Book as it is with other books, which when we have read through once, we immediately think that we now know enough of what is in them; that he also thinks, once he has read the Bible through, "I know well what is in there, and therefore I no longer need to read it diligently"—that angers the Lord our God to the highest degree. For we must rightly hold it to be true that in the Bible, being God's own book of which He Himself is the Author, thousands upon thousands of mysteries are set down which we still have to learn from it, even after we have read that same book through with attention a hundred and a hundred times.

This negligence must then also be avoided, if we wish for God to enlighten our understanding.

# Deformities, Reformations,

This blinds, confuses, misleads, and violently carries away the understanding; in such a way that even if a person is not afflicted with such manifest wickedness, disorder of the affections, curiosity, or negligence, they are nevertheless held back from acknowledging the truth by this accidental occurrence of prejudice. We see this in the Ethiopian <note>original: "Moor-man"; referring to the Ethiopian eunuch in Acts 8</note>. Acts 8:27. He was a pious man, diligent in searching God’s word; he read while on his carriage; he even had before him the clearest passage of Holy Scripture regarding the suffering of Christ. Christ had not only suffered, but everyone’s mouth was full of it; yet he did not understand that passage of Holy Scripture, because he was preoccupied with prejudice, thinking that the Messiah would be a magnificent personage according to the world. So it also went with Cornelius, even though he fasted for it. Acts 10:2. So completely does prejudice blind.

And what wonder; for it sets before us a wrong compass, a wrong star by which we sail. Whether a person then has ever so clear a light, or looks ever so sharply, once he has set his course wrongly, he runs entirely wrong; for he directs his whole course toward a wrong place. It is so harmful when a person first firmly adopts a path in his own brain as true, certain, and sure, before he has properly learned from the word of the Lord whether it

<column-break/>

is indeed true, certain, and sure.

Thus are the Papists <note>A historical term for Roman Catholics</note> misled; they adopt this: "the Church cannot err"; and yet that is not a firm foundation. Thus are the Anabaptists <note>original: "Wedertoo-pers"; literally 're-baptizers'</note> misled; they adopt this: "it is entirely unbefitting that the living God should take his flesh and blood from a sinful human." This they have laid firmly in their brains; they are pregnant with such prejudice, and with such intent they read the Scripture. Whatever clear passages to the contrary they then find—just like the Chamberlain <note>The Ethiopian eunuch</note>—they do not understand them; this prejudice blinds them. But if they read the Scripture without prejudice, in simplicity of heart, there is not a living soul who would not have to hold it as true that the Scripture testifies that Jesus Christ came forth from the seed of David.

Thus also are the Libertines <note>A group often accused of antinomianism or over-spiritualizing the Bible</note> misled; they think the letter of the Scripture is merely a dead letter, that it all depends on the spirit, and it must all have a spiritual meaning. But if they compared Scripture with Scripture, they would perceive that one letter of the Scripture explains the other, and so brings forth a spiritual sense without giving the human spirit so much room to play.

## Some things we must observe to get our understanding improved.

<margin>In general, we must exercise ourselves much in God’s word, and let it carry the highest authority with us.</margin>
In general: if you wish to have your understanding improved, then join God’s word and Spirit to the light of nature, and let God’s word have the highest word with you. Seek to furnish your brain everywhere and provide it well with good discernment of all kinds of firm foundations of knowledge and science of divine things from God’s word—concerning the service of God, the government of the Church, of Policy <note>Civil government</note>, of households, and of yourself. That is the light of the world.

<margin>And from there especially learn the knowledge of the crucified Christ.</margin>
And especially you must apply yourself to be well-instructed from God's word regarding the knowledge of God and of our Savior and Redeemer Jesus Christ. John 17:3. The Apostle brings everything to the knowledge of the crucified Christ, 1 Corinthians 2:2: he intended to know nothing else; it is also such a wonderful matter, bringing such bright, such clear light over all other things, and so fully satisfying the curiosity of the understanding and the desire to know something marvelous, that it may rightly be placed before all knowledge and before all science, just as the Apostle does.

<margin>Which is entirely wonderful.</margin>
And were it not for the fact that we were accustomed to hearing it, it would greatly amaze and terrify us to hear and to learn from the word of the Lord, which stands firm: that the great, terrible God of Heaven and Earth should become man, and allow Himself in His own human nature to be so cruelly mistreated by the children of men; yes, that He, who is the living God, the prince and the fountain of life, should allow Himself to be brought to death, to a shameful death, to the cursed death of the cross, and that by cursed, insignificant, mortal men, who perish like the grass in the field and are no more. Truly, this is so wonderful, so rare, that if we were not used to hearing it, and had we not accepted it from our youth, we would judge it unbelievable through our natural light <note>The "natural light" refers to human reason or common sense unaided by divine revelation.</note>, as the Jews and Heathens did. Therefore also the Lord our God Himself speaks of this matter,

<column-break/>

and says: *Behold, you despisers, and wonder, and perish: for I work a work in your days, a work which you shall not believe, though a man declare it unto you.* Acts 13:41.

<margin>And it must be believed by us, even if we cannot grasp it with our understanding.</margin>
So we must not be weakened in our Christian faith because the matter seems so very unbelievable to our natural understanding; but much rather (if we have otherwise accepted God's word as God's truth) believe it all the more. For were the circumstances of our Savior such that our natural understanding could easily believe it, or at least judge it to be plausible, then it would not answer to the aforementioned prophecy that had gone out concerning it beforehand; it must indeed be such a work that, when it is told to the natural man, presents itself in such a way that he must judge it as entirely unbelievable.

It also befitted the Majesty of God, when He now wished to do a greater and a new work that would exceed the wonder of the work of creation, that He should indeed do something such as no eye has seen, no ear has heard, nor has ever entered into the heart of man, if God Himself had not revealed it. # Misshapen, Reshaped.

will; and regarding this we must know that although no contemplations can properly be considered virtues in us if we only will them without our affections being moved, we must nevertheless know that it is a great matter that we will the good; indeed, it is also very praiseworthy that we contemplate the good even against our own inclination <note>original: "tegen heuge en meuge" - an idiom meaning to do something despite having no appetite or liking for it</note>.

<margin>What the Will is.</margin>
The will is the highest power of the soul (considering man’s own activity in relation to himself) through which man desires the good and resists the evil, and holds himself in suspense over the doubtful, or holds himself between two choices regarding the mediocre, having the freedom to choose this or that. I say through which man desires the good; for the will is a rational desire <note>original: "redelycke begeerlyckheydt" - a term used in scholastic philosophy to distinguish human will from animal instinct</note>, such as no living creatures possess except for the Angels and men. Irrational animals have a power of desiring, which we sometimes call their "will," but improperly; for their power of desiring corresponds to our natural appetite, of which we spoke above, which is awakened and guided solely by lust and not by reason, and which also, if left to itself, has no capacity to listen to reason.

But the will is such a desire which knows how to listen not only to lust, but also to reason: and therefore we call it a rational desire, not because it always follows reason, but because it *can* follow it, and consequently can restrain and withhold the lustful appetite, as it indeed often does.

And here now, namely with the will, properly begins the

<column-break/>

active life, where reason also comes into consideration: for in the preceding workings of the appetite, everything follows lust, unless the rational will interposes itself: for the appetite does not listen to the understanding, but is only restrained by the will.

Here then properly begins the active life; for man, properly speaking (namely, when one ascribes the action to the most immediate cause), does not do this or that because he understands and judges in general that he ought to do it; such as going to church on the Lord’s day; for many understand that well, are convinced of it, and yet stay at home because they do not will it. So also man does not do this or that because he desires or feels affection for it in particular through those lower powers of which we spoke before; for many often have a great lust and desire, being very ill, to drink much, and yet they do not do it, but abstain because they do not will it.

Thus man does only all that he does, or strives to do (which is also a doing), because he wills to do it: thus the thief steals, who yet well knows that he ought not to do it; thus the sick man drinks a foul potion, for which he has a loathing, and all that because he wills it.

It is also such with the will that, as soon as it has resolved upon something and <unclear>desires</unclear> it, it is immediately willingly served and strengthened by all the powers of man: but it is not so with the understanding, which often reproves and commands many things, and yet receives no

# Adam, Righteous

<margin>The will is like the Fountain of all actions,</margin>

Indeed, it appears from this that the will is the fountain of all our actions; yes, it is the very origin of all human conduct. This should be carefully noted here at the very beginning, for it provides a great opening to the following treatise and teaches us right at the start that we must truly learn to know our will thoroughly, and to watch it closely and pay attention to it, seeing as it is the principle of all our works.

### Of the General Character and Nature of the Will.

To understand the general character and nature of the will, we must examine these five things: 1. Its subject matter <note>The "object" or thing toward which the will is directed.</note>; 2. Its operations regarding it; 3. The manner in which it is awakened and works; 4. Its wonderfulness; 5. And its convenience.

<column-break/>

### Of the Object Presented to the Will.

<margin>The object presented to the will is everything that is known by man.</margin>
The object presented to the will is everything that is immediately known and perceived by man; (There is no desire for what is unknown <note>original: "Ignoti nulla Cupido." A Latin maxim meaning we cannot desire what we do not first know.</note>); with this the will occupies itself, either to desire it, or to resist it, or to leave it somewhere in between. For according to the common way of treating this subject, we also include the "non-will" <note>The act of choosing not to act or refusing.</note> under the category of the will.

However, the will, properly speaking, fixes itself only upon that which presents and offers itself as good; it matters not here whether the thing is good in truth, or whether it only appears to be good. For appearance and reality weigh the same to one who prizes and accepts the appearance as reality.

This serves to be explained more closely. For from this we shall also be able to understand the occasion of why a man does not will, or leaves a matter in between.

<margin>Thus man cannot will anything except under the guise of good.</margin>
Should a man then desire anything with his will, it must present itself as good in some respect or regard. For behold, evil and sin are so ugly, so foul, so loathsome, so unsightly, so horrible, so deformed—it draws so much toward the Devil and gives off such an abominable essence—that no one could desire it or pursue it, unless it were coated with something pleasant, lovely, sweet, beautiful, profitable, or esteemed, either in truth or at least in appearance.

Thus Eva could not will the eating of the forbidden fruit—which was evil—except when it was polished, adorned, and clothed by the Devil with the mantle of a new <note>The text cuts off at "nien," likely "nieuwe" (new), referring to the new knowledge promised by the serpent.</note>

# Adam, Righteous

<margin>Of spiritual good.</margin>
Spiritual good is the divine fear <note>original: "Goddelijcke vreeze"; a term for holy awe or reverence toward God</note> which properly has respect for God, for the things of God, and for the things of the future life, of which the Apostle speaks and mentions in 1 Corinthians 2:14. To this now belong:

2. All the contemplations of man that are serviceable and conducive to maintaining and putting into practice the laws of God.

And behold, these are the various kinds of good, by which the evil can then be recognized—namely, that which stands in direct opposition to the aforementioned, each in its own nature; and the indifferent <note>original: "middelmatighe"; referring to *adiaphora*, or things neither commanded nor forbidden</note> which stands between the two, and seems to be equally distant from that which has a consideration of good and that which has a consideration of evil.

<margin>Yet among these, one good is better than another.</margin>
Furthermore, among these various kinds of good, we see indeed that a distinction occurs, and one appears higher and better than the other; just as it is known to each of us through the light of nature that of two good things, one is often much better than the other, and that happens in two ways.

<margin>1. In regard to nature.</margin>
First, in regard to the general nature and character of things, a distinction falls between good and good. Thus, silver is justly judged better than the stones in the street, and also better than iron; to practice stately Religion <note>original: "Godsdienst"</note> is better

<column-break/>

than to watch a sheep.

<margin>2. In regard to the present occasion of use.</margin>
Secondly, in regard to the particular present occasion of use: it often happens that something which is in its nature incomparably better is nevertheless not as useful for the present use as something else that is not nearly as worthy; thus, if one wants to make a sword, iron and steel are better for it than gold or silver. If our sheep lies in the ditch, it is better to pull the sheep out than to occupy oneself with stately religion: likewise, generous wine is very good, but it is not good for those lying in a burning fever.

This distinction of things must also be noted and remembered; for the same shall be of great utility and use in all the following treatment. For when the will properly chooses that which is best in its present use, considered with all its circumstances, that is the singular goodness of the will, of which operation we now have to speak.

Behold, this is properly the operation of the will; with that, it now stands thus.

Because, namely, one stands in the way of the other: so in this case, man must choose the one and leave the other; sometimes only one matter offers itself for choice, which we shall either accept or reject as evil.

Regarding the first situation, it often happens that various things present themselves to man as being entirely good and worthy of pursuit. Thus it sometimes happens that there is offered to man, on the one hand, a merry company of the best friends, where one shall enjoy all kinds of joy and luxury, which man judges as good and deems not to be rejected; on the other hand, the assembly of the faithful, where spiritual things shall be pursued, which he must also confess are very good; here man stands between the two.

When both these things have been considered by him in general, he has judged them both to be good; but now that the matter should be brought to actual practice, and these good things come into competition, man stands bewildered and hardly knows what he shall choose—that is, what he shall will.

So likewise, he judges an honest trade to be good; but there falls before him the bait of a hundred pounds profit if he is willing to violate justice a little; here a greedy man stands bewildered; this we call temptation.

Thus Eve stood tempted, when she

<column-break/>

was enticed to eat of the forbidden fruit; on the one hand, she could not but judge the obedience to God's command as good; on the other hand, the new divinity <note>original: "Godtheydt"; referring to the promise that "ye shall be as gods"</note> which she thought to obtain by rejecting obedience appealed to her wonderfully well.

<margin>How the will works when a matter comes before it, over which deliberation falls as to whether it be acceptable or not.</margin>
Regarding the second situation—namely, when a matter comes before man over which deliberation <note>original: "deliberatie"; formal weighing of options</note> falls as to whether it be acceptable or not—it happens in such a way that the matter always clothes itself with something that is good, however evil it might be in its foundation; so it is then the work of the will to see to it that she does not take the appearance for the reality, just as happens in all false religions; and because she is a rational desire <note>term: "redelijcke begetlijkheyt" — a philosophical concept where the will is seen as a "rational appetite" that follows the understanding</note>, that is, a desire that can understand reason and listen to it, so here the work of the will is to investigate with reason what the matter is, and subsequently to give it its place. Here it should be known that it often happens in this, as also in the preceding situation, that the will is on the one hand urged and solicited by the lusts and affections of the heart toward such or such a matter, to accept it; and that she is on the other hand urged by reason and by the understanding to reject that matter and to accept the contrary thereof.

Here then the will stands between the two, being wooed like a beautiful maiden by both, and has the power to refuse or to grant to one or the other according to her pleasure. For as the will (as we have now heard several times) is a rational desire, and consequently has something in common both with desire and with reason; so she takes knowledge of both,
