# Deformed, Reformed

<margin>Thus presented things sometimes appear beautiful, even if they are the opposite.</margin>
**As** for the presented object, it often possesses a great power of allure within itself to win the will over to it, and vice versa.

<margin>See how the presented object, which encounters a person externally, often appears so beautiful at first instance that the person immediately desires it.</margin>
See how the presented object, which encounters a person externally, often appears so beautiful at first instance <note>original: "ter eerster instantie"</note> that the person immediately desires it as soon as he begins to perceive it. Thus, no sooner did Eve come before the eyes of Adam than she appeared so beautiful to him that she immediately found great favor in his eyes and won his will over to her, so that his heart immediately clung to her; although all this happened previously in such a way that the eye [informed] the common sense, that the imagination <note>original: "phantasie"</note>, that the desire, the desire the affection, and the affection, coming into agreement with reason, won over the will.

Now, when we desire in this manner, having been won over by the pleasantness of the object itself, then we are said to desire of our own accord.

<margin>Thus earthly things present themselves as very beautiful in themselves to earthly people; against which we must be on our guard.</margin>
In this way, all earthly and fleshly things present themselves to earthly and fleshly people; which must be carefully noted in order to guard our will well, so that it is not won over to evil, misled, or violated by the wicked "stuffer" <note>A "stoffiaan" refers to a decorator or upholsterer; here used metaphorically for the Devil who "dresses up" sin.</note> the devil, who is always lurking for that purpose, and who thus brings forth his evil coupling and horrible, deadly botch-job of sin. James 1:14. <column-break/>

Therefore the Lord, knowing this and wishing to keep us from destruction, warns us that we should watch our outward senses and take heed how we see and hear, so that our will, through the devil's cunning, might not be taken captive toward evil. And we must pay all the more attention to this, for the will is both the fountain and the balance <note>The "balance" or scales that weigh our choices.</note> of our actions; therefore we must guard it thoroughly and closely observe all the avenues, all the inclinations, and the outcomes thereof. Indeed, he knows where our "sleepy world" <note>Likely a metaphor for the dormant or unexamined parts of the human psyche.</note> is weak and sick, in order to creep through there, to seduce our will, and so to ruin us entirely and utterly; therefore we must watch and pray, and be on our guard.

# Adam, Righteousness

->**254**<-

<margin>
1. Preoccupied with distorted self-love.
</margin>
Regarding distorted self-love: it is impossible to express how very much the vain human being thinks of himself, and how much he is preoccupied with his own person. Indeed, it is certain and sure that ever since Adam and Eve desired to become Gods <note>A reference to the Fall in Genesis 3:5</note>, it has been the case with the natural man that he has always since made an idol of himself. He has always sought to please, gratify, and serve himself more than anything else in existence. In such a way, even those who are seized by a foolish love and risk their lives for their beloved, still do so fundamentally out of self-love—out of a desire to satisfy and appease their own passion and inclination (which is now so disposed, even though reason teaches otherwise). So it may be said with truth that no Heathen or Papist <note>A derogatory term for Roman Catholics, common in 17th-century Protestant Dutch writing</note> idol (no matter how great a following it may have had) was ever served as devoutly and zealously by anyone as the human being serves himself. Indeed, it is now such with man that he has such a strong, distorted love for himself that he wishes everything that opposes him to be annihilated and overthrown. It would be a small matter to him if Heaven and Earth were entangled and all things were turned upside down, if only he might have his way. Now, the human being being thus disposed, is always very ready to listen most of all to the petitions, requests, and appeals that are most clothed with respect and considerations taken from that which originally comes from himself, springs from himself, and can be regarded as his own. Such are the considera-

<column-break/>

tions and respects with which the lusts, desires, and affections clothe their requests. On the other hand, he is usually unwilling to listen to requests which are only clothed with respects and considerations taken from elsewhere—such as from God the Lord, and from those who take it upon themselves to change him, to break his lusts, to refuse his desires, and to advise and urge the opposite upon him. And thus it happens that very often lust is followed by the will more than reason.

<margin>
2. And is also unbelieving regarding the things of God and the future life.
</margin>
2. Regarding the unbelief concerning the things of God and the things of the future life: this is also very great. It is true that everyone boasts that he believes there is a God, a Heaven, a Hell, and a Last Judgment; but that is so testified among us Christians because everyone is accustomed to accept it as the truth among us, and because those people are regarded as very abominable among us who dare to deny it. Therefore, everyone confesses the aforementioned things with the mouth; but they are truly not well-impressed upon the heart. They do not stand there firm and clear, as one sees the Sun standing in the Firmament <note>The sky or heavens</note> on a bright midday. The aforementioned truths are very darkened in man; they are very dusty. For through the turmoil and the constant fleshly and earthly business, so much dust is thrown from all sides onto those certain truths that they lie as if smothered beneath it. So that the human being sees these same truths only as if from afar; thus he only weakly assents to them, and consequently is not much moved by them; he is but little [affected] there—

# Deformed, Reformed

->by Gerard<- <note>Likely Gerardus Wessels or a similar contemporary theologian; the text reflects 17th-century Dutch Reformed thought.</note>

Just as we see that one who only sees the King’s glory and the glory of his Court from a very great distance, or hears some melodious music of which he can barely discern the details, is but little moved by it; whereas those who are near to it, and come to behold it perfectly, are usually greatly moved by it.

See then, from this it also follows that lust and desire commonly gain more of a hearing than reason or conscience: For lust praises present, sensible things, of which one clearly perceives the beauty and loveliness, seeing them near before one's eyes, and therefore can easily and firmly believe in them, and consequently be greatly moved by them; whereas, on the contrary, reason and conscience use motives <term>beweegh-redenen: literally 'moving-reasons' or motivations</term> taken from such things that are still far off, such as the things of the future world, and the rewards of God in another life after this; which one does not see so clearly, and then also cannot believe so firmly, and consequently is but little moved by them.

And thus man is also led astray through unbelief in the things of God, to cling to fleshly things above spiritual things.

I say through unbelief; for even if a matter is not before one's eyes, but still far off, if one nevertheless certainly believes that it shall come, and if it is of weight, it usually still causes great emotion in this situation of which we now treat.

As for example, even if we do not yet see the enemy before our eyes, if we are nevertheless told with good certainty that he is already

<column-break/>

on the move, and is encamped with great power to surround us, that usually moves us greatly; it is then unbelief which causes great immobility in spiritual things.

3. As concerns now the third point, <margin>3. Because man is misled by wrong observations.</margin> namely the wrong considerations and observations by which man is misled; to rightly understand the nature of this, one must remember here that man, in his actual practice, never undertakes, follows, clings to, or practices anything, except because he otherwise recognizes it as good. If a man practices Usury, if he runs after harlots, if he breathes out murder and threats, he does that, and all that, under some appearance of good; he has something in mind there that seems good to him; he seeks something there that he judges to be good; and when man does thus, that "apparent good" which he follows does not always present itself as if the things set against it were evil—such as righteous dealing, a chaste life, or a gentle and forbearing spirit; but only comparing things with things for the present time, he judges foul gain, his sinful paramour, etc., as best for this present time; and that which he had generally judged and admitted to be good, such as righteous dealing, he now judges as not acceptable in present practice.

And this happens to the natural man very often, namely, that what he had judged as good in general—such as righteous dealing—while it still hung high above his head in mere speculation <term>speculatie: theoretical thought or contemplation</term>, he judges as not acceptable in the present...

To this end, a natural inclination within us greatly assists, which is to gladly put the "evil day" far from us (*Amos 6:3*). We let ourselves believe that it will not go so poorly for us on the final day as is preached; that we shall also have time enough to amend everything.

# Adam, Righteous,

If one very earnestly desires a matter, then he employs all means to bring it to pass; if it does not succeed through one means, he tries it through another; he does all that he can to reach his purpose; everyone knows this; daily experience teaches this irrefutably.

<margin>By this, man can test his will regarding the things of God.</margin>
By this, then, the Christian man has a proof of how his will is disposed toward the things of God and the things of the world to come. See, many people desire earthly things in such a way that they also continually employ all means with tireless effort to obtain them; that is then a firm proof that they earnestly desire those things. These same people are also commonly found to desire the things of God and Heavenly goods in such a way that they nevertheless cannot endure the pain of using and employing all the means of God in constant persistence and earnestness, which God has revealed in His word to obtain His Divine things; by this it then also appears that they only faintly desire those things of God. When we say that a person is forced by blows to *will* this or that, this is not properly spoken; but the flesh being forced by blows and feeling the pain, the lusts and desires begin to solicit the will, that she <note>In the original Dutch, "the will" (de wille) is a feminine noun, often personified as "she."</note> might indeed consent to do such a thing, and they sometimes overcome her; but when she consents, she does it freely, that is to say, in such a way that she could also have refused it. Do not say that you could not avoid it; but rather that although you wanted to refuse at first, you—being further urged—did not *want* to refuse it later; for you, who could refuse it at first, could also have done so at the last.

<margin>But it is limited in the power of execution in two ways. 1. In regard to man's own powers.</margin>

The will can pull man's powers up as high and apply them to its service as much as they can be pulled, but it cannot give any greater gifts nor new powers. It can make the eye see as sharply as it is capable of seeing, but it cannot make the eye see more sharply than it can by nature. The will cannot say to a lame foot, "walk straight now," or to a deaf ear, "hear sharply now." ### On the Wonderfulness of the Will.

<margin>The wonderfulness of the will is revealed.</margin>
Hitherto we have spoken very extensively of the condition and the particular nature of the will, from which the wonderfulness of this faculty is also recognized; therefore we may be briefer here, yet with a word: the wonderfulness of the will shows itself both in the things that it wills, and in the manner in which it is made willing, and how, being made willing, it acts.

<margin>1. From the extensiveness of its object.</margin>
1. There is nothing in Heaven, nothing on Earth, or beneath it, which it cannot will and desire, if it only pleases it; man can will to be King, Prince, God; and what not?

->On the usefulness of the will.<-

<margin>The usefulness of the will is revealed.</margin>
The usefulness <note>original: "gerieffelickheydt," meaning convenience or utility</note> of the will, when it is well set in motion and guided, is also very great; but it shows itself principally in three things.

<margin>1. Because through it, man brings to practice the things he knows he must pursue.</margin>
1. The will serves us so that we might bring into practice those things which we know and have perceived that we ought to pursue.

See, the Lord God created man for an active life: Read through the entire Book of God, and you shall find it so, namely that the Lord God made man for the practice of godliness <note>original: "Godtsalicheyt"</note>; there is not a chapter, not a leaf in the Holy Scripture, which does not make some opening and guidance toward godly reflections, and points, promotes, and advises man toward them. This, man perceives through his understanding; thus the will, which commands so absolutely, is serviceable to him, so that what he has perceived with his understanding, he may also immediately pursue and carry out with all his might.

So that the comprehension and the imagination, captured by the understanding, should not lie there idle, but that they should indeed, through the reflection <note>original: "weer-slag," like a rebound or echo</note> upon the will, break out into actions, just as the rays of the sun, through reflection, cast their heat—

# Adam, Righteous, VV

<margin>
2. Because through it the perverse lusts and affections of man are restrained, so that they do not break out into deed.
</margin>

2. The will serves us now to restrain perverse lusts, desires, and affections <note>The author uses "affections" to mean emotions or passions like anger or fear</note>, so that they do not break out into action, as they would always gladly do. Thus man is often held back by that power of the will, so that he does not do many things for which he otherwise has both the present opportunity and the inclination, being enticed by lust or affection; just as, on the other hand, man is driven by the will to do that which he otherwise has no mind for, which he does very unwillingly, being held back by distaste and opposing affections.

The beasts of the field do not have this benefit; for they, properly speaking, have no will, but are led only by lust and affections; of which this is briefly the explanation.

The lusts and affections of man are not in themselves rational powers—that is, powers that listen to reason—but are merely animal powers that neither understand nor use reason. Therefore, when they can be satisfied, they fall upon something without considering anything else. The furthest an animal goes is that it subdues its lusts through its affections: desiring a fatty broth, the dog restrains itself for fear of blows; the affection of fear tames the lust.

But there is nothing in an animal that goes higher, which might also tame and compel the affections. For that purpose, man has received the will, which is a rational power—that is, a power of desire

<column-break/>

that listens to reason; by the help of which reason and conscience, man knows how to subdue not only his fleshly desires but also the affections of his heart.

Thus, when it happens that foolish love, jealousy, or anger—against all reason and discretion (since the affections do not listen to reason anyway)—want to lead toward evil, the will can step in, restrain them, and stop them. It can lay the affections so fast in bonds that they can make no stir in the outward man, but must lie there fixed and consume themselves within the man, being compelled by the will.

<margin>
3. Because through it man demonstrates his virtue or vice.
</margin>

3. Thirdly, the will also serves as a proof of our virtue or vice; namely, when we break or give in to our evil affections and desires, as we are able to follow or thwart them through the power of our will.

So the will also serves as an occasion to show our virtue and uprightness toward God; namely, when we behave well and abstain from evil, having now not only good occasion and power to do so, but also being often violently assaulted by the Devil's cunning, the world's seduction, and our own corruption. How much more ought Adam, who was free from corruption, to have shown his virtue?

Thus virtue lies in the right use of our will, for the proper guidance of our affections and desires. And the matter stands thus: on the one hand, if something happens to us against our will, even if it were outwardly quite gruesome, it is no sin in us; just as when a maiden is violated with force against her

# Deformed, Reformed

For he no longer knows that he does evil, any more than a bull or a stallion.

On the other hand, the same applies here to the application of our will: that when we use it for the right guidance of our lusts and affections, and for the restraining of evil lusts and affections, then gradually, through the refusal of that which they desire, those evil lusts and affections are brought under subjection and killed; and so the human being, through contrary exercise <note>The practice of "agere contra" or acting against one's immediate impulses to build virtue.</note>, gains great power over the same, so that they no longer stir so tempestuously, and thus virtue is worked out through this, and the human being becomes virtuous.

### 11. Of the end for which God has given us the will.

<margin>God has given man a will, so that he might embrace God's will therewith.</margin>
The will is given to us by God so that we might embrace and observe His will therewith, according to the prayer, *Thy will be done*, so that we might also have our will from God, and be always and eternally blessed; Deuteronomy 30:16, Psalm 40:9. For truly, in God’s good will (Romans 12:2) all our good is wrapped up; indeed, all our salvation lies in this: that we will what God wills, whose will is always good and doing good toward all those who will as He wills; Psalm 84:12. For behold, this is also the truth: God the

<column-break/>

Lord desires our welfare more than we do ourselves: He has more interest in us; He made us Himself; He knows our nature better; He knows better what is good for us than we do ourselves; so He has also enclosed all our best good, indeed all our good, in His good will; if we then follow that, it must go well with us: wherein lies the advancement and promotion of a courtier, other than in this: that he aligns his will with the will of his Prince?

So also God the Lord had surely prepared many better things for Adam than the earthly Paradise, had Adam only listened well to the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God, wherein is laid up and wrapped up for man everything that is good, desirable, and joyful for man. Thus, God the Lord certainly did not give man the will so that he should ruin himself with it—although he has misused his will to that end—but so that he might be made more and more blessed through it.

From this we can now discern our bounden duty in the conduct of our will. Since we understand <margin>Therefore it is the duty of man.</margin> that all our salvation lies in God's will, it is our bounden duty to observe two things concerning the will of God.

1. That we diligently inquire <margin>1. To diligently inquire after the will of God.</margin> and prove what is the good, pleasing, and perfect will of God; Romans 12:2. To that end, we must exert ourselves most diligently: For seeing that we have received that noble gift of being able to "will" from God, in order to match it to His will; so we must surely, before any other work, properly learn what the will of God is, in order to [align] ourselves...

### Of the Uprightness of the Human Will Before the Fall.

<margin>The will of man was at first holy and blessed.</margin>
**The** will of man before the fall, like all his other powers, was upright and perfect, <margin>Ecclesiastes 7:29.</margin> equally holy and at the same time blessed.

<margin>I. Entirely holy toward all good.</margin>
**I. Holy:** man's will before the fall was entirely holy; which holiness of the will was uniquely situated in two things.

<margin>1. Above all, it had to be holy and approved of all that God willed and did.</margin>
**1.** That man agreed with, and approved as good and holy, all that God willed and did. Man possessed that perfectly of which the Apostle speaks, that he consented that it was good. <margin>Romans 7:16.</margin> This is a part of the holiness of the will, namely that man approves as good that which God the Lord does and prescribes—and thus reveals to be His will through His work and Word—and does not wish it to be otherwise than it is. This is well worth noting; for it can happen that a person perceives something with his understanding to be God's will, and is also convinced in his understanding that what God wills is good, and yet the person wishes it were otherwise: such as wishing that adultery might be permitted.

Man was disposed differently before the fall; he held everything as good that God prescribed: if God commanded that he should not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he immediately held it to be good.

<column-break/>

<margin>2. The will was more inclined to observe God than to do so only in part.</margin>
**2.** That man was also more inclined and disposed to observe the good will of God than to do the opposite: to understand which, we must remember here that the human will is entirely free, in such a way that of two things presented to it, it can choose one and reject the other, which we call <term>free choice</term> <note>original: "vrije willekeur" - the capacity for self-determination or "liberum arbitrium"</note>; so also could man before the fall, through the power of his free choice, choose to transgress God's command and to listen to the perverse advice of Satan, as the outcome has taught: but, although man had a free choice both toward good and evil before the fall, it was nevertheless so with man before the fall that he was most inclined through his free choice to choose that which God prescribed, although he could also choose the opposite. So it stood with man in this condition as with the courtier who presently loves his Prince from the heart, and is consequently, through that heartfelt love he bears his Prince, more inclined to obey his Prince than he is inclined to act against his will; although he, nevertheless having a free will, is changeable; and it sometimes also happens that in the course of time, through various occurrences, that courtier becomes unfaithful to his Prince and is found to have become a traitor.

So then, the holiness of the will of man before the fall was also situated in this: that man's will, as one who loved God from the heart, was more inclined to obey God...

Truly, this is a very common practice; it is also a completely base and damnable <term>weaving of the human will</term> <note>original: "vvebel van 's menſchen wille"; refers to the internal construction or "fabric" of one's desires</note> that he will not hold as good what God holds as good in His word, and what they themselves must confess is truly good.

And this is the general condition of all unregenerate men. Therefore the Apostle also brings this in as a particular virtue in himself, and a great fruit of his rebirth: that he consented to the Law, that it was good, <term>Romans 7:16</term> and that he had a delight in the Law of God, <term>verse 22</term>. By this he fully implies that it is something extraordinary; for indeed, very many are found who do not consent that the Law of God is good with a delight therein, but who instead reject the Law of God and wish that their lusts might stand as laws, and that God’s laws might be changed according to their lusts and desires. This is a

<column-break/>

proper deformity of the will, the causes of which we must briefly examine somewhat more closely.

This perverted weaving of the will is in the devil, and proceeds from a completely cursed, desperate, bitter hatred against God. Because of this, he will not, nor can he, allow himself to be pleased by anything that God does or prescribes to be done, being hostilely minded against the Divine Majesty. Just as some people are toward other people, against whom they are so full of hatred and envy—as a toad is full of venom—that whatever those others do, no matter how well it is done, they blame it, they criticize it, and they strain their minds to find something to use against it. This is "holding the truth of God in unrighteousness": <term>Romans 1:18</term>. The Devil does this in the most hideous way. But this perverted weaving of the will arises in man out of too great a love for the lust of his flesh, against which he finds and perceives that the truths and goodness of God conflict. So he is accustomed, being now corrupted (instead of striving that his lust might align with God’s truth and law), to desire and wish that God’s truth and God’s law would accommodate themselves to his lust, which is indeed a most damnable trick. For these people seek, like a crooked judge, to bend the justice of God’s Law to their own liking; thus these are also "men of a corrupt mind," <term>1 Timothy 6:5</term>.

This happens very often; walk through the streets, listen to what goes on there, and you will perceive that among the multitude of people—who themselves so greatly neglect to do the will of God—there is a constant complaint and grieving because they do not have their own way.

For the essence of the power of <term>free choice</term><note>original: "wille-keur"; refers to the capacity of the will to decide between options</note> does not consist in being able to carry out what one intends, but in the intending and striving toward the execution.

That such a power—to be able to accept or refuse, to pursue or to flee from something that is presented to us—exists in man, even after the fall of man and before he is restored again, cannot be denied. It can also easily be proven with clear evidence; because:

1. Man, even in his fallen state, has remained a <term>rational creature</term><note>original: "redelijcke creature"</note>; that is, a creature that does not only have desires and affections like the irrational animals, but also uses reason. Through reason, similar and dissimilar things, present and future things, are weighed and distinguished along with their circumstances and consequences. To what end would the power to distinguish, to some extent, various things that come before him as good or evil, as praiseworthy or blameworthy, serve man if, alongside his understanding and reason, he had no power to choose what he wants and reject what he wants from all presented things? Or to accept or refuse a thing presented to him for deliberation? If he did not have this power of choice, then man would not be Lord and Master of his own actions; and his deeds would be neither praiseworthy nor blameworthy. But now we know that it stands quite differently with the conduct of men; thus, he has still retained his free will.

<margin>Thus man has also retained his free choice of will in the Fall.</margin>
So it stands firm that man has also retained his choice of will in the Fall: for it is also certain and sure (which above all serves to be noted in this treatise) that through the fall of man no, indeed no powers at all, were taken from him: if he previously had sight, he still has it; if he had a power of desiring, of affection, of moving, he still has it; if he had an understanding and reason, he still has it: but they are merely corrupted, damaged, and become sinful, unfit for good, and ready instruments for evil. So it stands also with the free choice of the will of man, so then there falls no dispute over whether the unregenerate <note>The "un-again-born" or those not yet spiritually renewed by grace.</note> man has a free choice of will or not: But there only falls consideration and dispute as to how it stands with the free choice of the will of man who is yet unregenerate, and still lies in the fall and corruption. To judge rightly of this now, we must distinguish the objects or the presented matters with which the free choice of the will of man has to concern itself: now these are all such things which occur to man, and concerning which he has deliberation and consideration, whether he shall practice and do them, or avoid and leave them.

Now these things are not all of one nature and occasion; for they are either such which solely have a regard for the present natural or civil life of man; or they are such which have a regard for the things of God, and for the spiritual and future life in the

<column-break/>

other world; the former the Scripture calls <term>biōtika</term> <note>original: "βιωτικὰ" — things pertaining to ordinary life or livelihood.</note>, that is, the things that concern this life (1 Cor. 6:3); the latter <term>ta tou Theou</term> <note>original: "τὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ" — the things of God.</note> (1 Cor. 2:11). Now in regard to both of these, many things present themselves to man, either as good and acceptable, or as evil and rejectable, concerning which the free choice of the will of man is accustomed to have its operation; it follows then that we now examine concerning both of these, how it stands with the free choice of the will of man.

<margin>Concerning all things, so far that everything he chooses, he chooses voluntarily.</margin>
As for this, we must know in general that man's free choice of will has its operation concerning all these, namely, when any of these things are proposed, to either accept or reject the same; this cannot be denied. For man has not lost this power through the fall; but only this power, like the rest, is damaged and corrupted by the fall; so then here again the question is not whether man has a free choice of will concerning both these things; but how the free choice of the corrupted man is accustomed to apply and employ itself concerning these things; that then serves to be examined concerning both things separately: for the free choice does not employ itself in the same way concerning both.

<margin>And as much as concerns the things belonging to the natural and civil life, man can choose the good and reject the evil.</margin>

### Chapter XXXVIII
#### Concerning the Conscience.

<margin>What the conscience is.</margin>
Hitherto we have treated at length all the powers of man, which at first instance and appearance seem only to serve to highly exalt man in himself, and to make him worthy, more than all other visible creatures. Now there is one power remaining, which at first instance and properly was placed in man, to make man understand on God's behalf that he has received all the aforementioned powers from God, in order to serve and glorify God therewith. Therefore we recount this power last of all, as being inwardly created and placed in man for this purpose: to hold God's side, and to see to it that God the Lord might be served and honored with all the previously treated powers.

Now this power is called by one word the conscience <note>original: "conscientie"</note>, which is a particularly high power of man through which he takes knowledge of his own condition, as it stands before God.

So also Conscience in good Dutch signifies "joint-knowledge" <note>original: "mede wetenschap"; the author is explaining the etymology of the Latin 'conscientia' (with-knowledge) by translating it into the Dutch 'medewetenschap'</note>; that is, to know something with another; namely, that another also knows it; and because we know thousands upon thousands of things, and ten thousand, which others also know; and yet here in a special

<column-break/>

manner, this power is called "joint-knowledge" by the Holy Spirit in many places of the Holy Scripture, so there must be something special in it; and it is this.

This power, of which we now speak, is called conscience or joint-knowledge, not in respect to the fact that we know this or that with other men; but in respect to the fact that we know something with God, yes, very often with God alone; so that through this power of the conscience we know thousands upon thousands of things that no men in the world know, except only we and God; such as are all those things that commonly go on in our heart, of which God alone is a knower, or those things which we have committed in secret, of which no men in the world can be witnesses: See, the knowledge of these things is by excellence called conscience or joint-knowledge in respect to God; because it has, namely, such an excellent, preeminent, and certain "joint-knower" who knows all the things that go on in the secret of our heart as well as we do, being a knower of hearts.

And this power is indeed principally called conscience or joint-knowledge in respect to those most secret things that go on in our heart, which only we and God the Lord know: so also the Scripture often simply calls this power our heart, 1 John 3:20, 21 and elsewhere; and accordingly it is also testified that God the Lord shall reveal the hidden things of the heart, 1 Corinthians 4:5, Romans 2:15, 16, where the conscience is properly spoken of; looking upon which Job, when he was insulted in many ways by his friends regarding those things which solely and alone concerned his heart, and all the secret—

### Of the Nature and General Condition of the Conscience.

Regarding the nature of the conscience, to perceive it properly, we shall treat four things. 1. What the "proposed matter" <term>object: the thing toward which the conscience is directed</term> of the conscience is, with which it occupies itself. 2. What the manner is in which it works. 3. What its wonder is. 4. What its usefulness is.

#### 1. Of the proposed matter of the conscience.

<margin>The object of the conscience is, in general, all the conduct of man.</margin>
The proposed matter with which the conscience busies itself, and concerning which it works, is all the conduct of man in thoughts, in inclinations, words, works, doing, and refraining; as the same has a regard toward God, and falls into consideration whether it might please or displease God; whether it be well or poorly done. I say, all the conduct of man *himself*; for the conscience properly does not meddle with what concerns others, further than man takes that upon himself and makes it his own. So then the conscience meddles with all the occurrences of man's life and conduct, as they are viewed as permitted or unpermitted, profitable or unprofitable. **1 Cor. 10:27 etc.**

Many people make no difficulty when they have lied, cheated, danced, or jumped about, because their conscience is now so "broad" (being poorly instructed) that, like a fisherman’s boots, it does not notice small pebbles or even large lumps.

<margin>To the same end, it also has need of memory.</margin>
Furthermore, man also has need of memory. For he must remember things if his conscience is to have any operation concerning them. Because of this, it often happens that a forgetful conscience is judged to be a good and peaceful conscience.

<margin>Secondly, it has great power and authority from God.</margin>
As for the second point, namely the authority and power with which it must be provided to enforce what it proposes as being required by God: it has received a very great authority and power from the Lord its King, who placed it within man. For it is provided and strengthened with all that is desirable in Heaven and all that is terrifying in Hell. Thus it sits there in the heart of man, having as it were in its right hand Heaven and all its desired joy and glory, and in its left hand Hell and all its terrifying pains and torments. Thus it has great retribution at hand: on the one side, certain vengeance against those who will not listen to it; therefore it is also said in the Scriptures to "bite," to "pierce the heart" (Acts 2:37), and to "strike" (1 Samuel 24:6; 2 Samuel 24:10). And this is that worm that begins here

<column-break/>

to gnaw, and which hereafter never stops, if one does not provide for it in time (Mark 9:44). On the other side, it also has certain comfort for those who listen to it, and it strokes the heart kindly; even amidst the heaviest accusations (as happened to Job and Paul, 2 Corinthians 1:12), it gives a foretaste of eternal life.

And see, thus the conscience ignites, as it were, the glow of Hell in the soul and the mind of the one who will not do God’s work at its urging; and, conversely, it spreads Heaven out kindly over the head of the one who does listen to it and observes God’s work.

<margin>Who confirms its verdict.</margin>
And this power and authority of the conscience comes from this: that every person is convinced in their own heart and mind that God the Lord will uphold and confirm the verdict of the conscience. Just as those who are in dealings with a commissioner <note>original: "commissaris" - an official representative or deputy</note> of their own King, and hold it for certain that he follows his instructions correctly, cannot help but fear if they act against their King’s business—knowing that the Commissioner will complain about it to the King, and that the King will uphold his complaint; and so, conversely, when they do well.

And see, thus it stands with the operation of the conscience in general; it always stands on God’s side, provided with Divine power and authority. It always holds with God; it may be deceived, it may be misled, it may think that something is God’s cause which is not God’s cause; but deceived or not deceived, in intention and in...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the conscience, specifically contrasting it with the corrupted human intellect and detailing its active role in guiding future actions.</meta>

# Deformed, Reformed.

In its intent, the conscience always stands on God’s side; unlike the intellect—as it is now corrupted—which, even if it knows that God does not want a certain thing, or indeed does want it, sometimes speaks for the one and against the other, contrary to God’s will. The intellect allows itself to be misused by the will to strengthen sin and defend all manner of wickedness. The conscience does not do this.

<margin>The work of the conscience in particular regarding what is yet to be done, or looking at what has already been done.</margin>
II. Now it follows that we examine the workings of the conscience more specifically. The workings of the conscience, when considered specifically, look either toward that which is yet to be done, or they look toward that which has already been done.

Regarding what is yet to be done, or is currently being done, the conscience has two functions here.

<margin>1. To do what God wills.</margin>
1. Whatever God wants to have done, the conscience always advises toward it, without regarding anything else; whether King or Prince; life or death; loss or gain: it does not look at any of those things, nor whatever else of that nature there may be; but rather promotes what God wants to have done. It says to the person: "Do it, even if all Kings, Princes, and the whole world were against you; even if you had to walk into a fire for it; even if you had to lose your life for it." Thus, the conscience is like the overseers whom Solomon placed over the laborers working on the construction of the Temple, to drive them forward in their work. This gave courage to the Holy Apostles, *Acts* 4:19. <note>original: "H. Apostelen"</note>

<margin>2. Conversely, it advises against doing what is against God's will.</margin>
2. Conversely, whatever God the Lord does not want to have done, the conscience always advises against, no matter what profit, advantage, or gain might otherwise seem to lie therein; and even if the great and the

<column-break/>

mighty of the world, who hold the power of life and death in their hands, call us to it; the conscience nevertheless says: "Do it not, even if the whole world should fall upon your body, even if one were to roast you on a gridiron like a fish." And thus the conscience is like the wife of Pilate, who sent to him and had him told: "Have nothing to do with that righteous man: for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him: see to it that you do not condemn the innocent, not for the sake of the whole world," *Matthew* 27:19. This restrained Joseph, Daniel, and many other men of God.

And thus the conscience is, on the one hand, a spur to make us run in the way of God’s commandments, in all holy contemplations that God requires of us; on the other hand, it is a bridle to hold us back, so that we do not run into the evil way, and do not do that which displeases God and is against His will.

<margin>With arguments from the Natural Law or God's Holy Word.</margin>
And the conscience strengthens its counsel with arguments taken from the knowledge of those first fundamental principles <note>original: "gront-regulen"</note> that are imprinted in the human heart; as well as with the judgment further rendered in God’s Word on the matter. It adds to this God’s promises and threats, and shows that God is yet higher than the highest, and that He can cast both Soul and Body into Hell; therefore He must indeed be feared above all, just as we are always accustomed to most respect the commands that come from the highest Lords, because they have the most power to compel and punish us.

And see, since the Conscience, as God’s Officer, always sees to it that God’s work is done, so shall also

# Adam, Righteous

God always takes the matter of the conscience to heart and maintains it against whomever it might be.

<margin>Even when it errs.</margin>
And this is not only when the conscience is already rightly informed and truly drives God’s cause correctly; but also when, missing God’s cause, it thinks it is doing well. If it is then nevertheless not listened to by the person—even though the person themselves knows no better, nor thinks otherwise than that the conscience intends what is right and drives God’s cause—then the Lord God will also take that to heart and subsequently punish the person. This is not because they did what was fundamentally evil or left out what was in truth good, but because of the low esteem for His Majesty. For the person, thinking and knowing no better than that God Himself willed it so (as the conscience advised or discouraged), nevertheless did not heed it; but preferred to follow what pleased their flesh rather than doing what they judged would please God.

<margin>Thus we may never act against the conscience.</margin>
Therefore, in all things, a person must pay close attention to their conscience and look to it especially: first, that they never act against their conscience; for the Lord always counts that as being done against Him, because the conscience is God’s deputy <note>original: "gedeputeerde" - an official representative or legal proxy</note>.

<margin>And must also strive to be well-informed themselves.</margin>
Secondly, that their conscience might indeed be well-informed; for as long as a person’s conscience is poorly informed and has a bad grip and foundation, it stands so utterly piteous and miserable with the person that, whether they do it or leave it, they always sin against their God. If they do it, they sin because truly the matter is fundamentally unsound; if they leave it, they sin

<column-break/>

because they regard God so little that, where they hold it to be God’s will that it be done, they nevertheless dare to leave it undone.

And so much has been said regarding the working of the conscience over those things which are yet to be done, or are in the doing. Now, as for those things which have been done, the conscience has particular workings therein, both here in this life and in the future.

In this life, the conscience has a fourfold working regarding what has been done by the person. 1. It keeps a close record of all that is done. 2. It convicts of what has been done. 3. It terrifies over what has been done poorly. 4. It comforts over what has been done well.

<margin>1. The conscience keeps a close record of everything.</margin>
1. First, the conscience observes what the person does or leaves undone, whether it be good or evil, in thoughts, words, and deeds: nothing can slip past it that it wishes to note. See, it sits in the pit of the human heart, so it also knows all their secrets; it sits there where the origin of thoughts, words, and deeds is; it sees how they are stirred, set in motion, and brought forth. Even if there were no person in the world who knew anything of what we do, our conscience always knows it; therefore we are accustomed to saying that the conscience is like a thousand witnesses: for it keeps a record of all that the person does; it also notes with what heart they do or leave it; it keeps a book for the final judgment, which shall then be opened <term>Revelation 20:12</term> <note>original: "Apoc. 20. 12." referring to the Apocalypse or Book of Revelation</note>. So it is like an entirely alert and ready Notary, who always has his pen in hand and quickly records in his Protocol <note>A notary's official register or minute-book</note> all that is dictated to him. See, through the help of the memory...

# Misshapen, Reshaped.

This is how it proceeds: The conscience, through its operation and activity, impresses upon the mind of man the images and the forms of all human actions, exactly as they are in deed and in truth, whether good or evil. It is testified that the sins of Judah were written in their hearts as if with an iron pen, and with the point of a diamond, *Jeremiah 17:1.* This is what the conscience does; it places such an image within the person as the work itself brings forth; it presses like a counter-seal, entirely lifelike, upon the mind of man, which in this regard is like a tablet, ready to receive all impressions.

Thus, if a person commits adultery, the conscience impresses a foul, ugly stain and the image of the loathsome adultery upon the soul; likewise of murder, of theft, of usury, of lies and deceit; and it presses that so deeply and so firmly into the person that the impression of it will not go out of itself in eternity; nor can it be erased by soap, nor by much saltpeter <note>original: "sai-peter"; a reference to Jeremiah 2:22 regarding the inability of physical cleaning agents to wash away moral guilt</note> *Jeremiah 2:22.* No "strong water" <note>term: "sterck water" (aqua fortis/nitric acid); used here metaphorically for the most powerful solvents known at the time</note> in the world can remove it; but only the heart-blood of the Son of God *Hebrews 9:14.* On the other hand, the conscience also impresses upon the mind of man the images of all good works and deeds that we do: when we, with a good, fine, and moved heart toward God and our neighbors, give alms, do well to the miserable, defend the innocent, praise and prize our God, celebrate His Holy Sabbath, and use His Holy Supper well, then the conscience also makes impressions of these good works upon the mind of man, and that shall also remain standing firm there until the day of judgment.

<column-break/>

So also this Notary <note>The author uses "Notary" as a metaphor for the conscience, which legally records every human action</note> keeps a much more faithful book than that unjust Steward. *Luke 16.* And even though that which this Notary has recorded in the soul may be somewhat darkened for a time by the intervening dust of earthly business in this life—just as we see that what is written deeply and clearly in gravestones <note>original: "sarcken"</note> is sometimes so darkened by the dust and filth that gets upon it that one cannot read it—nevertheless, it remains firmly written, and if one merely wipes away that dust, one can clearly read what is written there; exactly so it is with that which the conscience records. It may be somewhat darkened by worldly business; but it remains nonetheless written there and remains clearly legible; and this is also recorded: that the person has allowed his conscience to be so fouled, which shall also all come to light on the last day, and God the Lord shall bring it to remembrance *Psalm 50:21.* This should be noted, and this ought reasonably to restrain us from doing evil and give us courage to do well; for even if no one knows it, our own conscience and our God know it: is that not enough? This consideration, then, ought to move us to the highest degree to avoid evil and to practice good. For truly, who shall not reasonably fear to do evil? Who shall

<margin>Secondly, she convicts the person of what he has done.</margin>

For they may have a poor memory regarding that matter, from which their tranquility arises; but now everyone knows that a poor memory cannot make a good conscience; indeed, since the conscience must use the memory for her service, a poor memory must result in a poor operation of the conscience.

<margin>Thirdly, the conscience strikes and gnaws over the committed sin.</margin>

# Adam, Righteous

<margin>
In the life to come,
</margin>
In the life to come, the conscience has these further functions: that it accompanies man until he stands before the judgment of God; it goes with him and carries its protocol <note>original: "protocol" — a record-book or register of deeds</note> with it, in which it has noted all the deeds of men, in order to give a testimony of everything according to the truth, Revelation 20:12. See, thus it stands with the conscience: it is born with us, but it does not die with us; it lives on in the world to come and accompanies the soul until the judgment. It is a companion from whom we cannot depart, whom we cannot dismiss, who always clings to us and always goes with us. Now, the testimony of the conscience is twofold, according to the twofold condition of men: believers or unbelievers, godly or godless.

<margin>
The conscience shall accuse the godless.
</margin>
As for the godless, who live and die in such a state, it stands thus: all the good that they think they have done shall only be found as a filthy garment before the judgment of God, and it shall in no way be remembered, Ezekiel 18:24. On the contrary, all their sins, all their evil whims, and all their abominations shall be remembered on the last day; and regarding this, the conscience shall have this function: it shall convict the man of his stubbornness, resentment, and disobedience. There, the conscience shall complain against the man thus:

> "See, Lord God, you had placed me within the man to warn him and turn him away from evil, to urge him toward the good. I have continually acted according to the information I received from the understanding. At such a time, Lord, when this man practiced impurity, practiced usury, lied, deceived, etc., I told him he

<column-break/>

must not do it; but he struck me on the mouth and commanded me to <unclear>be silent</unclear>. I nevertheless frequently persisted <unclear>after</unclear> <unclear>that</unclear>, but could obtain nothing. He <unclear>often</unclear> ran there, against <unclear>my</unclear> <unclear>warning</unclear>, to do evil. I also <unclear>frequently</unclear> admonished him toward the good, but I only seldom received a hearing. And even then, he did not do it as I said he ought to do."

See, thus shall the conscience accuse the godless, and God the Lord shall also judge accordingly, in so far as it serves to weigh down the godless. For otherwise, God sees even further than our conscience, 1 John 3:20.

<margin>
And justify the faithful.
</margin>
As for the godly and faithful, all their sins shall not be remembered in the judgment of God; but they shall stand clothed with the righteousness of Christ, which shall cover all their unrighteousness; and all their good works shall follow them, Revelation 14:13. And their conscience shall only give testimony of that which they have done well, and declare how firmly and diligently they always sought to listen to the good conscience, and to preserve it, 1 Timothy 1:19, to exercise themselves therein, Acts 24:16, and in all things to maintain a good conscience, Hebrews 13:18.

<margin>
Which ought to make us strive greatly for a good conscience.
</margin>
This, then, should rightly and powerfully urge us again to strive in every way to maintain a good conscience, so that we might be found in Christ Jesus on that day, not having our own righteousness but the righteousness of Christ, Philippians 3:9, so that our conscience might testify nothing but good of us.

# V Deformed, Reformed.

<margin>
The conscience is the most wonderful power of all.

### §. On the Wonderfulness of the Conscience.

THE wonderfulness of the conscience is very great: Although we have truly said much above regarding the other powers of man, the conscience nevertheless seems to surpass them all in its marvelous nature.

<margin>
As if it were another person within the person.
</margin>

See, the conscience sits there within the human being as if it were another person inside the man, and as if it did not belong to the man in whom it sits, but to someone else. We see that where man is accustomed to making an idol of himself—so that he is very single-minded in his own cause, always speaking in his own favor, defending and excusing his own actions (which is why a man may not legally give testimony in his own affairs)—and while all other powers of the man exert themselves alongside him and help him wherever they can and may: there the conscience remains alone by itself. It seems to have no fellowship nor love for the man; and although it is also a power of the man, it nevertheless takes the side of God. It testifies as readily against the man, when he is truly guilty before God, as the most bitter enemy he could have on earth. It pays heed neither to the will, nor to the <term>fleshly understanding</term> <note>original: "vleeſchelijck verſtandt" - the human intellect when driven by worldly or selfish desires rather than spiritual truth</note> of the man, nor to any affections or desires; it does not care how much the man is distressed, tormented, burdened, and troubled by the testimony it gives against him; it nevertheless

<column-break/>

proceeds with it; it does not for that reason cease in the least to give full testimony to the truth.

<margin>
Never adapting itself to flatter the man through self-love.
</margin>

We see how some people lie so burdened by the testimony of their conscience that they seem to have a Hell in their heart and are likely to perish with it: yet the conscience has no pity for this; it bites, it stings, it strikes just as unmercifully as it finds that the man has done evil. Thus the conscience sits in the midst of the man like a small God <note>original: "klippe God" - literally a 'small' or 'petty' god, acting as a local divine representative</note> and does the things of God, and not the things of man; nor will it in any way allow itself to be reconciled with the man, unless the man first reconciles himself with God. It holds fast, as much as it can and may, to those first <term>fundamental rules of godliness</term> <note>original: "grondt-reghelen der Godtſalicheyt"</note>; such as that God must be honored and served above all; that the wicked are to be punished: and even if the fleshly understanding seeks with the perverse reasoning of the flesh to obscure these fundamental rules, it stands on God's side and seeks to maintain them, in such a way that it is like a God to the man. If he behaves well, the man shall find no better friend in the whole world than his own conscience: if he behaves poorly, the man shall find no fiercer enemy than his own conscience. See it in Judas; he had done wrong, but meanwhile he had the friendship of the greats of the world; no one accused him of his misdeed; he now had his purse full of money: yet being pressed by his conscience, he did not rest until he had destroyed himself.

<margin>
Which wonder
</margin>

This is now all quite clearly...

# Adam, Righteous

very wondrous; but we shall touch a bit more closely upon this miraculous condition of the conscience.

<margin>From its omniscience regarding the affairs of man</margin>
Is it not entirely wondrous that the conscience is such an all-knowing Secretary in this little world <note>The "little world" or microcosm refers to the individual human being, a common Renaissance and Baroque concept.</note> that nothing can happen, however secretly it may be planned, but that this Officer of God immediately comes to the knowledge of it? The Lords of the Land have many an Officer to watch over the various doings of men; but much escapes them: there are thousands upon thousands of things they cannot uncover, though they would gladly do so; but this Officer of God has immediate knowledge of everything that goes on in this little world, if only it chooses to pay attention: For it sits in the pit of man’s heart, from which all man’s actions proceed, so that nothing can stir there without it becoming aware. Even if man can separate himself from other people when he wishes to do something, or if he can hide himself from them, he nevertheless cannot separate himself from his conscience; all things lie naked and bare before it: That is indeed wondrous.

<margin>Secondly, in its alertness to record everything.</margin>
2. Is it also not entirely wondrous that the conscience is such an alert Notary, who always sits there with pen in hand, and knows how to faithfully record all that is done by man, keeping a book of it against the great day of judgment? When we have forgotten it, it still knows how to bring it up—on this or that occasion twenty years later, or more (Genesis 42:22)—and set it before our eyes, for comfort or for terror. Is it not entirely wondrous that men have in their

<column-break/>

heart such a Secretary who knows everything? Such a Notary who records everything so perfectly, and writes it as if with iron pens, as if with the point of a diamond, which no passage of time or years, no scratching or destruction can ever erase in eternity: truly, that man has such a Notary on God’s behalf within him is also very wondrous.

<margin>Thirdly, in its faithful counsel.</margin>
3. Is it also not entirely wondrous that man has, on God’s behalf, such a resolute Counselor in his heart, who fears neither Prince, nor King, nor life, nor death; fears no loss, waits for no gain; but only observes what God the Lord wants done or left undone, and proceeds upon that, and peremptorily advises man against everything that it perceives God does not want? In such a way that even if a fiery furnace stands there fully stoked and hot, and man is brought to such an extremity that he must either go against God’s command or go into a fiery furnace, into a den of lions: this resolute Counselor, the conscience, advises man, without further hesitation, that he should rather go straight into the den of lions, into the fiery furnace, than go against God’s command (Daniel 3:18). Thus all the Martyrs of God, through the counsel of a good conscience, have chosen rather to let themselves be killed through all kinds of torments and pains, than that they should have wanted to break God’s command.

Instead, they fear and tremble before them, and would not for anything in the world dare to leap about with them as some of our wild folk <note>likely referring to iconoclasts or perhaps those newly converted from paganism</note> used to do in the beginning when they could get behind them. And all this happens because they have a conscience of the idol; that is, because they hold it in their conscience that there is truly something Divine in, with, or around it; therefore they believe that it [deserves] all honor.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

#### On the condition of the conscience before, during, and after the Fall.

Thus we see now how worthy and useful a talent the conscience is, which God the Lord has placed in man; and what our bounden duty is regarding the same. We may therefore also hold it for certain that the Lord our Master, who

<column-break/>

gave us that talent, will demand an accounting from us in His time as to how we have used and applied it. Therefore, we should now properly examine how it was given to man in the creation; how it stood before the Fall; how it stands now in the Fall; and how it is in the restoration <note>referring to the spiritual renewal or "rising up" of man through grace</note>.

For just as it stood with the other faculties, that they were subject to change, so also the conscience was created changeable—not so that it *should* change, but that being changeable toward evil, it should remain good; but, oh, alas, it has changed.

->On the uprightness of the conscience before the Fall.<-

<margin>The conscience was in the first creation.</margin>
The state of the conscience before the Fall was entirely well-disposed, just like all the other faculties of man: indeed, it was holy and blessed.

<margin>1. Holy</margin>
1. The holiness of the conscience before the Fall consisted in this: that it did not allow itself to be deceived, nor did it "close its eyes" <note>original: "d' oogen upsteken," an idiom for turning a blind eye or being bribed</note> like a faithless bailiff; but was always awake and ready for the work for which it was appointed by God; not only constantly and earnestly, but also faithfully exhorting and urging man to the work of the Lord, always giving a right account; neither offending nor erring; neither praising the Devil's work as God's work, nor the reverse; as often happens now with the conscience of man.

<margin>2. Blessed.</margin>
2. The blessedness of the conscience consisted in this: that it always had occasion to [commend] the man...

### Concerning the corruption of the conscience through and under the Fall.

<margin>The conscience is quite miserably corrupted under the Fall, although it still stands for the things of God more than any other faculty, etc.</margin>
Through the Fall of man, the conscience has also fallen from its good state, so that the conscience is in a pitiful condition; like other faculties, it is quite miserably damaged and corrupted.

### CHAPTER XXXIX.

#### Concerning the state of the conscience before, during, and after the Fall.

Thus we see now what a worthy and useful talent the conscience is, which God the Lord has placed in man; and what our bounden duty is regarding the same. So we may also hold it for certain that the Lord our Master, who gave us

<column-break/>

#### Concerning the integrity of the conscience before the Fall.

<margin>The conscience was in the first creation.</margin>

It was through this misleading conscience that *Paul* consented to the death of *Stephen*, breathed murder and threats against the Christians, and persecuted the Lord *Jesus Christ* in his members <note>referring to the body of believers</note> *Acts 8 and 9*. So it is truly that a person, being burdened with this perverse conscience, takes great pains to destroy himself and to accuse himself more deeply unto damnation, even while he thinks that he manages his affairs for the best and makes the best progress on his journey toward Heaven. This is also a very miserable state, yet it can be set right through better instruction, with God's grace added thereto; for truly, if these people knew better, they would do better. Therefore Christ prays for such people, testifying that they do not know that they do evil.

<margin>3. The conceited conscience.</margin>
3. The consciences of these people after the Fall also excuse the person far too much, where they might only be slightly excused; and they praise them too much, where they are but little to be praised: and this is a conceited conscience <term>verwaende conscientie: a conscience characterized by spiritual pride or false security</term>. This occurs when a person, because he behaves reasonably well, imagines that he cannot miss out on Heaven, while—alas!—he is still very deficient in all his deeds and has not sought, as he ought, to become a partaker of the Lord Jesus Christ, through whom alone he can be helped. This is still an evil conscience, for it

<column-break/>

makes the person entirely careless, and causes him—laughing and playing without reflection, thinking he is going to Heaven—to run toward Hell. Many people are possessed by this evil conscience and are accustomed to calling it a "quiet conscience." Likewise, when they are exhorted or better warned about something, they are accustomed to appealing to their conscience; and instead of all reason, they say that they are quite at ease in their conscience about it. They forget, meanwhile, that their conscience can give a very bad report through misunderstanding (Romans 10:2, 5) and also that God the Lord is greater than their conscience (1 John 3:20). Therefore, they ought rightly to think of the reasoning of Paul, who, even though his conscience did not accuse him, did not dare to pronounce himself innocent because of it (1 Corinthians 4:4). He did not say this to teach people to doubt, but to teach them to boast not in themselves, but in Christ; as the Apostle teaches us (1 Corinthians 1:30, 31) and did himself (Galatians 6:14, 15). These people do the opposite, being sloppy and negligent in the things of God, and having nothing other than a strong presumption, which they call a "firm faith," upon which they rest their conscience.

# Adam, Righteous,

it happens that the bell of conscience does not ring as a warning.

And even if men now place their rest and their comfort in this sleepy conscience, we nevertheless count this as a part of the misery <note>original: "rampsaligheyt"</note> of the conscience; for it is indeed easy to perceive that it is a very wretched conscience which, having as much upon its horns as Adam had when he had sinned—and even more—is nevertheless neither terrified nor startled as Adam was, but runs along cheerfully and happily, having nonetheless found no reconciliation, Job 33:24. This is indeed a very destructive conscience, which hinders man entirely from his salvation.

It was indeed better to have an uneasy conscience, which was full of fear and terror, and yet might advance toward the fellowship of Christ, upon which eternal rest shall follow; than to have a happy and restful conscience, and therewith to go cheerfully along in firm hope of eternal life while one nonetheless sticks in a damnable guilt, and if one does not look to it otherwise, will certainly reach hell thereby.

Truly, this rest of the conscience is merely like the golden dream of those who, being in prison and already condemned to death, dream that they are free and loose, and are happy about it; but waking up, they find themselves still in the shackles, and are terrified all the more: such a miserable dream, which shall only serve to greater torment, is the rest of the conscience of the unregenerate <note>original: "onweder-ghebozene"</note> and natural men; and even if this dream of theirs lasted their whole life long, it is still less in comparison to the eternal sorrow that is approaching them, than the dream of the condemned, even if that lasts but an hour.

And thus it happens then, that people who previously would not endure the lovely admonitions and knockings, nor listen to them, now fall into such a terrifying state that they cannot endure or suffer the admonitions and knockings of their own hearts; indeed, that the same pinch and press them like an unbearable burden.

# Adam, Righteous,

the smart and pain begin to take hold; then King Belshazzar’s countenance changes, the joints of his loins are loosened, and his knees knock against one another (Daniel 5:6). Yes, then Judas looks out for a rope and strangles himself (Matthew 27:5). Then Saul takes a sword and falls upon it (1 Samuel 31:4). But if the person remains alive, he goes about mourning all his life long, like Cain. He is then like a restless sea that foams up muck and filth; then he can no longer keep his own horrible sins secret. They lie as heavy as millstones upon his heart; he reveals them; he speaks of them to all who come near him, seeking relief. And in this tempest—unless God comes to his aid through a very extraordinary grace—the person finally perishes in soul and body, forever and ever without end, in the Hellish fire with the Devil and his angels.

And see, this is the wretchedness of the sinful conscience through the Fall; although some godless people die entirely unfeeling, like a stone—as Nabal did—and though they seem to enter the grave in peace, they are nevertheless not free. For however quietly they die here, they are nonetheless led before the Judgment of God, and there at last their conscience—like a raging dog that has slept until now—begins to fly at their throat, to accuse them, and to help condemn them (Luke 16, Isaiah 23, etc.).

And see, this is the pitiful state of the conscience under the Fall;

<column-break/>

and Adam and Eve became aware of this immediately, as soon as they had sinned; for through it they fell into great terror, although nowadays many of Adam’s children laugh it off for a time.

### Concerning the Restoration of the Conscience through Christ.

<margin>Concerning the restoration of the conscience through Christ.</margin>
Having now understood the nature of the conscience and what our bounden duty regarding it is—as well as how sinful and miserable the consciences of all men now are as they are by nature since the Fall, and how the same miserably misleads man—it is only right that all people who hear these things should be awakened and stirred to look out for a good conscience, to strive for it above all else, just as we are exhorted (1 Timothy 1:18-19) and as the Apostle did (Acts 24:16, Hebrews 13:18).

Now, for this purpose the Lord Jesus Christ also came into the world: to cleanse our conscience through his precious blood from our dead works <note>The author refers to "dead works" as religious or worldly acts performed without faith or spiritual life.</note> and from all that used to disturb our conscience (Hebrews 9:14). Therefore, we shall briefly point out two things regarding this:

1. In what the improvement of the conscience consists, or what the state of the improved conscience is.
2. How we might obtain it.

<margin>The improved conscience,</margin>
As for the first, we must note both the holiness and the blessedness of the improved conscience; and there...

<margin>n- last lesson and ed.</margin>
1. It makes a person strive to walk well in all things; this is what the Apostle had in mind in Hebrews 13:18, Acts 24:16, and 1 Corinthians 4:4. <note>The author cites these verses to support the idea of a clear conscience before God and men.</note> It is a very faithful proof of a good and well-reformed conscience when one is constantly admonished and spurred on by their conscience, not only to shun and avoid some sins, but all sins; and not only to observe some, but all of God's commandments.

Indeed, this must be carefully noted, for this is the only faithful proof of a good and upright conscience, as the Apostle presents it in Hebrews 13:18. This is also easy to guard: we have heard above that the conscience does not look at that which the flesh usually notices, but solely at the will of God; now the will of God calls us against all sins and toward all virtues; so the good conscience does the same, and in this, it regards no fleshly considerations.

All those must now pay attention to this who indeed make a matter of conscience out of great and horrific sins—which they would not want to commit for all the world—such as Murder, Adultery, Burglary <note>original: "Huysbrake"</note>, Perjury <note>original: "valschen Eedt"</note>, etc. But they daily give themselves over, with the consent of their conscience, to other sins: lying, cheating, fickleness, carnality, pomp and pride, excess, wantonness, foolish talk, and many such vanities; and they

<column-break/>

do not wish to be turned away from these, nor to be admonished against them, even though they know it is sin; they have trained their consciences to overlook these things <note>original: "door de vingher te sien" — to look through the fingers</note>, and are at peace even though they live in those great sins. Truly, these people must look to their situation, for it is greatly to be feared that they are still unregenerate <term>un-reborn <gloss>on-herbozene</gloss>: those who have not undergone spiritual rebirth or conversion</term> people, and are still stuck in their old coarse sins, 2 Peter 1:9. For the renewed conscience makes a person move against all sins, great and small; yes, even against such sins that are otherwise considered very convenient and profitable; it also commands a person to cut off his hands and pluck out his eyes; yes, even to cast away his most convenient members if they are a hindrance to him in the service of God.

So, on the other hand, those must also pay attention here who are accustomed to being urged by their consciences to keep their ordinary church attendance and to observe the use of the Lord's Supper, and thus to attend to public worship; but they can get permission from their conscience to let Christian house-exercises <note>family worship or private devotions</note> fall by the wayside, and make no work of them at all; yes, they consider it a mere trifle <note>original: "simelinghe" — a triviality or whim</note> that one would insist so much upon it. Oh, that these would also take heed! For the good conscience teaches us indeed to observe the great things of the Law above all; but it also admonishes us not to neglect the others; for one must always do the former, and not leave the latter undone, as Christ has taught us.

### CHAPTER XL.
#### Concerning the Image of God.

UNTIL now, by God’s gracious help and assistance, we have explained the various powers which God the Lord, according to His rich loving-kindness and wisdom, has placed in the soul of man. From these we may, in some measure, infer the condition of the human soul: namely, as we said at the beginning of this treatise, that it is a most excellent creature; spiritual and intelligent, raising man very high in honor and glory. By this, the excellence of man, as he was in the first creation, becomes more and more known.

<margin>The outstanding glory of man is evident from the fact that he was created in God’s image.</margin>
<margin>To understand this more closely, we must understand: 1. What the nature of God is.</margin>
This (namely, how glorious a creature man was in the beginning) is made most clearly understood when it is testified that he was created after God’s own image. Whoever merely reads or hears this with the proper attention must immediately be drawn to consider that man was indeed created very gloriously and excellently; seeing that God the Lord Himself testifies that he was created after His own image. That is, that he was made in the beginning as such a creature who possessed this unique quality above all other creatures: that he, in a special way, displayed and represented the nature of God his Creator Himself. This was so close and so glorious that he is testified by God Himself to bear His image, which in effect means as much as saying he was like a little God. <note>original: "kleenen Godt"</note>

# Misshapen, Reshaped.

God on earth; and that he possessed within himself, above all other visible creatures, a particular form and likeness of God the Creator himself; what greater or more glorious thing than this could be spoken of by man? And seeing that God himself testifies to these things—whose words are all seven times purified <note>A reference to Psalm 12:6, implying the absolute purity and truth of divine scripture</note> and found to be pure faithfulness and truth—it follows irreducibly that man was created very glorious and excellent. Therefore, humans, as well as the Angels, are called children of God <note>original: "Job. 1. 6."</note> and are expressly testified to be created after God’s image <note>original: "Gen. 1. 26."</note>. Thus, man was so created that he, in some measure, displayed and expressed the nature and form of his God within himself; so that, where we previously heard that the soul within man was like an Angel of God, we now understand here that man himself was like a little God <note>term: "kleenen Godt" (Microcosm/Little God) — a common Renaissance and Reformation concept where man is seen as a miniature reflection of the divine and the universe</note> in this great world.

Since so much is contained in the testimony that man is created after God’s likeness, we must investigate the nature of the Image of God, with which man was clothed at creation, somewhat more closely. To do this well, we must first briefly look into both what the nature of God is, and what the nature of an image is; and from there, proceed to show what the nature of the Image of God in man consists of.

Regarding the first, namely what the nature of God is: we do not intend to speak of this at great

<column-break/>

length, but only a word, as much as fits this present occasion. The Lord our God testifies of himself that he is a God who hides himself <note>original: "Esa. 45. 15." (Isaiah 45:15)</note>. So he also testifies of his own, who are renewed after his image, that they are his hidden ones <note>original: "Psal. 83. 4."</note>. In such a way, they are not recognized by the world for who they are. Nevertheless, the Lord our God, who is such a hidden God, has in some measure revealed himself through the Creation of the world, so that he shows himself therein to be eternal, infinite, almighty, entirely wise, and good. This is shown by the great design of the world, but the great design of the world itself does not comprehend it; nor does it bear the Image of God in the sense spoken of here regarding the Image of God; but only those creatures who are endowed with reason; as we shall presently better understand from the consideration of the nature of an image, and with what distinction the Image of God is described here in man.

As for the first, namely what the nature of God is: we do not intend to speak of this
