<margin>
2. What the nature of an image is.
</margin>
As for the second, namely what the nature of an image is: the nature of an image is not only to resemble the thing of which it is an image in some aspects, but to display and present such a likeness of that thing by which it is distinguished from other things, and is recognized to be the very thing that it is.

In our judgment, this should be well noted; for the understanding of this matter can give much light in this treatment. That this is the true nature of an image is evident from this: a dog and a cat sometimes resemble each other in many things

# Adam, Upright

very nearly—in size, in color, in shape, in almost everything; nevertheless, there is something in which a cat is markedly distinguished from a dog. Therefore, he who knows them both will never mistake one for the other; so too must one not hold that a cat is the image of a dog, or the dog of the cat. For the cat does not represent that specific quality in which a dog is distinguished from all other animals, nor does the dog represent that in which the cat is distinguished. But if a Painter <note>original: "Schilder"</note> merely makes a clever outward likeness of a dog or cat with his brush on a panel, even if there is no life in it—indeed, even if a thousand things are lacking and the painting is not like the dog in those respects—yet the cat is certainly like the dog in those same respects <note>i.e., both are living, breathing animals, whereas the painting is not</note>. Nevertheless, one will not recognize the cat, but rather that painting, as the image of the dog. This is because, whatever it may or may not have in common with the dog, it possesses that by which the dog is distinguished from other animals; it represents that, and so it is the dog's image.

So we see then, that it is the nature of an image to represent that by which the thing portrayed is distinguished from all other things.

<margin>3. With what distinction man is said to be created after God's image.</margin>

Having understood this thus far, it follows that we must examine with what distinction man is said to be created after God's image; that is, to be so created that he represented something of God in which the Lord God is properly distinguished from all other things.

<column-break/>

Since the Lord is then distinguished in all things, it seems in vain that one should place His image in anything. Nevertheless, we must also hold this for certain: that the Lord God does not testify here in vain and without distinction concerning man—which He does not testify of the other creatures—that he was created after God's image.

But the same is found only in good men and angels; thus also the children of God and the children of the world, the angels and the devils, are distinguished from one another by holiness—even by holy blessedness and blessed holiness. # Misshapen, Reshaped,

The lower powers of man—such as the desires of the flesh and the affections of the heart—when they are set in motion, often blind the understanding and always hang upon the neck of the will, soliciting it to consent to their desires. From this, great disorders arise within man and in his conduct; just as it always tends to happen when those who ought to be guided themselves begin to take the rudder in hand. It stood quite differently with man when the image of God in him was yet unblemished; for then the movement did not begin from the bottom upwards, but from above and from the highest powers downwards; the enlightened understanding was the leader, etc., and then all things also went quite well.

But here a matter now falls into consideration, which we must observe a little; we have understood above that although the will has great power and command in man, there are nevertheless still powers in man which the will can only restrain, but cannot change according to its own mind, nor make them otherwise disposed than they are—such as the power to draw nourishment to oneself <note>The vegetative or involuntary functions of the body</note>. And regarding this, the following consideration now arises: since it is natural for the hungry stomach of man to desire food, and since this power is not in the power of man's will to change, to command, or to set according to its pleasure; whether it does not follow from this that, by occasion of these powers, confusion or discord must necessarily have arisen now and then in man? Namely, when these lower powers, according to their character and nature, should desire to eat and

<column-break/>

to drink, and the higher powers, such as the understanding and the will, should find it otherwise advisable and could not approve that it should happen at that time.

This seems to be the case; from which it would then also follow that man, even in his first creation, would have been subject to the aforementioned confusion—which, indeed, is in no way to be admitted. Therefore some, to avoid this, have argued that man, viewed simply as he first stood created by God, was truly so disposed that he would have been subject to the aforementioned confusion, but that the Lord God therefore further endowed him with a supernatural righteousness <note>original: "boven natuerlijcke gerechticheydt"</note>, with which he would have been able to rightly guide the aforementioned lower powers. This assertion, however, is not to be accepted; for by it the preceding difficulty is not warded off, but rather conceded—namely, that man, in his first creation, would have been subject to that same confusion from the very character and nature of the created powers. This truly is in no way to be admitted, for it attributes imperfection to God and brings with it this absurdity: as if the Lord God had so imprudently created that glorious creature, man, that He had let him leave His hand so defectively that He would have been necessitated to improve it by providing him with supernatural powers and gifts, in order to restrain the untamed lower powers with them, as if with a bridle. Which is entirely un- <note>The text cuts off mid-word: "un-fitting" or "un-reasonable"</note>

### On the condition of the image of God before the fall.

<margin>The condition of God's image before the fall.</margin>AS for the condition of God's image before the fall, the same was in every part most glorious and excellent, just as we have explained here above.
For all the powers of man in the first creation were entirely holy, even as He who had created and made him; all his powers were well-disposed, in good order, rule, and measure, and so also were all his actions; God commanded, and man obeyed; the understanding grasped and comprehended rightly the sense and meaning of the Creator, so far as it pleased Him to reveal His will; the memory retained the same, without forgetting anything that was necessary to remember and which concerned the conscience; the will took up with all readiness to practice that which the right understanding had grasped and comprehended of the Lord's mind.
Upon this followed all the inclinations, lusts, and desires; these let themselves be guided by those higher powers of the soul: none of those which had to be obedient and guided rebelled or were striving against the powers whose office it was to guide and command.
The will did not rise up against the understanding; nor did the inclinations thwart the will; no lusts or desires manifested themselves

<column-break/>

in man which did not agree with right reason and with the will of God; from this arose also great peace and tranquility of conscience, the man being conscious of no evil, rejoiced in the awareness of his glory, and that was to him a continual feast. Thus man was like a well-set clockwork <note>original: "uyrwerck" - a common 17th-century metaphor for the soul's harmony</note>, of which the will of the most high God and Creator was like the weight, which fittingly set in motion all the cogs and wheels of the same, from which then arose not only the right striking of the bell at the proper time, but also a very pleasant and lovely prelude and postlude, a very sweet and lovely accord; and how could it be otherwise, for the Lord God Almighty Himself had set it, Psalm 119:73. # Adam, Upright,

and to perform works.

And the reason for this is as follows: because the renewed person, now having the Spirit of Jesus Christ within them as a new origin and fountain of life, begins—following the previously mentioned order—to lead a new life from that new fountain and origin of life; to carry out new thoughts, desires, words, and works. For we have indeed now heard that as the fountain of life is, so also is the life and activity of the creature.

Regarding this, a reflection now arises which is very useful to note carefully, in order to properly grasp the matter of the Christian life, which is established in man through the renewal of the image of God. It is so expressly testified to us that the Spirit of Christ is given to renewed people, which clothes them as if anew with the image of God over all their powers; and yet it is maintained everywhere that these same renewed people still retain their old soul and all its powers. For indeed, all the changes of which we spoke previously take place in that very soul and in those very powers which the person received when they first received life. For this is certain and sure: that on the one hand, encroaching sin does not annihilate the soul or the powers of the soul, but violates and corrupts them; and on the other hand, the coming grace, the new Spirit, and the new image do not annihilate the old soul or its powers, but improve and restore them. All this being so, I say, this reflection arises: how things then stand with the person who is now renewed and recreated according to the image

<column-break/>

of God; whether they are then so completely and entirely renewed that nothing of the "old rag" <note>original: "oude vodde"; a colloquial term for the corrupt old nature or the "old man" in theological terms</note> remains in the person, or not.

<margin>Yet the fountain and origin of the corrupted life also remains in the renewed person during this life.</margin>

This must be noted very carefully; and the answer serves here: namely, that the renewal of the image of God in man is conducted in such a way that in this life it only happens piecemeal <note>original: "stucks wijse"; meaning partially or in stages rather than all at once</note>. That is to say, in such a manner that there always remains much of the old corruption in the person while in this life. Therefore the Apostle himself testifies that we "know only in part" (1 Corinthians 13:9) and that he "did not do the thing he wanted" (Romans 7:15). So it is that the fountain and the origin of the natural and corrupted life remains partially present even in the renewed person. In such a way, there are found in the renewed person two principles of life, as it were: a fountain of natural life, which is our soul such as it is; and a fountain of spiritual life, which is the Spirit of Jesus Christ. Because of this, it happens that whereas the unregenerate and unrenewed person leads only a naturally corrupt and sinful life—having only their sinful and corrupted soul as a principle of life, which is so corrupted, muddy, and troubled that all the actions of that life are found to be purely corrupt, muddy, and sinful—the renewed person, by contrast, can lead not only a natural life but also a spiritual life, as one who has within them not only the fountain of natural life (the soul) but also the fountain of spiritual life.

### Concerning the condition of the image of God before the fall.

<margin>Concerning the condition of the image of God before the fall.</margin>
**A**S concerns the condition of God's image before the fall, the same was in every part most glorious and excellent, just as we have explained above.

For all the powers of man were entirely holy in the first creation, even as He was holy who had created and made him; all his powers were well-disposed, in good order, rule, and measure, and so also were all his actions. God commanded, and man obeyed; the understanding grasped and comprehended rightly the sense and meaning of the Creator, so far as it pleased Him to reveal His will; the memory retained the same, without forgetting anything that was necessary to keep or that concerned the conscience; the will took up with all readiness to practice that which the right understanding had grasped and comprehended of the Lord's mind.

Upon this followed all the inclinations, pleasures, and desires; these allowed themselves to be guided by those higher powers of the soul: none of those which ought to obey and be led rebelled or were striving against the powers whose office it was to lead and to command. The will did not rise up against the understanding, nor did the inclinations thwart the will; no pleasures or desires manifested themselves

<column-break/>

in man which did not agree with right reason and with the will of God; from this also arose great peace and tranquility of conscience. Man, being conscious of no evil, rejoiced in the awareness of his glory, and that was to him a continual feast. Thus man was like a well-set clockwork <note>original: "uyrwerck" — a common 17th-century metaphor for the soul's harmony</note>, of which the will of the most high God and Creator was like the weight, which fittingly set all the cogs and wheels in motion; from which there arose not only the right striking of the bell at the proper time, but also a very pleasant and lovely prelude and postlude, a very sweet and lovely accord. And how could it be otherwise? For the Lord God Almighty Himself had set it;
> Psalm 119:73. The breath of the Almighty set it in motion, Job 32:8, and His oversight preserved it in good condition, Job 10:12. <note>The author combines these verses to emphasize God's sustaining power over the human "mechanism."</note>

See, thus it was with man in the first creation; thus he bore the image of God upon him. At that time, man could also be his own savior <note>original: "salichmaker" — here meaning the one who maintains his own state of grace</note>; it then rested upon him to preserve himself in that holy and blessed state. Man, being clothed with God's image in the first creation, had the power within himself to direct all his strengths for the best, according to the will of God.

Which, however, is not to be understood as if man would have stood on his own legs and powers in such a way that he would no longer have needed God's support and blessing to keep himself in good condition: for this has always been true, that *in God we live, move, and have our being*, Acts 17:28, and it is not possible

<margin>
The condition of God’s image during the fall.

**W**ITH REGARD to the condition of God’s image during the fall, we must know that Adam, through the fall, entirely marred and broke the image of God; and we likewise, all who have descended from him, are also involved in the same fall, so that we are by nature entirely marred and corrupted. And consequently, we also perceive in the scriptures that the Holy Spirit finds and judges two kinds of beings within the renewed man: namely, the old man and the new man. The old man still carries the old image <note>The "old image" refers to the corrupted nature inherited from Adam</note> and has only his corrupted soul and the corrupted parts thereof as the fountain of his life. As the renewed man observes this with all his might, there arises from it a constant struggle within the same man between the old and the new man, between the flesh and the spirit *Galatians 5:17; Romans 7:23.* Much is mentioned concerning this spiritual struggle throughout Holy Scripture, and the reborn are exhorted and awakened in many ways to exert themselves bravely therein as long as they are in this life. *Ephesians 6:10,* etc.

And see, from this condition of the reborn man arises the spiritual struggle of which so much is mentioned in the scriptures; which for the poor man, as long as he is in this life, proves very anxious and hard. For he is now not only attacked from without by Satan, but also has within himself the evil corruption of his flesh, which stands on Satan's side and constantly counsels the man toward evil. It was different with Adam before he had fallen; he had only a struggle from without, which Satan inflicted upon him, just as did the Lord Jesus Christ. *Matthew 4:4.*

<margin>How one can know if God’s image is renewed in us.</margin>
By this we shall be able to know: namely, that we observe whether we are truly led by a different principle of life than our corrupt soul; whether we are indeed led by the Spirit of Christ <note>original: "Geest Christi"</note>, or if He has the upper hand in us; whether the movements of Christ’s spirit tend to prevail in us more than the natural movements of our soul; for, as we have now heard, where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty (2 Corinthians 3:17). And even if it does not happen without a struggle, it nevertheless proceeds so that where the Spirit is, there is liberty, there is victory.

The Spirit of Jesus Christ now teaches us to walk in the footsteps of Christ (1 Peter 2:21, 1 John 2:6). If we then wish to know whether we are renewed after the image of Christ by the Spirit of Christ, let us see if we walk just as Christ walked (1 John 2:6). He was meek and lowly in heart (Matthew 11:29); let us see if we are also so. He was long-suffering and patient; let us see if we are also so. He was temperate, chaste, pure, and kind; let us see if we are also so. He was not one for speaking ill, uttering useless chatter, scolding, slandering, or rendering evil for evil; let us see if we also guard ourselves against such things. He was much in prayer, and continually observed the religious services and assemblies (Luke 4:16); let us see if we do likewise.

If it goes thus with us, then it appears that we are led by the Spirit of Christ; if we speak, think, and act as the Spirit of Christ gives us utterance (Acts 2:4); if we

<column-break/>

become conformed to Christ and show His image in us, then all is well. But if it goes thus with any person—that he lies, deceives, and uses falsehood—that is not the image of Christ, for the Lord Christ would not have done so. That a person mocks or utters useless chatter at meals and in company—that is not the nature of Christ; Christ did not do so when He was in the flesh. If a person quarrels, disputes, or fights—that does not display the image of Christ; His voice was not heard in the streets. If a person lives in lewdness, <unclear>unchastity</unclear>, or fornication—that mind was far from the Lord Christ; the Lord Christ did not do so. Indeed, it is certain and sure that such is the image of the devil; for if he were to show himself here in the flesh among men, he would lie, deceive, curse, <term>swear oaths</term> <note>original: "edelen," likely referring to noble-sounding but empty oaths or prideful swearing</note>, rage, roar, drink to drunkenness, commit fornication, practice usury, spit out venom, cause disturbances, set everything in an uproar, bicker, fight, smite, and do all such things. Yet many people do these things now and still wish to be called good Christians; but we know that such behavior is not Christian: that such conduct is truly earthly, fleshly, and devilish.

# Adam, Righteous,

for we have indeed now heard that much depends upon this for us.

<margin>By what one can know if God's image is renewed in us.</margin>
Now, we may know it in this way: namely, that we observe whether we are truly led by a different principle of life than our corrupt soul is; whether we are indeed led by the Spirit of Christ <note>original: "Geest Christi"</note>, whether He has the upper hand in us, and whether the movements of the Spirit of Christ usually carry more weight with us than the natural movements of our soul; for, as we have now heard, where the Spirit of God is, there is liberty (2 Corinthians 3:17). And even if it does not happen without a struggle, it nevertheless happens so that where the Spirit is, there is liberty, there is victory.

The Spirit of Christ Jesus now teaches us to walk in the footsteps of Christ (1 Peter 2:21; 1 John 2:6). If we then wish to know whether we are renewed by the Spirit of Christ according to the image of Christ, let us see whether we walk just as Christ walked (1 John 2:6). He was meek and humble of heart (Matthew 11:29); let us see if we are also so. He was long-suffering and patient; let us see if we are also so. He was temperate, chaste, pure, and kind; let us see if we are also so. He was not one to speak ill, to engage in useless chatter, to scold, to blaspheme, or to repay evil for evil; let us see if we also guard ourselves against such things. He was much in prayer, and continually observed the religious services and assemblies (Luke 4:16); let us see if we do likewise.

If it goes thus with us, then it appears that we are led by the Spirit of Christ; if we speak, think, and act as the Spirit of Christ gives us utterance (Acts 2:4); if we

<column-break/>

become conformed to Christ and show His image in us, then all is well. But if it goes so with any person that he lies, deceives, and uses falsehood, that is not the image of Christ; the Lord Christ would not have done so. That a person mocks and engages in useless chatter at meals and in company—that is not the nature of Christ. Christ did not do so when He was in the flesh. If a person quarrels, disputes, and fights, that does not display the image of Christ; His voice was not heard in the streets. If a person lives in lewdness, unchastity, or fornication, that mind was far from the Lord Christ; the Lord Christ did not do so. Indeed, it is certain and sure that such is the image of the devil; for if he were to show himself here in the flesh among men, he would lie, deceive, curse, do evil, rage, roar, drink to drunkenness, commit fornication, practice usury, incite riots, cause disturbances, throw everything into turmoil, bicker, fight, strike, and do all such things. Many people also do these things now, and yet still want to be called good Christians; but we know that such is not Christian—that such conduct is truly earthly, fleshly, and devilish.

Thus, these people are known to not have the Spirit of Christ, since they do not display the image of Christ; indeed (though they may little wish to know it), they are led by the evil spirit of Satan, since they display and express his image in many ways in their conduct.

However, since it happens now and then that even a born-again Christian person, a new creature, sometimes does something in which the devil plays a part (2 Samuel 24:1).

Those who might also become aware through this test that truly the image of *Jesus Christ* is not yet raised up in them, they must be terrified, grieved, and humbled to the highest degree; and hold this for certain and sure: that it is the most miserable state in the world to be without the image of *Christ*: then one lies naked before the wrath and the curse of God, *John 3:36.* What can it benefit a man, though he be beautifully and handsomely dressed above many of his neighbors; that he be well-armed against his enemies; if he is not clothed with this image; if he, being like kings' children in his clothing, is like the Devil in his soul.

# Deformed, Reformed.

Therefore, those who have already received the image of Christ must see to it that they obtain it more and more perfectly; and those who do not yet have it must use all diligence so that they might acquire it. To this end, he shall now propose some means <note>The author refers to himself or the instructional voice in the third person here.</note> by which the image of God might be renewed and strengthened.

### To this end, much could also be said; but we shall only briefly touch upon the most important points.

The means are of two kinds: the principal and the ministerial <term>ministerial: serving as an instrument or tool rather than the primary cause</term>.

The principal means is faith, even the true, soul-saving Christian faith: for that is like the hand with which we take hold of Christ; it is like the channel through which all those spiritual gifts that are in Christ Jesus flow down to us: to all of us it happens in this situation according to our faith; no faith, no image of God; little faith, little image of God. The renewal of the image of Christ is by the Spirit of Christ, but we do not receive the Spirit except through faith (Galatians 3:2): it facilitates the perceptible workings of the Spirit of Christ. Faith is the Mother-virtue; it is like the Divine Paintbrush with which the Spirit of God draws or paints the image of Christ once again upon our soul.

The ministerial means are of two kinds: some consist in the avoiding of that which is contrary to the image of God; others in the practicing of that which the image of God requires: and they are called ministerial means by us because they are serviceable both to faith and to the image of God

<column-break/>

itself, to promote them through faith.

1. That which we must avoid are all known sins: certainly, he who desires to have the image of God renewed in himself must guard himself, as much as he possibly can, from all known sins: there is nothing so contrary to the image of God as sin; sin is the color of the Devil, it bears the image of Satan through and through: as many sins as we commit, so many stains and smears we bring upon our soul, making ourselves more and more like the Devil, and causing the image of God to fade more and more within us.

Oh, that this were well considered! Many a man is afraid to bring a smear or a stain upon his new wedding garment; he guards himself against it with foresight—yet he is often accustomed to delighting in sin, which is the smearing and staining of his Noble soul, of that precious garment with which Adam, being clothed in his soul, was so glorious. Oh, let us guard ourselves from this, and consider that sin is a foul blotch upon the beautiful image of God; let us above all guard ourselves from sins, and say: "Shall I then go and stain that pure and shining fine linen, which are the righteous acts of the saints (Revelation 19:8 <note>original: "Apocal. 19. 8."</note>), with hellish blotches?"

2. That which we must practice is of various kinds, but especially these three things.

1. We must yield ourselves to the form of God's word (Romans 6:17). See, so it stands written there; if we desire to have the image of Christ in us, we must pay attention to the word of Christ, and conform ourselves to it in all ways: for the word of Christ has the image of Christ—the wisdom, the goodness, the power of Christ—within itself.

Think: "That is yet another beautiful, vivid color; that is yet another glorious Christian stroke <note>as in a painter's brushstroke</note> that shall make me more and more like the image of Christ," and seek thus to adorn yourself with it. And by thus practicing the counsel of the word of God, the image of God shall be more and more renewed in you through the Spirit of God, and you shall find yourself entirely clothed in every way with the image of Christ.

<margin>2. To set the walk of Christ as a pattern before one's eyes.</margin>
2. We must always set the conduct and walk of the Lord Jesus Christ, as it is related to us in the Gospel, before our eyes as an exemplar and pattern, and also arrange our doing and leaving <note>our actions and omissions</note> accordingly. We should accustom ourselves, whenever we wish to do something, to frequently imagine and ask ourselves: "What would the Lord Jesus Christ have done in this situation, had this happened to Him? How would He have behaved when He went to a wedding, when He made a different garment, when He was reviled and wronged, when He was enticed away from that for which He was sent?" We must present this to ourselves thus, and then pay attention to what is told to us in the Gospel concerning the conduct and walk of the Lord Christ, and subsequently behave and conduct ourselves accordingly. And by doing so, and thus following the exemplar and the perfect pattern...

Oh, that this were well considered! And that many a so-called Christian person, who walks about so unformed <note>meaning: lacking spiritual discipline or moral shape</note>, would take courage and practice this, and thus question themselves as to what Christ would have done in such a situation, and behave and carry themselves accordingly; what better Christians would we become? How would the image of Christ be displayed in us? How finely and Christian-like would all things then be conducted?

Indeed, all of us—who truly desire above all things that the Lord Jesus Christ might take a shape in us, that we might indeed be changed more and more into the image of Christ from glory to glory as by the Spirit of the Lord—must do in this case just as the craftsmen <note>term: "Ambacht-luyden" refers to skilled artisans or tradesmen</note> who are to make their masterpieces <note>term: "proeven" refers to the 'proof' or masterpiece required to enter a guild</note> in order to become free workmen; they surely set before their imagination in this situation some piece of work that is well-made, in which nothing is lacking, and they make their masterpiece according to it. # Adam, Upright,

these three: the understanding, the will, and the conscience.

<margin>1. The understanding.</margin>
1. The understanding, by which he—above all other things—knows how to make a distinction, not only between good and evil as perceived through the outward senses (such as what is good for the eye, the ear, the taste, the smell, and the touch, and what is conversely bad for the same, which the beasts also possess). But he further knows how to make a distinction in what is good and evil according to the soul, according to reason, according to equity, modesty, utility, justice, and godliness <note>original: "Godtvreeſentheyt"</note>. Thus, man knows that to lie and to deceive is evil; that to commit adultery and to drink to drunkenness is sin; on the contrary, that to pray to the Lord God, to fear the great God, and to love Him, is good for the soul. The animals of the field do not have this; one sees neither sign nor token of this in the animals.

<margin>2. The will.</margin>
2. The will, by which man knows how to restrain not only the lusts of his flesh (which the animals of the field also know how to do through the affections of their hearts), but by which man also knows how to restrain even the very affections of his heart, which is a higher power than any irrational animals <note>original: "onvernufte dieren"</note> possess. For the animals of the field always maintain a uniform course, unless they are diverted from the outside (just as the Heavens maintain a uniform course), merely following their natural instinct; but man is very changeable and variable in his conduct.

Thus, one well knows that a dog whose desire is set upon a bowl of fat broth standing before him, having been otherwise trained, refrains from it out of fear of a beating; but he has no higher power to restrain his fear itself,

<column-break/>

but we have heard above, and we perceive it daily, that man moreover has a higher power, by which he knows how to overcome and suppress his very affections—his fear, his hate, his anger—which is a will that is a higher power, which listens to reason.

<margin>3. The conscience.</margin>
3. The conscience, by which man has a reflection upon his own soul regarding that which he has done, even if no one in the world knows it but himself; and he has because of it a remorse or a comfort, proceeding from respect for the great God who breathed into him the breath of life. Indeed, it makes him fear even as he now lies and dies, and as he is now about to depart from everyone in view of this world—where he would certainly have nothing more to fear if it were so that when he dies, it were entirely over with him, as it goes with the dogs and the cats that run about our houses.

But finally, this alone can fully serve to convince all brutish men that the soul of man is truly eternal without end, unlike the soul of the beasts; since thoughts of eternity, which never has an end, occur to men. If there were not something in man that is truly everlasting, then the thought and imagination of eternity would never have entered man's mind; for there must be something in man that corresponds to the thing of which man would receive an imagination.

# Deformed, Reformed.

In order to understand this well, one must testify here that the soul of man, in regard to the things she <note>The author uses the feminine pronoun for the soul, following the gender of the Dutch word 'ziele'.</note> understands and possesses, has the likeness of a mirror, which receives, imprints, and displays within itself the image of the things placed before it. But now, as we all know, a mirror—being merely material—cannot receive the image of any things other than those which are also material. Therefore we see that the images of those words which a man speaks before a mirror are neither received nor displayed in a mirror, because they are not material like the mirror. It is exactly the same with the soul of man; the soul of man cannot receive any image for which she does not have some conformity within her own self. From this it follows undeniably—seeing as she can receive the images of eternity within herself—that she must have a conformity to eternity, and must herself be eternal; for she would not be able to receive such a matter within herself if she had no conformity to it within her. Just as we know that the beasts of the field can receive no image within themselves of the nature of reasoning or rationality, because they have no rational soul; but if they could have reflections upon reasoning and discourse upon it, it would have to be placed beyond all doubt that they also possessed reason and knew how to use it.

And from this it also comes that we cannot understand God the Lord in His essence, nor receive any

<column-break/>

image of His own essence within us, because we ourselves are namely not Gods, but must merely learn to perceive God the Lord somewhat in His attributes and from His works, through reasoning and faith.

Therefore this always stands firm: since man can receive the image of eternity within himself, he has something within himself that is eternal. Consequently, all "beast-like" <note>Referring to those who live only by their physical senses without spiritual reflection.</note> men can be fully convinced that indeed their soul is eternal, precisely because they know how to discourse on that which is eternal, and that they know how to contradict it and judge it. Just as one notices that children are intelligent and rational from the very fact that they begin to discourse on reason—even if there were no other argument than their own reflections, that would be enough.

<margin>
And in case someone were not yet convinced of the immortality of his soul by this reasoning, he must nevertheless choose the surest side.
</margin>
And even assuming that the wicked man, notwithstanding all that has now been said, should still continue to doubt whether his soul truly were immortal and eternal; surely the weight of the matter and all reasons ought to count for so much with him that he chooses the surest side. For suppose man were so reckless that he would not allow himself to believe that his soul is eternal, and would make no arrangements for how he might fare in the future world or how he might be received there—and yet it were found in the end that his soul truly is eternal and immortal, and consequently that he had to appear there before the judgment seat <term>judgment seat: original 'vierschaere', a historical term for a court of justice</term> of God with such a foul, unprepared soul as men have by nature, and still...

<sig>Zz 2</sig>
<meta>The text ends mid-sentence; the catchword 'noch' (still/yet) indicates the first word of the following page.</meta>

# Adam, Righteous,

Mark 8:36 <note>original: "Mar. 8. 36." - "For what shall it profit a man, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul?"</note>, so also have the Holy Martyrs of God been of that mind and resolution, that they preferred to lose their bodies by giving them up to the fire to be burnt to powder, rather than they should have done any damage to their souls. Revelation 12:11. With this same understanding, Moses also chose rather to be ill-treated with the people of God than to have the enjoyment of sin for a season, esteeming the reproach of Christ to be greater riches (for it did good to his soul) than the treasures in Egypt, through which he could have improved his outward state. Hebrews 11:25, 26. On this ground Paul also comforted himself when he encountered manifold difficulties in the body for the cause of Christ, testifying that despite all this he did not faint. And listen, then, to what reason he gives for this: For (says he) though our outward man perishes, yet the inward man is renewed day by day, 2 Corinthians 4:16. That is: even if our body suffers damage, our soul derives benefit from it, and that is all profit at hand. Therefore, on the contrary, the Lord Christ—on this same ground—declared that rich man, who had gathered great worldly goods to the damage of his soul, to be a simple fool, Luke 12:20, however wise he might have seemed according to the world.

<margin>This is well known but not taken to heart.</margin>
Now, all Christian people acknowledge all of this with full mouths; but there are few who make use of this holy and well-known truth of God as they ought. Which partly happens to them because they take this known truth too lightly, because they see that no one doubts it, without nonetheless ever thoroughly

<column-break/>

pondering within themselves what the significance is, and what the firm grounds are, why the soul truly must be held as incomparably more worthy than the body. For if people frequently and thoroughly considered this within themselves, their hearts would certainly be more occupied with arranging the movements of their hearts according to this truth of God, and so conducting their life's meditations that they would in all ways pay more attention to their soul than to their body; and take more care that it might go well with their soul. Whereas they now do entirely the opposite, and care only for the body and neglect the soul, even while they acknowledge with full mouths that the soul is better than the body. When they act in such a way, what else have they to expect than that the Lord our God and King shall say to them, as he said to the lazy and evil servant: "You lazy and evil servant, out of your own mouth shall you be judged: you have always acknowledged that your soul was better than your body; yet you have consistently sought more for your body than for your soul, therefore you shall now perish in both soul and body."

In order then to prevent this fitting judgment and all this mischief, we shall open up the firmness of the aforementioned truth of God somewhat more closely, and point out the usefulness of it, and apply it to our soul.

<margin>The reasons for the excellence of the soul above the body are:</margin>
1. The reasons and proofs that the soul far, far exceeds the value of the body are many and clear; we shall bring forward some of the most instructive and best ones serving our purpose.

3. The third reason is taken from the great Capacity, extensiveness, and vastness of the soul, with which it is so constituted that the entire world, and all that is in it, cannot fill nor satisfy the soul; indeed, the Lord our great God alone can do that, and no

See, while it is so with our body that it is quickly filled, indeed, overloaded and thereby burdened, it is not so with the soul. According to the measure of the things that the soul receives, it expands itself, and the more it has, the more it desires to have, and the more it can receive: those who have already furnished their souls with manifold knowledge, and with the science of many things, are by that very means even more capable of being able to know and receive more.

Because of this, it happens that the soul can be satisfied by no things of this world, even if they were all heaped up and multiplied ten thousand times over.

See, the soul which we carry in our bosom is of such noble condition, of such Divine origin, that no things in the world can fill or satisfy it: just as our precious soul was not created out of anything that is earthly or worldly, but was breathed into man by God without any intermediary <note>referring to Genesis 2:7; the "direct" creation of the soul compared to the "indirect" formation of the body from dust</note>: so also the soul is not filled, nor can it be satisfied, by anything that is earthly and worldly; but it can only be satisfied and made content by God. Therefore the Psalmist says, when the Lord hid His face, "my soul refused to be comforted" (Psalm 77:3). And when the Lord revealed Himself again in grace, he said, "Return unto thy rest, O my soul; for the Lord hath dealt bountifully with thee" (Psalm 116:7). All of this we shall go on to reveal more closely.

# Adam, Righteous, VV

When he had now come to himself again, and had returned once more to the House of the Lord, he brought this news home to us and testified to us that all is vanity, yes, vanity of vanities, Ecclesiastes 1:2. Understand that all things of the world which are enjoyed or pursued outside of God are all so vain and empty that, even if they were all gathered together at once, they would not be powerful enough to fill or satisfy a single soul. See, if one man alone possessed all the riches that all the wealthy people in the world have; if one man alone had all the pleasures and delights that arise from the foundation of the flesh or from the curiosity and great knowledge of the intellect which sensual people in the world possess; if he also alone had all the Glories and all the Kingdoms of the world which all mighty Princes and Potentates possess together—it would all, being heaped together, not be able to fill or satisfy his soul. See, the soul is too noble; she is of another origin and nature than that she could be appeased and satisfied with those things. The soul does not desire riches; she finds no taste in them. She also does not satisfy herself with great states and offices; no kind of fleshly pleasures or delights can fill or satisfy her. She is of another nature; she must have something else if she is to be content. Could one indeed satisfy and please a Lion by giving him the best words and leading him upon grassy paths? We know well, no; he does not eat grass like an ox, <note>original: "als een osse"</note> Psalm 106:20. He wants meat <note>original: "vleesch" - literally flesh/meat</note> if he is to be satisfied. So it stands with our soul; the right

<column-break/>

object of the soul is only the Lord our God; no worldly things can satisfy her. Experience teaches this: that even if one had all the goods of the world, yes, even if he had conquered the entire world, he would still ask for more. Having much does not stop greed; in this regard, there is like a wolf in the stomach. But it is truly the Noble soul, this Angel of God, which will not, nor can, nor shall allow itself to be satisfied with earthly things.
<margin>Especially as this appears in the distress of the conscience,</margin>
But it is perceived most vividly of all that the soul can be neither filled nor appeased with earthly things when the soul is awakened by God in the slightest degree and touched with the particular torment of the conscience. Then, when a person begins to take some thought of how he might stand before God, and what his account shall be hereafter; when a person's soul is thus in any way touched by God, then truly all the things of the world are to him but dust and ashes. The beauty and the strength of his body, the multitude of his goods, the greatness of his status, and all the physical and worldly pleasures and all the delights that one can offer him, are all nothing at all when the soul is restless. Lord, says Solomon, a broken spirit who can bear it? <note>original: "op-heffen" - literally lift up or bear</note> Proverbs 18:14. And the Lord Christ gives us to understand that a man cannot compensate for the loss of his soul with the gain of the whole world, Mark 8:36-37. Thousands of Rams and ten thousands of rivers of Oil, and all that the world can give, cannot then set the soul at rest, Micah 6:8.

# Deformed, Reformed.

## [Page 371]

Belshazzar <note>original: "Belsazar"; the Babylonian king from the Book of Daniel</note> the King; he was a mighty Monarch; he was healthy and in good spirits; he sat there among his best friends in a thousand joys, surrounded by all kinds of pleasures and delights; and yet, as soon as his soul was awakened by the writing hand <note>The "writing on the wall" from Daniel 5</note>, all his courage sank into his shoes; his limbs trembled, his knees knocked against one another; all his goods, all his glory, all his pleasures, all his Princes and Lords, all his Wives and concubines could not set him at ease. Nothing in the world could now delight him, because his soul was thus wounded and injured, Daniel 5:5-6. Just as we also know that indeed our first ancestors Adam and Eve, as soon as their souls were wounded by the poison of sin, they immediately lost all delight and pleasure, even while they were still in the Paradise of God, in the garden of pleasure itself; before they were driven out from there, they had already lost all their joy; and all that because their soul was corrupted. So entirely worthy a part of man is the soul; all the glory and all the pleasures of Belshazzar, indeed the delightfulness of the Paradise of God itself, is not powerful enough to take away the displeasure of the soul once it is thoroughly awakened; that only the Good God can do, who made the soul, whereby again the excellent worthiness of the soul above the body and above all that is in the world is made known.

<margin>The fourth reason: from the eternal duration of the soul.</margin>
The fourth reason is taken from the eternity of the soul. We see that all things under the sun perish; cities and lands are overturned; and as for the bodies of men, they are

<column-break/>

indeed entirely bound to perishability; they diminish, they wear out like a garment; with our bodies we make a thousand and a thousand things which still remain when our bodies are rotted and gone: the houses above our heads remain standing, and the inhabitants pass away; how many generations of people has the city of Middelburg <note>A prominent city in the Netherlands, likely the author's location or reference point</note> already worn out, seen arrive and seen pass through again, while she has remained standing. This is the perishability of worldly things; so the world passes away with its lusts; but the soul of man remains in eternity, it never withers and it never perishes; it also has its being in the other world, and there it is transported through death.

What then are our bodies, the goods of this world, which all perish with use, in comparison to the worthiness of the soul, which lasts eternally? Naked we came here into the world, and naked we shall depart from here again, stripped of all our goods, offices, statuses, pleasures, or whatever it might be that men here are usually so proud of, and upon which they hang their souls' cost. As much then as the Heaven exceeds the earth, as much as eternity is more to be esteemed than that which perishes with use; so much worthier also is the soul than the body, indeed than the whole world with all that is in it, which is perishable.

<margin>The fifth reason: because the welfare of the body depends on the soul.</margin>
The last reason is taken from this: that the hope and the well-being of the body depends entirely upon the soul. We see that in a weak, evil, sickly body there is often lodged a very brave, healthy soul; so the condition of the soul does not properly depend on the body,

For even when a person becomes mad through the derangement of the brain, his soul is not mad, just as we have explained elsewhere; on the contrary, the entire condition of the body depends upon the soul. Do we not perceive it daily, that when our soul is of good courage and well-comforted, it is then a light matter for us to overcome all the difficulties of the body and of the world? If He also gives them health, riches, honor, and reputation, He wishes to bind them therewith to greater thankfulness, to more diligent service, to the preservation of their souls. So that it is all for the sake of the soul, as it is truly the most worthy and excellent part of man, upon which everything depends; which is followed by the body, wherever it goes, into Heaven or into Hell. And see there, those are a few reasons among many why the soul is truly more worthy, more excellent than the body: which reasons—if they were properly weighed and laid to heart by all those who so readily acknowledge that the soul is better than the body, and yet so little conform themselves to that truth of God—they would be more persuaded not only to profess with the mouth that the soul is better than the body, but also to demonstrate it with their life and well-doing. This is so that they might not be condemned out of their own mouth and confession like evil servants. Therefore, we shall also go on to point out what our bounden duty is in view of this truth of God, which we all acknowledge: that indeed the soul is better than the body, yes, better than the whole world.

# Misshapen, Reshaped,

### CHAPTER XLIV.

*Of the general duties that we are bound to observe, from the fact that we know and acknowledge that man's soul is the most noble creature, even better than the entire visible world.*

The aforementioned truth of God is very well known and in the mouth of all the world; but very few apply it to such spiritual uses for which it serves, and for which the same has been revealed to us.

We shall endeavor to faithfully present the duties which we owe in this regard; and then to apply them to our soul; these are of two kinds: general and specific.

The general duty is this: that we must all alike value our soul above all else, watch over it, and care for it with all possible diligence; avoiding that which might damage our soul; practicing that which might do our soul good.

This duty flows clearly from this truth of God: that the soul is the most noble part of man; for it is entirely consistent with all reason and good judgment that we care most and first for that which is worth most. We are accustomed to use that wisdom in all other things, that we look after the best things first, especially if they are also very delicate and might easily be harmed, as is also the case with our souls: we are accustomed to take more care for our own hand and flesh than for our Cloak or Coat, although we also

<column-break/>

care for and watch over those in their proper place and turn; so is this also the counsel of our Lord Jesus Christ, when he says Mark 8:36-37: ->What would it profit a man, if he should gain the whole world, and suffer the loss of his soul?<- testifying that in this case he can find nothing that he may give as a ransom <note>original: "losinghe," referring to the price paid for redemption or release</note> for his soul.

So we see then that this duty stands firm; but for a closer understanding of it, we must explain two things here; namely, what it is that harms the soul, so that we might avoid it; and secondly, what it is that does the soul good, so that we might practice it.

<margin>Therefore we must avoid that which harms the soul, which is sin alone.</margin>
As for the first, there is nothing in the world that can harm the soul but sin, that is, the breach of God's commandment; when we break God's commandment, we break our soul, we do our soul damage; *he who sins against you, does violence to his own soul,* says the wisdom of God, Proverbs 8:36. *Lord heal my soul* (says David) *for I have sinned against you,* Psalm 41 verse 5.

We cannot violate God's commandment without violating our soul thereby. When we distort God's commandment, we distort our soul. See, God has given us His word as a support for our soul, as a rule and measure to keep our soul in a right state: When we then depart from it, we disturb and ruin <note>original: "ontramponeren," a term meaning to damage, fracture, or throw into disorder</note> our soul; we do it damage. That was clearly shown in Adam and Eve; the sinful bite of the forbidden fruit was like a hellish poison to their soul, and corrupted them to the core; it immediately corrupted all the powers of their soul, and so harmed and spoiled them that they became useless for any good, and inclined toward all evil.

On the contrary, when we hold ourselves to—

# Deformed, Reformed.

Therefore, it stands thus: that even if it were so, that man should win the whole world with lying and deceiving, by committing any of the aforementioned acts; even if he could thereby draw to himself alone all the riches and goods of the entire world, which are now divided among so many wealthy people; even if he alone could obtain all the glories, the estates, the kingdoms of the world; yes, even if he alone could pursue and obtain all the pleasures and delights of the world by committing sin, through lying and deceiving, through practicing idolatry, or whatever it might be—it would still be, according to the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ, a bad bargain; for he harms his soul, and the slightest damage to the soul is greater than the advantage of the whole world; it cannot compensate for the loss.

Whenever a person omits or neglects any of these things, even if it seemed that he could thereby gain a very great advantage in the eyes of the world, he also does damage to the soul; he is simply a fool; for he neglects the improvement of his soul, which is by far the best part. Just as we know that merchants count it as a loss when they miss such profits and advantages in their trade as would ordinarily fall to them; indeed, they calculate that they suffer as much loss as they miss of certain and ordinary gain through some accident. Does the Lord Christ not take this matter so seriously that He holds it thus: that even if a man, merely to preserve his life, so as not to be burned alive or the like, should only omit the confession of His name, that man in so doing nevertheless does damage to his soul? He may thereby preserve his life—which otherwise is the dearest thing a man has—yet he cannot thereby compensate for the damage he suffers to his soul because of it, Mark 8:34, 35, 36, 37, 38. How much more, then, does the Lord Christ hold that a man does immediate damage whenever he commits any sin, leaves any good undone, or does any evil—not to preserve his life, but for a handful of foul gain, pleasures, and delights.

### CHAPTER XLV.

->The particular duties that we must observe, since our soul is far more excellent than our body, indeed, than the whole world.<-

<margin>The particular out-working of the excellence of the soul, with the duties.</margin>
<margin>that come from the same virtue.</margin>
AND so much has been said concerning the general duties which we are bound to observe, from the fact that we know and acknowledge that our soul is better than our body, or anything else that is in the world.

Now follow the particular duties, of which the first is:

That we learn from this a point of wisdom: namely, to esteem and value all things with which we have to concern ourselves according to their right worth. It is a particular work of wisdom to rightly grasp the value of things; this shows itself in every calling; among those who deal with precious stones, that they know the right value of each of them; those

<column-break/>

who deal with medals, that they rightly distinguish gold from copper, and one type of gold from another according to its value; among those who deal with cloths and grains, that they also know which is the best, and so forth. Now, since we well know and acknowledge that our soul is indeed better than our body, we must learn this singular point of wisdom: namely, that we most value and esteem those things which have a special regard for our soul, in order to bring it virtue, to enrich it, and to improve it.

People are often wonderfully bewildered in their deliberation over what they shall do: on the one side the world is at their throats, urging them to choose this or that; on the other side they are exhorted on God's behalf to reject that and accept this. Here they often stand bewildered and can hardly resolve; but if we only remember the aforementioned truth—that our soul is better than our body—and subsequently test the value of things against that faithful touchstone <note>a stone used to test the purity of gold; here used as a metaphor for a moral standard</note>, then we shall immediately be able to resolve (unless we wish to be found purely foolish) that it is in every way advisable to accept that which most closely concerns our soul and would do it the most good.

Thus was Job minded; he had learned this point of wisdom from the fact that he knew his soul was better than his body, so that he esteemed the word of God, by which his soul is fed, more than his appointed portion of food, Job 23:12. And David, that he esteemed it more than thousands of Gold or Silver, Psalm 119:72, and that he would rather wish to be a doorkeeper in the house of the Lord than to be a great Lord himself in the palaces of Kings, Psalm 84:11. And subsequently, when he [found himself] in deli-

<margin>The third duty: to fear most the one who can kill the soul.</margin>
The third specific duty is that we fear Him most of all who can also kill our souls; that is the Lord our God, Matthew 10:28. Since the soul is the best part, far worthier than the body, why should we fear those who can only reach our body, and cannot touch our souls with even a finger?

On the other hand, we must also most highly esteem those who can do good to our souls, who are rich in spiritual gifts; more than those who are powerful in status or worldly means, of which we have also spoken above.

<margin>The fourth duty: not to let the body rule over the soul.</margin>
The fourth specific duty is that we by no means allow the body to rule over the soul, nor the lusts of the flesh over the counsel of the spirit, 1 Corinthians 6:12. If our soul is much better than our body, then it is fitting in every way that our soul has the upper hand, and is not smothered in the lusts of the flesh; indeed, that the flesh should bow beneath it and give way to it, unless we wish to bring all things into the greatest disorder and entangle everything.

<margin>The fifth duty: to give no offense.</margin>
The fifth specific duty is that we, above all, guard ourselves against giving any offense <note>In this context, "offense" refers to a "stumbling block" or leading someone else into sin.</note> through our actions, whereby the soul is wounded and corrupted, Romans 14:13, 1 Corinthians 8:13. We are usually very careful not to hurt anyone in their body; the soul is worth much more: we must then be much more careful that we do no harm to anyone's soul.

<margin>The sixth duty: to be most attentive to repairing damage to the soul.</margin>
The sixth specific duty is that when we become aware of having suffered any kind of damage to the soul, we seek to provide for it at the very first opportunity; and that everyone seeks to

<column-break/>

do good to the soul: those who are unruly, faint-hearted, weak, or needy in soul—these we must seek to help, 1 Thessalonians 5:14. When we see someone who is physically infirm, our hearts are moved; how much more should they be for the soul?

## CHAPTER XLVI.

### A complaint that the things of the body are much more cared for than those of the soul.

<margin>Man seeks the body and regards earthly things most.</margin>
And see, these are the duties that we owe, since we know that the soul is better than the body; of which the most important is surely that we must watch over and care for our soul above all: but in this, there is a very great deficiency. To obtain earthly things—profit, pleasures, credit, and promotion—what do men not do? What ingenuity, what diligence, what straining of the senses! How people bustle for these things! How early and how late are they busy with them! Look at them, how they run; observe what they intend; ask them what they pursue; it is all for money and goods, for pleasures and to indulge in lusts; and meanwhile, the poor soul lies in the corner, and is hardly even thought of. It is evident everywhere that the vast majority of people take the matters of the body most to heart: but this reveals itself especially even among the best of civil people in two cases: first, in the great diligence and time they spend on earthly things;

# Mis-shapen, Re-shapen.

They employ their earthly business to clear their conscience in their calling, according to the command of the Lord: *In the sweat of your face you shall eat bread* <note>Genesis 3:19</note>. But it goes further: that diligence is not driven by conscience, but by lust, as is undeniably evident from this: that when the damage to the soul and the advantage of the body come into competition, the damage to the soul is ignored. Sin is committed to work out the advantage of the body, as we shall hear more broadly hereafter. It is also evident in those things where they are not even obligated by way of their calling, yet they nevertheless spend a great deal of time and diligence upon them. For example, to dress and trouble oneself, to adorn <term>pareren</term> <note>from the French 'parer', meaning to adorn or dress up ostentatiously</note> the body; when one has to enter into respectable company, what is not always spent on that? What dear and beloved money is "licked up" <note>spent greedily or wastefully</note> for that? But to arrange the soul a little, and to prepare it for the great God when one shall appear in His house—that is nowhere attended to, hardly thought of, and by almost everyone greatly neglected. To prepare the food for the body, when feasts are to be held, one has a multitude of cooks—twice as many as one has Preachers <note>Ministers or Pastors</note>—to prepare the food for the soul. While every household can well prepare its own physical food, but cannot prepare the food of the soul; yet it is there that the cooks and pastry-bakers are visited, even if it proves very costly. The Preachers are treated as equals <note>or perhaps 'ignored' in context of value</note>, even though they prepare the food of the soul for nothing, even though they give it for free. Indeed, this vanity in clothing and banquets—which are things concerning the body—goes so far that one neglects the poor "little limbs of Christ" <note>a common metaphor for the poor and suffering members of the Church</note>

<column-break/>

to the great damage of the soul; one makes them lie there hungry, while they themselves go about full, stuffed, topped off, and fattened. Secondly, this is also apparent in the judgment regarding the worth and esteem which people generally have for the things of the body above the things of the soul, as is found to be the case in many instances, especially in these three: when a Marriage is to be entered into; when taking up a residence; and when choosing company. Then the soul is almost always pushed to one side, and the things of the body and the world are taken in hand.

1. When a Marriage is to be made, in which (to use a manner of speaking) one exchanges person for person, one generally sees that the things of the body are valued higher than the things of the soul: a beautiful body is preferred over a beautiful soul; a rich inheritance in the world over a soul rich in God; a descent from noble parents, even if they have been very ungodly, instead of God-fearing parents. This is not said to the end that, in the matter of marriage, the unions should not also be proportionately matched in respect to worldly things as much as possible, but only that the things of the soul should not be nothing, and the body everything.

2. # Deformities, Reformations.

The soul is possessed, in which the spirit of disobedience works, where he (namely, the Evil One) runs in and out; whom he goads toward all kinds of sin and shameful contemplations, which we pass by as if with blind eyes.

That one hears of someone who has unexpectedly drowned, smothered in the harbor, affects everyone who hears it: but if it happens that someone is found to have laid hands upon their own death <note>committed suicide</note>, it makes the hair of those who hear of it stand on end; it astounds the whole world. But that someone is visibly smothered in his misdeeds, dies in his sins; if only the outward and physical aspect is not present, it is quickly forgotten.

Let the enemy be on foot to come and take a city, everyone takes up arms against him, one offers him resistance: but let the spiritual enemy, the Devil, raise his banner at a fair <note>original: "kermiſſe," a local church festival often associated with revelry</note> or Shrove Tuesday <note>original: "vaſtelavondt," the carnival period before Lent</note> to wound many souls, and people set the gates open for him; they usher him in themselves with beating drums and flying colors, and with great joy and merriment.

That a madman, having broken loose, runs through the streets, wounding and stabbing himself with knives and awls, creates a horror in everyone who sees it; hardly one person fails to run toward him to hold him fast, and he is bound with a rope. But though there are yet so many so deprived of their senses that they wound their poor souls on all sides, no one sets themselves against it; they are left to their own devices.

# Deformed, Reformed.

The fact that the soul is possessed—in which the spirit of disobedience works, where he (namely the evil one) runs out and in, whom he incites to all kinds of sin and shameful contemplations—that is passed by as if with blind eyes.

That one hears of someone who has suddenly drowned, or suffocated in the harbor, it affects everyone who hears it: but if it happens that someone is found to have laid hands on their own life <note>original: "handtdadich te wesen aen zijn eyghen doodt"; referring to suicide</note>, it makes the hair of those who hear of it stand on end; it amazes all the world. But that someone there noticeably suffocates in his misdeeds, dies in his sins—as long as the outward and physical element is not present—it is soon forgotten.

Let the enemy be on foot to come and take a fort, everyone takes up arms against him, one offers him resistance: but let the spiritual enemy, the Devil, raise his banner at a fair <note>term: "kermisse" - a local festival often criticized by preachers for encouraging vice</note> or Shrove Tuesday <note>term: "vastelavondt" - the carnival period before Lent</note> to wound many souls, and the gates are set open for him; he is welcomed in with beating drums and flying banners, and with great joy and merriment.

That a madman, having broken loose, runs through the street, wounding and stabbing himself with knives and awls, it creates a horror in everyone who sees it; hardly one person fails to run to him to hold him fast, and he is bound with a cord: but though there are so many so deprived of their senses that they wound their poor souls on all sides, no one sets themselves against it; they are left to their own devices.

Indeed, where but one man is murdered in the body, the entire place where it happened is completely

<column-break/>

Yes, many are found everywhere who even persist in laughing and taking their pleasure in such whims that wound the soul: how could the Devil make it any worse? We grieve when we hear of expensive times <note>meaning periods of famine or high inflation</note>, of pestilence, of war, of great tempests: but if we suffer hardship in the soul, almost no one takes it to heart.

This proves everywhere that there is great insensitivity, deadness, and unbelief among those called Christians themselves in the matter of the soul; indeed, that the soul is almost entirely forgotten, and the dignity thereof is known by almost no one. The godly David acted differently, <margin>Psalm 119:136. Lot 2 Peter 2:8. Jeremiah Jer. 15:17.</margin> as did Lot and Jeremiah. If people are out of their minds in the soul, wounding and hurting their souls with cursing, with evils, yes, through a thousand kinds of sins, no one takes that to heart.

If someone becomes sick in the body, what a concern there is! What weeping is heard there! How the Doctor is sought, and means applied for healing? How many a small note <note>referring to "briefkens" or prayer requests submitted to the church</note> is handed over for that purpose, requesting the prayer of the faithful? # Adam, Righteous

If someone has missed a good meal, a turn at the tavern, or something similar, it affects him deeply; but that one misses a Sermon <note>original: "Predicatie"</note> or the Ministers, that is nothing; that one observes Saint Monday <note>A traditional day of skipping work for drinking or leisure</note> but neglects the Lord’s day of rest <note>original: "rustdach des Heeren"</note>, no difficulty is made of that. Indeed, are there not many found everywhere who place their wisdom in this: that they specifically choose the Lord’s day to go out riding for pleasure, as it is a day when they can best be spared? They would consider it great folly, being Shopkeepers <note>original: "Winckeliers"</note>, to do so on a Market-day during the week: yet this concerns only the body, while the other concerns the soul.

That some miss a merry company, it affects them; that they miss the use of the Lord’s Supper <note>original: "Abontmaels"</note>, it does not trouble them; for a small trifle of the world they will postpone their journey for a week: but so as not to miss the Lord’s Supper, they will not tarry a single day.

If a child is born to us who is physically defective, having only one hand, foot, or eye, or being blind, it affects us very much, it grieves the whole house: but that our children, in growing up, are found to be very defective in the soul, full of sinful traits—as long as they cause no inconvenience to the body—that is even satisfactory to many parents; they laugh about it.

That our Wife is well delivered of a child, that we are healthy, have good means to live by—how we thank God for that! But that we have the Holy Gospel, and the means of salvation <note>original: "salichept"</note> healing our souls—how little we regard that?

<column-break/>

That a young, fresh maiden is beautiful of body and face—how greatly that pleases many? Even though her soul is often worth nothing at all; even though the same soul is often entirely like the very devil of Hell, being merely a decoy-bird <note>original: "roer-vinke" - a bird used to lure others into a trap</note> of the devil to ensnare souls: but if a very beautiful soul dwells in a deformed body, in a hunched, lame, bleary-eyed, or otherwise disordered body, how few there are whose hearts are drawn to it, who can take delight in it?

And thus, in every way, the things of the soul are placed below the things of the body and of the world;

<margin>This also happens among the Rulers of Church and Land.</margin>

The things of the second table <note>The last six of the Ten Commandments, regarding duties to fellow men</note> are everywhere more upheld than those of the first <note>The first four Commandments, regarding duties to God</note>. Experience also teaches that very many are found who come to Church only for the sake of fashion, so that one perceives visibly that Civil <note>original: "Borgerlijcke"</note> matters lie much closer to their hearts than Spiritual <note>original: "Geestelijcke"</note> matters, whereas the former concern only temporary livelihood, and the latter the welfare of the soul forever and eternally.

# Deformity, Reformation.

...we should gladly give all that we have in order to provide well for our souls.

5. Fifthly, this must serve as an **Awakening** to everyone; seeing as this is how it stands with the soul, and that we all equally and so loudly confess that the soul is better than the body, let us then surely align our contemplations with our confession, as is proper. Let us indeed watch over our soul, and the soul of our neighbor, and provide for it above all else, as the **most precious Jewel** that is in the world. Do not all wise and sensible people in every case work in such a way that they provide for and watch over the most necessary and worthy things most? Shall this apply in all other things? Shall this be true in all other things, and shall it not be true in the care of the soul? Shall it be found false there alone, or do we doubt any longer whether our soul is truly worthier than everything else?

How then? Do we not find it daily, that as soon as the soul is out of the body, it is entirely over with the body, though many make so much of it? Take note of this, you who neglect, yes, even wound your soul to provide for your body: when your soul shall be out of your body, then your eye, which is now so full of vanity, shall see no more; your ears, which now listen so much to vanity, shall then hear no more; your tongue, which now perhaps overflows with foolish chatter <note>original: "sotte klap"</note>, shall then speak no more; your feet shall then walk no more; your hands no more grasp. All your pleasures and all your delights, and all the amusements of your body, they shall then have an end. Your body shall then lie there stiff and cold; then you shall no longer see those lovely faces with which you are now so infatuated; you shall then no longer hear the melodious music, or that lovely

<column-break/>

talk and speech of your beloved, which now so greatly tickles your ears. Your mouth shall then no longer taste any lovely wine, or eat pleasant food; your tongue shall then no longer strike up any jests, or carry on delightful talk; your arms shall no longer embrace. Your body shall indeed lie there insensitive, immovable as a wooden block; decay shall seize it, the worms shall consume it. See, thus it shall go with your body, of which you now make so much, when your soul shall be out of it. This you may have seen happen to thousands in your time; this shall also certainly happen to you. How then do you not see that your soul is by far the best part, which alone can keep your body from destruction? How! Shall you then not observe your soul, not watch over it, through which you have life, which makes your eye see, your ear hear, your mouth speak, your foot walk? How shall you indeed neglect or despise your soul, through which you have all the loveliness of life?

<margin>For one must serve God with the soul.</margin>
Is it also not so, that where all your happiness, salvation, and welfare depend entirely upon the Lord your God, you yet cannot serve the Lord your God pleasingly except with your soul? Unless you have your soul in good condition, renewed by the spirit of Christ, you surely cannot serve your God. How then shall you not watch over your soul above all, which is like a vessel of honor <note>A biblical reference to 2 Timothy 2:21, describing a person sanctified and useful to the Master.</note>, with which alone you can well serve and please the Lord your God?

# Deformed, Reformed

within this current year, yes, within this month or week, or even a shorter time; why then should I care so much for the temporal and perishable, while a whole eternity lies before me, and I have a soul to care for that never perishes.

Go further then in this meditation, and think also thus: when man shall have entered with his soul into the other world, into that abyss of eternity which never takes an end, and shall have come into the place of joy or of pains, what shall he then think of this tiny speck of life that he shall have lived here on earth, and which he now makes so much of? Indeed, when man shall have entered through death with his soul into the abyss of eternity, and shall then look backward toward this world, how lowly, how like nothing at all, shall this temporal life (which he made so much of, and for which many destroy their souls) then rightfully appear in his eyes. Shall not even the damned, when they find themselves in the abyss of eternal sorrow, curse themselves, that for the sake of such a short little end of a pleasure-filled life they neglected and damned their precious soul? Shall they not rightfully mock themselves for it? Shall this not be to them like a gnawing worm, always and eternally biting their soul? And on the other side, when also the blessed shall have entered into the joy of their Lord, into an eternity of the good life, shall they not rightfully bless themselves, and think to themselves: Had I not great reason, for a short speck of time, however my life in the world was, to deny myself, to break my lusts,

This must then be considered, and this must then be practiced, to indeed make us willing and awake in the good practice of the salvation of our soul, which remains eternally, whereas our body perishes with its usage.
