# Adam, Righteous,

It will not help if a man should think to say before the Judgment of God: "Look there, Lord, I was not only born naked, but also very poor into the world; my parents left me nothing; I did not inherit a single penny <note>original: "stuijver" - a small Dutch coin of little value</note>; nevertheless, I have gained many thousands; I died a man of such and such wealth; I obtained such and such positions and offices; I held the administration of them in my hand for so long. It is true, I sometimes committed some sin to gain money and goods, or to obtain a certain position or office; it is true that I thereby damaged my soul, but nevertheless, I greatly increased my means through it; I greatly improved my worldly standing thereby." See, if a man should think to say this, it shall not be valid; it shall not be able to excuse him. Much less shall it excuse him if he should think to say: "It is true, I have indeed damaged my soul, but in exchange, I have had so many pleasures, delights, and lusts in the world with my neighbors, more than many of my acquaintances." All of this shall not be able to excuse the man; indeed, it shall rather weigh him down in the Judgment. For that is not the work that God the Lord has given man to do—namely, that he should hunt for and obtain money, goods, worldly honor, positions, and offices. The Lord did not place man in the world for that purpose, but so that he should glorify God and work out the salvation of his soul, *Philippians 2:12.* So truly is the soul so noble and precious (as we have now heard) that the slightest damage to the soul cannot be compensated for by all

<column-break/>

the profit of the entire world, even if one had won it all fairly.
Thus, it is still utter foolishness, even if one could win the whole world, if one does damage to his soul. If we then gather many treasures through lying, through any kind of falsehood or sin; if we even win a thousand pounds by committing the smallest sin; if we draw a great position or office to ourselves by some sinful, clever trick—then we are merely poor fools, for we do not deceive others half as much as the Devil deceives us.
Is it not a great and manifest foolishness that we want to busily provide for and draw to ourselves that which the great God, our Lord and Master, has not commanded <note>original: "op-gelept" - tasked or laid upon someone</note> us to seek, which He will also not demand from us, and of which we shall not have to give an account even if we have not pursued it? And that we meanwhile neglect the care of our soul, which God has tasked us with, upon which everything depends, and of which we shall have to give an account when we come before the judgment of God. The Lord will not ask us how much money and goods, or how many positions and offices we acquired in this world; that will not even be looked upon. But this, God the Lord will demand of us: how we have watched over our soul, and whether we have cared to improve the state of our soul; everything will depend on that. Is it not then great foolishness, not only to bring this useless unrest upon ourselves—that we should go seeking money, goods, honor, and reputation with great effort, which has not been tasked to us, and of which the Lord shall say to us: *Who has required this from your hand?* *Isaiah 1:12*—but even to do that with sin, that is, to the damage of the soul?
<margin>Therefore we must first watch over our own soul.</margin>

# Deformed, Reformed.

...whereas God the Lord has strictly commanded us, above all and before every other work, to see to it that our soul might suffer no harm.
   Since this is how it stands with the condition of our soul, we can certainly see enough that it befits us in every way to care for and watch over our souls above all else. This is explicitly charged to us in Joshua 23:11: *Take diligent heed to your souls* <note>original: "Bewaert uwe ziele... neerſtelijck"</note> (he says). Of this we also have a very excellent example in the Lord Jesus Christ, whom we must follow in all things. For, dear ones, do take note: What has the Lord Jesus Christ done all his life long, other than care for the soul? Did he not come into the flesh for that purpose? Did he not do and speak all that he did and spoke here on earth for that purpose? And did he not die the bitter death of the cross specifically to win souls? When we see him lying in the garden, sweating drops of blood running down to the earth; when we hear him cry out, *My God, My God, why hast thou forsaken me?* <note>Matthew 27:46</note>; when we thus see his soul in labor; if we then ask what the cause of it is, the answer will be ready: it was solely to win lost souls (Matthew 18:11). For this reason, Paul became all things to all men, that he might by all means win at least some souls (1 Corinthians 9:19 and 1 Corinthians 10:31-33). These examples we must also follow, and therefore follow in these footsteps: first, to watch well over our own souls, and then also the souls of our neighbors.
   We must watch over our own soul well, for we must also love ourselves; indeed, we cannot well do any virtue toward the souls of others unless we have first set our own

<column-break/>

soul in good order, and come to speak from experience <note>term: "bevindinge" — a key Pietist concept referring to the internal, lived experience of faith rather than just head-knowledge</note>, saying: *Come and hear, I will tell what God has done for my soul* (Psalm 66:16). So we must, above all, watch over our own soul, and by no means think that the growth of our soul would spring up by itself like a weed; but hold it for certain and sure that we must watch closely if we are to obtain good fruits from it.
   As to how we shall now care for our soul well, much could be said about that; but briefly: you must with all your might and prudence shun what harms the soul—which is sin—and contemplate what does the soul good—which is communion with Christ and the counsel of God revealed in His word.

You must look upon that as a dagger <note>original: "moꝛtpꝛiem" — literally a 'murder-awl' or piercing weapon</note> to your soul; you must flee from it as from a destroyer, as from the devil himself. All you, then, who would gladly preserve your soul with the utmost diligence, accustom yourselves to always be mindful, whenever you take anything in hand to do, with this reflection: "Will this do any harm to my soul? Shall I suffer any disadvantage to my soul through this?" And then also with this resolution: that whatever you truly perceive might damage your soul, you will not do for any reason whatsoever. No, even if you could win the whole world by it, remembering the testimony of Christ, which is true, who says that the slightest damage to the soul cannot be compensated for by the greatest gain of the world. How then can one be with one who bears the image of the devil? Who would wish to associate with the devil, hire themselves out to him, keep him in their house, or wish to marry him, even if he appeared beautifully adorned; even if he offered us so much money and goods; even if he could do us such good service; even if he made such beautiful promises? 2. That we should have the most compassion for those who are troubled in their soul: as the soul is the most worthy part of man, so surely the disorder of the soul is the most harmful thing. Sin torments the soul, so we ought rightly to make our sins, and the sins of the people, our greatest sorrow. But to be more specific, the human soul comes into distress in two ways: 1. Through stricken sins <note>Sins that have deeply wounded the conscience.</note>. 2. Through heavy temptations; we must be heartily moved by both.

Regarding the first, some are miserably troubled in the soul by heavy temptations and torments of the mind, namely when God the Lord lets <term>Satan</term> loose against certain souls; it cannot be expressed how

<column-break/>

great this distress is. Now these poor people do not consider what a biting wound the wound of the soul and of the <term>conscience</term> <note>original: "conscientie"</note> is: If they considered that properly, they would have more compassion; and we must see in the fear of the Lord that we are moved most of all over such people, and that we apply the word of God to them:

We must surely do good to our neighbor; if he is in want regarding the body, we must come to his aid, and not merely say, *go in peace, be warmed and be filled* <note>A reference to James 2:16, criticizing hollow faith that offers words but no physical help.</note> James 2, Isaiah 16, 1 John 3:17, 11. How then shall we not also do this regarding the soul, which is by far the better part?

In this there is now a very great deficiency; many people neglect this; many who still give an alms for the need of the body do not even think of the soul of their neighbor; this we must improve. It is true Christ speaks only of the virtue done to the body in Matthew 25:35, 36. But that was in a situation where knowledge was great, and admonitions regarding the soul could not well be given, and the heart was closed against the poor; otherwise He has let us be taught that we must also especially look to the soul, saying: *when you are once converted, then strengthen your brothers* <note>original: "als gy eens ſult bekeert zijn, ſoo verſterckt uwe broeders"</note>, Luke 22:32. And therefore it must also be practiced by us, and in this we must follow this path.

<margin>And to that end 1. give no one offense.</margin>
1. We must take great care that we do our neighbor no harm through any kind of given offense <term>offense: in this context, "ergerniſſe" refers to a "stumbling block" or a bad example that leads another into sin</term>. See, we know this, that offense wounds and destroys the soul, as the Apostle teaches us, Romans 14:13, 1 Corinthians 10:32. So then, just as we would not want to stab our neighbor in the body with a knife, or give him a poison or a deadly drink to drink—

<column-break/>

<margin>3. Use their speech, a familiar one.</margin>
—so we also may not give our neighbor any kind of offense. Little attention is paid to this; oh, that people would only pay attention to this! How many are found everywhere who, through their pomp, show, and excess, give very great offense, wound many souls, turn them away from the truth, cause them to turn to Popery <note>original: "Pauſdom"; a common 17th-century Protestant term for the Roman Catholic Church</note>, or fall into Anabaptism <note>original: "weder-dooperije"</note>, and yet cannot be brought away from it. Oh, how heavy a judgment do you bring upon yourself for a handful of trifles? How anxious it will be for you to answer for the fact that, where you were called to edify your neighbor regarding the soul, you were inclined to offend him; and where you shunned hurting your neighbor regarding the body, you have so unconcernedly wounded him regarding the soul. The female sex is not accustomed to fighting, nor to wounding one another regarding the body; but through their pomp and show, various kinds of vanity and lightheartedness, they wound many people regarding the soul; that shall also go hard for them. That must then also be improved in every respect.

<margin>A discovery of how terribly they do this.</margin>
<margin>1. The soul wounds for one's own g[ratification?]</margin>
<margin>2. To lead with a good example.</margin>

### CHAPTER XLVIII.

->Concerning the union of the soul with the Body.<-

Having thus understood that the soul greatly surpasses the body, there now remains at last that we speak of the union of the soul with the body; which must also be rightfully considered. For it is truly in itself a most wonderful thing, how the soul and the body, being two such entirely different natures, are so well united together. Man's body is earthly, fleshly, visible, tangible, coarse, heavy, sluggish, and mortal; on the other hand, the soul is Heavenly or spiritual, invisible, intangible, very delicate, nimble, and immortal. <margin>Jeremiah 23:28</margin> "What has the straw to do with the corn?" says the Prophet Jeremiah (23:28). But well may we say here: what has Heaven to do with the Earth, the flesh with the spirit, the mortal with the immortal, the visible with the invisible? This is most wonderful.

Indeed, it is worth the effort that we also examine this matter somewhat more closely, and to that end, we shall discuss these things: 1. What the bond of this union is, and how firm it is. 2. What the consequences of this union are.

->What the Bond of this union may be.<-

<margin>The bond of the union of the soul with the body are certain internal, subtle, and nimble spirits.</margin>

As we are sometimes accustomed to say when we have been in particularly great distress, where we had nearly lost our lives, that namely at that time our life hung only by a **silken thread**; we should indeed always hold that for certain, even when we seem to be at our strongest and least in peril of life; that truly our life hangs only by a silken thread; that it indeed plays there upon the movements of the aforementioned spirits <note>The "spirits" or "animal spirits" were believed in the 17th century to be the subtle fluids that connected the soul to the physical body.</note>, just as we see the flame, which now wants to separate from the smoldering fuel, playing upon that dark vapor through which it still remains attached to the fuel.

And it is to be thought that the Psalmist also had this in view when he complained that the hand of the Lord pressed him so, that his moisture was turned into the drought of summer, Psalm 32:4. <note>original: "sap veranderde in somer drooghten"</note> thereby giving it to be understood that since his moisture thus dried up, he was as if losing his life, and his spirits perished, and the bond wherewith his soul was held to his body was stifled: regarding this, it also seems well that Job had a view; when he complainingly said, *the arrows of the Almighty are within me, the fiery poison whereof drinks up my spirit*, Job 6:4. thereby giving it to be understood that it also affected his life, and that he would not be able to endure it for long.

<margin>Particularly through two kinds of things.</margin>
Now there are two kinds of things which greatly weaken and finally break this bond of the soul and the body, and consequently the life of man; the first are such things as are truly found through natural reasons to shorten the spirits of man's life: the others which do it only because they provoke God, the Author of life, against man.

<column-break/>

<margin>1. Through such conduct of men.</margin>
As concerns the first sort of things, these are—beyond the outward physical violence of deadly weapons, or the inward physical violence of poison—all such conduct of men by which they exhaust or stifle the spirits.

<margin>1. That which stifles the spirits.</margin>
1. The spirits are particularly stifled by **excess in food and drink**; there is nothing in the world that so ordinarily shortens man's life as gluttony and drunkenness; therefore it is testified with truth that more die through excess than by the sword.

Oh, that all such people would take note of this, who greatly dread death and hear mention of it quite unwillingly, so that all their courage sinks into their shoes if even a persistent thought of death comes over them, who nevertheless are very immoderate in their food and drink; and are accustomed, as it were, to stifle from day to day more and more those **Noble spirits** by which their souls are held in their bodies; and thus they also become consequently complicit in their own death, murdering themselves: yes, such people truly shorten, as much as is in them, their own lives, and thus make themselves highly guilty before the Lord. Which then truly shall make a very heavy account on the last day, when the Lord God, who gave them the living soul, shall come to convict them that they, through their extravagance and excess, weakened those Noble spirits and helped themselves out of their lives.

Oh, that all those "good friends," as they call themselves, would also take proper note of this, who, when they invite their best friends to a meal, are accustomed to incite them to excess...

# Of Creation and Recreation.

Each retains its own properties; the body remains mortal and tangible, the soul remains immortal and intangible. Were it otherwise, it would not be a union, but a mingling <note>The author distinguishes between *vereeniginge* (union, where parts remain distinct) and *vermenginge* (mixture, where parts lose their identity).</note>. Thus, the soul is not affected by this union any higher than explained above, but there are other excellent consequences that we must consider for a moment, namely these:

<margin>1. A perfect human life.</margin> 1. From this union of soul and body arises a perfect human life. I say a perfect human life, for although it is true that the soul, separated from the body, remains in essence and in life, it is nevertheless not perfect except when united with the body. Therefore, it also constantly longs for this union, as appears from Revelation 6:20 <note>original: "Apoc. 6. 20."</note>.

It is also certain and sure that there are various excellent works of man which man cannot do unless the soul and body are united. He cannot praise and glorify God the Lord with the mouth, nor serve Him with the body—which he is nevertheless bound to do, according to 1 Corinthians 6:20—unless soul and body are united with one another. In this regard, the Psalmist testifies that the dead do not praise the Lord, Psalm 6:6.

Indeed, that very great and most weighty work, which is of the highest importance—namely, the working out of our soul's salvation—is not done, nor can it happen (as we just heard), except while our soul and body are still united together.

Which should rightly serve to make us strive with our utmost best to cherish and maintain our life as well as we

<column-break/>

possibly can; knowing that great things lie at our hand, which we also cannot carry out except while our soul and body are together. Therefore, it is also a very grievous sin for a man to shorten his life, and thus prematurely make himself unfit <note>original: "onbequycsaem," meaning useless or incapacitated for service.</note> for the service of God; therefore everyone must prepare for this and guard against it.

<margin>2. That the workings of soul or body are workings of the whole man: such as that he...</margin> 2. It happens through this union of soul and body that the workings which actually occur either according to the soul or according to the body are fittingly and rightly attributed to the whole man: such as that he hungers, or that he fears the Lord. The one actually refers to the body, the other to the soul; yet both are appropriately, indeed even properly, attributed to the whole man.

<margin>3. The quickening of the body.</margin> 3. Through this union, the body is made alive <note>original: "levendich gemaeckt," or quickened.</note>, which otherwise has no life in itself of its own; and the body is raised as high as it can be raised in glory and beautiful condition. It is not made invisible or intangible, nor is it made intelligent; for just as the body is not invisible, so it is also not intelligent—understanding lies in the soul. But the body is raised as gloriously as possible through the union of the soul with the body, and receives as many excellent things as it can receive, as has appeared throughout the preceding discourse. In such a way that, if the body had more eyes, it would see more through the indwelling of the soul.

This being so, man—who is usually so fond of his body and flesh—should rightly still

# Adam, Righteous,

one should always bear the greatest respect for one's soul, from which the body derives its life and all the agility <note>original: "gauwicheyt"; refers to both mental quickness and physical dexterity</note> that it possesses. Certainly, it shall not be excused in eternity that man so neglects his soul and so pampers his body; which truly—as anyone can easily understand—shall create a very heavy account before God, and must be improved in every respect.

<margin>4. A great love of soul and body for one another.</margin>
4. There also arises from this union a very great love and affection between the soul and the body in the whole man; in such a way that they are each highly moved by the other's state, as the closest and best of friends; as the Apostle teaches in 1 Corinthians 12:25-26. <note>The author refers to the biblical metaphor of the body having many members that care for one another.</note> So that, although it is true that the soul cannot be physically visited by the body, nevertheless, because the body is a part of man and the soul is intelligent and cares for all things concerning man, she is accustomed to being moved, as if from the outside, by the condition of the body, whether unto joy or sorrow.

Indeed, this is certain and sure: soul and body become such good friends through this union that they cannot bear to part at all; and they grow to love each other so much that they take great pains to keep themselves together, and employ great agility and prudence toward that end.

It is a wonder how the Lord, our wise Creator, has managed this matter; that man, without any prior reflection, but simply out of an established care in his heart to do well by himself, possesses such great foresight for his own preservation. A man walks along, his mind

<column-break/>

earnestly occupied with something else, so that he pays no attention to anything and passes by a thousand things which he, as it were, does not see; yet if it happens in this situation that he encounters something that might be harmful to him, he immediately becomes aware of it by instinct, avoids it in his busy stride, and protects himself from it, even though he was entirely preoccupied with something else; even though he also passed by a thousand other things that could not harm him without paying them any mind.

Again, should it happen that through one accident or another, a man is damaged or injured somewhere—even if it were but a splinter in his finger—the eye immediately looks toward it so quickly, the senses and the understanding work to relieve it, the other hand is also immediately there, and the foot runs for help; such agility does man have within himself to preserve his members. And internally within man, all things also proceed so finely for the convenience and well-being of the man; the head, through its influence, cares for the whole body in its situation, as does the heart; and they never suspend this, as Princes are often accustomed to suspend their favor from their subjects.

Thus there is a wonderful, mutual, and great love between the soul and the body, although this same love is not always right; for it often happens now in our corruption <note>referring to the "Fall of Man" or the state of original sin</note> that the soul, out of a misplaced love, gives in too much to the body's lusts, so that they both are lost and end up in the abyss of Hell.

and the body; they grow so accustomed to one another—just like Husband and Wife—and each has need of the other's help in this life: So that the soul does not serve without the body, nor the body without the soul, 1 Corinthians 11:11-12. Therefore, we may rightly apply to the soul and the body that which the Apostle says of the members of man in 1 Corinthians 12 verse 21: *The eye cannot say to the hand, I have no need of you: or again the head to the feet, I have no need of you:* likewise, the soul cannot say to the body, nor the body to the soul, "I have no need of you." Because of this, it happens that their parting <note>referring to death</note> feels very bitter to them; so much so that two friends do not part from one another as reluctantly as the soul and the body usually do.

Therefore the Lord our God takes the likeness of this mutual love of the soul and the body, and of the members of man, to awaken Christian people to mutual love, unity, helpfulness, and compassion. The Apostle teaches us this clearly in 1 Corinthians 12:12-13: that from the affection we have for ourselves, we ought to deduce how we should be inclined toward the fellow-members of Jesus Christ; namely, that we should not pursue our own comfort, advantage, and profit so recklessly without having respect for the <term>tender little members of Christ</term> <note>original: "teere ledekens Christi"; a common Pietist expression referring to fellow believers, especially the poor or spiritually weak</note>; regarding what might be good, edifying, and comforting for them, or not.

The pomp and splendor in clothing, the excess in banquets (while the tender members of Christ live almost naked and hungry, sighing over the excess of such people) would very quickly cease; we would not need to warn the good Congregation against it twice.

Because this does not happen now, we have reason to fear bitterly that, if we do not improve, our very own hands and feet, fingers and thumbs, shall rise up against us in the <term>Judgment</term> <note>The Last Judgment</note>; as these are the things for which we have taken special care, while we take no care for the tender members of Christ, who are much better than our physical limbs.

# To the Christian Reader.

<image-desc>Ornamental square initial 'S' decorated with floral and vine patterns.</image-desc>Whoever observes God's dealings toward us with a discerning eye shall quickly perceive that the Lord God is powerfully at work with us; indeed, that He is now making His final effort toward us for our salvation, should we be saved. The Lord is now employing His ultimate means and remedies to heal us. Long before this, He called out by the *Sword* <note>referring to war</note>; that being of no avail, He added a time of scarcity <note>famine or high prices</note>; and now, at last, He calls out through the gruesome *Pestilence* <note>the plague</note>. These are all *vengeful plagues* which He is accustomed to inflict upon His *covenant-breakers*. Thus the Lord comes upon us with these three terrible rods of His wrath, testing whether He might thereby break our stubbornness and bend our fair necks under the bonds of His *Covenant* <term>Covenant: the formal spiritual agreement between God and His people, often compared to a legal contract</term>. From this we can now sufficiently deduce that *the inhabitants of our Land (who for the most part have entered into God's covenant through Baptism, and many further still through receiving the Holy Supper)* have done great violence to God's covenant. For certainly, just as great plagues are a proof of *great sins, so also are vengeful plagues*—with which the Lord God is accustomed to *avenge the quarrel of His covenant, Leviticus 26:25-26*—a certain proof of the violation that the covenant-members have committed against God's covenant. In the past, many have cried out against *Precisians* <note>a derogatory term for those strictly observant of religious rules, similar to "Puritans"</note> and *narrow-sighted spirits*; and while men have sought to make the *strait gate* wide and the *narrow way* broad, they have denounced the *right path of Godliness* as mere *superstition*. But the Lord comes now and places the matter beyond dispute; He comes now to convince us, with harder blows that can be felt, that we have indeed done great violence to His covenant. He also comes to prove that this evil is a *general evil* <note>a universal or national sin</note>, for He comes to visit us with plagues that are general. And in vain does one seek to diminish the plagues so that our misconduct might appear the less; it appears

# To the Christian Reader.

But now, because God’s Covenant <note>original: "Godts Verbondt"</note> can be violated in many ways by his covenant-partners; so it would indeed be high time, since our dispute over the preceding matters has ended, that we all alike should rouse ourselves, and go to inquire thoroughly, *what is the iniquity, and what is the sin, for which the Lord brings all this misfortune upon us.* Jeremiah 16:10. When David perceived that the Lord visited the people with a time of dearth <note>famine or scarcity</note> for *three years* in a row, he took that occasion to ask the mouth of the Lord what was lacking among them, why the Lord did such a thing. 2 Samuel 21:1. We also ought to have considered such things thoroughly long ago, and not only to say so generally that it is *our sins* which *give birth to these plagues*; but to inquire more closely in particular, *which sins by name, and which iniquities they are, that bring these vengeful plagues <note>original: "Wraeck-plagen"</note> upon our necks.* We ought indeed to have asked long ago, with the plagued Jerusalem, *Why does the Lord do all these things to us?* Jeremiah 5:19. Yea, we ought justly to have said long ago with Job to our God, *Lord, do not condemn us, but let us know why you contend with us,* Job 10:2. Namely, so that we, *knowing such things, might amend them.*

But now, alas! such is the least thought in the hearts of many. Yea, sad experience teaches that some, who have already felt the signs of God's wrath struck into their own bodies, do not yet even properly notice God's anger, or once consider that such is a singular proof that the Lord is greatly incensed because such great violence has been done to his Covenant. But it goes this way now: because everyone who is struck sees that he is not the only one, and that many others are likewise afflicted with him, he readily thinks, "it is just a common occurrence <note>original: "gemeynen overganck"</note> that few are free from; what wonder then if I am also touched? That is surely no proof that there is something particularly disordered in me?" And because even the most Godly are not always spared in this, it is held as being beyond doubt. And through this it happens that one views *extraordinary plagues* (which should make us all terrified and tremble, and urge us most powerfully to notice that much is indeed disordered among us, and to a wakeful diligence to amend it) merely as *ordinary visitations*. And so we have—oh woe, woe to us!—the *pain of the plague*, and *miss the fruit of the same*; and live—

### To the Afflicted Hearts.

...people have most miserably infected, violated, and corrupted one another in their souls through the evil, poisonous breath of all kinds of useless talk and idle chatter. Mouths have overflowed with this everywhere—in boats, on wagons, at meals, and in all manner of company—to the unspeakable damage of human souls (1 Corinthians 15:33). And all this has happened without terror or dread; indeed, people took pleasure in such infectious behavior and mocked those who complained about it or wished to oppose it. 

But mark what followed: this began to grieve the Lord our righteous God (who is jealous over His people and is terribly angered by sin), and it provoked Him to great wrath. Thereupon, He began to let His vengeance go out among the people. And just as our corrupt talk and the unedifying breath of our mouths infected many in their souls—and people even laughed and joked about it at meals, in social circles, in boats, on wagons, in inns, and everywhere—so the Lord God has now brought it to pass that the breath of many mouths has also become <term>pestilential</term><note>plague-bearing</note> and deadly to the body. 

Because of this, people are now beginning to be terrified and to inquire after <term>remedies</term> and <term>preservatives</term><note>preventative medicines or charms</note>. People are now shy of one another; they are afraid to sit together on a wagon or in a boat; they dread going to an inn together or drinking from the same cup. But alas, how pitiful! The aforementioned infection of the soul has penetrated so deeply that, despite all this, there is hardly any further notice taken of anything beyond the physical. We may well ask with the Psalmist: *Who knows the power of Your anger? For as the fear of You, so is Your wrath* (Psalm 90:11). Even those who have the signs of God's wrath upon them, and feel it within themselves, hardly once consider that such things come from the wrath of God; they prefer to think it is merely a common passing occurrence. And those who stand by and see such things in others—even if they carry the same poison within themselves for which they deserve such plagues—nevertheless do not learn to fear, but remain in good spirits as long as they themselves are spared.

Therefore, as we gladly seize every occasion to move God's people toward the fear of the Lord by all means, we have felt moved by these observations to publish this <term>treatise</term>. In it, we do not only point out what a sharp rod the <term>Plague</term>, <term>War</term>, and <term>Dearth</term><note>famine or high cost of living</note> are with which we are now being struck, and how we ought to take the opportunity to better uphold God's covenant; but we point even more closely to the gravity of the <term>pestilence</term>. We show how the Christian person—who fears the severity of the plague or is already caught in it—must conduct themselves to be preserved from it or delivered out of it (for the remedies are much the same). Furthermore, we show how those who have sat in that same misery but are now free should behave hereafter in a way of thankfulness toward the Lord their God, who has kept them safe or mercifully delivered them. 

See, in this treatise we endeavor to give faithful instruction from the Word of the Lord, which cannot fail. And you are yet happy if you will follow the counsel of the Lord regarding this in His Word; if indeed, hearing daily of so many deaths and feeling deadly signs in yourself, you will take all the more occasion to contemplate the killing of the "old man" <note>the sinful nature</note> within you through the life-giving Spirit of Christ. Then you need not fear, even if you see the certain signs of death struck upon your body by the God of life. Simply use the following means of life properly: and if they do not deliver you from temporal death, they shall surely, through temporal death, translate you into eternal life; and what more could you desire? Therefore, for the furtherance of this, we add the following <term>prayer</term> here.

## Prayer for one who is stricken with the Plague.

->Lord God Heavenly Father, it has pleased You to strike me with this terrible rod of Your wrath, which creeps through all my limbs and greatly unsettles me, for which also nearly all people shrink away in horror, and even the best of friends often abandon the plagued; I confess Lord, Your chastisement is righteous over me, I have deserved such, and a thousand times more; I have provoked You in many ways with my sins, so You have quite fairly been able to come and strike me with the rod of Your wrath, I have also not observed all occasions to do virtue to my neighbor, while I was able to associate with him, as I well ought, yes I have even been contagious to my acquaintances now and then *according to the soul* <note>The author suggests that his past sinful behavior or bad influence was a "spiritual contagion" even before the physical plague took hold.</note>, through my imprudent conduct, therefore You also righteously thrust me out from the company of my known friends, and place me among strangers. But Lord good God, there is nevertheless grace and mercy with You; and even though this infectious disease makes my friends themselves stand far from me, and also prevents me so that I cannot come among Your children <note>Meaning the congregation or church community.</note>, yet nevertheless O Lord, I have indeed no less a free access to You my God, through Jesus Christ my Lord: Your affection toward me is not changed, even though my state is thus changed; and even though some of my friends hide their faces from me, even if I ask for them; so surely You will not hide Your face from me, if I only have a heart to seek You through Jesus Christ my Lord. For His sake I pray You then, forgive me all my sins, the cause of this my sorrow; bless also the means <note>Refers to medicines, poultices, or medical treatments of the time.</note> that are used upon me for my healing; lay no more upon me than I can well bear; and give me also always long-suffering, and patience in this heavy visitation, and be You O Lord my God, who are *a Father of mercies, and a God of all comfort* <note>original: "een Vader der barmhertigheden, ende een Godt aller vertrooſtinge" — a reference to 2 Corinthians 1:3.</note>, now all the more kind to me, the more I am now deprived of the comfort of many of my friends; let the comfort of Your good Spirit fulfill in me what I lack from the side of my friends. Let me also be well prepared O Lord, for the hour of death, give me a good fight to fight; do not permit then, that my spiritual enemy <note>The Devil.</note> should have any power against me, but rather give Lord Your Angels charge, that they watch over me in all ways, and keep watch over me in my extremity; so that I Lord God, departing from this miserable House of this Tabernacle <note>A biblical metaphor for the mortal human body.</note>, which presently is full of smart, pain, anguish, and sadness, might be taken up into the Heavenly dwelling, where no smart, no pain, can enter, where also is to be found, for that soul which here is nearly forsaken by all company, the most joyful company that can come from there, and the fullness of joys forever and ever. Oh Lord, grant me this, oh Lord, hear me, oh Lord, be merciful to me, in living, and in dying, through Jesus Christ my Savior. A M E N.<-

# The Right of God’s Covenant. 427

would stir up new plagues and punishments against them, even seven times more (that is) many more plagues; a certain number being set for an uncertain <note>The author explains that "seven" is used here as a biblical idiom for a great, indefinite quantity rather than a literal count.</note>, than they had previously experienced.
**Concerning God’s Method, how He approaches His people to cure them of their sins.**

<margin>Doctrine.</margin> When God’s people are not bettered by God’s lesser plagues and punishments, the Lord will employ even heavier plagues to correct the stubbornness of His people: this appears clearly from our text, so that no contradiction can arise concerning it. This then is the method (as appears from this Chapter) by which the Lord God approaches His people to cure them of sin: He first approaches His people with His word, and teaches them what is profitable, and shows them the way they should go, Isaiah 1:2. He adds to this beautiful promises; He entreats His people, just as one entreats a Bride, that they would indeed fear and obey Him, verses 3 to 14. When He does all this in vain, and sees that His words vanish into the air like a useless speech, like a vain word (though it is indeed no vain word, Deuteronomy 32:47, for He after all created the World and all that is in it through His word), then He begins to change His voice; calling heaven and earth to witness, protesting, and complaining very movingly, so that it might melt a heart of stone, Jeremiah 2:12, 13. **Question.** By what is it known that one does not improve through the lesser chastisements that God the Lord has brought upon us?

# The Right of God’s Covenant:

Even though we are currently spared, we are just as guilty as those already punished. For a very long time now, in many of our cities and villages, the Lord God has faithfully allowed us to be taught what is profitable and has shown us the path we must walk. He has coaxed us; He has visited our homes from time to time with lesser chastisements—various illnesses, losses by water and land, economic decay <note>original: "neeringh-loosheydt," referring to a stagnation of trade or industry</note>, and such. But who has taken heed? Who has been improved by this? If it were otherwise, what flourishing congregations, what godly people would we find everywhere among men!

But now it stands quite differently: the foundation of the Reformed Religion was laid among us over fifty years ago—so well that no other can be laid, according to 1 Corinthians 3:11-12. But where is the gold and silver, the precious stones and pearls that are built upon it? Where are the people who now shine as lights in the midst of a crooked and perverse generation? Who respond to all the trouble and expense the Lord has taken with them for their improvement and edification? Certainly, it goes as it usually does: we remain the same old people, neither more nor less, as if the Lord God had never been among us with His word and His rod. This is terrifying: for how shall the preachers thunder against our sins and we not be frightened? If the Lord God confirms the word of His messengers (even if at first with lesser punishments) and we, giving no heed, allow ourselves to believe that things will go well for us? 

Let all those take note who were once so moved by the preaching of God’s word that they became convinced they had to amend their lives; those who were once brought so low by God’s visitations of sickness

<column-break/>

or other hardships that they promised the Lord they would improve; and yet, having escaped, they have stuck their heads back out <note>an idiom for returning to old ways or showing defiance</note> and remained the same old people. Certainly, these people fall under this threat of God: that He will come to punish them seven times more severely for their sins; and if all that will not help, that He will at last bring the pains of hell and eternal damnation upon them.

<margin>Because the Lord is already visiting us with heavier punishments, it proves against us that we have greatly increased our sins against God.</margin>

From this we can also learn what we ought to feel regarding the present condition of our entire land, now that we see and feel that the Lord—beyond His usual custom—visits us not only with War, but also with Pestilence, and further threatens us with high prices <note>original: "dieren tijt," referring to inflation or the high cost of living</note> and famine. Certainly, what else can we conclude from this than that we have increased our sins and have not been improved by previous lesser plagues? Otherwise, the Lord would surely spare the effort of imposing new and heavier plagues upon us. 

We often want to argue at length that we still stand reasonably well before God, but the plagues of the righteous God demonstrate something else entirely. We still want to cloak <note>original: "bemantelen," to cover up or excuse</note> our affairs, but God tells us clearly through His plagues that they are not right, as in 2 Kings 17:9. Indeed, our sins are so great and so many that they cannot be brushed aside, so that we are like the fool: for even if one were to crush us in a mortar with a pestle in the middle of bruised grain, our folly would not depart from us (Proverbs 27:22). Therefore, we must be dealt with even more harshly, with plagues that we might feel more keenly. Indeed, that the Lord God thus begins to send His plagues and punishments over us...

# The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading

The fact that our burdens are increased is proof that our sins are so baked-in <note>original: "aengebacken," implying something encrusted or burnt onto a vessel</note> that we must be broken along with our sins; for we are now punished with a total destruction. The foul vessel, with all that is within it, is now being cast out together.

<margin>That we are indeed a people who can be bettered by nothing other than the hard blows that one feels.</margin>
This way of our God toward us—that He thus comes to seek us out at home with the heaviest plagues—is a certain conviction to us that we are all too stubborn, or rather (as the World now takes it) all too wise to allow ourselves to be bettered by God’s word or by lesser plagues. We have resistances, excuses, and a thousand-fold wicked tricks against it, with which we know how to deafen our conscience so that we do not reform, **Psalm 58:5-6.** So that even when we have made the narrow way broad and the strait gate of life quite wide, we still want to be in the right. Therefore the Lord must come over us with heavier plagues and plead the matters of His covenant quite differently (as He says in **Isaiah 28:21**).

Wicked people as we are, we would sooner call into question God’s word, truth, power, and providence than depart from our sinful dealings. If some evil befalls us because of our sins, we nevertheless refuse to acknowledge God’s power in it; if we ourselves do evil, we dare to blame God’s will for it. We persist in circumcising <note>i.e., cutting down or censoring</note> God’s word rather than circumcising our sins. We are blind Balaams who see neither God’s sword nor His hand, but recklessly and stiffly press on with our sins onto the point of God’s wrath; and we dare to strike with our tongues the men of God—as if they were donkeys—even the angels of God and faithful servants of the Most High, because they, seeing more than such people see, also speak more of the judgments of God than such people care to hear.

<column-break/>

Therefore God is necessitated, and as if forced, to come and strike us with such blows and plagues as may prove the all-overpowering hand of an incensed Omnipotence. Such are the plagues which the Lord threatens here in our text and now begins to lay upon us; so that He, who previously was neither feared nor respected by many among us, might now at last begin to be held in awe, because He begins to plead the matters of His covenant with the gruesome Pestilence <note>The Plague</note>, for which everyone trembles. Just so, the Lord was necessitated to teach this to the Egyptians, **Exodus 7:4-5**, and also to the reckless Gog and Magog, **Ezekiel 38:22-23.**

<margin>Which therefore shall also not tarry in coming, unless we hasten toward actual reformation.</margin>
Secondly, we come to learn here what we have to expect for the future: certainly nothing but more plagues if we do not reform. See, it stands written there: that we reform so little under previous plagues constantly stirs up new ones. The Lord, who is wise and merciful, sees that we have need of all this to drive away our insensitivity and deadness, and so He brings all these plagues upon us, **Isaiah 28:24 etc.** Yea, He is a God who will not leave His work unfinished, but will carry out to the utmost that which He has once begun, as He Himself said to Samuel: -> I shall begin it, and complete it. **1 Samuel 3:12.** <-
When He then takes it in hand to punish His people—because He does not want them to perish with the wicked World—He will not stop until He has broken their pride and stubbornness, and brought them under His yoke and to His hand. So we see also that the Lord still goes on, stiffly and strongly, punishing His people, whom He once took in hand...

# The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading

You who are now in sorrow ought to consider that if you do not improve yourselves through these temporal chastisements <note>The author refers to "temporal" or earthly punishments as a warning of eternal ones.</note>—whatever they may be—which the Lord now brings upon you while you are still on your way, He will certainly bring eternal punishments upon your neck hereafter. And learn from this, O man, to take heed even now, so that you might not come into the place of eternal torment. Consequently, take a firm resolution, on the occasion of this temporal punishment, to yield yourself to the hand of the Lord, to gladly take up His yoke, and to live the time that remains no longer according to human desires, but according to the will of God. Then these shall yet be entirely blessed visitations for you, however much they pain you now; then you shall yet thank the Lord that He took the trouble to send even the heaviest plagues upon you—take for instance the **Pestilence** <note>The Plague or Black Death, often seen as a direct divine judgment.</note>, or whatever might be even heavier—to break your wicked stubbornness and to make you come to His hand for your eternal salvation.

# The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading

->This must indeed be noted. So it stands.<-

We would all gladly escape the threatened punishments: of the gruesome **Pestilence**, of the destroying **sword**, of the black **Famine**; we shudder, if we but think of it properly, that they might fall upon our necks. When we also hear of hell and eternal damnation in hell, and think for a moment what a horror and terror it would be for us to be always and eternally in the place of torment without any relief or hope of escape, our hair seems to stand on end; we then desire most greatly to escape that place of torment. 

But what of it? Even if it stands thus with us, it is nevertheless true that the present comfort of the flesh, the foolish love we bear for present fleshly lusts, desires, and pleasures, so greatly blind us and so miserably lead us astray, that even though we greatly dread the **Pestilence**, the destroying **sword**, the **famine**, and even more so **hell** and **damnation**; we nevertheless have neither the heart nor the mind to properly take courage to enter into the ways and means through which we might flee the aforementioned terrifyingly dreaded plagues and punishments. 

To our flesh, it begins to feel like a new plague, a new death, a new hell, to have to employ such and such strict means to be released from the dreaded plague. Here we are found, through and through, to be of the nature of the devil; it seems to us that when one calls us to the use of those spiritual means to escape the dreaded plagues, that one comes to torment us before the

<column-break/>

time <note>original: "pijntzen voor den tijdt" - a reference to Matthew 8:29, where demons ask Jesus if he has come to torment them before the appointed time</note>; so we pull backward and want nothing to do with it. Thus, it is made true concerning the thoughtless person what **Solomon** says: *The turning away of the simple shall slay them, and the prosperity of fools shall destroy them.* **Proverbs 1:32.** And so, while we avoid temporary hardship, we cast ourselves into the eternal. 

And it would be something, O man! if you feared being tormented before the time, if there were no hope that by tormenting yourself a little now before the time, you might escape the eternal torment. But now it stands quite differently; there is indeed still hope, O man! of salvation, as **Shechaniah** said, **Ezra 10 verse 2.** 

Will you now still follow God’s counsel? Will you still resolve to properly take God’s means in hand? What is at stake? We do not wish to say with the **Ninevites**, *God might turn from the fierceness of his anger.* **Jonah 3:9.** But we can assure you, that yes, **God the Lord** shall turn from His grim wrath and spare you from death—certainly from eternal death, which alone is to be feared. For He has said it, yes, sworn it: *He has no pleasure in the death of the sinner, but in this, that he should convert and live.* **Ezekiel 33:11.** 

It might also be that **God the Lord**, seeing our humiliation and improvement, shall also further give His gracious blessing to the warding off of the dreaded temporal inconveniences themselves: of the **Pestilence**, the destroying **sword**, the **famine**; if we do not wait too long, if we indeed catch His hand <note>original: "in de roede vallen" - literally 'to fall into the rod', meaning to submit to discipline before the blow falls</note> in time. But otherwise, if we wish to follow our fleshly ease, if we wish to shrink from taking God’s means in hand, if we allow ourselves to think of them as too painful, too difficult, then we have, plainly speaking,

Therefore, let us all together follow the Lord our God; yes, let us all together take courage to improve ourselves and those entrusted to us, and to free ourselves from sins that provoke God. This is so that we might spare the Lord God the trouble of punishing us seven times more <note>A reference to the biblical warning in Leviticus 26 that continued disobedience leads to increasingly severe, "sevenfold" divine discipline.</note>. Now this Covenant is made in such a way that, on the one hand, if it were kept, a great deal of good has been promised to those who maintain it; on the other hand, many heavy plagues have been threatened against the transgressors of it, as can be read at length here in our chapter, Leviticus 26, and Deuteronomy 28. # The Sword of Vengeance, Defended

->**The Doctrine**<-

<margin>For indeed, the Lord God is accustomed to avenge the injury done to His covenant—whether through stubbornness, lack of zeal, or otherwise—with very heavy plagues.</margin>
When someone suffers oppression or is treated unjustly, and being powerless to help themselves against it, they cry out for vengeance to the one whom they know is both powerful and willing to stand up for them. In this same sense, it is said of Abel’s blood that the voice of that same blood cried out to God from the earth (**Genesis 4:10**), namely for vengeance (**Hebrews 12:24** <note>The author links the Old Testament cry for justice with the New Testament's discussion of Christ's blood which "speaks better things than that of Abel."</note>). In this same sense, then, the "vengeance of the covenant" is spoken of here. Now, to avenge this vengeance of the covenant means to actually carry out what the Lord had threatened against those who enter into His Covenant and then violate it. And to execute such upon them, the Lord testifies here that He would send a sword among them. Now, by this we must certainly understand, in the first instance, the destroying sword of enemies; but as we know that frequently in the Scripture, all kinds of severe plagues are understood by "the sword"—to the extent that not only the sword of war, but also the Pestilence is attributed to it, as in **1 Chronicles 21:30**. And as we also tend to say of Hunger, that it is a sharp sword; so it is not absurd that we also understand here by the "Sword of Vengeance" all kinds of severe plagues which the Lord God would bring over His people (if they did not speedily repent through lesser punishments) to avenge His Covenant.

The Lord our God, with whom we have to do, is accustomed to avenge the injury done to His Covenant with very heavy plagues. We see it here in our text: the Lord testifies here that He will bring forth the most terrifying weapons of His wrath to avenge the wrong done to His Covenant

<column-break/>

<margin>done to His covenant, to avenge it with very heavy plagues.</margin>
by His people. He testifies to them that He will bring upon them the Pestilence, the hand of their enemies, the necessity of hunger, and all that is terrifying. He testifies as much elsewhere as well; listen to what the Lord says in **Jeremiah 29:17, 18, 19**: "Thus says the Lord of hosts: Behold, I will send the Sword, the Hunger, and the Pestilence among them: and I will make them like the loathsome figs, which cannot be eaten because of their badness. And I will pursue after them with the sword, with the hunger, and with the pestilence: and I will deliver them to be a reproach to all the kingdoms of the earth, for a curse, and for a terror, and for a hissing, and for a shame among the nations where I have driven them. Because they have not heard my words, speaks the Lord, when I sent my servants the Prophets to them, rising early and sending them: but you would not hear, speaks the Lord." So also has the Lord actually and continually pleaded the right of His Covenant with His people through various plagues; the books of Judges and Kings are entirely full of this. Listen to what the Psalmist says to that end in **Psalm 78:10**: "They kept not (he says) the covenant of God, and refused to walk in His law, and they forgot His deeds, and His wonders that He had shown them" (which he then relates there specifically in detail). And then follow these words in **verses 31, 32, 33**: "Then the wrath of God rose against them, so that He slew the strongest of them, and struck down the chosen of Israel. Despite all this, they sinned still, and believed not in His wonders; therefore He made their days vanish in vanity, and their years in terror." For this is playing the hypocrite with the Lord, and treating His covenant as a mockery.

Now in this regard—oh, poor place!—our entire Land stands quite guilty. The Lord has chastised us many times, and what good things have we then promised Him! But alas! nothing further has come of it; indeed, we have become worse and worse from day to day; we have merely flattered God with our mouths, and lied to Him with our tongues, Psalm 78:36. For this reason, for this reason—oh woe, woe unto us!—the Covenant of Grace also cries out for vengeance against us.

<margin>2. When one, having entered into the covenant, nevertheless wanders along carelessly, as if one were under no covenant.</margin>
2. The second is this: that when one has now entered into the covenant of God, and appears to have dedicated oneself to God in a special way, Exodus 19:5 and 8, one then nevertheless wanders along carelessly, as if one were in no covenant, as if one had no Lord whom one must serve, or to whose word or punishments one had to pay heed. This sin is also noted here in our text, verse 23, and also makes the covenant of grace cry out for vengeance; for it is also a entirely harmful mistreatment of the covenant. It behaves as if the Lord God alone were so insignificant and lowly that one might abuse, deceive, and mistreat Him above all others without making any difficulty of it, or expecting any further trouble to come from it. But what does the Lord say through the Prophet? *Will a man rob his God?* Malachi 3:8. It is just as if someone should clearly bind himself to the service of this or that person, to look faithfully after his work and to do it; and should then never look back at it again, but let the work go as it would. May the Lord not justly say against such people: "If you would not do my work, why did you take it on? I might have looked for another..."

# The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading

Is then this conduct not exactly the same as the conduct of the wicked servant, who, receiving a talent from his master, instead of putting it to use, went and hid it in a cloth <note>Luke 19:20</note>, or buried it in the earth <note>Matthew 25:18</note>? Therefore his hands and feet were justly bound, and he was cast into the uttermost darkness.

Now, a great multitude of people in our land are also guilty of this sin that cries out for vengeance. Very many are found everywhere who have indeed entered into God's Covenant, having received Baptism, and many also the Holy Supper <note>The Eucharist or Communion</note> in addition; who henceforth live their lives entirely carelessly; they do not feel bound in their hearts and consciences to the service of the Most High God; but live on there loosely and unconstrained, just as it happens; as if they were their own masters <note>Psalm 12:4; original: "Ps. 12. 5."</note>, as if they had no Lord or Master in heaven <note>Colossians 4:1</note>, to whom they shall have to give an account of how they behave here on earth according to the content of His Covenant into which they have entered. Indeed, many of them are so ignorant and unaware that, even though they bear the seals of the Covenant upon them, they nevertheless do not know how to speak of any Covenant; they do not understand what is meant when one says to them, "this or that person is in the Covenant." They have perhaps heard some talk of <term>Sacraments</term> <note>Holy rituals, specifically Baptism and Communion, viewed as visible signs of God's grace</note>, and it may be that now and then they have even sworn by them, but they do not recognize them as seals of the Covenant; they know of no Covenant, so far are they from it that they would take any care to keep it. For this reason, for this reason (oh woe, woe unto us!) the Covenant of Grace also cries out for vengeance against us.

<column-break/>

Then there are yet two or three other common sins which also set themselves so directly against the Covenant of Grace that the same cries out for vengeance against them, because of the outrage it suffers thereby; and these are:

<margin>3. That one considers the things of the covenant (which are the most worthy things in the world) only sluggishly.</margin>
3. <term>Lukewarmness</term> <note>A state of spiritual indifference or lack of zeal</note> in the things of the Covenant: that, even if one does not seem to neglect the matters of the Covenant entirely or cast them out of esteem, one nevertheless proceeds with them in such a way that one does them most poorly, very sluggishly, just to keep up appearances and nothing more; that while one knows how to promote one's own affairs with great earnestness and drive, one takes up the things of God quite feebly <note>Haggai 1:4</note>. This lukewarmness in the covenant-members also presses and distresses the Covenant of Grace so greatly that it cannot suffer nor endure it, so that it indeed sighs over it and cries for vengeance: just as we can gather from this, that the Lord Christ, the Surety of this better Covenant <note>Hebrews 7:22</note>, expressly testifies that he can so little endure this lukewarmness that he is ready to spit such people out of his mouth <note>Revelation 3:16; original: "Apoc. 3. 16."</note>.

Of this, almost our entire land is also guilty; whose [own] affairs are done with earnestness, with diligence, with faithfulness, and great industry; but the Lord's things are everywhere observed quite feebly: we are lukewarm, yes, lukewarm are we in the things of God, and we cannot deny it; our own consciences fully convict us of it. I believe there is hardly one in the land who must not confess such of himself, so entirely has all zeal for divine things declined. Indeed, it has now come to the point that one can oppose and mock true zeal for the Lord...

<margin>5. That one abuses the grace of the Covenant for licentiousness.</margin>

<margin>II. From the inherent nature of the Pestilence.</margin>
This can also be understood from the nature of the Pestilence itself, which is this: It is an entirely harmful and destructive poison <note>original: "vergif"</note> expelled into the flesh of man, whereby a violent burning (commonly) is aroused in all limbs, with a very great anguish <note>original: "benautheyt" - a feeling of constriction or suffocating anxiety.</note> around the heart, through which many become raving and insane, so that they must be restrained and held fast like madmen, or they would readily do much harm to themselves and others. Also, few are cured of it; the very strongest are readily snatched away from life within a few hours; indeed, the stronger someone is, the more readily he is overcome by this deadly venom; and those who yet escape it commonly retain some deformed scars of this harmful disease; some also never regain the use of their senses as well as they had them before.

Here, immediately, all friendly communication and fellowship begins to cease; one no longer dares to hold meals together; one is now afraid even to drink a draught of beer from a strange mug; the ordinary visiting of friends is stopped. The best of friends hardly dare to visit one another for fear that they might infect others or be infected themselves. And where they would gladly open their minds to one another through written letters instead of visiting, such is also feared; and the pleasant letters of our friends, which we otherwise used to read with such great pleasure, are then accepted by some with dread and suspicion, and opened with anxiety for fear that some infection might cling to them. # The Sword of Vengeance, Pleaded

The Psalmist says of the Lord in Psalm 84:11 <note>original: "Psal. 84. 12." due to different verse numbering in older Bibles</note>, *He will withhold no good thing from those who walk in uprightness.* Therefore, whatever God the Lord promises to the pious, he also carries out for them, insofar as that thing is good and conducive to their salvation. But it can happen that it is sometimes more beneficial for their salvation to die of the **Plague** <note>original: "Pestilentie"</note> than to live in luxury; they do not know when such is the case for them, but God knows, and therefore one must let Him have His way and consequently rest easy in His actions, Psalm 37:5, 11. Furthermore, the general promises of God always carry this understanding: that they must be mixed with faith by the pious themselves if they are to enjoy the particular fruit thereof, Galatians 3:14. Now it readily happens that even the most godly are deficient in their faith, and that they do not accept the gracious promises of God regarding temporal assurances with faith as well as they should; therefore they often come to miss the fulfillment thereof, Matthew 17:19, 20. III. Thirdly, these promises must be taken in their full power, looking toward the final end of all our endeavors: God certainly preserves those who love Him, even when He lets them be struck down by the harmful Plague. To this end, Christ—promising His disciples God’s protection on their paths and testifying to them that not a hair of their head would perish—nevertheless gave them to understand at the same time that some of them would be killed, Luke 21:16, 17. To which we must know this: that the Lord our God, who is eternal, also arranges and fits all His affairs according to

<column-break/>

the circumstances of eternity: thus He sometimes brings temporal difficulties upon His children in order to prepare their eternal deliverance; as we shall understand more broadly hereafter.

**Question.** Nevertheless, it seems strange that God the Lord would strike His own dear children with that very plague and punishment which He specifically threatens against His enemies and against the godless breakers of His covenant?

<margin>And that the Plague is also specifically a punishment that the Lord sends upon the Godless Breakers.</margin>

**Answer.** All kinds of plagues and punishments, great and small, these and those, whatever they may be, are properly the lot and the portion of the godless; they drink even the dregs thereof. Nonetheless, the children of God themselves also drink somewhat of it; indeed, the very same outward plagues with which the most godless are plagued sometimes also fall upon the necks of the children of God; such as death itself—which is surely the most fierce plague—and terrifying manners of dying which appear to be very cursed, just as the death of Christ was, and the death of many **Martyrs** appeared to be. And for this, the Lord nevertheless undoubtedly has great and weighty reasons, even if we cannot always point them out; yet He reveals some to us that might quiet our "counter-cackling" <note>meaning: grumbling or complaining</note> flesh. those who serve Him might be known to do so through a singular Divine power of faith, which leads them further than flesh and blood can teach them; so that where the godless—seeing that it goes the same for the pious and the impious in this world—conclude from this that it is in vain to serve God, and to walk in mourning before the face of the Lord of hosts. *Malachi 3:14.* <note>The author cites Malachi to show the typical complaint of the cynical: that righteousness brings no material reward.</note>

Or is he slain according to the slaughter of those who were slain by him?*
<margin>Isaiah 27:7, 8.</margin>
*In measure you have contended with him.* The Lord God comes with the sword of the Pestilence upon the godless as with a deadly tool, to destroy them in soul and body, forever and eternally, as with a single blow. In contrast, he comes upon the godly only to discipline them in measure; they are disciplined by the Lord so that
<margin>1 Corinthians 11:32.</margin>
they should not be condemned with the world. He disciplines them here temporally in the body, to preserve them eternally in both soul and body; indeed, he disciplines them here with temporal punishments to protect them from eternal punishments, and to prepare them for eternal joy and glory. To this we must also know that the Lord our wonderful God, when he converts men and powerfully works in them toward true Godliness, making them into new creatures, that he then through his wonderful wisdom instills in them a certain secret virtue <note>term: virtue; here meaning an inherent power or quality</note> and strength, through which it stands with them so that all things

<column-break/>

<margin>
Although it otherwise seems strange that the Lord God would strike his dear children, who still keep his Covenant, with that sword wherewith he avenges the outrage done to his Covenant.
</margin>
that may befall them must work for their best and for their eternal
<margin>Romans 8:28.</margin>
salvation. Through this it then happens that even those things which in their own nature are merely signs and fruits of God's wrath and grim anger, become to them signs of God's love and fatherly care over them—such as are all the tribulations, difficulties, and chastisements that befall them in this
<margin>Revelation 3:19.</margin>
world. In such a way, that even when the most ruinous and deadly things strike the godly—such as the destroying Sword, Famine, or Pestilence—these same things must all alike serve and advance them toward salvation and eternal life. For Godliness has the promise of this life
<margin>1 Timothy 4:8.</margin>
and of that which is to come. We see this clearly in death itself; for there is surely nothing more terrifying, nothing more ruinous than death itself; it causes one to rot, to stink, to perish. Nevertheless, terrifying and ruinous death (which to the godless is a second Sergeant <note>A legal officer or bailiff</note> to summon them out of this world before the fearful judgment of God, to be condemned there and then thrust into the abyss of hell and eternal pains) is to the Godly only like a polite messenger, kindly inviting them to come out of this troublesome world into the house of their heavenly Father, where there is fullness of joy and lovely being forever and eternally; so that to them, death is only as a passage to eternal life.

**Question.** But further still, it indeed seems quite strange that the **Plague** is declared here to be a **Sword of God's Vengeance**, to avenge—

# The Right of God's Covenant.

...the vengeance of his covenant; whereas it is nevertheless found that sometimes those who are the most abominable *Covenant-breakers* go free, while others, who in comparison to them are as entirely innocent folk, are struck by it.

->*Answer.*<- The *Plague* <note>original: "Pestilentie"</note> is such a sword of vengeance, yet it is in the hand of a wise *God* who always directs it well, although his management of it is not always known: and that he then lets some outstandingly ungodly people go free, while he himself strikes some godly ones with the *Plague*, the *Lord* also does not do without discernment. In order to grasp this rightly, we must know that the *Lord* our *God*, who is eternal, does all his things concerning men—to whom he has also given an eternal soul—for the sake of eternity. The *Lord* does not strike men with the *Plague* merely to strike them here for a time, but he does it for an eternal end: He strikes the ungodly with the plague to destroy them eternally; he strikes the godly to preserve them eternally: and he is so wise and skillful a master-craftsman that with that same and very tool, he knows how to work such diverse effects, according to the different circumstances of those upon whom he employs the same tool. That he then, in time of *Plague*, lets some ungodly go free while he strikes some *Godly* ones, he also does especially with a respect to eternity; namely, to teach us all that he does not settle the accounts evenly here on earth; for then the *Ungodly* would have to be the first who would be most heavily punished here; and the *Godly* those

<column-break/>

who would also be most blessed here temporally; which, turning out otherwise through the management of our *God*, leads us to a consideration of the eternal judgment, and of those two great ends of eternity: salvation and damnation, toward which the *Lord* directs all his dealings concerning the children of men. Thus this way of our *God* also serves greatly for the maintenance of his *Covenant*, which is solely established to promote those eternal things, toward the observation of which the aforementioned wonderful dealing of *God* powerfully leads all men who have any observation of *God's* dealing.

To this is added that it is enough to confirm that indeed the *Plague* is a sword of vengeance, applied to avenge the vengeance of the *covenant*, that many *covenant-breakers* are punished by it, although they are not precisely all struck by it. For the *Lord*, who is kind, sometimes spares now this one, now that one, for a long time yet, to let their measure be filled, testing whether they would at any time reflect upon themselves and turn to the *Lord*, so that they might be saved; just as we then also see happen now and then, that indeed those who were formerly abominable *covenant-breakers* are, through *God's* all-overpowering power and kindness, converted in the course of time, and henceforth begin to observe the matters of the *covenant* from the heart; although many of them are hardened in their sins, and are merely preserved until the day of judgment for heavier punishments.

Indeed, it then also appears from all this, that yes, certainly the *Plague*, which there like death, [strikes] all kinds of people so...

# Sword of Vengeance, Vindicated

...falls upon the body, and creates such a fearful distress, it is certainly a very heavy plague: Do we not consider it a terrible plague sent over the inhabitants of *Jerusalem*, when the destroying Angels received this charge from God over it,
> Strike, let your eye not spare, and do not show pity. Kill the old, young men, and maidens, and little children, and women until they are destroyed. *Ezek.* 9:5-6.

Indeed, exactly such a destructive power (as we have now heard) the *Pestilence* <note>original: "Pestilentie"; used here to mean the plague</note> also has: wherever it comes, it comes armed with this commission from the Most High:
> Strike, let your eye not spare, and do not show pity; kill the old, young men, maidens, little children, women, rich and poor, noble and common, wise and unwise, lowly and prominent, all until they are destroyed.

Yes, even the godly and the ungodly, the children of the world and the children of God, who all likewise face death, although not the same kind of death. But that the *Pestilence* is indeed a very heavy plague shall appear even more clearly if we choose to observe from where and how the *Pestilence* comes upon men.

# The Justice of God's Covenant

...recognizing the oneness of this plague in its Author, who sends the Pestilence <note>The Bubonic Plague or any sweeping epidemic.</note> to the people because of the aforementioned sins.

The Author who sends the Pestilence is the incensed God; it is nothing less than a provoked Omnipotence that sends the plague of Pestilence among the people. It is indeed the vengeance of God; it is the grim raging of the Lord's wrath which ignites this fire of Pestilence. Hear, then, how the Lord himself speaks of it: <margin>*Jer. 21. Isa. 5, 6.*</margin> *I myself* (He says) *shall fight against you with an outstretched hand and with a strong arm: yes, with wrath and grimness, and with great indignation.* (And what do you think shall follow?) *And I will* (He says) *strike the inhabitants of this city, both man and beast: they shall die by a great Pestilence.* So also Moses immediately recognized, as soon as he perceived that the plague of Pestilence had broken out among the people, that a great wrath had gone out from before the face of the Lord. <margin>*Num. 16:46.*</margin> With that certainty, the Pestilence is also explicitly called in the Word of the Lord "the hand of the Lord," <margin>*Exod. 9:15.*</margin> "the Sword of the Angel of the Lord," <margin>*1 Chron. 21:30.*</margin> and "the arrows of God." <margin>*Psalm 38:3.*</margin> And this is so patently obvious—namely, that the Pestilence comes from the incensed God—that even the most skillful physicians among the Heathens <note>Non-Christian or Pagan thinkers, often referring to Greek and Roman authorities like Galen or Hippocrates.</note> call this plague the "Divine sword," and place the healing of it under their Gods; thereby acknowledging that it is a punishment that comes from God in a special way. Eminent Heathen writers call it a "heaviness" <note>original: *swarigheyt*—referring to a divine burden or affliction.</note> sent by God; others, a "Heavenly Lightning." They also commonly attributed the causes of severe Pestilences arising among the people to some high-

<column-break/>

reaching sins, such as *Sacrilege* <note>original: *Sacrilegie*—the violation or profanation of anything sacred.</note>, or a completely faithless breach of a Covenant. To such an extent did they believe this, that even the Heathen Poets, when describing the Pestilence, introduce their Gods as shooting the arrows of their vengeance. Therefore, this same Pestilence is also appropriately called by others "God's War" against sinful man. From this, it surely appears clearly enough that the Plague is indeed a heavy affliction. For we all likewise know full well that it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God when He is incensed against sin. <margin>*Heb. 10:31.*</margin> If then the wrath of God is to be feared, and the striking hand of provoked Omnipotence is to be dreaded, then the Pestilence, proceeding everywhere from a provoked Omnipotence, is a very heavy plague. This is further evident from the means that the Lord God uses from time to time to send the Pestilence among the people.

<margin>3. The means through which the Pestilence is brought upon the necks of the people are: 1. Infectious breath of men, and of the Air, which is very terrifying.</margin>

3. The common and well-known means, and that which is most spoken of among the people, is the infectious breath <note>In the 17th century, the "miasma theory" suggested disease was spread by foul air or the breath of the sick.</note> that comes from the infected, or the infectious air which proceeds from them, or which has become entirely tainted in the place where one lives. That indeed (even if it is not all that should be noted here) is a terrifying thing: namely, when the breath of one human being is made deadly to another. It is fearsome when the hand, the sword, the bow, or the firearm <note>original: *roer*—an early type of musket or gun.</note> of one man is turned into a deadly weapon against another; but what a sorrowful thing is it then, when the very breath of our best friend, of our father, our mother, of the wife who lies in our bosom, or of our dear and precious children...
