<meta>This page transitions from a general call to repentance to a practical and theological examination of the plague's nature. It specifically addresses contemporary debates about whether the plague is contagious—a contentious issue in the 17th century involving both medical observation and theological views on divine providence. The author argues that acknowledging physical contagion does not negate God's sovereignty, but rather shows how God uses natural means.</meta>

# The Right of God’s Covenant.

...to examine and look into things somewhat more closely: 1. Whether the plague is contagious. 2. Secondly, whether it is advisable, in times of plague, to leave the place where the plague rages. 3. Thirdly, what means we might further best use to be protected against the gruesome Pestilence, wherever we might live.

### Whether the plague is contagious.

<margin>Yes, the Plague [is contagious]</margin>
The plague (as experience fully teaches) is indeed contagious, just as several other diseases are, which nonetheless are not as hot and distressing as the plague. There is nothing in the world so common as the finding that an infected person, being incautiously visited and attended by others, causes several of them to be readily struck with the plague, and that the fire of the plague is thus further ignited in various places. This can be as little denied as that several of those who are in the front lines, where a hot battle occurs and many deadly bullets fly like hail, are hit and struck down, while others, who are a mile from there, go on unharmed; to this, then, may be applied that the Pestilence is compared to an arrow that flies by day, *Psalm 91 verse 5.*

But here some ask how it can be that the infected person would thus transfer his contagion to others; and because they see nothing coming off the infected with their eyes, nor hear anything (just as one can still sometimes see and always hear the deadly bullets, and can also feel and touch them), they can all the more hardly allow themselves to believe that the

<column-break/>

plague would be contagious.

Answer. But these must let themselves be informed by experience, which always teaches us that the scent, which one neither sees nor hears, transfers itself from one to the other and even clings to the clothes, in such a way that one who has been in a hospital <note>The original "Gasthuyse" refers to a charitable infirmary or guest house for the sick.</note>, even if he touched nothing there, finds his clothes smelling of it many days later. Likewise, a small musk ball <note>original: "Muſſcheliaet"; these were often carried in pomanders as a perceived protection against "foul air" or miasma.</note> placed in a large chest with clothes will make all those same clothes smell of it afterward; such a secret transferring power is in those things. So also experience teaches us that indeed Leprosy and the disease called the Spanish Pox <note>original: "Spaensche Pocken"; a common historical term for Syphilis.</note> are so contagious that merely drinking from the same glass from which the infected has drunk and breathed into has infected many, and transferred that evil to them. Experience also teaches that the Plague commonly comes first and begins most hotly in small huts, in the fouled corners of the city, and in besieged cities, where the people live cramped and musty, so that they can hardly breathe except into each other's mouths; whereas meanwhile those who live more airily, where they enjoy a freer air, often go free: although they are otherwise such people who have provoked God's Covenant just as much, and often even more, than others—the Lord working through means. And to that end also serves what is said in our Text, that the Lord will send the Pestilence among them when they shall be gathered in their cities before the sword of the enemy: thus giving it to be understood that when they should be packed and crowded closely together in their cities, that

<margin>Even though some come very close to the infected, and others are struck who are far away.</margin>
But some are nevertheless restrained from accepting all this so readily; for experience also teaches that although some seem to be so infected by the diseased, on the other hand, others—who have been just as near and just as much around the infected—pass by it safely, as one often sees happening.

**Answer.** To this we must consider that we also often see happening that where deadly bullets fly thick and fast toward a rank of the enemy, many of them—indeed, sometimes nine out of ten—are struck down, and the tenth comes away unhurt, who was nonetheless just as near and just as much in the work where the battle was at its hottest as the others. From this, we nonetheless cannot conclude that the bullets would not be deadly to those whom they hit properly, but only that a Divine Providence works beneath it, which governs and directs the shots fired, and makes them hit whom He wills, and miss whom He wills, just as we have a notable example of this. 2 Chronicles 18:33. <note>This verse describes King Ahab being struck by an arrow shot "at a venture" or at random, which the author interprets as being guided by God's hand.</note> So it goes likewise with the deadly arrows of the pestilence; the same are sent out from the infected and commonly strike those first who are nearest to them; nevertheless, they still stand under the providence of God, and

<column-break/>

are still so directed by His wise hand that, even if they commonly strike those who are nearest, they nevertheless do not strike everyone without distinction, but in such a way, and such persons, as the wise God finds advisable.

To this, some rightly suggest that in this matter, three things that meet here together must be noted: 1. the disease of the Plague; 2. the person who is threatened by it; 3. God the Lord, who has His all-governing hand over both.

1. The disease of the Plague is found everywhere (as we have now proven) to be contagious; experience teaches this, and the Holy Scripture nowhere contradicts it. 2. Regarding the person who is threatened with the Plague: it is so that although all people are subject to the infection of the Plague, nevertheless some people—due to their particular disposition, <term>temperature</term> <note>In 17th-century medicine, 'temperature' or 'temperament' referred to the balance of the four bodily humors (blood, phlegm, black bile, and yellow bile) which determined health.</note> and the constitution of their body, or due to particular preservatives and medicinal precautions they have about them—are less subject to the infection of the Plague than others. (Just as God the Lord has created in His creatures various virtues and powers to help one another in a natural way against destructive inconveniences.) That is, they are less disposed and fit to be infected with it than others. 3. But now further, as concerns the Lord our God, who alone

### Of the means we must use against the gruesome Pestilence.

<margin>Therefore it is most advisable for us that, staying in the place where we are obliged to remain, we further use all other lawful means, both spiritual and physical, to arm ourselves against the Pestilence. Namely:</margin>
Now follows thirdly, that we also look into what means we might best use to be protected against the gruesome Pestilence. To that end, we must first use spiritual, and then also physical means; above all, I say, we must use the spiritual means; for indeed (as we have now heard at length) it is God the Lord Himself who comes there with the Plague to "avenge the vengeance of His Covenant," *Leviticus 26:25-26*. How shall we then not return to Him who has struck us, *Hosea 6:1*, and see to this work before all else: that we fall before Him under the rod <note>To "fall under the rod" is a metaphor for submitting to divine discipline or punishment with humility.</note>, so that we might still His zealous wrath, which lights the fire of the Pestilence so hotly against us?

### Of the spiritual means we must use against the gruesome Pestilence.

**Answer.** The same may be presented to us in two ways; first in general, then more specifically.

<margin>First in general: That we beforehand put away that for which God the Lord sends the Pestilence among His people.</margin>
In general, there is this spiritual means to ward off the Pestilence from our Cities, Houses, and Persons: namely, that we ourselves beforehand put away that for which the Pestilence is sent by God over a people, before it comes. This is a singular preservative <term>preservative: in the 17th century, this referred to a preventative medicine or spiritual practice intended to ward off disease before it took hold</term>, and an entirely ready means to ward off the plague of Pestilence from the Cities, Houses, or Persons that are still at hand. We are accustomed to say, "no wise man will do a finished work twice." We know indeed that the Lord our God is such a God who "does not afflict the children of men from His heart," *Lamentations 3:33*. <note>original: "Thren. 3. 33." — *Threni* is the Latin title for the biblical book of Lamentations.</note> If He could pass that by, He would gladly spare Himself that trouble. Therefore He also warns long and often before He comes to strike, and stirs many to improvement for a long time, so that He might spare them. Therefore, if the Lord could once see that we ourselves had beforehand put away that for which He wished to send the Pestilence to us (because we were too slow in the practice of it), then we may indeed assure ourselves that we shall have no need of the Pestilence; or if it still comes among us, that it shall only come for our good and for the best. Praiseworthy, therefore, is the conduct of those Christian Authorities who, at the onset of the plague, are active early on and ordain that the citizenry, once or twice a week as needed, should gather together in the house of prayer, to there together even more abundantly offer the incense of prayers to God, for the reconciliation of the place. It would also be desirable if further order were established, so that indeed throughout the entire country, in every household, morning and evening, besides the common prayers, the **Lord** our **God** would also be explicitly petitioned concerning this plague.

This could provide a twofold fruit. First, it would be a strong <term>preservative</term> or <term>abstergative</term> <note>A medicinal term for a cleansing or purifying agent</note> against the Plague; secondly, it could also be a means to bring the household prayers—which should rightly be performed every morning and evening in all Christian households together with all the members of the house, and yet are now entirely omitted or often neglected in many houses—back into good practice throughout the entire land. This, in the course of time (if it were sincerely practiced), could bring unspeakable blessing over our land.

But we must also add to this a certain and fixed order of life, namely, that we know what we have to do at each time to serve **God** rightly; and that we also keep a good watch to carry this out well, as we have explained more broadly elsewhere. This is also of the highest necessity.

Now we must especially see to it that we work our hearts so that we might in all our ways rely more on the Creator alone than on all creatures together: indeed, we must now bring our hearts to the point where we rely on nothing else than the **Lord** our **God** alone; and that we use all other means and creatures only to serve the providence of **God**, from whence our help must come. # 491
## The Law of God's Covenant.

Just as we owe gratitude for all benefits and deliverances that the Lord grants us, so are we especially indebted for those benefits that are of great importance. Now, we all know that a deliverance is so much greater the greater the hardship was that had befallen us. Therefore, since the Plague is such a great affliction—as we have heard—the deliverance from that great plague is everywhere a very great benefit; thus, one is also indebted for great gratitude for it. So that those to whom such recovery has happened might show themselves properly grateful, they must guard themselves against certain things and must further consider others.

I. They must especially guard against two things: 1. That they do not treat lightly whatever small relief they receive, but learn to value it greatly, with all proper acknowledgement of their unworthiness—that they should receive any relief at all—and recognition of God's unmerited kindness in giving them any respite. This must be carefully noted: many a person who began to be delivered still missed out on a full recovery because he did not receive the beginnings of it gratefully, nor respond to them rightly. From this there readily arises, through God’s righteous judgment—who is angered by such ingratitude—relapses <note>original: "recidiven"</note> and new attacks, and so the last state is often worse than the first. Therefore, we should rather see to it that as we feel somewhat refreshed from the distress, we might also awaken to the service of God; and just as we feel our physical strength 

<column-break/>

beginning to grow again, we should see to it that our spiritual gifts might likewise grow.

II. Secondly, being completely delivered, they must also guard themselves that they do not, like Pharaoh, harden their hearts when they see there is relief <note>Exodus 8:15; referring to Pharaoh’s refusal to let the Israelites go once the plagues of Egypt were temporarily lifted.</note>. And take good care that they do not, like the dog, return to its vomit, and the washed sow to wallowing in the mire <note>2 Peter 2:22</note>. Such a path leads to total destruction and ultimately brings eternal damnation upon one's head. All those who have received some respite and now feel strong should take note of this, thinking thus: "Should I restrain <note>original: "besnijden"; literally "circumcise," but used here in the sense of pruning or restricting one's desires.</note> myself when I am healthy, given that I must do so when I am sick or in need; when then would I ever see a good day?" and then proceed to break out into sheer wantonness <note>original: "dertelhept"; implies frivolous, worldly, or unrestrained behavior.</note>, and thus give their hearts room for a new worldly lifestyle.

But these people ought to consider that God the Lord has visited them to wean them from the world—to teach them, indeed, that they should henceforth seek their joy and contentment not in a worldly existence, but in their God. If they will not learn this through the Lord's discipline, which He brings upon them here in great long-suffering for their conversion, then they have nothing else to expect but a total destruction from the Almighty, which will finally overtake them. And then they shall be forced—whether they want to or not—to endure not just a short time for their preservation, but always and eternally without hope of deliverance, gnashing their hearts with fitting sorrow and pain. Therefore, so...

The Law of God’s Covenant.

# Of the Plague of Destructive War; and what a fierce plague it is.

Now follows that we speak of the second plague which the **Lord** here threatens, that He would bring upon His people to avenge the vengeance of His covenant <note>In the theology of the time, God's "Covenant" with His people involved mutual obligations; breaking these obligations triggered "covenant vengeance," often expressed through natural or political disasters.</note>; to this end, the **Lord** testifies that He would deliver them into the hands of their enemies. Herewith the **Lord** gives it to be understood that if they did not let themselves be bettered by the plague of the pestilence, the **Lord** would not leave it at that alone, but He would weaken them on all sides through the plague of the **Pestilence**, and so strip them of their brave heroes and warriors, and of their wise and experienced Rulers; so that they would have neither the power nor the counsel anymore to withstand their enemies: and so all things among them would fall as if into a confusion and entanglement, and they would be found a completely weak and defenseless people, and would thus fall as a prey to their enemies; and so God would yet again avenge the vengeance of His covenant upon them. See, thus the **Lord** gives them to be understood that He would proceed from punishment to punishment, to surely bring His people to better discipline: if the **Pestilence** alone were not enough to work such an effect, He would add the destroying sword to it. Whereby we may then see that when the **Pestilence** begins to plague a people who are already under **Judgment** from the **Lord**, it is to deliver such a people thereby into the hands of their enemies. This is **God’s** method, this is His policy, as we may see here; this applies to us also in the highest degree. We are a people who are in a war; we are now being plagued by the **Pestilence**; if we then

<column-break/>

do not better ourselves, what else have we to expect than that we also shall be delivered into the hands of our enemies; since we then see that the **Lord** also begins to go to work with us in this way, we must then surely also begin to see with our own eyes; it is then indeed high time to hasten toward improvement; and to that end, we must also properly take to heart this following doctrine, which blooms out of this part of our text.

<margin>Which is indeed a quite heavy plague; and a most terrifying plague.</margin>
**Doctrine.** A destroying **War**, wherein one is defeated and our enemy has the upper hand, is a quite heavy plague. It is one of the heaviest plagues which the **Lord** presented to **David** 2 Sam. 24:13. And often threatens His people with, if they did not keep His **Covenant**, Deut. 28:25, Isa. 42:24, 25. So also the **Lord** shows in our text that He considers it a very heavy plague, a seven-fold plague, a vengeance plague. It is also so, however one looks upon the war, it is full of plague and punishments; but when one is further defeated in the war, then the misery is inexpressibly manifold and great.

<margin>For even War itself, although one maintains the victory therein, is still a terrifying thing.</margin>
However one looks upon the war, it always goes thus; humans (which is indeed a quite terrifying thing in itself), who are created for each other's help, comfort, and convenience, are then only harnessed to destroy, violate, and ruin one another, with all that concerns them; to that end the senses work, to that end the hands are ready, which they then also deem their greatest joy and honor: truly a terrifying thing. Is this not considered a terrifying madness, if it happens outside of war or combat? So is

### The Law of God’s Covenant.

Now this truth of God—namely, that a devastating war in which one is defeated is an altogether heavy plague—offers us the same usefulness that we heard from the previous teaching. For it must serve, firstly, as a warning to those of our allies in Bohemia, in the Palatinate, also in the Valtelline, and elsewhere <note>These regions were key battlegrounds during the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648), where Protestant forces suffered significant defeats against the Catholic Habsburgs.</note> who for some years now have been subjected to a devastating war, and are currently being very boldly trampled under the foot of the proud; namely, that they should take more and more occasion to confess that they surely treated the Covenant of God as a war beforehand through their sins. Indeed, they have done it great violence, which God now righteously comes to avenge with the Sword of Vengeance of this devastating war among them. 2. For it is from the Lord—from the Lord it is—that one side is above and the other below, and that because of the sins of the people; such has God’s people always confessed. The children of Israel, being conquered by the Philistines, asked: *Why has the Lord smitten us today before the face of the Philistines?* **1 Sam. 4:1.** We may find political causes as many as we can, but the Divine verdict is this: it is properly God the Lord who breaks the arm of one and binds the arm of the other, **Ezek. 30:21 etc.** and breaks the arm of His people because of their sins, **Isa. 42:24, 25.** This must then be taken to heart, and therefore all those Princes, Cities, and Lands that are now being oppressed by the Enemy in the War must see to it that they take knowledge of their God-provoking sins. How anxiously would we then go about? # The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading
<sig>Rrr 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: not</meta>

avenging the vengeance of His Covenant.

**The Lesson.** Famine is a most heavy plague, with which the Lord is also accustomed to avenge the outrage that His people commit against His covenant. We see this clearly here in our text; it is threatened here as a sevenfold plague upon the people for the violation they have done to God's Covenant. To this end, it also serves that—where we have heard that the plague of **Pestilence** and of destructive **War** (under which one falls) is very great—this plague of **Famine** is almost everywhere joined together with those other two great plagues. It is also specifically counted by the Prophet Ezekiel among the "evil plagues of God," which are so named for their excellence <note>original: "uytnementheyt"; here meaning "pre-eminence" or "notability" in terms of severity.</note>, *Ezek. 14:21*. Following this, the Lord Himself calls famine even more closely: "Evil arrows of hunger," which the Lord sends out in anger and wrath, and "terrible punishments" sent out for destruction to destroy, *Ezek. 5:15-16*. Likewise, this plague was presented to David (as one of the greatest) alongside the **Sword** and the **Pestilence**, as a punishment for his pride; and however terrifying the Pestilence is (as we have heard), David nevertheless chose the Pestilence over the Famine, so great is this plague.

Who can also tell, who can reckon up, all the misery and all the destruction which appears over the people once Famine begins to press hard? Just as the Prophet Jeremiah presents to us in his **Lamentations** <note>original: "Klaegliet" or "Threnen," referring to the biblical Book of Lamentations.</note>. Then the people sighed, seeking bread, *Lam. 1:11*, and their skin became black like an oven because of the terrible storm of hunger, *Chap. 5:10*. The rich then sell their precious

<column-break/>

treasures and give their desired things for food, to revive the soul, *Chap. 1, vs. 11*. And yet it is often still not to be had; so that even in great famine, the **Priests** and the **Elders** give up the ghost in the city as they seek food for themselves to revive their souls, *Chap. 1, vs. 19*. The infant and the suckling faint in the streets of the city. Those who are a bit older say to their mothers, "Where is corn and wine?" as their souls are poured out into their mothers' laps, *Chap. 2:11-12*.

Thus, one may see, walking through the streets of the city, some children already lying dead here, having died of hunger; going a little further, see others lying there who are nearly fainting from hunger and gasping for death. Everywhere one may hear the young children calling to their mothers for bread, and there is no one who gives it to them; then that which the Prophet says is made true, *Lam. 4: vs. 2, 3, 4*: "The precious children of Zion, once valued against fine gold, how are they now regarded as earthen pitchers, the work of the hands of a potter?" Even the sea-monsters <note>original: "ſeekalveren," literally "sea-calves," likely referring to seals or whales, which were believed to be more nurturing than the starving people.</note> offer the breast: they suckle their young: but the daughter of my people has become cruel, like the ostriches in the wilderness. The tongue of the nursing child cleaves to the roof of its mouth for thirst; the children ask for bread; there is no one who shares it with them. Then it is also made true regarding the dainty and the wanton <note>original: "brootdronckige," literally "bread-drunk," meaning those who were so well-fed they became reckless or arrogant.</note>; those who previously lived in such excess and constantly ate the fattest of the flock, of whom the Prophet says, *Lam. 4: vs. 5*: "Those who ate delicacies now faint in the streets; those who were brought up in crimson now embrace the dung." Yea, that we go no further, just think: how it affects us all when we have but a little...

### The Justice of God’s Covenant.
#### Sff 2

It is indeed everywhere the bounden duty of those who have more abundance to curtail their excess, in order to better assist the needy. Oh! Oh! Let all those who still have more abundance be moved by the aforementioned considerations—even now, before Famine <note>original: "Hongers-noot"</note> comes upon our own necks—to improve their excess in meals, banquets, and clothing, and to immediately reform their daily wantonness <note>original: "broodtronckentheyt," literally "bread-drunkenness," referring to the arrogance or recklessness that comes from having too much</note> and luxury. From this, they should save what they might send away for the relief of needy friends <note>The author likely refers to Protestant allies during the regional wars of the 17th century.</note> in many lands, and of our own needy poor here at home, as well as for the maintenance and upholding of our dear Fatherland, which is likewise in great distress.

<margin>And above all, we must see to it that from now on we do not further burden the Covenant of God, for which the Lord God is accustomed to bring Famine upon His people.</margin>

Finally, we must also see to it that we ourselves do not fall into Famine, and bring this heavy plague upon our own necks. Oh! Oh! How anxious it would make us, who are used to having all things so abundantly and in full; how it would pain us then! Therefore, it is surely necessary that we provide for this in time. Now, just as we have understood regarding the Plague <note>original: "Pestilencie"</note> and burning War, that these are provoked by the burden <note>original: "overlast," implying a violation or injury to the legal standing of the agreement</note> placed upon the Covenant of God, so it stands here also. If we then wish to keep Famine from our cities and lands, we must see that we also prevent the injury that is done everywhere to the Covenant of God. For behold, thus it stands: when all the members of a person (which should be weapons of righteousness to fight for God’s Covenant) are bound to be weapons of sin to do injury to God’s Covenant, the Lord takes that most poorly from His covenant-partners; therefore then also comes

<column-break/>

the Lord and sends **Famine** as a vengeance upon the **Covenant-breakers**, with which He plagues all their members with impotence and lingering weakness. This is so that those arrogant members, who have been so strong to break the Covenant of God, should now justly be weakened and broken themselves. So it is also certainly the injury done to the Covenant which shuts the Heavens so that it does not rain, and makes the earth like iron, so that it does not give its bounty. Hear what the Lord Himself says to this in **Ezekiel 14:13**: *Son of man, when a land sins against me by trespassing grievously, then will I stretch out mine hand upon it, and will break the staff of the bread thereof, and will send famine upon it, and will cut off man and beast from it.* Therefore, if we would keep these evil arrows of Hunger from us, we must take care that we do not sin against God; and if we still happen to do so out of weakness, that we—having sinned—do not yet despise the Lord our God as if it were a small matter to offend the great God. Rather, let us immediately rise from our sin to turn back to our God, so that we might yet be spared.

<margin>And to that end we must especially restrain ourselves.</margin>

But even more specifically, the Lord points out to us certain particular sins for which He is accustomed to bring Famine upon a people, against which we must especially guard ourselves; of which the foremost are these:

<margin>1. From all wantonness and useless wasting or devouring.</margin>

First, great **wantonness** <note>original: "broodtronckentheyt"</note> while we have the fullness of all things; that certainly prepares the way to great scarcity and want. Hear what the Lord Himself says to this in **Deuteronomy 28:47-48**: *Because thou servedst not the Lord thy God with...*

Now such crying and groaning of the creatures who suffer abuse through overindulgence comes before the eyes of the Lord of Hosts, stirring Him to anger, and causes Him to righteously swear that He will take away the abundance from such violators of His innocent creatures. # The Justice of God’s Covenant
## Page 509

...against the needy. When the inhabitants of Jerusalem had plenty, yet did not help the poor and needy (Ezekiel 16:49), the Lord soon brought a famine upon them (Ezekiel 4:16, 17). This is also an entirely righteous and sensible punishment for this crime: for how can the Lord better teach His people what a gruesome cruelty it is not to help the hungry than to let them fall into famine themselves? In this way, they learn the distress of those in hunger and how it feels in their hearts. Therefore, let all who still have plenty curtail <note>original: "besnijden," literally "circumcise," but here meaning to prune or cut back.</note> their own excess in meals and in clothing, and help the needy poor with it, so that they themselves do not fall into famine and want. Let no one think it is for nothing that the men of God <note>referring to preachers or prophets.</note> cry out so loudly against excess while people are narrow-hearted enough toward the poor; for such things will surely bring famine over us if we do not provide better in that regard.

<margin>
II. Concerning wicked leniency and mercy toward willful sinners.
</margin>

Thirdly, the Lord also brings famine over a land when it neglects to punish godless evildoers and to avenge the injustice done to the innocent and defenseless. So we read that the Lord raised up a three-year famine in the time of David because Saul's blood-guilt against the Gibeonites had been left unavenged (2 Samuel 21). This should be carefully noted everywhere. We often do not know what to think when times become so distressed and all things become so expensive, but we see here from where it comes: it also happens because many willful murderers get off unpunished; it happens because many innocent people are greatly oppressed, and there is no one who takes up their cause; from there blood cries out,

<column-break/>

which distresses the whole land. Let the lawful Authorities, and those who hold the sword of Justice in their hand, also see to this, and by righteous punishment of evildoers, spare the land from famine. And among others, special notice should be taken here of those willful abusers who, through their drinking and carousing, do all manner of violence to God’s good creatures <note>In 17th-century theology, "creatures" refers to any created thing, including food and drink.</note>, and then come home drunk and sated like wolves and bears to their wives and children. They often act in such a way that while they carouse and guzzle, their wives and children must be supported by the poor-relief. Truly this is a cruel abuse; this ought to be avenged, or else the Lord will visit us with famine. Just as all other willful evildoers should be strictly punished, so that the Lord does not bring this sharp rod <note>A common biblical metaphor for divine punishment.</note> over us.

This is also righteous with God; when we care so little for His things and take so little care to do His fieldwork, as if we had no need of Him, He then lets all our labor on our own fields be in vain, so that we might learn that it all depends on Him. # The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading the Covenant
## Page 510

...so that such things are also improved, if we do not want the Lord God to come over us with His **Sword of Vengeance**. There are often many complaints that the land yields so little of its wealth; but what of that? We are also wretched! and do not give our wealth to God; we hold our strength back when His work is to be done, and pour it out entirely when we have our own affairs to attend to. This grieves the Lord; therefore He sends heavy plagues among His people now and then. Let us then see to improving all these things, and thus spare God this trouble, and so we may also be free of these plagues; especially if we also carefully observe the following lessons.

### That it is firm proof that very heavy sins are circulating among the people when the Lord allows very heavy plagues to come over His people.

From all that we have heard so far, it appears everywhere that the Lord God does not send these three heavy plagues of **Pestilence**, **War**, and **Famine** <note>original: "Dieren Tijdt," literally "Dear Time," a term used for periods of scarcity and high food prices.</note> to His people except when He is very heavily angered against them for the sake of their heavy sins. Just as everywhere in Holy Scripture, where the Lord threatens these plagues, we find that heavy sins are then present and that the Lord is then entirely wrathful, angry, and incensed. Very notable for this purpose is that passage, Ezekiel 5:11, 12, 13: *As surely as I live, says the Lord God (because you have defiled my sanctuary with all your abominations and all your horrors), I will also diminish you, and my eye shall not spare you, nor will I have pity. <column-break/>

*winds, and I will draw out the sword after them. Thus shall my anger be spent, and I will cause my fury to rest upon them, and I will be comforted: and they shall know that I the Lord have spoken in my zeal, when I have accomplished my fury against them.* From this it appears quite clearly that for the sake of the heavy sins of His people, the Lord God, through His very heavy wrath, brings these three heavy **Plagues** of **Pestilence**, **Famine**, and the **Sword** upon His people. And the Lord sets this forth again so vehemently in that same passage, in the following verses 14, 15, 16, 17, testifying that He would do such with wrath, fury, and furious rebukes; so that He hardly has enough words to express how very incensed He is for the sake of the heavy sins of His people when He begins to call for the Pestilence, the Sword, or Famine. Therefore we have two further lessons to note from this our Text:

Or at the very least, if we can do nothing else, if we fail to trouble ourselves over it and be grieved in our hearts, as Paul was, **2 Cor. 11:29**, then we certainly become participants in those same unfruitful works of darkness through our lack of zeal, and the Lord our God has then laid the guilt upon us as well. 

And this certainly applies to us all; there has hardly been any zeal used to avenge the outrage committed against <term>God's Covenant</term> <note>A central concept in Dutch Reformed theology: a binding agreement between God and His people requiring mutual faithfulness.</note> by many of our fellow members. Many have been seen and known to behave quite wickedly, yet from one **Lord's Supper** to the next, they continue to come to the table again and again, unhindered. Yes, even those who have been brought under <term>discipline</term> <note>The formal process (censura morum) by which church elders corrected the behavior of members.</note> to the extent that they were barred from the Lord's Supper—even when it was observed that they were not in the least bit dismayed by it, nor improved by it in the slightest—yes, even while remaining under discipline, they have gone from bad to worse and become entirely cruel mockers and harmful deceivers among the people, yet no further action was taken against them. 

Is it not the truth that there are large and very many wealthy Congregations, of a thousand, two thousand, or even many more Members, where after 40 or 50 years of the preaching of the 

<column-break/>

Word, not a single person has ever been cut off from the Congregation of God through the public <term>Ban</term> <note>Excommunication; the final and most severe stage of church discipline, where a person is officially cast out of the spiritual community.</note> for their unholy breaking of the Covenant? What shall we say? That our people are so orderly and submissive that there has never been an occasion to do such a thing? If we wished to say that, our own consciences would put us to shame. It is then certainly our lack of zeal for maintaining the cause of God's Covenant which is the cause of this. 

Therefore, the Lord Himself is now forced to come and plead the cause of His Covenant. This, at the very least, must finally make us open our eyes. Oh! That we would take this to heart in time and embolden our zeal for the future, seeing that we must be reconciled for our previous indifference and sin. Do we not, when we have angered someone of high standing, seek reconciliation? Shall we then not seek it much more with our God, through the blood of His Son? So that the arrows of His wrath, which still remain in His quiver, might be kept therein. 

Knowing then that this blow comes from God, let us above all look up to God if we truly intend to be healed. When Heaven is upset with us, we seek help from earthly things in vain. When God is angry, no human wisdom or power can help us until God is appeased. We must first be healed from above if we are to be healed properly. And this shall best happen if we begin to be zealous for God's things and seek to magnify Him in all ways. # The Right of God's Covenant.

**Column 1:**
...to root out sin. Some persons He calls out <note>original: "roept hy uyt." In this context, it refers to God removing people from life through death or judgment.</note> in whom sin is so entrenched that it cannot be separated from them; and He does this furthermore to better root out sin in others, who, seeing this, might learn to fear and avoid doing such destructive evil. Deuteronomy 21:21. The Lord also disciplines some pious souls out of this world through War, Pestilence, or other misfortune; He does this to terrify the rest even more regarding sin, so that they, seeing what happens in the green wood, might consider what will become of the dry. 1 Peter 4:18. <note>This is a reference to the words of Jesus in Luke 23:31. If the "green wood" (the righteous) suffers such discipline, the "dry wood" (the wicked) will face much worse.</note> It is therefore all about the sin to the Lord: He does not want to destroy us, but our sins. He does not desire the death of the sinner, but of the sin. And therefore, as long as any wicked, willful sins remain clinging to us and will not be separated from us—which the Lord hates with a perfect hatred—the Lord will continually be upon our necks with His healing plagues and punishments.

### Warning, to which we must attend.
Are we not otherwise God's people, and are we disciplined by God for the sake of our sins, which God hates? If we do not better ourselves, and the Lord our God has disciplined us even more, yet we remain the same, Psalm 55:20, then it shall go thus with us: He will not leave it at that. If there are anywhere sharper and heavier punishments than those He has already laid upon us, He will also bring forth the weapons of His wrath; yes, He shall shoot them all against us. Is the War we have had until now not been sharp enough to humble us? He shall make it seven times heavier. Does this Pestilence which He has already ignited not cure us? He shall ignite it seven times more. Have we had some scarcity, and has it not im-

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**
proved us? He shall make it seven times greater. The Lord our God is not like the foolish mothers who let their children perish in their filth because they cannot bear to cause them any pain; but He is like a wise Physician—if a gentle purge does not help, he gives his patient a stronger one. Oh! Oh! that we might then become wise and turn to the Lord in time: That we indeed set the Lord before us now, making destroying locusts, calling for fire, and for yet worse, Amos 7:1, etc. Yes, filling His hands with the fiery coals of War, of Pestilence, of the <term>Dear Times</term> <note>original: "Dieren Tijdts." A historical term for famine or periods of extreme scarcity when the price of food became "dear" (expensive).</note>, with plagues seven times heavier than we have had before, to send them upon our necks if we do not improve ourselves. That we indeed notice from that which the Lord has already done concerning us, that He is certainly and firmly busy with us (while He thus sends War and the Dear Time over us, and now also adds the plague of Pestilence to them) to make His ultimate effort over us for our preservation. In such a way that we certainly have great reason to fear that if all this does not help, the Lord will grow weary of curing us and give us over to His grim wrath, unto a total destruction.

### Lament.
That so little notice is taken of this: we still go on as if there were nothing special happening among us, whereas the Lord is busy with us as with His sick daughter who lies at her last gasp, where He indeed applies His ultimate remedy concerning us to preserve us (should we be preserved), even to <term>lanceting</term> <note>original: "vlijmen." The medical practice of bloodletting using a lancet.</note>, to cutting, and to amputating, through the destroying sword of War, through the biting Dear Time, through the gruesome Pestilence. Oh, that we are so dull! That we are so unfeeling!

# The Avenging Sword, Pleading the Case

...be! That we give so little heed to what the great God is so busily doing with us! Shall the Lord stir up War, shall He stir up Pestilence, shall He stir up Famine <note>original: "Diere Tijt." Literally "Dear Time," referring to periods of extreme scarcity and high prices, often resulting in starvation.</note> to cure us? Shall He take all this trouble, and shall we still go along as unfeelingly as if nothing were being done around us? What a stupidity is this? What a lethargy has seized us? With what a destructive, reeling spirit are we struck? How can our heart be so hard? How can our soul be so hardened and we so senseless and without all judgment? How do we dare to oppose God in this way, or are we stronger than He?

### Awakening
Since then matters stand thus, and we now learn from the Word of the Lord that the Lord has so heavily charged our sins, and is so intent upon them that He would rather use the ultimate remedies than to excuse us in them, so let us then finally take this once properly to heart. Let us, yes, also in this all alike follow the Lord our God; let us also all alike set ourselves against that which God the Lord sets Himself against. 

And above all, let each one see to bettering his own sin; let each see to forsaking the sin of the age, and the sin of his profession, and the sin of his person. Let us shun sin as we would a plague—yes, more than the plagues themselves. For God the Lord has tied these two together <note>The author argues that sin and its punishment are inseparable links in a chain.</note>. Let us each set ourselves most against our greatest and strongest sins, and see to putting Godliness in their place, so that we might be able to hold out in the battle against sin until the end. And the more we see that many are slack in this, so much the more let us be awake to it, while the laborers in this work are so few. For is it not entirely lamentable,

<column-break/>

and a loathsome corruption, that while we all alike so greatly dread the punishment of sin, we nevertheless concern ourselves so little with guarding against the crime of sin, which certainly brings the punishment upon us? Is this not a foolish matter and an entirely lamentable thing, that so many are nevertheless thus bewitched? 

Well, although very many go to work so poorly in this, yet those must indeed who are wise—who have their eyes in their forehead <note>An idiom for having discernment and looking ahead to consequences.</note>—see more clearly here, and care both for themselves and for others, just as is accustomed to happen in all civil matters.

<margin>Which must indeed greatly spur us all on to henceforth seriously maintain the matters of the Covenant for the warding off of sin.</margin>

Therefore, just as it is certain and sure (now that the Lord comes to visit us with a heavy War, with Famine, with the gruesome Pestilence—in a word, plainly with those plagues wherewith He is accustomed to plead the outrage done to His Covenant) that we have indeed done great outrage to God’s Covenant; so we must also take this for certain and sure: that if we are to be blessedly delivered from the aforementioned plagues which are now upon our necks, it is then of the highest necessity that we all alike henceforth not only guard ourselves, so as to no longer do such evil outrage to the good Covenant of God as we have long done; but that we also all alike quite faithfully lend a hand so that the Right of the Covenant <note>original: "Recht des Verbonts." The legal and moral claims God holds over His people according to their sacred agreement.</note> might be properly maintained against all those who would still wish to remain, doing outrage to the Covenant of God through their willful sins. And to that end we must rightfully, all alike, bind ourselves as if by a new oath (2 Chronicles 15 verse 14). To that end all those who still consider themselves Covenant-partners <note>original: "Bont-genoten." Referring to the members of the religious community bound to God.</note> must gladly go to renew their...

# The Right of God’s Covenant

...approach the Table of the Lord, who does not have such a heart and mind, such a resolution and intention, let him not make himself guilty of the body and blood of the Lord Christ, and thus eat judgment upon himself <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 11:27-29, which warns that those who partake in Communion in an "unworthy manner" bring judgment upon themselves.</note>. And that they should then also be given to understand more clearly that before God and the world it shall be held (as the act itself implies, whether one wishes to hold it so or not) that indeed all those who still come to the Lord’s Supper do so with such a spirit and heart (as intends to maintain the matters of the Covenant in all sincerity). And that they receive the Lord’s Supper with such a disposition, motivation, resolution, and intention, that they truly eat the bread of the Lord and drink the wine of the Lord upon that basis. 

And on the other hand, with a friendly encouragement to all those who find themselves so minded and resolved to still approach the Table of the Holy Lord with all humility, assuring them—regardless of what their previous neglects might have been—that the Lord is willing to graciously overlook them (for the Lord’s Supper is, after all, a **seal of the Covenant of Grace** <note>In 17th-century Reformed theology, a "seal" is a visible sign—like a wax seal on a legal document—that confirms and guarantees God's promises to the believer.</note>) if they only now desire to walk in sincerity from the heart, observing the matters of the Covenant, each according to their ability. And then, upon that basis, let the Lord’s Supper be administered; and let this also be properly reminded and laid upon the conscience of all people, of both high and low station, in the afternoon sermon; and further, let this obligation be frequently recalled in other sermons, to stir everyone up to make a matter of conscience of it, and to conduct themselves accordingly, each to their utmost power.

<column-break/>

See, this would create great expectation in these fireless and faint times <note>The author describes his era as "fireless," meaning a time of spiritual coldness or lack of religious zeal.</note>, for the better maintenance of the matters of the Covenant; and for the averting of such plagues as we have now heard the Lord wishes to bring upon a people who neglect the matters of His Covenant. Through this, many sleepy souls might be awakened—indeed, certainly—as many as have any true Christian blood in them. These would all alike, through these reflections, however faint they might have been before (having been swept away by the current of general decay), begin to come to themselves and begin to maintain the matters of the Covenant from the heart, to the inexpressible benefit and edification of God’s Church, and to the powerful averting of many **Plagues of Vengeance** <note>original: "Wraek-plagen." We must not merely trouble or punish them as minor offenders, but truly kill them, just as one is accustomed to killing all sacrificial offerings, and never sparing the heads of the rebellious. To this end, we must gladly exert ourselves; it is the advice of Christ himself: "If your eye offends you," he says, "pluck it out; if your hand offends you, cut it off." Mark 9:47. In this, we often fall short; we spare ourselves far too easily. We do not wish to cause our hearts so much grief; it weighs too heavily upon us. Mark what we say: when a person is set on something, he is so fixated on the means through which he hopes it might be achieved, that he often lets himself be led astray, even to the use of **evil means**, to carry out his intention. # **The Sword of Vengeance, Pleading**

...the entire multitude of the people, as many as can and will come there, as a warning to all!

Let the **Honorable Authorities** <note>original: "eerweerde Overheyt," referring to the civil magistrates and governing bodies.</note> also pay attention to this. What! Shall God the Lord give them the Sword of Vengeance and let them be His place-holders, and shall they not follow God in this? And shall they still let any sins of **Covenant-breaking** <term>Covenant-breaking: In this context, it refers to the violation of the spiritual and social contract between the Reformed community and God, which was believed to bring collective punishment upon the nation.</term> go by unpunished and uncorrected? Should they not rather begin to use the most extreme remedies than to leave it be? Shall the Lord cry out in our Land for the **Sword**, for **Famine** <note>original: "Diere Tijde," literally "Dear Time," a period of high prices and food scarcity.</note>, for the **Pestilence**, to avenge the vengeance of His Covenant, and shall the lawful Authorities—who are **Gods on earth** <note>A common early modern reference to Psalm 82:6, implying that rulers act as God’s representatives in executing justice.</note>—sit still? Shall they not then also justly begin to take courage to avenge the vengeance of God’s Covenant, so that the fierce Wrath of God might cease?

Indeed, considering that we may all clearly perceive that the Lord God is beginning to use sharper remedies to cure our Land of the increasing sins than He was accustomed to; shall not then all those to whom the care of the people in the Land is in any way entrusted also gladly begin to embolden themselves against all kinds of wicked impulses, which they can certainly perceive are greatly increasing in our Land?

Notice especially, you in the Land to whom this care is entrusted: the abuses and sins against which we rouse you are like the **Devil’s Army** and Troops; they are indeed nothing but a band of hideous Rebels who set themselves up against the Most High, and they are already condemned by the Almighty to death and damnation. Be

<column-break/>

then simply of good courage like **Joshua** <note>The biblical successor to Moses, known for leading the Israelites in the conquest of Canaan with divine strength.</note>, quit yourselves like men, set yourselves valiantly against this most guilty monstrosity, and know for certain that you shall earn nothing but honor and fight for victory. Therefore the Lord your God calls for the **Sword of Vengeance**, for the Pestilence, for War, and for Famine, that He might destroy this monster; you must each also stir up your zeal, each calling upon the power you have for punishment and for the prevention of sin, <margin>That the plague over your Land might cease.</margin> over your own people; and so you shall spare God the Lord this labor, and quickly and faithfully free our dear Fatherland from all this calamity. 

For if we would judge ourselves, we should not be judged by God. **1 Corinthians 11:31.** But should we neglect such things (which God forbid), then the plague of our Land would not cease; or if we were to receive some temporary relief for a time, we would still have something worse to fear. For it stands written: unless there be found here or there some zealous **Phinehas** <note>Phinehas was a priest in the Old Testament who stopped a plague by executing a couple who had defied God's law; he became a symbol of "holy zeal."</note> who does not spare the evildoers, who indeed begins to boldly punish the wicked Covenant-breakers, it is to be expected that the plague shall not cease, or shall quickly fall upon our necks much harder. 

Here you see life and death before you; may the Lord our good God give you understanding in all things, that you may choose life, so that we might still see the happiness of **Jerusalem** <note>A common metaphor in Dutch Reformed theology for the "New Jerusalem" or the blessed state of their own Protestant nation.</note> rise all the days of our lives; and that we might again be gladdened according to the days in which the Lord has afflicted us: according to the years in which we have seen evil. **Psalm 90:15. <meta>This page continues the introductory front matter of the work, moving into the formal dedication addressed to the administrative leadership of the Dutch Republic. The tone is one of humble submission and political philosophy regarding the "Mysteries of State."</meta>

# Noble, Honorable, Wise, and Very Prudent, Mighty Lords,
## The Council of State of the United Netherlands.

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'M' featuring a landscape with a building and trees.</image-desc>MY LORDS,
It has always been the way of things that those matters which affect everyone are also discussed by everyone. Would that the Lord granted that each person simply remained within the bounds of their own calling, and that no one meddled with things that are too high for them. But in this, the poor human can hardly maintain moderation. Even the things of the Most High God are often looked into by many much more deeply than God allows, or than is useful for us, as seen in Deuteronomy 29:29 and 1 Samuel 6:19. <note>These biblical passages warn against prying into the "secret things" of God or looking into the Ark of the Covenant.</note> So too, the affairs of the "gods on earth" <note>A common 17th-century metaphor for magistrates and rulers, derived from Psalm 82.</note> are not free from this; everyone meddles with them, and many go much too far. Nevertheless, these affairs are of such a nature that they cannot be rightly understood except by those who can see into the very heart of the State. We, who only look at matters from the outside, cannot penetrate or pierce those depths, nor those *mysteries of state* <note>original Latin: "Arcana Imperii"; a political concept referring to the secret or hidden powers of government</note>, which must be known if one is to rightly judge the actions of the High Powers. Often that which is most essential is hidden from our eyes; private individuals can never account for everything that must be considered to form a sound judgment on the affairs of state, or to say with authority what should be done and what should be left undone.

Therefore, it is always our heart’s wish to God that while we each contribute what we can to the well-being of our dear Fatherland, and while each respectfully declares what we have observed for the strengthening of our dearly won freedom and the promotion of our desired prosperity, we should still always think well of the actions and deeds of the High Powers. To them, the highest care is entrusted; they alone know the matters through and through, and know where the state is moving and where it stands firm. We should, accordingly, hold it for certain and sure that if they do not follow exactly the path that we believe to be best, they have great and weighty reasons—resulting from a closer knowledge of the whole matter, which is unknown to private citizens—why they act otherwise.

Yet there are general maxims and foundations of government that must never be neglected by the rulers of a Christian people, if things are to go well there. Such as that the Lord our great God *establishes kings and removes kings* (Daniel 2:21); that indeed *by Him kings reign, and princes decree justice; by Him rulers rule, and nobles, even all the judges of the earth* (Proverbs 8:15, 16); that He alone

<meta>This page continues the dedication to the Council of State. The previous page ended mid-word with "affai-", which completes here as "affairs," leading into a description of God's sovereignty over human governance.</meta>

affairs, <note>The previous page ended with the partial word "affai-", referring to the "affairs of the High Powers."</note> who is great in counsel and mighty in deed, for His eyes are open over all the ways of the children of men, to give to every one according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his dealings, *Jeremiah 32:19.* That the watchman wakes in vain, unless the Lord keeps the city, *Psalm 127:1.* That it is also all the same to the Lord to help by many, or by few, whether the mighty or the powerless, for against the Lord no mortal man prevails, *1 Samuel 14:6* and *2 Chronicles 14:11.* That the eyes of the Lord run through the whole earth, to show Himself strong on behalf of those whose heart is perfect toward Him, *2 Chronicles 16:9.* That the Lord will honor those who honor Him, and lightly esteem those who despise Him, *1 Samuel 2:30.* And consequently, that righteousness (which God loves) exalts a nation, but on the other hand, that sin is a reproach to the nations, *Proverbs 14:34.* 

See, these Maxims <note>original: "Maximen"; fundamental rules of conduct or political principles</note> are all as firm as the earth stands firm; on these grounds the Ministers of the Word are also accustomed to promise a people happiness or misfortune, and it then happens exactly according to their word. For these are all fixed Principles <note>original: "Principia"</note> and certain, sure Foundations laid by that God, who turns the wise backward and makes their knowledge foolishness; who confirms the word of His servant and performs the counsel of His messengers, *Isaiah 44:25, 26.* Therefore we, looking away from all other considerations and looking up to these fixed and certain Maxims of our great God, have sought in this Treatise <note>original: "Tractaet"</note> to open up what we—according to God’s word and pronouncement—must feel and expect regarding the present condition of our state; and we have shown that the good and gracious God has placed it as if in our own hands, whether we shall succeed well or poorly.

If we will fear the Lord our God, follow His counsel, avoid evil, and apply ourselves to good, then we shall be built up.

> For thus says the Lord, *I am the Lord your God, who teaches you what is profitable, who leads you in the way you should go; O that you had listened to My commandments! Then your peace would have been as a river, and your righteousness as the waves of the sea: your seed also would have been as the sand, and those who come from your bowels like the stones thereof; his name should not have been cut off nor destroyed from before My face, Isaiah 48:17, 18, 19.* And *the labor of the Egyptians, and the merchandise of the Moors <note>The original "Mooren" refers to the people of Cush or Ethiopia in this biblical context.</note>, and of the Sabeans, men of great stature, shall come over to you, and they shall be yours; they shall follow you; in chains they shall come over, and they shall bow down to you, and they shall make supplication to you, Isaiah 45:14.* And so the Lord would soon subdue our enemies, and turn His hand against our adversaries, and those who hate the Lord would submit themselves feignedly to us, and our time would be forever: and He would feed us with the finest of the wheat, and satisfy us with honey out of the rock, *Psalm 81:15, 16, 17.*

If we will only listen to the Lord, then it shall go well with us, even if we were ever so weak, and our enemies ever so strong. For truly, if our weakness, or the power and cunning of the enemies, could have destroyed us, then we would have been lost long ago—we who now still stand firm to face our enemy, should the need arise.

On the other hand, if we will not fear the Lord our God, nor follow His counsel, nor avoid evil, nor apply ourselves to good, then we are lost: for so says the Prophet, *Jerusalem has stumbled...*

treatises, and Judah has fallen. And this he says, even while Judah and Jerusalem were still in great outward prosperity, and had the fullness of all things: and that was not because their enemies were stronger and mightier than they; but because their tongue and their actions were against the Lord, <margin>*</margin>to provoke the eyes of His glory, *Isaiah 3:8.*

See then, honorable Lords, <note>original: "gheduchte Heeren"; literally "dread" or "formidable" lords, a standard respectful address for high-ranking government officials</note> this is what it comes down to: if we prepare our hearts to seek the Lord, and to seek out and root out our sins, then we shall live, *Amos 5:4*; indeed, it shall surely go well with us. If we believe the Lord our God, we shall be established: if we believe His prophets, so shall we prosper, *2 Chronicles 20:20.* This is a <term>Secret of State</term> <note>original: "Secreet vanden Staet"; here referring to a fundamental principle of governance where spiritual health determines political stability</note> which the Lord reveals to those whom He loves; and happy, indeed thrice-blessed, are those who take it to heart.

To this end—to move the hearts of the inhabitants of the land (on the occasion of the expectation of those things about which all hearts are concerned)—we have drafted this following Treatise. It is indeed true that everyone is very ready and full-mouthed in admitting that sin is the ruin of a people, but this knowledge is rarely put into practice. People do the opposite every day of what they profess; and many still want to help themselves with sin when they begin to get to work, even though they previously admitted that it was all ruin. And because this is a matter about which no one disputes, it is often laid aside so lightly that almost no one pays attention to it. Therefore, we have proven this well-known truth somewhat more extensively, and have also taken the opportunity to deter all classes of men, each from their beloved sins, and to move them toward the fear of God and the <term>reformation</term> <note>referring to a moral and social correction of behavior and laws</note> of the sinful abuses that are prevalent among us.

We know well that it feels as bitter as gall to our sinful flesh merely to hear of the Reformation of abuses upon which our heart is set; nevertheless, we cannot be helped otherwise. If we do not wish to better ourselves, we make all the promises of God—as many and as glorious as they are—entirely fruitless and useless, for none of them then apply to us; for if one reads through the entire Holy Scripture from the beginning to the end, one shall find that the Lord God constantly requires on our part, in order that we might succeed, that we put away our sins from before His eyes through an unfeigned reformation; and where this does not happen, He will give neither salvation nor blessing, but rather threatens all kinds of calamity and grief, *Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 28.*

So it is also sure and certain that the reformation of abuses appears much more difficult (through the craftiness of our flesh) than it actually is. For we cannot sooner take this work in hand with sincere hearts, but the helping hand of the great God, who is capable of all things, is immediately there to further our work. In this, we are positioned very much like the <term>drowsy person</term> <note>original: "vakerige"; someone overcome by "vaeck" (sleep/slumber)</note> whom one cannot get up for a necessary task upon which much depends; who, however, having once stood up, is immediately delivered from the torment of drowsiness, and would then for no reason (seeing what they have to do) lie down to sleep again.

<meta>This page concludes Willem Teellinck's dedication to the high-ranking officials (likely the Council of State). He moves from warning of God's judgment to a call for spiritual reformation as the only true national security.</meta>

Pay heed to what we say, Noble Lords, (and may the good God give your Honors understanding in all things) if only the Sovereign Powers would apply half as much effort, expense, and ingenuity to ward off sin and to gain God’s favor—where everything truly rests—as is daily applied to settle certain inconveniences of the <term>Civil Governance</term> <note>original: "Politie"; in the early 17th century, this referred to the general administration, policy, and public order of the state</note> and to obtain the favor of Sovereigns and Princes (which also must not be neglected), then we would soon grow wise to the fact that this task is not so heavy, and the fruit of it would be found to be unspeakably great. For let our state but once be fastened to the Lord our God through an unfeigned Reformation of wicked sins—that certain nail upon which everything hangs <note>A biblical metaphor referencing Isaiah 22:23, where a "nail in a sure place" represents stability and support for a household or nation</note>—and we shall dwell as securely as if we had no enemies in the world; *His angels shall then encamp around us*, Psalm 34:7 <note>original cites Psalm 34:8, following the numbering in older Dutch bibles</note>. *He himself shall be a wall of fire around us*, Zechariah 2:4-5, 8. *Then we shall have a strong city; our walls shall be salvation, and our gates shall be invincible; and all who set upon us shall bear guilt; God shall reveal His grace for us, and show His power to our enemies: and even if they think we shall fall into confusion among ourselves, they shall be deceived in this; they shall stoop and fall, but we, on the contrary, shall rise and stand upright*, Psalm 20:8-9.

Heartily wishing this, we humbly dedicate this work of ours to your Honors. Kindly requesting in God’s name that whatever your Honors find within it that is worthy of consideration, you would also (according to the high standing the good God has given you) lend a hand to promote it.

And in this trust, we commend your Honors to God and to the word of His grace, for whom we also pray daily for your Honors' prosperous government. Farewell.

->In *Middelburg* on the 26th of June, 1621.<-

->Your Honors' humble Servant<-

->**WILLEM TEELLINCK.**<-

### CHAPTER III.

**Further proof that such lands, cities, generations, households, or private individuals must necessarily perish who give themselves over to sin: taken from the condition of sin itself, and from God's disposition toward sin.**

<column-break/>

As concerns the character, nature, and condition of sin, it may be viewed in two ways.

First, as it is simply in itself and in its own nature, without regard to any <term>accidents</term> <note>In 17th-century theology, an "accident" (Dutch: "toeval") refers to a non-essential quality or circumstance added to the core nature of a thing.</note>. Second, as it is situated when clothed with this accident: that one does not wish to repent of it.

<margin>Sin is, in its own character and nature, an entirely destructive thing.</margin>
Sin, considered simply in itself and just as it is in its own nature, is entirely hideous and destructive; it is the very brood of the arch-devil of hell. For sin is a wicked breach of the Law of God, a violation of the image of God, and consequently the ruin and destruction of mankind. For indeed, what is more just than that those who break the just Law of the great God with their sins should be broken with many pains? What is more reasonable than that those who violate God’s image with their sins should themselves be violated with heavy plagues? Thus, sin in its own character and nature is the ruin of people; it is like a moth that consumes them like a garment; it is like a maggot which destroys them like a dead carcass; it is an eating cancer upon lands, cities, generations, households, and private individuals.

What wonder then, when people take no care to keep this consuming, destructive thing of sin away from themselves, if they themselves come to fail, be corrupted, and be destroyed?

<margin>But most of all when it is clothed with this accident, that one [refuses to repent]</margin>

Men may arrange it as lightly as they wish, but this is how it stands in truth and in fact; and thus shall the Lord God judge it on the last day.

<margin>Fast days in other regions.</margin>
For consider, dear friends: since the Lord God has so very often and frequently—on Fast-and-Prayer Days <note>original: "Vasten-biddagen"; official days of communal repentance and fasting decreed by the government during times of crisis.</note>, on other days, and on other occasions—allowed us to be warned against all the aforementioned sins; since He Himself has begun to bring us, for the sake of these same sins, into great danger and manifold confusions (in which we have seen our land and church in recent years): what has improved? Who has taken the opportunity to look within themselves and reform what might displease God in their own person, trade, household, or where they have influence?

If the hearts of many so-called Reformed Christians were previously empty of that solemn fear of God, trust in God, and love for God, they are so still. If the holy and stately ordinances of God, and those most Christian devotions which devout souls used to practice daily between God and themselves, were daily neglected by very many so-called Reformed Christians before this day,

<column-break/>

they are so still. And this is so much the case that it seems a "strange doctrine" <note>An unfamiliar or foreign teaching.</note> to many when one begins to speak of it. If, in the past, those who profess the faith have given themselves the liberty to accept one thing presented to them from God’s Word while rejecting another, it still happens daily.

If people previously neglected to profit from God’s blessings and the means given to us to awaken godliness, they neglect them still. The judgments of God are also still passed by with blind eyes; the benefits of God are still swallowed up as if they did not come from God, and are even misused against God. His holy Day of Rest <note>The Sabbath/Sunday.</note> is still so hideously profaned and violated daily that it is beyond words.

If many so-called Christians have previously shown through their conduct in all places that they had truly chosen the world or their belly as their God <note>A reference to Philippians 3:19: "whose God is their belly."</note>, it still happens daily. If holy household order <note>original: "huys-ordre"; the practice of family worship and religious discipline within the home.</note> was neglected in many families before, it is neglected still. If people did not previously spare the weak through the untimely use of "Christian liberty," <note>Referring to the theological concept where believers may do things that are not explicitly forbidden, but which might cause a "weaker" person to stumble or be offended.</note> they still do not. If the Congregation of God was filled with scandals and offenses—through pride and pomp in clothing, through excess in meals and banquets, through many kinds of wantonness and lewdness, through fraud and falsehood, through lying speech, slander, and gossip—it also still happens daily.

If, on the contrary, the holy works of love—which one owes to one's neighbor regarding both soul and body—were set aside by many in the past, many still do so daily.

<margin>
And this so shamelessly, that those who wish to conduct themselves otherwise, and admonish others against it, become almost a laughingstock to all men.
</margin>

Thus sins break in and are still daily committed as if they were obligations among us, notwithstanding that the Lord has in many ways allowed us to be warned against them through His word, and that He has also now and then shaken the rod over our heads and shown us a wrathful face against our sins. So very passionate are many in these sins of theirs. Indeed, many people are so set upon their sins, and the offense of their misdeeds is—through the fire of evil lusts—so hard-baked and burnt into many (*Ezekiel 24:11-12* <note>The prophet Ezekiel uses the metaphor of a bronze cooking pot whose impurities are so encrusted that it must be set empty upon the coals until it glows to burn the filth away.</note>) that they cannot even stomach or tolerate those who wish to behave better, or those who do not want to run along with them in that same unrestrained excess. 

If there is one or another to be found among us who begins to make a matter of conscience regarding the commands of God; who would gladly observe the one as well as the other; who takes courage (being spurred on by the fear of God, by a holy trust in his God, and by the love he bears for Christ his Lord) to rebuke his fellow Christians for their extravagance and their flippancy, and wishes to begin establishing some good order in his own household, and personally perform works of love and mercy for the "little ones" and despised members of Christ: he is almost immediately made into everyone's mockery. He is at once singled out and denounced as a fanatic <note>original: "bijs-hooft"; literally an 'extra head,' a term used for an eccentric or someone who has lost their mind to religious zeal.</note>, a precisionist <note>original: "precisiaen"; a derogatory term for those who were "too precise" in their religious observance, similar to the English term 'Puritan.'</note>, and I know not what else. Indeed, such people must go about labeled as secret hypocrites and shams, although even their bitterest adversaries cannot charge them with anything other than that they

<column-break/>

wish to be too holy. Yes, even though their greatest enemies, who track their ways most sharply, must confess that they are civil and just in their calling, pious in their dealings, and faithful to their word.

Since things go thus among us—and even among those who otherwise pass for respectable people—it is indeed proven in every way that very many among us are "heated" in sin. Consequently, it is also true that the Lord our God has great cause to whet His sword against us, to bend His bow, to prepare His deadly artillery, and to set us as a target. For truly, if we properly look into the situation and the state of our Christian people, and how the <margin>Which then proves in every way that the Lord is also armed for War against us.</margin> aforementioned sins have overflowed all sorts of estates and conditions of men, and have crept into the houses and bedrooms even of the most prominent—just like the lice and frogs in Egypt—and then if we also remember what high-reaching and abominable sins are still sometimes committed here and there in our cities and lands (of which we have not even spoken), we may see everywhere among us much fuel for the sword of the Lord to cut us down, and for the arrows of the Almighty to pierce us. 

Indeed, we may see with the eyes of the mind—more surely and certainly—the Lord our God, the Great Warrior, standing in the posture of war against us, than we perceive that the Spaniard <note>Refers to the Spanish Empire, the primary military adversary of the Dutch Republic during the Eighty Years' War (1568–1648).</note> is making himself ready and arming for war to invade us.
