# BALM OF GILEAD

<margin>Thus we must not think, when we attempt to do something—being driven by a high-pressing necessity—that which God has forbidden, that</margin>
Daughters of Zion. For what would that be other than young children, who have no understanding, attempting without any advice from an experienced Doctor <note>original: "Doctoors"; here referring to a learned physician or a spiritual authority.</note> to mix deadly poison into their drink for their own healing? Therefore, this must also be firmly imprinted on our hearts: that no one among the people of God may attempt to speak unrighteously before the Lord our great God, or to speak deceitfully for Him, Job 13:7. As if He were a powerless Idol of the Heathens, who could not establish His affairs and intentions without our help, or without the help of our wicked and sinful hand. On the contrary, the Lord our good God is so far from needing to be helped by our evil maneuvers to keep His Church standing, that even our virtues do not reach Him, Psalm 16:2, Job 35:6, 7—so all-sufficient a God is the Lord our God. Even if the Church of God wavers, the Lord does not require that **Uzzah** <note>Reference to 2 Samuel 6:6-7, where Uzzah touched the Ark of the Covenant to steady it and was struck dead by God for his irreverence.</note> should stretch out his sinful hand to hold it up. God the Lord will keep it standing well enough in the greatest needs, even if we do not stretch out our sinful hand to it, and even if we do not stain ourselves with sinful means.

II. And it cannot excuse us here to try to pretend that when one—in such a situation of particular distress as the people of God may find themselves—does something that does not exactly align with God's word, that it then ceases to be evil because it is excused by urgent necessity: certainly this is not the truth. For indeed, even though it may sometimes be beneficial for the people of God, due to high-pressing necessity, to suspend or set aside certain

<column-break/>

<margin>it would be good for them.</margin>
good and holy meditations for a time: nevertheless, no one is free, no matter what urgent necessity presses him, to actually do and commit that which is evil and forbidden by God. And the reason for this distinction is this: we cannot do all the good works commanded of us at the same time; therefore, there is choice and distinction to be made there. But we *can* leave all evil works at the same time, and we must also strive to leave them all, and rather go into a fire than into sin, as the Martyrs of God have done. And therefore, there is neither choice nor distinction here in the sense we are speaking of. For while we can leave a thousand, and a thousand, and a thousand things at once, we can only do one thing at a time. And for us Christians, this is always the highest urgent necessity: that we do no evil. Thus, no necessity can overcome us that is so great that it could outweigh the greatest necessity of not sinning.

<margin>For the highest necessity that lies upon us is that we do not sin: And if any great distress comes upon us, unless we commit some sin, then God does not call us to sin but to suffering.</margin>
And when the Lord our good God brings us into such distress that we cannot be helped out of our difficulties unless we employ evil means, we must in that case hold it for certain and sure that the Lord our God is calling us then, not to use evil means, but to endure evil difficulties. He calls us then, not to sin, but to suffer; and thus have all the Martyrs of God and holy Confessors <note>Confessors: Those who maintained their Christian faith under pressure or torture but were not necessarily killed.</note> understood it completely.

<margin>And the willful must be borne.</margin>

# FOR ZION'S WOUND

<margin>
In our heart, that we may do no evil, so that good might come from it.
</margin>

...we must do no evil, so that good may come of it. Romans 3:8. It is also nothing but a mere deception of the devil when he comes to make us believe that we could bring forth something good out of sin. Can one also suck health from a deadly poison? Or gather figs from thistles? Matthew 7:16. Can any human hand do that? Does not the Lord our God—our Supreme Physician <note>original: "Heelmeester"; a term for a surgeon or master healer.</note> who must heal and help us—testify to us that if we are to be healed and helped (Jeremiah 17:14), He will have no mixture of sin in the healing elixir <note>original: "heel-dranck"; a medicinal potion or tonic.</note> of the daughter of Zion? See concerning this Deuteronomy 23:9, Deuteronomy 25:16, Joshua 1:8, 1 Thessalonians 5:22, Ezekiel 18:31, 32. Even though earthly physicians sometimes mix a little poison into their healing potions, it does not work that way with the spiritual medicine of the soul. The poison of sin that one mixes into it is like the colocynths <note>original: "Coloquinten"; wild gourds that were accidentally shredded into a pot of stew, making it poisonous until the prophet Elisha performed a miracle. See 2 Kings 4:39-40.</note> in the pot of the children of the Prophets; it brings no healing, but death. 2 Kings 4:39, 40.

<margin>
Even if we consider the evil we would do to be very small, and conversely the good we would obtain from it very great.
</margin>

V. And if one should think that the evil we commit is only small, and the good that offers itself from it is very great and excellent—such as, for example, the preservation of the people of God—that is also but a deception. The good that we think to obtain through sin is entirely detrimental at the outset. Listen to what our Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself, says of this: "What would it profit a man," He says, "if he gained the whole world and suffered the loss of his soul?" Mark 8:36. Indeed, we truly obtain no kind of good through sin; for the good acquired through sin is so poisoned by that sin that it becomes entirely harmful to us as well. Titus 1:15, Haggai 2:

<column-break/>

<margin>
For such good that is poisoned by sin is turned by the sin in such a way that it always turns to our harm.
</margin>

14. Even the blessing thus obtained is turned into a curse from the Lord for us, Malachi 2:2; it bites at the last like an adder, Job 20:12, etc. Therefore, such lusts that lead us to the practice of sins are called "deceitful desires." Ephesians 4:22. For they namely promise much good but do not perform it, but in the end bring forth nothing but gravity and trouble, Romans 6:21. This is something our first father Adam became well aware of upon his first sin, Genesis 3:8, etc., and since that time, sin has not changed its nature, but has much rather become even more sinful and destructive.

Therefore, all reasonable people must rightly maintain that it is better and more blessed for the people of God that, by abstaining from sin, they remain in temporal misfortune, and contempt, in heavy persecution and oppression, than that they should be delivered from their difficulties by helping themselves with sinful means. This holds true even if the sin committed in order to be helped does not seem to be very great; for as the Apostle Peter says, "Who is he that will harm you, if you be followers of that which is good? But and if ye suffer for righteousness' sake, happy are ye," 1 Peter 3:13, 14. And it is also truly the case with sin that even the smallest sin has the poisonous sting of death within itself, Romans 6:23, 1 Corinthians 15:56. How then can we still consider that as small which brings the great wrath of the infinite Majesty of God upon us? Ephesians 5:3, 4, 5, 6. Can it then also be considered but a small matter to deserve hell? Indeed, is there any good so great, contained within this life and this present world...

### CHAPTER XIX.

->On the bearing and paying of burdens and taxes which are necessary to withstand the common enemy and to help the people of God out of their distress.<-

<margin>
We must all equally, according to our ability, gladly bear such burdens and taxes as are laid upon us to withstand the common enemy, so that God’s people may indeed be helped.
</margin>

<margin>I.</margin> If the misfortune of God’s people—and the difficulties that now also press upon them externally—are to be warded off, then work must also be done toward this: that all lovers and well-wishers of God’s people, and every one of them, according to their utmost ability, gladly contribute and pay all such imposed burdens and taxes for the payment of the manifold expenses which arise in order to withstand such a heavy war with which God’s people are now oppressed. Look, very great and unbelievable costs must be incurred, by sea and by land, to face the enemy, to stop the course of his victories, and to pull the prey he has already seized back out of his molars. <note>original: "back-tanden" (molars); a vivid metaphor for rescuing territory or people already captured by the enemy</note> Now the means for this must come from the people, of every rank, of high and low status. So then must all allies <term>Bont-ghenooten: "covenant-allies," referring to the provinces or individuals joined in a political and religious union</term>, each according to their condition, circumstances, and ability, contribute to this; each region, province, city, village, household, and following that, all private persons and residents. To this end, many are indeed very slow, and some seem unable to pay what is laid upon them. We shall therefore excellently <note>original: "costelijck" (preciously/excellently)</note> point out how we are bound to be willing, and how we might also be empowered to do so.

<margin>Earnest exhortation</margin> II. So that everyone and each individual

<column-break/>

might be willing to serve according to their utmost ability from their means, for the help and assistance of God’s distressed people, then one must thoroughly weigh and lay to heart all the evidence we have brought forward above: how much we are obligated and bound to help and assist the people of God with all our strength and to our utmost ability. For whom shall we save our means if we refuse to apply them for the help and assistance of God’s own worthy people and of His holy Church? Do we not also know, and must we not admit, that everything we have, and what the Lord our good God has given us, He has given us solely for that purpose: that we should spend and apply it for the good and relief of His own people? Indeed, has not the Lord our good God partially blessed us and dealt wonderfully well with us, just as with the house of Obed-Edom <note>The text uses "Obedmelech," but refers to the biblical Obed-Edom (2 Samuel 6:11), whose household was blessed because he sheltered the Ark of the Covenant</note>, because the Ark of God has been among us? Have not many of the inhabitants and residents of the land become rich and powerful while they have had and maintained the Gospel among them? How then shall we not gladly apply and spend those means and that power which God has given us to further support His Gospel? ->### A BALM FOR ZION'S WOUND ###<-

Furthermore, it also greatly harms the **common good**: because those who are deprived of such opportunities—which would serve them best—are kept so far under that they are not capable of bearing the public burdens alongside others. From this arises not only a weakening of the country’s resources, but also a great alienation of minds and a great dissatisfaction with the present government, to the inexpressible detriment of the general welfare of the land.

Therefore, we wish from the bottom of our hearts that in this, too, the rule of God’s Word (which shall indeed be found in every way to be the most wholesome, both for the **State** <note>original: "Politie"; referring to civil administration and governance rather than a modern police force</note> and the **Church**) might be properly observed; and that every person would seek not only his own gain and advantage, but also that of others, as in *Philippians 2:4*, and do unto others as he would have done unto himself, *Matthew 7:12*.

In writing and wishing this, we nonetheless testify in all sincerity that we do not have a particular eye on any specific **Province**, **City**, **College** <note>an administrative or judicial body</note>, or **Guild**, etc. For we freely admit that although we often hear one Province complain about another, one City about another, or one Guild about another, we nonetheless cannot, nor dare we say, where the injustice lies. Instead, we leave that to the wisdom of those to whom the care of the Government of the land and the Cities is entrusted; and we only wish from our hearts that they, in their manifold wisdom, would also seriously see to it and labor so that everyone might be civil and upright

<column-break/>

in their trade, and that every person should not only seek his own advantage, but also that of others.

And behold, if we are thus willing to be diligent in our calling, moderate in our food, drink, clothing, and household goods, and civil in our trade, then we shall everywhere be easily able to pay the taxes and burdens laid upon us. Thus, with our means and efforts—God’s blessing working therein—we may further the recovery of the misfortune of **Jerusalem** <note>a common metaphor for the Dutch Republic or the Reformed Church community</note> even in our days. Concerning this, we have given some further account in our *Trumpet of Zion* and our *Lamentation*.

### CHAPTER XX.

Regarding the faithful keeping of the **Oath**, which has been sworn by the inhabitants of the land for the maintenance of good order and for the raising of the necessary resources of the land; and how it must be observed so that the people of God might be well-aided.

<margin>

</margin>

Should the people of God be well-aided, it is also of the highest necessity that all and everyone—according to their opportunity, state, and condition—should, in all good conscience, keep their **Oath** and promise, which they have made for the maintenance of good order and for the raising of necessary funds for the common cause of the people of God, and to their **Governments** and **Magistrates**. Behold, the Oath is an entirely Divine means, serving the wonderful ease of the children of men, when the same is properly applied and also observed.

...men shall. And the servant said to him; Perhaps the woman will not want to follow me into this land: must I then bring your son back into the land from which you departed? And Abraham said to him; See to it that you do not bring my son back there. The Lord, the God of Heaven, who took me from my father’s house, and from the land of my kindred, and who has spoken to me, and who has sworn to me, saying: To your seed I will give this land; He Himself shall send His Angel before your face, so that you may take a wife for my son from there. But if the woman does not want to follow you, then you shall be free from this my oath: only do not bring my son back there. Then the servant laid his hand under the thigh of Abraham his lord, and he swore to him concerning this matter. *Genesis 24:1, 2, and so forth.* <note>original: "Et." (Latin for "and others" or "and so forth"). This refers to the continuation of the story in the Bible.</note> <note>Placing a hand under the "thigh" or "hip" was an ancient Near Eastern custom for swearing a solemn oath, often related to the sacredness of progeny and lineage.</note>

And we wish from our whole hearts that we all would likewise observe this discretion of our father Abraham in the administering of an oath—which is the first instance where the manner of doing so is expressly set forth in the Holy Scripture. For it is truly beyond words what damage and disadvantage it breeds when people begin to perceive that the intention and meaning of those who impose and demand the oath does not seem to have been that everything should be kept as exactly as the words expressly sound, but only "roughly" or "in a reasonable manner," as some say. For such a thought (since all men by nature crave leeway) <note>original: "ruymicheydt" (literally "roominess"), meaning the freedom to interpret rules loosely.</note> immediately causes people to begin giving themselves the liberty to somewhat dispense with what they have sworn; and once a

<column-break/>

door has been opened to this, there is neither end nor measure to be kept. For once a person comes so far that he dares, on his own authority, to dispense—however slightly—with his oath, he is gradually led further and further to violate his oath in everything where he finds that it stands in his way. And holding it to be true that it is indeed not the intention of those who took the oath from them that they should keep it all so strictly; so they begin to embolden themselves to keep that which pinches them most the least, to the unspeakable disadvantage of all good ordinances. And so, too, consciences are gradually so devastated that they finally begin to make no further business of their oath than their fear of being caught. And so it also happens that that great and terrible Name of God—which was granted to the children of men to keep them in all good order, even in their most secret reflections where no men know of or can discover—is completely and utterly despised. In such a way, men are the boldest in their most secret reflections, of which no one knows, to act against their oath; to the unspeakable damage of the land and the provocation of our great God; whose curse then goes out like a fire to avenge itself over such great and loathsome contempt as is done to Him through such conduct. And so this also becomes the ruin of many a person and household; which might have been prevented in many ways if labor were done thoroughly on all sides so that everything which is clearly confirmed with an oath, also...

### for Zion’s wounds. ###

...might be maintained with faithfulness, and that the <term>Contraventeurs</term> <note>original: "Contraventeurs" — those who act against or violate a law or agreement.</note> thereof should be strictly punished in every way, so that everyone might learn to fear that glorious and terrible Name, the Lord our God, Deut. 28:58, and be very careful not to do the slightest thing against their oath.

To this end, it would also help much if those who administer the oath did not do so carelessly, as a mere common custom or order; but with all possible solemnity, and with prior encouragement and Divine warning to those who have to take the oath, that they should take good heed of themselves—what it means to bind one's soul with an oath to God; and with a subsequent bold exhortation, once the oath is taken, that it be kept with all faithfulness and integrity.

III. The common man must also see to it here that oaths are well maintained; and that in two ways: First, that they themselves, each for their own part, use all good conscience in observing their oath: And secondly, that they seek to expose those who act against it, wherever they can or may.

<margin>3. That everyone should personally make it a matter of conscience to keep their own oath.</margin>
As for the first point, all lovers and well-wishers of God's people and Church must especially see to it for their own part that they use all good conscience in observing and keeping what they have sworn by oath. Indeed, they must impress this upon themselves and make it thoroughly understood: that they can do themselves no favor through anything they achieve by 

<column-break/>

the breach of their oath. For we all know that the Lord our God must help us if we are to be helped; so it is also customary to take the oath with this clause, **So help me God**; which signifies this: that just as we wish and desire that God help us, so we promise that we shall faithfully keep and fulfill the oath we thus take, and consequently we pray in effect that God not help or bless us, but rather oppose and curse us, if we do not keep our oath; in such a way that if someone violates his oath, he places himself in the tracks of the cursed, faithless man, of whom the <term>Psalmist</term> <note>The "Psalmist" refers to the author of the biblical Book of Psalms, usually identified as King David.</note> speaks thus:
> Since he loved the curse, let it come upon him: and had no delight in the Blessing, so let it be far from him. And let him be clothed with the curse, as with his Garment, and let it enter into his innermost parts, like water, and like Oil into his Bones. Let it be to him as a Garment with which he covers himself, and for a belt with which he is always girded.
*Psalm 109, Vs. 17. 18. 19.* Is this then not terrifying? Must not everyone indeed rightly see to it that he keeps his oath well? What profit or advantage is there so great that we think we can obtain through the breach of our oath, which can outweigh this heavenly curse of God, which surely ruins everything? Is it a small matter to put on the curse of God like a shirt, and that it should crawl through all our inner parts like water, and go into our bones like oil? ...consume them / our state, and ruin us here and hereafter, forever and eternally? Shall anyone among us then be so foolish that, even if he might win a thousand pounds <note>original: "duyfent pont" — a substantial sum of money, used here to illustrate the temptation of greed.</note> at a single stroke by the breach of his oath—and do it so secretly that no man could ever catch him—he would dare to do so? Since the great and terrible Name of God, which he has invoked, always stands over him; and God the Lord will take the matter all the more to heart the less that men are able to discover it; and consequently, He will not help that person, but oppose him; not bless him, but curse him. What profit can his gain be to him if he brings the devil into his house along with his profit, if he shuts God’s blessing out of the house because of his ill-gotten gain, and drags the curse of God into it? Therefore, it is only right that everyone who wishes to prosper in the world should shrink from doing such evil. And no one should dare to take it upon themselves to dispense with or weaken anything in their oath through self-invented and vain, sought-after excuses, or secret meanings <note>original: "hepmelijcke beduydingen" — mental reservations or private interpretations used to justify breaking the literal word of an oath.</note> which he keeps to himself and does not put to the test: for a person can very easily and miserably deceive themselves in this, and give in too much, being led astray by their own greed to their eternal ruin. <column-break/>

upon which the blessing or the curse of God so significantly hangs, depending on whether one conducts oneself well or poorly in it, dare to do nothing otherwise) than having first well-investigated everything with those very people who administered the oath, and other God-fearing people who understand such matters.

4. That all pious people lend a hand to catch and expose the perjurers.

Although this may benefit the individual soul but little, it will nonetheless bring great ease and benefit to the state and the land. Therefore, all those who love God's people and wish them success must labor toward this end.

-ured out to us by the Lord our good God, in that time when we shall have the most need of comfort and help, Luke 6:38. For as the Apostle Paul says: *God is not unrighteous, that He would forget your work and the labor of love which you have shown toward His name, in that you have served the saints and do still serve.* Heb. 6:10. Mark well this manner of speaking; "God is not unrighteous," says the Apostle; so that God's righteousness is, as it were, held as a pledge (to speak with all reverence) that He shall bless those who do good to His oppressed people. All the labor then, and all the effort that we spend for the oppressed people of God, all the good that we do therein, shall return again into our own bosom, just as if we had cast it up toward heaven; and the more we seek to do good to the oppressed members of Christ, the more we ourselves shall be blessed. ## CHAPTER XXIV.

### That if we do not take heart to come to the aid of God's people in their need, matters among us will go from bad to worse, and our accountability will be very heavy on the final day.

<margin>But if we do not come to the aid of God's people in a timely manner and also improve ourselves, things will go from bad to worse.</margin>
If, on the contrary, we do not rouse ourselves nor offer a hand to help the sick daughter of Zion <note>The "daughter of Zion" is a biblical personification of the Church or the community of the faithful.</note>, to assist God's people in their need, and to help ward off the ill humors of base sins whereof we have spoken above in Chapter 5 of the first part and Chapter 4 of the second part of this Treatise; and to do even further what must be done to help God's people out of their misfortune: to practice unity, to be willing to contribute, for each of us to fulfill our oath, and to see to it that the Land might be served by the most pious and brave persons.

# BALM OF GILEAD, #

Who will also take the matters of God’s Church in hand, if the members of the Congregation themselves do not consider it? Reflect then for once, all you who act this way: how will you be able to answer for this in eternity, if you do not improve your ways at the first opportunity?

V. Imagine indeed that you are now lying on your deathbed (and you must certainly die one day) and are making final preparations to appear before the judgment of God—for there you must also certainly appear one day. *For it is appointed for man once to die, and after that the judgment, Hebrews 9:27.*

<margin>As they can quickly learn, if they would only once go into the house of mourning <note>Dutch: "claech huys," referring to a place where the dying or bereaved are found.</note> to the dying, where they will hear those who lived as they do now complaining bitterly on their deathbeds.</margin>
Imagine then the hour of death, the day of Judgment, and consider for once whether this conduct of yours—from which we have sought to turn you throughout this entire Treatise, yet in which you take such great pleasure and so boldly persist against all warnings of the Men of God, yes, even sometimes against the promptings of your own conscience—whether you will indeed be able to defend this conduct in the hour of death and on the day of judgment? Or will your conscience not then bite you because of it? Will you not then truly wish that you had acted otherwise and followed our advice? If you still doubt this, follow me into the house of mourning where people lie dying, stretching and gasping for death: Listen to me how they complain that they also acted just as you do now; how they wish that they had managed their affairs differently and followed the faithful advice of the Godly more closely, *Proverbs 5:11, 12, 13, 14.* And hearing and perceiving that, consider also that the Heathens <note>A common term for classical Greek and Roman authors.</note> themselves have known how to say that in 

<column-break/>

the hour of death, man no longer fakes his thoughts, but speaks faithful and true words:

> At last, from the bottom of the heart, true voices break forth. <note>Original Latin: *Tunc demum pectore ex imo, veræ erumpunt voces.* This is a quote from the Roman poet Lucretius, suggesting that the proximity of death forces a person to be honest.</note>

Therefore, you should certainly pay close attention to this.

VI. For see, this is how it stands, and it is well worth noting;

<margin>When the Lord God makes Himself master of them, and causes them to be accused and their godliness besieged, whether they will or not.</margin>
It often happens that the Lord our gracious God stretches out His hands all day long to a disobedient and contradictory people, *Romans 10:21.* Yes, it often happens that God’s word and work, and all that He does concerning man to convert him, to bring him away from his evil ways toward more blessed thoughts and a better walk of life, counts for nothing at all; nor does it move the hard-hearted man to repent thoroughly and from the heart, or to better his life, *Proverbs 1:20 etc., Romans 2:4, 5.* Nevertheless, the Lord God wants to be and remain Master, among and over all, over all the children of men alike. He wants to address even the Heathens in such a way, at one time or another, that they must all finally acknowledge that they are but men, and that He is Lord and Master over them all, *Psalm 9:21.* So the Lord God also brings it to pass that no matter how recklessly or godlessly a man has acted and behaved here in the course of his life while he ran about fresh and healthy; no matter how little he cared for the Word of the Lord; how boldly he mocked all warnings; how jokingly he treated serious things in the days of his luxury and wantonness, in his meals, weddings, in his drunken gatherings, or in his fleshly recreations, songs, dances, delights, and pleasures...

...convicted and violently convinced (by the gnawing and biting of the worm of their own conscience, which then begins to live, and thereafter pricks and strengthens, *Mark 9:44, etc.* <note>The "worm of conscience" is a common seventeenth-century metaphor for the internal realization of sin, referencing the biblical "worm that dieth not" in Mark 9:44.</note>) that the godly have advised them well, but that they themselves have done poorly; so that they all must alike confess that faithful obedience to God's commandments, shown in the course of one's life while one was still well, is worth more than the glory of all the Kingdoms of the earth, however many and however great they might be.

VII. See, experience teaches this, and it is well worth noting. For through this gracious dealing of our God (for so we may rightly call it, a completely gracious dealing of our God, since thereby all the living are powerfully warned not to do any longer in the course of their lives that which they shall so bitterly lament in the hour of their death) all people who are willing to pay attention are most faithfully convinced that, however much they delight in their vanities and however pleasantly they know how to excuse and defend them now, it shall not go well for them in the end. Indeed, they shall at the last be extremely distressed and troubled over it in the hour of death, as they make preparations to appear before the judgment of God. This they can fully perceive in as many dying people as they happen to encounter; for then the Lord makes true regarding them what He, on another occasion, threatened the disobedient people through the Prophet Jeremiah, saying:

> See, a storm of the Lord, a fury has gone forth, a persistent storm: it shall remain upon the

<column-break/>

head of the Godless. The heat of the Lord’s Wrath shall not turn away, until He has done, and until He has established the thoughts of His heart: in the latter days you shall pay attention to it. *Jer. 30:23, 24.*

Therefore Solomon also says, *It is better to go to the house of mourning than to go to the house of Feasting: for in the same is the end of all Men; and the living lays it to his heart. Eccl. 7:2.* <note>The "house of mourning" refers to a home where someone has died or is dying; the author argues that witnessing death forces the living to reflect on their own mortality.</note> And we mention this here also in order to drive away—if it were possible, as if with an iron rod—all those who, despite everything we have said so far, will not let themselves be turned from their vanities and God-provoking sins, and lead them toward more soul-saving thoughts. And therefore we also wish to give those—who as of yet have not taken the misfortune of God’s Church to heart, but rather, through their vanities, lightheartedness, wantonness, spitefulness, pride, and other indecencies, further ignite God’s wrath against God’s people (among whom they also count themselves)—the following things to consider most seriously and deeply. Indeed, we pray most heartily that all of you members of God’s Church, of high or low station, and all who have any interest therein, and who are well aware that you do not take courage to come to the aid of God’s Church in her need, would consider these following things deeply.

## CHAPTER XXVI.

Some noteworthy things, to be deeply considered by all those who are still aware within themselves that they do not take the affairs of God’s people to heart as they ought.

<margin>
1. With what conscience we can pass by the salvific <note>The word "salvific" (heylsame) here means leading to safety, health, or salvation.</note> counsel of the only-wise God, which He gives us in His word for our preservation, and follow our own mind, which is surely not good.

->for Zion's wound.<-

We certainly know better. What less could we do for our great God, who wants to do so much for us, than to gladly break away from wicked usages, the vile customs of the world, to forsake destructive sins, to practice the Christian faith, hope, and love, and to learn all Christian virtues? Shall we then remain any longer proud, extravagant, excessive, unjust, and deceitful, frivolous and wanton? Shall we do so, when God advises us otherwise, so that it might go well with us?

<margin>
And while God’s martyrs gave up property, blood, life, and everything to keep God’s word; people today do not even want to give up their intemperance, injustice, and godlessness for the preservation of God’s people.
</margin>
Consider what the martyrs had to do, what they had to endure, what they had to suffer—what difficulties, what grief, what anxieties they had to withstand. Consider what they had to leave behind and forsake to cling to the Lord Christ, to keep their Christian faith, and to adorn their profession of it. And yet, consider how they overcame all this, how through all these distressing cases and great difficulties, they clung to their Lord Jesus Christ above all else and confessed His truth. Well then: what they did, we would also have to do if God the Lord called us to it, unless we expect to arrive elsewhere than where they have 

<column-break/>

arrived; unless we expect to inherit eternal rest, joy, and glory with them hereafter in the Kingdom of Heaven by some other way. Now, all that the holy martyrs of God in the time of our fathers gladly underwent; thus also their blood was the "seed of the Church" <note>original: "zaet der Kercke" — a reference to the famous quote by Tertullian: "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church."</note>; thus they have also with their blood rebuilt for us the fallen walls of Jerusalem <note>A metaphor for the restoration of the true Church after a period of spiritual ruin.</note>. Indeed, through their steadfast confession, through their death and dying, they brought the affairs of God's Church to where we see them now. The flames of the fire with which they were burned have lit the clear light of the Gospel so brightly throughout the whole world that we also rejoiced in that light for a time. Indeed, that saving light still appears and teaches us that, renouncing all ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly in this present world, **Titus 2:11-12.** To keep this heavenly light among us, we do not need (as the martyrs of God had to do, and as many Christians in other parts of the world still must do) to forsake wife, children, status, offices, honor, reputation, property, means, freedom, life, blood, and all. No; the Lord, who knows our weakness, does not test us so severely. We only need to forsake worldly customs, wicked usages, vile sins, and fleshly vanities, which we can spare as easily as the clippings from our nails or the dust from our shoes.

If we then will not even do this much, though the Lord God makes it so easy for us—whereas in the time of our fathers it ended so harshly—think then further...

# BALM OF GILEAD,

So too, those excellent **Martyrs of God** who, in the times of our fathers, staked their lives, property, blood, and everything to preserve and advance the **Holy Gospel**; who also, through their steadfastness, patience, and death, truly confirmed the Holy Gospel among us. If they were to raise their heads now from among us and see how we, their children, treat and regard that Holy and precious Gospel for which they suffered death; and if they began to perceive how we weaken, bend, and push aside the Holy rules, commandments, and **Ordinances** of the Holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus, all for the base habits and evil customs of this corrupt world; how we, their children, have merely cast off the **yoke of the Antichrist** <note>In the context of the Dutch Reformation, the "Antichrist" was a common polemical term for the Pope or the Roman Catholic Church.</note> but have by no means taken up the **yoke of Christ**; indeed, how we instead wear the yoke of the world and break out in all splendor and excess, lewd wantonness, and frivolity, in unjust and deceitful trade, in ambition and power-seeking, in vanity and partisanship; and how we cannot be won over by all the counsel of the Holy Gospel to do even so much as to lay aside our scandalous finery, trimmings, and pageantry, our excesses and intemperance, and the lewd wantonness at **Feasts** and **Weddings**; while they were comforted to lay down their own positions and offices, their honor and reputation, their property and blood, and their very lives—

<column-break/>

—and to lay all of that down in the dust for the love of the **Gospel**. Seeing this, would they not rightfully be ashamed of such degenerate and bastardized children as we are? Would they not be ashamed of such an ungrateful generation as we are now found to be? Would they not rightfully think to themselves (silently looking upon us): "Did we take so much trouble and labor for these people to confirm the Gospel for them, and do they now dare to regard it so lightly, to distort it <note>original: "hersoolen"—literally to 'resole' a shoe, here meaning to rework or tamper with the faith to make it fit a worldly lifestyle</note>, to wrinkle it, to bend it, and even to make it give way for the base, evil customs of the world?" What else could they conclude from this but that the Lord God will surely soon withdraw the Holy Gospel from us and give it to another people who will better yield its fruit?

What else can we conclude, when we act in this way, than that if we had lived in our fathers' time and had been persecuted with fire and sword, robbed of our goods, stripped of our positions and offices, separated from wife and children, cast into a foul-smelling and difficult prison, sentenced to death, and burned with fire—if we had wanted to remain clinging to the Gospel as happened to them—that we, who now will not even leave our lewd wantonness, scandalous pageantry, our intemperance, and other improprieties for the sake of the Gospel, would surely rather have abandoned the Gospel than put ourselves in any difficulty for its sake. Consider then further, you who [do] this...

Give unto the Lord, you children of the Mighty, give unto the Lord glory and strength for the service of his people, which he has given you, Psalm 29:1. Follow then the Lord your **God**, who has exalted you, in this matter as well; arrange your entire Government so that it might best serve the good of the people of **God**. Let your eye, like **God's** eye, be upon the Congregation of **God** from the beginning of the year to the end, to build and edify it. Make it always the first, the greatest, and the most prominent of all your Deliberations and Consultations: how you might, through **Holy Reformation** according to **God's** counsel, come to the aid of **God's** people and help them out of their distress. Discharge your conscience in this, and hold it for certain: the Lord **God** expects this of you; the Lord **God** shall also call you to an account for this in his time. If you do it not—if anyone among you remains sluggish and unwilling in this—then you must

<column-break/>

nevertheless know that the Lord God has nonetheless exalted you for this purpose, just as he once exalted Esther for that end. And you shall also have to answer for it; for even then, the Lord **God** will not leave his people without help; refreshment and deliverance shall arise for them from another place; but you and your Father’s house shall perish, Esther 4:14. Indeed, their deliverance will then bring little honor to you, Judges 4:9. Cast off, then, all sluggishness in this matter; lift up the drooping knees and the idle hands; and stand—yes, stand in good earnest—with those people who, though they may be oppressed for a little while, shall nonetheless at last lift up their heads again and hold the victory over all their enemies.

<margin>The Ministers and the Overseers.</margin>
IV. Let also the Ministers and the Overseers <note>Referring to the clergy and elders or bishops of the church.</note> of **God's Church**, and all the Lord's Servants, embolden themselves to this; let them constantly and quite diligently awaken themselves and the people to come to the help of the Lord, to the help of the Lord against the mighty. Let them indeed make this their work, as they are especially called to it; let them indeed devote themselves quite faithfully to this. For truly, if time is found to do anything—to eat, to drink, and to sleep, and whatever we might deem most necessary for the maintenance of this life—so must we also find time for this work, upon which the glory of **God** and the welfare of the people so greatly depend. # PREFACE.

<meta>catchword: for</meta>

to grieve our God, so He has also let the affairs of the Reformed <note>The "Ghereformeerde" refers to those following the Calvinist tradition of the Protestant Reformation.</note> (as they stood in counter-weight to the Antichristian Kingdom) <note>A common polemical term used by Reformers at the time to refer to the Roman Catholic Church and the Papacy.</note> fall miserably into ruin, and our affairs have, for some years now, gone powerfully backward. Almost everything we have taken in hand has failed: heavy wars, expensive times of scarcity, Pestilence, unusual diseases, and deaths have broken in upon us, along with even more other particular inconveniences and difficulties that have struck various individual churches and families. Of which your Honorable Congregation, for some years now, has also had great and sad experience. Thus, we have seen enough hardship in temporal matters, just as we had seen all too much decline in spiritual matters. And so, from contrary causes, contrary effects have arisen.

Now, there is also no godly heart among us which does not long and sigh that our first Love might be awakened; for then our first blessing might also come upon us again in full measure, and we might not only escape many feared difficulties that still further threaten us, but also ourselves receive many benefits which we now hardly dare to hope for—so poorly have we repaid the Lord our God for His previous benevolence. And all the more must all lovers of Jerusalem <note>A biblical metaphor for the Church or the community of faithful believers.</note> rightly and most earnestly wish for this, for we can indeed see that at this time, even the work of our Reformation and the Holy Truth, which is still among us, begins to be despised because of the misconduct of many of those who profess this Holy Truth. 

It has come to the point that our adversaries even dare to proclaim loudly that the Doctrine confirmed in the National Synod of Dort <term>Synod of Dort: A major international assembly held in 1618–1619 in Dordrecht to settle a theological conflict regarding predestination and grace.</term> is a doctrine solely directed toward stifling godliness and allowing godlessness to break in everywhere. # PREFACE.

...to shame such impudent slanders of that Holy, and in the Scripture firmly grounded, and altogether comforting Doctrine, through a Holy and Godly conduct? Which might fully stop the mouth of foolish gainsayers: as it shall more and more appear that indeed the *knowledge of the truth*, which God the Lord graciously grants to us, is in all our hearts as a well-rooted *Seed of Godliness*, bringing forth all kinds of good fruits of the Spirit; now again, and were it possible even much more than it ever did at the first dawning of the Holy Gospel. 

To further this then, and to assist the affairs of the Reformed in some measure, and to bring back the first zeal and blessing, we have, according to our humble gift, employed some meditations; and among others, we have previously set forth for that purpose a WARNING to our Churches, from the words of ZEPHANIAH 2:1–2 <note>Zephaniah 2:1-2: "Gather yourselves together... before the decree bring forth." A biblical call for a nation to humble itself before God's judgment.</note>. Which we have noticed that, by God’s grace, has awakened quite some attention in some. 

We now presently add thereto *another* WARNING, from the words of CHRIST, Revelation 2, verses 4 and 5 <note>Revelation 2:4-5: "Nevertheless I have somewhat against thee, because thou hast left thy first love... and do the first works."</note>, trying whether perhaps the Lord God might grant that the one Warning, strengthening the other, our hearts might be convinced, as by two true witnesses, of our falling away, and how very necessary it is that we repent, and do our first works. 

With that aim and longing, we now also make these our reflections public to the People through the press, and have seen fit to dedicate the same to Your Honors; both because we presented the same some years ago, when we were with Your Honors in LONDON, in a Sermon to Your Honors’ attention, to the good satisfaction of many: as also because we observe the particular situation of Your Honors’ Congregation, how the greater part of it is descended from those old, faithful zealots, who risked goods and blood for the Love of the Holy Truth, which the Lord had revealed to them, and who *accepted the plundering of their goods with joy, knowing that they had in themselves a better and enduring possession in the heavens.* <note>The author is quoting Hebrews 10:34 to describe the Protestant refugees who fled to London to escape religious persecution, likely from the Spanish Netherlands during the 16th or 17th century.</note>

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut drop cap 'T' featuring leafy scrolls and floral patterns.</image-desc>THE Lord Jesus, being absent in the flesh from His <term>Church</term> <note>original: "Gemeynte." # Christ’s Warning, to prevent downfall.

...to quench the smoldering wick. 
Matthew 12 verse 20. He who alone can also stand for us: even when He has something against us. For we ought to act in such a way that, even if the world has much against us, the Lord Christ might truly have much in our favor: which happens, not when we are entirely without sin, but when we are upright of heart, when in our spirit there is no deceit: Psalm 32 verses 1, 2; Psalm 37 verse 1. When we do not stubbornly keep any sins within us that we could easily better if we only willed it. Isaiah 1 verses 18, 19, 20, 21. When we do not grow weary, but increase in the best gifts, like the <term>Church of Smyrna</term> <note>Smyrna was another of the seven churches in Revelation, praised for its faithfulness under suffering.</note>. From this, the following teaching arises.

The Lord Christ has a keen-eyed gaze, to perceive even the failings of His people. *I have something against you* (He says). He presents Himself here as a **keen-eyed Suitor** <note>original: "Vyper." While this word literally looks like "viper," the context of "nausiende" (keen-eyed) and the comparison to lovers and mothers indicates it refers to a "vrijer" (suitor) or a meticulous inspector who looks for any blemish on a loved one's face.</note> (spoken with reverence) who immediately notices where there is a blemish or a smear on the beautiful face of His beloved. Thus we learn in the **Gospel** <note>original: "Euangelio."</note> that the Lord Christ perceived the failings of His **Disciples** and rebuked them for it from time to time, as in Matthew 17:20, Mark 16:14, and elsewhere. So the Lord Christ keeps a close eye on all our conduct; He watches how we manage our households, how we behave toward our family members, whether we neglect those holy domestic exercises to which we are justly bound: how we conduct ourselves in the works of our calling, whether we commit any injustice or unfaithfulness therein; He also pays special attention to whether we neglect the promotion of His honor, the building up of His holy **Church** <note>original: "Ghemeynte," referring to the congregation or the body of believers.</note>, and the welfare of His people; and He pays heed 

<column-break/>

to it, in order to bring it against us if we are found guilty, as we see here in our text.

The reason for this is that Christ's love for His holy Church is not like the blind love of **foolish Mothers** or **Lovers**, who see no faults in their beloved; but it is a well-tempered and very useful love, whose work it is to perceive clearly what is disordered, and also to point it out helpfully so that it might be improved. Leviticus 19:17, 2 Corinthians 2:4, Hebrews 10:24.

An awakening to diligently examine ourselves, how we stand, and whether there might be anything in us that the Lord Christ might have something against; we should gladly consider this: so that we do not deceive ourselves in such a weighty matter as this is; all the more because we are so inclined to quickly convince ourselves that all things are well, rather than to diligently take care that they might truly be well. We do not gladly allow ourselves to believe that Christ would have anything against us.

This has deceived and ruined many Churches of Christ in **Germany** <note>original: "Duyts-landt."</note> and elsewhere, and we still follow that same path; and rather than making certain work through examination, we want to assure ourselves through vain delusion that all is well; while yet—alas, poor souls!—it is far from it. For dear ones (that we may also add a word here), does not this complaint of Christ also apply to us? I speak to the best of us all, who live so securely and imagine that all is well: would not the Lord Jesus also have something [against us]—notwithstanding the boast of our **prosperity** <note>The page ends with "wel-stant" (prosperity/well-being), providing the catchword "stant" for the next page.</note>

If an earthly **Prince**, who had command over us and upon whose grace we lived, let us know through his servants that he had something against us: would we still be able to go to bed at peace? How poorly then do those people care for their souls, who so rely on the favor and love of Christ that they embolden themselves in their sins through it; and no matter how much the **Lord Jesus** complains about them, and lets them know that He has much against them—against their hatred and envy, wantonness and frivolity, against their pomp and pride, against their desecration of His **Sabbath** <note>original: "Rust-daeghs," literally "Rest-day."</note>, against their neglect of Divine Service, misuse of His **Holy Supper**, and whatever more of those things there are—they nevertheless pay no mind to it, nor even once take it to heart to improve it: but when they have heard all that in the house of the Lord, they turn around like the hardened **Pharaoh** and go to their house, and do not set their hearts to it.

### CHAPTER II.

->**Concerning the specific fault that was in the Church of Ephesus, and which needed to be improved, namely: The abandonment of their first love.**<-

The fault over which the **Lord Christ** particularly complains against those of **Ephesus** is this: *That they had abandoned their first love*, that is, that they did not remain in the zeal for which they were praised by the **Lord Christ** in the preceding verses.

This is a very remarkable thing. For is it not a wonder that the **Lord Christ**, here like a **Bridegroom** who had set his love upon his **Bride**, stands and complains about the lack of our love toward Him? Why does the **Lord Christ** care about our love? What need does He have of us? Everything, after all, comes from Him. What a singular love is this then?

If a mighty **Prince**, and an exceptionally handsome one at that, set his love upon a lowly girl whom he had raised from the dust to a very high state, and complained about the lack of her love: would that not be a sign of great love? Should that not work upon her heart, and awaken a reciprocal love, and stir it up? What kind of hearts do we have then, if we are not moved by this to the awakening of our love for **Christ**, when we have fallen away from it?

But let us look a bit more closely at the words of our **Text** themselves; in order to understand them well, we must briefly explain these deep things.

### Christ’s Warning, to prevent [the loss of love]

First: what the nature is of that affection or passion of the heart called love.

Second: what the first love of Christians is.

Third: what the leaving of that first love is.

<margin>What love is.</margin>
Concerning the first point: Love is an affection, or a passion of the heart, which, by stirring the heart with a friendly inclination toward someone, sets all the powers of a person in motion to seek and pursue their well-being, favor, and goodwill, *Matthew* 6:24. It is a completely sweet and powerful passion of the heart; love makes all the powers of a person precious to itself and leads them through a pleasant compulsion—or rather, through a willing-making constraint—into the soft bonds and cords of kindness, wherever it wishes. This is evident in a lover: there is no trouble too great, no labor too heavy that he does not gladly and willingly undertake to promote the well-being and favor of his beloved. We see a shadow of this in greedy people and in pleasure-seekers: they spare neither effort nor cost to obtain that which their heart desires. See then, this is the nature and the quality of love. When a person’s love is placed upon the Lord Christ, then that love is in its right element, for the Lord Christ is love itself, 1 *John* 4:8, and the Son of love, *Colossians* 1:13, more so than Cupid <note>The author contrasts the pagan Greek god of desire with the divine, sacrificial love of Christ.</note>. Then all our powers go toward Him and are kindly led through a free-willing constraint into His obedience, to seek and pursue His honor and His favor above all else.

<margin>What the first love is.</margin>
Now, the first love spoken of here

<column-break/>

is the heartfelt affection that we placed upon our Bridegroom, Christ, when we were first converted to Him; when our eyes were first opened by conversion to see not only the exceptional beauty and majesty of Christ, but also His benevolence toward us. Indeed, it is when we first came to see that He loved us so exceptionally that He—being so beautiful in Himself—gave Himself up for us, poured out His precious heart’s blood for us, and that He, like a Blood-Bridegroom <note>original: "Bloet-Bruydegom." A term used in Dutch pietism to emphasize that Christ won His "bride" (the Church) through His own blood and suffering.</note>, laid down His life to redeem us and to betroth us to Himself. He died a cursed death for us to deliver us from eternal death, and to provide us with eternal life and a glorious marriage. Behold that heartfelt reciprocal love <note>original: "weerliefde," meaning a responsive or returned love.</note> which we placed upon Christ when our eyes were first opened to see this great love of His toward us; the reciprocal love which leaped upward in our (otherwise cold and troubled) hearts toward the Lord Jesus, after He had first shone upon and warmed our hearts through the powerful brilliance—indeed, the fiery glow—of His great and Heavenly love toward us. This reciprocal love (for love awakens love, just as one fire ignites another) is what the Lord Christ calls here the First Love, by way of excellence, <term>the first love</term> <note>original Greek: "τὴν ἀγάπην τὴν πρώτην" (tēn agapēn tēn prōtēn).</note>. This manner of speaking, according to the phrasing of Scripture, signifies that which is of singular excellence and preeminence in its kind, as in *Luke* 15:22, <term>the best robe</term> <note>original Greek: "τὴν στολὴν τὴν πρώτην" (tēn stolēn tēn prōtēn), literally "the first robe," meaning the finest or best garment.</note>. So these words also look upon the occasion of

<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion on the nature of "first love," moving from a definition of its intensity to an explanation of what it means to "abandon" or lose that initial spiritual fervor, specifically referencing the biblical address to the Church of Ephesus in the Book of Revelation.</meta>

# Christ’s Warning to Prevent Falling

...entirely beautiful and pleasing in the eyes of God; it is the exertion of all our powers in the service of Christ. Where this first love is, there all the things of Christ are performed in the very best way. One does not withhold bread from friends. <note>Original: "Men slupt geen broodt voor de vrienden." An old Dutch idiom meaning one should not be stingy or hesitant when serving those they love.</note> Christ’s work is the principal work there, and for that purpose, one's strengths are especially exerted. If one must worship the Lord Christ, love awakens all powers to do it well; if one must hear the word of Christ, it is the same. Yes, first love is like the weight on a clock, which sets all the wheels in motion. And see, this is the nature of the first love spoken of here, which those of Ephesus are testified to have abandoned. Therefore, it also remains to be examined what it means to "abandon one’s first love."

<margin>
What the abandonment of our first love is.
</margin>

To abandon one’s first love means here not to cast away all love for the Lord Jesus entirely and completely—as the wanton <note>Original: "dertele." In the 17th-century context of 1 Timothy 5, this refers to widows who have lost their spiritual focus and become self-indulgent.</note> widows are testified to have nullified their first faith, *1 Timothy 5, verse 12*—but rather to let that youthfulness, that vigor, that strength, that readiness and intention of the love of Christ (which we had when we first set our love upon Christ) decline and grow sluggish. It means that one no longer devotes oneself to the things of Christ with such ready zeal or with such earnestness as one formerly did.

Now, that the "abandonment of first love" must be understood in this way here is evident from the whole logic of our text, since those of Ephesus are not condemned here as people who were no longer Christians, or who had fallen away entirely and completely from the Christian faith.

For the candlestick <note>A reference to Revelation 2, where the "candlestick" or lampstand represents the presence and recognition of a local church by God.</note> was still among them; Christ still walked among

<column-break/>

them; He still held the star—the Angel <note>Original: "Engel." In the context of the Book of Revelation, the "angels" of the seven churches are traditionally interpreted as the bishops or leaders of those congregations.</note> of this Congregation—in His hand. There were also still some Christian virtues to be found among them, and so they could also be raised up again through repentance. This cannot happen to those who have entirely and completely fallen away, *Hebrews 6, verses 4, 5.* Thus, they are not accused here of having entirely and completely fallen away from the Christian faith—which indeed never happens to those who have once intentionally loved the Lord Christ, *Romans 8, verses 37, 38, 39.*

Rather, they are accused that their love for the Lord Christ had greatly declined; that they no longer performed the things of Christ with such zeal and earnestness as they had done previously; that they did not continually press forward with such effort, labor, patience, foresight, and diligence to maintain and perform the things of Christ as they had indeed begun to do at the start. Therefore, they are also exhorted hereafter to "do their first works" again.

And because this had happened to them in the midst of all the good means to the contrary—and since they ought to have grown in their love in every way rather than decreased—they are therefore testified against. It was not that their first love had slipped away from them through some heavy accident, but that they themselves had abandoned it. Namely, they had allowed their hearts to be won over too much by the love of the world and of earthly things. Through this, the love of Christ in them was cooled and declined, so that it happened through their own fault, whereas they otherwise [would have]...

# CHAPTER III.

### That the abandonment of our first love for Christ is a most lamentable sin.

<margin>To abandon one’s first love is a lamentable sin.</margin>
Indeed, it is a blameworthy and lamentable thing to slacken in one's zeal for God; it is a pitiful sin to cool in one's love for Christ and for Christian contemplations. We see here in our text how seriously the Lord Christ—who is usually so friendly—takes this: He even threatens to remove the lampstand <note>Original: "candelaer." In the Book of Revelation, the lampstand represents the church's presence and divine favor; its removal signifies the end of that congregation's spiritual standing.</note> if they do not repent, verse 5, and testifies enough that their zeal against the deceiving spirits will no longer be able to excuse them in this case, verse 6. Nevertheless, He does not charge them with being otherwise defiled by gross and abominable sins; He does not accuse them of false doctrine, nor of recklessness of life, but only that they were very faint in His service. This very thing He takes quite seriously; this very thing He cannot forget; this very thing He wishes to address in such a way that if they do not quickly

<column-break/>

repent of it, He will punish them for it and take away their lampstand.

<margin>For then we slacken entirely in the service of Christ.</margin>
And that is quite justified: for first, the defect is very great in itself: to abandon one's first love is to weaken in that <term>Holy Earnestness</term> <note>Original: "H. ernst." This refers to a deep, sincere, and active devotion that drives all religious practice.</note> which must be present within us in all our worship, since we are bound to serve the Lord our God with all our hearts and all our strength. It is to loosen those holy bonds by which all our powers are exerted in the service of the Lord, without which all our service to the Lord is a loathing. Thus, it is also a pervasive sin, a sin that spreads itself over all our contemplations and causes them all to be lukewarm and faint: our prayers, the hearing of God’s word, our acts of charity <note>Original: "hantreykinge." Literally "reaching out a hand," referring to alms-giving or helping those in need.</note>, and all that we do in the service of our Lord Christ. The <term>pith</term> <note>Original: "keest." A 17th-century term for the kernel, marrow, or essential core of something.</note>, the youth, and the strength of it all completely fall away as soon as one begins to abandon one’s first love. This is indeed a most pitiful thing and a lamentable matter: for truly, for whom shall we keep the utmost capacity of our strength if we do not offer it to Christ? For whom shall we exert our powers if we forsake and let them loose before the Lord Christ? Is there anywhere a Lord or Master who has more right over our strength, who has better deserved it at our hands? Are we not also explicitly accepted into the service of the Lord on this condition: that we should grow up like newborn babies in the love of Christ (*1 Peter 2:2*) and that we should indeed grow and increase in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ (*2 Peter 3:18*)? # Christ’s Warning, to prevent

[the children of] God sometimes very miserably falling away from their first love. Now, these causes are, according to our present understanding, primarily three.

<margin>When they neglect to exhort themselves every day, and to awaken themselves to the love of Christ.</margin>
**First:** the neglect of exhorting oneself every day, according to the advice of the *Apostle*, as long as it is called "today," so that one is not hardened through the deceitfulness of sin. *Hebrews 3, verse 13.* See, in the demonstration of our love for *Christ*, and in the contemplation of the things of *Christ*, we are going as if against the current of our natural and fleshly affections and desires; unless it be that we habituate ourselves to constantly awaken our hearts again and again to the service of *Christ*, we naturally drift backward. This first love is like the weight on a clock <note>original: "uerwerck"; the author uses the mechanical weight of a seventeenth-century clock to illustrate how spiritual fervor naturally sinks unless regularly "wound up."</note>; it sinks downward of its own accord (being pressed by the flesh) unless we pull it up again, otherwise it eventually hits the bottom. Indeed, the devil, the world, and our own flesh all join forces to completely extinguish or at least cool our Love for *Christ*, unless it be that we exhort ourselves daily; that we daily wind our hearts up toward Heaven and toward *Christ* through holy consolations, as if by a windlass <note>original: "wint-ase," a mechanical device like a winch used for lifting heavy loads.</note>; that we indeed daily overlook our situation, that we pay attention to it and give heed to what has fallen away or become damaged <note>original: "ontramponeert," a term meaning out of order or broken down.</note> in us through any deceitfulness of sin, in order to repair it; otherwise, we eventually fall into such a state of disarray that there is no more helping it. From this neglect comes a great falling away, and because we are by nature very unwilling to exhort ourselves every day, to demand an account, and to set our affairs right before the Lord, so it

<column-break/>

happens easily that our affairs regress and our love cools.

**Secondly:** the imprudent or immoderate use of our *Christian* freedom regarding earthly and physical things, against the warning of the *Apostle* in *Galatians 5, verse 13.* This also cools the first love of *Christians* exceedingly much; for see, it is written: friendship with the World is enmity with God. *James 4:4, 1 John 2:15.* And when a *Christian* person imprudently and abundantly gives themselves over to the use of otherwise lawful worldly things, their heart is thereby gradually won over more and more to the love of worldly things; and the more sweetness and taste they find therein, the more their heart begins to cling to it, and consequently, to be led away from the love of *Christ*. And thus it happens that in the measure that the love of the World becomes strong in us, the love of *Christ* in us slackens; for see, there is a secret distracting power in the things of the World, through which the hearts of men (who do not act prudently with worldly things) are gradually led away from *Christ* toward the vanity of life. It is not easily expressed what it is, but the results prove it; experience teaches it inarguably; one sees it clearly, that in the measure that *Christians* let their heads hang toward the world, their hearts are stolen away and led away from *Christ*.

Now, because many people do not pay attention to this secret distracting power which is in worldly things, many are very miserably deceived and come

### The Decay of the Church of Ephesus.

...to fall away from their first love, because they look only upon the most beautiful and pleasant things of the world: and merely occupying themselves with such worldly business as is not evil in itself, but permissible (for it is of such circumstances that we speak here), they are gradually and unexpectedly won over to a great love of this world. <margin>This happens when one does not habituate oneself—when finding sweetness in the things of this life—to notice that Christ gives them to us, and that we must therefore love Christ all the more.</margin>
Now, if someone here should ask: what does it mean to use the otherwise permissible things of this world "imprudently," <note>The author uses "onvoorsichtelyk" (imprudently/unwisely) to describe a lack of spiritual caution.</note> through which—as if by so many thorns and thistles—the love of Christ is choked in our hearts? This is so that our hearts might be set even more upon the Lord Christ (who is the fountain of all those good things) than upon those things themselves.

<column-break/>

-fit in our labor and trade, or a singular sweet delight in our wife and children; if we do not then, on such occasions, lift up our hearts to Christ and recognize Him to be the fountain and the giver of all those good things, and even of that sweetness and delight which we find in them; then our hearts remain hanging upon those worldly things. Our love is gradually led away from Christ toward those things, and so we cool in our first love. But on the contrary, if we use these things prudently, and take occasion from them (as was just said) to constantly notice the friendliness of Christ and His goodness toward us, and consequently take occasion to stir up our hearts more and more to consider what might please Him as a sign of gratitude, then our love for Christ would be even more ignited thereby, and we would be preserved in our first love.

They, not doing this, allow the things of this world to gradually weaken the first love of Christ more and more; just as the good seed is gradually and imperceptibly oppressed and choked by the weeds, the thorns, and the thistles. *Luke 8, verse 14.*

# The Decline of the Church of Ephesus

...[hidden from the] wise and understanding and had revealed the same to the little children.
<margin>Matthew 11:25</margin>
So also experience teaches that very little-esteemed, clever minds according to the world, also happen to be zealous Christians according to the Spirit (1 Corinthians 1:25 etc.). The genuine love of Christ, and the continuous zeal for the things of Christ proceeding from it, is a matter which is not esteemed among the worldly-wise; indeed, it is entirely resisted and despised. Yes, one generally sees that worldly discretion consumes all Divine zeal, and that political considerations <note>original: "Politijcke consideratien" — in this era, this referred to worldly prudence, social status, and "playing the game" of society rather than just government politics.</note> almost swallow up all Divine reflections in all those who give themselves over to them. And still these people, with all their wisdom, will not even once notice that God catches them in their own wisdom, and that they are also those (as long as they act so) to whom it applies what the Lord Christ testifies: that God the Heavenly Father has hidden the things of His Kingdom (which alone can help us to salvation) from the wise and understanding.

<margin>When they fall into some great sin through poor oversight.</margin>
Lastly, Divine love is also cooled very much whenever the Christian person, through any kind of poor oversight <note>original: "quadelycke toeficht" — refers to a lack of spiritual watchfulness or negligence in guarding one's soul.</note>, falls into some great sin, as is evident in David in Psalm 32. For sin is of an entirely hostile nature against Christ, and where it can once become strong, it devastates the heart quite miserably and numbs all lovely feeling and movement toward Christ. A great sin is like a heavy blow <note>original: "bolslach" — literally a strike from a ball; used here to mean a stunning or concussive spiritual impact.</note> which so dazes a person in their spiritual life that they are, for that time, entirely useless for all reflections on Divine love. And see, these are the causes of the cooling...

<column-break/>

...of Divine love; against which every true Christian, who places all his joy in his love for Christ, must take special care to watch, if he does not wish to cool therein and be deprived of his comfort.

# Warning of Christ, to Prevent the Cooling of Love
<meta>catchword: first-</meta>

Thereby it is found that the love for the temporary profits of sin is stronger in us than the love of Christ, which at first had the upper hand over us and must always be maintained if it is to go well with us.

And we gladly set forth this general rule here, both for simple hearts <note>The "simple-hearted" (Dutch: eenvoudige herten) refers to humble, sincere believers who may be prone to self-doubt or anxiety about their spiritual standing.</note>—who are easily led to believe by their spiritual enemy that they have fallen from their first love <note>A reference to Revelation 2:4, where the Church of Ephesus is told "you have forsaken the love you had at first."</note> when it is not actually so—to help them against their despondency, as well as to timely warn the false-hearted <note>The "false-hearted" (Dutch: valshertige) describes those who are hypocritical or complacent, believing they are righteous simply because they avoid scandalous sins.</note> against their vanity. For these people, as long as they do not act completely crudely, immediately imagine that nothing at all can be said against their Christian conduct. For this is certain and sure: that even if a person does not find themselves in gross sins, yet if they do not daily and sincerely humble themselves over their shortcomings, the love of Christ is not in them; it is certainly not fresh and blooming in them. On the other hand, even if the Christian person still finds themselves burdened daily with many weaknesses, if they nevertheless sincerely humble themselves daily over them, mourn over them, struggle against them, and guard against them to their utmost ability, then indeed the love of Christ is still fresh and blooming in them.

See, where it goes thus, there the first love of Christ has already cooled very much. 

For every Christian knows that when the love of Christ was first poured out into their heart, they sought to please the Lord Christ in all His institutions; their heart went toward Christ when they prayed or when they heard God's word. If they found themselves sluggish, that affected them; they blamed themselves for it, they would not give in to it, they set themselves against it—for they well knew that their labor in the service of Christ could not please the Lord Christ nor be well-pleasing unless they did it from the heart, with all their strength. Unless their powers were warmed and ignited by the heat of the love of Christ, they were not at peace until they had brought it to that point. This is evident from all those pitiful complaints that the children of God otherwise make when they feel that things are no longer going that way for them (Isaiah 63:17 <note>original: "Esa. 63. vers. 17" — Isaiah 63:17: "O Lord, why do you make us wander from your ways and harden our hearts so we do not revere you?"</note>). # The Downfall of the Church of Ephesus

...[that your] first love has cooled.

<margin>
If one does not want to endure, or be found accountable, concerning the word of admonition for one's faults.
</margin>

**Secondly:** when one cannot bear nor endure that someone should come to faithfully rebuke us for our failings and defects, but instead takes it poorly and begins to speak up for, excuse, and gloss over those failings and defects. This is a great sign that one has fallen from one's first love: for where the love of Christ is fresh and blooming, there it makes us hate sin, *Psalm 97:10*. "You who love the Lord, hate evil" (says the *Psalmist*). So it is that the children of God, out of their love for Christ, long and wish that they might be rebuked and corrected for those defects that still remain in them, and which they themselves cannot detect, so that they might improve them. In this way, they become even more pleasing to the Lord Christ, removing from their path everything that might in any way displease Him. See on this *Psalm 141:5* and *Psalm 19:13–14*. Whenever a person falls into such a track that he cannot endure anyone speaking against his sin, he shows clearly enough that the "usefulness" of sin lies closer to his heart than the love of Christ. For although it is true that his sin is like a thorn in the side of the Spirit of the Lord Christ—so that He cannot rest, *Ephesians 4:30*—these people nevertheless will not allow their sin to be disturbed. Thus, sin is indeed the "beloved" of their soul, whom they cannot tolerate being disturbed or awakened. *Song of Solomon 2:7* <note>Original: "Cantic. 2. Vs. 7." This verse in the Song of Solomon—"Do not arouse or awaken love until it so desires"—is often used allegorically in this period to describe the soul's rest or, in this negative case, its spiritual lethargy.</note>. For there is no greater sign of love for a thing than that one cannot endure anyone speaking harshly of it. Whoever thus excuses sin, loves sin; he now prefers the embraces of sin over lying down in the ar-

<column-break/>

-ms of Christ. When someone commands that no noise should be made, but to be quiet, and puts out the candle and draws the curtains, is that not indeed a sign that he intends to go to sleep? He who then likewise prepares himself to lie down quietly and undisturbed in sin, what does that prove other than that he wants to lie there sleeping peacefully, even though it grieves the Spirit of Christ? How could this happen if the first love for Christ had not cooled beforehand?

<margin>
If one indeed endures the admonition, and yet pursues no improvement because of it.
</margin>

**Thirdly:** when one bears it well enough that our sins and defects are pointed out and rebuked, but takes no care that it might produce any fruit in the heart—so that the admonition of the Lord, like a healing medicine, might spread through our inner strength and take root in our thoughts, words, and works, *Psalm 119:11*. True Christians are accustomed (when the warmth of Divine love is with them) to take the matter to heart and give their souls no rest until they have perceived the power of Divine admonitions in their souls, leading to the awakening of holy contemplations. And truly, this is the only thing in this case that proves some Divine love is still in us. Otherwise, if one endures the rebuke but then makes no further effort, it is certainly a sign that our first love has fallen away. For there are people of such a comfortable and slow-moving <note>Dutch: "voetvoerighen," describing a sluggish or passive temperament.</note> nature who can endure even sharp rebukes very calmly; yet they are also of the mind that if the admonition is to work any improvement in their deeds, [it must do so on its own]...
