# Christ's Warning, to Prevent Failure

...[to act] <note>The text likely refers to people doing good deeds for outward appearance or out of habit rather than love.</note>; they may do so, but that they themselves would then later see to it that it might work toward improvement—that is the least of their heart's thoughts. These people are far enough from the fresh, Divine love that ought to be in us all. Those who are so disposed may freely know that, even in the best light, they have already cooled significantly in the love of Christ.

<margin>If one can digest and swallow down one's daily failings and faults without being saddened or troubled by them.</margin>

**Fourthly**, and finally: when one can digest and swallow down one's daily failings and faults without much effort or disgust, without being remorseful or troubled by them; but instead, one goes about freely and unburdened, as if there were nothing there over which one ought to be saddened and humbled. This is also a very bad sign of the weakening of the first love for Christ. For whenever a Christian has their love fresh for the Lord Christ, it grieves them greatly that they cannot serve their Lord Christ better. Oh! That they see they still stumble in many things, misstep in many things, and catch themselves doing so—that makes them feel overwhelmed, just as a loving **Bride** would trouble herself that she was still so clumsy that she did many things incorrectly and backward for her **Bridegroom**. This made the Apostle complain so piteously in *Romans 7 verse 24*: *O wretched man that I am, who shall deliver me from the body of this death!* <note>original: "Ick ellendigh mensche, wie sal my verlossen van het lichaem deses doodts!"</note> and David in *Psalm 119 verse 5*: *O that my ways were directed to keep your statutes!* <note>original: "och dat mijne wegen gherichtet werden, om uwe insettingen te bewaren!"</note>

And see, these are the causes and workings of this sin—namely, the desertion of the first love—by which the ugliness of it can also be more and more recognized.

### CHAPTER VI.

->Application of all the preceding, containing a sorrowful complaint over the desertion of our first love, with an earnest awakening to improve it.<-

<margin>Complaint regarding how we, like those of Ephesus, have deserted our first love.</margin>

Would to the Lord God that the complaint which the Lord Christ makes here—concerning the fact that people had weakened in the first love they used to bear for Him—only affected those of Ephesus. But oh, poor alas! This accusation also applies to us; we, we also have a great hand in this offense. There was a time for us once: when we also, with toil and patience, with labor and expense, with love and zeal, observed the things of Jesus Christ; but that has now mostly vanished.

<margin>How great the love was in the beginning of the Reformation.</margin>

There was a time once when people risked goods and blood for the sake of the Gospel <term>Euangelium; the message of the New Testament</term>; when people wanted—yes, not only to have the Book of God in their own houses, but also to have it daily in their hands and read it, even though there was great peril involved. There was a time once when people would follow the preaching of God's Word and the gathering of the believers in **forests and hedges** <note>This refers to the *hagepreken* or "field preachings," clandestine Protestant services held outdoors to avoid persecution by Catholic authorities.</note>, even if it had to be done with great toil, discomfort, and danger. There was a time once when people left house and home, father and mother, and everything, and went wandering in foreign lands to follow the Gospel. There was a time once when people kept such good household order that the little children were catechized, and holy prayers were offered to God daily with the whole household, even though it was very much hated in the neighborhood. There was a time once that as soon as one had learned anything from the Word...

### The Downfall of the Congregation of Ephesus

...to proceed further, to prove that many among us have also fallen from our first love, and that the complaint of Christ <note>original: "Christi"; referring to Revelation 2:4, "Yet I hold this against you: You have forsaken the love you had at first."</note> also applies to us; for as we heard in the beginning, things used to go quite differently—indeed, things used to go much better among us—so then this is also a most lamentable matter, a grievous sin.

<margin>Therefore, every one of us ought to test ourselves to see if we are not also guilty of this transgression.</margin>
But if the abandonment of our first love is such a great sin, such a lamentable matter, and also as common as we have now understood, then we must rightly test ourselves to see if this defect has not penetrated into our own selves in particular. Let everyone then examine their own self, their household, their circle of associates <note>original: "Collegie," referring to a professional or social group or a board of elders/officials</note>, and all those entrusted to them. See and learn if you now take the warnings of the Lord regarding moderation, justice, and godliness <note>original: "Godtsalicheydt"</note> as much to heart as you used to do in the past. Note whether you have not become puffed up in the pride and pomp of clothing, or in the excess of banquets. See also if you now use more deception or greed in your trade and business, doing things that are not quite honorable, than you used to do when you first joined God's holy Congregation. Check if you have begun to leave behind some holy exercises that you used to practice before; whether you do not neglect to admonish yourself every day, and furthermore, whether you cannot bear it when others admonish you—or at least, that you seek no improvement because of it, but simply let it all pass by.

Oh, if it stands thus with you! (Setting aside for now those who actually oppose such zeal, who certainly need no further conviction

Can you remember that you used to have such and such holy stirrings frequently in your heart, and have they now vanished? That you used to have such and such fervent exercises in your household, and are those now neglected? Or are they merely performed out of habit, just to keep up appearances? Then it truly stands miserably with you. If you, being a man of standing and authority, used to be moved by the love of Christ to apply your power against sin, to call it out—and do you now think that to be too much trouble or a task that brings too much resentment? Then surely Satan <note>original: "Sathan"</note> has come too close to you and has cooled the love of Christ in you. Truly, your state is very pitiful.

Or perhaps it stands thus with you: that up to this hour you have never had a sensible love for the Lord Jesus <note>original: "Jesum"</note>, though you still give yourself out to be a Christian; then you must also know that your situation is very wretched. For if those who merely slacken somewhat in the love of Christ are in a bad way, in what a miserable state must those be who have never borne any true love for Christ?

Therefore, seeing as it is such a lamentable matter to slacken in the love of Christ, and yet so common, we must also consider ourselves warned to be on our guard with all our might against falling from our first love, and to keep ourselves in the love of Christ. This is entirely necessary...

# Christ’s Warning to Prevent Falling Away

...[right?] <note>The text begins mid-sentence from the previous page.</note> — this is entirely just.

Is not the first love <note>A reference to Revelation 2:4, describing the initial, fervent zeal of a believer.</note> which we bear toward Christ the strength of our soul, by the help of which we are strengthened to perform the service of Christ and of our God most joyfully? Should it not then rightly grieve us, and affect us deeply, that this strength should decay in us, by which we must lead our Christian life? Should it not grieve us that this light—through our poor oversight—should go out within us, the very light by which we must see to walk in the way of life? Is it also not the Lord Jesus Christ who has done all good things for us, and still does? How then shall we not rather cling to him than to the World, which has never done us any good? Is it not the Lord Jesus Christ who has brought you forward, brought you thus far, and made you so rich and powerful—if indeed you are rich and powerful? And will you then, for the sake of those things which he has given you, cease to love him, and let your heart hang upon those vain things, and abandon him who gave them? That would indeed be quite wrongly done, and a very unjust matter.

If you would now also gladly see how unjust it is that any Christian person should abandon their first love for Christ, and also guard against such in yourselves, then know that much could be said on that. However, that we frequently and earnestly reflect upon all the beautiful and desired things that are in Christ Jesus is a powerful means for this, as we have explained elsewhere.

Indeed, their own consciences and hearts can sufficiently testify to this, for those who have thus fallen...

But, whatever such people might be inclined to do or not to do, we surely—who also would not wish to abandon our **first love**, or finding that we have in some way grown cold in it, would gladly be re-awakened—we, I say, must surely be willing to be warned about this. We must allow ourselves to be moved by this: that, since there is such a very secret distracting power in worldly things to cool the love of **Christ** within us, we should accustom ourselves to see to it that we conduct ourselves with all caution regarding the things of this world. We must always be on our guard, so that we are not led astray from the love of **Christ**. Therefore, when a wedding occurs, or a journey, or a commission <term>deputatie: a formal assignment or representative role</term>, or any business in which much is at stake and great profit or loss is to be made, or anything similar, we must then truly watch ourselves with special care. We should always fear that we might be harmed by these things. And to that end, we must once and for all firmly resolve within ourselves that we will follow or pursue no worldly things further than the love of **Christ**—without its harm or cooling—can allow. Indeed, we must make all our pleasures, profits, and all the honor and reputation we might have in the world give way to the

See, this must stand firm with us if we are to be preserved from falling away from our first love. Yet little attention is paid to this, and therefore the love of **Christ** grows so very cold in many hearts.

People think: luxury and pleasures are delightful; riches and goods are convenient; honor and reputation are of great power in the things of this life. Lured by that bait, they run headlong toward it "without looking for a door or a window" <note>A Dutch idiom meaning to act recklessly or without considering the consequences or the proper way out.</note>. Thus they only look at the outward appearance and the beauty of worldly things, and thereby they are ignited with great love for the things of the world. They do not even notice that beneath that bait is a hook; that there is indeed a secret distracting power in the things of the world to make us abandon the love of **Christ**, if we do not proceed cautiously. They do not wish to notice this, and so they run toward the world, swallowing up worldly things—the pleasures, profits, and the reputation of the world—with great greed, and so entangle themselves in a great cooling of their first love.

Indeed, this folly is constantly committed by those **wise in the ways of the world** regarding the things of **Christ**, upon which their eternal welfare depends. They perform their Christian duties (as matters arise): they go to Church, to the **Lord’s Supper**, and outwardly perform the things of Christ alongside others. But beyond that, they do not even notice how they fare, nor do they seriously consider what they have gained or lost, or whether they have regressed or advanced through their religious practices. And so they continue from one week to the next without ever properly examining the **book of their conscience**. This is a folly greater than can be imagined, especially since the soul is better than the body, **Heaven** better than the earth, and the things of the **Kingdom of Christ** better than the things of this **world**.

Most certainly, our spiritual enemy has a hand in this. He is intent on keeping the hands of incautious people full of work from all sides, seeking to occupy them so that they have neither time, nor effort, nor heart, nor mind, nor desire to ever properly notice how it might stand with their poor soul, or whether it is going backward or forward. Indeed, the **Devil** constantly piles on more work and entangles people so that they fall into great spiritual arrears <note>A term for debt or falling behind in one's obligations; here used for a soul's neglect of God.</note> before they are even aware of it. And once he has brought it to the point that their own **conscience** begins to testify to them

<column-break/>

that their affairs do not stand very well before **God**, they become even more reluctant to reflect upon their state. Just like reckless traders who, realizing they are deep in debt, have no desire to set their books in order but let everything run into a mess, thinking it is best to "fish in troubled waters" <note>An old proverb meaning to seek personal gain or find excuses within a chaotic or confused situation.</note>.

Through this, **Godlessness** breaks in like a sea. This is why so many Christians are found who have fallen completely behind in their souls, who possess nothing but a broken state, lead a completely unformed life, and conduct un-Christian business. This must then be improved if things are to go better for us. We must accustom ourselves to admonishing ourselves every day, and frequently reflecting on our **first love**.

See, the human heart has received a power from **God** to look inward and to take knowledge of its own state: the eye of the body cannot see itself, but the soul can do so. Thus, the human heart also has many depths and turnings (**Isaiah 57 verse 17**), but there is no better nor more wholesome turning of the heart than when a person "comes to himself," like the **Prodigal Son** (**Luke 15 verse 17**) and begins to seriously consider from what height he has fallen in **Adam** <note>The author refers here to "Original Sin," the theological belief that all humanity "fell" from a state of grace through the first man, Adam.</note>, and through his own reckless and active course of life. **Reason:** Because the repentance spoken of here aims at the improvement of our own heart, and consequently of our entire person, just as the word implies and as the Apostle explains it when speaking of this repentance in *2 Corinthians 7 verses 10 and 11*. Now, it is also certain and sure, as the Lord Jesus Christ
<margin>For we can do nothing good until our heart is improved.</margin>
testifies to us: That the tree must first be made good before it can bear any good fruit. *Matthew 12 verse 33; Titus 1 verse 15.* As long as our heart is still evil and filthy, the lovely and pure love of Christ cannot thrive therein; nor can any good works flow from it, in which the flowering youthfulness of our renewed love for Christ must reveal itself. See, our hearts and our own persons are like the **instruments** and **tools** through which we must do all things—through which we love, and through which we perform works of love. Thus, if our own heart is filthy and corrupt, and if the tools (with which we have to work) are of no use at all, then it is also impossible for our work to be of any use; just as if someone wished to work with a sore hand that is full of pustules and sores. The heart must therefore first be good before its affections, its love, and its works can be good.
<margin>Herein is discovered the great folly of those who still call themselves [Christians].</margin>
From this wise counsel of Christ, and from this prudent management in the improvement of things which Christ prescribes to us, we learn to notice the great folly of many people who, without paying any attention to their heart in order to practice the 

<column-break/>

improvement of it, think
<margin>on the improvement of their lives, and pay no attention to the improvement of their hearts and minds.</margin>
that they will immediately be able to love Christ well and do good works, if they only intend to set their hand to them. Whereas the truth is that they can do nothing good, nor love Christ rightly, until their heart is improved and purified through true repentance.

Nevertheless, many do not wish to acknowledge this; they do not wish to take any trouble to have their hearts improved through true repentance and faith. For they strongly convince themselves that whatever might still need improving in them—even if their works are of little value—nevertheless their heart is very good, and that it is not their heart's fault that they do not manage their affairs better.

Thus, even while they do evil, they still imagine that they themselves are good; though their life is evil, they still persuade themselves that their heart is good. Thus, when they engage in drunkenness, fornication, or deception, they certainly admit that their conduct is very evil and of no use at all, but nevertheless they will not admit that they themselves are evil and of no value. They do not even want to notice that they must not only see to the improvement of those evil works, but also get their own heart improved, where the wickedness actually resides. For truly, neither they nor their works are of any use, and to them applies what the Prophet says: *their course is evil, and their power is not right.* *Jeremiah 23 verse 10.* But because they do not want to pay attention to this, and do not want to follow the counsel of Christ to be diligent above all else in getting their own heart and mind improved, therefore nothing they do is of any value.

<margin>2. The loveliness of Christ.</margin>
Secondly, we must also behold with the eyes of faith the loveliness of our Lord Jesus Christ, just as it is presented to us in the Gospel, and there we shall find that the Lord Jesus Christ alone is the one who can deliver us from hideous sin (*Matt. 1:21, Acts 4:12*). He alone can still the wrath of God, which sin has quickly ignited (*1 Thess. 1:10*). He restores the image of God, which was defiled in us by sin, and can deliver us from Hell and damnation (*Rom. 3:25*). He is indeed the most beautiful, the friendliest, and the most gentle (*Matt. 11:28*), and from Him flow (as from a living Fountain) all desired things (*John 1:16*). We are indeed never well, nor can we otherwise be saved or kept, except when we cling to Him and love Him (*Matt. 11:29-30*). See, these and many similar lovely things, which are revealed to us concerning the Lord Christ in the Gospel, we must observe with the eyes of faith. Thereby also our heart shall be so purified and improved that we, in good earnest, shall begin more and more to hate sin, which displeases Christ, and to gain a firm desire and inclination for all good works that well-please the Lord Christ.

...with the eyes of faith, to consider the vanity of all worldly things (for the sake of which we tend to grow sluggish in the love of Christ), just as we may perceive from the experience of our own lives. To this end, we must also open our eyes and notice how the joys of this world **are only like the crackling of thorns under a pot**, <note>original: "het gheluyt der doornen onder eenen pot" — A biblical metaphor from Ecclesiastes 7:6 meaning that worldly pleasure makes a lot of noise but burns out instantly, leaving only cold ashes.</note> which indeed make a great noise, but are immediately turned to ashes (*Ecclesiastes 7:6*). We must see that the riches of the world make themselves wings and fly away (*Proverbs 23:5*) from one person to another, from one city to another, and from one household or family to another. We must see that even the honor and reputation of this world flies away like a bird (*Hosea 9:11*), so that in one and the same year, the very same person has been seen in great honor and afterward in great shame and disgrace. Indeed, consider how it goes with all these things: they all perish with use, and we must soon be separated from them all by death, carrying nothing in the world away with us (*1 Timothy 6:7*). Truly, these same things shall only accompany us before the judgment of God to accuse us and help to damn us even deeper if we cling to them more than to Christ—if, for the sake of these idle, earthly, and perishable things, we leave Christ (as Demas did) and go to cling to the world (*2 Timothy 4:10*). <note>Demas was a companion of the Apostle Paul who eventually abandoned the ministry because he "loved this present world."</note> All this we must consider and contemplate with the eyes of faith, and through this, our heart and understanding shall be so purified

<column-break/>

and improved that where we previously thought these earthly things were something of substance, we shall now begin to esteem them very little. We will not hold even the best of them worthy of causing us to grow sluggish in the least in the love of Christ or in His holy service.

Certainly, the reason why many people do not love the Lord Jesus with all their heart—and why others do not love Him much at all, while they conversely cling so tightly to the world—is this: they have no wakeful eyes of faith to see how insignificant all earthly things are in comparison to the dignity of Christ. They are deceived by this. Otherwise, if they once came to notice that Christ is a thousand times better than the world, and that the least of the things belonging to Christ is better than that which is most highly esteemed in the world, they would surely conduct themselves quite differently. As Paul said (*Philippians 3:7–8*), who—if they are merely in their right senses and truly know the things of Christ—would want to exchange gold for copper?

<meta>This page continues the exhortation to the Ephesian church, arguing that God's original laws for church governance are timeless and adaptable to any size or political situation, much like the miraculous clothing of the Israelites in the wilderness.</meta>

# The Downfall of the Congregation of Ephesus

If you would truly demonstrate your first love upward toward God, then you must also resume your first fervent considerations and boldly put them into practice. You also need not fear that the first good Christian order—which you maintained in your congregation when you were still few in number—could not be practiced now that you are many. No; simply let your first love be fresh <note>The author uses "fresh" to mean a renewal of the original zeal or passion found in early converts.</note> in order to do your first works; that will arrange itself, and you will realize that my laws and ordinances, which I have given for the government of the congregation, proceeded from a Divine wisdom. Through that wisdom, I have so tempered them that they bow, arrange, and fit all sorts of congregations: rich or poor, large or small, in peace or in persecution. It is the case with brittle, mortal lawmakers that they cannot give laws, nor devise a kind of government and civil policy <note>original: "Politie"</note>, which might fit all sorts of people and all nations. But I am not so narrowly bound that I could not devise laws for my congregation and provide an order of government that would fit every circumstance of the congregations equally well. And since I well knew that my holy congregation here on earth would be gathered from all kinds of nations, under all kinds of states of people, under Kingdoms, and under free Republics; and that she would also be subject to many changes—now in prosperity, then in persecution and adversity; now large in number, then small—therefore I have also, according to my manifold wisdom, such...

<column-break/>

...laws, and order of government <note>original: "regieringhe"</note>, and of conduct, prescribed to my people, which can be used and practiced among all sorts of congregations, wherever they might be gathered. Yes, just as I knew how to make the clothes and shoes on the feet of my people Israel fit well in the desert, all that time that they had to struggle in that fearsome wilderness; and I made it so that the same clothes, as if they had grown with them, adapted themselves well, no matter what size or circumstance they were. <margin>Deuteronomy 8:4 <note>This verse refers to the miracle where the Israelites' clothing did not wear out during their forty years in the desert.</note></margin> So it is likewise now a light matter for me to establish such an order among my people in the spiritual realm, which fits well enough all their manifold changes to which they are subject in this desert world, and knows how to adapt itself rightly and appropriately.

It is then also nothing but a harmful invention, arising only from the wisdom of the flesh <note>A theological term for human reasoning that is not guided by the Holy Spirit.</note>, when people want to make others believe that my congregation will have to take up another fashion of government than she has already begun to use, whenever she shall become larger in number and possess greater prosperity and outward blessing. No, no; the order that I have once given must always be practiced. Search for it diligently in my word, and there you shall find a complete account. and just as you had begun well at first and had arranged yourself nicely according to my prescribed order—through which the Church <note>original: "Kercke"</note> was also greatly edified—but have now fallen away from that through poor oversight: so I exhort you now again to proceed thus, and to do your first works.

# Christ’s Warning to Forestall Judgment

and that is what the Lord threatens here: which was also no empty threat, for the outcome of the matter has shown that it struck those of Ephesus immediately. The Lampstand <note>The "Lampstand" represents the local church as a vessel of divine light; its removal signifies the end of that church's status as a true congregation.</note> was removed from its place there; and because they did not follow Christ’s counsel, so Christ’s punishment followed them, and they soon lost the prestige, the power, and the authority of a true church, and in the course of time, even the very form, the name, and everything else, being now taken over by the Turk <note>A historical reference to the Ottoman conquest of Ephesus, which the author views as the final fulfillment of the prophecy in Revelation.</note>.

<margin>The decline of zeal puts the Congregation of Christ in danger of falling from all its glory and from the light of the Spirit.</margin>
From this we must now learn: that the decline of zeal puts the Congregation of Christ in danger of falling from all its glory, of losing the presence of Christ, and consequently being deprived of the power of Christ, and the authority and dignity of a church of Christ. We see it here in our text; the Lord threatens it here to the fallen Christian people of Ephesus: and he does it too; he carries out his threat, and that most justly.

<margin>And that most justly.</margin>
For tell me, what is more reasonable than when the Lampstand no longer gives light—when indeed the stars and the lights that are placed upon it are darkened and extinguished by the Lampstand itself. That is to say: that those very people who still have some zeal about them, and would gladly see the "first works" <note>A reference to Revelation 2:5, "do the first works," meaning the works of love and faith performed at the beginning of their conversion.</note> performed by those who hold the management of the Church's power, are not heard, but rejected; that their zeal is effectively quenched. And so, those who ought to bring forward such lights so that they might shine for the benefit of the whole Congregation, instead seek to dampen and extinguish them; when, I say, the Lampstand, which

<column-break/>

ought to receive and display the lights, instead darkens and extinguishes them. What is more just then, than that the Lord Christ, the Master of the Congregation, should remove such a Lampstand from its place, and do away with such a Lampstand? Yea, what is more just, than when the Congregation of Christ (which formerly received the Lord Christ so very kindly in his members, that they did not count their own eyes or their lives too precious to lay down for the Lord Christ) begins in the course of time to become so familiar, so bold, and so arrogant toward the Lord Christ, that they treat him very poorly in his own house? They thrust him out of his own place (which is, by all rights, the best place in the house) and withhold from him his proper service (which is justly the best and the utmost we are capable of). On the contrary, they let various ungodly "Canaanites" enter the house, of whom it was prophesied that they would not be tolerated in the house of God (**Zechariah 14, Chapter 21**) and they endure many wicked notions there; they give those things the best place in the heart; they give them their utmost effort; they serve them with their best strengths. Dearly beloved, when the people of Christ begin to act in this way, what shall the Lord Christ do? Is it not just, since the Congregation of Christ so rudely begins to thrust the Lord Christ out of his own house through such scornful treatment—as if pushing him out by the shoulders—that he himself should be moved to wrath? And that according to his great dignity and power, he should shove such a Congregation from its place, enrage it, and take the Lampstand away from such a Congregation, and thus depart from it himself, withdrawing his presence...

### The Downfall of the Congregation of Ephesus

withdraw from her, and so take away at the same time his power and his authority? 1 Cor. 5 <note>The author refers to 1 Corinthians 5, which discusses the church's authority to discipline members; without Christ’s presence, the church loses the divine right to govern itself.</note>. Which then, when it occurs, results in no true Congregation remaining anymore; thus it is removed from its place.

Furthermore, consider the Congregation of Christ, which in former times valued all the things of Christ at the highest level, and *regarded all things as loss and dung* in comparison; she held it to be her greatest honor and glory that she was deemed worthy to preserve the holy Ordinances and institutions of Christ. But when that same congregation begins to despise the ordinances and institutions of Christ, to slacken his holy Discipline, to misuse his holy Baptism and holy Supper out of habit or *superstition*, to profane or violate his holy Day, to entirely neglect his holy household order, and to contemptuously ignore his commended moderation, righteousness, and godliness—in such a way that Christ is hardly noticed anymore.

For example: if there is a meal to be held, no one pays attention to what command Christ gives regarding it—that it should be done moderately, without detracting from Divine Service, and without excess or wantonness. If there is a garment to be made, one does not even consider what Christ says about it. If there is a dispute or quarrel to be settled, one does not wish to listen in that counsel to the gentleness and reconcilability that Christ teaches; instead, one repeatedly pushes the commands of Christ out of their place in these matters and refuses to give them their due place. Dearly beloved, if the Christian people (I say) begin to act in this way—if they thus push Christ’s institutions, ordinances, and commands out of their place—is it not only fair that the Lord Christ, in response, should remove their Lampstand from its place?

And so we may see that this threatened punishment fits the committed crime very precisely, and that it is a very just punishment, measuring out such a portion as was measured to him. Since they push the things of Christ out of their place, they are in turn pushed out of their own place.

<margin>Although it is a very heavy punishment.</margin>
But just as this punishment is very fair, so it is also very heavy; it is indeed surely the heaviest judgment that can come upon a people. For when the golden Lampstand, upon which the lights of God are placed—the lights of his holy Ordinances and institutions, the lights of his holy Children and Servants—is removed from its place, then the people are left in darkness and in the shadow of death. There they can no longer see how to walk upon the path of peace; there they must necessarily (like those who walk in the dark in unknown, dangerous places) stumble and bruise themselves at every turn, and finally fall into ruin. No greater plague than this can be imagined. Everyone realizes what hardship it causes a person's body when they must walk in the dark or do their business in the dark. Oh! If we had the slightest feeling for the soul, we would much more fear that spiritual darkness—walking there in the midst of the Devil's snares, and that without light, without a guide, and in the dark. What could be thought of as more terrifying?

# Christ's Warning, to Prevent [Judgment]

...it would be better for a people to be overwhelmed by their bitterest enemies than to lose this **Lampstand** <note>original: "Candelaer"; a reference to Revelation 2:5. In this context, it represents the light of the Gospel and the status of a true church.</note>. For when the yoke of our enemies presses upon us, yet we may still enjoy the light of God's **Gospel** <note>original: "Evangelium"</note>, then we have indeed torment of the body, but our souls are still visited by God. On the contrary, when one loses the light of the Gospel, no matter how much more luxury, better trade, or greater prosperity one has, the worse off one is: for then one walks carelessly and unremarked through a thousand delights toward eternal sorrow and Hellish damnation. But now it also stands that usually the Lampstand is not removed unless all matters of **Civil Governance** <note>original: "Politie"; referring here to the public order, administration, and social stability of a city</note> and outward government are also thrown into utter chaos, to the unspeakable distress of the inhabitants, as we have seen in some conquered cities.

And thus, in every way, the slack service that weak Christians offer to the Lord Christ brings very strict and sharp punishments. Thus we may see that this threatened punishment is indeed just, and also very great.

<margin>
From this it appears that all those who fall away from their zeal prepare the way for their own destruction.
</margin>

From this it follows now that all those prepare the way for their own destruction who abandon the love of Christ and treat the things of Christ lightly and push them aside. See, so it stands: If one undertakes to blow the love of Christ—and consequently the **Ordinances** <note>original: "Ordonnantien"; these are the specific rules and religious practices established by Christ for the church</note> and institutions of Christ—lightly into the wind and to push them aside, then the Lord Jesus Christ also wants to scatter such a **Congregation** <note>original: "Ghemeynte"</note> to all the winds, and shove it out of its place. Jeremiah 49:32.

<column-break/>

This also applies to private persons and actions: See, if you shove Christ out of your heart by treating his commandments lightly, the Lord Christ will erase your name from the book of life; if you push the commandment of Christ regarding **moderation** <term>the practice of avoiding excess in food, drink, and lifestyle as a religious duty</term> out of your house through pomp and parade in clothes and banquets, Christ will also push you out of your house through war, through plague, or through death. If you throw the commandment of Christ regarding righteousness behind your back and conduct an unrighteous trade, the Lord Christ will also throw you down and drive you out of all your trade and business through one plague or another, or through death. Oh! that people would consider this, that they would indeed pay attention to this—would they not then do better than they do now? If they thought: "To the degree that I act against the Commandments of Christ and push them aside, so I gradually push myself out of everything," would they not then see better with their eyes and observe the things of Christ better?

likely that he who should come to us in grace, with a rich blessing, and healing under his wings, Malachi 4, verse 2, that he (I say) should come to us with flaming fire to take vengeance? 2 Thessalonians 1, verse 8. They do not even remember that Christ here so explicitly testifies that he wishes to approach such people, and that he himself wishes to punish them heavily and devastate <note>original: "verwoelen" — to churn up, disturb, or ruin.</note> them. Oh, that man is so foolish and so willingly deceives himself in such weighty matters, and that he does not once notice that even though the Lord Christ is a friendly Lord to all those who seek and cling to him from the heart, he is nevertheless a jealous Judge and an avenger over all those who, under the Christian name, lead an un-Christian life; over those who follow not the counsel of his Spirit, but the lust of their flesh in their deeds; over those who would rather suffer being separated from Christ—whom they nonetheless call their dear Lord—than be separated from their beloved sins. Therefore, let such people let go of their boasting and learn here what a terrifying thing it is to go on in one's sins against all warnings: for such conduct rouses the Lord Christ himself, the Savior of mankind, against mankind, so that instead of saving, he wishes to condemn them all the more deeply, and [treats] them like filthy vessels that do not want to be cleansed,

# The Downfall of the Church of Ephesus

<margin>That we were faithfully warned of approaching punishments, and that not only with words.</margin>
We follow our own course: neither more nor less as if the message of Christ were only a wind spoken into the air, while He is nonetheless that great Lord who, through the breath of his lips, is able to strike down an entire land.
<margin>Isaiah 11:4</margin> <note>original: "Esa. 11. vs. 4." — This verse refers to the Messiah judging the earth with the "rod of his mouth."</note>
This threat also applies to us: that the Lord Christ shall indeed come quickly to destroy us if we do not quickly mend our ways. And it has truly been a miraculous grace of Christ until now that He has not snatched us away long before this—the day before the evening—after He has found us so many times, again and again, in our sins.

<margin>But also with deeds, and still we have not improved ourselves.</margin>
Yes, what is more: the Lord Christ has not only let us be warned of this through his word, but has also begun to warn us in deed and with his works. He has caused our land to shudder and tremble through the ambitious schemes of power-hungry men, as the proclamations of our Fasting and Prayer Days <note>Days of fasting and prayer were officially mandated by the Dutch government during times of war, plague, or political strife.</note> testified to us. But who, for that reason, has begun to prune the ambition in his own head, or begun to curtail his own thirst for honor? The Lord our God has, through our disagreements and differences, through our partiality and one-sidedness, placed the entire Church and the entire Land in great danger, so that while everyone pulled for the longest end <note>Dutch idiom: "om het langhste eynde trecken" — to compete for the best position or personal advantage at the expense of the whole.</note>, we would all have quickly fallen as a prey to our common enemy and lost everything. But who among us has, for that reason, let go of his petty grievances, his particular quarrels, partialities, and disagreements, his

<column-break/>

bitterness against this one or that one, whom he cannot tolerate? The Lord our God has—while we give ourselves over to great wantonness and excess—begun to restrict us in our trade and shortened our means in many ways: but who among us has for that reason in any way pruned and shortened his pomp and display, his excess and flightiness? The Lord Christ has caused many a brave Preacher, who previously addressed the people with zeal, to have their tongue (according to the threat in Ezekiel 3:26) cleave to the roof of their mouth, and through the pursuit of I know not what fleshly gain or profit, allowed them to fall away from their zeal and boldness: but who has therefore begun to fear that these were signs that the Candlestick <term>Candlestick: A biblical metaphor from Revelation 1:20 representing the presence and status of a local church; to remove it means the community loses its spiritual standing.</term> itself would also at last be removed from us, if we wished to continue longer in such disregard for God’s word and His holy Ordinances? What are you thinking? What sign is it when Christ thus lets the lights go out in a Church, which should always be burning?

From this we may then see that we have been sufficiently warned before this of even greater approaching punishments, so that we shall have no reason to complain, should they come, that we were taken by surprise.

Has not the Lord Christ also used great long-suffering toward us for a long time now during these his faithful warnings? Has he not long endured us and had patience with us, one day after another, as if waiting for us to wake up in our first zeal, so that he might do us good again.

# Christ’s warning to prevent what is coming

The man still has to settle / the pain he has inflicted on me / I must yet seize my opportunity for that. But poor man / how do you forget / that the Lord Christ shall swiftly come upon such people, for if he came to you this night / at an hour when you least expect it / and smothered you in your sins; would you then not have time enough to lament your foolishness / and none at all to improve it? how can you then still let yourself believe / that there is anything else in the world / that you have to consider with greater haste / than the improvement of your life? to which Christ calls you. Rev. 18. vers. 8. <note>original: "Apoc. 18. vers. 8."; referring to the sudden downfall of Babylon in the Book of Revelation.</note> and let him conclude from this that / if there is anything in the World / that he must do with all haste / it is this / that he should turn away at the first opportunity / from his evil ways to God / through true repentance of the heart / which is the only means left / to escape the swiftly approaching punishments / without which it is also not possible / that a Church should be preserved / as it is explained to us in the last part of our text.

# The Downfall of the Church of Ephesus

Lord, and he is not satisfied that he had made those of Ephesus understand clearly enough that things would go all the more poorly for them if they did not quickly improve; but he goes on to present it to them again, so that they might indeed take notice of it, saying: *I shall come unto you quickly, and shall remove your Lampstand <note>original: "Candelaer"; in the Book of Revelation, the lampstand represents the church's status and presence before God.</note> out of its place, unless you repent.* By this, he seeks to stir them up to improvement in every way, and gives clearly and powerfully to understand—on the one hand—that he himself most earnestly wished and desired that those of Ephesus would yet allow themselves to be told and would improve, so that they might be spared. On the other hand, he shows that there was no counsel nor way out in the world for those of Ephesus to escape the threatened punishment, if they would not listen and practice the required repentance. As for the words themselves, they are explained above, except that here we must take the word repentance <note>original: "bekeeringe"; refers to a total "turning about" of one's life and orientation.</note> somewhat more broadly than in the preceding speech, where it was placed alongside the doing of the "first works." Here it encompasses the conversion of the whole person, and all his outward works and intentions, just as it is also so often used in the Scriptures, such as in *Luke 13, verses 5 and 6.*

Now, from this established condition and its explanation, we could point out various teachings, and among others this one: That whenever a Church of Christ falls away from its first zeal and love for Christ, and having been faithfully and frequently warned about it, does not improve itself, then the same

<column-break/>

shall at last, by God’s righteous judgment, also be abandoned by the Lord; so that it justly loses and is deprived of the dignity and worthiness of a true Church of Christ. We see this in the Roman Church <note>The author is writing from a Protestant perspective, arguing that the Catholic Church lost its divine mandate by straying from early Christian simplicity.</note>, which, gradually abandoning the love of Christ and refusing to be improved by any warnings given to her so many times, has at last lost all dignity and worthiness of a true Church in the eyes of all those whose eyes have truly been opened. So now, all those who are taught by God rightly separate themselves from her, and take up against her those convincing reasons which the children of Israel once used against Babylon, *Jeremiah 51, verse 9:*

> We have treated Babylon, but she is not healed; forsake her, and let us each go into his own country, for her judgment reaches unto Heaven, and is lifted up to the highest clouds.

->Nevertheless<-

we do not intend to dwell upon this now. The teaching that touches us more closely, we shall now alone present, and therewith conclude this text; and this teaching is:

<margin>And there it also truly stands: that there is no other means in the world to escape the coming punishments than that we improve ourselves.</margin>
The improvement of ourselves must be practiced, if our destruction is to be prevented. **See, whenever a Church of Christ, or a particular person in the Congregation, has grown slack in his zeal, or has fallen away from his first love, there is no other way in the world to escape destruction than to improve that which is disturbed.**

We see here the Lord Jesus, the Savior of the world, who can and will advise us so well; he testifies it to us here quite expressively, so that we should certainly not let it pass by unobserved, but should have good knowledge of it...

### Christ's Warning to Forestall Judgment

...they should take [heed], yet he is not satisfied with having said it once; rather, he repeats it, says it yet again, and urges it most earnestly. Just as he does here, up to two times, he also does in *Luke 13, verses 5 and 6.*

He has also taught all his ministers to do this at all times. If you read through all the Prophets, you will become fully aware that they promise no grace, nor salvation from approaching destruction, except on the condition of improvement. We have a beautiful account of this from the Prophet Jeremiah, specifically relating to the circumstances of our text, in *Jeremiah 4, verse 1.* There, God the Lord speaks through the Prophet in this way: *If you will return, O Israel, says the Lord, return to me; and if you will put away your abominations from my sight, then you shall not wander.* Here we see that the Lord explicitly requires—if the Lampstand <note>original: "Candelaer"; a reference to the divine presence and status of a church congregation.</note> among them was not to be removed from its place—that they must then remove their sins and cast them away through true repentance. So we also see throughout the Book of God that the Lord God has not helped His people, when they began to fall into hardship, in any other way than when they began to repent. They first had to change themselves before God the Lord was willing to better their condition, just as we have a beautiful example of this, among others, in the Book of Judges, *Judges 10, verses 10 to 16.* We also see that the friends of Job (whom they considered to be miserably estranged from God) knew how to give no other counsel than that he should improve himself, and upon that, they also promised him grace and reconciliation. See *Job 22.* So greatly has

<column-break/>

this truth of God been known since ancient times and urged by the godly; it also stands with entirely good reason.

For dear heart, what is more reasonable than that you first improve yourself, if you want your condition to be improved? Is it good that your outward state and circumstances might be well, and do you therefore greatly wish that, being in good external circumstances, you might be preserved in them—or, having been cast out from them, that you might regain them? And is it not yet much better that your own heart and soul might be good? And should you not justly desire and strive for that above all things? Indeed, must it not also justly be enough for each of us that the Lord God still wants to pardon us and receive us in grace, after all the evil we have done, and after we have now (as he speaks through the Prophet *Jeremiah 3, verse 1*) played the harlot with many lovers—if only we will henceforth still go and improve ourselves and refrain from such wicked whims? Is it not all the more very just, when an honorable man is on the verge of separating from his adulterous wife, that if any reconciliation were still to be reached and she were pardoned and taken back into grace, she should put away her adulteries <note>original: "overfpeelderije"</note> from her breasts (*Hosea 2, verse 1* <note>In most modern Bibles, this verse is Hosea 2:2.</note>) and repent? And would it not also be an intolerable lack of discretion if the adulteresses should want to be taken back by their husbands without letting go of their tricks, without improving themselves?

### The Downfall of the Church of Ephesus. 1119

<margin>Revelation 3:19.</margin>
...so that we might improve ourselves <note>original: "beteren"; this refers to moral reformation and repentance.</note> and thus escape the plagues: is that not the fruit that He expects from it? How then shall the Lord spare us, if we do not also improve ourselves, if we make Him miss out (as much as lies within us) on His fruit which He intended? He will surely bring plagues upon us seven times more, and that rightfully so. <margin>Leviticus 26.</margin>

<margin>And it is but mere folly and wasted labor that we seek to have our condition improved while we neglect to improve ourselves.</margin>
1. An uncovering of the folly of those who constantly plot and are intent upon this: that when they are in difficulty, they might have their condition <note>original: "staet"; referring to their external situation, social standing, or national security.</note> improved, without however considering improving themselves. These people certainly perform wasted labor; the counsel that our wise and merciful God gives them, they do not even notice, even though He is the only one by whom they must be helped, should they be helped at all. Instead, they follow their own counsel, which the Lord, for that reason, will not bless. For He has testified (and He shall also keep to it) that He will never again associate Himself with the throne of harmfulness <note>original: "stoel der schadelijckheden"; often translated in English Bibles as the "throne of iniquity."</note>. <margin>Psalm 94:20.</margin> So then, the woe that the Lord pronounces over Israel through the Prophet also applies to these people: <margin>Isaiah 30:1.</margin> saying: *Woe to the rebellious children, says the Lord, who take counsel, but not from me, and who cover themselves with a covering, but not of my Spirit, that they may add sin to sin.* The curse that the Lord also pronounces against such people shall strike them: <margin>Isaiah 8:10.</margin> *Take counsel together, but it shall be brought to naught; speak a word, but it shall not stand.* And this is so certain—namely, that the enterprise of those who, giving themselves out to be God's people, seek to escape their difficulties

<column-break/>

and to improve their outward condition without seeking to improve themselves—that it shall hardly succeed. Even if it were the case that they seemed to be somewhat improved and to rise above their difficulties, and that they had now defeated all their enemies <margin>Jeremiah 37:9.</margin> so that they began to expect all salvation, happiness, and prosperity, it would nevertheless quickly come to an end; it would nevertheless be of no value; it would nevertheless be the same story all over again within a short time (perhaps even the very next year) and it would turn out poorly for them again and remain just as precarious. So it shall often go with those who seek to improve their outward condition, just as the Israelites complained that everything went for them when they acted in such a way, saying: <margin>Jeremiah 14:19.</margin> *We looked for peace, and there is no good; and for the time of healing, and behold, there is terror.* It cannot be otherwise, for the cause of our grief and confusion, which comes upon us at any time, is our sins; as long as we do not improve those—as long as we do not improve ourselves from our sins—then the cause and the reason for our sickness and our grief remains just as strong. Thus, our evil cannot be healed; our guilt remains just as great. All other means of help that one employs are no different than if one were to poke out the eyes of the bailiff <note>original: "deurwaerder"; a court official or process-server sent to collect debts.</note> who was sent to demand payment from us, and so sent him away without giving him anything. Though this may release us from the immediate trouble for the present time, the debt remains, and we can expect an even worse experience the next time. In this regard, it is quite sufficient...

### Christ’s Warning, to Forestall Evil
<meta>catchword: well</meta>

it appears that it is indeed a great folly to wish to have one’s condition <note>original: "staet"; referring to one's social or political circumstances.</note> improved, and to escape from hardships, without improving oneself and striving to escape from one's sins.

<margin>A Lament.</margin> This being so true, it is indeed a very lamentable thing that so many people nevertheless enter this path. Yes, all the worldly-wise are lodged here; they contemplate this, they attempt that, when they are in difficulty and need, in order to get out of it. But the improvement of themselves, which the wise and merciful God (who alone can help them) advises as the best and readiest means to be helped, they do not pay attention to. It does not even occur to them that they should, on that occasion, go and consider bringing their own heart into a better state, bringing their household into better order, and warding off all godlessness, worldliness, and vanity from it. Instead, they should introduce all holy exercises and contemplations; this (I say) does not even come to their minds. Yes, even if they are earnestly exhorted and urged to this, they have neither desire nor inclination for it; nor can they believe, nor hold it to be true, that these things would best help them out of their difficulties. For they, viewing matters with a fleshly eye, and finding that such spiritual contemplations do not directly serve to rescue them from their difficulties—and hearing that the improvement of ourselves would only, as if by a detour, bring a secret blessing from the invisible God—and having no eye of the Spirit to perceive this, they are not accustomed to even look back at it. But all

<column-break/>

worldly wisdom <unclear>in this</unclear> is in a hitch, or some difficulty, so that one might manage oneself, those external things that bring something about, so that one might get those on one's side—that one goes bound here and there, with such and such other earthly means at hand. All of which to consider, if it is done in the fear of God, is not to be disparaged. But that one employs these means alone, and does not consider the improvement of oneself according to the word and counsel of the Lord; that is sheer folly. It is for this reason that many otherwise good and well-planned means often turn out so poorly and so unluckily. For namely, the people do not want to recognize this wisdom of God, nor improve themselves according to His counsel, but they want to have their condition improved, and do not want to improve themselves—which yet cannot succeed well.

**A Terror for those who nevertheless enter this path,** and having fallen away from their first love, and therefore also, through visitation <note>original: "besoeckinge"; a trial or punishment sent by God.</note>, come into some difficulty, yet do not consider the improvement of themselves: Certainly, it stands miserably with these. They may hope for peace, but no good shall come to them; they may hope that they shall be made whole, but behold, even more damage shall be at hand. If they belong to God, and are not people of this world (who would have their portion and part here in this life), then certainly the Lord God shall not leave them in peace nor in rest, until they consider themselves better and go about the improvement of themselves, who perhaps before this only considered and sought the improvement of their outward state.

# Christ’s Warning, to Forewarn [against sin]

Take Christ's exhortation to heart; you must indeed strive for your improvement at the very first opportunity, and not think to say in your heart: "My conversion will surely come later; I must take my pleasure in the world for a while longer, and after that I will join myself to Christ." You must not think this way, if you do not wish to destroy yourself; rather, think this: that the Lord Christ will come quickly to bring the deserved punishment upon all those who delay in following His warning. 

You should rather consider that the Lord Jesus—to whose love we now exhort you—is the one who died for you to save you. Will you then still keep running against Him? Should it not fairly be enough for Him that you have previously scorned and angered Him in so many ways and so horribly, rather than that you should continue to do so for some time longer? 

See, when you drink to drunkenness, behave proudly, lie and deceive, or persist in wantonness and lust, it is as if you were striking Christ on the jaw, as if you spat in His face, as if you crucified Him all over again. <margin>Hebrews 6:6</margin> Should it then not be enough for you that you have done this many times until now, without wanting to do it even more? If you have previously spat in the face of the Lord Jesus Christ through your drunkenness, do you want to continue doing so? If you have previously crucified Him anew through your unchastity, wantonness, and lust, can you bear in your heart to continue practicing such things for a while longer? Have you previously betrayed and sold the Lord Jesus, as it were, through your lying, cheating, and ill-gotten gain <note>original: "buyl gewin"; refers to profit gained through greed or dishonest means.</note>, for a few

<column-break/>

silver coins, and would you want to keep doing it? Have you sufficiently scorned the Lord Jesus through your finery, pride, and excess in clothing and banquets, and rejected and mocked His humility and poverty—in which He lived when He was here on earth in the flesh for your sake—and would you still want to do it once or more? 

Oh! Let this mindset of the ungodly be far from every one of us! Let us rather all together, with all haste, improve ourselves according to the counsel of our Lord Christ. Let us all likewise consider that as long as we walk on unrepentant, without true love for Christ, we are certainly walking on the broad road of damnation, even if our lives were otherwise ever so respectable <note>original: "burgerlijck"; meaning civil or law-abiding in a worldly sense, but lacking spiritual depth.</note> in the eyes of men. 

What person would dare to go on any longer like that, in certain peril of eternal destruction? Is it wisdom, is there any sense in a person choosing—even if it were only for one hour—to pursue such vain things as all the things of this world are (the reason why people usually postpone their improvement), with the great and certain peril of eternal destruction, should something sudden happen to him in that hour and he were to drop dead <note>original: "de moort stake"; an old expression for dying suddenly or being struck down.</note> (as has happened to many thousands)? Those who died in their sins, and were recklessly snatched out of the world by one unexpected event or another—oh, oh! Woe, woe be to us! Indeed, eternal woe be to him, whoever he may be, who meets such a fate; he would have time enough to forever drown in sorrow over it <note>original: "versaepen"; literally to drown or over-drink, used here to mean being consumed by eternal regret.</note> and to be terribly lost, but no time...

Members of high courts or governing councils.</note>, or others who hold the authority of the Country in hand—that they do not seek to apply all their latest influence which they have with the aforementioned Gentlemen so much to advance their own private matters, or the matters of their friends and acquaintances, as much as to advocate for this most necessary part of **Reformation** <note>original: *Reformartie*. This refers to the "Further Reformation" (*Nadere Reformatie*), a movement seeking to bring personal and public life into stricter alignment with Reformed Christian doctrine.</note> and to win them over to it, so that they might take it to heart and consider it. For certainly, our Country has such need, and there is still hope, but it is high time that it be done at the first opportunity and with all earnestness.

Yes, what is more, even those who still live without reflection on these matters and have no feeling yet in their heart of the Love of Christ—be they of great or small standing, in authority or outside of it—must at least learn to endure the great necessity of our Country's need, so that some may then begin to be zealous for the things of Christ, thinking thus to themselves: it appears quite clearly in the word of the Lord that God the Lord flatly demands that one should remove the **abominations** from before His eyes, if He is to spare the Land, **Jeremiah 4** <note>A reference to Jeremiah 4:1: "If you will put away your abominations out of my sight, then shall you not remove."</note>. This stands indeed in the word of the Lord, clearly expressed everywhere, and yet I find in myself neither desire nor pull to take it to heart or advance it in myself or in others; nonetheless, it were to be wished that such were taken to heart...

# The descent of the Crucified Christ

The **descent** <note>original: *onderganck*. This term literally means "down-going" or "sunset." The author uses it to describe the *Kenosis*, or the voluntary emptying of Christ’s divine status to become human.</note> of the **Crucified Christ** is to say as much as His laying down of all His **glory**, which He had with the Father before the world was; for He emptied Himself, having taken on the form of a **servant**, and became like men: And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself, becoming **obedient** unto death, even the death of the **Cross**. <note>This is a paraphrase of Philippians 2:7-8, a central text in Christian theology regarding the incarnation.</note> This is the true descent of Christ, which He suffered for our sakes, so that He might exalt us to the highest honor and glory. For just as He humbled Himself, so God has also highly exalted Him, and given Him a **Name** which is above every name.

From this we learn, firstly, the great **humility** <note>original: *ootmoedigheyt*.</note> of our Lord Jesus Christ, which He has left us as an example, so that we should follow in His footsteps. For if He, who is the Lord of Lords, so humbled Himself: how much more does it befit us, who are **poor little worms of the earth**, <note>A common 17th-century Dutch expression used to emphasize the vast distance between human insignificance and God’s majesty.</note> to humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God.

<unclear>Secondly, we learn from this the great love of God the Father, who did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all. And how should He not also, with Him, freely give us all things? This is our comfort in all **temptations**, <note>original: *aenvechtingen*. This refers to spiritual trials or "buffetings" of the soul.</note> that we have a God who has loved us so dearly.</unclear>

<unclear>Thirdly, we learn from this the great power and worthiness of the death of Christ, through which He has taken the Curse of the Law from us, and has **reconciled** us with God His Father.</unclear>

<summary>This page reflects on the "descent" or humiliation of Christ as described in the Book of Philippians, using His example of humility as a model for believers. It emphasizes that Christ's voluntary suffering is the source of human exaltation, comfort in trials, and reconciliation with God.</summary>
<keywords>Humiliation of Christ, Humility, Atonement, Servant, Cross, Grace, Reconciliation, 17th-century theology</keywords>

## To all sincere lovers of the <term>Church of God</term><note>original: "Ghemeynte Godts," referring to the collective body of believers or a specific congregation.</note>, who now in our time, in many parts of the world, are greatly oppressed.

<image-desc>Large decorative woodcut initial 'B' containing intricate foliate and floral patterns.</image-desc>

<margin>Ecclesiastes 7:3</margin>
Beloved in the Lord, although Solomon testifies to us that mourning is better than laughing—and adds a good reason for it, for through the sadness of the countenance the heart is improved—and although we all have equal, indeed very great, weighty, and many reasons for mourning in this sinful, sorrowful time and heavy onset of tribulations which have come upon God’s people in all corners of the world: we are nevertheless very unwilling to give ourselves over to mourning. Our hearts still hunger for joy and cheerfulness; and because we have no desire to mourn, we also put the "evil day" far from us and gladly convince ourselves that even if other Churches have fallen into great misery and contempt, it will nonetheless go well with us—which we also wish for with all our hearts. 

But in the meantime, it is truly no wisdom, since God calls us in every way to mourning through so many great and evil signs of His wrath as He allows to come upon His people, that we nevertheless refuse to mourn over it. If just some small thing in our worldly business goes against our will, it plagues us, it saddens us, it affects us; but that it goes very poorly for the people of God, that we pass over lightly, and we can hardly take it to heart. We ought to be exceptionally sorrowful about this, for we have indeed received the "heart-passion" of sorrow for this very purpose: but we twist that noble power which God has given us, misuse it, turn it toward the wrong objects, and force it to mourn over trivial things; yes, even sometimes over the fact that we cannot satisfy our evil desires, which we ought to be putting to death. 

The Lord Christ says to the Daughters of Jerusalem, *Do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves and for your children; for behold, the days are coming in which they shall say, Blessed are the barren, and the wombs that never bore, and the breasts that never nursed,* <margin>Luke 23:28, 29</margin> So we may now also say: Do not weep because you are thwarted in some worldly matters—that is often entirely useful and blessed for you—but weep over the misfortune of God’s people, which is, after all, the most lamentable of all things. The tears from the eyes of true Christians are such precious dew that they can be poured out over nothing better than over the misfortune of God’s people; <margin>Psalm 126:5</margin> and he who sows in tears shall in due time reap in joy. We should gladly give ourselves to this; and not only when we ourselves are in grief and difficulty (which is an easy thing), but also when we are still in good circumstances while God's people are in great misery and contempt. <margin>1 Corinthians 2:2; Psalm 119:136</margin> For just as we must not only mourn for our own sins, but also for the sins of others, so we must not only mourn for our own misfortune, but also for the misfortune of God’s people. <margin>Amos 6:6</margin> All the more because, certainly, our sins have also contributed to this common onset of difficulties. Had some of us stood in the breach, had we taken the misery of God's people to heart early on, had we constantly prayed fervently for their deliverance, the

### CHAPTER II.

That God the Lord sometimes allows His own people to fall into great misery and contempt.

<margin>God the Lord sometimes allows His own people to fall into great misery and contempt.</margin>That God the Lord sometimes allows His own people to fall into great external difficulties, we see clearly here in our text; in the people of <term>Israel</term> <note>The ancient Israelites, whom the author views as the spiritual ancestors of the Christian church.</note>, the inheritance of the <term>Lord</term>, whom He had chosen for Himself out of all nations, <term>Deuteronomy 10:14, 15.</term> This was in the time of <term>Nehemiah</term> <note>A Jewish leader who served as cupbearer to the Persian King and later oversaw the rebuilding of Jerusalem’s walls.</note>, in such great difficulty that they could not rebuild their capital city; its walls were broken, its gates burned, and they remained lying so. Thus, they could not establish any form of civil government <note>original: "Politie," referring here to organized social and political order.</note>, but were deprived of their liberty, and in every way insulted by their adversaries; the daily sacrifice ceased, the places of their religious assemblies were laid waste, the shepherds were struck, and the flock scattered. And this had now lasted for many years; and even though they had often tried to improve it, it had not yet been successful. Being in such great misery, no one yet had compassion for them; they were still mocked and ridiculed, so that they were in great misery and contempt at the same time.

There is also nothing so common in the Holy Scripture as to find the precious people of God in great difficulties. Read for me the beginning of <term>Exodus</term> <note>The second book of the Bible, which tells of the Israelites' enslavement in Egypt.</note>, and there you shall find them everywhere in great misery and

<column-break/>

contempt, even in a fiery furnace of misery, <term>Exodus chapters 1 and 2, etc.</term> After that, you find them in the wilderness, also oppressed by many kinds of difficulties and hardships. And even in the promised land, in the land of <term>Canaan</term>, how often do we also find the people of <term>God</term> there in great oppression, in great distress, mockery, and tyranny, being dominated by foreign lords who oppressed them; so that they often and many a time had to cry out to the <term>Lord</term> their <term>God</term> and say, "other lords besides You rule over us." <term>Isaiah 26:13.</term>

<margin>Because even His own people sometimes fall into great sin and transgression.</margin>It cannot be otherwise; even the people of God themselves must now and then fall into great misery and contempt; for, setting aside other reasons (which we have handled extensively elsewhere), the people of God, through poor oversight and remaining corruption, sometimes fall into great sin and transgression. From this, great misery and contempt must always arise among the people of God, just as the dregs <note>original: "spantchelen," referring to shavings or impurities that rise to the surface of a liquid.</note> rise from beer when it is stirred. For so has the Lord <term>God</term> Himself testified to them and said: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you for all your iniquities." <term>Amos 3:2.</term>

See, when the people of <term>God</term> have been in prosperity and luxury for a long time and in great measure, they begin gradually (I know not how) to love the world—which now smiles so kindly upon them—all too much; they begin to make too close and internal an acquaintance with the world; thus the world also has a certain seductive power in itself, by which it secretly chokes/ <note>The catchword "keelt/" refers to "ontkeelt," meaning to choke, throttle, or cut the throat of one's spiritual life.</note>

<summary>This page explores the theological concept of why God permits His chosen people to endure suffering and mockery, using the ruins of Jerusalem in Nehemiah's time and the slavery in Egypt as primary examples. The author argues that such misery is often a divine response to the people's own sins and their tendency to become too attached to worldly prosperity.</summary>

--- Page 1220 ---
<meta>This page continues the theological reflection on the suffering of the faithful. The previous page established that God allows His people to face misery; this page explains that such suffering often serves as a necessary "bitter cup" to cure the spiritual decay brought on by excessive worldly prosperity.</meta>

...steals the very hearts of God's people away from God toward vanity. Because of this, it often happens that once God’s people have lived for a long time in luxury and prosperity, they begin to be tainted by the world. They then start to become decadent, wanton, frivolous, proud, ostentatious, ambitious, power-hungry, and excessive in their feasts and clothing. Thus, they gradually become more and more conformed to the world, leading to great blasphemy of God’s name and causing the godless to open their mouths in mockery against the Holy Truth that the faithful profess. 

Now, if God’s people begin to behave so poorly, how will God deal with them? When they thus misuse their luxury, rest, peace, prosperity, and abundance—which the Lord God granted them out of His great grace—turning it into lewdness, wantonness, intemperance, and excess; is it not then righteous for God to withdraw that luxury from them and prune that abundance which they so greatly misuse? If God’s people indeed persist in swallowing the poison of sin to their own destruction, what else remains but for the Lord to place the bitter cup of oppression in their hands and make them drink it to the dregs for their own preservation? Is it not better, even in this case, that they lose their peace rather than their zeal entirely? Is it not better that they lose their prosperity rather than their souls?

## CHAPTER III.

->How we ought to conduct ourselves when God’s people fall into great misery and contempt.<-

<margin>2. We must not, therefore, take offense at this.</margin>

I. **A** warning that we should not take offense, even if we hear or learn that the

<column-break/>

people of God, the professors of the faith, have fallen into great contempt here or there; that the walls of their cities are torn down, and their gates burned with fire. No one should begin to doubt the holiness of the faith they profess because of this. If such things had never happened to the Church of God before, then one might be troubled by what befalls these people. 

But now we know—and it has been shown from the preceding—that the militant Church <note>The "militant church" refers to Christians currently living on earth, struggling against sin and worldly trials, as opposed to the "triumphant church" in heaven.</note> here on earth is just as subject to such events as any other people in the world. Indeed, such external difficulties—like wind, rain, hail, and snow—fall upon this earthly Paradise, or the flower-garden of the Great King, just as they do upon a common farmer’s field. We see it here in our text with the people of Israel themselves, whom God had chosen as His portion out of all the generations of the earth; they are here in misery and contempt. Jerusalem, the city of the Great King <note>original: "de stadt des grooten Conincks." See Psalm 48:2 and Matthew 5:35.</note>, lies here devastated; the walls of Jerusalem (of which the Lord said He had engraved them on His palms, so that they were always before Him, Isaiah 49:16) lie here broken; the gates of Jerusalem, which the Lord loved more than all the dwellings of Jacob (Psalm 87:2), are now burned. 

And though the godless might cry out at this sight, "Ha! This is the day we expected! Where is their God now?" <note>A common taunt used by enemies of Israel during the Babylonian exile, as seen in the Psalms.</note> yet we see that the God of Israel alone was the true God, and the people of Israel alone were God's people on earth. So it also stands firm forever: God's people may be oppressed, but they cannot be rooted out <note>original: "uytghe-roept," meaning to be called out or extirpated.</note>. According to Psalm 129, the gates of hell shall not prevail against them, Matthew 16:18, even though...
