...might accustom themselves to a hard life, in order to better withstand the approaching difficulties. <note>original: "swaricheden"</note> Jeremiah 35.

<margin>2. That we constantly occupy ourselves with pulling out the sting of reconciliation; the prick of death, 1 Corinthians 15:56. Oppression causes more pain through sorrow than unreconciled sin.</margin>
2. Secondly, that we constantly occupy ourselves with pulling out the "sting of reconciliation," <note>This likely refers to the "sting" that prevents reconciliation—unconfessed sin.</note> that is, unreconciled sin; the prick of death is sin, 1 Corinthians 15:56. There is nothing that makes tribulations hurt more than unreconciled sin; it is like a raging poison in the wound of oppression, which bruises and tears the conscience. All the blows then that one receives while in such a state are like blows to a tender wound, which therefore cause more pain. So we read that the need of hunger would sting the ungodly—who were not reconciled with God regarding their sins—so much that they would even eat their own children, Deuteronomy 28:57. Whereas the godly, whose sins are reconciled, can endure and overcome such needs much better. Therefore, in these perilous and troublesome times, we ought to do our utmost to reconcile ourselves with the Lord our God through Jesus Christ for all our sins; and sincerely try and strive to put away our sins from us as much as lies within us, as much as possible, so that we might have peace with God, and consequently be comforted by God, who is well able to comfort, in all needs and difficulties.

<margin>3. That we now already in time gather a good provision of spiritual gifts, so that we might stand firm in the evil day.</margin>
3. Lastly, that while things go well for us, we look to gather a good provision of all Spiritual gifts, and see to it that Christ's word (which is the word of comfort, Romans 15:4) might dwell richly in us, Colossians 3:16. So that when heavy times come, we might then be able to strengthen our hearts with it, and remain standing in the evil day, and be found steadfast

<column-break/>

in the holy doctrine which we once confessed, until the end; and so finally obtain the goal of our faith, namely the salvation of souls, 1 Peter 1:9. See, we do not know to what trial the Lord our great God might please to call us before He gives us the crown of salvation. But this we know always: it is written that *whoever perseveres to the end shall be saved,* Matthew 24:13. We also know that many who had received the word with joy were prone to fall away when temptations and heavy trials arose concerning the holy doctrine they had confessed, Matthew 13:21. Therefore, it is greatly to be feared that all those who do not now strive to gather a good provision of God’s word in their hearts—and see to it that they are well-founded and rooted in the true faith early on (Colossians 1:23)—would very readily fall away if any difficulties arose for them for the sake of the Gospel. Matthew 7:26, 27. Therefore, everyone must provide against this in time. And especially we must try and strive to mourn the misfortune that has struck our brothers; for that is also a precious means to be either wholly spared or well-comforted in all kinds of difficulty, as we shall hear more broadly hereafter.

Thus we perceive in this day that a Papist <note>original: "Papist," a common 17th-century term for a Roman Catholic</note> is now not to be spoken with; he is now so hardened in his lack of understanding, he now so blesses himself in his blindness, and now so boldly prognosticates in his foolish heart the total downfall of the Beggars' cause <term>Geuserye: a term for the Dutch Protestant movement, originally a label of "beggars" adopted as a badge of honor by rebels against Spanish rule</term> (as they speak), that he believes it cannot fail. The Libertine <note>A term used here for those who advocated for religious indifference or the idea that outward conformity to any church did not matter as long as one believed in their heart</note> also looks out now and then, and many a time seeks by these occasions and persecutions to make people believe that they are but simpletons <note>original: "slechte bollen," literally "simple heads"</note> who undergo any kind of bodily difficulty for the sake of the outward confession of their faith, since they might keep their hearts for God and otherwise adapt themselves physically according to what their Superiors or those who are too powerful for them desire; forgetting that it stands written: *You are bought with a price, therefore glorify God in your body and in your spirit, which are*

The reckless and immoral people also gather hereupon more and more poison, so as to go forward boldly in their sins, and they loiter everywhere in the gates and in drunken gatherings to the detriment of God's Church; certainly holding in their godless hearts that it is all in vain to lead a hard life before the Lord of Hosts <note>original: "Heere Zebaoth"</note> Mal. 3:13-14, while they see that even those who give themselves out to be the only people of God, themselves still fall into such great misery and contempt; forgetting that the Lord God truly has a book of remembrance <note>original: "gedenckcedel"</note> and that He shall yet, in His time, make a notable distinction between those who fear Him and those who do not fear Him. # LAMENTATION.

God's people fall into misery and into contempt; so that certainly the time of hardships for God’s Church is an evil time (Amos 5:13). All of this distresses the Daughter of Zion <note>A biblical personification of Jerusalem or the community of faithful believers</note> not a little; this makes her heart even more anxious in her weakness; this is indeed like a piercing in her bones (Psalm 42:11). This causes the Daughter of Zion to weep, to complain, to throw out her hands, and to say: "O woe is me now, for my soul is weary because of the murderers" (Jeremiah 4:31). Thus, it is everywhere a very pitiful thing and a lamentable matter when God’s people fall into great misery and contempt, because from it arises all kinds of discomfort and so much calamity, and so many poor people are misled and set further and further away from the path of salvation.

<margin>
3. Then God's great and holy name is also terribly blasphemed.
</margin>

III. When God's Church and God's people fall into great misery and into contempt, then on that occasion, God’s holy, great, and fearsome name is very much blasphemed. For see, God the Lord has taken it upon Himself to protect His Church as the apple of His eye (Zechariah 2:8). When it then goes differently with God’s own people—when the Israel of God falls into great misery and contempt—then the children of the world (to whom the wonderful ways of God over His people are unknown, and who cannot see how God Himself preserves and keeps His people through those very means by which they seem to be entirely destroyed and annihilated, Ezekiel 20:38–39) immediately think that the God of Israel is not the true God. Indeed, when those of the Reformed Church <note>The "Gereformeerde Kercke" refers to the Dutch Reformed tradition, the dominant Protestant group in the Netherlands at this time</note> fall into great difficulties, the children of the world are ready to think that the God of the Reformed Christians is not the true God (though

<column-break/>

He alone is); instead, they much sooner believe that the Papal Image-God <note>original: "Paepschen Beeld-God." A polemical term used by Protestants to describe the Catholic depiction of God, which they viewed as idolatrous due to the use of statues and icons</note>, who now seems to gain the upper hand, is the only true God. Thus, the true God of the Christians is greatly blasphemed for that reason, is rejected (O abomination!), and is called a powerless God who could not help His people. This is what Moses feared when the Lord intended to annihilate the people of Israel once and for all in the wilderness—namely, that the foreign nations would take the opportunity to blaspheme the name of the Lord and say the God of Israel had let His people perish in the wilderness because He did not know how to bring them into the land He had sworn to them (Numbers 14:16). And the heathens also interpreted it this way whenever God’s people fell into difficulty. "The enemy," says the Psalmist, "has reproached the Lord, and a foolish people has blasphemed His name" (Psalm 74:18). This also caused Rabshakeh <note>A messenger of the Assyrian King Sennacherib who mocked the Israelites' faith</note> to open his blasphemous mouth and boast that the God of Israel would not be able to deliver Jerusalem from the hand of his King, since he had already overpowered a large part of God's people and brought them into great misery (Isaiah 36:18, etc.). So we also know that the Papists <note>A common, often derogatory, term for Roman Catholics in 17th-century Protestant texts</note> interpret it thus now. If the honor of our God is worth anything to us, if His holy name is glorious and fearsome among us, then it is certainly a entirely lamentable and pitiful matter that God’s name has fallen into such great decline, that it must be blasphemed through such means, on which occasion the name of the true God is so terribly blasphemed.

His wrath is notably sent to blaze against his own people.

The heathens have come into his inheritance, defiled the temple of his holiness, and laid Jerusalem in heaps of stones. <note>original: "Psalm 79. 1."</note> Thus, God's fierce wrath is quite clearly revealed from heaven; so one may indeed rightly ask: how long, Lord? Will you be angry forever? Will your zeal burn like fire? <note>original: "Pfal. 79. 5."</note> For it is easy to sense that the Lord our long-suffering God must be exceedingly provoked and pushed away when he begins to perform such a "strange work" <note>A reference to God's judgment being "strange" because His primary nature is mercy.</note> upon his people, Isaiah 28:21. That he himself—who had undertaken to do them all good, to build, and to plant—begins thus to strike with unmerciful lashings; that he begins himself to break down what he has built, and to pluck up what he has planted; even the whole land. <note>original: "Ier. 45. 4."</note> Everyone can indeed easily sense that the Lord our long-suffering God must be exceedingly provoked and angered when he begins to enter into such rare ways with his own people, which also so grossly tend (through the wickedness of men) at that time to the blaspheming of his own name. But now, is that not a very lamentable and a truly very sad thing, to see the good and merciful God so pushed away and angered? What do you think? If some good-natured children saw that their friendly and gentle father, being provoked by their misdeeds, began to throw everything in the house upside down, striking now this one, now that one on the jaw, and thus completely enraged, went storming through the house; would that not break their hearts? Would they not consider that the saddest spectacle they had seen in all their lives? So it is also certainly—

<margin>
4. Then also God's wrath is revealed.
</margin>

<column-break/>

—certainly of all lamentable things, the most lamentable: to see God's people in great misery and contempt. For that makes us see the fierce wrath of our otherwise entirely long-suffering God blazing very greatly against his own people; that makes us see the Lord our gentle God overturning his own house, breaking down what he had built, uprooting what he had planted; to wound and to hurt those he had undertaken to heal and to cure. What more lamentable thing than this can be imagined?

<margin>
Therefore God the Lord also calls all his people to great mourning and grieving when any of their brothers are in great misery and contempt.
</margin>
Therefore God the Lord also requires everywhere so very earnestly, whenever his people are in misfortune and contempt, that one should take that very much to heart, and heartily mourn over it, as over the most lamentable thing that can be imagined. "Let the bridegroom" (he says) "go out of his inner chamber, and the bride out of her bedroom. And let the priests, the Lord's servants, weep between the porch and the Altar, and let them say: Spare your people, O Lord, and do not give your inheritance over to a reproach, that the heathens should rule over them: why should they say among the nations; where is their God?" <note>original: "Ioel. 2. 16. 17."</note> Yes, the Lord wants people to rise early for this, and make a business of weeping and mourning, whenever the Lord's people are in great misery and contempt. "O you wall of the Daughter of Zion" <note>The "Daughter of Zion" is a poetic biblical term for the community of believers in Jerusalem.</note> (he says) "let tears flow down day and night like a stream: give yourself no rest, let not your eyeball cease. Arise, cry out in the night from the beginning of the night-watches, pour out your heart before the face of the Lord like water; lift up your hands to him for the soul of your little children, who have fallen into a faint." <note>A reference to Lamentations 2:18-19 describing the famine and distress during the siege of Jerusalem.</note>

And He threatens heavy punishments if one refuses to do this.

### On the Hardships of God's People.

From what was said before, it is well enough understood that these evil times have also come upon God’s people in our century. Wherever we turn or look, we may become aware of various troubles and hardships that have befallen God’s people in these days. Just as we read here of Prince Nehemiah <note>original: "Nehemia de Vorst" — Nehemiah was a high official in the Persian court who led the rebuilding of Jerusalem's walls.</note>, how he asked Hanani and the other men from Judah how the Jews were doing—those who were preserved and left over from the captivity—and how things stood in Jerusalem; he received as an answer: *The survivors who are left from the captivity there in the province are in great misery and contempt; and Jerusalem's wall is torn down, and its gates are burned with fire.* <note>original: refers to Nehemiah 1:2-3.</note> So we, likewise, for some years now, have from time to time received such sorrowful tidings regarding the condition of God’s people from various quarters of the world. For indeed, is it not the same there? When some of our brothers come over to us from France, and we ask them how it goes with God's people there, do we not receive as an answer that God's people there are in great misery and contempt, that their wall is torn down and their gates burned with fire? 

<margin>God's people are also in terribly great misfortune and contempt.</margin>
If some come to us from Switzerland, from the Cantons <note>The sovereign states that make up the Swiss Confederation.</note>, do they not also testify to the same? That there, too, God's people are in great misery and contempt, that their walls are torn down and their gates burned with fire? If we happen to meet some from Moravia, from Silesia, from the Palatinate <note>Regions in Central Europe that suffered heavily during the religious wars of the 17th century, such as the Thirty Years' War.</note>, and from even more quarters, do they not also bring us that very same news: that indeed God's people there also 

<column-break/>

are in great misery and contempt, that their walls are torn down and their gates burned with fire? Thus, from all sides, we also receive those same sorrowful tidings regarding God's people in our time, which Prince Nehemiah received from Judea.

Oh, oh! If only the spirit of Nehemiah were now also in our Princes, and in our common people, and in all those whom it concerns! That we all might have such hearts as Nehemiah, to be ready to receive all such impressions of holy mourning and sorrow, just as the sorrowful tidings—which we have received from time to time for some years now—offer us. Indeed, that we might now also get those very same stirrings of Nehemiah in our hearts! So that we, who still have things well (as Nehemiah also did), could also be heartily sorrowful over it, weeping, abstaining from our vanities, and being much in fasting and prayer, until the Lord God of heaven looked upon it and helped His people. This is no more than what we owe; yet in this—oh, woe, woe to us—we fall far too short. The stirrings of Nehemiah are little found among us. While we have so much material and such great cause for mourning everywhere, yet very little mourning and sorrow over the misery of God's people is perceived among us. And above all the sins—alas, woe to us!—that we have committed so many of, we still add this one: that we do not mourn over the misery of God's people as we ought.

One finds many everywhere who mourn like Amnon <note>original: "2. Sam. 13. 2." Amnon was a son of King David who became physically ill with "sorrow" because of his forbidden lust for his half-sister Tamar.</note>, because they cannot better satisfy their fleshly lusts; or like Ahab <note>original: "Ahab" — The King of Israel who sulked and fasted because he could not seize Naboth's vineyard (1 Kings 21).</note>, that

<summary>The author draws a parallel between the biblical report given to Nehemiah about the destruction of Jerusalem and the contemporary suffering of Reformed communities across Europe (France, Switzerland, Germany). He laments that modern leaders and citizens lack Nehemiah’s compassionate spirit and fail to engage in proper communal mourning.</summary>

# LAMENTATION.

...that they cannot seize Naboth's vineyard for themselves, <note>original: "1 Coning. 21. 4." — King Ahab became despondent and refused to eat because Naboth would not sell him his ancestral vineyard.</note> or like the Israelites, who wailed upon their beds over the lack of corn and wine that had befallen them. <note>original: "Hof. 7. 14." — A reference to Hosea 7:14, criticizing those who cry out for material needs rather than seeking God.</note> When some of our ships are lost to a tempest, or captured by the enemy, we can mourn for them from the bottom of our hearts; when a worldly but helpful friend has died, we can bewail them; when we suffer any kind of damage or misfortune to the body, no one needs to urge us to mourn; no one needs to send for professional mourners to sing us dirges and teach us how to be sad—we take it to heart well enough on our own. <margin>That we nevertheless lament so little, or take so little to heart, the misery into which God's people have come in our time.</margin> But that the worthy people of God, the dear Bride of Christ <note>A traditional theological term for the Church.</note>, God’s holy Congregation—the most beautiful thing the world possesses—has fallen into great misery and contempt, who takes *that* to heart? Indeed, where are those to be found who, in the midst of an abundance of all desired worldly things, nevertheless mourn with Jeremiah because God’s people are in great misery and contempt? Where are those to be found who are so minded with David that the insults falling upon God, or upon God's people, also strike them? <note>original: "Psal. 69. 10."</note> Where are those to be found who wish with Jeremiah that they had enough water in their heads, and that their eyes were fountains of tears, to weep for the slain of the people of God? <note>original: "Jer. 9. 1."</note> Indeed, who takes all the great and utterly lamentable hardships of God's people—which we still hear of from time to time—to heart in any way other than as common news? We chat about it for a bit from week to week, and no sooner have we heard it one day, than we are already asking

<column-break/>

immediately the next day for something else, and we forget the first report; or we store it away in a cabinet of convenience without troubling our hearts much with it. And even when such moving, sorrowful news first arrives and spirits are somewhat stirred and moved by it, is it not immediately worn away so that before the [week] is over, everything is back to how it was in that regard? Is it not so that the very gravest and saddest tidings we hear are just like a heavy stone thrown into a canal, which makes a ripple and spreads itself out across the whole canal, causing some stir in the water—but a quarter of an hour later, it has all vanished again? Does it not happen exactly the same way with us, even with the most lamentable news we hear? It moves us for only a short time, and after that, everything goes on as before. After all these great and sorrowful hardships of which we have heard so many from time to time, they have served us for nothing else than to provide us with subject matter in our walks, in our gatherings, in our meals, at weddings, or on our travels; as soon as people come together, it gives them something to talk and gossip about. Often, some jesting or drollery is even mixed in with it—and that is essentially all we make of it.
   This is how it generally goes among the common man, with the exception of a few; and for that reason, those few are often regarded as being far too "heavy-headed" <note>original: "swaer hoofdighe" — Meaning melancholic, pessimistic, or overly serious.</note> people...

<margin>Further proof that we take little to heart the misery of the people of God.</margin>
But perhaps someone would still like to convince themselves / or imagine / that it is not so bad with us / that indeed we still reasonably take to heart the misery of the people of God; to him we will, for further measure, preciously present / the certain and sure signs of right mourning / over the misery of God's people / and by this it shall undeniably appear / that there is everywhere a great lack of holy mourning among us / although we have very great cause for mourning. We shall take these tests / and signs from the very nature / and operation of true sorrow / which are principally four / best suited to the present matter with which we are occupied.

1. The first / and proper operation / which sorrow has regarding the human heart / and eye / is this: that it shuts up / constricts / and burdens the heart; to this end serves the complaint of the Prophet, **Lamentations 1:20.** <note>original: "Thren. 1. 20" — Threnorum is the Latin title for the Book of Lamentations.</note> *Behold, O Lord, for I am in distress, my bowels are troubled, my heart is turned within me, for I have been very rebellious.* See also **Isaiah 16:11, Habakkuk 2:16.** Thus also does heartfelt sorrow / when it has settled a little / cause the eye to leak / to weep / and to cry. The anxious distresses of the heart / make the head into an <term>alembic</term> <note>original: "Alambijck" — a chemical apparatus used for distilling liquids; here a poetic metaphor for the head producing a "distillation" of tears.</note> and cause it to weep out in watery drops. # SCRIPT OF MOURNING. #

But here, perhaps, some will immediately think that the signs of sorrow we are presenting here are too extreme, and they will want to argue that a person cannot long endure being constantly gripped by such great sorrow, to have their heart always so constricted, and to refuse all outward comfort. Therefore, for these delicate people—and indeed for all well-meaning Christians—we shall present two other signs of true sorrow, by which it may further be shown that, in truth, very little sorrow is being shown among us over the great misery that has befallen God’s people.

<margin>Zechariah 12:10</margin>
III. Thirdly, we must know that where a person is heartily grieved over something to which he himself has also contributed through his imprudence, poor oversight, and his own fault, he is accustomed to loathe himself for it from the heart, and to take vengeance <note>In this context, "vengeance" refers to the practice of self-mortification or intense penitence—punishing one's own desires to show remorse to God.</note> upon himself in that regard. For example, if someone through imprudence had given his beloved mother a fatal stab-wound with his own knife, would he not loathe himself most heartily for it? So it is testified of the mourning in Zion, that when they should come to hear that their sins had pierced and killed the Lord of Glory, that very thing would also wound their hearts, so that in view of their sins, they would wail over him as with the mourning for an only son, and would cry out bitterly over him, just as one cries out bitterly over a firstborn. Now, it is certain and sure: we have each of us, man for man, helped bring about the misery of Jerusalem. This general overflow of

<column-break/>

difficulties across the entire Reformed world <note>The author is likely referring to the geopolitical and religious conflicts of the 17th century, such as the Thirty Years' War or the pressures on Protestant states.</note> is caused by nothing other than a general abundance of sin. Thus, we must rightly maintain that even those sins that cry out for vengeance—of which there are so many in this land—as well as our numbness, our lack of prayer, and our continuation in all kinds of vanity and wantonness after we have heard so many sorrowful tidings (at which we should have long ago taken the opportunity to humble ourselves and to excise <note>Original: "besnijden," literally "to circumcise," used here metaphorically to mean cutting away or pruning sinful habits.</note> such things), these, these sins of ours have steadily kindled the wrath of God more and more. They have also helped ensure that, from time to time, we have heard heavier and heavier news. Thus, we may well say and cry out: We have transgressed and we have been rebellious; therefore You have not spared us.

<margin>Lamentations 3:42 <note>Original: "Thren." for Threni, the Latin name for the Book of Lamentations.</note></margin>
If we then do not hate our sins, if we take no vengeance against ourselves for them, if we do not cast them away from us and break them—just as one would do with a sword with which he had unintentionally stabbed his mother to death—then truly our sorrow over the great misery of God’s people is little, or nothing at all.

<margin>Galatians 4:26</margin>

# ON THE HARDSHIPS OF GOD'S PEOPLE. #

<margin>3. Because we do not humble ourselves over our sins, which are the cause of all the misery of God's people, nor do we properly oppose them.</margin>
...can deny whether his own sins, together with the sins of others, have also helped kindle God's wrath against God's people? If it were otherwise, would there still be so much lustful frivolity, intemperance, pomp, pageantry, immorality, injustice, deceit and falsehood, so much spitefulness, quarreling, hatred, so much ambition and greed for status, so much ingratitude, and contempt for God's holy and precious word circulating among us? If we took the matter to heart, if we were truly sorrowful that we too, through our sins, have kindled the wrath of God against the people of God, would we not—according to the nature of true godly sorrow—have long since with all diligence detached ourselves from these sins that provoke and cry out to God? Would we not have better sought our accountability and reconciliation for this through the Lord Jesus Christ? Would we not long ago have shown displeasure and loathing regarding the fact that we had behaved so poorly that nothing but the heart's blood of the Son of God could atone for it? And would we not have grieved that we also, through our sins, had brought the <term>Congregation of God</term> <note>original: "Gemeynte Gods"; referring to the collective body of believers or the Reformed Church.</note> into hardship and misery? And would it not make us take vengeance <note>In the context of 17th-century repentance, "taking vengeance" refers to the Pauline concept (2 Cor 7:11) of being severe with one's own failings and disciplining the "flesh" to avoid future sin.</note> upon ourselves, and over our evil flesh and wicked whims, which have so misled us into provoking our God, and causing...

Everyone well knows that such people are very thinly sown <note>A metaphor meaning "few and far between."</note>, from which it once again appears that certainly very little spiritual and godly sorrow is being felt over the misery of the people of God.

V. Finally, where a person is heartily grieved over something, he wishes it to be improved; thus he is also accustomed to employ all possible means for that purpose, and to do what is in him so that it might be otherwise. For this reason, man is by nature always inclined to ward off and remove everything that naturally grieves him; and when he knows not what else to do, he breaks out in supplication and in prayer, as we see here in the Prince Nehemiah. He, being heartily grieved over the misery of God's people, devotes himself to fasting and prayer; indeed, he seeks the God of heaven (Nehemiah 1:4) and the god on earth <note>The "god on earth" refers to the Persian King Artaxerxes, whom Nehemiah petitions for help in Nehemiah 2:3-4.</note> to ward off the misery of Jerusalem, the cause of his sorrow. <margin>It is a great sin to feel only a small distress over the great misery of God's people.</margin>
...great misery of the <term>Church of God</term> <note>original: "Kercke Godts"; refers to the collective body of Reformed believers</note> / but little mourning is expressed. wherever there is true love for God's people, there is immediately great compassion and concern over the misery of God's people. Why was David so grieved over Absalom's fall (2 Samuel 18:33)? Why is a child so grieved over the death of his mother, while a stranger feels no distress at all, but hears it told and immediately forgets it? Why else, but that the child loves his mother? The child has placed his love upon his mother; the stranger has not. And even if the misery that has befallen God's people occurred in distant lands, our hearts would nonetheless be seized with sadness over it, if we had placed a heartfelt love upon God's people. Understand it this way: there is an honorable matron who has her husband in France and her son in Germany; and she comes to understand that her husband in France has been murdered by highwaymen, and that her son in Germany has been killed by the enemy; shall that wound the heart of the wife and mother any less because it happened far away? Does the death-blow given to her husband in France not pierce her heart here in our own land? It would happen exactly the same way to us, had we placed our love upon God's Church; hearing that she is wounded and devastated in France, in Germany, etc., it would also cause us pain here. experts know that the disease is most dangerous when some great evil is about to break out all at once, even when a person is truly very sick and yet does not feel it. <note>This refers to the medical concept where a lack of pain in a severely ill patient was seen as a sign of imminent death or a "mortification" of the flesh.</note>

<margin>4. Those who do not take to heart the misfortune of God’s people are not improved by it.</margin>
IV. A fourth base effect of this insensitivity toward the misfortune of God’s people is this: that we then gain no spiritual profit from God's heavy plagues and punishments. One has then—alas!—along with all the others, the pain, the torments, and the discomfort of the plagues, punishments, and chastisements of the Most High, and yet one misses the benefit of them if one does not take the misfortune of God’s people to heart. One does not repent then; despite all those worldly torments and difficulties, one continues to perish in their sins, *Jeremiah 5:3.* In this state of insensitivity, one is just like those who have taken a bitter, loathsome drink which makes them very distressed and anxious, yet which does not work, nor brings about any purging <note>original: "purgatie"; referring to a medicinal cleansing of the bowels, here used as a metaphor for the spiritual cleansing of repentance.</note> afterward. This, then, is also a foul fruit of base insensitivity.

<margin>By all of which it fully appears that an insensitive state regarding the misfortune of God’s people is a high-ranking sin.</margin>
And thus we may now fully observe from all of this that it is indeed certainly base, high-ranking, and entirely harmful sin to be insensitive and unmoved when God’s people are in great misery and contempt. The causes are entirely evil and terrifying, and the fruits thereof are most hideous and damaging.

<margin>Nevertheless, it is very common.</margin>
Yet, however gruesome and high-reaching this sin may be, it is nonetheless very common, as may have appeared from what was previously discussed. Indeed, it is a wonder, when the misery of God's people

<column-break/>

is so great, and when all professors <note>term: "belijders" (confessors/professors); those who publicly profess the Christian faith.</note> of the true faith have such a great interest in it, that so little mourning is made over it all. Certainly, if something evil were not at work, these emotions would come upon us of their own accord; they would indeed spring forth from the abundant seed of sorrow, which the Lord God, our spiritual Farmer, has himself sown with "heart-blood" <note>original: "hertbloedelück"; meaning with intense, life-giving passion or sacrificial effort.</note> for some years now in the field of his Church. There are many who, upon hearing a pitiful story recounted with emotion, are touched in their hearts and weep over it, even though it is often but a fictional tale. That we then are not moved by the entirely heavy, certain, and sure misfortunes of God’s own precious people—surely something evil is at play underneath that. Therefore, we must all the more embolden ourselves against it. This is also certain and sure: since holy sorrow is a fruit of the Spirit of God (*Zechariah 12:10, 11, etc.*), it does not grow in everyone's field. If we are to obtain it, we must awaken the gift of the Spirit and apply all spiritual motives and means toward that end from within our hearts. Therefore, we shall speak a bit more on both of these.

That which we have already said to confirm the doctrine we have at hand; all the reasons we have brought forward for it (which must certainly be well-considered and thought upon again here), as well as the observation of the hideous causes and the loathsome fruits of base indifference in this matter: See, all of that may serve as powerful motives to strive for holy mourning and sorrow over the misfortune of God’s people. But, for further abundance, we shall present specific motives here for this purpose; for indeed, our hearts are wonderfully unwilling to feel any sadness. Our hearts are by nature luxurious and frivolous, hating sadness and hungering for all joy and pleasure; therefore, what we can say here is barely enough.

So we read that when the Lord God intended to bring heavy plagues upon the city of Jerusalem, and sent out six men—that is, God's angels—for that purpose, with harmful weapons in their hands, giving them this command: that they should go through the city and strike, and that their eye should not spare, and that they should not have pity. **Yet the Lord God still took care, before these six men with their harmful weapons should fall upon the city, that a man clothed in linen, who had a writer’s inkhorn at his waist (which was the Angel of the Covenant), should go before them; and that he should first mark with a sign on the forehead those people who sighed and cried over all the abominations occurring there: with express command to those**

<column-break/>

**other six men, that even if they had to kill old men, youths, maidens, and little children even to the point of destruction, they should certainly not touch or harm those who bore the mark—those who had sighed and cried out over Zion. <note>Ezekiel 9:3, etc.</note>**

Yea, those who heartily mourn over the sin and the misfortune of God’s people shall not only be spared in the time of need and the evil day, but moreover, they shall be most gloriously comforted in due time. Behold, the time shall come when all tears shall be washed from their eyes, and it shall be most kindly said to them: *Rejoice with Jerusalem, and be glad with her, all you who love her; rejoice for joy with her, all you who mourned over her; that you may nurse and be satisfied from her consoling breasts; that you may drink deeply and be delighted with the abundance of her glory.* <note>Isaiah 66:10-11</note> It shall then be rewarded in its proper time, so that *those who have sown in tears shall reap with shouts of joy,* <note>Psalm 126:5</note>. Their sorrow and mourning over the misfortune of God’s people has truly been the seed of their new spiritual joy and glory. Who is there then, who, considering and believing this, would not gladly take heart to mourn heartily over the misfortune of God’s people, so that he might not only be spared in the evil day, but moreover be gloriously comforted in the proper time of help?

4. And means may be found through the misfortune of God’s people to help rescue them from their misfortune and contempt.

4. If we heartily mourn over the misfortune of the people of God, then by God's grace, there may yet be means to help the people of God out of their misery and contempt. For truly, holy mourning and sorrow over the misfortune of the people of God is a very serviceable means to obtain the help of God for His people: it is indeed the very means that the Lord God himself prescribes for that purpose, and therefore it shall surely provide strength, if only it is applied properly. <margin>
How we might best work upon our hearts—which are by nature light and ready to hanker after joys—toward holy mourning and sadness over the misfortune of God’s people. Namely:
</margin>

From all that we have already said, it appears fully sufficient on all sides that it is indeed our bounden duty in every way to engage in great mourning and begin holy sorrow whenever God’s people fall into great misery and contempt.

But alas, oh misery! Although this is our bounden duty, we may well perceive that our hearts are so vain and frivolous, so always hankering after joy and merriment, that our hearts are nevertheless with difficulty won over to this. We are ready to mourn and be sad over some temporal inconvenience, over all kinds of vain earthly things that perish with use; and that often beyond measure, and much more than we ought; and yet we can hardly shed a tear over the misfortune of the Church of God. Our hearts are generally in this regard as hard as cobbles <note>original: "kepen", likely referring to hard stones or flint</note> and as dry as a pumice stone. Therefore it is necessary that, besides the aforementioned Motives, we point out some Means through which we might work upon our hearts and bring them to actual holy mourning and sadness. Now, the following means are primarily very useful for that purpose.

<margin>
1. That we thoroughly press God’s commandment upon our souls, by which He commands us to weep with those who weep.
</margin>

I. That we thoroughly consider and well press upon our souls God’s own commandment and will in this, clearly presented to us in His word. See, it stands written there: the Lord wants it straightforwardly that we should indeed mourn and be sad, make mourning and bear grief over the misfortune of God’s people; He wants, when they are in difficulty, that we should also take it to heart as if we ourselves were in difficulty. How we might best prepare our hearts, which are by nature flighty and eager for joy, for holy mourning and sadness over the misfortune of God’s people. Namely:

misfortune, damage, or contempt which strikes you, then you can weep and be sorrowful; but see, you must also learn to mourn—and that quite thoroughly and with all your strength—over the **breaking of Joseph** <note>original: *verbrekinghe Iosephs*; a biblical reference to the affliction of the people of God, taken from Amos 6:6</note>, when God’s own people come into great misery and contempt. <margin>3. That we should strive to have a heartfelt love for the sorrowing people of God.</margin>
III. Thirdly, that we should strive to have a heartfelt love for the people of God, and that shall of itself cause us to mourn heartily over the misfortune of God’s people. Nature itself teaches us this: those whom we love, we always mourn over their misfortune; and the more we love someone, the more it affects us when they fall into any hardship or grief. Therefore, the Holy Spirit also joins the Lovers and the Mourners of Jerusalem together, **Isa. 66. 10.** And truly, the reason why many people are so little grieved over the misfortune of the Church of God is this: because they do not love the Church of God. They mourn more over a misfortune in their trade, their ship, their shop, their field, their cattle, or their horse, than over the misfortune of the Church of God, because they love their worldly business more than the Church of God. If this is to be improved, then we must see to it that our hearts are worked toward a deep, heartfelt love for God’s Church; we must see that we make Jerusalem our chief

<column-break/>

joy, and then we shall also be able to mourn most of all over the misfortune of Jerusalem and over the ruin of Joseph <note>original: "verbrekinghe Josephs"; a biblical reference to Amos 6:6, meaning the affliction or destruction of the faithful</note>. A wound given to Jerusalem—even if it were very far from our hand, in France, in Germany, or wherever it might be—shall also cause us pain here in this Land; it shall hurt us here as well and make us mourn heartily and bear sorrow, if we love Jerusalem from the heart.

Now, we can be encouraged to have this deep, heartfelt love for Jerusalem, for the people of God, and for the Church of God, through serious and deep meditation on the worthiness, beauty, and friendliness of it, and how great an esteem and estimation the Lord God Almighty holds for it; likewise, by thinking of the great benefit that all those shall have who love Jerusalem, and by the urging of God’s command, which wills and requires that we should love God’s people above all, **Gal. 6. vs. 10.**

<margin>4. That we heartily pray to the Lord our God, that He would give us softened hearts regarding the misfortune of His people.</margin>

It is as if they had set their minds to it—that they, along with the **rich glutton**, <note>A reference to the biblical parable of the Rich Man (Dives) and Lazarus from Luke 16.</note> would live it up in all excess and splendor without once taking to heart poor **Lazarus**, who lies hungry and naked at their door. They do not once take to heart the hungry and naked members of **Christ**, who (now that God’s people have come into such great misery and contempt) are found in such great numbers throughout the Christian world.

Truly, this is to utterly despise the Church of God. Shall our brothers be in great misery and contempt, and shall we be in great joy and wantonness? Shall they sigh and we laugh? Shall the beloved of our soul sit in sackcloth and ashes, and shall we live it up in all worldliness? Surely this is a sign of an entirely wicked nature; especially when one considers that in all this misfortune of God’s Church, **God’s fierce wrath** (which comes to visit His own house and overturn everything) is quite clearly perceived. Consider then, what kind of nature such children have, who, when they see their father in such

<column-break/>

great wrath and indignation, throwing down and destroying everything high and low in the house, can nonetheless go and sit laughing and engaging in their usual joy? Are these not surely blemishes in the house of God, rather than children? Do not all these surely consider themselves as the most harmful enemies we can have? They devise injustice and give evil counsel to **God’s people**, and harmful plots over God’s people, even if they intend otherwise (*Ezekiel 11:2*). Do not all these who are so little moved—not at all terrified—by the fierce wrath of the Most High God, have a sad sign upon their souls? They are themselves **children of wrath**, whose nature is not to fear the coming wrath of God until a swift destruction comes upon them from the angry face of God, like labor pains upon a woman in childbirth, from which they cannot escape. Must these then not rightly expect that surely, when the days of the Lord’s **visitation** <note>original: "thuyssoeckinghe," a term for divine inspection and judgment of a household or nation</note> shall also come upon our land (and this might happen to us soon, and such people greatly contribute to it), they shall then be the first among those who shall be led away captive, or fall by the sword (*Amos 6:7*). For to them especially applies (if it applies to anyone) what the Lord says (*Isaiah 65:12*): "I will also destine you for the sword, so that you shall all bow down to the slaughter, because I called (to mourning and wearing of sorrowful garments, *Isaiah 22:12*), but you did not answer; I spoke (through my plagues and...)"

### IV. Awakening, to all members of the Reformed Church and all those who present themselves as her favorable friends and well-wishers.

even greater decay has come than the current state of God’s people across the **Reformed world** <note>original: "gereformeerde weerelt." For also, that which the Prophet [Jeremiah]—after this earnest exhortation to mourning—gives as a reason for it, also applies to God’s people at this time. That the people whom the Lord chose as his heritage from all nations, to whom he revealed his Divine truth and granted the ministry of his Sacraments, that this people in so many places in the world is so devastated and scattered; is that not truly the most lamentable of all lamentable things?

Thus no one should think that this awakening to wailing would be harmful to the people, as if their hearts were made faint-hearted by it against their enemies; rather, it serves only to make them humble before their God; and that is the readiest way to succeed. not in ourselves, nor in our own power, but in God must boast and place our trust, Phil. 3:3. It is then our bounden duty in such circumstances to conduct ourselves very humbly in ourselves, so that we might gain courage in our God; and only then are we in a state to do some good for ourselves and the people in general. Nor did it weaken the courage of **Nehemiah** <note>A biblical leader who mourned the destruction of Jerusalem's walls before seeking permission from the King of Persia to rebuild them.</note> that he mourned so bitterly and wept over the misfortune of God’s people, but it rather gave him new courage and strength—not only to pray to the God of heaven, but also to approach King **Artaxerxes** <note>original: "Arthahsastha"</note> with boldness to seek help for God’s people. ### CHAPTER XII.
### That we must all alike, to our utmost ability, when God’s people are in great misfortune and contempt, lend a hand to help the people of God out of their hardship.

<margin>
That we must all alike lend a hand, and do our utmost best to help the people of God out of their hardship.

That we must not only be heartily sorrowful / over the people of God / when they fall into great misfortune and contempt / but also lend a hand / each according to our situation / and utmost ability / to help God's people out of their distress / is also taught to us by Prince **Nehemiah** <note>Nehemiah was a high official in the Persian court who returned to Jerusalem to rebuild its walls in the 5th century BCE.</note> / through his reflections. # ### Concerning the difficulties of God’s people.

Christian people [seek] such mountains <note>The Dutch "bergen" can mean "mountains" (metaphorical for high status) or be the end of "herbergen" (to harbor/shelter).</note>; and because one must admit that many things in war cannot be managed as effectively as might be desired, hardly any thought is given to the **Regulation of Christ**, which he also provided regarding such matters. Instead, the course of the world and the ways of nations who do not know God are followed more in these times than the rule of Christ our Savior. And thus, in every way, the laws of Jesus Christ—oh, the horror!—are bent under the base practices, customs, and ways of doing of this corrupt world, through an intolerable and exhausted ingratitude. Thus, the <term>Angel of the Covenant</term> <note>original: "Engel des verbonts," a title for Christ representing his role as the messenger of God's promise to humanity.</note> in whom the name of God dwells, is embittered among us. Is it any wonder, then, if we are not better helped? Is it any wonder, then, if the Lord Jesus Christ, who is *mighty to save* (Isaiah 63:1), no longer rouses himself to help us, and no longer stands at our side to be an *enemy to our enemies, and an adversary to our adversaries*?

<margin>Therefore he also refuses to take up our cause.</margin>
When we were in our greatest distress and need, and sought help wherever we could find it from the higher powers here on earth, did we not have to keep such conditions as we had entered into with those who came to our aid if we wished to be helped by them any longer? Did we not have to accept the **Governors** <note>original: "Gouverneurs," likely referring to the political or military leaders sent by allies during the Dutch Revolt.</note> that one or the other sent to us, just as we had agreed? How obsessed were we then! Should we not also, if we wish to be truly helped by the Lord our God, the true Helper-in-Need, accept, receive, honor, and obey the Lord Jesus Christ—the Savior and Redeemer whom He gives us out of grace and great faithfulness and 

<column-break/>

power—just as he finds necessary and advisable? When we do not do this, when we do not want to recognize the Lord Jesus Christ our Savior as our **Teacher** and as our **King**; when we do not want to subject ourselves to his teaching and his laws, how can things go well for us? If we sufficiently affront him in all our gatherings, meals, dealings, and even in our clothing—doing him all manner of insult and disdain, paying no heed to his word, his given order, or his regulation—but instead bend all his laws and ordinances under the base customs and ways of this evil world, which is his enemy; if we drink, flaunt, mock, jest, engage in useless chatter, and are proud, excessive, ambitious, greedy for money, and do all such things that are not virtuous; do we then not embitter his spirit? Can we then expect that he would want to stand on our side any longer, to be an enemy to our enemies and an adversary to our adversaries? Indeed, must things not necessarily go poorly for us? Do we not provoke his high **Majesty** to turn his own hand against us and to scourge us as if he were scourging an enemy? Just as he has done for several years now in many parts of the world with his people, and that quite justly.

For how shall the Lord Jesus be revealed to us as that great Savior and Redeemer of both soul and body, and how shall he consequently be offered to us as our Savior and Redeemer, unless it is on the condition that we also accept him as our **Teacher** and **King**; and—

### On the trials of God’s people. ###

God's. See, we lack nothing else but his help; if we can get that on our side, then we are on top. Would he but turn his hand against our enemies, they would soon be suppressed; would he become the enemy of our enemies, and the adversary of our adversaries, then we would have won. Let everyone, therefore, labor toward this end; let everyone lend a hand to this; indeed, let the Lord Jesus Christ, our Great Savior <term>original: "Heplant," a 17th-century term for Christ, combining the idea of a "Healing Plant" or Physician with that of a sovereign Protector.</term>, have his proper honor among us, so that he is recognized and obeyed as our commanding Lord and King, and he shall be bound faithfully to his covenant, and we shall be helped. See, from time to time, from year to year, we have begun to go backward in our faithfulness toward him; we have gradually fallen away from our first love <note>A reference to Revelation 2:4, often used by reformers to describe a decline in religious zeal.</note> which we once bore for Christ, turning toward the love of the world; thus we have begun to weaken the laws of Christ and have made them bend under the base customs of the world; thus we have begun to break the condition upon which he offered himself as our Savior. The Lord Jesus Christ has noticed this for a long time now; it has also embittered his Spirit; it has begun to grieve him, and so he has also begun to withhold his great power and to leave us to our own devices; from that time on, our affairs have regressed <note>original: "geaerselt," literally "moved backward like a crab."</note> and fallen from bad to worse in many parts of the world.

<margin>Therefore, this must be seen to on all sides; this must indeed be improved, following the counsel of the people of God.</margin>

King, and subject ourselves to his laws; hear, then, what the Lord himself says to this, and how clearly he gives his people to understand that he will not be merciful to them unless they observe his commandments and are obedient to the laws: It shall come to pass (he says) because you shall hear these judgments, and keep them, and do them, that the Lord your God shall keep unto you the covenant and the mercy which he swore unto your fathers. *Deut. 7:12.*

For in strife, each seeks to oppose his adversary, and even to reject good counsel simply because it comes from a person who is offensive to us, and whose reputation we envy, lest it be said that such a thing was resolved and done through his advice and proposal. # LAMENTATION

...to report? so that if they can divide us, they can win us? Therefore, all the **High Powers** <note>Referring to the sovereign governing bodies of the various provinces and states</note> of the **Reformed world** must stand firm in this common need of Christians; each must look not only to his own interests, but also to the interests of others, **Philippians 2:4**. And laying aside (at least for a time) all **animosities** <note>original: *simulteyten*; refers to private grudges or rivalries</note>, all occasions for dispute and misunderstanding, and each maintaining his own claims, they must—as is only right for this time—hand in hand, work together to resist the common enemy as one. And that, if anything, shall still be able to quiet these great disturbances and bring them to an end without bloodshed: namely, that one sword (as the saying goes) shall keep the other in its scabbard; and when equal powers meet one another, they shall cause the scales to weigh evenly and remain still. Therefore, all lovers of the people of God and of the peace of a **shattered Christendom** <note>original: *ghescheurden Christenheyts*; a reference to the religious wars and divisions in 17th-century Europe</note> must especially labor toward this end; and those who have no other power must at least seek the Lord God with constant prayers regarding this matter.

### concerning the hardships of God’s people.

...necessities bind [them], for the maintenance of the true **Religion** and of the affairs of the land; and without which they do not see how they could hold the land or secure the state against the common enemy; and in which they also spend their own money. Indeed, we can also in no way doubt that if the good Community only knew well how things go in other Provinces—in this one, what necessity there is, what means are raised, and how they are handled there—they would yet bless themselves that things still go so well here; all the more because very mature consideration is now being given to how everything might be better provided for everywhere; and where there might have been some unevenness here or there while there was great abundance, that should also be improved in this present great necessity.

<margin>And to that end, consider how richly God the Lord has blessed the inhabitants of the land, while they have had the Holy Gospel among them.</margin>
Therefore, let all lovers and well-wishers of God's people also consider here in the fear of God how richly and how abundantly the inhabitants of the land have been blessed by God, while the holy Gospel and the Reformed Religion have been among us and well-received. What rich harvests, what great **Trade** <note>original: *Negotie*</note>, what good business, and what a mighty profit there has been in the land in the years past; how the Lord has truly opened the windows of Heaven over us and poured out the fullness of blessing over our land; so that even now the chests of many remain full, and many a rich and powerful **Merchant**, many a rich and excellent **Investor** <note>original: *Rentier*; one who lives off the interest of their wealth</note>, and many a rich and respected Citizen is to be found everywhere; besides that, even the common man in our land, who uses only proper diligence to support him-

<column-break/>

-self (in comparison to many other peoples and nations, whose heads are as much directed toward Heaven as ours) lives like a Prince, having not only food and clothing, but also an abundance of both, and often of the best quality: even those who are so heavily burdened that they cannot care for themselves; the abundance in the land and Christian **Charity** <note>original: *Charitatie*</note> is still so great that even they are still well-cared for in every way, provided they behave well and decently. Truly, the Lord still feeds us with the finest wheat and satisfies us with honey from the rock.

<margin>Therefore they should indeed reasonably and gladly give back something of their ability for the protection of the Holy Gospel and of our dear Fatherland.</margin>
See how richly God the Lord has blessed us while we have had the Gospel among us, and how well He has dealt with all the inhabitants of our Land; what then remains but that we, in the fear of God and by way of proper gratitude, should gladly devote those means and that ability—which the Lord God has granted us out of pure grace through the blessing of His Holy Gospel—to the defense of His Holy Gospel and the security of our dear Fatherland? How could we ever answer for it in eternity if we were found wanting here, or if we were stingy and sparing in this? Especially since one sees everywhere that the inhabitants of the Land are still so excessive and costly in their meals, their daily table, in their clothing, in their houses and furniture, and everything pertaining to them. What? Shall we have the heart to give our money away for a tasty morsel for the mouth, or for a fine adornment <note>original: *getopsel*; refers to fashionable trimmings or head-dress</note> for the head, the neck, the back, the hand, or the foot?

31. So too is our worthy **Fatherland**—together with God’s **Church**—in great want and need. ### Description of God’s people.

uprightness <note>original: *vroomigheyt*; in 17th-century Dutch, this term encompasses piety, moral integrity, and religious devotion</note> and courage <note>original: *kloeckheyt*; implying a combination of bravery, strength, and shrewdness</note> must go 
paired with one another: for uprightness alone 
is often rash, and courage 
without uprightness is mostly cunning 
or wicked: therefore one must 
properly strive for wisdom, so 
that uprightness may be guided 
by the same. Furthermore, 
an upright man will not lightly 
undertake any matters, upon 
which he has not well and ripely 
deliberated: but after he has 
well deliberated the matter, then shall he 
accomplish the same with a 
good and upright courage. An upright man 
is also such, that he would rather please the 
upright, good God, than the 
evil devil: for he 
well knows, that God through 
uprightness makes men happy, and 
the devil makes them through wickedness 
unhappy. He also chooses 
rather that he be upright in poverty, 
than that he be godless and 
ungodly in great riches. 
It is also characteristic of an upright man 
that he would rather uphold 
the right, than promote the wrong; 
for he well knows, that injustice 
brings more harm than advantage. 
An upright man is also restrained: 
for although he has a righteous cause 
in hand, yet he shall 
seek to carry it out not with violence, 
but through proper means. 
An upright man is also patient: 
for although he is often for his 
uprightness hindered and 
persecuted by the wickedness of 
other men, yet he bears 
that nonetheless with patience, and relies 
upon the good God. An upright 
man is also faithful, as well in 
words as in works: he shall also 
gladly keep his promise, though 
the same may already have 
resulted in his own loss. He is also 
ready to help and 
advise another, yet always 
for the best, and not for the worst. And 
to say it all in a word: 
an upright man is such, that he 
loves to do nothing more than what is good, 
and leaves nothing more gladly than what is evil: 
for God the Lord is himself an 
upright God, who 
loves the upright, and hates the godless.

<column-break/>

Nonetheless one must know, that there 
are various degrees of 
uprightness: for one person is 
more upright than the other, so that one 
may also increase in 
uprightness, just as the Lord Christ 
says: *He who is upright, let him become 
yet more upright.* <note>A paraphrase of Revelation 22:11: "He that is righteous, let him be righteous still."</note> And Paul says: That 
we must daily increase 
in uprightness, and in the true 
knowledge of God. We must also 
consider, that uprightness must 
not only be an outward appearance, but 
an inwardness of heart: 
for the uprightness that is 
only from the outside, and not from 
within, that is hypocritical, and 
the same is not acceptable 
before the All-knowing God:

# On the warning of Christ, to prevent the downfall of the Congregation of Ephesus.

Introduction to the following treatise. Explanation and application of the first part of this text. Page 1055.
Of the particular defect that was in the Congregation <note>original: 'Gemeynte'; refers to the local church body or community of believers.</note> of Ephesus, and which had to be amended, namely the leaving of their first Love. 1057.
That the leaving of our first Love for Christ is a very lamentable sin. 1061.
Of the causes of the leaving of the first Love of Christians. 1063.
Of the signs of the cooling of Divine Love. 1067.
Application of all the preceding, containing a sorrowful complaint over the leaving of our first Love, with an earnest awakening to amend that. 1070.
The remedies through which the aforementioned defect must be amended, three are proposed here. 1078.
That we must above all remember from whence we have fallen, in order to amend the leaving of our first Love. 1079.
That we must strive to have true repentance over the falling away from our first

<column-break/>

Love, should we be able to rise up from it, and that to this end our hearts must be improved. 1085.
That we must strive to do our first works, should we be awakened in our first Love. 1094.
That those Congregations of Christ which have left their first love, and cannot be moved to their former zeal by any warning, stand in great peril of being devastated. 1101.
That the Lord Christ himself will devastate such Congregations that will not awaken in their first Love through any warning. 1108.
When the Lord Christ will bring about the threatened punishment, namely very quickly, if one does not repent. 1112.
With what discretion or condition the Lord Christ threatens the aforementioned punishment. 1117.
Conclusion; Containing an earnest exhortation to amend that which is disturbed among us, so that we might be preserved, and the Lampstand <note>A reference to Revelation 2:5, where the 'lampstand' represents the church's presence and God's favor.</note> of the Holy Gospel might be confirmed among us. 1123.

WE Christians know from the word of God that the sin of pride <note>original: "hoovaerdye"; in this context, it refers to an arrogant self-sufficiency that rejects God’s authority</note> is one of the most abominable and most harmful sins to the soul of man: which in an outstanding way makes God an adversary to man; whereas, on the contrary, the virtue of humility <note>original: "nedrigheyt"; a central theme in Teellinck’s spirituality, meaning a posture of complete dependence on God</note> is one of the most glorious and most profitable virtues for the souls of men. As this appears irreutably from the testimony of the Apostle Peter, 1 Pet. 5: verse 5. Where he says: *God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.* What is more harmful and destructive for the soul of man than to have God’s opposition against oneself? One would much rather have all creatures as our adversaries than God alone. How can it go well for the soul of man when God resists him? Since man can perform nothing good without God. How carefully should every Christian then guard themselves from the sin of pride. What is there also, on the other hand, more profitable and glorious for man than to receive grace from God? For *God’s loving-kindness is better than life*, Psalm 63: verse 4. And therefore, how every Christian ought, according to the lesson of Christ, to learn from Him, his Master, this virtue of humility, Matthew 11: verse 29. How every Christian ought to investigate with diligence and search out the holy truth of the Reformed Christian Religion <note>The "Gereformeerde Chriſtelijcke Religie" refers specifically to the Dutch Reformed faith established after the Synod of Dort</note> presented to us in the Holy Scripture; which is also particularly directed toward this end: to cast down all high-minded thoughts of the naturally proud heart, and to place man rightly humble before the Lord his God.

Therefore, beloved Reader, do you have any desire for this glorious virtue of humility? Do you wish to be adorned with this excellent ornament of this prominent virtue, so that you may be pleasing in the eyes of your spiritual Bridegroom <note>A common metaphor in devotional literature referring to Jesus Christ as the husband of the believer’s soul</note>; then learn, meditate, and seek to press upon your souls that which is found in these treatises of this hon—

But so that man, through the consideration of his lost blessedness and present wretchedness, should not become despondent and be placed beyond all hope of restoration: the Author goes on in that first **Treatise** to point out time and again how the Lord Christ—the second Adam <note>In Christian theology, Christ is called the "second Adam" because he undoes the spiritual damage caused by the fall of the first Adam.</note>—and His own people through His Spirit, go about restoring that blessed state which they had lost through the sin of the first Adam. For the doctrine of Faith shows and reveals to man that the right to eternal salvation is not to be obtained through our own works that we perform, but only through the merits of the Lord Jesus Christ, which the Christian must receive through Faith if he ever wishes to become an heir of eternal life. But if you wish to have general rules from God’s Word in this so doubtful matter of clothing, against which you can mirror yourself and your attire to see if they are good and proper: then read this third *Treatise* by this *Author*, and it shall give you thorough instruction from God’s Word, and also strip away the veils of shame with which this sin seeks to hide its ugliness.

## Beloved
# R E A D E R .

<image-desc>A large decorative ornamental drop cap 'A' featuring intricate floral and scrollwork patterns within a square frame.</image-desc>
As one observes with attention the behavior of the children of men in these our days, one finds that many labor for the food that perishes, but very few for the food that remains for eternal life <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 6:27: "Do not work for the food that perishes, but for the food that endures to eternal life."</note>. Many are preoccupied with an excessive, even heathen concern regarding their livelihood in this present life: yet they care nothing at all for that exceedingly great eternal weight of their salvation. It is so sorrowful in this regard that one might justly confront almost everyone with a rebuke, that they trouble themselves with many things when only one thing is necessary <note>An allusion to the story of Martha and Mary in Luke 10:41-42, where Jesus says, "Martha, you are anxious and troubled about many things, but one thing is necessary."</note>, which is nonetheless lamentably neglected by them: <margin>Matthew 11 verse 12.</margin> for how few there are who take the Kingdom of Heaven by force, and thus seize it with violence <note>Original Dutch: <term>geweldt doen</term>, referring to the biblical concept of spiritual zeal or "holy violence" in pursuing God.</note>. One might be amazed and astonished by this, thinking how can it be that God’s people (who are daily instructed in the glory of eternal happiness and the terror of eternal damnation) so little work out their salvation with fear and trembling. But if one considers the matter more maturely: one shall find that it is not so much to be wondered at. For although all who attend the ministry of God’s word are abundantly instructed, both in the glorious happiness that God’s children shall perfectly enjoy in God above in Heaven for all eternity; and also in the unbearable pains that the ungodly shall suffer in Hell for all eternity, both in soul and body after the Day of Judgment: yet it happens that many of those who enjoy such instruction nevertheless do not believe it in their hearts; even though they outwardly acknowledge the truth of it with their

<summary>In this preface, the author laments that people prioritize their physical needs over their eternal salvation, noting that despite constant religious instruction, many fail to truly believe in the realities of Heaven and Hell.</summary>

->To the Reader.<-

...confess with their mouth. It cannot be said how greatly atheism <note>In the 17th century, "atheism" often referred to "practical atheism"—living as if God does not exist—rather than just a philosophical denial of His existence.</note> has crept in among us: so much so that God’s servants, when they preach of Heaven and of Hell, may also complainingly say, "Who has believed our preaching?" <note>A reference to Isaiah 53:1 and Romans 10:16, expressing the frustration of a preacher whose message is ignored.</note> For how many are there among us who, if they were to pour out their hearts before the Lord, would have to confess that they have no inclination nor desire for heavenly happiness; nor any horror or fear of hellish damnation, and thus live entirely carelessly. It is no wonder then that they do not concern themselves with what shall happen after this life, since they do not believe in it.

So there are also many who indeed believe with a <term>historical faith</term> <note>Historical faith (<term>historisch geloof</term>) was a theological term for an intellectual acceptance of Biblical facts that lacks the transformative power of "saving faith."</note> that after this life the glory of Heaven is prepared for God’s children and the torments of hell for the godless and unrepentant: who nevertheless have such a perverted sense of His grace, that they imagine to themselves that God is so gracious and merciful that He will take the sinner—who has lived in sin his whole life—into grace even at his departure from this world, and will grant him heavenly happiness if he but once calls out to Him, "Lord be merciful to me, a poor sinner." Yet our Savior has so expressly said in Matthew 7 verse 21: *Not everyone who says to me, "Lord, Lord," shall enter the Kingdom of Heaven: But he who does the will of my Father who is in Heaven.* Few among us rightly consider that although God’s grace and mercy are infinite, they are only for those who are in Christ, who are incorporated into Christ through true faith. Thus, as long as the sinner is outside of Christ, he is also outside of God’s grace; so that God will deal with all those who are and remain estranged from Jesus Christ not according to His infinite mercy, but according to strict, avenging justice. It is no wonder then that people, who imagine such a perverted mercy of God for themselves, and think that heavenly happiness is so easily obtained, employ no labor or effort to be saved.

But furthermore, even many of those who now believe that God’s grace for salvation is only for those who accept Christ through true faith, wrongly convince themselves that they believe in the Lord Jesus because they believe that the Lord died for them—just as if all those who can merely imagine that the Lord Jesus is their Savior, possess the true...

For this reason, it is most highly necessary that the Lord’s Congregation be thoroughly opened up and the entire nature of true <term>saving faith</term> <note>Saving faith (*zaligmakend geloof*) refers to a faith that actually leads to salvation, characterized by a heart-change and devotion, as opposed to a mere intellectual belief or "historical faith."</note> be plainly revealed. For *Satan* and man's own corrupt heart are very much intent on miserably deceiving each and every person in this matter: just as they hand those who are still completely devoid of true saving faith a false faith <note>The original Dutch uses *waen-geloove*, meaning a delusional or imagined faith.</note> as if into their hand, and then seek to make them believe that such is a true faith—in order to keep them in it to their eternal ruin. And therefore, to expose the deceit of our spiritual enemies in this matter on both sides, it is necessary that it be plainly pointed out from the Word what true saving faith is; this present *Treatise* shall now clearly show us this.

For our *Author* in this *Treatise* very clearly points out—even for the understanding of the simple—the nature and working of true saving faith, as he particularly does in the 5th chapter of the 2nd Book of this *Treatise*. There he teaches that the nature and working of true faith is to accept the Lord *Christ* just as *God* presents Him to us in His Word: not only as our High Priest to reconcile us with *God* for our sins through His Sacrifice; but also as our *Prophet*, to teach us the way of salvation, and as our *King*, to command and rule us. And so he exposes the deceit of those with false faith, who satisfy themselves with the idea that they are reconciled with God for their sins through *Christ's* blood (as they think), without concerning themselves with also being sanctified by *Christ* through His *Spirit*. And so this *Author* is throughout this *Treatise* especially busy convincing those careless *Christians* of the deception of their false faith; which truly is a matter that is exceedingly necessary in these careless, easy-going, and false-faith-filled [times]; for very many among us suffer the shipwreck of their salvation upon this rock. ### To the Reader.

...[it] seems to be intended to convince us all that a faith in Christ which is separated from true holiness is not that <term>salvation</term> <note>The original Dutch uses *zaligheid*, which implies both the state of being saved and the state of eternal blessedness.</note>—it is not that true faith through which one can be saved.

If you then, beloved Reader, love your soul, and would not wish it to be lost through smooth-talking <term>carelessness</term> <note>The original Dutch *soetvoerige sorgloosheydt* describes a dangerous state of spiritual apathy or unconcern that feels pleasant or "sweet" but leads to ruin.</note>, but rather to be saved through a true faith in Christ; then live, love, hope, and believe that which is presented to you here from the Word of God. Thus (with God’s Spirit working therein), this Treatise may be a means toward your eternal preservation and salvation: which I wish for you with all my heart from that God, who is able to do all things.

# THE TOUCHSTONE
## Of
# FAITH
## CHAPTER I.

That God the Lord has uniquely established faith in His Son Jesus Christ as the way through which mankind must be saved; in order to further spread His glory, and to strip man of all boasting. But that many wicked people pervert this path of God toward salvation into a blasphemy of the name of God, and to their own deeper destruction.
