## CHAPTER II.

->That the ungrateful people of this age only scheme how they might serve God the Lord with the least labor and effort, although the Lord very graciously invites them to serve Him abundantly.<-

Thus also the days of this age are so evil that we perceive everywhere that love has grown remarkably cold, and that true faith is hardly to be found on earth: Indeed, we now live in a time in which the base, ungrateful person seeks to deceive his God, and is only out for this; how he might serve the Lord his God, from whom he has everything, with the least labor and effort. Nevertheless, the Lord our great and entirely gracious God has so richly opened the bosom of His grace and love to us—to indeed restrain us within the <term>godly life</term> <note>Teellinck uses "Goddelıjcke leven" to describe a life lived in accordance with God's will and Spirit.</note>—when He gave His own only-begotten Son from His bosom among the children of men, and also let Him become man, and die the cursed death of the cross for the salvation of men and the <term>satisfaction</term> <note>original: "voldoeninghe." This refers to the theological concept of "Penal Substitutionary Atonement," where Christ pays the legal debt for human sin.</note> for all their sins and crimes, such as should rightly soften hearts of stone: for surely no greater, more wonderful, higher, nor more alluring kindness and grace can be imagined to awaken godliness in the hearts of men; Titus 2: verses 11, 12, 13. It being a work of grace, worthy of the benevolence of the great God, surpassing all the kindness of the children of men in an infinite manner: which therefore should also rightly awaken all hearts and minds that come to hear of it to a completely

<column-break/>

great and fiery reciprocal love toward the Lord our good God; so as to likewise hold nothing, nothing in the world too dear nor too precious that they would not gladly give up to please this, their good God, who did not consider His own, only, and well-beloved Son too precious to give for them.

Thus, certainly all those to whom this exceeding wealth of God’s grace is revealed (for that does not happen to everyone) are, among all people on earth, most of all obligated to serve and cling to this our good God with all faithfulness and earnestness; and to spare no effort nor labor to please Him.

But although it should be so, and this should rightly be practiced in this way; yet we see (which truly can never be lamented enough) that not only among those to whom this great mystery has only been outwardly revealed, many are found who in no way respond to this exceeding kindness of God with diligent obedience (just as we know that among the so-called Christians, to whom this grace is also proclaimed, very many are found everywhere who live so entirely un-Christianly that they justify the heathens themselves by their actions) but also even among those who not only boast of knowing this exceeding grace of God (which the double-

## CHAPTER V.

### That although it is true that we can only be justified before God's Judgment through the perfect righteousness of Christ: nonetheless true godliness is not empty within us.

Although we may not place our confidence for salvation upon anything that we can do, but only upon the grace of God over us, absolutely for the sake of the perfect satisfaction of **Christ Jesus**; yet when the question arises: how a person shall assure themselves whether God the Lord, for Christ's sake, will be merciful to them for salvation (since it is indeed certain and sure that the Lord is not merciful to all people, nor grants heaven to all, for the sake of the perfect satisfaction of Christ Jesus) then we must see what God the Lord has wrought in us toward godliness for Christ's sake. For even the rough jailer <note>original: "Stockwaerder." Refers to the Roman official in Acts 16 who guarded Paul and Silas.</note> could not assure himself that God would be merciful to him for Christ’s sake in any other way than by what he felt now wrought within him: a different heart and mind, namely to do good to and cherish the members of Christ whom he had previously treated very poorly and insulted, *Acts 16.* Just as **Rahab** the harlot <note>original: "Hoere." Rahab is a biblical figure from the Book of Joshua praised in the New Testament for her faith.</note> could not have expected through faith that she would be spared above all those of **Jericho**, except as she found wrought in her heart by God that she would henceforth acknowledge and cling to the God of Israel as her only God; and so it still stands with all other true believers.

It can also in no way consist with any orthodox Scriptural judgment, nor with the proper reverence and respect for the high Majesty of our God and

<column-break/>

His holiness, that anyone, whoever they might be, should or could assure themselves on the ground of God’s word that God the Lord would want to preserve and save them for the sake of the perfect satisfaction of Christ, who was still so vile, so enslaved, and servant-hearted toward sin that they would (even while thus assuring themselves of God's grace toward them for Christ's sake) still be and remain resolved to continue in their evil life, as is the case with many; and would not have a free, sincere, unfeigned, and effective intention and purpose (which involves the use of the means <note>The "means of grace" typically refer to prayer, studying scripture, and participating in the sacraments.</note>) before God the Lord, who knows hearts and minds <note>original: "herten, en nieren," literally "hearts and kidneys," a biblical idiom for one's innermost thoughts and emotions.</note>, to break off their sins from now on, and to go and serve their God, and to live for God, and to cling with all their strength to Him who has given them His Son and eternal salvation in Him.

pride and arrogance often tend to carry themselves very high (as their own consciences know and their words sometimes clearly reveal) whenever they think they have done something good; they tend to secretly harbor in their hearts certain conceited virtues (if they have even that many) to set against their known sins, and thereby to deaden the gnawing and remorse of their conscience now and then. In contrast, it is quite different with the true believer, who, in the matter of justification <note>justification: the theological concept of being declared righteous or "in the right" before God.</note> for salvation, constantly cries out to God: *Lord, do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no one living will be righteous in your sight,* Psalm 143 and Psalm 32. And this movement and working is so sincere and so powerful in true believers that they find in practice that the more they feel strengthened to do many good works, the more they sincerely renounce all trust in those good works. For as they apply themselves to good works, they also become more and more aware through their daily practice of their great imperfections, and how everything they do is merely "piecework" <note>piecework: an expression meaning incomplete or fragmentary effort.</note>; for nothing but that which is perfect can stand in the Judgment of God, which is weighed according to the truth, Romans 2: verse 2. Indeed, what is more, they also vividly experience that it is not they, but the grace of God within them, that makes them work more abundantly than others, 1 Corinthians 15:10. From this it results and

<column-break/>

arises that the more good works they do, the more they feel their own insufficiency, because they perceive better through those works how much they fall short in many things. They also come to realize more clearly that the good works they perform are so far from putting the Lord God under any obligation to them (since it is the truth that even when they have done all they can, they are still useless servants in God's sight, and have merely done what they were obligated to do) Luke 17:10. On the contrary, the good works they do bind them even more to God, because it has pleased Him so graciously to nourish and strengthen them through His Spirit to be willing and able to do such good, Philippians 2:12, and then to still accept those works with favor for Christ’s sake, however imperfect they may be.

This holy, humble, and sincere impulse we find very vividly expressed in the godly David, when he and his people were found willing and ready to so heartily promote the great work of building the Temple; for his heart breaks out in this thanksgiving to his God, saying: 1 Chronicles 29: verses 14, 15, 16, 17, 18.

> 13. Now then, our God, we thank and praise your glorious name.
> 14. For who am I, and what is my people, that we should have obtained the power to give so willingly as this? For everything is from you; we give to you out of your own hand.
> 15. For we are strangers and sojourners before your face, just like all our fathers: our days on earth are like a shadow, and there is no hope.
> 16. Lord our God, all this abundance—

<page-num>437</page-num>

...which we have prepared to build you a House for the name of your holiness, <note>David is referring to the building of the First Temple in Jerusalem.</note> that it is from your hand, and it is all yours.
17. And I know, my God, that you test the heart, and that you have a pleasure in uprightness; I have, in the uprightness of my heart, freely given all these things, and I have now with joy seen your People, who are found here, that they have behaved willingly toward you.
18. O Lord God of our Fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, preserve this forever in the inclination of the thoughts of the heart of your People, and direct their heart to you.

Now, who is there who reads this with a God-fearing heart and does not immediately perceive that David considered himself very greatly beholden to God—that He had made him and his people powerful enough to do that good work (to promote the building of the Temple so heartily)? He was so far from any thought that he would have wanted to come boasting and bragging before his God, or introducing it as a <term>meritorious work</term> <note>A "meritorious work" refers to the idea that a human action can earn a reward, like salvation, from God—a concept the author is arguing against.</note> for which the Heavenly Temple should rightfully be given to him as a reward. From this, we can also conclude that although David labored greatly in the work of the Lord and very diligently applied himself to <term>Godliness</term>, he nevertheless did not (as the Apostle teaches) rely on his good works or piety in the matter of <term>justification</term> <note>justification: the theological act of being declared righteous in God's sight.</note>. Instead, he only expected or trusted to be kept and saved through the simple grace and unmerited <term>satisfaction</term> <note>satisfaction: the theological belief that Jesus' sacrifice "satisfied" or paid the debt of sin.</note> of Jesus, Acts 15: verse 11. And so, this faith of his was also credited to him as righteousness, Rom. 4: 5. And thus have all other Godly and right-believing people

<column-break/>

behaved and conducted themselves, always praying to God the Lord that He would not enter into judgment with them, Psalm 143: verse 3. They have even sought and desired <insert>pardon</insert> from God for their best works, wishing that He would deal with them not according to their merits, but according to His great mercy, Neh. 13: 22. So it is that the true nature, power, and working of <term>saving faith</term> shows itself here: it makes the Christian person observe good works as diligently as if Heaven itself were to be earned by them; and yet, once they are done, the Christian person learns to rely so little on them as a matter of merit as if he had never done any good works in his life, Philip. 3: 3. For the whole purpose of Christian faith is to magnify the Lord Jesus Christ and His atonement, and to glorify Him in our salvation. Therefore, it not only makes us renounce all trust in our good works, but it also makes us take heart all the more in doing good works, the more earnestly to go out of ourselves toward Christ; to esteem the satisfaction of Christ all the higher, and to observe the fellowship of it more diligently. Just as we certainly know that the more Godly a person becomes, the more he prizes the merits of Christ. One finds every day that there are no people under the Sun who observe the fellowship of Christ with greater diligence than those who have increased the most in Godliness; see Phil. 3: verses 7, 8, 9.

And here now the case of the true believer turns out so happily, whereas otherwise only grounds for mistrust and desperation would follow: namely, that he feels, finds, and perceives that even his best works still...

...piety and godliness / which then ensures that he does not rely—in the work of <term>justification</term> <note>Justification is the theological concept of being declared righteous before God, not through one's own deeds, but through faith.</note> for salvation—upon the worthiness of his own faith / but solely upon the worthiness of the <term>satisfaction of Christ</term> <note>The "satisfaction" (Dutch: *voldoeninge*) refers to the belief that Jesus’ death paid the full debt for human sin.</note> / which he can receive through true faith / and through that alone; Consider with me a common analogy of a man guilty of a capital offense / who has received a <term>pardon</term> <note>The original uses *remis*, a legal term for the remission of a penalty.</note> from the Prince; and now pleads his case before the judgment seat.

### Touchstone of Faith.

**Column 1:**

For people who doubt their faith or salvation, and to whom we might more closely reveal the character, nature, power, and true condition of true **Saving Faith**; we must first and foremost hear a little what the specific literal meaning of the word "faith" is, as it is used in the text of Holy Scripture.

**To believe**, both according to the nature of our **Dutch** <note>The author uses "duytsch" to refer to the Dutch vernacular of the 17th century.</note> word, and according to the nature of the word that the Holy Spirit uses in the **original text** <note>original: "Grondt-text," referring to the original Hebrew of the Old Testament and Greek of the New Testament.</note> of the Holy Scripture, signifies holding for truth that which is presented to us, because we consider the one who presents it to be **trustworthy**, or because we judge the arguments of knowledge that he brings forward to be so sound that they arouse our consent. From this it appears that **to believe** something, or **to know** something for certain, are distinct in the common meaning of these words. For that which we know for certain—that which we have indeed seen ourselves, or understood through certain and firm reasons—we do not say (if we speak properly) that we **believe** it; rather, we say that we **know** it well, and that we are sure and certain of it. But that which is related to us by others, and which we do not know otherwise than through their account and through the evidence they give us of it; that we say we **believe**, when we hold it for truth. And if we do not believe it, if we do not hold it for truth, then we are accustomed to say: "I believe that," when we want to indicate that we hold it for truth, and conversely, "I do not believe," when we want to indicate that we do not hold it for truth. What we then do not know for certain through our own senses or understanding, but accept only on trust or on some kind of probable evidence—

<column-break/>

**Column 2:**

—holding it for truth, is then [called] **to believe**. Now, the belief [or acceptance] of what is said to us [is not] always equally strong; sometimes [it is without any] doubt at all, because of [the cer]tainty that we have [from the truthfulness] of the person [whom we] rely upon, or from the firm[ness of the] reasons by which we [have been] won over. And then [we are] well-accustomed to say, not only [that we] believe, but also that we [know it, as if] we knew it for certain; [at other times] we indeed have doubt about [it, yet] hold it rather for [truth than for a] lie. In which case [it is] common to say [that we "think"] that it is so; and this is [often not called] **faith**, but **opinion** <note>original: "opinie"</note> [though] we may also be said [to some] degree truly to believe [it, since] our consent there [is stronger] than toward the opposite; [here] we struggle against the [uncertainty], as is commonly [the case in the] faith of the children of God [regarding] salvation.

And in both these meanings, the word "faith" [is used] throughout our common speech, and [also] in Holy Scripture. But [because there] are two kinds of things [presented to us] now and then by occasion [to be believed], that is, to be held [as truth]; [one kind] contains a naked account [of things] which otherwise do not [concern or] affect us; others which also [contain] such things as [personally] concern us, to do them [or to experience] them; so there falls, regarding [those thin]gs about which faith [is exercised], although otherwise to [hold for truth] what is said to us is [the same] act in the nature of [the soul, a] distinction also in the matters themselves.

saving faith <note>original: "saligmakende geloove." In Reformed theology, this refers specifically to the faith that leads to eternal life, as opposed to a mere intellectual belief.</note> is particularly given to us by God, namely to receive the Savior of the World with it; for in this also consists our only well-being and salvation: that we receive the Lord Jesus Christ—who is generally presented to us as a Savior in the Word—specifically through faith as our Savior. For this is also certain and sure: that true saving faith justifies and saves us in no other way than by making us receive Christ, the Savior of the World, and by which we are subsequently united with Christ. True saving faith looks to the whole Word of God and has its operation therein; it accepts the commands of God, the threats according to their nature, and especially all the promises of God, of whatever kind they may be, per-

<column-break/>

taining to this life and the life to come: promises of strengthening in the godly life, in the time of tribulation, and such; but through all these, faith does not justify us, nor does it make us saved through these; it justifies us and makes us saved only because it rests upon Christ; because it receives the Lord Jesus Christ, the Savior of the world, and unites us with him, and consequently makes us partakers of all his treasures and riches, for our complete reconciliation and salvation.

Thus, from these receptions of Christ follow all the other glorious workings of saving faith, some of which we have touched upon above; of which we shall speak somewhat more closely and distinctly in the following Chapter.

# CHAPTER VII.

->What beautiful workings or fruits come forth from our<-
->union with Christ, by which true Saving faith<-
->can also be tested.<-

---

The workings, or fruits, that spring forth from our union with Christ are very many and very glorious, but can all be brought under two main headings. The first are such workings as the Lord God Himself has prepared for the believers—yet apart from their own work <note>original: "buyten haer werck." This refers to 'monergism,' the theological idea that God acts alone in certain aspects of salvation, such as adoption, without the human being 'earning' it.</note>—for their comfort and salvation, in view of the fact that they are now truly united through faith with Christ His Son. Others are such as are wrought within them by virtue of the union itself, and from the fact that we are partakers of the power of Christ.

<column-break/>

As for the first kind, they are these four:
1. The Lord God adopts the believers, who are now united with Christ, as His children.
2. He credits to them the merits of Christ <note>original: "verdiensten Christi." This is the doctrine of 'imputed righteousness,' where Christ's perfect life is legally credited to the believer's account.</note>.
3. He considers Himself thus perfectly reconciled with them.
4. And consequently, He justifies them and declares them free from damnation, and grants them eternal life; and with all these, the matter stands thus:

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the spiritual benefits of being united with Christ. <header>Touchstone of Faith.</header>

3. The growth in the same.
4. Our glorification.

In this regard, it stands thus:

First, we, being made one with Christ through faith, receive not only a share in his merits, but also in his life-giving Spirit, and in the power of his death and his resurrection. Through this, our corrupt nature is so subdued, and we are so fashioned after the image of Christ, that we truly become **new creatures** and **partakers of the Divine nature**. In this respect, we are said to be **born again** from the incorruptible seed of God’s Word (1 Peter 1:22; 2 Peter 1:4). This occurs in such a way that we now receive a more noble birth than we ever had before; for through this rebirth, we are entirely changed and renewed in all the powers of our souls and the members of our bodies, receiving a **new heart** and a **new Spirit**. Thus, where we were previously inclined toward all evil and useless for any good, we now begin to be turned away from evil and become fit for all good works.

Secondly, being made one with Christ through faith, and thus being reborn to a new life (1 Peter 1:3) and provided with a **new heart** and **new Spirit** (Ezekiel 36:25, 26), we then immediately begin to lead a new life and to live by faith. We express the life of Christ in our mortal bodies, so that we may say with the truth: *I live, yet no longer I, but Christ lives in me; and the life which I now live in the flesh, I live by the faith of the Son of God* (Galatians 2:20). Everyone knows that life is active; wherever it exists, it shows itself more or less, even if it were only in a

<column-break/>

quiet breath or in the beating of the pulse. Just as it is with those who sleep or lie in a faint, so it is with believers: however poorly they may sometimes seem to be doing, if a <term>discerning Christian<note>original: "verstandigh Christen," referring to someone with spiritual maturity and insight.</note></term> comes to "feel their pulse" (as the saying goes), he will find that there is life in them. Through God’s grace, he shall soon bring them back to themselves and to a better life.

Thirdly, regarding the **growth** in this new life, we must know that just as in nature, newborn infants—if they have the spark of life and are healthy—grow and increase in size and strength from day to day, so it is with the children of God (1 Peter 2:2). Now, this growth in the new life consists in this: that from day to day, one puts off more and more the "old rags" of the **old man** and adorns oneself with the virtues of the **new man** (Ephesians 4:22, 23, 24). Thus we cleanse ourselves more and more in preparation for when we shall come to **see God as he is** (1 John 3:3). This then causes a constant struggle between the flesh and the Spirit for as long as we are here—between the **old man**, who is being crucified in us and struggles against it, and the **new man**, who is more and more expected in us and who will not excuse the old man in the least (Galatians 5:17).

Fourthly, after the believing person here on earth has thus endured until the end in the Christian life through faith in Christ, he is given the **crown of righteousness** when he departs from this world; that is, the eternal life of joy (2 Timothy 4:7, 8). First, this is given to the soul as soon as he dies (Philippians 1:23), and thereafter to both soul and body when the Lord Christ shall come in the clouds,

And by this proposition, God-seeking hearts are best comforted, and all those minded toward the world are best terrified: for all God-seeking hearts find this, that they are always so minded that they wish to seek their salvation in no one else but in Christ, and that they also sincerely intend to walk according to all the commandments of God. Those who then do not wish to seek their salvation in Christ are certainly not worthy of any Christian comfort; nor are those who are not minded to live henceforth according to the will of God (who knows the <note>The original Dutch uses "herten en nieren" (hearts and kidneys), a biblical idiom for a person's innermost thoughts and emotions.</note> hearts and minds); it does no harm that such people, as long as they are so disposed (even assuming they were once right-believers themselves, but were snatched away by an evil turning), can draw no comfort from this Christian doctrine, but are instead terrified by it in every way. For as long as a person is so disposed that he will not conform himself to God’s word, then God’s word must look upon such a person as sour and stern; it cannot comfort such people, nor speak peace to them.

And furthermore, since much deception occurs because everyone boasts that he seeks and wishes to seek salvation only in the Lord Jesus Christ—for even the deceptive Spirit gladly makes some believe that they do so—we therefore judge that one of the surest and most infallible tests of true saving faith is this: that truly the person who testifies that he seeks his salvation in Christ alone, should further see whether he also has the unfeigned desire to live the time that remains according to the will of God by way of gratitude; see, we consider this to be

<column-break/>

the very surest and most infallible test: the Devil will never preach this to us.

Nor does it conflict with this that it is also often found that some seem for a time to embrace the commandments of God quite diligently, to obey them to the honor of God, who nevertheless are found in secret not to have been right-believers, since they soon become weary of it and turn back to the world. For it also cannot be denied that many who seemed to greatly rejoice over the gracious promises of God made in Christ, and to rest themselves upon them, are also found in secret not to have been right-believers, since they also soon fall away from that joy of theirs whenever any difficulty or trouble meets them regarding the confession of their faith.

Then this is also added: that one finds in deed and in truth that even the right-believers are now and then, in the time of <term>spiritual assault<gloss>The original "aenvechtinge" refers to intense periods of doubt, temptation, or spiritual struggle.</gloss></term>, led away or pushed back from that joy of comfort which flows from the gracious promises of God, established in Christ Jesus our Lord, and are thereby cast down as being entirely disconsolate. In such a case, even the right-believers have no other instruction by which they can be distinguished from the unbelieving or those with a <note>original: "waen-geloovige"</note> false faith, than that in all this they still seek the Lord according to His commandment; and by practicing His prescribed means, they sincerely strive to avoid the evil that He forbids them and to fulfill the good that He commands them, making that still the always-held course of their lives; wherein the unbelieving and those with false faith always fall short.

### ->Touchstone of Faith.<-

...it is found to be a principal and most excellent distinction (one that is especially felt and must always be present where there is to be comfort) between the right-believer and the unbeliever: namely, that right-believers, in the course of their lives, so rely (according to the Holy Gospel) upon the Lord Christ for salvation that they always seek to present themselves as pleasing to the Lord and to walk according to all His commandments. This is in contrast to the unbelieving and the deluded-believers <note>The original Dutch *waen-geloovige* refers to someone whose faith is based on a "waen"—a delusion, fancy, or false impression.</note> who, in the vain pride of Christ, expect salvation regardless of how they live, and only serve the Lord as far as it suits them, is convenient, or pleases them. In such a way, even if the deluded-believers sometimes seem to intend to live according to all God's commandments, it is found in practice that their intention is merely like an untimely fruit that has no root, and therefore quickly withers and perishes, <note>original: "Matth. 13:6"</note> *Matthew 13:6*. Whereas, on the contrary, it is found that the intention of true believers to walk according to all God's commandments grows stronger and stronger over time, and brings forth true obedience better and better, <note>original: "Prov. 4:18. Psal. 37:31. 1 Tim. 4:8."</note> *Proverbs 4:18, Psalm 37:31, 1 Timothy 4:8*, as being well-rooted; for truly the right-believers have the root of the matter within themselves, <note>original: "Iob 19: vers 28"</note> *Job 19:28*. Thus, one can clearly see that true believers lead a steady course of life according to the commandments of God; and their transgressions are merely human stumbles and wanderings from the right path, on which they are nevertheless found to be proceeding all their lives; just like a man who goes to Jerusalem, and wants to go there, even though he 

<column-break/>

sometimes stumbles and wanders slightly, he constantly turns back again to the right way, so that anyone who watches his step can notice that the man is going to Jerusalem. On the contrary, the situation with the unbeliever or deluded-believer is such—as they know in their hearts, or as their conscience can tell if they watch their steps closely—that even if they sometimes have the purpose and intention to please God and walk according to all His commandments, nevertheless the constant course of their lives is otherwise. Thus, the transgressions of the right-believers are not just stumbles on the way of God’s commandments or unforeseen straying from the same path (from which they then immediately return), but the walks of the unbeliever or deluded-believer are merely like apparent departures from the way of the world, to which they themselves soon return.

Since this is found to be the case, we still deem it necessary, as we said before, that saving faith can best be distinguished from all other types of faith which do not save by the "obedience of faith," <note>original: "Rom. 1: vers 5"</note> *Romans 1:5*. This is provided one remembers that we are speaking here of how one distinguishes for oneself and for others all kinds of professors <note>In this context, a "professor" is someone who "professes" or openly declares their faith.</note> of saving faith; or to say it more clearly, how one shall distinguish between two people who both confess the true doctrine of Christ and both boast of trusting to be saved through Christ alone, of whom one is yet but a deluded-believer and the other a true believer; for it is for this purpose that we have specifically established this treatise.

# CHAPTER IX.

->Removal of a singular objection concerning the previously discussed test of true saving faith.<-

---

<margin>Rom. 4:5</margin>
But there is yet another passage of Holy Scripture, Romans 4:5, which thoughtless people tend to use as a pretext (just as Satan also teaches people to twist Holy Scripture itself to their own destruction, <note>original: "2 Peter 3:16"</note> with which soft-hearted, careless Christians want to excuse their actions, and which they very unwisely apply to their wrong feelings and to the nature of their unfit faith, which they maintain); it says thus: **to him who does not work, but believes in Him who justifies the ungodly, his faith is credited as righteousness.** From this they secretly conclude in their hearts (as is to be feared, although they do not dare to say it aloud, but their lives show it and shout it out with a loud voice) that practicing much in godliness, and in the working out of good works, would rather be a hindrance than a help for them to reach the certainty of true faith: since the text says so clearly, *not he who works, not he who is godly; but he who does not work, he who is ungodly, his faith is credited to him as righteousness*, as if that alone were the true old faith of Abraham, through which alone one can and must be justified and saved: that if one believes, even if one does not exert oneself in good works, nor diligently pursue godliness, one can and shall nevertheless just as quickly and just as well be justified and 

<column-break/>

saved. A more harmful claim than this cannot be imagined; nor a falser one; for the Apostle's meaning in that place is not that to him who does not apply himself to good works, nor exerts himself to live godlily, his faith shall nonetheless be credited as righteousness: for it was not so with Abraham and David, whose examples are brought in by the Apostle to confirm his proposition; indeed, it is found to be true in the whole Scripture that Abraham and David, although they also had their failings, were nevertheless the most godly people in their age; indeed, even people after God's heart, true examples of holy zeal; right models of true religious devotion, sincerity, and godliness.

Therefore we shall say, as the Apostle testifies, that God the Lord *justifies the ungodly*, that he speaks there according to the order that God the Lord maintains in leading people to salvation through faith in Christ, which is this, as we can note from the previously mentioned 7th chapter: namely that God the Lord, when we are engrafted into Christ, first accepts us as His children, and consequently deals kindly with us as with His children, credits the merits of Christ to us, and reconciles us with Himself, and thus justifies us; while we are still ungodly in ourselves, so that we have nothing of which we might boast; but since the unsuit- <note>The word "unsuitable" or "unbecoming" continues on the next page.</note>

<meta>This page continues the refutation of the idea that one can be "justified" while remaining intentionally ungodly. The author is explaining the "order" of salvation: how God's grace leads to a new life of gratitude.</meta>

<header>Touchstone of Faith,</header>

...likely it is that those who are chosen to be members of Christ, God's children, reconciled with God, and justified by God, should not stand out above other people; so the Lord also, out of pure grace for Christ's sake, goes on to make them into **new creatures**, <note>A "new creature" (Nieuwe Creatueren) refers to the biblical concept of regeneration, where a person is spiritually transformed by God's power.</note> gives them a new life, and makes them grow and increase therein, until they come to eternal life.

If we then pay close attention to this order, it is pertinently said by the Apostle that **God justifies the ungodly**; <note>referring back to the quote from Romans 4:5 on the previous page</note> and yet it by no means follows from this that anyone could assure themselves that they are truly justified, or that the testimony they feel within themselves—that they are reconciled with God—is not a deceptive testimony, but the testimony of the great and true God; even if they continue to live an ungodly life. For this is also certain and sure: that the testimony God gives of our reconciliation with Him is always powerful and is accompanied by the other concurrent workings of which we are now speaking. And this happens in such a way because all well-disposed children, as soon as they begin to perceive that God has been so graciously willing to be reconciled with them, immediately also begin to long and desire that they might show themselves grateful for it. To this end, they then need that renewal and that growth through which they prove their gratitude; and from this arises the greatest joy of their hearts, since nothing is more pleasant for a well-disposed heart (such as the heart of all true believers is) than that they can be thoroughly grateful for the benefit they have received.

When this believing person also...

<column-break/>

...who thus exerts himself most diligently in all good works, has to consider his justification before God, he cannot and may not regard himself as anything other than an **ungodly person** in himself. For he well knows that when God graciously justified him in Christ, he truly was such a one in himself. He also understands well that all his good works, which he has done thereafter, could not serve before God as a means by which he might be justified; for he knows well that he was previously justified by grace before God, even before he had done those good works. 

But he sees clearly that these works must fairly be shown by way of gratitude by all those who are already justified by grace before God, without works. And therefore, though he does his works, he does not consider himself justified before God because of them, <margin>1 Cor. 4:4</margin> <note>original: "I do not even judge myself... but it is the Lord who judges me."</note> but acknowledges solely by grace to have his justification from God, without works. This is true even though, through his works, he is increasingly recognized as being justified before God in Christ, both before men and before his own conscience, just as the Apostle James <note>original: "Iacobus"</note> teaches us: <margin>James 2:24</margin> <note>original: "You see that a person is considered righteous by what they do and not by faith alone."</note>

From all this, it then appears irrefutable that no one in the world can assure themselves on any grounds of God's word that they shall be justified by the satisfaction of Christ unto salvation, except those who also apply themselves to godliness. For throughout the whole of Scripture, the grace of God and salvation in Christ Jesus is promised not to those...

# Touchstone of Faith.

...those who vainly boast of faith, but rather to those who prove their faith by their works, James 2:18; to those who are truly converted to God from their evil works, Acts 16:18, 19; <note>The text cites Acts 16, though the author may be thinking of the broader call to conversion in Acts 26:18-19.</note> to those who do the will of the Father, Matthew 7:21; who are obedient to the Son, Hebrews 5:9; who listen to the voice of the Spirit, Hebrews 3:7; and observe the commandments of God, throughout Psalm 119.

And this is so certain that we can find and perceive everywhere in the Holy Scripture that wherever the Holy Spirit is pleased to give us any description of **saving faith**, He generally directs it in such a way that He clearly gives us to understand that true faith necessarily produces the **practice of godliness**. <note>The Dutch term *Godtsaligheyt* (godliness) refers to a life lived in active, reverent devotion to God.</note> We shall briefly take up and explain some passages for this purpose. They are these:

The Apostle, speaking of the **Faith of the elect**, Titus 1:1, 2, declares to us there that it is *a knowledge of the truth, which is according to godliness, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, has promised*: by which he indeed very clearly gives us to understand that true saving faith is such a knowledge or science of the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, or of the Divine revelation presented to us in the Holy Scripture (which is here called "the truth" by excellence, John 17:17). This is *according to godliness*; that is, it in every way extends and promotes the **Christian life** and the **divine walk** in which true godliness is situated, Titus 2:11, 12, in the hope of eternal life, which God, who cannot lie, has promised in Christ Jesus. In such a way that true faith is such a knowledge of Divine

<column-break/>

things through which we come to see and acknowledge that the Divine things revealed to us in the Holy Scripture (which all invite and direct us toward godliness) are far, far, yes, far and away the very best, most precious, and most worthy things to be found in the world, as they contain within themselves the most precious treasure of eternal life. Therefore, it is only right that all those who come to truly know and acknowledge these things in their right value through the enlightenment of the Spirit, are accustomed to gladly forsake all advantages and all highly-esteemed things of this world, and all that their flesh holds dear and precious in themselves, and to "sell everything" in order to buy and obtain that **precious pearl of the truth** of God, Philippians 3:7, 8. <note>The author is likely alluding to the Parable of the Pearl of Great Price from Matthew 13:45-46 while citing Paul’s personal sacrifice in Philippians.</note> Therefore the Apostle also witnesses elsewhere: that those who have thus learned Christ, as the truth is in Jesus; that they should put off the **old man** who is corrupted through the lusts of deceit, and put on the **new man** who is created after God in true righteousness and holiness, Ephesians 4:21, 22, 24.

This is where many people fall short, even those who also boast of true faith: namely, that they have not truly opened their eyes to see the glory of the mysteries of the Kingdom of God, nor the preciousness and the great value of the glorious pearl of truth that is set before them. Therefore (whatever they may confess with their mouths) they do not come to properly "sell everything" so that they might buy that pearl; they do not come, for the sake of the love of that same precious truth, *to forsake all ungodliness and worldly lusts, that they might live temperately and righteously in this present world*. <note>A paraphrase of Titus 2:11-12.</note> Just as true believers do, Titus 2:11, 12.

For the truth that is presented to them, and which contains eternal life within itself, appears so beautiful in their eyes, that all the things of this world are as nothing in their eyes, in comparison to it.

Observing this, the Apostle further describes true faith thus: namely, that it is *a certain ground of things hoped for, and an evidence of things not seen*, Hebrews 11:1. <note>The Dutch *vaste gront* (certain ground/foundation) translates the Greek *hypostasis*, suggesting that faith gives reality or substance to future hopes.</note> That is, that true faith is such a knowledge of heavenly things (which God the Lord has promised us in His word, and which we expect through hope) which assures and confirms us of those heavenly things, so that they are as real and as glorious as if we saw them with our own eyes; and this because it is also an evidence—a strong conviction—of those same glorious and excellent things of the life to come, which God the Lord has promised us in His word, and which we do not yet see, but expect in hope. From this, the following effect inevitably follows for all those who are sober of mind—as all true believers are, Luke 15:17, 2 Timothy 2:26. <note>The reference to Luke 15:17 describes the Prodigal Son "coming to himself," which the author links to the "sobriety" or clarity of mind found in true repentance.</note>

<column-break/>

To this end also serves the description which the Apostle Peter gives us of true faith, 2 Peter 1:2, 3, 4, where he also declares that precious faith lies in such knowledge of Him who has called us to glory and virtue; through which the greatest and most precious promises have been given to us, so that through them we might become partakers of the Divine nature, after having escaped the corruption that is in the world through lust. Thus also giving us to understand more clearly that true faith is such a knowledge of Divine things whereby, through observing that glory presented to us, we are also most powerfully stirred up to virtue—that is, to true godliness—so that we might thus come to accept those very great and glorious promises; through which we are then made into new creatures, receiving another, yes, even a Divine nature, <note>The "Divine nature" (*Godtlijcker natuure*) refers to the spiritual transformation or "new birth" where the believer begins to reflect God's character.</note> which causes us to escape the corruption and reigning sinfulness which is in the world through lust; which then once again results in this: that true and precious faith causes us to pursue God's promises, to avoid godlessness, and to express godliness.

If one were to ask further whether the true saving faith <note>original: *salighmakende geloove*</note>—through which we are made one with Christ—precedes conversion (when conversion is understood as the total renewal of the person), then we may freely and without concern answer plainly that faith precedes that conversion. Or, to put it at its lowest requirement, at least those who wish to come to Christ, Revelation 22:17 <note>original: *Apoc. 22: 17*</note>. That is, those who are now so minded, and seeing that the Lord our God everywhere in His word requires of all those who wish to be His people (who must be made so through the Lord Jesus Christ) that they should forsake ungodliness and worldly lusts and live moderately, righteously, and godly in this present world <note>A reference to Titus 2:12.</note>; they must yield to this and desire to practice and begin this with the help and under the grace of their God, who must work in them both the willing and the doing of this matter. See, thus must a person be minded, and sincerely minded: namely, that they wish to turn from their sins and surrender themselves to Christ in the practice of the will of God; so should they come to Christ, receive Him through faith, be united with Him, and be saved through Him. This sincere <note>original: *ongeveynsde*, meaning unfeigned or without hypocrisy.</note> will must indeed be present; Revelation 22:17.

# Touchstone of Faith.

This kind of conversion necessarily precedes true faith; just as the Lord our God, in the administration of the means of salvation, follows that very path: that He first lets hearts understand through the Law <note>The "Law" refers to the Ten Commandments and biblical moral requirements, which theologians argued were meant to show people their own shortcomings.</note>, and through the offered grace of the **Holy Gospel**, allures them to a better disposition, so that being thus wrought upon, they might come to believe in **Christ**. See **Hosea 12:6**, **Matthew 21:21**. To this end it also serves that He sent **John the Baptist** as a forerunner of **Christ**, who was a preacher of repentance <note>original: "bekeeringe"; in this context, it refers to a turning away from sin.</note>, **Mark 1:2, 3, 4**.

Now, all this can be laid open clearly and plainly to even the simplest person, if we would only pay a little attention to how a person proceeds (being wrought upon by God) when they accept the Lord **Jesus**—who is presented generally to everyone in God's Word—specifically as their **Savior**, in order to be effectively saved and preserved by Him. For if we look closely at this, we shall find that the same is brought about through this, or a similar, faithful **syllogism** <term>syllogism: a logical argument where a conclusion is drawn from two premises (e.g., All men are mortal; Socrates is a man; therefore, Socrates is mortal).</term> leaning on the promises of God:

All those who are contrite <note>original: "verslaghen"; literally "beaten down" or struck with guilt.</note> and sorrowful for their sins (says the poor sinner), who indeed only wish to sincerely convert from their sins to God, to them the Lord **Jesus Christ** is specifically promised by God as a **Savior**; they may receive the Lord **Christ** as their **Savior**. **Isaiah 59:20**, **Matthew 11:28**, **Revelation 22:17**.

But (says the poor sinner, who

<column-break/>

would gladly receive **Christ**), I find through God’s grace this wrought in me: that I am sorrowful and contrite over my sins, indeed, that I now sincerely wish to convert to God from all my sins.

Therefore (concludes the poor <insert>sinner</insert> <note>The original OCR text "ar-daer" appears to be a typesetting error or abbreviation for "arme sondaer" (poor sinner).</note>), the Lord **Jesus Christ** with all His merits is also promised to me in particular; thus, I may freely approach to receive Him, so that through Him, I may be saved.

See thus, or in a similar manner, the heart of a person is led to receive the Lord **Christ** as their **Savior**: from which it fully appears that no one can grasp the Lord **Christ** through true faith who is not previously minded to separate from their sins and essence, and to give themselves over to **Christ**. Consequently, this kind of conversion precedes true saving faith and is like a preparation <note>original: "toe-beschickinghe"</note> of the person to be allowed to receive the Lord **Christ** the **Savior** in faith for their salvation.

Therefore, also, all those who wish to calmly assure themselves that they have a right saving faith must first find themselves so disposed: that with an unfeigned will they intend to separate from all worldly ways and henceforth conduct themselves according to the Law of God. This observation—just as it is the pure truth of God—is also of incredibly great utility for the building up of the **Church of Christ**, and must be [upheld] by all build[ers]...

<summary>This page explains that repentance and a sincere desire to turn from sin must precede saving faith, illustrated through a logical "syllogism" used by a believer to find assurance. The author argues that God uses the Law to prepare the heart before the Gospel can be received.</summary>
<keywords>conversion, saving faith, John the Baptist, syllogism, kontrite heart, Law and Gospel, assurance of salvation, Church of Christ</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the "order of salvation," specifically how a preliminary form of conversion (a turning away from sin) relates to "saving faith." The author is explaining that while this initial change of heart isn't the same as salvation itself, it is a necessary step that pleases God.</meta>

# Touchstone of Faith.

...must be properly noted and practiced in the house of the Lord.

So we must also know this: that although this kind of conversion <note>original: "bekeeringhe"; here referring to the initial turning toward God and away from sin.</note>—which we testify a person must have if they are to believe in **Christ**—is by no means sufficient for salvation, it is nevertheless so acceptable and pleasing to **God** that He will give the Lord **Christ** to no one except those who are already so minded.

This does not conflict with the testimony that it is impossible to please **God** without faith, **Hebrews 11, verse 6**. For we have sufficiently proven above that such a faith—believing that we are sinful and that **God** wants to be merciful to us if we repent—is necessary before a person can practice this conversion in any way. Therefore, this conversion is not entirely without faith. However, if one wishes to understand that passage as referring to *saving faith*, then one must also hold that it speaks of a "pleasing" that leads to eternal salvation. When we say that the aforementioned conversion is pleasing to **God**, we do not mean that this conversion is so pleasing that a person could be saved by it if they went no further; for we have previously proven that a person cannot be saved unless they are united with **Christ** through true saving faith. We only wish to say this: that the aforementioned conversion, which precedes saving faith, is pleasing to **God** insofar as it is

<column-break/>

a work of His **Spirit**, which prepares the person to be able to believe in **Christ**. Thus, we also find in **Holy Scripture** that many things are testified to have pleased **God**, even though they were done by those who did not yet possess true faith. Examples include **Jehu's** zeal in **2 Kings 9 and 10**, and the pious conduct of the **Young Man** of whom it is testified that **Christ** loved him, **Mark 10, verse 21**, even though he might still have been lost in his sins.

This, in turn, does not conflict with what is written: that whatever does not proceed from faith is sin, **Romans 14, verse 23**. For it is also clear from that same text that it speaks of a specific kind of faith <note>original: "bysonder gheloove"; referring here to the "faith of assurance" or confidence in the rightness of an action.</note> by which a person can be certain, on the basis of **God's** Word, that what they are doing is commanded or permitted by **God**. Anyone who does something without such faith—even if they otherwise possess saving faith—is certainly sinning, for they act against their conscience. Otherwise, we are accustomed to saying (and **God** also speaks thus in His **Word**), even to those who do not yet have true saving faith, that when they do what **God** has commanded them, it is "well done." On the other hand, we also know that if we look at the strictness of **God's Law**, the purity of His will, and our own frailty, even the best works performed by believers themselves are stained with sin. We know that all of this in no way hinders the truth of the preceding statement.

<summary>This page clarifies the relationship between preliminary repentance and saving faith, arguing that God is pleased by the initial work of the Spirit that prepares a heart for Christ, even before full salvation occurs. It distinguishes between the "faith" required for a clear conscience in daily actions and the "saving faith" required for eternal life.</summary>
<keywords>conversion, saving faith, Jehu, Rich Young Man, Hebrews 11, Romans 14, conscience, good works, preparation for grace</keywords>

# Touchstone of Faith.

Thus, the previously mentioned truth remains firmly established; we also hold it to be so and shall, at a more convenient opportunity by God’s grace, prove it more extensively: that this observation, along with the preceding ones now discussed in these two parts, can shed a very great light on many of the most difficult controversies <term>Controversien: theological disputes, particularly the intense 17th-century debates between Remonstrants and Counter-Remonstrants over the nature of grace and free will</term>, and on the most cunning objections and most harmful doubts,

<column-break/>

<header>To the Honorable, Pious, and God-fearing</header>

### ELDERS and DEACONS,
->of the Congregation of CHRIST in MIDDELBURG.<-

<image-desc>A decorative woodcut drop cap 'W' featuring a pastoral landscape with a figure and trees inside an ornate rectangular frame.</image-desc>
WE present to Your Honors <note>original: "U. E. E." (Uwe Edele Erwaerdigheden), a formal honorific for church officials.</note> here several Sermons, which we have given concerning the clothing of Christians; and now also present them to the good Congregation in print, as a faithful Mirror, made from the unadulterated substance of God’s word, which therefore shows the nature of clothing not according to the course of the world, but according to the word of the Lord. In which whoever shall be pleased to observe themselves with only a spiritual eye, may also soon become aware of whether they are so adorned in their clothing as might please the eye of the Lord *Christ*, or not. So also is our heart's wish to God, that all pious Christians would look away a little from the common corruption that is now in fashion <note>original: "in swange gaet," literally "in full swing."</note> everywhere in clothing, and that they would finally mirror themselves in the word of the Lord: and no longer (as many are accustomed to do) compare themselves with themselves, or with others, who just as well as they, have gone far beyond the limit. For we well know that many, who still stand in their [own] righteousness, would have to confess that they also have a hand in this transgression. Therefore it is right that each of us, whom the Lord has placed as leaders <term>voor-gangers (leaders/forerunners)</term> of the true Christian people—who must more and more die to the world—should offer a hand to help prevent such mischief; and to that end, to lead the good Congregation well in all ways, with a modest garment in ourselves, and in ours <note>Meaning within our own families and households.</note>: Considering that even the most excellent friends of the Lord, of whom the World was not worthy, *sometimes walked in Sheep-skins and Goat-skins, wandering in deserts, Hebr. 11. 37. 38.* And consequently, that it is God's great and undeserved grace that we (who are of the same confession with them) live in easier times, and may wear an honorable garment. With which we indeed ought to be well-satisfied in every respect, without in any way following the vanities of the world in this. All the more, because it is after all the people of standing (of which Your Honors are also especially so in God’s Congregation) who give the fashion of clothing to the people, since everyone indeed wants to follow such [people].

Now because we hope, that whatever others might do in this, that Your Honors will observe this, as those who well know that we should rather put on no worldly ostentation <note>original: "snof," referring to a trend, scent, or fashionable puffery.</note> or garment in eternity, than that we should offend one of the least of the Congregation of Christ therewith, *Matth. 18. 6. 1 Cor. 8. 13.* So we dedicate this Mirror of Modesty to Your Honors, so that Your Honors also might arrange and fit all your bodily ornament, and that of yours, according to it, as far as Your Honors shall find in conscience to be proper. And to that end, we conclude our discourse with the Apostle’s friendly admonition, which thus addresses his beloved in similar circumstances: *Whether you eat, whether you drink, or whether you do anything else (and therefore also dress yourself) do it all to the glory of God; be without giving offense, both to the Jews, and to the Greeks, and to the Congregation of God. Just as I also please everyone in all things, not seeking my own advantage, but the advantage of many, so that they might be saved, 1 Cor. 10. 31. 32. 33. Amen.* Fare well in the Lord. This 1st of January, 1620.

->Your Honors' willing fellow-worker in the Lord,<-
->Willem Teellinck.<-

<summary>Willem Teellinck dedicates his sermons on modest dress to the church leaders of Middelburg, urging them to set a pious example by avoiding worldly fashions. He argues that since common people imitate those of high standing, the elders and deacons must lead by dressing with Christian sobriety.</summary>

<header>PREFACE.</header>

...bewitches [us], so that truly not nearly as much effort is made, nor so much cost, time, and trouble spent by many to work out their eternal salvation, as is spent to obtain a beautiful garment. Indeed, people heat themselves up in this evil of finery <note>original: "pronckerye," referring to ostentatious or showy display</note> so very much that they would rather—if it cannot be otherwise—let their own souls and consciences, their honest trade, and their well-being go, and take up wicked, deceitful tricks to hunt for filthy lucre <note>original: "vuyl gewin," a biblical term for ill-gotten gain</note> with which they might dress themselves beautifully, than give up and lay aside their finery. Likewise, many modest parents know how heavily their children burden them for beautiful clothes, and what trouble and strife they have in keeping their children within any degree of moderation.

Furthermore, it is also the case with this wicked sin, committed through pride and the finery of clothing, that it is constant and shows itself shamelessly everywhere the showy person walks or stands. And where other sins seek the darkness and shun the sight of men, this one strives most of all to show itself in the largest gatherings, as if it were specifically intended to defy the Most High. Yea, the very look on the faces of proud people testifies against them: *and they declare their sin as Sodom, they hide it not* <note>original: "ende hare sonden spreken sy vry uyt, gelijck Sodom, sy en verbergen se niet," quoting Isaiah 3:9</note>. For this reason, the Prophet also speaks a woe over such people, saying, *woe unto their soul! for they have rewarded evil unto themselves. Isaiah 3: 9.*

And just as there is no offense that is so eye-catching as this "show-market" of clothing, so too is there nothing that a person can more easily improve if they only wished to. Every evening he lays aside his finery; he could also leave it off forever if he only desired. Hypocrites and dissemblers can do it when it suits them, though they have no power of the spirit; that Christians then, in a matter they can so easily improve—and can do without as easily as the clippings of their nails—still constantly oppose the Lord Christ and dare so openly to despise His warnings: truly, that signifies a great deal; there is more evil stuck in that than one might think at first glance.

Nevertheless, we have noticed that this is not even perceived by many whose hands are already deep in this misdeed. Indeed, many (and those not even of the worst sort), when they have acted quite grossly in this matter, do not even notice that they are doing wrong. And even if they are faithfully warned against vanity in clothing, they do not take it to heart at all, but look at others who act even more grossly, imagining that only those others are meant—whereas, nonetheless, hardly anyone is free from this transgression. And thus we have almost lost the ability to notice this sin because we see it so constantly before our eyes. Indeed, this evil has broken in so forcefully that those who do not act in an utterly abominable way do not even seem to be doing wrong, even though they forget themselves quite a lot. This being so, who can rightfully blame us—whom the Lord has appointed as <term>Watchmen</term> <note>original: "Sienders," literally "Seers," referring to the prophetic duty to observe and warn the people of spiritual danger</note> among the people—seeing this mischief, which nonetheless...

# PREFACE.

...people do not see it clearly, should they [the leaders] not faithfully warn them against it?

Therefore, my very dear and longed-for brothers and sisters, please take this labor of ours in good part, and let it go to your heart. Look there: by God's great grace, you have this praise in our land, that you are a very generous, excellent, and zealous Congregation; you also demonstrate this in deed in many instances. However, this blemish <note>original: "blaem," a mark of shame or fault</note> still lies upon you: that you excel too much in the outward appearance of your clothing. It is truly so: the Lord Christ, among other things, still has this against you, which is indeed very much to be lamented. The Lord has, according to His great mercy, given us great peace and prosperity for a long time now, undoubtedly to this end: that we, tasting His kindness therein, should love Him all the more, and serve Him all the more diligently in the abundance of all things (*Deuteronomy 28:47-48*). We, on the contrary, have gone and misused God’s kindness for wantonness; indeed, as if the Lord God had done us well and given us prosperity solely so that we might go and love the world, like <term>Demas</term> <note>Demas was a companion of the Apostle Paul who eventually deserted him because he "loved this present world" (2 Timothy 4:10).</note>. Thus, according to the measure of our prosperity and luxury, we have begun to puff ourselves up in <term>pride</term> <note>original: "hoovaerdye"</note> and <term>finery</term> <note>original: "pronckerye," referring to ostentatious or showy display</note>. So the Lord has also begun, according to His threat, to cut back our abundance (*Hosea 2:8*); and yet, we are so entangled in these vanities that, notwithstanding this, we have not trimmed our finery in the least. Rather, as if we wished to defy the Most High, we practice just as great an excess in our clothes, and even increase in it every day. 

If you still doubt this, and wish to know how far you have exceeded the measure, simply go and look at the clothes of your parents—their collars, their bodices, their ornaments, etc. And you will be able to find and perceive that you have now, in comparison to them, put on an entirely worldly appearance; indeed, you would be judged as such, if custom did not excuse you. And although our parents also had their transgressions in clothing (just as the sin of <term>pride</term> has always been in the world), yet this is certain and sure: that we people have, within the last dozen or two years, become much more depraved in this matter. For example: we can still remember that among common people, <term>ruff-irons</term> <note>original: "lob-yfers," metal tools heated and used to press pleats into large ruffs or collars</note> were judged to be "the Devil’s pitchforks" <note>original: "Duyvels Peck-ftocken," literally "pitch-sticks," suggesting tools used by demons in hell</note>, and that many would have feared (as a wicked <term>instrument</term>) to have one in the house, much less to use it. Now, on the contrary, there is no household so lowly, even if it lives on charity, that is not provided with this gear, or at least borrows it. Custom has made this so common that the simplicity of setting one's own <term>ruffs</term> <note>original: "Lobben," the starched, pleated collars fashionable in the 16th and 17th centuries</note> with one's own fingers is almost entirely forgotten. But now, you surely know this well: that the Lord our God, the Ancient of Days, is not blinded by custom. You know well that the Lord God, who sees this market of finery, with all that attaches to it, and...

...with all the newly-adorned gear <note>original: "getuych," referring here to the "equipment" or "trappings" of fashion</note> belonging to it, [you have] gradually seen it arise and creep in, and have always had a loathing for it, and have had you faithfully warned against it through His messengers <note>The "messengers" or "boden" refer to the ministers and preachers of the gospel.</note>. Therefore your guilt is all the greater, because you, notwithstanding this, have nonetheless broken out in such excess. Which has also moved us all the more to devote this present labor of ours, with such earnestness as you may see here, to your warning. For when we see you, at every gathering of the faithful, appearing so costly and so outward in your display—from the servants on up—we often think to ourselves: "These people have nonetheless been faithfully warned through the Word of the Lord; all their **pride**, all their **finery**, and all their vanity has indeed been nakedly exposed and rebuked many times by the men of God in the ministry of the Word." Thus those sermons also stand before the Lord; so too the Lord knows well that they were warned. And even if they have forgotten what was brought against their finery, nonetheless the Lord, who confirms the word of His messengers, has not forgotten; so they will nonetheless have to answer for it. They were indeed told what is good, so it is also their fault that they let the Word of the Lord fall so to the earth and do not profit better by it. 

And as we consider this within ourselves, we think further: what does it help our Congregation that she is warned against her finery if she proceeds in it just as much? Truly, it would be better for them (if it is not improved) that they had never heard anything preached against it, for then they would have less sin. This then ignites a zeal in us so that we cannot keep silent; this makes us search the Word; this makes us pray to the Lord God that He would bring *words* to our mind that might be like goads and nails, through which we might truly prick you to do what you were taught in *Ecclesiastes 12, verse 11* <note>The verse says: "The words of the wise are like goads, and like nails firmly fixed are the collected sayings; they are given by one Shepherd."</note>. Furthermore, it happens that we often fear within ourselves that—just as the Lord God, for many other sins, visits His people with various worldly hardships—you indeed have it worse in many things because of the **pride** and the **finery** that goes on among us. # Necessary Warning

### TO THE

## CHRISTIAN READER.

->*Since we notice that the greatest cause of the*<-
->*sin of finery is the pride of the heart*<-
->*(however much the vain person may deny it),*<-
->*so we provide this additional*<-
->*necessary report against it.*<-

**Remedies to ward off the natural pride of our hearts (which is the womb <note>original: "baer-moeder" — figuratively meaning the source or birthplace of a vice</note> of ostentation in clothing) from us.**

->I.<-

Consider, O human, what you are in yourself, and how little reason you have to exalt yourself; indeed, how great a reason you have on every side to humble yourself: *Is not all flesh grass, and all fine goodness like a flower of the field? Isaiah 40:6.* Shall not your body also, which you now deck out so much, *be covered with worms (Isaiah 14:11) and have the grave for a father? (Job 17:14).* Indeed, if death (which shall surely happen before long) has sat upon your body for only a few days, shall it not immediately be entirely loathsome to all eyes? So much so that even those who have loved you *shall bury it out of their sight (Genesis 23: verse 4).* What sense is there in this then, that you still wish to have so much upon the trunk of your body? That you still wish to be so bold in your life, when *your days are set by God as a hand-breadth (Psalm 39:6) and are yet full of unrest (Job 14:1).* But above all this, consider well that your body, which you now deck out so much, is merely *a body of sin (Colossians 2: verse 11), a body of death (Romans 7: verse 24).* And your soul, which is also understood therein, is merely a womb for all that is abominable, having within itself the seed of all damnable sins; *seven abominations are in your heart (Proverbs 26: verse 25; James 1:14).* You are by nature such an entirely ruined work and a corrupted vessel. So much so that of every human, as he is by nature, it may

can be said, as the Prophet says of King *Coniah* <note>original: "Chonia" — a reference to Jeconiah, King of Judah, used here as a symbol of fallen earthly glory</note>, is then this man *Coniah* a despised, broken idol? II. Consider further, O human, what you have also deserved to be, and what by nature already hangs over your head through your sinful nature—which you still wish to cherish with your finery. Is this not truly the portion of the godless man from God, and the heritage of tyrants which they shall receive from the Almighty? *Job 27: verse 13.* What reason is there then, that while the Lord God can bring so much against you, you nevertheless still wish to exalt yourself and show yourself off in all ostentation? Is it fitting for a condemned criminal <note>original: "verwefen mifdadighe"</note> to still be prideful? Does it make any sense that those who are draped in so many death-deserving sins should hang all kinds of vain toys around themselves? Become wise then, and make of your past sins—as if from dragon's poison—a healing medicine of humiliation, to humble the pride of your heart. But if you think you are released from the guilt of your sins through the merits of your Savior <note>original: "Salighmaeckers"</note>, then consider this also: that your Savior who has released you demands that you should be humble and put away all your finery. *Matthew 11:28; 1 Timothy 2:9; 1 Peter 3: verses 3, 4.* Consider then also, if you are released through *Christ* <note>Latin: "Chriftum"</note>, that you have also become a member of *Christ*, and consequently that it is fitting in every way that you should dress and adorn the members of *Christ* not according to the course of the world, but according to the prescription of His Word.

Indeed, has not the Lord *Jesus Christ*, to amend our pride, been pressed even into the dust of the earth? Marc. 14. vers. 35. <note>A reference to Jesus falling on the ground in the Garden of Gethsemane.</note> Was He not afterwards also shamefully crowned with a crown of thorns? Was He not stripped, and hung naked as one cursed, upon the wood of the cross, to cover our cursed nakedness, and to clothe us with eternal glory? This we Christians certainly all know. But now tell me, you Christian person, what sense is there in this: shall the Lord of Heaven humble Himself, and shall the worms of the earth puff themselves up? Shall God be humble, and shall man be proud? Shall the Lord *Christ* lay aside His glorious state to save us, and shall we still constantly exalt ourselves above our station to ruin ourselves? Shall the Son of God humble Himself unto the death of the cross, and also leave us an example of humility (which is beyond all comparison), Philip. 2 : 5. etc. And shall we, children of men, still pride ourselves in this life of vanity? Shall our Savior hang naked for our sake on the wood of the cross, and shall He desire of us—that we should be humble all our lives for His sake, and guard ourselves against finery <term>finery: "pronckerye," referring to the showy, ostentatious display of wealth through clothing</term>—and shall we nevertheless clothe ourselves with all kinds of vanity? Truly, whoever wishes to keep the comfort of their Christianity must indeed let go of the vanity of their finery. For this also always stands firm, that the Lord has nowhere promised that He would save our decked-out bodies (such as many make their bodies): but has only promised, *that He shall change our lowly bodies so that they may become conformed to His glorious body, Philip. 3. vers. 21.* If we then wish to expect in hope that our bodies shall hereafter be glorified in Heaven, so must we presently here on Earth prepare <note>original: "toe-maken" — literally to "make up" or "prepare," here meaning to dress or groom oneself</note> our bodies in all humility.

IV. Consider lastly, O human, the words of the Spirit, who says there, *Be clothed with humility, for God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble, 1. Pet. 5. vers. 5.* And again, *The Lord shall humble their pride with the ambushes of their hands, Esai. 25. vers. 11.* <note>This Dutch phrasing "laghen harer handen" likely refers to the "movements" or "schemes" of their hands.</note> *So that certainly the lofty eyes of men shall be humbled, and the haughtiness of men shall be bowed down. Esai. 2. vers. 11.* Consider then also, O human, what you do, when you puff yourself up out of pride, in the finery of clothing; for you exalt yourself against the Most High, who shall in His time strike you down into the dust of the earth. And notice, you cannot so quickly present yourself before the eyes of the children of men with your finery to exalt yourself, before the Lord God has you immediately in His eye to humble you; indeed, He sets you as a Target, to shoot the arrows of His wrath against you, Psal. 7. vers. 13. 14.

To this, those of the lowest status in the land must now pay special attention—aside from those of high state, whom this also concerns, for both great and small are equally fathered from sinful and corruptible seed; their souls and bodies are likewise bound together by the same fragile bond. Thus both, the great as well as the small, are by nature subject to mortality and the curse. Yet the lowly must take heed, for the Wise Man <note>original: "Wijfe-man"; likely a reference to the Book of Sirach 25:2, which expresses God’s hatred for a proud poor man.</note> testifies that a poor person who is proud stands as a complete abomination before the Lord.

And yet we see, to our sorrow, that even the lowliest break out in all kinds of excessive clothing. Common domestic servants <term>domestic servants: "dienft-boden," at this time often young women from rural areas working in city households</term> walk about outwardly adorned as if they were noble young ladies, with the only exception being the fineness of the fabrics; many young men do the same. The lace and other decorations they put on are excessive. And as if they had not yet made it coarse enough, they constantly practice ways to set their lace and other trimmings (which are like Satan’s teeth, with which he bites and tears apart many souls) even larger and higher.

This also gives birth to much mischief in the Congregation <term>Congregation: "Ghemeynte," referring to the local church community</term>, for by this, others who are of some status—and believe that they must therefore surpass the lowliest of the place—are so provoked that it grieves all simple hearts. We know that many are greatly offended by this and often complain with tears about the scandal that is given in our Congregation. Furthermore, the lowly of the city, having become accustomed to this finery <term>finery: "pronckerye," ostentatious or showy dress</term> while they serve good people and only have to care for themselves, cannot let it go when they become householders themselves. Thus they continue it and teach it to their children from a young age. Because of this, the entire era within the last twenty years has become so corrupt among us that we cannot doubt that, if it continues this way, the Lord will be forced to finally come and humble our pomp with the arms of His hands.

Thus all young people must consider here that even if they might think—because they present themselves so attractively to the fleshly eye through these outward adornments—that this might be a means to make a better marriage, it is not so at all. For it is certain and sure that by these outward adornments, the truly Godly <note>The "Godsalige" refers to those who live a life of active, sincere piety.</note> (with whom alone a good marriage is to be made) are frightened away. In contrast, only those who are still vain and lightheaded of heart are stirred to love by such things. But every Christian person knows that no good marriage can be made with such people, as experience daily teaches us.

How much better it would be, therefore, if young people, considering what an anxious time it is, would save something from their surplus against the evil day <note>A biblical reference to times of hardship or judgment.</note>, and not spend and squander it on vain finery (to the great offense of all). Thus, when they come to marry, they might have some provisions with which to begin their household decently. That would cause no unrest for their souls in any way, and would give our Republic and Church a better fashion and do more virtue. **AMEN.**

...wants it, and still and daily practices it; from this it then also appears that you do not love the Lord.
