And how do you think He will take it, that for a lot of <term>doll-play: "poppe-werck," a derogatory term for frivolous finery or childish vanity</term> of idle vanity (which we have after all proven to be entirely useless for any good, and very fruitful in all kinds of troubles and offensive whims), one would still willfully and knowingly break His commandment and despise His request? Can this also produce good work for the soul? Must it not in the end result in the worst possible outcome?

## Conclusion of it all.

He who knows how to say that it does not matter much what clothing someone wears, let him then also know this: that it matters a great deal in every way that no one, for the sake of that which "does not matter much," should break even the least of God's commandments (Matthew 5:19), or grieve the least of God's children (1 Corinthians 8:12).

## Concerning
# The Nature of Clothing, which
### should be observed by Christians, so that they might show themselves in their attire as true Christians.
### Delivered upon the words of Matthew 3, verse 4.

> And the same John had his clothing of camel’s hair,
> and a leather belt around his waist.

### FIRST SERMON.

<image-desc>Decorative square initial 'D' with floral scrollwork designs.</image-desc>

The Evangelist Matthew has pointed out to us in the preceding verses of this chapter how John the Baptist, the forerunner of our Lord Jesus Christ, came preaching repentance, for the Kingdom of Heaven was at hand. He further declared, drawing from the Prophet Isaiah 40, that John did so not on his own authority, but having been called and appointed by God for that purpose; for he was the "voice of one crying," of whom Isaiah had prophesied. He was that very <term>Echo: "weer-klanck," a resonant sound that repeats what is spoken</term> which cried out loudly there in the wilderness (just as echoes are often found in desolate places), "Prepare the way of the Lord, make his paths straight" (verse 3). For namely, the Lord God had first called this into his heart, and so John in turn—following the nature of an echo, which cannot remain silent when it is spoken to, and cannot speak anything other than what is spoken to it—cried this out to the people with all boldness. With this explanation, the Evangelist

<column-break/>

Matthew also proves that John indeed performed his preaching by Divine authority: since he did not begin to speak until God had first spoken to him, and he spoke nothing other than what the Lord God had placed in his mouth, being merely as a voice of the calling God, as an echo or resonance of the Most High. This is the proper condition of all faithful ministers of the Divine Word, as we have explained in the preceding sermons.

II. Now the Evangelist proceeds in the description of John, and points out to us what John was like in the <term>course of his life: "treyn sijns levens," referring to his daily habits and lifestyle</term>, and in his manner of <term>conduct: "conversatie," meaning his social behavior and way of living</term>, as the same could be observed and perceived in the outward man. Regarding this, he explains what his covering and his nourishment were like, testifying to us that his clothing was of camel’s hair, and that he had a leather belt around his waist, and that his food was locusts and wild honey. All of this is introduced to further confirm the authority of John <note>The author suggests that John's simple dress and diet proved he was a true prophet, unaffected by worldly luxury.</note>.

->Mirror of Modesty.<-

III. Someone might now wonder here, for what reason only the clothing and the food of John are mentioned here, when Matthew wants to give proof of his godly course of life. Answer: John was a Preacher; all his outward conduct consisted primarily in his voice and Sermons; furthermore, he did not have much interaction with the children of men, nor did his calling allow it: thus he could not be praised for outward worldly things; the most remarkable thing by which he could still be outwardly known—what kind of man he might be—was his covering and food. These being two common things with which all people, good and bad, young and old, steady and frivolous, Preachers and others, must concern themselves: so the person is also made very well known therein: for they are like two little clappers <note>The author uses the metaphor of "klapper-kens" (small rattles or clappers) to suggest things that announce or signal one's character to others.</note> (namely the clothing and the food), yes, like two trustworthy witnesses, which there often reveal what the person is inwardly, and what one is to feel about him: so then our Evangelist also very appropriately takes his description from this, concerning the particular condition of John's life, just as the Lord Christ, who best understood of what weight these matters were, also draws upon both there, Matthew 11 verses 8 and 18. So it is then also our bounden duty that we likewise pay close attention to it. The more so, because not only the children of the world, but even the children of God themselves, in these two things, in our time—I know not through what cunning of Satan and poor oversight—have very miserably

<column-break/>

forgotten themselves. Therefore we shall, on this occasion, treat both somewhat more closely: and first the first, namely, the clothing.

IV. Concerning the clothing of John, it is testified there that his clothing was of camel’s hair, and that he had a leather belt around his waist. And the same John (says the Text, even this John, who was inwardly clothed with such glorious gifts, who was there the calling voice of the Most High) had his clothing of camel’s hair, and a leather belt around his waist. Two things are pointed out here: First, what his outer garment was: It was a rough garment of camel’s hair, that is, as it appears, of a camel’s skin with the hair still on it: not of fine <term>Camlet: "Kamelot," a luxury fabric made of silk and wool, often used to imitate camel hair</term>, such as is used now: for the whole intent of our text leads elsewhere, and it also conflicts with Christ’s words, who testifies of John: That he was not clothed in soft garments, Matthew 11:8. Such as Camlet is: It was then a rough garment: he was indeed clothed with a rough skin, just as our first Forefathers were right after their fall, Genesis 3:21, and that also fits best: John had to strictly preach to the people the improvement of their lives because of their sorrowful fall, so he comes thus clothed, just as Adam was clothed right when he had fallen. Secondly, the addition to his garment is also pointed out, which was a leather belt, which served to tuck up his rough <unclear>frock</unclear> <note>original: "pije," a coarse, thick woolen cloth or the garment made from it</note> (since they then wore long garments) so that he might be ready for the service of his Lord, Luke 12:35.

[...modesty] adorn themselves, not with braids of the hair, or gold, or pearls, or costly clothing: But (as befits women who profess godliness) through good works, 1 Timothy 2:9-10. Now hear further what the Apostle Peter says to this: Let the adornment of Christian women (he says) not be that which is outward, consisting of the braiding of hair, and wearing of gold, or putting on of clothing: But the hidden person of the heart, in the incorruptible adornment of a gentle and quiet spirit, which is precious before God. For in this way the holy women of old, who hoped in God, also adorned themselves, and were submissive to their own husbands, like Sarah, etc. 1 Peter 3:3-5. See there—two decisive passages of Holy Scripture concerning the modesty which we must observe in every way in our clothing, and the avoidance of frivolities, which are now (God help us) so common, even

<column-break/>

among those who bear the name of Reformed Christians <note>The author is addressing members of the Dutch Reformed Church, urging them to live up to their "Reformed" title.</note>, in use directly against this Divine decree, and as if in defiance of the Most High. Now, because in these passages the text expressly gives instruction only to Women—for they are most accustomed to forget themselves in this regard—the Holy Spirit therefore teaches the place where the need is greatest. Since clothing is nothing but doll-work <note>Original: "poppe-werck," referring to childish trifles or vanity.</note> upon which the weakest hearts gaze most longingly, it follows much more strongly that, if Women may not indulge themselves in this, then surely men may do so much less; they are expected to be of higher contemplations than to let themselves be ensnared by such child’s work. We may also see that both of these divine Apostles expressly forbid any Christian person—even if they might wear gold or silver or a costly garment due to the excellence of their calling <note>A person’s "calling" (Dutch: *beroep*) refers to their social rank or profession.</note>—from seeking their adornment in gold, pearls, hair-braiding, or costly clothes. Indeed, as the Apostle Peter speaks, one must not seek adornment in the wearing of any kind of clothing, whatever it might be (1 Peter 3), but only in those spiritual gifts. Since this is so clearly stated there, it is therefore all the less to be tolerated that it should be so visibly done by us Reformed Christians. For even the utmost excuse that can be said by those who wear pearls and costly clothing—namely, that their calling and the high state they hold assists them in it, so as to display the glory of their status—is [refuted]...

# Mirror of Modesty.
### 505

...[specific] / a particular modesty of clothing, suited to the specific circumstances of every Christian person.

Regarding the first point (we have understood in the handling of this doctrine that it is indeed proper) that everyone should arrange their clothing according to their calling <term>calling: "beroepinge," the social or professional station one is "called" by God to occupy</term>: since there are now various kinds of callings and states of men, some more distinguished than others, it follows that according to the circumstances of the calling, one may dress more elegantly than another; yet all must constantly observe Christian modesty and temperance in their clothing. In order to maintain this well, there are certain Divine rules concerning the suitability of clothing which must be followed: some of which concern the clothing itself, others our behavior regarding clothing, and they are these:

<margin>1st Rule. Not the purse, but the social state, must set the measure for clothing.</margin>

First, the closer someone comes in calling and state to sovereignty, and the more prominence they have in the courts of Kings, or in the court of a Republic, the more elegantly such a person may dress: A Lord of the Land more elegantly than a common Citizen; a Councilor than a Bailiff; a Burgomaster <note>The chief magistrate or mayor of a Dutch city</note> than a Clerk; a Merchant than a common Craftsman; a Prince than a common Nobleman. This rule arises from the fact that those who, by way of their office, are in authority and placed above others, must to some degree show the excellence of their supreme Lord and Master, whose closest servants they are, Romans 13.

Therefore also God the Lord, when He wished to bring Eliakim forward and [cl-]

<column-break/>

[-oser] to the King in service, promised that He would subsequently clothe him with a more stately robe and belt, Isaiah 22:21. Upon this also stands what the Lord Christ testifies: that those who wear soft clothing are in Kings' houses, Matthew 11:8. And this extends so far that not only they, but also their Wife (Proverbs 31:22), their children (2 Samuel 13:18), and their attendants (Psalm 45), may also present themselves more elegantly. Against this, then, all those sin who, having no prominence by way of their place or office, nevertheless deck themselves out in soft clothes and make themselves equal to the Lords of the Land; wise men do not usually act so. There are rich and powerful Merchants; they could go about dressed like Princes, but they act wisely in holding to the attire of Merchants. It is not the purse, but the social state, which must set the measure for clothing: Whether there be a Shopkeeper or Craftsman who, through inheritance or otherwise, has become very wealthy above others of his guild, he nevertheless ought to conduct himself in his clothing according to the order in which he belongs; the contrary gives birth to much trouble. As for example: when a wealthy Shopkeeper decks himself in costly clothing above his fellow shopkeepers, the others—so that they might not seem less than their neighbors—want to do the same; thus that whole order rises. The next group above them, considering themselves better than the first, then wants to do even more, and so everything falls out of order, and great extravagance breaks in on all sides: for one sees that according to how someone’s clothes are—which always catch the eyes of people—so also follows all the [rest...]

...rest happens: the housing, the furniture, the table, and everything else, which everywhere gives birth to great excess. <margin>II. Rule. One may dress more exquisitely on a feast day than on a common day.</margin>

Secondly, if there is a special occasion for rejoicing, and for maintaining and displaying one’s state, then those who have such an occasion may present themselves more exquisitely for that time (each according to the aforementioned specific circumstances of their calling) than at other times. Thus, someone may dress more exquisitely on a **Feast day** than on a **work day**: at a **Wedding**, than on a **common holy day**. This rule arises from the fact that the occasion of rejoicing draws everyone—of whatever calling they may be—one degree higher for that time, and brings them closer to the glory and excellence of the **Courtiers**; therefore they may also, for that time, set themselves closer to their equals in their clothing. For this reason we also frequently read in the Scriptures of *costly garments* <note>original: "Dyer-kleederen," meaning expensive or precious clothes</note>, *clothes of change*, *garments of the feast*, as also of a *Wedding garment*, **Matt. 22:11, Rev. 19:7, 8**, and of the *best robe*, **Luke 15:22**. So too the Apostle Paul had not only a traveling cloak, but a cloak for state <note>original: "mantel ter statie," a ceremonial or formal cloak</note>, **2 Tim. 4:13**. Nevertheless, a holy caution must also be used here, so that on the occasion of this our Christian freedom to present ourselves more exquisitely on Feast days, Weddings, and similar occasions than on common days, we nevertheless do [not]

<column-break/>

exceed the measure; for this is also certain and sure: that in such cases and moments, one can also wretchedly forget and catch oneself in excess of clothing. Indeed, experience teaches us that the mischief mostly begins there: when people are to go to a feast or a wedding, they think, "I may now dress myself more handsomely than on common days." They do so, and often do it much more costly than they should. This being done, those fashions <term>fashions: "moderen," the prevailing styles or modes of the time</term> please them so well that they also hanker to go more exquisitely on common days than they are accustomed. Thus evil breaks in, if it is not cautiously provided against. Yea, more; for the **Devil** also constantly plots there, so that when man has the most cause to seek God's favor—as, for example, on his wedding day—he might then most offend and provoke his God, so that the mischief might indeed be great. And this he brings to pass with many, for experience teaches that there is hardly a day in human life in which many so give themselves over to all kinds of vanity and pomp, wherewith God is angered, as on their wedding day. Against this, Christian caution must be employed and used. # Mirror of Modesty.
### 507

...as if he would do that every day or even every week. In this, our ancestors were prudent; they always kept some garment for "honor" <note>meaning formal or ceremonial clothing</note> which they did not wear except on very special and extraordinary occasions. Otherwise, they went about dressed very commonly. When our young people see their ancestors depicted in such portraits, they wrongly conclude that they too may go about so expensively dressed every day—which was not at all the custom of their forefathers. Sin is also committed here in another way: people keep too many changes of clothing and have an excess of **outer garments**—so many, in fact, that they can hardly keep the moths from them by wearing them, a vanity about which James complains in **James 5:2**, while meanwhile many poor "members of Christ" <note>a reference to fellow Christians in need</note> go nearly naked. John the Baptist desired that he who had two suits of clothes should give one to him who had none, **Luke 3:11**. From this, at least, it follows that we must not be over-abundant in outer garments or in "clothes of change" <note>original: "kleederen der verwisselinghe," referring to a rotating wardrobe of luxury items</note>.

<margin>
III. Rule. One must not spend much time in dressing oneself.
</margin>

Thirdly, one must dress oneself quickly; one must indeed see to it that one does not spend much time concerning one’s clothing, neither in preparing it nor in putting it on. This rule concerns our outward conduct regarding our dress and arises from this: because we Christians are commanded to **redeem the precious time**, **Ephesians 5:16**, and because our clothing is among those things in which the **Kingdom of God** does not consist. Since fine dress does not make us more pleasing in the eyes of our God—no matter how beautifully we are adorned—it follows in every respect

<column-break/>

that our business concerning clothing is one of the smallest matters of our lives. Therefore, we should by no means be much occupied with it, but rather dispatch it very lightly. Furthermore, anyone can well enough perceive that for Christians—upon whom such great work always lies, such as the working out of their souls' salvation, the spreading of God’s honor, the winning of the souls of others, the breaking down of the kingdom of **Satan**, and the establishing of the **Kingdom of Christ** <note>original: "Coningrijcke Christi"</note>—it is not fitting that they should waste their precious time with a deal of idle <term>primping and preening</term> <note>original: "topinghen en mopinghen," archaic Dutch for excessive fussing over appearance</note> of the sinful flesh. Therefore, whatever our calling or state might be, everyone must see to it that he spends not much time in his dressing. 

Against this many women sin, and even some men, who often care so much for their outward clothing and spend so much time therein that they can find no time to perform holy exercises in their homes as is proper, or to hasten to Church in a timely manner. Nor do they otherwise prepare their souls so that they might sit down in the assembly of the believers, appearing pleasing before the eyes of God according to His requirement, **Ecclesiastes 4:17**. Truly, it is terrible that man dares to waste his time to make himself outwardly <term>fancy</term> <note>original: "frap," meaning gallant or elegantly dressed</note> for the eyes of men, while meanwhile he neglects to adorn and prepare himself in his soul before the eye of his God. We hardly know if one can have a surer proof of a <term>worldly nature</term> <note>original: "werelts-wesen"</note>: we always know certainly that such people do not need to look far for sure signs of their vanity, for those signs hang around their bodies on all sides.

# Mirror of Modesty.
### 508

<margin>
Rule IV.
That we must always be humble of heart, no matter how exquisitely we are dressed. Against this sin those who...
</margin>

Fourthly, one must also—whatever clothing we put on and for whatever occasion it might be—always be humble of heart in our attire. This rule pertains to the internal state of our heart regarding our clothing and arises from this: that we must always be humble of heart (1 Peter 5:5) and not exalt ourselves in anything. Indeed, even a Prince and King may not exalt himself in pride of heart above his brothers, not even in the excellence of his authority and kingdom (Deuteronomy 17:20); much less may anyone then exalt themselves on the mere outward signs of such authority and excellence, such as clothing. Now, against this holy requirement of humility, one sins in two ways.

<margin>
1. Those who seek their own adornment in their clothing.
</margin>

I. When a person seeks their honor and their adornment in their costly clothing, which they may have to wear because of their calling. This the Apostle forbids in **1 Peter 3:3-4**; this is also unseemly for a Christian. See, honor must go from the person to the garment, and not from the garment to the person. If someone comes forward exquisitely dressed, and one asks who he is and finds that he is merely some "quidam" <note>original Latin: "a certain someone," used here to mean an insignificant or unknown person</note>, then he and his garment are justly despised. But if he is also a person of stature, then his garment is honored for the sake of his person. If then someone's calling is such that he may wear more exquisite clothes, let him do so, not in a vain pride of heart, seeking his own honor in his clothing, but let him do it in humble obedience to God's ordinance, and to keep in honor that order which God has established...

<column-break/>

...having meanwhile not a proud, but a true Christian heart, which, being highly exalted above all these earthly things and not regarding them, can put on a silk or velvet coat and yet be as little puffed up by it as another is accustomed to being when wearing a **rough frock** <term>rough frock: original "rouwe pije," a coarse, humble garment made of heavy wool, typically worn by the poor or by monks as a sign of penance</term>. For a Christian person, being clothed with the Lord Jesus Christ, the "Sun of Righteousness," must—like the Community of God, the Moon, and all that is under the Moon—tread underfoot all gold and silver, all silk and velvet (**Revelation 12:1**), and so wear them as if not wearing them. Indeed, the Christian person whom God exalts must **so use the world as not misusing it** (**1 Corinthians 7:31**) and must **boast in his humiliation** (**James 1:10**) and by no means place his honor in that externality, and thereby be more arrogant in his posture or gait. It is also childish and vain to be proud and haughty about one's beautiful clothes and to go mincing along, as the "Daughters of Zion" did, with haughty eyes and gestures, because one is so dressed—as if a horse were proud of its costly saddle! But therefore, when one looks at it, all earthly things of which you are proud are but the excrement of beasts, of the earth, or of the sea <note>A common 17th-century observation: silk is produced by worms, and expensive dyes like purple were extracted from sea snails</note>, and yet a "lily of the field" is more gloriously adorned than you yourself, as the Savior Christ Himself testifies (**Matthew 6:28-29**). What cause for exultation is there then in this? For this reason, even the King might not exalt his heart above his brothers, not even when he came forward hung with gold, silver, and all kinds of precious stones...

When a person seeks their own honor, or places their holiness in the plainness of their garments, just as the false prophets did in the time of Zechariah, Zechariah 13:4, and as the Monks still do now, and some of the Anabaptists <note>The "Weder-dooperen" or Anabaptists were a radical Reformation group often known for their plain dress and rejection of worldly social hierarchies.</note>, and other hypocrites; who, because they go about poorly dressed, let themselves believe that they are therefore the holier. There are also some among them who, more out of a certain whimsicality <note>original Dutch: "sinnelijckheydt," implying a physical or sensory preference rather than a spiritual conviction</note> than out of true godliness, go about so poorly dressed: and often have more pride in their plain attire than another has in their choice garment: as is evidenced by the fact that these people, in great pride of heart, immediately condemn as "children of the world" <note>A term used for those perceived as being more concerned with earthly life than spiritual salvation.</note> all those whom they see dressed a bit more handsomely than themselves. A humble Christian shall also guard himself against this. Otherwise, who are you indeed, O man, who so sharply judges another's servant? He falls and stands before his Lord. How do you dare so quickly to de-Christianize someone in your mind because he does not go about dressed exactly <note>original: "essen jupst," a colloquial emphasis on precision</note> according to your liking? It may happen out of thoughtlessness; the flood of corruption in this matter may have sullied him a bit without him even noticing; being warned, he would perhaps do better. Test that first, before you judge so sharply. For otherwise, we also wish to readily acknowledge that those who, against all warnings, still constantly flaunt <note>original: "uyt braberen," meaning to show off or parade</note> themselves above their

<column-break/>

status and calling, give very sad signs that they are indeed worldly-minded: whatever they might prattle about their humble heart that they carry beneath their magnificent clothes.

Fifthly, and lastly, we must, in everything that pertains to our
<margin>5. Rule. One must practice Christian purity, modesty, and moderation in everything that concerns our clothing. And therefore</margin>
clothing, point by point, make Christian modesty and moderation outwardly apparent, of whatever calling or status we might be: namely in the fabrics, accessories, colors, styles, and everything attached thereto. This rule arises from the fact that the commandments of our God do not only concern themselves with general things, but also with all particular cases and circumstances of things, Isaiah 3:13, etc. When our Lord God commends to us modesty and moderation in clothing, 1 Timothy 2:9, 1 Peter 3:3-4, then that must not only be understood of the garment in bulk, but also of all that is attached to it: for otherwise, as Solomon testifies, a dead fly spoils a whole jar of good ointment, Ecclesiastes 10:1, and a prideful addition to our clothing quickly spoils all the other propriety that might be present therein. Just as when someone comes into the King’s court and has some precious garment about him, yet is found to have worn-out shoes or patched stockings, he is immediately judged to be a godless and destitute squire <note>original: "berooyt Joncker," a term for a nobleman who has lost his wealth but tries to maintain appearances</note>; so it stands here as well: therefore, everything must be paid attention to, and so we shall also say something about everything.

<margin>1. The fabric must not be too costly.</margin>
I. The fabric of our clothing must, according to the circumstances of our calling, be neither too costly, through magnificence, nor too uncostly, through stinginess, whimsicality, or superstition. But this last we shall say no more of,

Furthermore, the material is bound too expensively in two ways: either because it is too costly for one’s social standing—as when someone wishes to wear velvet <note>A luxury silk fabric that was heavily regulated by sumptuary laws in the early modern period.</note> who ought to be satisfied with wool cloth, or wishes to wear the finest cloth when they should be content with common cloth. Or because it is too flimsy in its wear—namely, that the material does not cost much, but also does not last long, and once worn out, is of no further use, falling into shreds and being in no way fit to be used by a poor person for clothing. Our ancestors were prudent against this. By contrast, in the present day, many light fabrics have been invented which seem beautiful and entice people because they are a bargain, but are also quickly worn out and then useful for nothing. Thus they deplete the purses and prepare the way for all sorts of new fabrics and fashions, since there is a constant occasion to change clothes. Therefore, those who wish to practice moderation in clothing, as we all must do, shall guard themselves against this.

<margin>2. One's accessories should not be too many.</margin>

<margin>4. The style must be.</margin>

## IV. The style <term>fatsoen|The cut, fashion, or overall design of a garment.</term> of our clothing must also be very modest, and of such a kind that our Christian honor might be perceived and noticed through the modest style of our clothes. Now, there are three flaws in style which run like a plague among the people and infect many, which must be prevented.

<margin>Not too ornate.</margin>

### 1. Excessive Finery. 
All those styles which contain so many fripperies <note>original: "flickflackerijen"; a colorful term for flashy, unnecessary trimmings or "bells and whistles."</note>, so much finery, are no good; they are nothing but evidence of the vanity of the heart, and they also devour much time to prepare and to put on. It can never be justified before God in eternity that a person employs so many fripperies without any necessity to decorate their sinful flesh, while such a heavy task lies at hand: the decoration of their soul with spiritual gifts, which are precious before God. A Prince, Princess, or a noble young lady can let their splendor be seen without mixing such vanity into it. The Lord would not tolerate it, even in the noblest maidens of Israel, in the courtly young ladies who were in the King's Palace, *Isaiah 3:16.* <note>The author refers to a biblical passage where the Prophet Isaiah rebukes the "daughters of Zion" for their pride and elaborate finery.</note> Therefore, it must also be avoided.

<margin>Not frivolous.</margin>

### 2. Frivolity. 
All those styles that savor of frivolity <note>original: "Lichtveerdigheyt"; implies both a lack of seriousness and a lack of moral restraint.</note> are also no good. Such are all those styles which lay bare before the eyes of men that which modesty counsels us to cover. This is seen when women go about with open collars and bare necks; and even more so when they furthermore put their breasts, much or little, on display. What is that other than making oneself into a snare of the Devil?

<column-break/>

and opening a pit, into which foolish and incautious youths might happen to fall. The Lord ordains that if someone opens a pit, or digs one, and does not cover it, and an ox or a donkey falls into it, the owner of the pit shall make restitution, *Exodus 21:33, 34.* Shall these souls not also have to pay for the damage which their enticements <note>original: "aenritselen"; lures or provocations.</note> cause among foolish youths? Yes, certainly, it shall be required of their hands, and it shall bring in a heavy reckoning on the Last Day against those wanton maidens who behave so. Thus, no one who knows how precious the blood of souls is should any longer give such occasions for the damaging of the soul, especially after being warned. Everyone must indeed guard themselves against this.

<margin>Not new.</margin>

### 3. Novelty. 
If a style is merely new and unusual, it is scandalous <note>original: "ontstichtelijck"; literally "un-edifying" or causing a stumbling block to others' faith.</note>. For instance, if one of us wished to dress now as the Patriarch Abraham or the Apostle Paul might have dressed, it would be found scandalous. Custom <term>gewoonte|The established social norms of the era, which the author argues should dictate dress as long as they are decent.</term> carries much weight in this matter; as long as a style is not overly ornate or frivolous, custom makes it acceptable. However, custom cannot make an ornate or frivolous garment good, for that conflicts in the first instance with the modesty of Christians, which cannot and may not be obscured by any custom. Now, in the novelty of fashions, many sins are committed, whether by following foreign styles that come from other lands, or by introducing styles that are only appropriate for youths or nobles among elderly persons or the common citizens. Both are improper. Thus one casts...

<margin>*Zeph. 1:8*</margin>

And yet, as if such a threat from God did not exist, or as if God’s threat were not to be feared, everyone here emboldens themselves. 

New fashions run like a plague among the people and infect many. 

Therefore, they are also rightly called the "new snot" <note>original: "nieuwe snot"; a 17th-century Dutch slang term for a passing, irritating trend or a trivial but infectious novelty, much like a common cold.</note>; people pull and sniff it in like a foul air. 

Yes, the poor soul is so feverish in this matter that he would rather dress himself in the fashions of his mortal enemies (as some are found among us who follow the fashions of the Italians and Spaniards) than not have something new to distinguish himself among his peers. What is this other than a sorrowful sign that we might soon bring the tyranny of the Spaniard <note>The author refers to the political and religious tensions of the Eighty Years' War, where the Spanish Empire was the primary antagonist of the Dutch Republic.</note> back upon us, since we so readily dress ourselves in their fashions and seek our adornment therein? 

Indeed, this is certain and sure: those who occupy themselves with this prove by their deeds that they are the vainest people to emerge; they show that they have an entirely worldly heart, ready to be poured and molded into all the new fashions of the world that come forth. 

<margin>*Rom. 12:2*</margin>

<column-break/>

They are also, for one, monstrous people in a well-ordered Republic; for just as when any limb in the body is not proportioned in size, color, and essence to the others, but exceeds them all and stands out, it is found to be monstrous, so too are these people. Is it then not a pitiful thing that people take so much trouble to disfigure themselves, and to reveal their monstrous cursedness more and more? Therefore, a Christian heart shall guard itself as well against this "new snot" as he would guard himself against a pestilent air.

And see there: those are the general rules which must be followed and observed, so that everyone might properly conduct and carry themselves in their clothing according to their calling, and show and express the moderation that is expected of the people of God in all modesty <term>sedicheyt|The quality of being moderate, humble, and morally upright in appearance and behavior.</term>, including in their dress.

And we also, through long-standing bad habit, have almost entirely lost and brought out of use the right measure by which everything ought to be improved. We have indeed grown up under a bad custom and wrong measure in clothing (for it is not from today nor yesterday that this evil first began, although it has recently increased exceedingly among us) and are therefore so used to it that, even though things are far beyond all measure with us, we hardly notice it—just as we ourselves become accustomed to the most unregulated things over time through constant habit...

4. And even more especially if we also consider these following specific rules.

<margin>
1. That we do not follow the common course of the world in clothing.

1. That we do not follow the common course of the world in the matter of clothing: the Apostle forbids us this in general, in Romans 12:2; he does not want us to imitate the <term>outward form</term> <note>original Greek: "σχῆμα" (schema); referring to the fleeting fashion or appearance</note>—that is, the fashion—of the world. Scripture testifies to us that the whole world lies in wickedness (1 John 5:19). It would then be a wonder if, while the world is beyond proper measure in everything else, it had kept the right measure specifically here in clothing—in clothing, I say, in which the world has nonetheless erred most miserably. So this must stand firm and beyond dispute among us: that the common course of the world in materials, in accessories, in colors, and in fashions, is a bad course and unbecoming of Christians. Therefore, this excuse is by no means to be pardoned: that one can say they do nothing else in their clothing than what all the world does. For exactly that is poorly done; the world is beyond measure, and we must stay lower <note>meaning more humble or modest</note> than the world if we are to keep the right measure. Now, for each of us, "all the world" refers to those who are of the same calling and style <note>social station or profession</note> as we are: just as now all artisans <note>original: "Am-bachts-lieden"</note> who have some means go dressed according to the general trend, a Christian artisan may not exalt himself in clothing if he does not wish to go beyond the measure...

<column-break/>

...and so forth for the rest.

<margin>
2. That we do not act against the light of our consciences in our clothing.
</margin>
2. That we do not act in the matter of clothing against the light of our own conscience (Hebrews 13:18). If our own conscience testifies to us that we have gone too far with the corrupt world and have exalted ourselves too high in our clothing, then it is high time that we better ourselves, "circumcise" <note>in the sense of cutting away excess</note>, and cast that off. See, there are those who admit there is a fault in the clothing, and that they themselves are at fault; truly, these must improve their deficiency if they do not wish to be judged out of their own mouths like wicked servants (Luke 19:22). See there: it is a great kindness of the Lord when God is pleased to open our eyes and let a light of conscience rise for us in this cruel darkness which has come over the matter of clothing in our century. We must not put out this light in this confused darkness, but we must indeed walk in that light and arrange our clothing accordingly, if we do not wish—like wicked servants who know the Lord's will and do not do it—to be beaten with more stripes than others (Luke 12:47).

<margin>
3. That we do not act in the exalting of clothes where we doubt if we are free to do so.
</margin>
3. That we do not act in the excess of clothing in cases where we merely doubt whether it be permitted to us, whether it be modest, or whether it be beyond the measure (Romans 14:23). See, a thousand to one, if we begin to doubt whether it be evil, then it *is* evil. Modesty and moderation make themselves known enough when they are present; so long as we still doubt whether they are there, it is to be feared that they are still far off. This primarily applies when one sees others of his own calling <note>social or professional status</note> dressed more simply...

Now follows finally that we also point out the workings or fruits of splendor in clothing, by which the abominableness of this sin may be known more and more. And to that end, we must note these two things: First, that excess in clothing is entirely

<column-break/>

useless for any good; Secondly, that it is very abundant in all kinds of evil.

Excess in clothing is entirely useless for any good; for it is indeed an entirely unfruitful work of darkness. It performs no good virtue in the world, neither to those who do it, nor to others. No one is honored before God by it, nor is our neighbor edified; nor does the person themselves who wears the splendid garment enjoy any good fruit in the world from it, whether we look at their body, their mind, or their particular state before God or men.

As for the body, it enjoys no glory, no fruit from its glorious garment; for a beautiful and scarce, costly garment does not bestow its glory, beauty, and costliness upon the body for which it was made. It does not make the body any stronger nor any healthier than a good, modest garment could do. It does not make a person's food taste better when they wear it, nor their sleep more refreshing when they are covered with it. The exquisite garment also cannot ward off the pains and aches, illnesses, ailments, and many kinds of afflictions <note>The original Dutch uses "pichemuyen," an old term for petty physical miseries or nagging ailments.</note> to which the human body is subject; or even if they have already attacked the person, it cannot lighten or soften the pain, the fever, or the ache. Put a person in a velvet coat, and the fever, the toothache, and the colic will creep upon him just as well, plague him just as well, and hold him just as well as if he were in a rough woolen gown <note>original: "rouwe pye." A "pye" (or pije) was a coarse, cheap garment associated with the poor or certain religious orders.</note>. Thus then, in regard to the body, splendor in clothing is useful for nothing, and finally is an entirely unfruitful work of darkness.

# Mirror of Modesty
### 529

<margin>
Fine clothing does no good for the human heart: it cannot hide the heart's failings, much less improve them. It does not help a person against anger, jealousy, etc.
</margin>
Concerning the spirit <note>original: "ghemoet," referring to one's internal disposition or soul</note>, fine clothing can likewise do a person no good. Beautiful and magnificent garments cannot make a person more sensible or wiser than they already are. They cannot hide the failings of the heart, and much less can they improve them. They cannot help a person against their anger, fear, sadness, jealousy, ambition, vengefulness, envy, or whatever other defect might plague them. Thus, magnificent clothing—in regard to the human spirit—is of no use whatsoever, and is merely an unfruitful work of darkness <note>This is a reference to Ephesians 5:11: "And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them."</note>.

<margin>
Fine clothing does not make a person more pleasing to God, nor more fit to perform God's service.
</margin>
If we look further at the state of man toward God and his conduct therein, fine clothing cannot come to his aid there either. If there is something to be done before God, magnificent dress does not help. Nowhere do we find that a person was pleasing to God because they were dressed magnificently and above their station. Nowhere do we find that a person was reconciled with God through their fine clothes. On the contrary, we find that some found a kind of reconciliation with God when they laid aside their beautiful and magnificent garments, and clothed themselves in haircloth, and lay down in ashes, as seen in 1 Kings 21:27, Jonah 3:6, and Esther 4:1–2. If there are divine exercises to be performed before God, here too magnificent clothing is entirely useless. That someone is dressed in a velvet coat or a silk bodice <term>keurs: a laced bodice or stays, common in 17th-century Dutch fashion</term> does not make them more fit to pray; indeed, it hinders many, for they are afraid to kneel down upon the earth before the Lord their God (as is proper to do in solemn prayer). Nor can one

<column-break/>

thereby understand or carry away God’s word any better. One cannot sing any better for it, nor is one any better prepared to come worthily to the Lord's Supper. In short: fine clothing is also entirely useless regarding all those things we have to do before God, and is nothing but an unfruitful work of darkness.

<margin>
Fine clothing also does a person no good in their dealings with others; it cannot make them more prudent, nor protect them against deceit, etc.
</margin>
And as for the state of the magnificent in regard to other people, their fine clothing is also useless to them there. It cannot make a person more clever in their conversation and social interaction than they already are. It cannot protect them from being deceived or wronged by their neighbor. It cannot help them conduct their affairs better or have better credit, for sensible traders do not look at the clothes, but at the man. Thus, it can serve no purpose other than to better deceive the innocent and the simple, should they trust someone more because of their clothes than he is worth—but of such fruit no one shall boast. So this itself is a work of darkness. Thus it appears everywhere that, even in regard to our standing among men, excessive clothing is of no use, and is an entirely unfruitful work of darkness.

<margin>
Excess in clothing is very fruitful in all kinds of evil.
</margin>
And so we may see that indeed, excessive clothing is an entirely unfruitful work of darkness, and completely useless for any good. Now it follows that we also point out how fruitful it is in evil. There are many abundant evil fruits from the splendor of clothing, so that we hardly know where to begin; for whether we look upon the Lord our God...

# Mirror of Modesty
### 530

Whether it be God, or our fellow neighbors, or the people themselves who value expensive clothes so much, or the whole Republic—we find that magnificent dress, like an evil plant of Satan, brings forth very many bad fruits everywhere.

<margin>The excess in clothing that Christians practice greatly dishonors the Lord *Christ*.</margin>
First and foremost, then, we find that the fastidious, with their excess in clothing, bring forth this evil fruit: they cause the name of God to be blasphemed on their account, and they dishonor the Lord their God most shamefully with their improper vanity <note>original: "mopigheydt," referring to a state of being overly groomed or dressed up in a conceited manner</note>. To honor and adorn themselves with their splendor—supposedly <note>original: "quansijs," meaning ostensibly or as if</note>—they do indeed, as we have heard, offer great insult to the Lord *Jesus Christ* and His holy doctrine, which they are bound to adorn in all things (*Titus 2:10*). For through their outward appearance in dress, they make known to the whole world that they regard their God, the Lord *Christ*, and His commandment and teaching so little that they do not fear to act against them openly and before all the world. And they do this daily; not out of weakness or oversight, but with deliberate wantonness and intent, spending their money, consuming their time, and using their hands, eyes, and all their members to fashion themselves differently than the Lord *Christ* desires. They do this to deck themselves out and preen <note>original: "topen" and "mopen," archaic Dutch terms for excessive grooming and vanity</note> in their clothes, whereas the Lord *Christ*, the Master of humility, requires of His own that they should be entirely humble in their clothing. He only allows that they should adorn themselves in clean garments, but in no way in more expensive clothing than their calling warrants (*1 Timothy 2:9*). For so says the Apostle ex-

<column-break/>

-plicitly: That women adorn themselves in modest apparel, not in expensive clothing. Could one then more openly defy the Lord *Christ* than the magnificent do in their conduct? Is this the love you bear for the Lord *Christ*, your dear Lord: that while He requires humility and modesty <note>original: "sedicheyt"</note> in dress, you instead break out into all excess and frivolity? Do you choose to deck yourselves out and fashion yourselves according to what might please the wanton eye of the world, rather than arranging your clothing as it might best please the eye of the Lord *Christ*—Him whom you nevertheless call your dear Lord and your Bridegroom? It seems to you to be becoming to go so choicely dressed; the Lord *Christ* tells you that it is unbecoming, and that it displeases God's eye. Yet you do it anyway. Will you love what *Christ* hates? (*2 Chronicles 19:2*). Or will you approve of what He judges as evil, and still expect to fare well? How could you show the Lord *Christ* greater contempt? See there: the pleasure of the Lord *Christ* and God, and your own path and desire, stand on opposite sides. God the Lord sets you between them. When you are now at liberty to have a new garment made, *Christ*—who died for you, who also gives you the clothes, the power, and the voice to be able to clothe yourself—stands on one side, advising you against splendor and excess. The world—which never did you any good, which is as evil as itself, and which seeks to corrupt you even further in your greatly corrupted state...

2. Splendor in clothing provokes ill-will in other people against all those who practice it. "Well," they say, "what does this one want to be? From this, no small mischief arises even among the children of respectable citizens, who on such occasions fall into unchastity. Thus the house-holding folk suffer great inconvenience, as everyone complains; and it is truly a righteous punishment for our vanities, which we must then necessarily prune and better, if we wish to be better blessed in our servants and household.

# Mirror of Modesty
### 543

**Mirror of Modesty**

It is a most lamentable matter that a great power of darkness is at work here, and that it is truly an entirely unseemly thing for true Christians to still gape at these worthless vanities. Indeed, every true Christian who finds themselves in any way guilty of this transgression ought to heartily humble themselves over it and sincerely set themselves against it. Therefore, resolve all together—my very dear and desired Christians, who are now gathered here in the name of the Lord and have heard of the fruitlessness of splendor in clothing, and have now been taught its manifold harm—that you will no longer have fellowship with such unfruitful works of darkness. Instead, put them away at the first opportunity, just as the Lord Jesus, your Savior <note>original: "Salighmaecker", literally "Bringer of Salvation"</note> himself advises, and as your Christian profession requires and demonstrates. If you have a great abundance of means and it does not pinch you so tightly, look there upon the poor members of Christ <note>original: "ledekens Christi"; a common metaphor for the poor and suffering within the church community</note> who go about nearly naked; look there at the Deacons who stand ready to receive your alms for them. Give to them what you used to spend on the splendor of your clothing, and so make for yourselves friends there above in Heaven; that shall comfort you in that day and hour when you shall have the greatest need of comfort. Amen.

### The Third Sermon.

<margin>
Humbling of all those who have transgressed
</margin>
Humbling of all those who have introduced this filthiness of clothing into God’s pure house, or have followed the same and still cling to it. Oh! The plague of worldly vanity has also struck them; it has also, like an evil leprosy, penetrated even into

<column-break/>

<margin>
in excess of clothing.
</margin>
their clothes (Leviticus 13:47). So they must also rightly, to their shame and humiliation, cry out with the leper: "Unclean, unclean!" (Leviticus 13:45). It is also high time that, in place of their splendid garments—which are nothing but signs and evil eruptions of a proud and worldly heart—they put on the signs of their humiliation and their unfeigned repentance for their worldliness. See, the law of leprosy required that the clothes of those found infected with it had to be torn, their head bared, and their upper lip covered; moreover, they had to cry: "Unclean, unclean!" for so the words of Leviticus 13:45 actually read. No less should be done by those who, from the preceding sermons, may have become aware that they too have been infected with this evil plague of worldly vanity, even unto their clothes. Indeed, they ought to tear those clothes of theirs, bare their heads of such frivolous top-knots <note>original: "getop"; likely referring to the 'fontange' or 'commode', an elaborate, tall headdress made of wire and lace popular in the late 1600s.</note>, and if they will not (with King Ahab) not only tear their clothes but also put sackcloth upon their flesh, and fast, and lie in sackcloth, and walk slowly (1 Kings 21:27), let them at least henceforth wear only a garment that is no more costly than their calling and status can well afford. And let them, according to the advice of the Apostle, no longer adorn themselves in all-too-costly clothing (as many have done for all too long), but only in modest apparel, with shamefastness and sobriety.

To this end, many and various powerful motives and persuasive reasons can be brought forward from the Word of the Lord and from all that has been said before, some of which we shall briefly touch upon.

Now, this is His livery, these are His colors in clothing which He desires His subjects to wear: namely, *that they adorn themselves, not in costly clothing* (for that is the livery of the world, which is His mortal enemy, John 15:19, 20), *but in honorable attire, with modesty and moderation*, 1 Tim. 2:9.

Is it not then also quite right that every Christian person should conform and adapt themselves to this? That they should indeed put off **excess** in clothing, which is the livery of the world, and conversely clothe themselves in **honorable attire, with modesty and moderation**, which is the livery of Christ? Would it be fitting if some <term>soldiers<note>original: "lants-knechten," referring to infantry or mercenaries.</note></term> who were in the service of the <term>States General<note>The governing body of the Dutch Republic; the author uses the contemporary political conflict between the Dutch and Spanish as a spiritual metaphor.</note></term> should want to wear the colors of the King of Spain? Likewise, it is not becoming for someone who identifies as a Christian to attempt to put on the livery of the world, which is a sworn enemy of Christ. Therefore, the servants and handmaidens of Jesus Christ may no longer carry upon themselves those excesses and various attachments in clothing, since all of those are nothing but the mere vanities and frivolities of this world. Indeed, our own mouths testify to it, for we are accustomed to say of those who "puff themselves up" so much in their clothes that they are "very worldly." And on the other hand, we must be all the more ready to observe the livery and colors of the Lord Christ in our clothing; for according to His manifold wisdom, these are so established that a Christian person can wear the livery of Christ in their dress—which is **honor, modesty, and moderation**—and yet, if they are also in the service of a great [earthly] Lord, they may still wear whatever livery that Lord requires. For the Lord Christ has not prescribed this or that specific fashion, but only requires in general **honor, modesty, and moderation** in dress.

<margin>
Therefore, he is indeed happy who is found to be the first in cutting away the excess of clothing, which has risen too high among us.
</margin>
What else follows from this, but that we must necessarily let go and put off our vanities and frivolities in clothing—the costliness and the excesses, which are entirely a worldly way of being? Yes, we must cast them away like <term>filthy dung<note>A common biblical metaphor (Philippians 3:8) for things considered worthless in light of Christ.</note></term> and cast them from us as a useless burden, if we do not wish to suffer shipwreck of our Christian profession and confession in the waves and billows of this wild, frivolous world. Therefore, let us indeed all—

<summary>The author uses the metaphor of "livery" to argue that Christians should display their allegiance to Christ through modest dress rather than following worldly fashions. He compares wearing worldly finery to a Dutch soldier wearing the colors of the enemy, the King of Spain.</summary>

-> ### Mirror of Modesty. <-

<margin>Excess in clothing is very difficult to reform in many, because it arises from an internal disorder of the heart; indeed, it clings to them like the leopard’s spots.</margin>
we have observed that those who have practiced [excessive dress] without considering how evil it was, behave very submissively and begin to prepare themselves for improvement. But there is a sort of people—and not a few—who have not only been stirred up to preciousness in clothing by the common example they saw before them, but who have themselves been the first **instigators** <note>original: "roer-vincken," literally "stir-finches," meaning ringleaders or agitators.</note> in this misdeed. For them, this evil of excess in clothing proceeds from an internal disorder of their hearts, or from pride, or from frivolity, or from a slavish servitude to the world; it sits in their very marrow and bones. It is truly to them like the **leopard's spots**, <note>A reference to Jeremiah 13:23: "Can the Ethiopian change his skin, or the leopard his spots?" implies that the sin has become part of their nature.</note> which are not painted on the outside, but spring forth internally from his natural constitution, within his skin and hide. See, so it is also with many regarding splendor in clothing: their excesses are to them like the leopard's spots. You seem to tear their very hearts when you wish to pluck those [excesses] away; they are wicked sores, boils, and pimples that have broken out from the internal pride and frivolity of their hearts. Therefore they cry and complain, and are very dissatisfied when one touches them even a little harshly. And what is most lamentable: as if these sores and boils were truly a beautiful ornament, they stand there defending them with knee and elbow, with hands and nails, as much as they possibly can, to protect and maintain them. Then there are yet others who, although they do not make so much work of these vanities, nevertheless believe that it does not signify much 

<column-break/>

whether one does it this way or that; and therefore they do not want the trouble of paying attention to it. We shall yet seek to help both of these to a better path, if perhaps the Lord God might grant that, noticing their disorder, they might also be moved to improve it. The first are arrogant people; the second are complacent; both have need of instruction.

<margin>People seek many excuses to justify their pride in clothing, which we subsequently set forth and answer here.</margin>
As for the first, there are people who seem to have the plague upon them that **Isaiah** threatens: namely, that they have eyes and see not, have ears and hear not, have a heart and perceive not <note>original: "Esa. 6 : 10."</note>. For although their pride convicts them in their very faces, and they do not hide their magnificent and excessive being in the vanities of clothing—but rather display their being in public for the very purpose of being seen and noticed—they nevertheless seek to justify their case through hollow excuses, and to make the people believe they do no evil. Therefore, we shall briefly touch upon these hollow excuses here and refute them with a word, and thus, as if with a sweep of the Lord’s hand, clear away those stumbling blocks that still lie in the path of many, and over which many still fall regarding excess in clothing. The excuses are very many; we shall present and answer them with little parade, yet very faithfully.

<margin>1. Excuse. It is "Monkery" to insist so strongly on the simplicity of clothing.</margin>
1. It is nothing but introducing a new **Monkery** <note>A derogatory term used by Reformers to describe what they saw as the legalistic, outward rituals and rules of Roman Catholic monks.</note> among Christians to insist and compel so strongly upon the manner of clothing. **Answer.** We do not place any holiness in clothing, as the Monks do; nor do we bind anyone to a certain garment, a certain fabric, or a certain fashion

<meta>This page continues the discussion from page 550 regarding the excuses people make for wearing extravagant clothing. The author is refuting the idea that "Christian freedom" allows for vanity, specifically addressing the theological concepts of "taken" versus "given" offense.</meta>

# Mirror of Modesty.

<margin>
4. Excuse.
It is only a "taken" offense when people stumble over the finery in clothing.
</margin>
...forgotten? <note>original: "vergeten"</note> Certainly, something evil is at work here. There is hardly a pair of terms in the whole of Theology as well known as this distinction between **taken** and **given offense**, <note>"Given offense" refers to doing something wrong that leads others into sin; "taken offense" refers to someone being offended by a neutral act due to their own weakness or malice.</note> yet the right use and application of it—which is also taught—is forgotten by almost everyone. Likewise, this distinction is throughout miserably abused by worldly people to excuse many intolerable improprieties and to embolden many in the practice of vanities. Certainly, this comes from the evil one, and he who loves his soul must be on his guard against this.

<margin>
5. Excuse.
It is the Ministers' fault that people take offense at our fine clothes, because they preach against them; if they could keep silent, no one would be offended.
</margin>
5. If offense is given through the finery and elegance of clothing, it is the Ministers' fault; they create the offense among the people because they stand and shout against it so much and incite the people; if they could only keep silent, there is not a mother's child who would be offended by it. **Answer.** Truly, this sin and excess in clothing is very shameless, when it is found so clearly on every corner and neighborhood of the streets, "in its own blood," <note>original: "in haren bloede"; likely a reference to Ezekiel 16:6, implying a blatant or raw state of sin.</note> yet it still dares to lay the blame for everything upon the men of God. 

But if we stir up offense over the finery and elegance in clothing, such as is practiced by you all, then the Holy Prophets and Apostles also stirred it up, for they shouted against it with all earnestness. They stir it up (let it be spoken with reverence) along with the Lord Christ and the Lord our God himself, who puts this into the hearts of his servants and lays it in their mouths, that they should indeed shout against it: Isaiah 3:16, Zephaniah 1:8, 1 Timothy 2:9, 1 Peter 3:3, etc. And

<column-break/>

since excess is evil in itself, we must not neglect to cry out against it, even if more offense should arise from it through your stubbornness. But we hope for better things from you, and that you will so behave that, conforming yourself to the word of the Lord, you will still give great edification <term>edification</term><note>The act of building up the faith or moral character of others.</note> in this matter in every way, as it shall be clear to all the world that you are indeed people who submit yourselves under the word of the Lord.

<margin>
6. Excuse.
Finery—silk, velvet, gold, and silver—is more common now than it was in olden times; therefore, we may now go about more finely dressed.
</margin>
6. Nevertheless, it is the truth that gold, silk, purple, and other fineries were not as abundant in the time of Isaiah <note>original: "Esaiae"</note>, nor even in the time of Paul <note>original: "Pauli"</note> and Peter <note>original: "Petri"</note>—at least not among Christians. Therefore, it is more tolerable now, and there is less excess in it, even if one goes about a bit more elegantly. **Answer.** Just as gold, silver, precious stones, silk, velvet, purple, and other luxuries are now more abundant, so on the other hand, modesty, temperance, honorableness, and other such spiritual ornaments—which are precious before God—are more rare and scarce. So too is the great abundance of all kinds of outward finery and ornaments a proof of the vanity, light-mindedness, and worldliness of these last times. <column-break/>

So likewise, it is not for everyone's dress to wear silk, velvet, gold, silver, pearls, or precious stones. Wine is good, but it is not good to be drunk by those who lie in a burning fever. Silk, velvet, silver, pearls, etc., are good, but they are not good for you, because your status does not reach so high. Indeed, as I say: when you come into the shop to buy some fabric, you being merely a common person, the fabric is praised to you, for it is said to you, "it is very beautiful, it is indeed lordly attire," <note>original: "Heeren dracht"</note> they say to you; upon that you buy it then: but do you not even once notice that it is not for common people to wear, but that it is lordly attire? And how do you not even once consider that you ought therefore to keep away from it? Note further: bread and wine are good things, but it is not good to eat too much bread or drink too much wine; it makes a person full and drunk. Silk, velvet, gold, silver, pearls are good—even if your status brought with it that you might wear some silk, some velvet, some gold and silver—yet it is still not good for you if it exceeds the measure and you would flaunt <note>original: "uyt-braken," literally to vomit or erupt out</note> too much with it.

Now, it displeases the eye of this your heavenly Husband greatly that you deck yourself out according to the eye of the world and present yourself so: it is not outward ornaments, but the meek and quiet spirit, faith, and moderation that please this heavenly Husband well. Furthermore, you must also know that marriages brought about and sought out through outward finery commonly have little blessing. The love that a woman must win through outward adornments <note>original: "parceerselen"</note> is fleshly, unstable, and comfortless. The best bonds and ties of love with which a woman must hold her husband to her are humility, chastity, purity, politeness, modesty, honorability, friendliness, ready obedience, and the respect she bears toward her husband. Let loose women <note>original: "lichte Vrouwen," implying women of ill-repute</note>, who have no better gifts, help themselves with those vanities, but that is entirely unbecoming for godly matrons. In saying this, we do not forbid anyone from making themselves clean and becoming in their clothing for their husbands, but only that they should not be outward, excessive, or frivolous in it.

13th Excuse. A good garment of honor gives standing and credit among people.
</margin>
13. Nevertheless, a good garment of honor gives standing and credit among people, and if we were to lay aside our costly clothes—in ourselves, in our wives, and our children—the people on the exchange <note>original: "beurse," referring to the mercantile Bourse or market where business was conducted.</note> would easily think we had lost our wealth <note>original: "van goederen af gegaen," literally "gone away from goods."</note>. Answer: We do not deprive

<column-break/>

anyone of wearing a good garment of honor according to his station and calling, but we set ourselves against the pride, the excess, and the frivolity in clothing which goes beyond one's station and calling. Furthermore, on the exchange, one does not look at the clothing, but at the man; it is an entirely vain fear that people would suspect you had lost your wealth if you set aside the vanities of your clothes. For there is not a single sensible person who does not know that merchants do not become impoverished so suddenly <note>original: "op een spronck," literally "at a jump."</note> that they would need to pawn their clothes and arrive in a poor garment. Thus, no one can gain true standing and credit through a magnificent and excessive garment; rather, he causes envy and malice to be stirred up against himself among those who know him. And as for those who do not know him, there is no one so foolish that, in this current general excess of clothing, they would give an unknown person any credit based on his fine clothes. If there are any so foolish, they are commonly deceived thereby; and surely you do not mean to say that you wear costly clothes above your station in order to be credited above your means? In all cases, a modest, sober garment will inspire more credit with a stranger than an outward garment, let it be as costly as it may. We also see that those who are most moderate in their clothing are the most secure people in their credit, as we also touched upon above; and because honorability teaches this, they therefore receive the best credit.

# Mirror of Modesty.

<margin>
It is now the custom to go about finely dressed; the whole world does so.
</margin>

regardless of rank, style, or profession, one goes about somewhat more expensively dressed than might be wished; and once a thing has become the custom in this matter, it always seems fitting, for custom indeed has great power in the manner of dress. **Answer.** Custom has great power in dressing and must also be followed, provided it is not tainted by excessive extravagance in the fabric, or frivolity, or an excessive variety <note>The original Dutch *veel-topigheydt* refers to a gaudy or overly complex variety of colors and fashions.</note> of colors or fashions; for it is certain that what is most common in this regard is best. But when the garment is tainted by excessive extravagance, frivolity, or gaudiness, then we must, according to the counsel of *Jude*, hate the garment that is spotted by the flesh, *Jude verse 23* <note>original: "den rock, die met het vleesch bevleckt is, haten"</note>; for such a custom conflicts with God's word, which can and may not be nullified by any custom whatsoever. Extravagance, frivolity, and gaudiness in clothing are evil in themselves; therefore, they cannot be made good by custom, any more than an evil garment can become good by being worn often. Here the command of God applies: *you shall not follow a multitude to do evil.* *Exod. 23:2.* Thus, it also cannot excuse us that "the whole world does it," for the world is set in wickedness, and broad is the way that leads to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat, *Matt. 7:13.* Therefore, the more common the taint in clothing has become through custom, the greater our prudence ought to be (as in a time of plague) to guard ourselves so that we are not also tainted, since this is, after all, the only proof of our true

<column-break/>

godliness: that we keep ourselves unspotted from the evil customs, traditions, commands, and ways of doing of this world, which lies in wickedness, *1 John 5:19.* Furthermore, we answer even more specifically: splendor, excess, and extravagance in clothing is not "the custom," or at least there are still those among us who set a better example for us, whom we ought rather to follow. For as *John* says to us: *beloved, follow not that which is evil, but that which is good,* *3 John verse 11.* It is not only the children of the world who are so excessive in their clothing, but also those who have been led astray from reason by the world; we must not follow them either, but rather restrain ourselves so that such mischief might be stopped. And certainly, though it may be the custom in our City to parade about so in one's clothes, it is not the custom among all our united and closest friends <note>The author likely refers to fellow members of their religious community or "brethren."</note> with whom we also share a distinction: those who are carried away and take offense when they see such outward and excessive display in clothing. Thus, it is not the custom, or else that custom is a manifold offense that should not go unpunished because of its commonness; and the garment that is stained by sin must be shunned, so that it might not also taint others.

Bear with us, you great and mighty of the world, that we say it to you: Sarah was noble; Sarah was indeed the noblest woman of whom we can read. Refers to Genesis 11, describing the lineage of Abraham and Sarah.</note> and so she was also married to the most noble and excellent personage then under the Sun. Nevertheless, Sarah did not wish to go about dressed so <note>Meaning: she did not dress ostentatiously despite her high rank.</note>, as Peter testifies, <note>Original: '1. Pet. 3:5.6.' Refers to 1 Peter 3:5-6, which praises the holy women of the past for their internal rather than external adornment.</note> The king’s children are surely the noblest in the land; nonetheless, the Lord will not tolerate that they should wear a strange garment <note>Original: 'een vreemt kleet'. This refers to Zephaniah 1:8, where God threatens to punish those clothed in foreign apparel, interpreted by the author as a condemnation of following international fashion trends.</note>, as you people do, <note>Original: 'Zep. 1: 8.' Refers to Zephaniah 1:8.</note>. The courtly daughters of Zion, which was the King's Palace, were noble daughters of great descent; nonetheless, the Lord took it poorly of them that they so flaunted themselves in so many follies as are there enumerated, <note>Original: 'Esa. 3: 16. Et.' Refers to Isaiah 3:16 and following, a famous biblical passage condemning the vanity and jewelry of the women of Jerusalem.</note> and such as you people now also tend to load upon yourselves. Oh! will you bear it that one says it to you, you noble, you great, and highest of state: you are the beginning of sin among the people of God in this matter as well, <note>Original: 'Hos. 5: 1.' Refers to Hosea 5:1.</note>. Look there: your status, your descent, your riches, your reputation, your persons are in all ways much esteemed by the common people; the multitude conforms itself to your example. What you hold in high regard, they also regard highly and think it to be worth something. When you people then put on those excesses in fashions, and thereby present yourselves before the people, it ignites in them a hot desire to mimic that as well, and through this it happens that those vanities, like a poisonous air, infect all the inhabitants of the land. And then this disaster is added to it: that when the common man

<column-break/>

has begun to adopt your fashions, you must then devise something new, and thus all sorts of new vanities come out of the court, and the transgressions become very many, and the disaster very great. All of this you could entirely prevent if you yourselves would lay aside your vanities, just as your Christianity exhorts you to do, and would present yourselves before the people in a choice, precious, yet also stately and dignified garment, as is fitting. So it is proper that you, you great and mighty, should ward off this disaster from the **Christian Republics** <note>The author uses 'Republijcken' (Republics) to refer to the organized Christian states of his time.</note> both through a good example and through good laws that are well-kept, just as both of those means were employed even in **pagan republics** to ward off the encroaching pride and excess in clothing.

[these] can be, and truly are often, great occasions for such pride in those who practice them; whereby some conceited people begin to exalt themselves more than is proper, or to pretend that they are better than others, solely and only because they do those things outwardly, while in the meantime their heart before God the Lord is worth nothing at all. But because some thus misuse these holy practices for vanity and spiritual self-conceit, should one therefore refrain from earnestly encouraging people to properly fulfill those aforementioned religious exercises and practices? And [should one] rather keep doing that, and even more so warn them that they should not practice those same exercises outwardly only in a blameless manner, but that they should endeavor to do the same with an upright, simple, and believing heart; which if they do, who can then deny that they truly show their deeds to be better than those who do not practice the aforementioned holy exercises at all? But now everyone knows that for such cases one may not omit the diligent urging of proper moderation and sobriety in food and drink. And it is enough for such people that one points out to them, alongside the abuse, the proper use of the good gifts of God, as we have also done regarding the matter of clothing, from which it has appeared that we in no way set ourselves against a decent, honorable garment for everyone, nor against a stately garment for those whose calling <note>The term 'beroep' refers to one’s social status or professional position, which in the 17th century dictated what was appropriate to wear.</note> requires it: but we set ourselves only against great costliness, frivolousness, and extravagance in clothing, which indeed misbecomes

<term>Mirror of Modesty</term>: The title of the treatise, suggesting the text serves as a spiritual mirror for the reader to examine their conscience.
<term>Excess in clothing</term>: Over-indulgence in fashion, considered a spiritual distraction.
<term>Ruff</term>: A "lobbe," the distinctive starched collar of the era, which became a symbol of vanity as it grew in size.
<term>Quibbling</term>: "Fymelinghe," used by the author to describe the act of making excuses for small sins that lead to larger ones.
<term>Fear of the Lord</term>: The beginning of wisdom, which the author suggests should be the true guide for fashion.

...worn out, that you yourself will sooner be worn out and eaten by worms than your clothes will be worn out: indeed, how do you not fear that the Lord in His wrath will Himself come to snatch those things from your neck with His own hand, through sickness and death, since you will not do it at His word when you could do it right now? <margin>
31st Excuse. We do not know what we should then do with our clothes, if we must set them aside and trim them down. <note>original: "besnyden" — literally "circumcise," here meaning to cut away excess finery or alter them for modesty.</note>

31. Finally, when those who are extravagant in their dress are thus stripped of all their excuses, they begin to complain that they do not know—if they must change their attire in this way—what they are to do with the many clothes they have already made and have lying by them. If these people had not burdened themselves, contrary to the counsel of Holy **Scripture**, with such very costly clothes or with so many bundles of garments—as if they wanted to set something aside for the moths as well (*James 5:2*)—then the loss would be small, and consequently, the complaint about this could not be great.
