Secondly, they must also know that the Lord God

<column-break/>

Himself provides them with a fitting answer to their complaint and question. For He testifies of *Tyre* <note>An ancient Phoenician city-state famous for its wealth and luxury</note> that it should be converted to the Lord from the heart (for that is how that text in *Isaiah 23:17-18* must be understood when all is well-considered): that then her merchandise and her "hire of a harlot" (that is, the profit she formerly spent on the worst things) should be holy to the Lord. It shall not (He says) be gathered as treasure, nor locked up; but her merchandise shall be for those who dwell before the Lord, so that they may eat their fill and be clothed in strong, durable garments (*Isaiah 23:17-18*). By this, the Lord clearly gives us to understand that when someone is converted in their heart from the pride and excess of their clothing, they should not gather their costly and extravagant clothes as treasure, nor hide them away. Instead, those who "dwell before the Lord"—that is, the true and needy members of the *Church of Christ* (see *Acts 2:44* and *4:34, etc.*)—shall enjoy the benefit of them for their food and their necessary clothing. Thus we answer these people from the mouth of the Lord: they should hallow to God those costly and extravagant clothes with which they have sinned, and hand them over to the *Almoners* <note>original: "Arm-meesters" — local officials responsible for distributing relief to the poor</note> or *Deacons* of the *Church of Christ*. These men will determine how to sell those same costly garments for the best profit of the needy, in order to provide the poor with necessary food and strong, durable clothing, made from those costly and superfluous clothes in which the proud (now being better instructed that they should no longer show off with them)...

As for the first point, it is certain and sure: the magnificent and extravagant dress that you should reject, but which you people still wish to keep wearing, must and will necessarily always be in your way. Ultimately, it will help lead you to ruin as an instrument and tool of Satan in the most significant cases and greatest needs that can befall you, if you do not lay it aside in time. There are no weightier events that can happen to a person than these four (setting aside personal matters where it is also constantly in the way), namely: 1. the practice of prayer; 2. the occurrence of difficulties and oppressions; 3. the hour of death; 4. the day of judgment. Well, in all of these, magnificent clothing is in a person's way.

<margin>1. Vanity and extravagant worldliness in clothing is a great hindrance to a person when they wish to devote themselves to the duty of prayer.</margin>

Must it not greatly weaken—yes, even break—the power of your prayer and of your faith in praying? ...and a completely faithful and excellent account has been given (above other things) against the manifold vanities that you are wont to practice from head to foot in your clothing. Behold then what the spiritual garment is, with which we may adorn ourselves, so that we might excel above others in precious finery.

<margin>
2. Proof that the spiritual garment is much better than the physical: because it performs all services to the soul which the physical garment does to the body.
</margin>

II. Yet many, even among Christians, when they hear mention of this spiritual garment, have no spiritual eye to see the glory and excellence thereof; so they then have neither desire nor inclination for it, like those who do not know its worth at all. They even think, when they hear it preached, that a choice and magnificent garment of <term>caffa<note>A rich silk fabric, often with a patterned weave similar to damask or velvet, highly prized in the 17th century.</note></term>, satin, silk, and velvet, adorned with gold and silver, is much more glorious than spiritual virtues—which are, after all, the only true adornment. Therefore, we must secondly open and declare the worthiness and excellence of this spiritual garment.

In order then to rightly understand that this spiritual clothing indeed far exceeds in value and glory all the most precious physical garments that a Prince or King can put on, we must know in general that this spiritual clothing is the covering of the soul. Inasmuch as the soul is better than the body, so much more worthy and precious is the spiritual garment that we recommend to you than that choice physical clothing with which you are so infatuated. For also this spiritual garment—which is our Lord *Jesus Christ* with His merits and virtues—does everything for the soul that common clothes do

<column-break/>

for the body of man; these serve a fourfold purpose. First, to cover the shameful nakedness of the body. Second, to preserve the body against the hardships of wind and weather. Third, to adorn the body. Fourth, to make a distinction between persons, of what honor, age, or state they might be. The spiritual garment serves the soul for these same ends.

<margin>
1. The spiritual garment serves to cover the cursed nakedness of our soul.
</margin>

1. The spiritual garment, which we recommend to you, and which is the Lord *Christ* with all His merits and gifts, can alone cover the shameful nakedness of our soul, into which sin has brought us. See, we all lie by nature naked and bare in our blood, and are by nature entirely loathsome in the eyes of our God, as you may read in *Ezekiel 16:4, etc.* Now there is no silk nor velvet, no precious cloth or linen, nor any kind of worldly or physical ornament that can in any way, before the eyes of our God, cover and hide the shameful and sinful, cursed nakedness of our soul. That can only be done by the wool which the Lamb of God wore—He who takes away the sins of the world. It is indeed only the bright-shining garment of the righteousness of *Christ* which can cover and hide before the eyes of God our sinful and cursed nakedness. That is that "wing of God" <note>original: "vleugel Gods"; a biblical metaphor (see Ezekiel 16:8) for divine protection and the covering of one's shame with the hem of a garment.</note> with which our nakedness is covered, *Ezekiel 16:8.* Those are the ornaments with which our sins were hidden before the eyes of God, *Psalm 32:1, 2; Revelation 16:8.* Just as we then, if we were naked in body among the people, would give much to have even a rag to cover our shame-

You take upon yourselves those manifold frivolous fripperies <note>original: "flickflackeryen"; referring to trivial, fluttering decorations or nonsense in dress.</note> which the Lord God has as expressly rejected in His word as a cursed and rejected fashion. <margin>Isaiah 3:16, etc.</margin> For dear indeed, who are so vain, who are so frivolous, who are so high-crested <note>original: "veel-topich"; a critique of the high, layered hairstyles or "fontange" headdresses popular in the late 17th century.</note> in their clothing as you, who are called the noble and the great of the world? 

Examine yourselves with a simple eye, and tell me: have you not truly picked up and put upon yourselves that frivolous, high-crested garment which the Lord once tore from the bodies of the haughty daughters of Zion and threw into the dust? Change your ways in this, and better yourselves at the first opportunity. For it truly becomes all of you, who are exalted by God, that you should in turn seek to exalt the Lord your God with David, <margin>Psalm 30:2.</margin> and that you seek in all ways to show that you have high and lofty thoughts—thoughts that can despise the finery in clothing, even that worthless doll-work <note>original: "poppe-werck"; implying that fashion is as trivial as dressing dolls.</note> which many respectable people, as if they were still children, stare at in amazement. 

We have shown above that there is indeed a garment of honor, a stately garment to be found, which would display your excellence above others, and at the same time display

This also applies proportionally to those who are the most prominent in their rank and calling: you rich and mighty merchants, you foremost among the shopkeepers, and the craftsmen; among your equals, see to it also that you go before others with sobriety, shamefastness <note>original: "schaemtigheydt"; a 17th-century term for a healthy sense of modesty or the capacity to feel shame.</note>, and moderation. ## Short Prayer, in which the sin of finery is confessed, amendment thereof is promised, and forgiveness and healing for it are desired.

> Lord God, Heavenly Father, you who resist the proud and give grace to the humble: I confess before your great Majesty that I have often trespassed in pride, and with the finery <note>Original: "pronckerye"—meaning ostentatious display or gaudy dress</note> of my clothing have angered your Majesty and offended your holy congregation. For this, I have well deserved that you should have long ago, through one heavy plague or another, snatched all my vain adornments from my neck and laid me down in the bed of sorrow <note>A common 17th-century metaphor for a bed of illness or divine affliction</note>. 
> 
> But Lord, you have been merciful to me and have spared me until now; and whereas you might have forced me to unlearn my finery through your striking hand, you have rather chosen to warn me against it in time through your friendly Word, so that I might improve and escape your punishments. Great then is your long-suffering toward me in every way. 
> 
> Therefore, I now also promise your high Majesty that I will no longer indulge in the finery of my clothing; indeed, that I will, at the first opportunity, put far away from me and mine all my vanities and offensive adornments, and henceforth clothe myself according to your counsel in clean garments, with modesty <note>Original: "schaemte"—referring to "shamefastness" or a humble, bashful disposition</note> and moderation: so that I might henceforth edify all those whom I have previously offended with my finery by my modest attire. 
> 
> Yes, Lord, this I promise your high Majesty, and I shall also keep it. Only for the sake of the merits of your Son, forgive my previous sins, graciously heal the vanity of my heart, and give me such a heart and mind that henceforth, all my life long, I might strive and endeavor, as one beloved of God, to be adorned with heartfelt mercy, kindness, humility, gentleness, and long-suffering: so that I might be found to be truly one of your children, and subsequently, upon departing from this world, be clothed—like all the Saints of God—with eternal glory, through Jesus Christ your Son, who with you and the Holy Spirit be all praise, prize, honor, and gratitude from eternity to eternity, *Amen*.

# Explanation
### concerning the Title
->Of this<-
## T R E A T I S E.

In many places, one finds paintings of a head crowned with thorns and covered in blood, bearing the inscription *Behold the Man* <note>Original Latin: *Ecce Homo*—the words spoken by Pontius Pilate when presenting Jesus to the crowd (John 19:5)</note>. This is a human invention intended to represent the inhuman passion <note>The "Passion" refers to the period of intense physical and spiritual suffering undergone by Jesus Christ leading up to and during his crucifixion</note> and the most bitter suffering of our Savior and Redeemer Jesus Christ. However, such things provoke only human emotions and a fleshly devotion. In this following treatise, we have instead endeavored to reveal the meaning of these words from the Word of the Lord; and through that, to explain the nature of the bitter suffering of our Savior and Redeemer Jesus Christ, and what sweet fruits we may obtain from it. In this, we have followed the example of many excellent men, both of the early centuries and of these present times; yet we have set the Holy Scripture uniquely before us as our pattern to explain Christ's suffering and its fruits, as those who know that:

> *the Word of God alone is living, powerful, and sharper than any two-edged sword, and pierces even to the division of soul and spirit, and of joints and marrow <note>A paraphrase of Hebrews 4:12</note>: useful for converting souls and strengthening them in true conversion.*

<summary>In this preface, Willem Teellinck argues that visual art (like "Ecce Homo" paintings) only stirs superficial emotions. He explains that his treatise will instead use Holy Scripture to provide a deeper, spiritual understanding of Christ's suffering and its benefits for the believer.</summary>
<keywords>Ecce Homo, Passion of Christ, Scripture vs. Tradition, religious art, spiritual devotion, conversion, Word of God, Middelburg</keywords>

# Most Honorable, Worshipful, Wise, Prudent, and very Discreet Lords:

## *The Delegate Directors, in the assembly of the Seventeen, representing therein the United and General Chartered East India Company of these free United Netherlands.*

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'A' at the start of the main text, depicting two cherubic or classical figures intertwined with scrolling foliage.</image-desc>

As we reflect within ourselves upon what the Lord *Jesus Christ* the Son of God has done and suffered for us children of men, it seems to us that all of us Christians, as many as there are of us, ought to do our utmost diligence to spread the honor of our Savior and Redeemer *Jesus Christ*, and to make it our primary work throughout our lives that we might make His Name great in every way among the nations. 

When we then further consider by what means we Christians could best do this, we can think of no better way than that we, with all passion and earnestness, should proclaim to the children of men to whom He has not yet revealed Himself, who the Lord *Jesus* the Son of Mary <note>Original Latin: *Mariae*</note> is—even the Son of God—and what He has done and suffered for us, and to reinforce this through a Christian way of life. This was also the mind of *Paul*, the Apostle to the Gentiles <term>Gentiles: historically referred to here as "heathens," meaning non-Christian peoples encountered in the colonies</term>; for he testifies that even among the Gentiles themselves, among the learned Corinthians <note>OCR: "Corinheren"—a 17th-century spelling for the people of Corinth</note>, and among all the clever worldly-wise, he desired to know nothing else but *Jesus Christ* and Him crucified, *1 Cor. 2:2.* 

It is also certain and sure that nothing in the world can be conceived or imagined more powerful and moving to turn people away from the vain way of life they learned from their parents than the thorough explanation of the nature of our Savior and Redeemer *Jesus Christ*, and of His bitter suffering and death, *1 Pet. 1:18.* For truly all of this is such a great, so wonderful, so incomprehensible a matter for human intellect, exceeding so far all that humans could ever have imagined or thought of themselves, *1 Cor. 2:9,* that whenever the same is properly presented and revealed to the children of men, there immediately appears such a wonderful Divine wisdom, and such utterly lofty and excellent mysteries, that all hearts and minds that can only be won over to pay attention and notice with care, must also be convinced...

# PREFACE.
### Hhhh 3

difficulties, such as appeared in the propagation of the Christian faith, the Christian faith would never have driven Heathendom <term>Heathendom<note>A historical term used to describe non-Christian religions and cultures</note></term> out of these parts of the world. Concerning all matters of exceeding great importance and weight, great difficulties usually present themselves, which must first be overcome in order to accomplish something great. But against this, if the cause we have before us is good, we must place our even greater God; otherwise, one will never, never accomplish any great thing in the service of our great God. In such circumstances, one ought indeed rightly to consider that it is written: *He who is in us Christians is stronger than he who is in the world* (1 John 4:4). And looking upon this good Spirit of God, who *works where He wills, just as the wind blows where it wishes* (John 3:8), and who can do great things alone, then all those who have great things at hand under the guidance of this great Leader must also take great courage and heart. They must in no way despair over a thousand inconveniences that arise, if they only know that their work is the work of their God.

Whatever zealous heart might find itself moved further toward this, we give this advice: do not think, "this we shall be able to accomplish and bring about, but that we cannot," when the Lord God nevertheless requires both. Rather, surrender yourself entirely to the will of your God (1 Peter 4:2), looking to nothing else but His help; then you shall be strong. Do not despair, therefore, that the wickedness of the world is great, or that there are not many upright Christians to be found who are willing to undergo the hardships of such a difficult journey to then spread the honor of Christ among the Heathens. Consider instead how great the power of God is, and how great and precious His goodness is toward all those who are zealous for His honor. Take hold of Him then—of His power and His goodness—through faith. Make good laws, establish strict orders and see that they are well maintained, looking to your God; and what does it matter? For you shall accomplish more than you could pray for or even think (Ephesians 3:20). Only believe, only dare, only trust your great God whom you serve, whose work you wish to do, and you shall surely succeed. Imagine that the poor Indians <term>Indians<note>In this 17th-century Dutch context, this refers to the indigenous peoples of the East Indies, modern-day Indonesia</note></term> stand before you and plead, just as the Macedonian man once did to Paul (Acts 16:9), saying: *Come and help us.* Consider also what a great gain it is to win souls.

To this end, may the good God move all your Honors' hearts, and give His blessing over your weighty trade, to the spreading of the honor of Christ, the winning of many Heathens, the great benefit of our dear Fatherland, and the comfort of His holy Church. AMEN.

# TREATISE,
## Regarding the bitter suffering of Christ, and the sweet fruit that we may obtain therefrom.

Set forth upon the words of John 19, verse 5.

> Jesus then came out, wearing the crown of thorns and the purple robe, and (Pilate) said to them, "Behold the Man."

---

### CHAPTER I.

-> The Text is opened, and an introduction made to the following discourse. <-

<margin>Pilate’s worldly <note>literally "fleshly"</note> wisdom failed him in his previous counsel to release Christ with the favor of the Jews.</margin>
Pilate, being convinced of the innocence <note>literally "un-guiltiness"</note> of the Lord Christ / and furthermore warned by his wife / that he should have nothing to do with that righteous man / desired to let the Lord Jesus go; and to that end, he had presented Barabbas the murderer and Jesus the righteous one to the Jews, so that they (according to the ill custom they had at the high feast of Passover) should choose / which of the two / they wished to have set free; trusting that the Jews would surely have preferred to choose Jesus the righteous one / rather than Barabbas the insurrectionist <note>literally "uproar-maker"</note>. However, the perversity <note>or "corruption"</note> of the Jews was so great

<column-break/>

# Of the Bitter Passion of Christ,

you are no friend of Caesar <note>original: "des Keysers vriendt"; a reference to the Jews' threat in John 19:12 that if Pilate released Jesus, he would be acting against the Emperor.</note>, John 19 verses 6, 12.

However, although Pilate failed in the goal he had intended with this speech to the Jews, when he said of the Lord Jesus, *Behold the man*, there is nonetheless a great power of observation in Pilate’s words. We may rightly believe that he spoke them through a special steering of God; just as Caiaphas the High Priest, in a similar situation, once spoke a word concerning the Lord Jesus that contained much more than he himself knew, John 11:50. Therefore, we shall examine these words of Pilate more closely; and seeing that Pilate spoke more here than he himself realized, we Christians may rightly bring to it that light and closer explanation which can be given to us from the Word of the Lord. To that end, we shall look at things more closely: **First**, of whom Pilate speaks here when he says, *Behold the man*. **Secondly**, what he says about him.

### CHAPTER II.

->Concerning who is spoken of here, when Pilate says, *Behold the man*, and what that signifies.<-

<margin>Who is understood here by "the man."</margin>
What is spoken of here is the only-begotten Son of God, who was now in great contempt according to the flesh, but who had nonetheless many times shown himself to the believers in the flesh in such a way that they had seen his glory—a glory as of the only-begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth, John 1:14. So, what is spoken of here is the Lord of Glory, the Prince of Life,

<column-break/>

the King of Kings, through whom all things were created, who also carries all things with his powerful word, and does all that he wills in heaven, on earth, and in all depths. Behold, it is of this dearly beloved Son of God, in whom God has taken all his pleasure, who is also that strong Hero, that strong Lion of the tribe of Judah, who can do all things, who was also a completely righteous King, in whose mouth no deceit and in whose heart, side, hands, and feet no sin was or could be found; of him, I say, it is spoken when Pilate says, *Behold the man*. All of this must be kept in mind from the start; for throughout these various reasons, it can be very useful for the greatness of salvation.

Behold then, of this Lord of Glory, of this only-begotten Son of God, Pilate says: *Behold the man*; thus we may notice here: **First**, that the Son of God is here called "the man": **Secondly**, that the Jews were stirred up to see him; *Behold the man*.

The Son of God is called "the man" here, and Christians may observe this in three respects.

**First**, because the Son of God became a true man in the fullness of time, born of a woman, Galatians 4:4, so he might rightly be called a man. Indeed, everyone knew him to be a man: on the other hand, the Jews rose up against the Lord Jesus,

# ...and the sweet fruit thereof.

...mercilessly, without any mercy, as if he were (with all respect, let it be said) a dog, and not a human being. Therefore Pilate says here: *Behold the man* <note>original: "Siet de mensche"; the Dutch translation of the Latin phrase "Ecce Homo."</note>, as if he had said: "Oh dear people, take note; he is surely a human being just like you, against whom you rage so much; show him some human pity and compassion."

Secondly, the Son of God is called "a man" here because he now stood there quite pitifully and lamentably, as a poor and insignificant man. For not only is it the custom of the Holy Scriptures to call those who are nothing "men" in a particular way (Psalm 9:20-21 <note>original: "Psalm 9. 21." Verse 20 in many English translations: "Put them in fear, O Lord: that the nations may know themselves to be but men."</note>), but we also use this in our common speech when we see some grief: "What has become of the man?"

Thirdly (so that we, through the light of the Word, may look into the matter a bit further than Pilate did), the Son of God is called "the Man" by way of preeminence <term>preeminence|the quality of being superior or surpassing all others</term>, and that in three respects:

1. Because this man, Jesus Christ, is the **second Adam**, the trunk and stem of a whole world of people—even all those from the entire human race who are saved and preserved (1 Corinthians 15:47, 48, 49).

2. Because this man, Christ Jesus, has taken as his portion and share all the **states** of men, which are fourfold: 1. The **blessed state**, in which man was first created. 2. The **miserable state**, into which he fell through sin. 3. The **state of grace**, to which many are restored through rebirth. 4. The **state of glory**, which the reborn children of God enjoy hereafter. Now, the man...

<column-break/>

...Christ Jesus alone, while here on earth, has had as his portion and share a part in all these states of men. For from the **blessed state** in which man was first created, he possessed innocence; from the **state of exile** <note>original: "verballinghe"; referring to the state of humanity being cast out of Eden into misery.</note>, he possessed the misery and the infirmities of man; from the **state of grace**, he possessed the fullness of grace and an abundance of spiritual gifts—more than even Adam had in the first Creation; from the **state of glory**, he occasionally displayed, while still in the flesh, a greater majesty than any man could have (Matthew 17:2, etc. <note>A reference to the Transfiguration, where Jesus' face shone like the sun before his disciples.</note>).

3. Because this man is also truly God; he is indeed God and man, true God and true man in one Person (John 1:14, 1 Timothy 3:16). Therefore, he is rightly called "the Man" by way of preeminence.

<margin>All people are awakened to see him.</margin>
Now, all people are awakened here to see this singular man: *Behold the man*. David wonders that God the Lord would look upon man and the son of man to do him good (Psalm 8:4-5). Indeed, Job finds it strange that God the Lord would open his eye over such a lowly thing as man is, to bring him into judgment (Job 14:3). If the great God still deigns to look upon poor man, how could man think himself too great to open his eyes to behold God-as-man (oh wondrous! oh most glorious sight!)? So it must also be far from us that, even though the Lord our God, in his righteous judgment, often hides his face from us...

# Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

little more than fish for his ordinary fare <note>The author suggests Christ lived a life of extreme simplicity, eating the humble food of the poor.</note> / being served by no one / and mocked and scorned by many.

<margin>
He is opposed and slandered by the prominent men.
</margin>
For during the time that he constantly went about doing good (Acts 10:38), working great miracles, healing all diseases, and preaching the Kingdom of heaven, he was nonetheless opposed by all the great and mighty. Thus he suffered altogether much contradiction from sinners; one calls him a glutton and a wine-bibber <note>original: "wijn-supper"</note>, a friend of tax collectors and sinners; another cries him out as a Samaritan; and a third accuses him of (O horror!) having a devil. Thus do the children of men quarrel and bicker against this man, who truly had come to reconcile men with God. How great then is this humiliation? Behold then the man; behold the Son of God; gaze upon his suffering.

<margin>
And he suffered most at the end of his life.
</margin>
However, so that we might better understand the suffering of this man, even our Lord Jesus Christ, we must now observe more specifically what this man, the Lord Jesus Christ, suffered at the end of his life, when the time had come that he should satisfy the justice of God for the sins of his people.

That which the Lord Christ suffered at the end of his life surpasses all that went before, and it began in the Garden of Gethsemane, thereafter before his Judges, and finally it was completed on the wood of the cross.

### CHAPTER IV.

->What the Lord Christ suffered in the Garden of Gethsemane.<-

<margin>
In the garden his soul is [troubled].
</margin>
In the Garden where the Lord Jesus Christ had withdrawn

<column-break/>

with his Disciples, after he had eaten the Passover with them and held the Last Supper; there the ultimate suffering of our Lord Jesus Christ began. There, even while alone, a great anguish came over him, so that there his soul became sorrowful on every side <note>original: "om ende om" — literally "round and round," meaning completely surrounded by grief.</note>, "deeply grieved" <note>original Greek: "περιλυπος" (perilypos), meaning surrounded by sorrow or sorrowful unto death.</note> (Matthew 26:37-38). Indeed, he was so sorrowful that he, who is the brave Lion of the tribe of Judah, became terrified and very anxious (Mark 14:33). He was so full of woe that he could not keep silent but had to lament to his Disciples, declaring to them that his soul was sorrowful unto death (Matthew 26:38).

Indeed, the anguish that bit into him in the Garden was so great that he was pressed down to the earth by it, being bent as if by a heavy burden, so that the text says that "he fell on the ground" (Mark 14:35). Then one could see the Lord of glory, to whom the highest place in the heavens belongs, lying writhing in the dust of the earth like a worm of the earth, as was prophesied of him (Psalm 22:7).

And as our Lord Jesus Christ lay there pressed down for so long, like a worm of the earth that could easily be trodden upon, yet "the foot of the proud" (Psalm 36:12) came over him; the devil of hell bestirred himself and attacked him quite harshly in his greatest difficulty. There [the devil] on one side (as we must rightly assume) set before the eyes of the Lord Christ all the horrible sins we had committed, for which he had become surety <note>In a legal or financial sense, a "surety" is someone who takes responsibility for another's debt; here, Christ takes responsibility for human sin.</note>; and on the other side, the [terrible judgment of God].

They did not sleep on the matter, but with all haste hurried his death. They then dragged him to the place of execution, called the "Place of the Skull" <note>original: "hooft-scheel plaetse," referring to Golgotha or Calvary</note>, and—troubled and exhausted as he was by his bloody sweat and other mistreatment—they laid upon him his cross, which he had to carry for our sake and which was very heavy, without any mercy. And later, realizing that he would collapse under it, they forced one Simon of Cyrene to help him carry it; so that they would not lose the cruel spectacle of his crucifixion, upon which they were so intently set.

Then the Lord Jesus might justly complain and say, 
> O my people, what have I done to you? and wherein have I wearied you? Testify against me. <note>original: Mich. 6. 3. referring to Micah 6:3</note> That you press me so hard, insult me, and without any mercy thrust me forward to my death!

<margin>He is nailed through hands and feet to the cross between murderers.</margin>
Having come to the place of execution, they nailed him there to the cross; through his hands and his feet they hammered great nails, and thus fastened him to the cursed wood of the cross; and there they hung him (who was the Lord of heaven and earth) between heaven and earth, as if he were unworthy of both; yes, they crucified him between two murderers, as if he were the head, the Captain, and the Prince of all thieves, rogues, and base men. There he hangs indeed, his hands and feet most painfully pierced (for the hands and feet are among the most sensitive parts of the body, because

<margin>The Lord Jesus had to carry his own cross.</margin>

<column-break/>

so many veins and nerves come together there) he who alone can take away all our smart and pain; there his life-sap is dried up by the running out of his precious blood, as when it is parched in the Summer; because of this he became faint and thirsty, <margin>There he hangs faint for refreshment, and is still mocked.</margin> but little refreshment was granted to him; on the contrary, he was mocked and laughed at by all who passed by, even those hanging next to him did the same; and what vinegar mixed with gall was merely served to him on a reed in a sponge—if he desired to drink that, it was all that was granted to him.

Here is great distress in every way, that someone being in great anxiety of thirst seems to perish, and not even a draft of cold water may be granted to him, but only vinegar mixed with gall in a sponge; that is a heavy thing. Nevertheless, these are only the beginnings of the sorrows, in view of the distress that was yet further to come upon him.

<margin>The Devils are let loose upon his soul.</margin>
For while the Lord Jesus was thus despicably hanging there on the wood of the cross, the abyss of hell was as if opened against him; the Prince of Devils, with all his hell-hounds, was released there against his soul; they fly at his body, they surround him, they gape their jaws against him like roaring and tearing lions (Psalm 22); they attack there, in the most cruel fashion, his lonely and already sufficiently distressed soul, and distress it even more, wherever they can or may.

# On the bitter suffering of Christ,

...therefore, to every human, to all you Christian hearts: behold him indeed with understanding, and in a different manner than the Jews did. Behold there the Lord of glory / like a beast of burden / forced to carry the heavy wood of the cross; so that we might be released from all the heavy burdens of the law. Behold the Mighty One of Israel / as if fainting under the weight of a wooden cross / so that we poor, frail, weak humans / might be strengthened to bear his lovely yoke (the burden of which is not heavy) well. Behold those blessed hands of your Savior / which alone are worthy to bear scepters <note>A scepter is a staff held by a sovereign as an emblem of authority</note> / those feet / with which he tramples the head of the Devil as if underfoot / pierced through with hammers and nails to the wood of the Cross / so that we might not be bound hand and foot (as we have indeed deserved) / and thus cast into the outermost darkness. Behold the Lord of Heaven and Earth / hanging between Heaven and Earth / as if unworthy of both / so that we might be made heirs of the new Heaven / and of the new Earth. Behold him (who clothes the lilies of the field with greater glory than even Solomon was clothed) / hanging naked there on the wood of the Cross / so that he might cover our cursed nakedness and clothe us over with glory. Behold the Fountain of living waters / himself faint and thirsty / so that he might give us to drink from the streams of living waters. among the angels. Behold the well-beloved Son of God / forsaken for a short time by the Father / so that we might be accepted into eternal grace. Behold the Prince of life / dying death / so that we might be delivered from death / and live eternally. And consider then / how much / how mightily / how inwardly / you ought to be moved by all of this.

### CHAPTER VIII.
### Of the fruits of Christ’s suffering in general.

Up to now we have heard what kind of suffering our Lord Jesus Christ’s was, both what he suffered beforehand, before he was presented to the people by Pilate in such a wretched form; and what happened to him after that until death; now it follows that we also look upon this man in the fruits of his suffering.

<margin>There is great fruit in Christ’s suffering, for he suffered everything for the benefit of mankind.</margin>
It has now been sufficiently shown from the preceding discourse that the suffering of this man, our Lord Jesus Christ, was wonderfully great, the likes of which no man has ever undergone: nevertheless, as we have heard, all that this man suffered, he suffered for mankind: so we may surely be certain that a special fruit and great usefulness is to be found in the bitter suffering of our Lord Jesus for mankind.

<margin>And he is the only-begotten Son of God.</margin>
Especially when we remember that he who suffered all this was not only a righteous man, and also a quite excellent personage in himself; being truly of a great lineage and descent, the born King of the Jews according to the flesh; but even more (O incomprehensible matter!) the well-beloved and only-begotten Son of God himself, equally God, praised into eternity; what has

<column-break/>

then such a righteous, such a worthy person, been able to deserve and acquire through such a fearful, such a bitter suffering? And even more specifically, hearing that this righteous one died the death for us, so we may, so we must rightly long for the fruits; for he himself has testified of himself that he indeed is that grain of wheat, which having died, brings forth much fruit, <term>John 12:24</term> <note>Jesus uses this agricultural metaphor to explain that his death is necessary for spiritual life to multiply.</note>; that he is the bronze serpent <note>original: "metalen slange"; referring to the story in Numbers 21 where looking at a bronze serpent on a pole healed the Israelites; Jesus applies this to his crucifixion.</note> which being lifted up <term>John 3:14</term> draws all to him, <term>John 12:32</term>; so it has also long been prophesied of him that when his soul should have so labored, he should then see his seed <note>Meaning his spiritual offspring or followers.</note>, and have a portion of many, <term>Isaiah 53:10, 11, 12; Psalm 22:30, 31, etc.</term>

Now of the fruits of Christ’s suffering, much could be said; for truly the Lord Jesus Christ has through his bitter suffering conquered devil, sin, death, hell, damnation, and all. Judas, the Pharisees, the Scribes, the Chief Priests, the godless band, the soldiers, the fierce Jews, the devils of hell, and all, have all toiled and exhausted themselves in vain to overcome him and to bring him down: even though he was pressed hard by them, yet he finally triumphed over his enemies on the cross itself; having overcome all his enemies and satisfied his heavenly Father, <term>Colossians 2:14, 15</term> <note>The text refers to Christ "blotting out the handwriting of ordinances" and triumphing over principalities.</note>; so that we may see lying defeated at this man's feet (just as they were still nailed to the wood of the cross) all his enemies: the devil, sin, death, hell, and damnation, all gasping as if for their final end, <term>Psalm 110:1, 7</term> <note>The OCR lists verse 9, but Psalm 110 only contains 7 verses; the author likely refers to the imagery of enemies being made a "footstool" and the victory of the King.</note>.

Of the bitter suffering of Christ,
<meta>catchword: house</meta>

But we shall not speak of all these things in detail now, but only touch upon the immediate fruits of the suffering of our Lord Jesus Christ, which come forth and spring from the victory over the aforementioned enemies <note>The "enemies" refer to Sin, Death, and the Devil, which the author discussed in previous sections as being defeated by Christ.</note>; and through which we ourselves obtain all salvation, comfort, and blessedness. Now, these are also very many, but they can briefly all be brought under these four main headings: 1. Forgiveness of our sins. 2. Healing of our defects. 3. Comfort here in all circumstances. 4. And hereafter eternal life: greater benefits than can ever be imagined.

Behold then here again the human being: yes, behold him whom you have seen before, hard-pressed by his enemies; behold him now overcoming his enemies, treading as if over their heads; behold him triumphantly rising from the dead, ascending into heaven, seating himself at the right hand of God His Father almighty, and from there distributing gifts to his own: forgiveness of sins, healing of defects, great comfort here in this life, and hereafter eternal joy and glory. We shall now also speak of these things in particular.

### CHAPTER IX.

->Of the forgiveness of sins, which is one of the principal fruits that we have from the suffering of Christ.<-

<margin>Through Christ’s suffering, we have forgiveness of sins.</margin>
The first fruit that we have from the suffering of Christ is the forgiveness of our sins, in which also our reconciliation with God is situated.
Of this the Scripture speaks thus in Romans 3:23, 24, 25: They have all sinned, and lack the glory of God. And are freely

<column-break/>

justified by His grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus. Whom God has set forth to be a reconciliation <note>Original: "versoeninghe," often translated in biblical contexts as "propitiation" or "atonement."</note> through faith in His blood: to demonstrate His righteousness through the forgiveness of sins that occurred previously. For this reason the Prophet also says thus: He was wounded for our transgressions, He was bruised for our iniquities, the punishment that brings us peace was upon Him (Isaiah 53:5), so that He might bring us to God (1 Peter 3:18) and reconcile us with Him (Colossians 1:20, 21, 22; Ephesians 2:16, 17, 18; 2 Corinthians 5:19; 1 Timothy 2:5).

For the Lord Jesus Christ fully satisfies the justice of God for all that we have misdone; through His bitter suffering, He is found in every way to be a perfect <term>Mediator</term> <note>A "Mediator" is a middle-man or go-between who reconciles two parties—in this case, God and humanity.</note> and pays the penalty for everything that was committed there. Because we have sinned in the body, He has suffered in the body; because we have sinned in the soul, He has also suffered in the soul. If our sins are great, if they are many, if they are bloody—His suffering is great, many, and eternal. Indeed, if they are in every way deadly sins that we have committed, His bitter suffering extended even unto death. Just as Paul once wrote concerning Onesimus, in order to reconcile him with his master Philemon (from whose house he had treacherously run away, and had also taken with him what was not his): *If he has wronged you in any way, or owes you anything, put that on my account; I, Paul, have written it with this my own hand, I will repay it* (Philemon 1:18, 19). So the Lord Christ may say much more for us, to reconcile us with our heavenly Father, from whose

# and the sweet fruit thereof.

If they have wronged you in anything, or owe you anything, put that on my account <note>This phrasing echoes Paul’s letter to Philemon, used here to illustrate Christ’s role as our advocate who takes on our debt.</note>: and thus the Lord Christ makes peace between God and us, satisfying the justice of God for us, through His bitter suffering and perfect obedience shown on the wood of the cross, by which He then wipes out the record of debt that was against us, and takes that same record out of the way, Colossians 2:14, 15; Ephesians 2:16, 17. And thus, through the suffering of Christ applied to our souls, we obtain forgiveness of sins and are justified before the Lord our God.

<margin>This now is a most glorious matter.</margin>
Now, to be justified before God, to regain the forgiveness of our sins, and to have peace with the Most High, is for a poor sinner the greatest matter in the entire wide world; it is easily said, but it carries great weight. Do you wish to sense it somewhat? Imagine how one used to feel who is at odds with someone who seeks his life, that person being a capable man of his hand, bold of heart, and of great authority, who has indeed often struck down some of those he was after. Truly, merely to have such a person against him in a city, who continually seeks his life, keeps a man very troubled. What then, if the great God seeks our life, if He Himself lurks for us, Hosea 13:7, and is intent on bringing eternal death upon our heads, and casting us into hell and damnation, just as He has already done to many, such as Sodom, Gomorrah, Korah, Dathan, Cozbi, Zimri, and the like,

more, whom He, binding them in their sins, snatched away as if on the spot and cast into hell; so as to send away all those who still go there unreconciled with Him, so that they might seek peace with Him in time through Jesus the crucified.

### CHAPTER X.

->Of the healing of our defects, which is another fruit from the bitter suffering of Christ.<-

<margin>Through Christ's suffering, our defects are also healed.</margin>
The second fruit that we have from the suffering of Christ is the healing of our defects: for so says the Prophet: *By His stripes we are healed*, Isaiah 53:5. And the Apostle testifies to us: *That He bore our sins in His body on the tree: that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness, by whose stripes we are healed*, 1 Peter 2:24. So He is truly the right Samaritan <note>The "Good Samaritan" from the parable in Luke 10, frequently used in this period as a metaphor for Christ healing the wounded soul.</note>, who pours out His own heart’s blood to pour into the wounds of our souls, so that we might thereby be cleansed and healed, 1 John 1:7.

See then how it goes: the sin of the first Adam made all of Adam's children sick and weak; the wound of the second Adam <note>The "Second Adam" is a theological term for Jesus Christ, who undoes the fall of the first Adam.</note> makes all His members strong and healthy, and this is the cup that His heavenly Father gave Him to drink, John 18:11. This is truly wonderful: we were the sick ones, and He takes the medicine; He drinks the bitter drink, and we are healed; He is bled <note>This refers to the medical practice of bloodletting, common in the 17th century; the author suggests Christ underwent the "treatment" so the patient could recover.</note>, and we are lightened; He sweats a bloody sweat, He dies the death, and we receive life, 1 Thessalonians 5:10. We had been proud, and He was humbled:

# Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

we were traitors, and he was therefore himself betrayed; we were greedy, wanton, and excessive, and he suffered hunger, thirst, and want; we had swallowed the tasty morsel of the forbidden fruit, and he was therefore fed with wormwood <note>original: "alsem"; a plant known for its extreme bitterness, often used in the Bible to symbolize sorrow or divine judgment.</note> and given gall to drink; we were evildoers guilty of death, and he suffered death; the measure that we had measured out was measured out to him. Now he might well say, *I must restore that which I did not steal*, Psalm 69:5. Now we might well say: as David said in another situation, *We, we have sinned, and we have acted unjustly: but what has this innocent Lamb of God done?* 2 Samuel 24:17. He was beaten for the sake of our sins, so that by his wounds we might be healed.

   Truly, the suffering of Christ has a healing power; yes, if only we look rightly upon the crucified Christ, even this very man: he has within himself a transforming power to turn us toward his image, and to heal us of our ailments.

   But this is easily said: namely, that the Lord Jesus Christ heals us from our sins through his wounds. But it is truly a very great matter, and few are moved by it as they ought to be. Imagine it thus: think for a moment if you found yourself in the same state as poor Job once was, who had no health in him from the crown of his head to the soles of his feet; how it would refresh you to hear of a Physician <note>original: "Medecijn-meester"; literally a master of medicine.</note>? Yes, of one who would certainly heal you. If you only have a toothache or suffer from gout <note>original: "flerezijn"; an old term for gout or aching joints.</note>, how greatly do you wish to be healed of it?

<column-break/>

but now, by as much as the soul is nobler than the body, by so much more is the healing of the infirmities of the souls to be esteemed than the healing of bodily infirmities: for with all the sicknesses of the body, even when they are perfectly healed, temporal death soon follows; but upon the sicknesses of the soul follows eternal death, if they are not healed. This the Lord Jesus now does for his own through his bitter suffering, his Spirit working through it: he certainly heals them of willful sins, Psalm 19:13, and also breaks the power of devilish weaknesses, so that no sin reigns over them, since they are under grace, Romans 6:12. Indeed, this is a certain fruit of Christ’s suffering; because David had become aware of this same thing, he broke out in thanksgiving and said: *Bless the Lord, O my soul, and all that is within me, bless his holy name. Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not any of his benefits, who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases*, Psalm 103:1, 2, 3.

# and the sweet fruit thereof.

are signs of God’s wrath, fruits of God’s curse, and likenesses to the devil of hell, who is a cursed and disordered spirit, full of sorrow. Consequently, these are also certain beginnings of eternal sorrow, being merely like the smoke before the fires of hell. However, all the afflictions that we encounter in this life are made into signs of God’s love for us through the suffering of Christ <margin>Revelation 3:19</margin>, fruits of His fatherly care over us <margin>Hebrews 12:7</margin>, and certain means to advance us toward the Kingdom of Heaven and eternal joys <margin>Acts 14:22</margin>. So it is that even temporal death—which by nature is a "King of Terrors" <note>A common biblical personification of death, specifically from Job 18:14.</note> and a fierce Sergeant who drags criminal men by their stubborn necks <note>original: "taeyen halse"; implying a resisting or unyielding prisoner being forced along.</note> out of the prison of this world and away to God’s judgment, to be carried from there into the abyss of hell—is changed for us through the suffering and death of Christ. It is made into a friendly Messenger who comes to release us from the troublesome prison of this world and lead us into heavenly joys, eternal freedom, and glory <margin>Luke 16:22; Revelation 14:13</margin>. For indeed, through the death of Christ, our death is made a passage to eternal life <margin>John 5:24</margin>; therefore it is also said that those who share in the death of Christ shall not taste death.

And this is truly a very great benefit, for as we all know, it is written: all who desire to live a godly life in Christ Jesus shall be persecuted; they shall have much trouble and hindrance here in this world <margin>2 Timothy 3:12</margin>. Now they are tormented by evil men,

<column-break/>

heavily insulted and slandered; now visited with sickness, with loss of property, and the passing away of their best friends; now assaulted with heavy temptations of the Spirit. Thus, it is a great thing in every way that they know that through the cross of Christ, all these trials are sanctified and blessed for them, and consequently will turn out and work for the best. This sweetens all the bitterness of life; just as we are often willing to swallow a disgusting drink, paying money for it and gladly rewarding the Doctor <note>original: "Doctor"; here referring to a physician.</note> who prescribes it to us, all in the hope that it may do us good.

## Chapter XIII.

### A powerful example in the conversion of the Thief. From which it appears that we truly can obtain all the aforementioned fruits from the bitter suffering of Christ.

<margin>The believing thief on the cross obtained all these fruits of Christ's suffering.</margin>
See then, all these fruits and benefits we have from the bitter suffering of Christ; so has our dear Lord Jesus Christ Himself—to indeed fully assure us that we have to expect all these advantages, all these fruits, and benefits from His bitter suffering and death—wished to leave us a very excellent example thereof, through that which He Himself did, while He now hung on the wood of the Cross, suffering for our sins, to one of the two thieves who were crucified with Him. For as all know, the Lord Jesus Christ, applying the power of His suffering and death to one of the two thieves crucified with Him, has granted him the forgiveness of his sins, the healing of his defects, patience in his present sorrow, and thereafter eternal life. Yea, the Lord Jesus has reconciled him with God, and where he was previously a blasphemer (even while he already hung on the cross, as the Evangelist Mark tells us, Mark 15:32), yet He nevertheless healed him of that afterward, and made him a

<column-break/>

proclaimer of Christ's praise, as Luke witnesses to us, Luke 23 &c. so that he thereafter patiently and willingly bore the punishment that lay upon him, confessing that he suffered it justly, and thereafter passed through death into life, and was taken up with the Lord Jesus Christ (following His promise) into the heavenly Paradise, Luke 23:43.

This example is notable, for this person, if anyone, seemed to be placed entirely beyond all hope of salvation: the course of his wicked life had been altogether unholy and godless; he had committed such villainous acts <note>original: "schelm-stucken"; referring to serious crimes or outrages.</note> that he was condemned to death by the worldly Judge, yea, to the accursed death of the cross, which was not done except to the most wicked people in the world (and in this no injustice was done to him, Luke 23:41). Now, being already nailed to the cross, he remained obstinate in his wickedness and blasphemed, along with the other thief, even the Prince of Life, the Lord Jesus Christ. How could any man be further away from all hope of salvation? How could anyone be closer to eternal damnation than this man was? Nevertheless, the Lord Christ, through the power of His suffering, still delivers him and makes him blessed. How strange the Devil must have looked upon this; it was as if someone were snatched from his mouth <note>original: "muyl"; literally the snout or jaws of a beast, here referring to the "mouth of hell."</note>, yea, from hell itself. And the Lord Jesus willed to do this so as to indeed fully assure us that the power of His suffering and death is so great for the preservation...

### Of the bitter suffering of Christ;

<columns>
If there were to be seen somewhere an image or likeness of a great, mighty **Prince**, or **Potentate**, who was of such **virtue** <term>virtue: *virtuut*, here meaning an inherent power or medicinal-like efficacy</term> and strength, that all those who came daily to behold it were thereby more and more drawn up toward the same glory and excellence which that Prince and Potentate possessed; and that they, through the beholding of his image, received more and more a share and communion in all his goods and glories: how eager would everyone be to behold that image! How diligent would each person make themselves to be at that work daily, as much as they possibly could, in order to see it also? Especially if it were immediately found that whoever showed more and more diligence in inspecting that image, was truly more and more blessed in earthly things, and was drawn forward to excellent states and offices, in conformity with the glory of the Prince himself.

Well now, see, so it stands with the image of the **crucified Christ**, that whoever often and properly looks upon it is thereby more and more changed into that same image. This power and virtue the Lord Christ gives to all those who—with proper **devotion**—behold the Lord Christ the crucified, painted vividly before their eyes in his holy word: just as experience undeniably teaches. For it is found daily that truly all those who most **empty themselves** <note>original: *ontledigen*; a spiritual term for clearing the mind of worldly distractions to focus on God</note> to consider the bitter suffering and death of our Lord Jesus Christ—those who are most taken up with beholding, with the eye of faith, this man, the Lord Jesus Christ the crucified,

<column-break/>

as he is painted before us in the **Gospels** and the preaching of God’s word—that they are truly the **most Christian-like**, the **most godly**, the most "dead to the world," and the most crucified to the world (and the world to them). In their lives, they also begin to most clearly express and print out the form, the essence, the likeness, the conduct, the manner of living, and the virtues of the Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, it is indeed very much to be lamented that among those named Christians, many are now found who forget this; who indeed do not even properly move themselves—I do not say every day, but hardly once a week or month—to earnestly meditate upon the bitter suffering of the Lord Christ. People toil and turn, one day after another, year out, year in, and let themselves be entirely taken up by—indeed, I know not what—vain, brittle, perishable **trifles** <note>original: *beuselingen*</note> of the world, which cannot come to their aid in the time of need or in death, when they shall have the most need of comfort and consolation. And the Lord Jesus Christ the crucified is forgotten; indeed, almost no one looks toward him, even though the Son of God has the principal power, having come from the bosom of his Father into these deepest parts of the earth to work out our **salvation** <term>salvation: *salicheydt*, meaning spiritual rescue and eternal well-being</term> through his bitter suffering and death. Indeed, that we might at least have properly learned those things from the crucified Christ which are of the highest necessity to know for our own preservation and salvation; and yet, these can be learned most vividly and movingly by everyone through the close and right consideration of the condition of this man, even our Lord Christ the crucified.

Truly, this is so wonderful and so rare that, were we not accustomed to hearing it, and had we not accepted it from our youth, we would judge it by our <term>natural light<gloss>human reason and intellect unaided by divine revelation</gloss></term> (as the Jews and Heathens did) to be entirely unbelievable. Therefore the Lord God himself speaks of this very matter and says: *Behold, you despisers, and wonder, and perish, for I work a work in your days, a work which you shall not believe, though someone tells it to you.* Acts 13:41.

natural

unbelievable.

<column-break/>

For this circumstance of our Salvation <note>original: *Salicheydt*; meaning the state of being saved or blessedness.</note> is such that if our natural light could well believe it, or at least held it to be believable, then it would not answer the aforementioned prophecy. Nor would it match what was declared as a blessing of our Savior: that such a work, when told to the natural man, presents itself as being quite unbelievable and unbefitting the glory of God. For if he wished to do an entirely new work, this work should then be the most wondrous among the work of creation itself: it should do such that *the eye has never seen, and the ear has never heard, nor could ever rise up into the heart of man,* that which God himself had not revealed.

Holy Job witnesses to us in Chapter 26 that the Lord God *stretches out the north over the empty place, and hangs the earth upon nothing.* And after mentioning yet more other entirely wondrous things, he further witnesses that all those things (which indeed all seem so wondrous) *are but the outermost ends of his ways, yes, that we have heard but a small portion of him,* Job 26:14. Consider then: if the Lord wishes to do a work in which he will fully reveal himself and make himself known to his beloved Christians, should it then not be infinitely more wondrous than the creation of the world? Must not the Lord, our great and almighty God, in this case do such a thing that would be far over and above all the reach and understanding of man's intellect?

# and the sweet fruit thereof.

...frivolities and earthly trifles, with which all unregenerate <note>Those who have not experienced a spiritual rebirth.</note> worldly people are still constantly ensnared; so that they are violently driven and carried hither and thither in every way, one after this, another after that, each where their heart leads them, like a storm-tossed sea stirred by many winds. For as soon as we receive the true knowledge of Christ in our hearts, and consequently fellowship with him; then our stormily raging heart is stilled; we begin to see that the things of the world are nothing at all; that indeed the Lord Christ is all, and in all, Colossians 3:11; that he alone is the Lord, Nehemiah 9:6; and so our heart is drawn away from the world and begins to seek its delights in Christ, now that it sees and finds that which infinitely exceeds in worth, all-sufficiency, contentment, and satisfaction everything that the world gives, or can give. And whenever the Christian person—who has once obtained the true knowledge of the crucified Christ (and through that also fellowship with Christ)—happens to miss the presence of Christ in their soul and heart; then their soul does not usually fall back into the lusts and desires of earthly things, but it begins to mourn the absence of its Bridegroom, and goes to seek him above all, whom its soul loves, as is beautifully presented to us in Canticles <note>The Song of Solomon</note> 3 and 5, and Matthew 9:15.

Since it is thus with the true knowledge of the crucified Christ, that it is useful in all ways to thoroughly satisfy and please both the curiosity of our understanding and the covetousness of our will,

<column-break/>

we must surely strive after this knowledge above all else, for the improvement of our understanding and the satisfaction of our hearts. This is especially true because we have now also understood that this same knowledge brings such light to our understanding that through it we can better see and comprehend all other spiritual things and mysteries of the Kingdom of God; of which these three following main points are surely the most important:

First, the abominable nature <note>original: *grouwelickhept*</note> of our sins, and subsequently our great misery; for we are hung about with horrible sin inside and out, all around. Secondly, the perfection of the satisfaction <term>satisfaction: the theological concept that Christ’s suffering paid the debt for human sin</term> of Christ, from which our deliverance from misery arises. And finally, the exceeding benefit that Christ has done for us, or what the Lord Christ has earned for us, satisfying so perfectly for us through such a bitter suffering, from which then flows the right sense of the duty of gratitude. All these things, along with many others, just as they are entirely necessary for everyone to know thoroughly, so they are also perfectly set before us in this Man, in the Lord Christ the crucified; so that we only need to look closely at this Man, and with understanding consider his circumstances, and we shall immediately be able to learn in full all that is necessary for us to know regarding these things for salvation. Therefore, we shall deal with these three things somewhat more closely, seeing that they are the certain foundations of the Christian Religion and of the true Christian life, to which we must all apply ourselves.

### Chapter XVIII.
#### Concerning the horribleness of sins, and the knowledge of our misery, through the crucified Christ.

<margin>Contemplating the crucified Christ through faith allows us to see the horribleness of sin.</margin>

<margin>For the sins of the elect were the cause of Christ's suffering.</margin>

# Of the bitter suffering of Christ;

<column-break/>

...would devour; if but a small droplet of that full sea of God's wrath, which passed over his head, were sprinkled upon us, it would penetrate our inner parts and so go even into our bones, so that we would perish under it forever and eternally.

<margin>
The suffering of Christ also reveals to us what sin shall bring upon us, if we do not provide against it in time.
</margin>
And thus we can also easily perceive, from the close observation of the bitter suffering that the Lord Jesus Christ underwent for the sake of our sins, what workings, effects, and fruits our own sins are likely to produce upon our own selves, if they are not timely provided for. For truly, if our sins pressed the Lord Christ so very hard and terribly, when he had only become a surety <note>original: "borge" — a legal term meaning one who takes on the debt or legal obligation of another; a guarantor.</note> for them; how then shall they press us? What distress, what anxiety shall they cause us, if we let them be, and if we are not on our guard against them?

We must indeed rightly, remembering this, feel thus about all our sins: that truly within them lies wrapped up against our own souls and persons everything that is fearful, horrible, and abominable; that also all the grief, all the difficulty, all the evil, and all the trouble, and all the misery, sickness, pain, scorn, damage, shame, or whatever it may be and might be, that goes against us here and plagues our soul and worries our hearts, all stems originally from our sins; for so it is written: *Fools because of their transgression, and because of their iniquities, are afflicted,* <note>original: "De sotte worden om den wegh harer overtredinge, ende om hare ongerechtigheden geplaeght"</note> Ps. 107:17. Our old proverb also says, *Had we no sins, we would have no wounds.* And

<column-break/>

then we must also yet, considering the bitter suffer[ing of Chri]st, which far, far, yes [in an unutterable] manner surpasses our [own] suffering and grief that we [undergo in this] world, however grea[t it] may also be; [we must learn] therefrom that no man, through all [the thi]ngs that he suffers here on earth, [however lon]g he may live, or how many [pains] he also has, is mighty [to make satisfaction] for the misdeed of his [sins]; and consequently [conclude] therefrom that all the grief, all the [difficul]ties, and all the pains [whi]ch the poor sinner, who is still [in his] natural state, undergoes in [this world], are but the b[eginnings] of pain, the forerunners o[f eternal] grief, that shall befall him hereaf[ter], if he does not timely [provide against] the raging poison of s[in]: for behold, al[though as a] man, the Lord Christ [on the] cross suffered for a time [and] underwent [this], it shall [the wicked] man in some measure [bitterly] regret forev[er]; mis[ery] more fearful and terr[ible] than which, how can [be imagined]?

And see, thus may we [behold in] the crucified Christ, the gr[eatness] of our sins, the greatne[ss of our] misery, the wretchedness <note>original: "catijvigheydt" — an archaic term for misery or extreme wretchedness.</note> of [the pr]esent life, and the ce[rtainty] of our death, yea the terri[ble nature] of the cursed death, [which] those must die who [from] the raging poison of their sin[s] have not obtain[ed] a proper cure.

From this it is now also [clear to] perceive, how we ought to be minded concerning our sin[s], [to be] rightly [distressed] over all our sins, [over our] worldliness, wantonness, <note>original: "dertelheyt" — refers to frivolous, wanton, or luxuriously playful behavior often associated with sin.</note> vanit[y], our excess, pomp, pride a[nd...]

<summary>This page warns that if God's wrath against sin was so great that it overwhelmed Christ, it will surely destroy the unrepentant sinner. The author argues that all earthly suffering is merely a precursor to eternal punishment for those who do not seek the "cure" for sin in the crucifixion.</summary>

### ...and the sweet fruit thereof.

...arrogance, greed, ambition, wantonness, gluttony, hate, and envy; excessive living, slovenliness, and negligence in the service of God; for our profanation of the day of rest <note>original: "rust-daghs" — the Sabbath</note>, the misuse of God’s holy name and of his holy ordinances; for all our sins and for all our crimes, we must humble ourselves to the lowest degree; and in every way make all our sins our greatest sorrow, and loathe them to the highest extent. For it has now been fully revealed in the crucified Christ that our sins and crimes were like the rods, the thorns, and the nails with which he was pierced; yes, they were truly like the tails of scorpions and the stings of serpents with which the blessed heart of the Lord Jesus was wounded unto death, and with which our souls are still pierced daily, which shall also lead us to eternal death and hellish damnation if we do not provide against them in time.

<margin>
Yes, with a great sorrow we must mourn them.
</margin>
What sorrow over our sins can then be enough, which brought the Lord Christ such great sorrow? What remorse over our crimes, which caused Christ such great remorse? What pain over our transgressions <note>original: "begrijpinghen" — here used in the sense of moral failings or things "apprehended" by the conscience</note>, which gave the Lord Christ such great pains? What anguish over our sins is indeed sufficient, which so entirely and severely anguished the Lord Christ? Truly, even if we did nothing but mourn all our lives long, we could not sufficiently mourn the abomination of our sins; if we wept all our eyes out, we could never sufficiently bewail them; even if we wept bloody tears, coming from a wounded heart with the greatest pain that can be imagined, we would do no more in all this than the abomination of our sin has well deserved.

Indeed, should we not quite rightly weep as bitterly over our sins as we have so sweetly laughed over them? It is indeed prophesied of true Christians that they should do so; thus sounds the holy prophecy:

> They shall look upon me whom they have pierced: and they shall mourn for him, as [one] mourns for an only son; and they shall be in bitter lamentation for him, as one that is in bitter lamentation for a firstborn. Zechariah 12:10.

Imagine that a father had unexpectedly wounded his only-born child to death with a weapon, and saw his child bleeding to death there before his eyes; how would he feel? Would he not be most deeply humbled and grieved over such a deed? Would he not also hate and cast away from himself the deadly weapon with which he had done such a thing, beyond all thought? Well, this is our state: with our sins, as if with our own hand, we have pierced him whom we call our dear Lord, in whom we testify to have all our joy; how greatly then ought we to be grieved over this? How greatly then ought we to hate our sins, which have done such things? What tongue can express, yes, what heart can conceive how great this remorse of ours rightly ought to be?

<margin>
Thus we must humble ourselves more deeply over our sins.
</margin>
<margin>
And we must also hate all our sins with an unfeigned hate.
</margin>
Thus we, considering this thoroughly, must also be led by this to an unfeigned <note>original: "ongheveynsden" — sincere or without hypocrisy</note> hate against all kinds of sins; we must indeed rightly be much more horrified against...

-># On the Bitter Suffering of Christ;<-

...would devour; if but a tiny drop of that full sea of God’s wrath, which passed over his head, were sprinkled upon us, it would penetrate our inner parts and go even to our bones, so that we would always and eternally perish under it.

<margin>The suffering of Christ also reveals to us what sin shall bring upon us, if we do not provide against it in time.</margin>
And thus we can also easily perceive, from the close observation of the bitter suffering that the Lord Jesus Christ underwent for the sake of our sins, what workings, effects, and fruits our own sins are likely to produce upon our own selves, if they are not timely provided for. For truly, if our sins have pressed the Lord Christ so entirely hard and terribly, when he had only become a guarantor <note>original: "borge" — a legal term for someone who takes on another's debt or bail</note> for them; how then shall they press us? What distress, what anxiety shall they cause us, if we let them be, if we are not on our guard against them?

We must indeed rightly, remembering this, feel about all our sins that truly within them lies wound up against our own souls and persons everything that is fearful, horrific, and abominable; that also all the grief, all the heaviness, all the misery <note>original: "pbal" — likely a transcription error for "quaal," meaning ailment or distress</note>, and all the trouble, and all the misery, sickness, pain, scorn, damage, shame, or whatever it may be and might be, that goes against our breast here and plagues our soul and troubles our hearts, all originates from our sins; for so it is written: *Fools, because of their transgression, and because of their iniquities, are afflicted.* Psalm 107:17. Our old proverb also says, *Had we no sins, we would have no wounds.* And

<column-break/>

then we must also still, considering the bitter suffering of Christ, which far, far, yes, in every way exceeds our suffering and grief that we undergo in this world, however great it may also be, conclude from it that no little man <note>original: "menschje" — a diminutive used to emphasize human frailty and insignificance before God</note> through all that he suffers here on earth, however long he also lives, however much he also has, is able to do penance <note>original: "boete" — payment or satisfaction for a crime</note> for his misdeeds; and consequently conclude from it that all the grief, all the difficulties, and all the labor-pains that the poor sinner, who is still in his natural state, undergoes in this world, are merely the beginnings of the pain, the precursors of the eternal grief that shall strike him hereafter, if he does not timely provide against the raging poison of sin: for look, all that the Man, the Lord Christ, underwent when crucified, being tormented for a time, that shall the godless man, in some measure, have to endure always and eternally; oh, how much more fearful and terrifying is that state than any other can be described?

And see, thus we may learn from the crucified Christ the greatness of our sins, the greatness of our misery, the wretchedness of this present life, and the certainty of our death, yes, the terror of the cursed death, which those must die who find no suitable healing for the raging poison of their sins.

From this it is now also easy to understand how we ought to be minded regarding our sins; how we should rightly be moved over all our sins, over our worldliness, wantonness, vanity, our excess, splendor, and pride <note>original: "pzael" — likely "praal," meaning ostentatious display</note>...

<summary>This page argues that Christ's suffering serves as a terrifying warning of the natural consequences of sin, suggesting that if a mere 'guarantor' suffered so much, the actual sinner faces eternal peril without repentance.</summary>

# Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

against our sins, rather than against the wicked Scribes, Pharisees, and Chief Priests, the fierce Jews, and the wanton band of barbarian soldiers; for see, all whatever evil, all whatever suffering they have done to the Lord Jesus, they have done being set to work through our sins. Your sins, mine, and the sins of us all have set them in motion and incited them to do what they did. We, we are also as it were complicit <note>original: "handtdadigh" — literally 'hand-guilty' or caught in the act</note> and guilty in our hearts of all the suffering that they have done to the Lord Jesus. If we then hate them, we must hate our sins much more, which made them do that which now makes them so hateful in our eyes.

And if we judge thus—that truly those wicked Pharisees, that godless band, and the fierce Jews stand completely damnable before God because they so shamefully mistreated the Holy One of Israel, the innocent Lamb of God—then we may also easily understand from this that we, who truly set them to work and for whose sins' sake the Lord Jesus Christ suffered all that He suffered, also lie very damnable before the Lord because of our sins. Consequently, we must rightly humble ourselves to the lowest degree over our sins and hate them to the highest degree; indeed, we must flee and shun them more than the plague, the fire, the sword, and all that is terrifying and deadly—yes, more than all of those. For this reason, the Lord Jesus Christ also said to the daughters of Jerusalem who lamented and wept for Him: *Daughters of Jerusalem, do not weep for me, but weep for yourselves, and for your children,* Luke 23:28. It appears that they thought

<column-break/>

that the Lord Christ (who previously had conducted himself so <unclear>piously</unclear> <note>original: "v[r]dragen" — likely "vroom gedragen," meaning he conducted himself piously or virtuously</note> and had done them so much good) was now truly being forgotten and forsaken, and that He had been slandered by their leaders, the Priests and Scribes (of whom they still held a very high opinion), who felt they had to persecute Him unto death. It was with this mind and intention that they lamented and wept for the Lord Christ; therefore He told them that they should not lament Him so, nor mourn Him, but rather weep over themselves and over their children. For they truly carried within themselves the very cause of why the Lord Christ was in this state and why He had to suffer, and because they would yet live to see heavy and anxious times, verse 29. Thus the Lord Christ points us, in the warning He gives to the daughters of Jerusalem, to the fact that we should especially mourn, grieve, and weep for our own sins, which have done all that evil to the Lord Christ and shall yet do the same to us in this life and the life to come, if we do not provide against them in time.

## CHAPTER XIX

### A serious complaint that people rejoice in sin, which has grieved Christ to the highest degree, and how some embolden themselves to sin by contemplating the bitter suffering of Christ.

See there then; thus we must mirror ourselves in the crucified Christ, and in Him learn and understand the abomination of sin and the depth of our misery, and consequently how we ought to mourn over it.
