665

...and the sweet fruit thereof.

to be. It is also certainly our bounden duty that we should consider this with all earnestness; but here we have everywhere great reason to complain that this is so little thought of, and even less practiced.

<margin>It is much to be lamented that so few Christians look upon the faith.</margin>
But are they to be found among the Christians themselves, those who have this holy habit of daily beholding this man, and in the **crucified Christ** <note>original: "gekruysten Christo"</note>, as in a spiritual mirror, contemplating the hideousness of their sins, the greatness of their misery, and learning from this a sorrow for their sins and a hatred toward the same? Oh, oh, what poor Christians we are! Among us, it goes quite differently; one gazes daily into the mirror of vanity, and instead of humbling oneself and grieving over one's sins, one puffs oneself up and parades in one's sins, rejoices in them, and boasts of them.

The baptized Christians go about with heads held high, raised eyebrows, and parade in all kinds of pride, wantonness, splendor, spitefulness, and injustice, and bathe themselves in lusts, while their Lord and head Christ—whom they still call their "dear Lord"—is as it were crucified anew by them.

<margin>And that many can take no pleasure except in sin.</margin>
Indeed, it has gone so far, and fallen so miserably among us named Christians, that very many baptized Christians are found who can create no delight, joy, nor merriment in anything, unless the cursed sauce of sin (which oppressed the Lord Christ, our very own dear Lord, to the highest degree) is mixed into it.

<column-break/>

It was our sins which, like so many hellish and bitter spices, made the cup of the Lord Christ—which He had to drink—so loathsome that a bloody sweat broke out from Him when He merely thought of it. What sense is there then in this: that even those who give themselves out to be members of Christ, and boast that they have the Spirit of Christ (for *if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him*, Romans 8:9), nevertheless can find no taste nor sweetness in anything, unless these cursed, loathsome, hellish drugs of sin are mixed in? This is nevertheless found daily: their meals cannot make them merry, their clothing does not please them, their games and amusements do not refresh them, unless sinful excess, pride, show, wantonness, and leafiness <note>original: "dertelheyt" — meaning decadence or frivolousness</note> are mixed therein. Their trade, dealings, commerce, and conduct cannot satisfy them, unless they may strike into it falsehood, lies, deceit, or any of such sins. Indeed, there is hardly anything good in the world that man can allow himself to enjoy, unless some sin is crumbled into it, as if it were truly a magnificent sauce, a very precious and pleasant spice. How is this "Christian"?

<margin>So that they will not leave their sins even though He entreats them through His suffering.</margin>
And the base, earthly, fleshly, and worldly man is so miserably fond of this foul and hellish sauce of sin, that even though the Lord Jesus Christ Himself warns them very faithfully in His Word that the sauce of sin, however well it tastes, is but a deadly poison that shall truly bring eternal death upon the soul; yet they do not ask about it...

### Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

<margin>
Indeed, many use Christ’s suffering as a spur to sin.
</margin>
...not after. Yes, even though the Lord Christ stands and pleads—through his bitter suffering and death, through his bloody sweat, through his mortal wounds, which our sins have given him—it counts for nothing with many people; they nevertheless swallow the poison of sin right greedily.

One finds also (which is surely of all shocking things the most shocking) those who dare to use the bitter suffering and death of our Lord Jesus Christ (which he underwent for the sake of sins) as an occasion, yes, as a spur and encouragement to commit more sins. Thus there are those who, having heard that the Lord Christ underwent such bitter suffering for the sake of sins, conclude from this that there is then no need for concern about how they behave, since the Lord Christ has paid for it all anyway. Oh, horrible! Oh, hellish conclusion! Oh, my soul, my lonely one, do not enter into this counsel; let this mindset of the <term>godless</term><note>The author uses "Godtloose" to refer to those living without regard for divine law, regardless of their nominal faith.</note> be far from you. Yet this is also what happens. Thus one finds daily that everywhere there are many who boast with wide mouths that they trust they shall be saved through Christ just as well as the best of men (although they live as unchristianly as the worst), as if the Lord Christ had shed his precious blood to earn them the freedom to be allowed to sin. Thus the drunkards, <term>usurers</term><note>original: "woeckeraers"; those who lend money at unfairly high interest rates.</note>, spendthrifts, the entirely worldly, light-minded, fickle, and base people—who show or express in themselves no sign or likeness of the life of the spirit of Christ—nevertheless comfort themselves with the suffering of Christ and lay that to their hearts, not

<column-break/>

in order to die to sin according to the demand of Christ’s suffering, but to live all the more boldly in sins. What greater horror than this could be imagined? Namely, that the Son of God—who came to "destroy the works of the Devil" <note>1 John 3:8</note>—is used to strengthen the work of the Devil and to make the snares of sin even tighter.

Certainly, this is exceedingly horrible, nor can this ever be sufficiently lamented; for truly, when things go this way among Christians, what is that other than "crucifying the Lord Christ anew and putting him to shame"? <note>Hebrews 6:6</note> And when we see these things, do we not then see the Lord Christ daily crucified anew before our eyes? Just as the Apostle speaks, though in a completely contrary sense. Can this then ever be sufficiently lamented?

<margin>
Such a thing does not rhyme with...
</margin>
For dear heart, whoever you may be, Christian person, consider for a moment with me how this <term>rhymes</term><note>The author uses "rijmt" (rhymes) as a metaphor for consistency or logical harmony.</note>: what sense or reason, what ground or account is in this; shall we bathe in the delights of sin, while the Lord Christ was bathed in his blood for the sake of our sins? Delicate limbs under a head crowned with thorns—how does that rhyme? What Christian fashion is this? Would the Lord Christ also have undergone so much suffering, such a bitter and anxious passion, so that we—who boast to be his members—should let ourselves go in all kinds of wantonness, luxury, and worldly bravado? Shall then our dear Lord Christ die the bitter death for our sins, and shall we still lead a joyful life in our sins? Shall that which grieved Christ and ended his life...

# 667

-> and the sweet fruit thereof. <-
Pppp 2

...has sold his life; shall the Son of God be distressed unto death over our sins, and shall we still treat them lightly? Shall our gossip, drunkenness, injustice, unchastity, spitefulness, wantonness, frivolity, hatred, and envy be like so many spears in the side of *Christ*, like so many stinging scorpions at the heart of *Christ*, and shall we still commit them daily and even sharpen them against him? Shall the Lord *Christ* himself truly warn us so faithfully that the sting of sin—in which we take such delight—contains a deadly poison within it, and shall we nonetheless still swallow it down? Shall he stand before us praying and beseeching, through his bitter suffering and death, through his wounds and bloody sweat, that we should make a renunciation of our sins; and shall we nevertheless not be turned away from them? What sense is there in this? Is that behaving like *Christians*? Do we thus thank our dear Lord for all his bitter suffering and for all the distress he underwent for our sake? How could the devil make it any worse than to rejoice to the highest degree in that which grieves the Lord *Christ* to the highest degree? Is this not to be an enemy of the cross of *Christ*? <margin>Philippians 3:18</margin> Is this not as if to crucify him all over again, and to put him to shame, and to trample the Son of God, and to count the blood of the New Testament as an unholy thing; and whatever more such sins there are that lead toward the <term>unforgivable sin</term><note>A reference to the "sin against the Holy Spirit," which was viewed by theologians of this era as a final, willful rejection of God's grace.</note>?

<margin>Indeed, if we wish to do so, it would be better for us</margin> If we truly intended to act this way, would it not have been better for us that we had never known anything of the crucified *Christ*, nor of the way

<column-break/>

of truth? That we had indeed never perceived nor heard that a *Jesus*, a *Savior*, was sent into the world by God, who also died the death to deliver us from death? Would it not have been better that we had been born somewhere in a corner of the world, in the remotest *Indies* <note>original: "Indien"; a term used then to refer to distant colonies or lands perceived as the edges of the known world.</note>, where one never hears mention made of the Lord *Christ*?

<margin>it would be better that we had never heard of the crucified *Christ*.</margin>
<margin>Or that we were by confession *Jews*, *Turks*, or *Heathens*.</margin> Indeed, if we are truly so minded that we will not heed the warnings of *Christ* at all, nor allow ourselves to be moved by the friendly beseeching and praying he does for us—through his bitter suffering and death, through his wounds and bloody sweat—to make a renunciation of sin; would it then not be much better that we were not *Christians* by confession, that we were indeed *Jews*, *Turks* <note>original: "Turcken"; a common historical term used to refer to Muslims.</note>, or *Heathens* by profession? For then at least his great and holy name would not be blasphemed on account of our sins, as happens now: when we boast of being *Christians* and yet live so entirely un-Christian lives; when we care so little, or not at all, for the Lord *Christ* (whom we yet call our dearest Lord); so defiantly and so scornfully casting to the wind his beseeching and his prayers, which he makes to us through his bitter suffering and death. going to crucify the Lord **Christ** and put him to shame.

And what is most to be lamented of all: the conduct of so-called **Christians** is so much more horizontal in this regard than the wild madness of the fierce Jews; for, oh poor souls, *they knew not what they did* <note>original: "zy en wisten niet wat zy deden"</note>, Luke 23:34. These people crucified the one whom they believed to be a traitor, and who did not pray or beseech them to spare him. But these [Christians] mistreat the one whom they acknowledge to be the Son of God, the Savior of the world; indeed, they call him their dearest Lord, who also stands and prays and beseeches them by his bitter suffering, by his wounds and bloody sweat, that they should not make him suffer anew through their sins, and that they would please spare him and let him rest. From this, it appears in every way that truly the Lord **Christ**, the Savior of the world, is treated much more shamefully and horribly by all those **Christians** who—constantly ignoring his faithful warnings and pleas—deliberately give themselves over to their sins and will not be turned away from them for any reason, than he was ever mistreated by the Jews.

What does it matter then if these **Christians**, who behave so un-Christianly, hate and loathe **Pilate**? They cry **Hosanna** with a loud voice, yet as long as they indulge in their sins against the counsel and prayer of **Christ**, they crucify **Christ** anew. Thus they are even worse than Jews; thus they are truly **Judases** in their hearts; they are as wicked as the murderous soldiers, for they do this to **Christ** in the most scornful way possible.

<header>Of the bitter suffering of Christ,</header>

### CHAPTER XX.
#### Of the perfect deliverance from our sins, through Christ the crucified.

<margin>
Christ has brought about perfect deliverance through his suffering.
</margin>

In order that we may rightly perceive the perfect deliverance from our sins, we also simply need to behold this man, the Lord Christ the crucified, with understanding, just as we have explained above. For it has been shown there that everything the Lord Christ, that innocent Lamb of God, suffered and underwent, he suffered not for his own sake (for there was no sin found in him), but for the sake of his people. Consider now: what could the Son of God—the only-begotten Son of God, the dearly beloved only-begotten Son of God—not earn and acquire through such a great, such a bitter, and cursed suffering as he underwent?

So also Holy Scripture testifies to us most expressly that he is able to save to the uttermost those who come to God through him (Hebrews 7:25); that we have all received from his overflowing fullness grace for grace (John 1:16); that he has also become for us wisdom from God, and righteousness, and sanctification, and <term>deliverance</term> <note>Original: "verloffinge." This refers to the act of being set free or ransomed from the debt of sin.</note> (1 Corinthians 1:30); yes, that his divine power has given us everything that pertains to life and godliness (2 Peter 1:3). Just as he was also anointed by God his heavenly Father with the oil of joy above his companions (Psalm 45:8), precisely to bring good news to the humble, to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of

<column-break/>

the prison to those who are bound; to provide for the mourners of Zion, that there be given to them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for a spirit of heaviness (Isaiah 61:1, 3; Luke 4:18). Likewise, the punishment that brings us peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed (Isaiah 53:5; 1 Peter 2:24).

Thus we have also heard from this that the Lord Jesus Christ the crucified has received for us comfort, forgiveness, and healing: comfort in all struggles and difficulties, and hereafter eternal life. So it is that for us he is "all, and in all," as the Apostle testifies to us (Colossians 3:11). Therefore, the Apostle Paul counted all things as loss for the excellence of the knowledge of Christ Jesus his Lord (Philippians 3:7–8); and as the merchant sold everything to buy this pearl (Matthew 13:45); for they clearly understood that in gaining Christ, they would find in him everything they needed for salvation and for comfort.

Providing heart to all poor-spirited, death-guilty sinners who, hearing and perceiving the aforementioned horror of sin—and what a damnable thing it is not only to have sin, but to sin willfully (where the Lord Jesus Christ is set before our eyes as vividly crucified for our sins' sake)—and being thereat crushed in heart and faint in spirit, wish and desire to be reconciled with the Lord their God over their sins and unfaithful ingratitude; and these prepare themselves for this, [to] behold and go...

<header>...and the sweet fruit thereof.</header>

<margin>Encouragement to all <term>death-guilty</term> <note>Original: "doot-schuldige." This refers to sinners whose offenses are so grave they warrant eternal spiritual death.</note> sinners who wish to be reconciled with God over their sins.</margin>
...from the crucified Christ, that it pleased him to pour out his blood / for those / who demanded his death / if they only afterwards better themselves / and convert / *Acts* 2:36-37, *Acts* 3:17, 19.

It also cannot well be / O human whoever you are / who lives here in the light of the Gospel / and now and then also stumbles into church / or at least moves here among the Christians / where you now and then hear mention of heaven / of hell / of damnation / of sin / of Christ / and what more of those things there are; or you must sometimes be struck / by many thoughts / and considerations / of what will finally become of you / and where you might end up / when you must depart from this world; your heart must indeed now or then / give you these or similar thoughts: It is not all well with me / certainly my affairs might stand quite poorly before God / I have fallen in Adam / who will lift me up? I have corrupted myself even further through my own actual sin / who will deliver me? I have greatly angered my God / with my sins / who will reconcile me? I am mortally wounded by my sins / who will heal me now? I am subject to many painful / hardships / and sorrows in this life / who will comfort / and strengthen me therein? I have no lasting place here / I shall soon have to go from here into the other world where one goes to heaven or to hell / who will deliver me from hell? who will bring me to heaven? See, these or similar considerations must necessarily strike the people / who live here in the light of the Gospel / now or then.

Come forth then / O human / whoever you may be / who with

<column-break/>

these troublesome considerations / and melancholy thoughts are taken up; see here, that there is yet hope for all this / come and look upon the man; look upon this crowned / mocked / crucified Christ, and see in him perfect deliverance from all your hardships / and from all your melancholy thoughts; if you only henceforth will love him / and hate your sins; if you only henceforth will look upon him / and leave your sins / then you shall certainly find in him perfect deliverance / you shall indeed find in him forgiveness and healing of your sins, comfort in your suffering here / and hereafter eternal rejoicing.

<margin>For in Christ there is help against everything that torments us.</margin>
For dear one / what is it that torments you / what is it that afflicts / and keeps you worried / against which you shall not be able to find ready help / and comfort / in this man / in the Lord Christ the crucified? Is it your past sins that worry you / because they are so many / because they are so great; well / let the sins be as many / as the hairs of your head, as the sand on the seashore / let them be so great / that they are found blood-red, all of them death-guilty sins;

<margin>As well against our past sins;</margin>
look only upon the crowned / the crucified Christ, with an <term>unfeigned heart</term> <note>Meaning a sincere or honest heart, without hypocrisy.</note> / and a mind to leave your sins and cling to him; and know then for your comfort / that the blood of the Son of God, cleanses us from all sin, 1 *John* 1:7. Look upon the man / who is also God / and know that he has been able to satisfy more / than you have been able to misdo. Have you committed sin upon sin / he has received wound upon wound; have you committed death-guilty sins / he has also received mortal wounds / to deliver you from death. It does not depend on / how many / how great your past sins...

<header>Of the bitter suffering of Christ,</header>

...have been; but here it all depends on whether you wish to cling to those sins any longer; if you wish to do so, then we know of no counsel in the world for you: but if you wish to leave them, and cling to the Lord Christ, if you wish to follow him, then you shall certainly experience that just as the sins you committed in the flesh <note>The "flesh" refers to the fallen human nature prone to worldly desires.</note> have corrupted you, so the wounds he received in the flesh shall preserve you; so it happens to you as the Lord says by the Prophet, *Though your sins were as scarlet, they shall be white as snow; though they were red as crimson, they shall become as [white] wool,* Isaiah 1:18.

<margin>As also against your present, tormenting sins.</margin>
Or is it perhaps your present failings that still torment you? Is it that very pressing sin which burdens your heart? Well, look also upon this man; he is that exalted metal serpent <note>A reference to the "Brazen Serpent" from the Book of Numbers; just as the Israelites were healed of snake bites by looking at the bronze snake, Christians are healed of sin by looking at the crucified Christ.</note> who heals us from the poison of sin; truly, there is power of healing in him; only look at him with a faithful eye; he shall make you free from all willful sins, so that they shall no longer rule over you, Psalm 19:14, Romans 6:14. It cannot be otherwise; only take the matter thus, and you shall soon realize it: When you are in your wanton luxury, when you bathe willfully in pleasures; then only look at this man, bathing in his blood for the sake of your sins, having nothing but vinegar mixed with gall to drink; and tell me, considering this properly, would you then still dare to indulge in excess, in gluttony and drunkenness? When you walk along boldly and proudly, full of arrogance, spitefulness, and vengefulness; then only look once at this man, full of all scorn and con-

<column-break/>

tempt, full of humiliation for your sake; and tell me then, would you then still dare to be high-minded, spiteful, vengeful, and so on with other sins. For what shall heal our pride, if the humility of Christ cannot heal it? What shall better our unrighteous greed and wantonness, if the distress of Christ cannot do so?

Indeed, only accustom yourself, whether you are enticed to any kind of sin or are already ensnared in some kind of sin—of levity, of anger, of intemperance, etc.—and are entangled thereby, so that Satan already has all his fingers on you through his snares and bonds (which are the beginnings of sin); just as experience teaches that even the best Christians find it most difficult to restrain themselves once they have already begun to entangle themselves in certain sins. As an example: That they have now already conformed themselves to the world in outward things and worldly <note>Original: "er licke," likely "wereltlicke."</note> ornaments; that they are already in bad company, in an unseemly meal or wedding; or that they are already inflamed with wrath or are already quarreling, though they well know they do not do well therein, yet for that time they know not how to overcome their evil mouth, even if they wish to do so; even in this case, accustom yourself to bring the crucified one vividly into your thoughts; set before you the Lord Jesus Christ, treading forth crowned with a crown of thorns, clothed with a rag of a purple garment, all bloody and scourged, spat upon and disfigured, through the cruel treatment of the fierce Je- <note>The text cuts off here; likely "Joden" (Jews).</note>

<meta>This page continues the pastoral encouragement by explaining the "sweet fruit" of Christ's suffering. Having established Christ as a mirror for the soul, the author now addresses the theological weight of Christ's abandonment on the cross, presenting it as the definitive victory that provides a "city of refuge" for all sinners.</meta>

->### and the sweet fruit thereof.<-

The righteousness of God set an appointed time, during which He was as if in danger of being abandoned, because He did not want to abandon you, or me, or all of us together—who seek our salvation in Him—but rather He persisted so that we, who were dead through trespasses, might be made alive again with Him, and be seated with Him in heaven, *Eph. 2:5-6.* This provoked the struggle for Him; this brought anguish upon Him; nonetheless, He did not remain in it; He wrestled through it; He maintained the victory; He was still accepted in grace while He held us in His arms; and so for us, together with Him, an ample entrance has been opened into the eternal Kingdom, *2 Pet. 1:11.* Upon this we may then take courage and let the fear of hell pass away, and take up the hope of Heaven.

<margin>As also against the fear of being finally rejected at the last.</margin>
For certainly, the Lord Jesus Christ held, as it were, the whole of hell in His bosom, and conquered it there; otherwise He would not have cried out so mournfully over a small matter, <note>original: "Myn God, myn Godt, waerom hebt ghy my verlaten"</note> *My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?* <note>Matthew 27:46. The author argues that this cry of abandonment proves the intensity of the spiritual battle Christ was fighting on behalf of humanity.</note> But He saw before His eyes all our sins; He saw all the curses and punishments that we had deserved for the sake of those same sins; He saw hell as if opened to swallow us up; He saw the devils of hell preparing themselves to go off with their prey; He saw the grim wrath of God ignited and burning against our sins, and against Him for our sake: this distressed Him, yet He wrestled through it; thus He was as if abandoned for an appointed time, so that we might be accepted with eternal mercy.

<column-break/>

Let then all troubled souls set out toward this Jephthah, *Judg. 11:3,* toward this David, *1 Sam. 22:2.* <note>In the Old Testament, Jephthah and David were leaders who gathered "worthless" or "distressed" men around them; the author uses them as types (foreshadowings) of Christ welcoming the marginalized.</note> Let all who flee from the avenger of blood hasten to this city of refuge, *Num. 35:25.* Let all the guilty grasp the horns of this altar; let all the wounded look up to the exalted serpent, the crucified Christ, *Num. 21:9.* Let all the thirsty run to this free, open fountain, *Zech. 13:1;* all the hungry to this bread of life; yes, let all eagles fly to this carcass, *Matt. 24:28.* <note>A common Reformation-era interpretation of this verse was that believers (eagles) are drawn to the body of Christ (the "carcass" or prey) for spiritual nourishment.</note> Let all who are weary and heavy laden come to this burden-bearer, *Matth. 11:28.* Behold, indeed, all you who are thus positioned as men, look upon the Lord Jesus Christ, crowned with thorns so that you might be crowned with glory; see Him hanging on the wood of the cross with bowed head, and outstretched arms, and an opened heart, as if inclining Himself to you, as stretching out His arms for you, and opening His heart to help and deliver you in every way. Let no one go forth any longer despondent or comfortless, who is merely minded to leave his sins, and has now learned that there is a man who is also God, who has died the death on the cursed wood of the cross, to reconcile the death-guilty, sinful man with the righteous God, and thus to deliver him from death and grant him eternal life.

<margin>Complaint: that few seek Christ from the heart.</margin>
It is a complaint that, even though it stands so gloriously with this man, so few are to be found who seek the Lord Jesus Christ from the heart, as if His suffering were worth nothing at all, as if He had been able to merit only a little. The things of this world present themselves so...

# ...and the sweet fruit thereof.

<margin>
The presumptuous, who live in their sins yet convince themselves that they shall be saved through Christ, must know that Christ also heals the sin of all those for whom he is the Savior.
</margin>

Concerning the first point: there are presumptuous Christians in the world who boast loudly that they have indeed been made partakers of the Lord Christ, and consequently that they have obtained through him the forgiveness of their sins and shall be saved by him; yet they behave in an altogether un-Christian manner in their dealings and conduct. These truly deceive themselves, as they might soon realize here if they would only consider: that to whomever the Lord Christ is a Savior, he is a <term>whole Savior</term> <note>The author emphasizes that Christ cannot be "divided"—one cannot accept his mercy while rejecting his moral authority.</note>; that he does not only acquire for them the forgiveness of sins, but also grants them the healing of the same—so much so that they become distinguished from the common masses of the world.

For the Lord Christ truly brings it about through his cross and suffering that his people are "crucified to the world, and the world to them" (*Galatians 6:14*). As we have also heard above, there is a great power of healing in the cross of Christ; from which it necessarily follows that the drunkard who is not yet healed of his drunkenness, the fornicator who still lives in his impurity, and the greedy man who still constantly practices usury and dishonest trade, all boast in vain that they have accepted the Lord Christ as their Savior. For behold, it stands thus: the Lord Christ may not be divided; his robe may not be torn <note>original: "sijnen rock mach niet gescheurt werden." He must not only acquire for you complete forgiveness, but also the true healing of your willful sins. This is

<column-break/>

the test by which many are exposed (who yet live so comfortably) as having no part in Christ: for they are in no way healed of their sins, but remain slaves, each to their beloved sins.

<margin>
The careless must know that if they do not become partakers, they themselves must bear the wrath of God which Christ bore.
</margin>

There are also the careless, who, even if they notice well enough that they are not truly partakers of the Lord Christ, nevertheless cast it to the wind and make little trouble of it. These are also very ill-advised; no carelessness in the world is more harmful than being negligent in so great a salvation as is offered to us through Jesus Christ (*Hebrews 2:2-3*). No <term>false security</term> <note>original: "soetvuerigheyt." Likely meaning a "sweet fire" or a deceptive, comfortable zeal that lacks true foundation.</note> is more damnable. Indeed, if we choose that path, it would have been a thousand times better for us never to have heard anything of the Lord Christ. To awaken these people and bring them to more blessed thoughts, these two considerations serve:

Behold, first and foremost, it stands thus: if we do not become partakers of the Lord Jesus Christ and his bitter suffering, then we ourselves shall have to endure inhuman terrors and anxieties, always and eternally, just as the Lord Christ suffered for a time. Look at the man once more; had your soul stood in his place, how could you have endured it? Well, if his soul is not placed in your stead, then you shall yet come to that, and endure it always and eternally. # ...and the sweet fruit thereof.

Therefore we must often gaze upon this man, and cast our eyes upon the Lord Jesus, the crowned and the crucified; and through this sight, we must strive and seek to awaken in our hearts such a sensible movement, **affection**, and stirring of the mind as usually arises in the hearts of those who love, when they hear of or see their beloved in great distress and sorrow. Just as we may perceive that when we contemplate the martyrdom <note>original: "martelisatie" — referring to the torture and execution of martyrs</note> and the great suffering of certain excellent men and martyrs of God, we are singularly ignited thereby with a lovely and moving affection toward them, even though the event passed long ago. And this is a **work of faith**: that although the bitter suffering of the Lord Christ is long past, we nevertheless, through faithful meditation, still set it daily and vividly before our eyes. By observing this, we maintain a tender, moving, lovely, and friendly affection—fresh and blooming—within ourselves toward the Lord Christ. We do this so that we might be moved and set in motion by this same affection to always do, gladly and willingly, whatever we know might please him; just as a fresh, sensible love is the most serviceable and always most gladly performs everything it knows will best please the beloved. Now, this affection and love of ours for the Lord Christ the crucified must also manifest itself in all circumstances: in adversity, in prosperity, and in various other situations, if we are to show ourselves properly grateful for all the good he has done for us. We shall say more regarding this.

<column-break/>

<margin>And making us patient in adversity.</margin>
In adversity, we must indeed everywhere—as a sign of gratitude toward the Lord Christ the crucified, who suffered so much for us—learn to be long-suffering and patient. For how shall we not quietly endure and bear all kinds of grief which we have brought upon ourselves through our own sins (just as the converted thief reminded his companion), when we lift our eyes to the man, the Lord Christ, who, being **innocent** <note>original: "onnoosel" — in this period, the word meant innocent or harmless rather than its modern Dutch meaning of "silly"</note>, suffered so much for the sake of our sins? How can we do less as a sign of gratitude than, seeing the Lord Christ our head bearing our cross for our sake, to also gladly take up our cross and thus follow him? If the head is crowned with thorns, must not the members be comforted even when they are in heaviness and sorrow? Surely the servant is no better than his Lord.

Would it even be fitting for the head to be crowned with thorns while the members bathe themselves in pleasures? That the Lord and Master should be a man of sorrows, who knew nothing but affliction, and that the disciples should be **pursuers of trifles** <note>original: "papier-jagers" — literally "paper-hunters," a term used to describe people who chase after worldly honors or fleeting, fragile vanities</note> who knew nothing but luxury?

To this is added that all our grief, all our suffering, and our cross are sanctified and blessed through the suffering of Christ; so that it only serves for our good and our best, if only we receive it well. Yes, in all our grief, in all our cross, lies a blessing wrapped up, which the Lord Christ has placed therein if we are only wise enough to draw it out. Indeed, this our light affliction, which passes so quickly, works for us an exceeding...

# Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory, *2 Cor. 4:17.* How shall we then grow weary because of this? Are we poor? Are we in pain? Are we mocked and slandered? Do we have the world against us? This is all the seed of our glory and our joy. It happened the same to the Lord Christ; he entered into his glory through much suffering, *Luke 24:26,* and he has overcome the world, and commands us to be of good cheer; we shall also overcome it, *John 16:33.* Temporary sorrow and the hardships that strike us here are then also the liveries <note>original: "leveren" — distinctive clothing worn by servants to identify which master they serve</note> and marks of the Lord Jesus himself, *Gal. 6:17.* They are like the after-pains of his bitter suffering and death, *Col. 1:24,* which we should therefore gladly bear upon ourselves. # Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

...of that man <note>Referring back to the contrast on the previous page between worldly leaders and the suffering Christ.</note> who has not earned salvation for us; that we must indeed be servants of Christ, who died for us, and bought us with a precious price; then we would conduct ourselves better in our meals: and likewise in a thousand other such cases.

<margin>2. To pursue our sins even unto death.</margin>
Secondly, as a sign of gratitude toward the Lord Christ for his bitter suffering—which he underwent for the sake of our sins—we must also pursue our sins with all our might even unto death. To this, the Holy Scripture exhorts us everywhere through the consideration of the bitter suffering of Christ. Thus Peter says: > Since Christ then suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves also with the same thought, with that same feeling; that whoever has suffered in the flesh (meaning as a member of Christ, who has also felt the power of his suffering) has ceased from sin, 1 Pet. 4:1. For also, as Paul testifies to us: > Our old man <note>The "old man" is a theological term referring to the sinful, unregenerate nature of a person before following Christ.</note> is crucified with him, so that the body of sin might be destroyed, that we should no longer serve sin, Rom. 6:6. So also the Holy Scripture (awakening us to godliness) uses manners of speaking taken from the cross and the death of Christ: > those who are Christ’s have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires, Gal. 5:24. And again: > mortify <note>original: "doodet" — literally 'kill' or 'put to death'.</note> your members which are on the earth, Col. 3:5. Thus it has also been made clear enough from all the preceding discourse that truly our sins were solely the thorns and scorpions that brought the Lord Christ to his death; yes, our sins were the price of his blood; how then should we not abstain from them?

<column-break/>

We read of David, when he longed for the water of Bethlehem, which was in the camp of the Philistines, that three of his heroes broke through the camp of the Philistines and brought David the water he desired; yet King David, noticing in what danger his heroes had placed themselves to provide him with that water, would not drink it (even though he longed for it greatly). But he poured it out before the Lord and said: > Far be it from me, O Lord, that I should do this. Should I drink the blood of the men who went at the risk of their lives? And he would not drink it, 2 Sam. 23:16, 17. Thus, all kind-hearted Christians ought much more to say, in view of all fleshly lusts and sinful desires for which their fleshly longing still strives so much: "Far be it from me that I do that; is it not the blood of the Son of God? Has not our Lord, the Lord Christ, not only risked his life for it, but actually died the bitter death of the cross for it? How then should I still give in to it?" In this way, all pious Christians must act, even when the opportunities are at hand where fulfilling and satisfying their fleshly lusts and sinful desires would seemingly cost them nothing. Thus did Joseph, when his young and persistent mistress, Potiphar's wife, presented herself and offered him unchastity, he refused her. Thus we must do in all cases; when we now have abundance, and eat costly and delicious food every day, how [could we] provide for our flesh for lusts, and splendor, for show, for wantonness,

> Reward her even as she rewarded you, and double unto her double according to her works. Revelation 18:6.

And subsequently, we must crucify them, kill them, give them over to the law of God, strike them dead by the power of the Spirit, and leave them there to languish and perish like criminals. Thus must we do to our evil desires; thus must we pursue, torment, and crucify the old man in every way. By doing so and thus acquitting ourselves against the old man and his wicked ways, we shall properly demonstrate our bounden gratitude to the Lord Christ for the bitter suffering he underwent for the sake of our evil sins.

<meta>This page continues the theological discourse on how a believer should respond to Christ's sacrifice. ### Of the bitter suffering of Christ,

Oh, that all those called Christians would take careful heed of this, those who still have so much to do with the **old man** <note>The "old man" is a biblical term for the sinful human nature that exists before a spiritual rebirth.</note>, who still provide for his lusts and serve his desires; oh, whoever you may be that acts thus, consider this once: is this truly acting like a Christian? That you would still maintain, cherish, and fulfill the desires of the mortal enemy of Christ—the one who gave the Lord Christ his death-wound—yes, even running against the Lord Christ to please and satisfy this enemy of Christ? Is this truly acting like a Christian? Oh, consider this once very thoroughly; consider it deeply in your solitude, between your soul and the Lord your God. And then, noticing how utterly abominable these ways of acting are, break them off and henceforth cling better to the Lord your God and your Savior, Christ Jesus the crucified, as is fitting.

<margin>3. To uphold His members and the Holy Congregation.</margin>
Thirdly, and finally, as a sign of gratitude to the Lord Christ for the bitter suffering He underwent for our sake, we must also go and uphold His **Holy Congregation** <note>The "Congregation" refers to the community of the Church.</note> and His dear members <note>The "members" of Christ are individual fellow believers who together make up the "body" of Christ.</note> in every way, and strive to observe all His Holy Ordinances and institutions. This we must also contemplate in every way. Holy Scripture also admonishes us to this through the consideration of Christ’s suffering; for this is it: *not to live for ourselves anymore, but for the Lord Christ, who died for us*, 2 Cor. 5:15.

If a special friend had died for us, and through his death had acquired great goods and glory for us; if he had left behind any friends or kin, would we not

<column-break/>

repay them for the good that our friend had done for us, since we could not repay him himself? Thus we must also repay the members of Christ for the good He has done for us, and practice works of love toward them in every way. The Apostle admonishes us to this through an argument taken from the suffering of Christ: *Walk* (he says) *in love, even as Christ also hath loved us, and hath given himself for us an offering and a sacrifice to God for a sweetsmelling savor*, Eph. 5:2. From which the Apostle John then also concludes that, seeing as the Lord Christ *laid down His life for us, that we ought also to lay down our lives for the brethren*, for the members of Christ, 1 John 3:16. So also has the Lord Christ left His poor, needy members here on earth in His place, so that we might prove our good-heartedness toward Him, Matt. 26:11. Thus He will also recognize on the last day in His judgment what is done to His poor little members as if it were done to Himself, Matt. 25. Toward this we must also embolden ourselves and be diligent, that we do as much service and virtue to the members of Christ and His Holy Congregation as we possibly can and may, as a sign of gratitude for all the good He has obtained for us through His bitter suffering and death.

Oh, that many **name-bearing Christians** <note>A term for those who are Christian in name only, lacking true devotion or practice.</note> would take note of this, who have already reached twenty, thirty, or more years of age, yet who to this very day—except for some alms they may have given out of habit to the members...

### CHAPTER XX.

**Communion with Christ** to be sought above all and in everything.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;is shamefully abused by many,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;hope of grace emboldens [one] to sin,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;if abused, it is more severely punished,
&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;neglecting offered grace increases damnation.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;**is a great matter.**

**Feeling** <note>the sense of touch</note> in the body, how noble a sense.
